This game is incredible and among my personal top games. I played it on the playstation 4 but I bought it here to give a review. Here's why:
The story is told perfectly. People now-days forget that video games are an interactive medium. Telling a story through just cutscenes is lame and unimaginative. Bastion solves this problem by having everything tie in perfectly. The narrator is able to describe what you're doing and give context on the world you're exploring. It seems like he's telling you little, but it adds up to a huge amount meaning as you play the game you're also learning about it. For example when you go to one new location the narrator tells you about it by warning you about the obstacles and how people in the past got hurt there. Through that you learn about how that place was before the game started.
Next, the gameplay is amazing. First you choose a difficulty and start playing the game. As you play, you collect these statues which actually add mechanics to your enemies. For example, one statue makes your enemies faster and more eager to attack. Each of the statues adds gameplay mechanics forcing you to change up your style, but only if you want to. If you enjoy the current difficulty you can just play on it, but if you want more of a challenge you can use the statues. After using al 12 the game plays at a much higher level and forces you to do the same.
The Art is more subjective. For me, I loved the environment and the world itself with it looking exactly like how it should after the events in the game. On the other hand I wasn't a very big fan of the character models.
The Music is also amazing. You can listen to the soundtrack online to get a glimpse, but playing the game to it is a whole different ballgame. It draws you in and immerses you in the world.
Controlling wise, I would advise playing with a controller. You can play with mouse or keyboard, but personally I found the controller to be the best way to play.
Overall, this game is amazing and you should buy it, especially now when it's only 3 dollars. The gameplay, story, art and music are wonderful.

The game is amazingly well done.  It is quite daunting at first and the game throws you into what feels like the deep end right off the bat.  It's a trial by fire, but you must endure.  If you do, you'll get better and better and better and be able to handle it.  That's the beauty of the series.  You will die... a lot... but it's okay.  Dying is part of the experience and doesn't really cost you anything.  Continue to explore different paths as it is a nonlinear game and try not to get discouraged or give up.  You'll love the experience by the time its over.
The lore is perhaps the best part of the game.  It is kind of hidden in item descriptions, subtle environmental clues and vague character dialogue, but it is there and its very, very rich.  It's honestly the most ingenious and deep story telling I've seen in my 30 years of gaming.
The fact you can now get this game for $5 is quite honestly a total steal.
Bottom line: It is challenging, but manageable with practice.  Stats and equipment aren't super important.  You can upgrade almost anything to be a viable piece of equipment to get you through the game and that's great.  Certainly some stuff is better, but if you don't find the best weapon or armor in the game it doesn't matter.  Don't worry about missing stuff - just keep slogging forward and you'll be rewarded with a brilliant experience.

ShellShock Live is a fantastic multiplayer tank game that brings back fond memories of Pocket Tanks Deluxe and, of course, SSL2. It is a fantastic game already, and relatively cheap as well. I personally bought the game for a few friends, and we've played a lot together, but it's a testament to the game that I really enjoy playing it alone as well.
The Pros:
Matchmaking often works very well, and the internal chat system makes games far less boring.
Wind and atmospheric nudge as well as the one weapon mod make for challenging, skilliful play.
6 game modes means a lot more time until you get bored.
Tons of weapons to unlock is a great incentive to just play one more game over and over.
The campaign is great, and challenging.
The Cons:
Quick Join is just broken, as of this review. It without fail adds me back to the last lobby I was in, or tells me the lobby I joined was full.
Tournaments. You cannot invite steam friends to join your tournament, nor can you kick anyone. As of right now, tournaments are solely 1v1 games in a bracket, and in the future I'd like to see 2v2 games as well.
Overall, this is an excellent game that I would recommend to anybody. It's especially impressive that the game is so polished in early access.

Hiveswap is an absolute must for Homestuck fans just like myself. But even if you're not a fan, it's still a pretty good adventure game. The only major thing hampering it, at least on release, is the amount of bugs. Most of them are visual bugs with the environments and UI. It can break the immersion just a bit. They will most likely get fixed. It happens, usually, when you first switch to fullscreen and to a higher resolution. It goes away upon restarting the game.
Nothing else seems to be wrong, technically speaking. Vertical Sync is available with good Resolution Options, Volume Levels, and Windowed Mode. When loading, the game suffers some framerate issues, but that literally means nothing since there isn't a thing on screen during this process. Moving around does feel clunky, especially on stairs in cramped spaces.
Other than that, there's very little wrong with this game. It's almost "perfect", despite it having this sort of "cheap" feel to it... but it's so minor, that it barely affects the game at all.
This game is a crap load of fun, with plenty of laughs to be had. The 90s pop culture references are off the charts, and the nostalgic feel is wonderful to the point of being palpable. Sadly, this wonder only lasts about 5 hours. It ends too quickly. The price justifies the length at least. There's some replayability, especially since you're practically encouraged to try every item and weapon with everything. I actually didn't think of trying every item with everything. I was just using the weapons with everything, and even then I eventually stopped doing that. So there's probablly quite a few things I'm missing, which is evident by me having 57% of the achievements after beating the game.
What makes this game so great is the text, which is amazingly written and hilarious, and the sheer amount of things in each environment that make them feel "real". Trying out stuff on everything will give you this text, making each action you do rewarding just for the downright fun writing to read. Don't even get me started on the story, it's very good and keeps you playing all throughout. Andrew Hussie has crafted yet another fantastic story of youth and the celebration of the people, hobbies, dreams, or things we care about. If you haven't read Homestuck, go and do it right away, it will take you weeks! Even after hours of binging per day!
Hiveswap is worth so much more, I would've paid $15.00 for it at most just for the fun it gave me. I can't wait for more. As a Homestuck fan, it was more than I hoped for!

'State of Decay' puts the "survival" in the zombie survival genre. People going in expecting it to be a shooter will be dead in minutes. As an open-world third-person survival game, it's all about strategy and resource management. Ammunition is scarce, but you won't be using guns much without suppressors anyway, as a small hoarde of zombies can easily kill you if you're not careful. There are a few special zombies to watch out for, and are best dispatched quickly, several of them requiring different strategies. Using Influence as a currency of sorts, you can have survivors follow you on expeditions, order construction projects, retrieve supplies from the communal storage, and request help scavenging. Characters run off of their independant health and stamina guages, which will have their maximums reduced as you take damage while downed and explore for long periods of time respectively. Switching characters will allow them to replenish lost max health and stamina, so be sure to do so frequently; characters die permanently, and because of the autosave system there's no way to try get them back once they've perished. Coupled with the RPG element of raising stats through use, providing bonuses and specialties, 'State of Decay' offers deep and challenging gameplay with a good story.
The game is somewhat unpolished with a relatively low frame rate and zombies frequently clipping through walls, but that takes away very little from the overall experience and is still a very well thought out game with fantastic core mechanics. 'State of Decay' is likely the closest we'll ever get to the perfect zombie survival game.

Way too many game breaking bugs (on release day even one is one too many, but this "game", after an overly long beta period, has a lot more bugs than features, and probably needs to be rewritten from scratch in some other engine to have any hope of being fixable), that the "developers" seem to have no intention or capacity to fix (many of the most blatant ones are now apparently "features"), making the game mostly unplayable, and almost definitely unfinishable.
Beyond that (if you can even play, and in that case keep playing once you start encountering broken quests and game-breaking bugs, mostly related to the extremely fubared game saving), besides graphics (which, with technical improvements over time, are a given, and even then frankly sub-par compared to current games), in the good old times this would have been considered a mediocre copy of the classics it claims to be inspired on (for eff's sake, it doesn't even have companion AI or tactics... instead of playing you have to spend every second of combat constantly micromanaging every action of every character, vainly hoping that they won't disregard your orders and stand still while being attacked without fighting back, walk aimlessly into an identified trap, a wall of fire, or some other hazard - if they could fall down cliffs they wouldn't last more than 30 seconds -, or start attacking their stunned, charmed or disoriented companions... and the "developers" apparently have the gall to claim this travesty is intentional! Apparently it's not a bug, it's an effin' feature!).
The story could be relatively interesting (for the current uninspired times, at least, compared to the classics it'd be mediocre to bad) if the quests worked, and the graphics could be relatively pretty - if bland and dated - if the fog of war didn't render them almost too dark to see (even with gamma correction, which does little to fix the darkness while managing to almost turn the game to grayscale) forcing you to strain your eyes till they pop out of their orbits and rub all over the screen your nose is glued to in a futile attempt to see anything, but the mechanics are poorly designed (and even worse implemented), the classes are badly balanced, most of the mechanics that made the classics classics are completely missing (and the ones that are there have been warped into an unnecessarily overcomplicated and poorly designed unbalanced and extremely buggy mess), and all in all attempting to play (if the bugs even let you) quickly becomes a tiresome chore, and instead of relaxing over a good game you end up stressed and angry at a "game" that does anything but let you play, leaving you in a state of mind that leads you to attempt to vent by angrily writing reviews like this one (which, frankly, doesn't seem to help, as I'm only getting more angry and frustrated if that's even possible after a couple days of trying to play this thing).
One more nail on KickStarter's coffin; one more entry in the way too long list of kickstarter games that ended up being an utter disappointment (much easier to list the very few that have managed to deliver something passable, sadly... you can count them with the fingers of one nose...), and probably one of the last ones I'll ever waste money in.
If you're not a masochist, wait a few years till it's in the discount bin and the community has managed to fix the myriad of game breaking bugs through a community patch, and even then you'll probably have  more interesting games to play.

When will developers realize that videogames are meant to be fun? Because THIS GAME ISN'T FUN.
I mean I could complain for hours about how little death matters in this game because there is literally no punishment for death but the biggest complaint I have is simply the fact that this game is a faff and the only reason it is is because like most early access games, the developer's choice of direction for the game absolutely stinks.
Now this game coulf be something great but they would have to remove almost every single feature and start from scratch using the same assets.
Food and Warmth are a really irritating mechanic as it restricts exploration. Plus the compass is so damn complicated, how the hell is anyone supposed to know where the hell they're going. Building stuff is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as hell simply because everywhere you build it leaves seams in the wall because if doesn't match the terrain.
In addition, combat so far (I say so far because there may be improvements in the future) is basically whack an enemy to death simulator and pray you don't bleed out. You can't block which is stupid and overall, combat just isn't fun.
Now I realize this is in Early Access and it's constantly improveing but this doesn't change the developer's direction of the game.
Do you want to know what the problem with this game is? I'll tell you. REALISM
Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ realism in games. If it's done right then fair enough but this is not done right, it's just pure tedium. Everywhere looks the same and exploration isn't fun to do and even if the devs worked more on the world mapping, it would still be boring because of the heat and food feature. Plus the fact that every time you use your weapons damages them is a pain because it's a constant back and forth to repair it. Another problem is mining. Why is it some rocks can be mined and others can't? I just want some stone so I'll hack at that rock on the coatsline... wait why am I not getting stone?
The worst part about this is, the game has you running back and forth doing very repetitive tasks. I mean, sure a lot of survival games do this but it's not as extreme as this.
Adding survival gauges doesn't make the game harder, it just makes the game mroe tedious. Management in this game doesn't exactly take skill, it's just a nuisance. As such the so-called "difficulty" of this game is nonexistant, rather instead of difficulty, it's just painfully tedious to play.

So, I used to hear bad things about this game...
"It's just another early access buggy mess"
"Day Z clone..."
Blah blah blah. After seeing these large changes made and hearing a lot of positive things about it, I decided to get the game on sale (10$) and I'm pleasently surprised!
Let's start off with the obvious stuff... the graphics...
The game looks great. My first time loading into the world I was at an abandoned trailer park and noticed the world looking great on ultra graphics but the most important part to me was the performance...
WOW. The game runs beautifully... I'm not sure how they've managed to optimize the game so well but it runs amazing (even better than the game it's supposed to be "immitating")
I explore the trailer park a bit, finding food to eat, clothing items to wear, bandages for wounds, and items to help me repair vehicles, should I find one. Then I found the most beautiful thing ever... A crossbow. I was later ran up on by not a zombie...  but a mutant. An obvious human experimental abomination that surprised me (first scared drops of pee out of me) but surprised me when I found out it wasn't zombies in the game... Killed him with a few crossbow bolts to the face (and unfortunately realizing I couldn't retrive my bolts which made me sad.)
After my initial point of contact with the mutant, the world started to change... the weather got dark and gloomy and it started raining heavier than I've seen it rain in a video game before. The water effects and enviornments were beautiful.
The game needs work obviously, as it's in early access, but I think the devs would do a great job moving forward in making honestly one of the best survival "simulation" games that not only looks great but plays extremely smooth. Definitely check this one out if you're a fan of the genre, ESPECIALLY if you can get it on a discount, which it is at the point of writing this impression.

Hello, I am Steven and I have played 33.3 Hrs on record. I must say that in the beginning the game was pretty bad and had a lot to catch up on. Because a lot of other zombie survivals were already alot ahead, this game was essentially thrown under the bus. People tend to not read as well because it says PRE-ALPHA yet they still rate it bad because they expect a full game, when it is clearly stated on Steam AND startup. This game has developed in a short time, but is already ahead most other zombie survivals. It has good mechanics for walking, running, looting, good inventory setup, UI is good, however they could add an auto-run feature because after awhile your pinky finger tends to start to hurt, but other than that basic mechanics are good. The player-base is pretty friendly and not everyone is a KOS, I actually have made a few friends with people who were completely looted to the teeth and did not KOS me on sight. The game is absolutly beautiful for being a newer survival game (Thank you Cry-Engine). I was actually stunned how good the game was when it first came out, and even more things have made it stand out. There are signs posted around the map to really help find your positioning, literally... every town has at least 4 signs describing your location.. or just blatantly stating it. Overall I think it is worth the buy because unlike other survivals this game is heading up-hill at a fast, yet precise rate. The devs always are in contact with the player-base and they always have hotfixes if there are any problems with a new update that was release and had issues. Please, if you are interested at all in buying this game (Which not to mention I have found no hackers / scripters, ect. to be in) at all please take the time to read the NEWEST feedback on the game. Plus your contribution to buying the game will help the Devs create even more fun things to do in future releases. Hope this helps, happy playing! :)

Ok...the UI is ever so slightly clunky (it's an old game), but this has to be one of the best games I've ever played, hands down. I put 127 hours into this game. One game. Now, it doesn't take *near* that long to do a playthough, but I'm one of those nuts who saves and tries...every...option ;) ... However, even doing that..even seeing all the conversations in one go...I'm *still* aiming to get the DLC for this game. I also already own ME 2 and I just got ME3.
Best of all, this game series has a *genuine* combat level adjustment. My husband *loves* hardcore combat. I do too...when I raid or PVP...but when it's just me and a good story, I'd prefer *not* feeling like the phone ringing is going to spoil an hour of grueling work to get somewhere and shoot something. This game is a *completely* different experience depending on how you set the comat difficulty. I *love* that.
Characters live, laugh, love, cry....and die by your side in this series in a way that I've not experienced in many other games. By ME3, I was *crying* at the death of some characters (even ones I knew from other play options I could have kept alive)...and I am *so* not the weepy girly girl type.
If you like sci-fi, buy this game. If you love story-driven adventure where it feels like your conversation choices *matter*, buy this game. If you enjoy some shooting but don't want it to be the absolute be-all end-all of the gaming experience, buy this game.
Getting from me1 to me2 was *jarring* beause of the changes to the UI, but I *still* loved it. Seriously, buy this game.

So the AI is stupid.  AoE units will target single enemies that are closest to it when there are a large group of enemies within it's firing arc. AI will chase around a unit and circle around it before attacking.  AI will not move or attack for about a second after it is spawned.  AI will often sit there and do nothing when mind controlled.  Some units will stop attacking after they use their activated attack.
Commander abilities don't work as intended.  There are a few that are exploitable, and there are others that affect both enemies and allies when they clearly state they effect either your enemies or your allies but not both.
Units are extremely unbalanced.  Some units are the be-all-end-all-only-need-to-make-this-unit, while others are so useless you are not only hurting yourself, but helping your enemy by using them.  This goes for all units ranging from early game to end game.  While the 3 different factions all have their useful and useless units, 1 of the factions is overall better than the other 2, while another of them is the weakest of the 3.
You're also probably going to have to invest some serious time if you plan on unlocking every single unit for all 3 factions.
And if you have read this far, you are probably wondering why I am recommending it.
Well, this game is awesome.  Even with all the bad there is so much more good that the bad is overshadowed.  Not only is the good better than all the bad points I made, but the game is in Beta.  That means that bad stuff I listed, most if not all of it is going to go away, which will just add onto this games awesomeness.
What makes this game awesome?  Well for starters, 3v3 battles are done in such a way that it is possible for 1 person with well timed commander skills, and the right units to carry their team.  And 1 or 2 well timed and placed commander skills is all it takes to turn the tide.
Another thing that makes this game awesome, most matches only last about 10 minutes.  Meaning you can get several battles in the corse of an hour, see what you are playing against, what starts your enemies and allies are using, and continue to tweak your own build without worrying about losing too much time.
Community doesn't seem toxic.  Though most of the communicating I do is through the emotes that game lets you use, but I have had some fun with enemy players using them.
All in all great little gem, and I can't wait to play the game in a few months from now.
TL;DR:  There is no TLDR, because if you can't be bothered to take the time to read a review you shouldn't be bothered to form an opinion about what you are reading reviews about.

This game is incredible and among my personal top games. I played it on the playstation 4 but I bought it here to give a review. Here's why:
The story is told perfectly. People now-days forget that video games are an interactive medium. Telling a story through just cutscenes is lame and unimaginative. Bastion solves this problem by having everything tie in perfectly. The narrator is able to describe what you're doing and give context on the world you're exploring. It seems like he's telling you little, but it adds up to a huge amount meaning as you play the game you're also learning about it. For example when you go to one new location the narrator tells you about it by warning you about the obstacles and how people in the past got hurt there. Through that you learn about how that place was before the game started.
Next, the gameplay is amazing. First you choose a difficulty and start playing the game. As you play, you collect these statues which actually add mechanics to your enemies. For example, one statue makes your enemies faster and more eager to attack. Each of the statues adds gameplay mechanics forcing you to change up your style, but only if you want to. If you enjoy the current difficulty you can just play on it, but if you want more of a challenge you can use the statues. After using al 12 the game plays at a much higher level and forces you to do the same.
The Art is more subjective. For me, I loved the environment and the world itself with it looking exactly like how it should after the events in the game. On the other hand I wasn't a very big fan of the character models.
The Music is also amazing. You can listen to the soundtrack online to get a glimpse, but playing the game to it is a whole different ballgame. It draws you in and immerses you in the world.
Controlling wise, I would advise playing with a controller. You can play with mouse or keyboard, but personally I found the controller to be the best way to play.
Overall, this game is amazing and you should buy it, especially now when it's only 3 dollars. The gameplay, story, art and music are wonderful.

Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is by far one of the best games I have ever played. Its like combining the moving controls from any Assassin's game and the battle mechanics of the Batman games. Now, sure it brings together the controls from two other great games, but what really makes this game shine is the nemesis system. What this is, if you don't already know, is a system that sets up ranks for the enemy. There will be 30 or so random and unique enemies all with their own names. What I loved, playing throuh this, is that I found an Orc named Zog Brawler. He killed me instantly. When I came back to fight him again, he made a little remark about how he killed me once and would do it again. Except this time I killed him. Usually in games, when you kill an enemy, the enemy stays dead, but with the nemesis system, unless you decapitate your enemy, there is a possibility of it's return. I ended up fighting Zog Brawler 10-20 times before he finally stayed dead. At first it was frustrating because I wasn't used to gameplay like that, but after a while I started to make a history with this orc as my arch nemesis if you will. No longer was Zog an ordinary orc, but he was the Joker to my Batman, and when he was finally gone for good, I kind of started to miss battling him and hearing his witty comments on how he would kill me. Without the nemesis system, this game wouldn't be what it is, and quite frankly I am surprised you are still reading this. Stop reading this and buy the game already, you'll thank me after you stop playing your first binge play of a couple of days.

The game is amazingly well done.  It is quite daunting at first and the game throws you into what feels like the deep end right off the bat.  It's a trial by fire, but you must endure.  If you do, you'll get better and better and better and be able to handle it.  That's the beauty of the series.  You will die... a lot... but it's okay.  Dying is part of the experience and doesn't really cost you anything.  Continue to explore different paths as it is a nonlinear game and try not to get discouraged or give up.  You'll love the experience by the time its over.
The lore is perhaps the best part of the game.  It is kind of hidden in item descriptions, subtle environmental clues and vague character dialogue, but it is there and its very, very rich.  It's honestly the most ingenious and deep story telling I've seen in my 30 years of gaming.
The fact you can now get this game for $5 is quite honestly a total steal.
Bottom line: It is challenging, but manageable with practice.  Stats and equipment aren't super important.  You can upgrade almost anything to be a viable piece of equipment to get you through the game and that's great.  Certainly some stuff is better, but if you don't find the best weapon or armor in the game it doesn't matter.  Don't worry about missing stuff - just keep slogging forward and you'll be rewarded with a brilliant experience.

I'm one of the early backers, having been a huge fan of Infinity Engine RPGs. I was incredibly excited about Pillars of Eternity, so naturally my expectations have been incredibly high, perhaps impossibly so. Of course Pillars of Eternity is not a gift from gods, it's just a game. Not without flaws, but a very good game still.
Things that I enjoy about Pillars:
- The setting that felt a bit bland at the begging is growing on me immensely. It's introduced slowly and will probably confuse you or send you to "cyclopedia" at one point, but as I keep immersing in it, I like it more and more. And it's all original material, hopefully offering more opportunities for exploration in the future.
- The game is visually very solid. Lightning is beautiful, animations are smoth, backgrounds are rich and finely detailed. It's pleasant to look at.
- It preserves the spirit of its old predecessors, while introducing new welcome quality of life functionalities. Slow mode/fast mode are some of my favorites so far.
- NPC party members, just like setting, can feel a bit bland at first, but they grow on you. I don't have the same level of emotional attachment I had to guys and gals from Baldur's Gate 2 or more contemporary Mass Effect, but they are definitely better fleshed out and interractive than BG1 and many other RPGs out there. Plus, as I haven't finished the game yet, I might still be in for a few surprises.
Things that I hope would be improved in the INEVITABLE sequel (I hope to gods there will be sequel. PLEASE!)
- Companion AI (and battle movement). A lot of times due to companion collisions, simply telling a party member to go somewhere sends them running in a random direction, often into a group of carefully herded enemies.
- More companions! More interaction! More companion subplots! Not necessarily a dating sim that is some of the recent BioWare games, but more companion interaction makes us more emotionally involved in the game.
- More open-ended exploration chapters. Some of the best times had in BG2 for me and I'm sure for many others was Chapter 2 where the only major story-related goal was to accumulate a heap of money. It gave us the opportunity to travel the world, go on cool, completely unrelated adventures, get to know our companions, and generally have fun. Sticking to the main plot too closely risks railroading the game, making every playthrough feel the same.
Overall, I'm very happy with Pillars and will definitely recommend it to any fan of IE RPGs. It's not going to beat BG2, but it's a very solid game nonetheless and you will enjoy it if you approach it with open mind.
Oh, and bugs, Obsidian. Please, look to that. Double clikcing weapon bug is brutal.

I am only ten hours in but the expansiveness of the world is simultaenously exciting and terrifying. PoE is equally rewarding and punishing while maintaining an engaging sense of strategy that comes from it's Dungeons & Dragons influences. If you are looking to a throwback to the earlier days of fantasy RPGs then Pillars of Eternity is for you.

I'm aware it may seem unfair to give a game a bad review with so little play time, but I feel I've gotten a good idea about everything there is to this game. If any developers are reading, I'd like to offer some constructive criticism. Conceptually this game is pretty unique, apart from the early access survival aspect. The atmosphere of waking up on the shore of a cold unforgiving island, plagued by undead creatures, and a dragon (which becomes ever so annoying once you realize it simply flies in circles for eternity) is truly awe-inspiring. Intrigued by the atmosphere you soon realize that there isn't much to offer upon exploring the crafting, combat, and building system. You will find yourself running back to the beach over and over trying to collect flint and other resources, which is very tedious. Simply, the game suffers from poor structure. I'm not sure if it is technical limitations caused by the game's engine, or the lack of experience from the developers. The map isn't big enough to leave any room for exploration, you simply spawn in and see what appears to be your main objective (the dragon). If you're going to leave this big of a gap in map design, atleast make it randomly generated. I recommend starting from scratch with the map, perhaps hire some new employees with the money generated from the Steam sale, maybe even invest in using a better game engine. It all just seems bland, next is combat; after interacting with some skeletons I discovered they had some sort of disability that allowed me to simply run to a safe distance, get a whack in and continue running. There needs to be a proper block and parry system, and more intelligent A.I. I hate to continue to bash, but I'm simply trying to conceptualize some ideas for the developers, so I can get my money's worth from this game. For example, the building. It's simply a bunch of pre-fabs, to build said pre-fabs you must go spam left click countless trees until you die of old age. After you've collected enough resources to build your desired structure, you simply spam "E" until this structure magically appears. (This system is similar to that of The Forest". Referring to the gathering of resources, perhaps players could create a lumber-mill of sorts allowing for increased productivity in wood gathering, and rather than running to the beach to collect flint, you could find nodes (these nodes should respawn eventually) scattered across the map. But, once again with the size of the map, after building your pre-fab riddened village of nothingness the wilderness becomes barren due to the lack of trees. Ultimately, this game needs a fresh-start. I do not intend to insult any developers, I simply would like to see this game to shine in the way it should.

Singularity combines first-person shooting and time device manipulation in a great way. You can shoot enemies to death, or expend energy to kill them using time itself (advancing or reversing it). Not only is this usable in combat, but you can also reverse time to fix broken stuff like machines or stairways, and age obstacles to the point of degradation so you can get past them. The gameplay is fun, and the story is surprisingly good for a first person shooter a lot of people haven't heard about. It's no BioShock, of course, but it's got a good plot for an action-heavy shooter, including multiple endings. I've beaten the game once on PC and once on PS3. It's a good game.

It's set on a Soviet research facility dealing with a mysterious newly found source of energy. Things go wrong, you know it goes. The story is not anything special, but it helps to paint a pleasant spooky atmosphere along with audio logs and some memos scattered around.
The game is nicely paced and varies things a bit between shooting soldiers and various mutants. You'll have a Time Manipulation Device to help you through this, giving you various superpowers related to time and reverting objects and enemies. There's of course the standard FPS arsenal of weapons, of which I'll mention a rifle with a bulletcam you can steer and also a steerable grenade launcher. Weapons feel fine to shoot and you can upgrade them with doodads you find along the way.

I just finished my first play-through of Bastion, and I'm really happy with it. I'm really into games that won't be a huge time commitment to complete, and Bastion is short enough for me to finish in a day or two, but substantial enough to leave me satisfied at the end. I plan on opening the game sometime soon to unlock some more achievements.
The art and music are fantastic (seriously), the setting and story are original and intriguing, and the variety of weapons was great. I found myself wanting to keep playing so I can learn more about the world they live in. As for the narration, I actually really loved it. It had all the potential to make the game terrible, but it enhanced the game instead. The narration was seamless with gameplay, and if I happened to replay an area for some reason, the narration wasn't repetitive; it had new content.
My only real complaint about the game is that sometimes the character can move a lot slower than seems appropriate, and some of the fighting sequences seem more like a chore because they are so long. (You get good rewards, but it almost doesn't seem worth it.)
In the game you unlock new weapons, abilities, and enhancements that you can choose between to move forward with your journey. I'm one of those people who likes to fully upgrade every weapon possible. If you enjoy that too, then Bastion will be fun for you.
Overall, I'm really happy that I purhcased this game, and I will definitely open it again for another playthrough in new story plus mode.

The First Game That Put Novel Developer 'Supergiant' On The Gaming Hall of Fame. Its Not Surprising Why. It Easily Distinguishes Itself in The RPG Genre, You'll See How Below. If You've Played Transistor and Pre-Ordered 'Pyre', or You Just Found Out About All These Aforementioned Titles... Now's The Ideal Time to Give This Game A Whirl. By the By, This Game is SUPER Cheap Right Now With The Summer Sale 2017 On... That Has Ended. Don't Fret! There's Always The Next Sale.
Post-apocalyptic premise known as the 'Calamity' has plagued. You play as a character known simply as 'The Kid', highlighting your helplessness and anonymity. On your search for survivors, you are to also locate pieces of fragments to restore the 'Bastion', a safe haven. You witness the remains of many that you've known... and those that you could've gotten to. He Matures and Takes On Responsibility.
(a) A Simpler Time-
The art style is breathtaking, despite exploring the after-effects of the tragedy that took so many lives. One cannot help, but envision a period when the places were crowded with people and not rubble.
Additionally I love how it seems as though The Kid is a newborn. What I mean by that is how the pathway falls into place and gradually unravels before our eyes when he navigates the field. Its a neat little feature, that shows his being distant and how everything has changed after the Calamity.
(b) Nothing Held Back-
There's just so much diversity! Combat system, in real-time allows the flow of battle to be followed. Equipped with two weapons at a time. Choosing to deal quick attacks, special attacks, swapping between the two instantaneously and then rolling away, strategize on the go! The environmental hazards plays a large factor too.
Not to forget there are more than enough weapons to suit the differing playstyles. Be it, Long range- 'Dueling Pistols', 'Fang Repeater' and many more! A much necessary alternative, Close range- 'Cael's Hammer' and More!! Or the combination of the two- 'Brusher's Pike', 'War Machete' and MANY, MANY, MANY.... (Cuts Off)
(c) Growth Spurt-
There are upgrades to the core of the Bastion that unlocks new structures, to tap into greater power. Each weapon can be further modified in either one of two options, three times- dealing more damage, critical rate up or better accuracy (some are weapon specific)
With cumulative experience points, The Kid gains a slot for an upgrade per level up. The in game currency 'Spirit' gives access to buying stats increasing items or parts/materials for weapon upgrades. It absolutely feels as though he as ageing, although not physically and the Player is the parent.
(d) Milestones-
Apart from story levels, The Kid can undertake 'Proving Grounds' where he will be promisingly rewarded with 'Spirit', weapon materials and new weapons-exclusive arts. Each one is accommodated to a particular weapon, so you have to adapt accordingly. Varying tests of reflex, wits and brawn, the Proving Grounds have them all!! Not for the faint of heart.
Of course, there is the structure where you invoke 'Idols'. They are where buffs can be granted to the enemies in exchange for more XP, Spirit and all-round misery. If you love get-rich quick schemes but even faster deaths, you are welcome to have a taste.
At a certain point, The Kid will stumble onto 'Who Knows Where' A 20-Waves fight it all out, where additional backstory is narrated! Lets not forget New Game Plus, where the enemies will be tougher? (Though I have yet to actually do it....)
(e) More Than Words-
So the game is filled with narration by an old, wise man. They're well implemented mostly, with every action that The Kid does, its given a nice touch of commentary. (To draw on the pointlessness and to humor us) These can occur when falling off, doing repetitive things, dying, destroying certain objects multiple times.
The story itself is also heavily narrated, every key item that is found can be given to others for their thoughts (also narrated by the same old guy) which leaves us to symphatize (to a degree, emphathize)
(f) Life-
The plot felt complete. Nothing too long, probably able to finish in 5-6 hours. This game will force you to feel every emotion. It had some twists that plunged The Kid into moments of despair. There were some instances of hope where the sanctuary had survivors. But never overwhelming amounts.. At the end, it did tell its story. (and a story it was) (PLAY IT!!)
(g) In The Country-
Sountrack was awesome for a first impression (Shout out to DARREN KORB!) It had a Folksy, acoustic tune with a modern vibe. There was a track featuring Ashley Barrett (LUV!!) and anything with lyrics, is always appreciated.
(i) Third Person-
I know I said the narration was a good move. However, it also means that throughout the entire game, (we'll all be hearing an old voice) Not that there's anything wrong.. He can be believeable at least, but monotonous at worst. Its like as some have pointed out, an aged sage telling a story.. Our attention does wander off right? After prolonged durations..
Furthermore, it ruins the immersion. I think since there are other characters... They should have their own voices when they speak/share their thoughts. Just to add characterisation. Instead they are expositioned through narration, which becomes depersonalized. (But hey, its their project, I get it. Their vision, so I am not gonna b-word about that)
(ii) Survival of The Fittest-
This is probably, definitely me being biased but it shouldn't have included a top rankings feature.The game does has a score attack mode... Yes, I feel that ruined it. You play the campaign to discover a fascinating story but you then go gung-ho to compete with others. Where's the drama gone? (I am still glad its included, because you got to please some people that aren't me)
(iii) Not in Stock-
Since they've included all that weaponry, they could've gone one notch higher and give up the option to change some equipments (armor, accessories) altogether. (Not a big issue, I'd just prefer some cosmetic changes) (Also, where would they even find a supplier..)
Bastion Is One of My Personal Favorites. I Cannot Generalize This As One of The 'Best' in The RPG Genre, (Reason being I have not played a whole lot...) But Its Safe To Say That It Is of The Few That Stand Out. With More Good Than Problems, It Will Surely Take Shelter In Our Memories.

The game is amazingly well done.  It is quite daunting at first and the game throws you into what feels like the deep end right off the bat.  It's a trial by fire, but you must endure.  If you do, you'll get better and better and better and be able to handle it.  That's the beauty of the series.  You will die... a lot... but it's okay.  Dying is part of the experience and doesn't really cost you anything.  Continue to explore different paths as it is a nonlinear game and try not to get discouraged or give up.  You'll love the experience by the time its over.
The lore is perhaps the best part of the game.  It is kind of hidden in item descriptions, subtle environmental clues and vague character dialogue, but it is there and its very, very rich.  It's honestly the most ingenious and deep story telling I've seen in my 30 years of gaming.
The fact you can now get this game for $5 is quite honestly a total steal.
Bottom line: It is challenging, but manageable with practice.  Stats and equipment aren't super important.  You can upgrade almost anything to be a viable piece of equipment to get you through the game and that's great.  Certainly some stuff is better, but if you don't find the best weapon or armor in the game it doesn't matter.  Don't worry about missing stuff - just keep slogging forward and you'll be rewarded with a brilliant experience.

Miscreated is an open world post-apocalyptic sandbox developed by Entrada Interactive. It is the best survival game that I have played because of its phenomenal graphics and the way it immerses players.
Miscreated immerses players with ambient sounds and overgrown landscapes to create a fun and enjoyable environment. The game creates a sense of fear (e.g. when you hear footsteps that are not yours in a dark and eerie town) The mutants can become a threat if not avoided or dealt with properly but the real threat is the vulnerability of other survivors. Any survivor can be a threat even if they appear to be ‘friendly’ or not.
The extreme detail put into this game by the developers is fantastic. Miscreated has a long and realistic day/night cycle with harsh weather conditions such as the many levels of rain, fog, wind, tornados and many other weather conditions. The downtown city recently added into Miscreateds patch #36 is amazing. The city features locations such as the police station, a hotel, scaffolding around buildings and many more.
Miscreated keeps players playing because of random encounters that could happen which may result in life or death situations and the exciting updates which happen regularly.
This game is definitely worth your money and time so I strongly suggest you pick up this tittle and play it. Congratulations to Entrada Interactive for creating this stunning game, keep up the effort and great work.

This is what happened on the first server I joined:
- Spawned near a highway.
- Followed it to a gas station, which I explored.
- Followed highway a bit more to a city.
- Saw a mutant hobbling toward the town square, so went to a minimart.
- Saw someone stalking me from a cargo container, went up and said hi.
- 5 people came running toward us, chasing another person. They killed him and said he was a robber. They showed me around the minimart to a backpack before killing me.
- Respawned and came into contact with a few friendly people. We eventually met up and started exploring.
- Explored for a while withe the group, came across two nice people, seperately, one with a shotgun.
- On our way up north, we came across a medium sized town to the east, so we explored.
- Went into a house that had a sign that said "DO NOT COME INSIDE THIS HOUSE". Found a rifle upstairs and a full magazine.
- As soon as I picked the rifle up, I heard a loud bang and ran outside. One of our people had been shot dead.
- We all went back to searching for supplies in the town. After a while, I got lost, and we all agreed to meet at the bridge we used crossed into the town.
- On the way to the bridge, I heard multiple shots, and came running to see what happened. I saw a friend running from the scene, and followed him. He explained that another person was killed by an unknown assassin.
- We went to the corpse and inspected it, taking all needed materials from him. Then, another of our friends came running up to us with a shotgun taken from the corpse. I immediately pulled my crosshairs up toward him, and he did the same to me. I told him to lower the gun, but began shooting at my friend and I. I quickly shot him multiple times in the chest, and he fell over, dead.
- After looting his body, it was only my friend and I left. We were wondering if he was the killer, or if he was just scared and confused like us, and thought I was the killer because of my newly found rifle.
- We walked along a path away from the town, and into a forest. We had to keep heading North. Eventually, we took a look at our map, and stalled in a forest, trying to figure out where we had fled to. Suddenly, a man dressed in all camoflauge ran out from the trees and began firing his shotgun at us. I fired a few bullets into him before getting filled with holes, and my friend tried hobbling away before bleeding to death seconds after I died. Turns out, this guy had been stalking us, killing us, and making us paranoid of each other until he could finish us all off. He must have been watching us for an hour.
The lesson is, don't go into a house that says to not go in.

I just finished my first play-through of Bastion, and I'm really happy with it. I'm really into games that won't be a huge time commitment to complete, and Bastion is short enough for me to finish in a day or two, but substantial enough to leave me satisfied at the end. I plan on opening the game sometime soon to unlock some more achievements.
The art and music are fantastic (seriously), the setting and story are original and intriguing, and the variety of weapons was great. I found myself wanting to keep playing so I can learn more about the world they live in. As for the narration, I actually really loved it. It had all the potential to make the game terrible, but it enhanced the game instead. The narration was seamless with gameplay, and if I happened to replay an area for some reason, the narration wasn't repetitive; it had new content.
My only real complaint about the game is that sometimes the character can move a lot slower than seems appropriate, and some of the fighting sequences seem more like a chore because they are so long. (You get good rewards, but it almost doesn't seem worth it.)
In the game you unlock new weapons, abilities, and enhancements that you can choose between to move forward with your journey. I'm one of those people who likes to fully upgrade every weapon possible. If you enjoy that too, then Bastion will be fun for you.
Overall, I'm really happy that I purhcased this game, and I will definitely open it again for another playthrough in new story plus mode.

DaRevieweD #8
The First Game That Put Novel Developer 'Supergiant' On The Gaming Hall of Fame. Its Not Surprising Why. It Easily Distinguishes Itself in The RPG Genre, You'll See How Below. If You've Played Transistor and Pre-Ordered 'Pyre', or You Just Found Out About All These Aforementioned Titles... Now's The Ideal Time to Give This Game A Whirl. By the By, This Game is SUPER Cheap Right Now With The Summer Sale 2017 On... That Has Ended. Don't Fret! There's Always The Next Sale.
Post-apocalyptic premise known as the 'Calamity' has plagued. You play as a character known simply as 'The Kid', highlighting your helplessness and anonymity. On your search for survivors, you are to also locate pieces of fragments to restore the 'Bastion', a safe haven. You witness the remains of many that you've known... and those that you could've gotten to. He Matures and Takes On Responsibility.
(a) A Simpler Time-
The art style is breathtaking, despite exploring the after-effects of the tragedy that took so many lives. One cannot help, but envision a period when the places were crowded with people and not rubble.
Additionally I love how it seems as though The Kid is a newborn. What I mean by that is how the pathway falls into place and gradually unravels before our eyes when he navigates the field. Its a neat little feature, that shows his being distant and how everything has changed after the Calamity.
(b) Nothing Held Back-
There's just so much diversity! Combat system, in real-time allows the flow of battle to be followed. Equipped with two weapons at a time. Choosing to deal quick attacks, special attacks, swapping between the two instantaneously and then rolling away, strategize on the go! The environmental hazards plays a large factor too.
Not to forget there are more than enough weapons to suit the differing playstyles. Be it, Long range- 'Dueling Pistols', 'Fang Repeater' and many more! A much necessary alternative, Close range- 'Cael's Hammer' and More!! Or the combination of the two- 'Brusher's Pike', 'War Machete' and MANY, MANY, MANY.... (Cuts Off)
(c) Growth Spurt-
There are upgrades to the core of the Bastion that unlocks new structures, to tap into greater power. Each weapon can be further modified in either one of two options, three times- dealing more damage, critical rate up or better accuracy (some are weapon specific)
With cumulative experience points, The Kid gains a slot for an upgrade per level up. The in game currency 'Spirit' gives access to buying stats increasing items or parts/materials for weapon upgrades. It absolutely feels as though he as ageing, although not physically and the Player is the parent.
(d) Milestones-
Apart from story levels, The Kid can undertake 'Proving Grounds' where he will be promisingly rewarded with 'Spirit', weapon materials and new weapons-exclusive arts. Each one is accommodated to a particular weapon, so you have to adapt accordingly. Varying tests of reflex, wits and brawn, the Proving Grounds have them all!! Not for the faint of heart.
Of course, there is the structure where you invoke 'Idols'. They are where buffs can be granted to the enemies in exchange for more XP, Spirit and all-round misery. If you love get-rich quick schemes but even faster deaths, you are welcome to have a taste.
At a certain point, The Kid will stumble onto 'Who Knows Where' A 20-Waves fight it all out, where additional backstory is narrated! Lets not forget New Game Plus, where the enemies will be tougher? (Though I have yet to actually do it....)
(e) More Than Words-
So the game is filled with narration by an old, wise man. They're well implemented mostly, with every action that The Kid does, its given a nice touch of commentary. (To draw on the pointlessness and to humor us) These can occur when falling off, doing repetitive things, dying, destroying certain objects multiple times.
The story itself is also heavily narrated, every key item that is found can be given to others for their thoughts (also narrated by the same old guy) which leaves us to symphatize (to a degree, emphathize)
(f) Life-
The plot felt complete. Nothing too long, probably able to finish in 5-6 hours. This game will force you to feel every emotion. It had some twists that plunged The Kid into moments of despair. There were some instances of hope where the sanctuary had survivors. But never overwhelming amounts.. At the end, it did tell its story. (and a story it was) (PLAY IT!!)
(g) In The Country-
Sountrack was awesome for a first impression (Shout out to DARREN KORB!) It had a Folksy, acoustic tune with a modern vibe. There was a track featuring Ashley Barrett (LUV!!) and anything with lyrics, is always appreciated.
(i) Third Person-
I know I said the narration was a good move. However, it also means that throughout the entire game, (we'll all be hearing an old voice) Not that there's anything wrong.. He can be believeable at least, but monotonous at worst. Its like as some have pointed out, an aged sage telling a story.. Our attention does wander off right? After prolonged durations..
Furthermore, it ruins the immersion. I think since there are other characters... They should have their own voices when they speak/share their thoughts. Just to add characterisation. Instead they are expositioned through narration, which becomes depersonalized. (But hey, its their project, I get it. Their vision, so I am not gonna b-word about that)
(ii) Survival of The Fittest-
This is probably, definitely me being biased but it shouldn't have included a top rankings feature.The game does has a score attack mode... Yes, I feel that ruined it. You play the campaign to discover a fascinating story but you then go gung-ho to compete with others. Where's the drama gone? (I am still glad its included, because you got to please some people that aren't me)

**A game that tries to do too much with too little.**
It tries to be Bioshock with its mixture of "magical" combat and "conventional" combat--but neither one of them is exceptionally interesting unless the individual items are progressed through leveling them up.
It tries to implement item progression for both the "magical" and "conventional" weapons through a currency found through "exploration"--but the maps are extremely linear and don't provide any real rewards for finding the items that allow you to level up the items.
The weapon progression doesn't seem to help a lick with your capabilities in the game. As soon you have enough time to level up particular weapons--the enemies get harder. This makes the unupgraded items worse and puts the upgraded items back at square one. This removes a good deal of player choice in loadout.
What I do like though: When you are actually in a circumstance where a particular weapon would be situationally useful--the game actually straight up gives them to you. "Oh, boss fight. Here is a weapon locker that allows you to swap out." "Oh, an open field? Here is a sniper right and a minigun. Pick one" I appreciate that immensely.
But back to upgrading. The progressive upgrades themselves are not very differentiated: Magazine size, reload speed, and damage. With no clear indicator of *how much* those stats are improved--its impossible to make an informed opinion. Not that it will matter any way because the vaguely scaling enemy difficulty will render your upgrades pointless anyway.
And then towards the end of the game--an entire line of upgrades is completely obsoleted by the removal of particular limitations on a specific item.
There is decent variety in enemies but some of the enemies are either obnoxious to deal with (ticks) or are boring to fight against (normal human soldiers). What unique and creative enemies they *do* have are easily mitigated by certain skills and become rote to defeat.
The boss battles--and I use that term lightly--are uninspired and boring. Once you figure out the mechanic of the boss, its a rinse-and-repeat affair.
And the ending(s). I'm not going to say much but lets just say "multiple endings" is a little disingenuious.
The most annoying part, though? The game also plays ridiculously fast. I beat it on hard in four hours. HLTB claimed a completion time of 7.5 so your mileage may vary. I would only consider buying this if it was very cheap. I cannot believe the publisher is trying to get someone to pay $30 for a game published in 2010!

Singularity is a game that was released in 2010 and kinda flew under everyone's radar, especially mine. However, now I've played it, so it's no longer under my radar and I can tell you that it's basically alright.
Singularity is a fairly standard linear FPS, with two weapons, iron sights, sprinting, and other features fairly common to console shooters from the mid-to-late 2000s. It's got a story involving time manipulation and a miracle element and Russians taking over the world, which is a bit less involving than it sounds. Singularity's main selling point, however, is that it rips off much more popular games a lot.
The game it takes most from is BioShock, with weapon upgrades, a miracle element that both fuels the plot and is used for upgrades, a wrecked environment that was state-of-the-art in the 30s-50s, a survival-horror-y tone, audio logs, a silent protagonist, enemies that are insane mutated humans with magic miracle-element powers, ghostly flashbacks, and health/ability power bars in the upper-right-hand corner. It also just has a very prevalent BioShock-y feel. I don't have anything against art copying other art, but it gets fairly ♥♥♥♥ing blatant in this case.
Additionally, Singularity takes plenty from other games. It has Fallout 3's gore and dismemberment system (excellent), as well as its futuristic aesthetic. It also has Half-Life 2's gravity gun (that gets an upgrade right at the end that makes it blue instead of orange and much more powerful), physics puzzles, and and setpiece fixation. Again, there's nothing wrong with any of this, but the game doesn't seem to have too many ideas of its own.
The game has a variety of upgradeable weapons, which start out pretty standard but get fairly wacky as time goes on. There's a railgun, a minigun that makes the most of the gore effects, a sniper rifle whose rounds you can guide around corners, and a roller grenade launcher that you can also guide around. Complementing this are a variety of fun time-based and gravity-based abilities, including the ability to age enemies to death, create a sphere in which all time is stopped, and lift objects into the air (including enemies' shields, which can then shield you). All this is cool to use, but I found that none of it was as useful as the more standard fare, like the shotgun and sniper rifle. It's a shame that the game wasn't balanced to make the ridiculous weapons more fun, but I can see how that'd be difficult.
For some reason, every Russian person on the Russian island where the game takes place speaks and writes in English, even to each other. I'm not sure if a reason is ever given.
Overall, Singularity's alright. It has some good ideas that it stole from other games, but it doesn't really do much to make them into someting interesting. It's not bad, but it's not especially memorable either. I recommend it because it's completely passable, but if you've got something else you want more and you're trying to decide, go for that other thing.

Mass Effect is the first instalment to the franchise of what could be the greatest player driven story ever made in a game. Mass Effect is what I will term "a diamond in the rough'. Some people will find that it's just their cup of tea, while others won't be able to look past its clunky gameplay. Mass Effect features some of the most complex menus I've seen in a game. It contains a ton of gear, weapons and armors. It's all a bit overwhelming at first, but soon the player will just start looking for higher stat weapons and it becomes a simple matter of finding the highest damage gun. The conversations that you participate in are very dynamic and change more than you sometimes expect when you try different classes of Shepard. The story telling and characters are superb, if a bit shallow. I purposely avoid the phrase one dimensional, because that's defiantly not the problem. You meet characters who seem more interesting than the game lets them be.
Mass Effect joins every other RPG game I've touched in the "I hate this class system" pile. It's especially annoying when you choose one of the power based classes who can only use pistols. I understand what they were trying to achieve, but either powers should have been developed more, or each class should have had access to pistols and assault rifles. Another issue that comes up is that guns lack interest. The player will quickly realize that pistols are overall the best class at most ranges. They're only out classed later in the game by guns with superior DPS. The movement controls also seem clunky on the ground, while the Mako moves smoothly but can be sent flying be even small bumps.
However, Mass Effect is a very enjoyable game. The world is interesting and when you visit most planets you feel like you're on a planet. The sky above really give you the feeling that you're traveling among the stars. It a very rewarding experience and I'd recommend playing it if you're interested in a unique sci-fi franchise.

This is a very hard game to pick a positive/negative review upon.  More so due to RNG elements within the game and trying to 100% complete it rather than anything wrong in the actual game.
In and of itsself the cons of this game are very small compared to how utterly addicting this game is.  But the couple of cons could have easily been play tested and altered to create a far more enjoyable experience.  Since at its core this is a crafting game in the same vein of 'holy potatoes it's a weapon shop'.  Which I also enjoyed but have not beat as of yet.
The pros are primarily that the game is incredibly addictive trying to build the perfect equipment or complete a quest, or get enough money for the next goal is so insanely addictive.
There are several small cons though:
The music is incredibly repetitive (sure it fits but when going for 30-60 hours and only having a total of like 5 or 6 tracks is a bit dissapointing)
There are two lines of 'failure' achievements, one for crafting 'inferior' grade equipment which you will get pretty easily, but the other is for running from adventures the sheer amount of times they want you to run from an adventure is silly I was less than 5% of the way to the final achievement in this category when I 100% everything else.
There is a 'clicker' based achievement strand for clicking on your pet, the amount of money required for this if you do not use an auto clicker makes this achievement strand is PAINFUL, I only got the first and the other two I used an achievement unlocker to obtain.
The true final boss can actually be easily cheesed.  However to do so requires you to idle the game for around 42 minutes (and yes I timed it).  If you don't this requires you to grind your characters to darn near max stats.  Including health.
You have to play through the game 3 times.  This is actually my smallest problem with this game since this game after beating the true finale on impossible is in all honesty rather short.  It took me less than 20 hours to complete my last 2 playthroughs.
Overall despite my criticisms the gameplay for this FAR more makes up for it.  The only unfortunate this is mouse control only no controllers allowed :(

Dragon's Dogma is a game that came out of nowhere for a lot of people.  For a lot of people, Camcom doesn't have the best track record for PC ports, and when a PC port for Dogma was announced many people worried that it would receive the same treatment as their other games.  Fortunately, Dragon's Dogma's PC port is very, very good.
Dragon's Dogma is an open world action adventure RPG where you can create your own NPC ally and recruit other people's allies, known as Pawns.  This is the multiplayer aspect of the game: You can use the pawns other people created, and vice versa.  The Pawn system is interesting because they learn with the player (assuming your first time playing the game); picking up on enemy weaknesses, effective tactics, etc.  The cool part about this system is that if someone else uses your pawn, the next time you rest at an inn your pawn could come back to you with knowledge of enemies you've never even encountered yet, making said future encounters much easier.
The combat is a mixture of a hack n' slash game along the lines of God of War or Darksiders, mixed with a bit of Devil May Cry for combos, and the best part of all: Shadow of the Colossus style climbing on giant enemies to go after weak points.  Although, after you've played for some time the encounters with these enemies might just become an exercise in mototony.  It's dependant on how well you deal with repetition.
The story is honestly nothing to write home about.  The main draw (to me) of Dragon's Dogma is the exploration, combat, and pawn system and how they all blend together to create a very unique gaming experience.

State of decay is a third person action survival roguelikesque rpg. The game starts with you returning from a fishing trip with your buddy Ed to find the main land over run with zombies. The game combines third person melee and ranged combat with a scavenging resource and community management system.
The starting area is fairly easy with sparsely positioned zombies in a camp ground area. You quickly find the rangers station and begin exploring the area and looting for supplies.
The combat system is fairly competent as is the driving system, however controls for this game currently are restricted to controller but the developer is working on full keyboard and mouse control so keep this in mind before buying this title.
The graphics are decent enough but nothing spectacular, however this is not a AAA title so this is understandable. Music, ambient sound and voice acting are pretty good considering this is not a AAA title.
What makes this game really shine is the community management system. You don't play one main character as you need to manage fatigue and people need to rest, so this has you swapping out for other community members as need be, but you will quickly find your favourites and tend to cycle between them.
The inventory management system is decent but transfering items between characters is frustrating making you return to base and stash it before switching characters and retrieving the items.
All in all this is a great game and definitely a refreshing approach to the zombie survival genre and for $20 or equivalent it is worth your time to pick this up. If you enjoy the zombie genre and looking for something a little different then this may be the game you have been looking for.

I always thought the hype over Dark Souls was a bit exagerated at first.
That was until I had an opportunity to get the game. It was a long time since I last spent 90 hours on a single game within a week.
What do you have to expect from the first episode on PC?
A quite bad port, let's say. The textures looks a bit weird and the game is capped at 30fps (Which isn't a problem for me as I don't ♥♥♥♥ing care as long as it's fluid, but 12yo with GTX960s and♥♥♥♥♥♥are gonna be ♥♥♥♥ing mad for that, I know it.)
But I'm not here to talk about port. Those "reviews" where people only care about the performances shouldn't even exist. What counts in games is the gameplay.
Also, I strongly recommend you to play with a pad. Well, first of all because it's a RPG, but secondly because the Keyboard+mouse control are... yeah. Messed up.
But oh boy, Dark Souls.
The clichee about it, present even in the title, is quite not a lie.
At first, you will die.
Much.
A lot.
So much.
But then, you will improve. You will learn over your death to perfect your skills.
Plenty of basic RPG elements are present, such as leveling, weapon grinding, magic and all- but what really struck me in Dark Souls is the fact that, as an absolute normal human(or rather undead, actually) you're going to fight armies of hollows and demons, swinging your weapons at a quite realistic speed. There's no super skill or any kind of irrealistic actions in this game (well, aside from magic and pyromancies, but they make you quite vulnerable); you really feel like you're a human like another, whose only advantage is the spirit.
You have a whole lot of armors available, though the tougher ones may not always be the more adequate choice, as you may need to improve your inventory capacity first - which means, soul grinding - souls being both money AND XP in this game.
There's also an entire pannel of weapons of various kind, such as swords, hammers, halleberds, axes, knives, bows... The list just goes on. It only depends your favorite fighting style, or what you do better with.
The soundtrack at first wasn't too appealing for me, when I fought the first boss. But through the game, I quickly discovered that this first taste was wrong.  In fact, I actually do listen to the OST quite often when not playing. That should be enough to understand...
The lore, now. It's dark. It's obscure and vague if you just go through the game without reading items descriptions (Or if you do not discover some secrets and covenants, some which are literally impossible to aknowledge without guides). But as the game would suggest, the lore is sad and rather melancholic. Don't attach too much to the characters you see...
I would like to give other constructive arguments, but Dark Souls surprised me so greatly that the only thing I can tell you is to go try it for yourself. If you got skills in videogames, you should finish it all right. For beneath 4$ in sales, it's completely worth a try if you're unfamiliar or skeptical with it.

Dark souls is now one of my favourite games ever.
Sure, graphically it's a bit dated, but it's a 4 year old console port. There are mods that make it look good at 1080p and run at 60fps (mostly).
The level design and lore is probably the best part. Everything intertwines and each area (in the first half of the game at least) is meticulously designed. It feels like a living world. The second half was clearly rushed (Lost Izalith and so on) but it is still enjoyable to complete the game.
Combat is of course a challenge, as it should be, but is also rewarding when you get it right. You will die a lot (as the name implies), but thats all part of the game and the learning process. Dying should be a punishment in all games, it makes you value your character and makes you think before running in to do the exact same thing again.
Considering how cheap it is now, and how much gameplay you get for your money, its a highly recommended purchase.

Maybe it's only the most recent patch that made this game worth playing, but it's fantastic.
As a huge fan of DayZ's gameplay model of bare bones, high risk survival, but not a fan of DayZ's infinite development progress despite getting over $60,000,000 in early access sales, this is exactly what DayZ would aspire to be in a beta build or even close to release.
The graphics are rich and detailed, the engine handles hit detection very well, crafting is mature, weapons and vehicles behave well and whilst they're rare they're not too rare. Looting is also much more realistic and requires attention to scrounge through piles of things and scanning environments for things that look useful, rather than the DayZ paradigm of opening inventory and walking until ground items show up in 'items nearby'.
There's other negative reviews where people say it's crap because they got shot on sight. These types of reviews reflect poorly on the game but they're really other player behaviour. Of course people will shoot you on sight, it's a hostile environment. Perhaps it you don't like the type of game where you need to excercise constant caution you should play a different game that doesn't have guns, or survival, or any form of competition.
Sure there's plenty to still sort out, like putting car tyres in your pockets, but this game is miles and miles ahead of DayZ. Get it.

The atmosphere of Miscreated, a survival post-apocalpyse type game, is extremely well crafted. Rats scurry about garbage strewn streets, alleys and old shops. Forlorn, tattered flags flutter from flagpoles jutting from the remnants of buildings, both large and small. The graphics of this game are some of the best I've seen, particularly the rain, which falls in realistic sheets and spatters and splutters on the ground in little pools.
The mechanics of the game are similar to Dayz, except it all seems to work and the zombies aren't also half-ghosts who can phase through walls and punch you without moving their limbs. In fact, the PVE enemies are actually not zombies, rather mutated people.
The game has vehicles already, something that took Dayz almost 2 years to implement. My play so far has been largely stable and consistent, with little lag or rubberbanding.
Miscreated deserves to be highly regarded for a number of factors. It has a robust and stable platform, it has truly beautiful graphics, and the atmosphere of the game is very well done.
I highly recommend this game, and urge you to give it a try. Don't miss this hidden gem of a game.

It's a very simple but difficult game. Similar to Asteroids, except you're an immobile circle in the center of the screen that can only rotate 360 degrees but not move otherwise. Enemies (triangles of varying sizes) come directly at you from all directions. Smaller enemies take fewer shots to kill than larger ones.
Arrow keys rotate. Spacebar fires your main weapon. Hold spacebar for a larger shot that does more damage. Each shot you take depletes the shot power bar.
Press Q to fire heat-seeking missiles, of which you have a limited supply, so use them only in emergencies. The main missle will break off into a series of smaller missiles after striking its first target.
Your shield deflects enemy shots back at them, but does not hold up for long. It will replenish itself occasionally.
Defeating bosses (giant triangles) will drop powerups that you can use to levl up your shot power, regain health, etc.
There is an element of randomness which can make it frustrating, but also leads to the urge to try it one more time.

Dragon's Dogma is a game that came out of nowhere for a lot of people.  For a lot of people, Camcom doesn't have the best track record for PC ports, and when a PC port for Dogma was announced many people worried that it would receive the same treatment as their other games.  Fortunately, Dragon's Dogma's PC port is very, very good.
Dragon's Dogma is an open world action adventure RPG where you can create your own NPC ally and recruit other people's allies, known as Pawns.  This is the multiplayer aspect of the game: You can use the pawns other people created, and vice versa.  The Pawn system is interesting because they learn with the player (assuming your first time playing the game); picking up on enemy weaknesses, effective tactics, etc.  The cool part about this system is that if someone else uses your pawn, the next time you rest at an inn your pawn could come back to you with knowledge of enemies you've never even encountered yet, making said future encounters much easier.
The combat is a mixture of a hack n' slash game along the lines of God of War or Darksiders, mixed with a bit of Devil May Cry for combos, and the best part of all: Shadow of the Colossus style climbing on giant enemies to go after weak points.  Although, after you've played for some time the encounters with these enemies might just become an exercise in mototony.  It's dependant on how well you deal with repetition.
The story is honestly nothing to write home about.  The main draw (to me) of Dragon's Dogma is the exploration, combat, and pawn system and how they all blend together to create a very unique gaming experience.

Singularity is a pretty well made game. At first glimpse you won’t know much about it. But once you learn the backstory or just watch the intro of the game you will instantly fall in interest with it. In a short summary I will give a brief description of the story without going into too much detail or popping an accidental spoiler.
After World War 2, the Soviet Union was looking to make their own Atomic Bomb. Whilst searching for Uranium on a tiny island of the South East Coast of the Soviet Union. Soviet Engineers discover on the Island E99. Also Known As Element 99. A powerful source of Energy which would make Uranium and Plutonium obsolete. After some time Khrushchev orders the Scientists and Engineers on the now named Island of Katorga 12 to begin experiments. Moments later a tragedy occurs killing off all of the Islands inhabitants. Moscow buries the existence of the Island. Not until 2010 when a American Satellite starts reading massive radiation levels from the Island. Fearing another Chernobyl. The USA sends in Elite Soldiers to investigate.
