I’ve always been a fan of casual simulation style games and when I saw one reviewer compare Weapon Shop Fantasy to games by Kairosoft, a well-known developer of excellent mobile simulation games, I knew I had to play it.
Weapon Shop Fantasy is played entirely with your mouse. You can choose to play as male or female and select from a handful of pets, whose purpose is to look cute and sometimes yield coins when you click on them.
The game begins with a cut scene that explains the ridiculous situation leading up to you, a vampire, running a weapon shop in order to pay back a whopping sum of five million gold to another vampire. This absurd exchange is the driving force—the “why am I doing this?”—behind the game and sets up the ultimate goal at the end of your mercantile grind. You start with 2000g, lent to you by your debtor as a sign of good faith, and the game walks you through a tutorial. Then, it’s up to you what you make of your time; you’re immortal, after all, so you have the option to work for the rest of eternity.
Naturally, you don’t want to have to work for the rest of your immortal life, so it’s time to put your shop workers to good use.
Crafting, adventuring, completing missions, and selling or equipping the items you create makes up the bulk of gameplay and you’ll spend a lot of time tabbing between your storefront and the adventure screen so that you can keep track of your operations.
In your store, you’re able to..
The gold you earn can be spent on a variety of workstations and Boss Skills. I’ll explain crafting and adventuring a bit later. Boss Skills, while costly, make your life easier and streamline your sweatshop. These include things like bigger queues for your crafting stations, reduced staff wages, increased storage space for the equipment you’ve crafted, and the like.
What you can craft depends on what station you use. There are a total of five stations:
Each crafting station has an associated attribute (listed next to it) that will make crafting or enchanting successfully and with a higher ranking more likely.
Your stables are where you’ll send your workers on adventures, which is how you’ll acquire raw materials for crafting. You can tab between your storefront and the adventure screen using the triple arrow icon on the middle right side of the screen. You can have up to four simultaneous adventures running at a time and there are 8 possible places to send your adventurers, each with their own elemental affinity, materials, and monsters.
Adventures are automated; your would-be hero will fight whatever is in their paths, mine, cut down trees, and eat wild foods which will have positive and negative effects that will last the duration of their adventure. The only thing they won’t do is save their own skins, which means you’ll need to pay attention to their health if you aren’t on the adventure screen, watching the adventure progress.
The game shows the health bar of your hero(es) when you’re on your shop screen and lines of text appear at the top of that screen to warn you of monsters they’ve run into. If your hero is slain, he’ll run back to your shop without any of his loot (unless you buy a Boss Skill that allows for a percentage of your loot to make it back with you), so there’s no shame in turning tail.
The boss monsters and chest monsters (Mimics) pose a serious threat to even the most seasoned adventurers, so it’s best to avoid them until much, much later.
Adventurers will also gain stats and skill exp points from successful adventurers. Skills are tied to pieces of equipment and are divided into active and passive skills. After you've earned enough exp, you’ll have mastered the skill and it will still be available even after you change equipment.
There are three types of missions:
1) Main Missions. Finishing these gives you bits of the main story. They consist of milestones given to you by your vampire debtor and their conditions will typically be fulfilled eventually through regular play
2) Sub Missions. These are given to you by shop patrons . They’ll ask for specific items and quantities and in exchange they’ll give you new recipes, gold, and even new staff
3) Staff Missions. Your staff will request equipment and sometimes to defeat a specific monster. It’s in your best interest to finish these missions, because the rewards upgrade your employees.
Any characters can equip a one-handed weapon and shield, or two-handed weapon, a helm body armor, and an accessory.
Whatever you don’t equip can be sold from your shop inventory. The higher the quality, the more the item will sell for.
You can equip anything you make to your employees as there are no class or level restrictions.
The BGM consists of a single chiptune track that loops, but it never really got irritating or overly repetitive.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
If you’re a fan of casual simulation titles, Weapon Shop Fantasy is a solid investment. Even in its current form, you're bound to get your money's worth out of it with the content available and there's more to come--more skills, craftable items, maps, and more fun to be had. The writing, while clumsily translated at times, is amusing. Completing the campaign will take several hours and if you’re like me and you like to unlock every recipe and employee and beat every boss, you’ll get even more out of this title.
Even if you aren’t a fan of the genre, this game will keep you entertained for hours at a time between the more involved titles in your inventory.

In 5:30 hours I managed to build a 5-square hut with door and bed inside, a fire spit, a stockpile of crabs and drinkable coconuts, I found bandages, antibiotics, morphine shots, bucket for water purification, a solar-cell lamp that's endless, motor/tank/carburator parts, hammer, stuff and stuff and stuff. Finding those tools is wonderful, it always feels like a great win.
But I burned through in less than 6 hours, I think there are some 4 hours left but I don't think there will be much more. Maybe a story would be nice like pages of an album or something... I don't know but some higher-order gameplay that sits atop everything that's currently there. Also more items types and different ingredients/recipes. But don't overdo it, avoid those 200 pointless recipes with 400 ingredients... keep it relevant (stuff that actually enhance the experience). Good examples are the compass and the lamp. They are real game-changers. I'd like binoculars to better spot distant islands or a GPS device that requires a lot more work than the usual stuff. Also temperature (hot/cold) mechanics would be nice. But I can't come up with more without falling into useless stuff. So to stay "relevant" with the current gameplay it is difficult to come up with good examples.
Next, direction. Right now it is a nice sandbox, but it also lacks a feeling of progress. Just survival is good at the beginning but once you have your hut nailed down and a cache of food and the water bucket you realize you can go on ENDLESSLY. Just go to the next island, reap the resources and get back to your home island. Soon, there is no real limit to how long you could go on. Exactly then, the game feels like pointless. With "direction" I mean that the devs understand how to progress the gameplay when it stops to engage the player (keep him in the "flux").
So, when these problems are solved I'll definitely recommend this game. For now, it's a thumbs up but it needs to be corrected and expanded or the thumb will go down very quickly!

This forgotten title is a mix of all the big FPSes of our time. A big chunk of BioShock, some Half-Life 2 and a tad of Call of Duty. (it's a game produced by Activision, so of course "press Shift to steady a sniper rifle (time dilation)"...) The first half of the game is a top fun. You'll enjoy the wonderful environments of a Soviet town and a futuristic research facility. The game looks especially good when it is raining. However, it looks very much like the one year older Batman: Arkham Asylum (also running on Unreal Engine 3) as it shares the same colour palette and for example, the plants that spread on the island of Katorga-12 are almost the same as Poison Ivy's foliage. This is not game-breaking though. You'll enjoy the subtle horror atmosphere in the first third of the game and the exploration of cleverly designed levels while collecting Element 99 Tech that is used in upgrading abilities and perks found on blueprints throughout the game. I hated that this game doesn't have any subtitles. Because of that, I missed a fair portion of the game's interesting writing. The TMD (Time Manipulation Device) is quite original in that it can age or renew objects (in order to gain resources or solve puzzles) or kill enemies by making them too old to live. This all happens during specific animations and is wonderfully satisfying to witness. The second half of the game can quickly turn you down with its chaotic graphical design, the uncovered corridor-shooter nature of the level design and the abundance of resources, ammo and powerful weapons that make you OP. I highly recommend playing on Hard. I also recommend playing with the Flawless Widescreen FOV mod. The game is very short, lasting only about 9 hrs.

Singularity is, hands down, one of the best FPS games I've layed my hands on in a long while. Despite being 7 years late to the party, I still managed to enjoy myself quite a lot on Katorga-12.
What is so good about this game, is that it offers variety. From weapons to powers, to enemies, it has enough to satisfy you throughout it's campaign, which, albeit a little bit short ( I beat it in under 9 hours ), is packed from start to finish with different exiting aspects of gameplay. And it ties everything so nicely, making you use different abilities to not only dispatch enemies in quick and exsiting ways, by aging them to a pile of dust, or by grabing their projectiles  out of the air and hurling them back, but also to solve different puzzles to progress or find hidden items. It's simply feels amazing to be able to do so much in a first person shooter and to not be confined by your ordinary weapons or feel like you have a set path that you can't stop following. The gameworld is by no means open, and posseses the usual invisible wall here and there, but you never feel like there's nothing more to it,with the graphics aging quite well, in my opinion, giving you  sence of mystery and urgency, feeling strangely dystopian, as you explore what's left of the finest the Soviet Union was able to offer, and with exploration promoted by hidden areas everywhere, with notes and audiologs left around that tell the story of the island through it's previous inhabitants.
All in all, it uses game mechanics brilliantly to offer choise and variety to the player from start to finish and is simple enough to not be overwhelming, but still never manages to get boring or too easy to be enjoyable.
Forget all those FPS games, Crysis? Pfft. Bioshock? Pfft. Call of Duty? Forget about it. This game has everything from Time Manipulation to Bullet Curving Sniper Rifles.
Strongly recommend.

Why the neagive review then?  Theres a major gamebreaking flaw in the design.  Limited resources.
Note:  there is the immersion breaking and outright cheaty workaround.
You can wipe the server and move your character from world to new world,   You'll have to rebuild all the buildings every single time OR spawn a new world, loot it for resources, and take it all back to the "real" game world.
If you don't use the workaround, your character will peak and then spend a precipitous dive back to the stone age and then die when everything is gone.
All the forests gone,
The Stone/ore nodes gone.
The flint used.
You will be forced to survive on loot and vilage respawns.
but
No more cooking fires because you cant get wood or flint.
You then die of starvation after surviving against all these critters and undead baddies.
Why? Not because there isn't food to eat.  It'll be because  you can't cook your food.
Game over, the end.
You lose.
You will die in just a few (realtime) days of gameplay on that first map.
On the upside you get to starve sooner if you play with friends (you'll collectively be using the resources faster) .
Bottom line, I'd wait for some resource respawn mechanic before you invest in this game. After it's in, Go for it.

THE SONIC 06 OF ISO GAMES.
This game is a shell of what I expected it to be. I let the hype train, and the 3.9 million budget (on kickstarter) isometric rpg game, make me think it was going to be an epic that would allow me to relive Baldur's Gate. And I was wrong.
I'll start off with a few things I liked. Inventory management is much easier. You can place the majority of loot in a huge container. The Prologue I found to be extraordinarily fun, and I felt everything about that part of the game was well fleshed out. The fast forward that allows you to quickly walk around is a dream come true. The stronghold mechanics were extremely fun and well done.
EDIT: I'd like to update the news on this review, the devs caved into SJWs to remove a limerick that was pathetically not offensive. In addition to that, the devs have stated modding on the Baldur's Gate scale is unlikely. So yeah, enjoy this objectively worse game. Funnily enough, they largely stated they would "support" mods. By support, they must have meant "allow" mods, supporting them in a metaphorical sense rather than an actual implementation sense.
I'd also like to mention the absolute shameless moneygrab the upgrade packs are. It makes EA look generous.
But sadly, for a story rich rpg, if you find the story and characters uninteresting and the combat unfun, you will not like this game.
I found myself fairly uninterested in the story. In Baldur's Gate you were the spawn of a dead God, in planescape Torment you were an amnesiac immortal who can die, in this game you're a ghost whisperer.
The prologue was fun until the end, and the game kinda felt like it just kept rolling downhill.
First, like most obsidian games, it's been released with numerous bugs, though you wont notice them at first (loading game with some stat boosting armor stacks the effect, saving and reloading enough will make you invincible.)
Combat is terribly unbalanced. There are SEVERAL situations where my backline (the damage on the team) is simply rushed by most persons of the enemy group. In order to stop them, I use tank-warriors, whom are immediately ignored and practically walked through. Warriors in general don't do very much damage so you HAVE to rely on your backline. But if you can't peel the enemies off, GG better reload.
Then you can form a party of max/min rangers. 4 rangers, a cleric, and a tank/rogue are unbelieveably strong because they each get an animal companion. The hardest difficulty with this group is relatively easy.
Mages and Clerics cannot cast buffs before battle. So no preperations can be used save for just "winging it." In battle tactics often involve simply having your backline hope the front line can prevent the fast moving rush monsters from touching the backline. In baldur's Gate, this wasn't nearly as bad an issue, as you could summon monsters or even buff characters before a battle, in this game u kinda just hope and pray.
Mages have been SEVERELY weakened relative to what you probably expect. Many of the spells you'd expect them to have have been split up between roles, such as chanter, and chanters can't learn mage---excuse me, wizard spells. In Baldur's Gate you'd use all your mage spells in a battle early on. But it wasn't too big an issue, you could rest all you needed, though it would risk combat. In this game, you CAN'T rest without supplies, and you can only bring 4 rests worth in normal difficulty, plus they're relatively hard to come by.
Then there's the skirmishes. They only programmed party ai to auto-attack. A very lazy way to go about things considering just about every iso game in the infinity engine allows your party to auto-battle with more developed ai.
The game's built in characters "tag along" with your party without any real reason to do so. The only character that actually seems to have a reason to tag along is the Grieving Mother and Sagani. The others are just risking their lives for you and doing chores around your keep because "it seems less boring than waiting around." The writers make little effort to conect the characters to you at a personal level in any way. They barely even seem to notice each other, and while they do banter, the banter will likely remind you of Dragon Age rather than Baldur's Gate, they say a few voiced lines, instead of arguing or having something meaningful to say, they just feel like they're making minor comments. In Planescape: Torment, the characters could all connect to the main character because they were all suffering torment and at one point or another, dealt with experiencing their nature jurassically change. And the reoccurring question: "What can change the nature of a man." Was pure icing on the cake. I could analyze that game and its merit all day.
In this game: Many of the characters aren't particularly interesting to begin with, and are shockingly low in number. BG1 had 25 companions available and 5 temporary companions. This game has 8 companions and 2 temporary. Something is amiss if the amount is a THIRD of available in game party members of a 1998 game it tries to succeed that have much less dialogue than Planescape: Torment despite much better technology not to mention recieving 4 times their asking budget. None of the in-game characters seem nearly as special or interesting.
There's a LOT of writing in this game, but quantity doesn't necesarily mean quality. There's *some* great immersive dialogue, but there's just moments where I can't help but not care. The characters' motivations are poorly constructed, the quests are immersively flawed, ex: a certain paladin: ("I have to go to this location that is currently unavailable at this point in the story, so I'll just ignore my meager existence because my plotline isn't important enough to give an explanation as to why I can't guide you to this location on the map yet.")
I recall PoE was CONSTANTLY advertised as free of publisher-based restrictions and a free creation envisioned by the developers. Yet, it plays textbook safe, as one of the most generic, word swamped, fantasy adventure games I have ever played.
An example: A man who is witnessing the memories of himself in a different life is watching himself♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman in tears. The dialogue should describe a pained expression on his face, so that I PERSONALLY am able to figure out he feels a sense of shame and regret. Instead, the writing is, "he makes a face as though he is ashamed of what he's done and that he regrets doing such a thing." I'm supposed to figure that out by watching his face, stop flipping the narrative to omnipotent God who understands the feelings of others, start telling me what IM seeing so I can make that judgement.
Don't even bother with the lore. Some creatures are just called "tall." There's no specifics given.
Oh and the FAN CREATIONS EVERYWHERE. Oh God. At first I was reading the various tombstones wondering why this was all over the place. Turns out if u paid 500-1000$ you got to add some of ur own fanfiction to the game. The npcs created from this are mostly hardcore Mary Sues. Thankfully, holding tab allows you to determine who's real and who isn't. But if you want, you can "reach out for the soul" to read about the fanfiction character that semi-cannononically made it into the game.
There's also a Kickstarter only achievement if you're a completionist.
As another reviewer said:  "For 34.99, it's a been one huge and, frankly unacceptable disappointment. It piggy backs on the reputation of much older and far superior games, without ever matching their achievements. Baldur's Gate will be remembered in another fifteen years. Barring bargain basement sales, POE will have been forgotten"
Having said that, maybe I'm being unfair? I keep wanting a game to top Baldur's Gate and Torment, but I have yet to see a fraction of what this game could and should have been.
TLDR; If you hate yourself and your money, purchase this game.

Short review: Awesome.
Longer review: Awesome and addictive.
For anyone who played and loved the old classic infinity engine games (BG, BG2, PS:T etc), this is the true spiritual successor of those games. You'll love it. If you're not that old there is probably a good chance you'll like it anyway. EDIT: If you usually only play fast-paced shooters, this will probably not be your cup of tea, but if you like tactics, reading and occationally thinking, you should like PoE.
Warning: If you plan to actually do anything else in the near future, don't buy this game.
Detailed review (EDIT):
Graphics: Adequate.
Pleasing to the eye, but nothing special. Not a main attraction in this type of game. I would have liked a transparency feature for objects that your characters might walk behind, but that is no big deal.
Sound: Pleasant. More voices for your main characters would have been nice, but again, this is no game-breaker.
Gameplay: Awesome. Take one of those nice D&D-based crpgs, chuck the d&d ruleset as far as you can and start over with something that makes sense for a crpg. I really like the ruleset of PoE, it is obvious that the developers have invested a lot of thought into it. The classes might not be "balanced" in a one-on-one way, but they complete one another well. The wizard is awesome, but if you don't have a few meat-shields you are toast. The Chanter (bard) and the Paladin are great, but need a party to shine. Anyhow... gameplay is excellent!
Story: Great. I'm only halfway into the second chapter but so far I like it, a lot. Even if the main story is somewhat linear there is some room for actual roleplaying, there are some situations where I would have preferred if there were possibilities to solve situations with diplomacy instead of fighting. The dialogues are well written and the dialogue options allow you to connect with your main character by selecting choices that make sense. The game world is relatively open, but you need to advance the main story to open up some areas.
Replayability: Well... I've restarted my chararacter 5+ times (because I couldn't decide on a class/race combination) and I'm not that bored with the beginning yet, so replayability seems rather good!

Time continues during story events so you get stuck in dialogue and meanwhile your adventurers die and drop all their loot.

Its not a clicker because there are too many menus required.
It's not an idle game because you can't automate anything.
It's not a store game because you just click 'Deliver' to sell an item; no one is ever browsing your store; there is no way to attract patrons; there are no world events influencing prices.

Bastion is a must have. Right from the get go, in true above average indie game fashion, the game sports a beautiful art style and a riveting soundtrack. But those are not the only things Bastion thrives at. Despite it's many unique gameplay and conceptual elements, it is an RPG at heart and it nails that brief perfectly.
Combat, which while at first may seem a little aimless, quickly reveals itself to be very well layered. Once the weapons start piling up, a multitude of options open up to tailor your very own play style (along with the usual passive perks, in the form of 'liquers'). Even while in combat, no matter how chaotic there's always a window where the game allows you to catch a breath and do something satisfactory and clean. This is something many games with heavy combat fail to do.
Among the side quests, each of the 11 upgradable weapons offer a specific training level dubbed 'proving grounds' where you can learn to master said weapon and make it your own. 'Vigils' are little in game challenges which can be completed for extra cash and 'dreams' can be visited both for extra cash and to hear some character backstory. All of these 'shops' are present on the main home area and the story levels and other accessible areas are tied to it via the 'The Skyway'. Not only is this an neat way of doing things, it also provides a sense of the smaller scope of the game.
Story wise, it's just okay. But again, I don't see how they could've done any better with the style of narrative they had. That said, like any good example of world building, the lore unfolds as you progress through the levels and certain items that you retrieve. You'll find yourself genuinely caring for what happened and curious for what's to come. While not exactly character driven, the game does bless us with memorable characters. Whatever goes on in the game is narrated by 'The Stranger' in a dynamic fashion. It's very fascinating and sometimes even hilarious to hear rather simple things in his godlike voice. The Kid himself is a little bit more than your usual mute protagonist. He adds in his own flavor of steadfast agression and composure to his actions. Sure, the guys only have basic animations and don't really do much outside control, but that's okay.
Bastion carves it's own special area and flourishes right there while providing a memorable experience and if not immediate, a definite replay value. Deep inside it's lush artwork, it gives us food for thought and a few morals along the way. Did I mention the epic soundtrack?
8.5/10

There are many great things about Bastion, so I'll start with them. It's difficult to order its great aspects in a list of most-least/least-most noticable ones, so I'll just start firing without order. The story could be described as relentless, daring, and retrospective. These qualities of it are so easy to go wrong with, but the game does it correctly. Often, the danger the characters are placed in is daring, and often does it feel relentless with so much action and drama, and near the end, it simply makes you feel retrospective over what you accomplished (and that is all I will say as for the story's end, without spoiling much). The soundtrack is intense, which fits the game. The enemies all come in a large variety. The way the game allows you to explore background stories and lore is not done in a way that feels shoved in your face, or in a way where you feel you will miss out on potential game-changing information (because none of the optional pieces of lore or background stories contain any of that sort of information).
As for the flaws, there aren't any noticeable ones, besides the fact that a few people may find the dramatized narration voice of one of the characters to be rather over-the-top (I didn't, but it's a possibility I realized).
Overall, while the game has many great aspects, none of them are stretched to the point where you may feel this to be a masterpiece. Instead, it is more of a memory from the past, a good one nonetheless, which is what Supergiant Games (the developer) seems always able to provide. It's a game that will sit with you as a fond memory, one that you can easily suggest to others.

Singularity. The name alone got me hooked up...
...and it sure was a ride! I really like sci-fi themes that involve time-travel and time-manipulation. As you start the game, you'll think it is some scary game as you go explore the first areas. That however fades away pretty quick, but it doesn't matter when the action is there to compensate.
The beginning is the setting stone for disaster, because you basically travel back in time through a freak coincidence, save some non-descript guy who later turns out to be the Russian Adolf Hitler, and find yourself in mess upon returning to your time period. What to do? Go find out what the heck happened, thus beginning the actual story.
You will find several weapons which then you can get from lockers that are scattered throughout the game. You shouldn't go without the assault rifle, it'll be your bread and butter for pretty much everything. Your secondary gun should be a strong one, as a backup solution for tougher enemies. You will find weapon tech, which can be used to upgrade weapons.
The TMD is your tool of everything. Repair/destroy bridges, boxes, crates and act as a HL2 gravity gun in order to solve simplistic puzzles. It can age or mutate enemies. If you want enemies to get off of your skin, use the pulse ability to knock them back. It can create a statis bubble that is effective crowd control. Also, you will find out that the main antagonist really wants that thing.
Items? There are E99 tech thingies that add to a credits system to upgrade the TMD. Stimpacks give you HP, first-aid kits heal on demand. Energy cells recharge the TMD. Other than ammo, there is not much to say about it.
If you play things right, then you won't die once.
The enemies are Russian blokes and mutants. They don't scream to rush B, but I can't understand what they're saying - because there are no subtitles. Easily dispatched. However, I find the dismemberment from simple shots kind of excessive...
The game is pretty linear. You can get disoriented, but the ChronoPing ability shows you footsteps on where to go - so you can't make wrong turns.
On your way through, you will find recordings on tapedecks, notes and scribblings on walls. Sometimes questionable, sometimes outright sad. You might wanna give them a listen / read.
At the very end of the game, you have choices. There are three endings. Either you shoot the good guy, which gives you the 'bad' ending. If you go back in time and kill your past self, you get the 'good' ending. If you kill both, you get the second 'bad' ending.
In conclusion, I really enjoyed this game. The story was reasonable for a sci-fi game and keeps you entertaining for its pricetag. Give it a try if you liked games like Time Splitters.

Singularity succeeds when respecting itself and it's own ideas, when it tries to replicate what other games did such as Call of Duty, or Bioshock, the game seems to apall in comparison, as it should, given the fact that those games have already "perfectioned" in a way their own ideas, while games such as Singularity are still experimenting with their own.
And it's wonderful that they do, because it's for that reason alone that games such as this one are still remembered fondly by plenty of people including myself.
Right of the back I should mention Singularity runs perfectly well on my gtx 970, has a couple of options, nothing to special, nothing to terrible, but sadly most of them are hidden within it's "regedit" directory, (if you can believe it) making it also have some problems with it's limited but fixable fov, either by using external programs (FlawlessWidescreen) or by making sure to edit some files.
Overall it's fine as a port, it's what i'm trying to get at.
That being said, the game has some terrible storyline, but that I personally appreciate if anything because the game makes an effort into trying to tell somewhat of an original idea, with the game taking place bouncing back and foward between to periods of time and really experimenting with the whole concept, and/or idea, of time manipulation, as a narrative aspect, or as a gameplay mechanic, it doesn't matter, when the game tackles it, it succeeds in doing so, at the very least for me.
The story characters and scenarios however always range between being unique and excellent, while in other cases they just simply fall into the whole spectrum of cliches and replicas of the games that i've mentioned minutes ago.
When the games attempts to do that, through it's narrative, set-pieces, or gameplay elements, the game fails to succeed in delivering a "fun" or "enjoyable" experience, while when it sticks with it's own ideas, the game manages to captivate me, and engage me in an excellent way.
Having said that, the gameplay is excellent either way, before you get the ability to manipulate time, and of course, after you get, said ability.
Everything changes...
Everything.
The game's use of time manipulation allows you to do several different small changes to objects around you, some that will allow you to progress, others that you'll be able to use as weapons, while other times they'll simply reveal hidden messages written in decaying walls, or alternatively allow you to move some objects for the fun of it.
Everything feels incredibly tight and smooth, whether it is the combat system of time manipulation, (slowing your enemies down, or aging them until they're nothing but bones), or the general gunplay, (shooting hundreds of bullets with an assault rifle, or firing from a shotgun shells that send your enemies flying into the air) everything seems to make the game feel amazing, and satisfying to play.
But there are problems.
You can upgrade the device that allows you to manipulate time, you can, as a matter of fact, upgrade a lot of stuff, your health, your energy (which allows you to use the device), your weapons, or even something as discovering different blueprints scattered around the game which you can use to upgrade your own device with their own unique features.
That's wonderful.
But why is there a two weapon limit in this game?
See... This is what I mean by borrowing nonsensically mechanics from other games for the sake of borrowing them in a hail mary attempt to try and think that just because a certain game is popular, maybe, if you choose to replicate it, yours will become popular as well.
How does that sound for a well thought out logic for anything?
And there are hundreds, upon thousands of different games doing it up to this day, It doesn't make any sense!
Don't believe me, look at every game needing to have some aspect of "survival gameplay" after the whole fascination with Minecraft and DayZ.
Why hinder an otherwise incredible game with this sort of thing?
Some might say i'm making a very big deal about this, but hear me out.
The game doesn't offer more than a couple of instances to change your two currently equipped weapons, actually for the first couple of hours you will just straight out have to leave some weapons behind completely, for a while at least, then you find this sort of "upgrade weapon centers" they're pillars that stand in specific places in-game, you can interact with them to upgrade your weapons, buy ammo, or... You guessed it!
Change the two weapons you currently have equipped.
Great...
But why is this here? It was personally a massive let down and a surprising thing for me when I discovered this, it's minor, but it's an issue, and an issue that shouldn't even be here in the first place, the fact that it's here just in an attempt to borrow a mechanic from another game it's unbereable to me, the reason as to why that two weapon limit works in other games such as Call of Duty, or Halo, it's because weapons are always flowing in those games, each enemy that you kill, you can take their weapon, and so on, and so forth.
Why is this here if you can't do that here?
Because of "realism"?
Considering that the game deals with time manipulation, mutants, and an alternate timeline in which there's a different ruler for the soviet union, I think is safe to say the game can take certain liberties with that.
Either way, overall it's nice, and really that last bit of negative points, (altho it only seems like one and a minor at that) really don't do much to hinder an otherwise fun experience with a unique and original concept.
Without spoiling to much the game is light-hearted fun, it's extremely violent of course, with limbs flying away from mutants, and massive gaping bullet wounds showing in your mutilated enemies, but even then the game always toys with all of this, it's just a crazy fun little game with a silly narrative, but with enough heart to making it something memorable, and still recommendable to play to this day, the fact that you can get this game now, and get it on Steam, makes all of this the more better.
Get it now, or wait for a sale, it's your choice, other than that.

I don't really know what to say other than, "meh".
This software isn't really that great, but it's a step forward in terms of getting this kind of feature into the consumer market, so I'm okay with supporting it. I purchased it specifically because of the Live2D module, but that's also been a bit disappointing.
The face tracking is fine, but the rigging and parameterization aren't really up to snuff, so the subtler gestures of the human face are really under-expressed, and the more overt ones are sometimes overexpressed. There's also little accounting for the differences in expressiveness between the various human facial structures and ranges of human physical expression. Some people show teeth when they smile, some don't. Some people's lip edges actually point downward when they frown, some don't. Some people open their mouths wide when they speak, some people make subtler lip motions. I can see the tracker keeping up with all of this, but the model does not seem to account for it correctly. Tuning is long and tedious and only helps a little bit. Most furstrating, though, is the
latency in the model's expression.
I don't think Holotech has been lazy here. I think the tech is just still in its infancy. Live2D was particularly disappointing because the range of expressiveness for the models tends to be so very low to begin with.
Still, I consider this to be prototypical tech; breaking ground in a new consumer segment. I'm hoping that FaceRig gets some competition and that all of the involved tech (especially Live2D) makes large strides forward.

MyWorld is a new take on a classic, that combines many great aspects from many great games in one, allowing for total player creation and an absolutely unlimited amount of worlds to explore and conquer. If you had ever played games like RpgMaker or Dark Souls, or just like creative games, then this is definitely for you. Every world that you venture into, is created by another player. Everyone who owns the game has access to develop their own map and quests, and literally make their own RPG, which other players can then play through by downloading the map from steam workshop. After about an hour and a half of game play and reading thirty-or-so reviews (about half positive and half negative) I still can't recommend this game. Keep in mind this is not a comprehensive review, simply my observations. If you disagree, thats's fine. If you feel the overwhelming urge to be offensive, get bent. Here's a summary of my pros and cons list.
Pros:
-Lots of character customisation.
-Good game premise (story line).
-Interesting story set up (how they started the story line).
-Combat is responsive.
Cons:
-Community has a lot (and I mean tons) of caustic people. And I mean tons. Lots of tons. Metric and SAE. In great, huge, furry, green, clumpy tons. What this means is if you have an issue and you don't like an aspect of the game for it, there will definitely be a hostile response. Buy the game, like it and shut up.
-Any negative comments, as simple as a dislike of any game aspect, posted on the forum will get you harrased at the minimum and possibly censored to include removal of your post. It happened to me when, due to the rabid dog-like responses I read to what I considered fair and ballanced negative reviews, I posted a disapproval of those practices on the forums and questioned whether or not it may be the devs or their friends attacking the reviewer. "finalBoss" (spelling?) stated I had to prove it was or I was "ranting like a mad man" or something to that effect. I disagreed, saying it was an opinion and needed no proof. My post was removed.
-The combat, while responsive, lacks definition, meaning, it's simply button-mashing, not directed at anywhere specific.
-Damage modeling is nowhere to be seen. Cutting anywhere on a monster doesn't show up beyond blood splashes and scripted removal of the part. It doesn't happen when you do it, or where you do it.
-Antagonists seem to be overwhelmingly overpowered, but unimaginative when it comes to combat, in what seems to be simply for the sake of dragging it out. No new attack themes, just a variation of the same, simplistic event over and over. I refer to my fight with a Chimera. It went something like this:
Climb its front leg, mash button quickly to cut off its snake tail.
Climb its front leg, mash button quickly to kill its goat head.
Climb its front leg, mash button quickly to kill the beast.
If, as a few people stated, the combat is repetitive, this would be a tiresom chore instead of an exciting event after a small portion of this game, much less the entirety of this game. Never once during the combat did I ever feel my character was in any sort of peril, thus there was no adventure in the event, breaking any sort immersion and I can see, if this is a reoccuring theme, it will become irritating, instead of exciting throughout the game. There really isn't anything to make this type of combat entertaining.
-The graphics are extremely dated. On cutscenes, there is pretty obvious pixelation of textures. Think circa, early nineties for PC's.
-Inventory management is not as streamlined as it should, much less could be, and is slightly clunky.
Neutral observations:
-Voice acting is adequate. Neither extremely good, nor very poor.
-UI is ok. Neither simple and intuitive nor offensively vague.
-Music is neither memorable nor invasive, simply there.
To summarise my review:
-Lots (and I mean lots) of bad eggs on the foums.
-Nothing sets this apart from run-of-the-mill.
-There just aren't enough good things to warrant paying for this.
-If you want better, games like Neverwinter Nights 2 or Diablo 2 did a much better job for cheaper prices, or if you want to pay more, Diablo 3 or Skyrim. Whether you like these or prefer others, there is definitely better out there than this game.
-Way overpriced for what you get. Keep in mind this is a port from a console game several years ago. There are those out there who did the same thing with better results.
-Censorship burns me and is counter to what I put my life on the line to protect, The U.S. Constitution. If I had used profanity I could understand but I simply disagreed with forum members harassing reviewers.

Mass Effect is a story-rich FPS where you play as Shepard, in a time where the universe is starting to realise the potential of the human species in taking up bigger responsibilities alongside others. Initially under Captain Anderson's command, you are tasked to investigate a distress signal on a planet and during which, you discover that a trusted ally is setting something shady into motion. Throughout the game. you hunt him down and discover the secrets that would have implications on everyone in the known universe.
The game focuses strongly on the story, during which you would have to make a number of decisions that although may not change the story itself, they translate to your character stats, and also the (remaining) crew that you fight with. (And also your sex life lmao.) The combat system is pretty good in that you fight in a section of 3, where your crew could provide interesting powers or just be meat shields as you recharge your own powerups. However, some hostiles such as snipers or rocket turrets could possibly one-shot Shepard and you would have to restart from where the game last saved. Hence, I do recommend that you consistently manual save or you might have to replay a large part of the mission.
I find the game very well-rounded and enjoyable, back by an interesting story. However, one major set back to the action for me would be the extremely long elevator rides. Seems silly but you would have to play it to understand the agony :)

Short and sweet review here.
A nod to the classics of Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, the gameplay is somewhat solid, environments detailed and classes varied and unique.  Combat has that familiar feel to it while being unique in its own way by adding derived stats like accuracy and deflection to make combat more about landing hits and damage reduction rather than simple hit or miss AC based combat.  Classes have x per encounter and x per rest abilities similar to 4th edition Dungeon and Dragons.
There are many pros to this game but some -big- cons in my opinion.
PROS
-Good graphics for the kind of game it is
-Nice variety in races and classes to chose from
-Interesting story so far
-some memorable characters
-Combat system that while odd in places, plays well and stands on its own two feet without depending on the BG legacy.
-Game stability (no crash or significant bugs so far.)
CONS
- Endurance/health system is absolutely abysmal and in my opinion the worst thing about this game.  It is frustrating and counter intuitive and a real wtf if you come from a Infinity Engine background of games.
- Wizards seem somewhat useless.  Too often I want enemy mages cripple my party while my own struggles to contribute with their spells.
Overall I recommend this game but do not go into it expecting the Infinity Engine of 2015.  Not as good as Baldur's Gate or Planescape torment, but definitely good enough to be its own thing worth playing.

Be warned, if you do not have some sort of gamepad or controller, do not bother with this game. Dark souls is terribly optimised for keyboard+mouse. Although there are some mods available online that can help fix this problem. (Also you may want to consider getting the 60fps mod) But it is still generally much better to use a controller.
If you do own some sort of controller, let me tell you why you should play this game.
Dark Souls is a series infamous for being unforgivably difficult and challenging. Especially for new players. and believe me, it certainly is difficult, but it's difficulty holds a certain beauty to it.
Dark souls is unique in today's age of games, games that hold your hand and help you along your journey step by step, telling you where to go and what to do. Dark souls does the complete opposite of this. In fact, Dark souls pretty much kicks you in the face and laughs as you scramble helplessly to try and get up, only to get kicked in the face again.
On my first play of the game, I got stuck in an extremely tough area and quit, only to be told a few months later by a friend that I had actually stumbled into an area that is supposed to be visited much further through the game. So I came back to Dark Souls and started again, but this time I was determined to finish it and go the right way. And boy did I realise what I had been missing out on when I finished it.
But the difficulty of Dark Souls is what to me, makes this game so damn awesome and unique. Dark Souls taught me to appreciate difficulty in games, to always seek a challenge and to find fun it. Ever since the day I finished Dark souls for the first time I have always set the difficulty in new games to hard or above as I find playing through a challenging game to be much more enjoyable than breezing through an easy one where there is no sense of accomplishment.
And if the difficulty of the game is something that is stopping you from buying it, don't let that be a reason to stop you. It's well worth playing because Dark souls teaches you how to overcome difficulty, with persistence. You will die, over and over and over. But when you finally beat that boss that you have been stuck on for hours, well, nothing can rival the sense of accomplishment a satisfaction that fills you with.
Dark souls is not only a difficult game, but is also riddled with cryptic story about this strange world you are placed in. The lore and story is there for people who care about it to uncover, but not thrown in your face so people who just want to play the game don't have to worry about it.
I haven't even touched on how much I adore the mechanics of this game as opposed to the mechanics of a game such as Skyrim. Dark Souls has an absolutely insane skillcap due to these mechanics. If you are good enough, you can beat any boss in the game without taking damage or without using a weapon, or wearing no armour or pretty much anything you want. Dark Souls has been pushed to the absolute limit by many talented members of the community who play the game in many unique and challenging ways. You can watch some of these guys on twitch to see just how much depth there is to this game.
I highly recommend Dark Souls and it's one of my favourite games of all time. And If you play Dark Souls it might just change your perspective on games as a whole and teach you to appreciate a challenge. I know it sure did for me.

Sometimes you kick a ball around. You kick, kick, then kick the ball some more. And it becomes a bit of a slog. Wouldn't it be nice to break the monotony of kicking a ball by say, kicking balls?
In Soccer Rage you win a match by either scoring more goals than your opponent, or by kicking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their team until they have less than seven players left. It's a sports game AND a fighting game!
It looks, and to some extent plays like a mix between FIFA and Mortal Kombat, though I should say it doesn't have the depth of either of those games. It's also still a work in progress with some bugs, small annoyances and features yet to be implemented.
But even as it is, the game's fun, cheap and it definitely tries something new. Worth picking up to mess around with if you want something to play in short, quick bursts.

Amazing experience and a totally overlooked gem. So much fun, inventive, deliciously sadistic weapons. Totally linear, but a good story, great set pieces. Well-designed levels never get too frustrating, it's never samey because the art direction keeps the visuals fresh. Boss fights are epic. Honestly, I enjoyed it more than Bioshock. I don't think it's as well-developed as a world and characters, but I'm talking about pure entertainment value. Graphics aside, it doesn't feel particularly aged. Most current FPS games are no better, just a little prettier.
Only annoying thing is, when using a gamepad, the buttons aren't shown in on-screen prompts, only keyboard keys. An oversight which will never be remedied now, but it hardly ruins the game.

overall pretty nice gameplay which is on the one hand quite simple (more or less 3 attacks with the 2 weapons equipped) but on the other hand rewards timing, planning and skill.
You have a couple of different weapons which all behave quite diversly and complement one another well. For each weapon there's a training stage where you can achieve bronze, silver and gold ranks while getting to gold actually forces you to really understand the weapon's mechanic which is insofar relevant as it prevents you from button mashing through the levels without a sense or deeper understanding of the game: once you mastered for example the shield's training stage you a) learnt a lot about proper timing b) soaked in the enemy's behaviour and c) are now setup for the more ranged oriented enemy's in those plant-heavy levels which otherwise could become rather annoying :)
So the game is accessible, rewarding and fun. can recommend it!

Bastion is one of the first games I ever played. It made me realize that games could be a piece of art, and that the storytelling and emotional potential of a game is massive given the right presentation.
So many things to applaud about Bastion: its music, art, and narration. The gameplay is good, but it is the story where Bastion really shines through. Although games with an emphasis on story usually has less incentive for a second playthough, Bastion cleverly establishes through its storyline a reason to do a second run (New Game Plus), provided that the player chooses Restoration and not Evacuation on the first. It is a touch of ingenuity on the creators' part, and it makes the second playthrough feel much more satisfying instead of feeling repetitive.
Recommended if you like witty dialogue and tough decisions.

First off, there are a lot of ups and downs for this game.  Depending on why you want the game makes all the difference.
I purchased a 4-pack because I intended to play with my friends and my friends only.  We had tons of fun! We skipped the tutorial and still learned how to play very quickly.  There are over 200 weapons and learning to use them is half the fun.
As you level up, you earn more weapons and can spend more skill points to upgrade your tank.  I understand if you play against other people and they happen to be significantly higher level than you, then you are at a decent disadvantage which can be frustrating.  This can also be a problem is you've been playing for awhile and have tons of items and your friends just get it and are low level, lacking certain items.
There is a single player mode, but I believe the games intent was to play with others and if that's what you're looking to do (especially with friends) I would definitely recommend it.  8/10
If you would like to see some gameplay, you can check my video below of my first experience with it.  I had lots of laughs as my friends and I figure out what the hell we were doing.

Surprisingly good for the small price. Main quest line took me roughly 25 hours and I still have plenty to unlock from the looks of it. The core gameplay is fairly simplistic - grind resources, use resources to upgrade/equip your adventures, grind more/better areas, craft better items, sell, profit, repeat. The early game is VERY grindy. Skills get learned by equipping certain items and the combination of certain skills can lead to powerful combos so there is also a pretty cool strategic aspect to the game. Overall the game exceeded my expectations even though there are a lot of areas that could be improved still.
Don't expect this to be a 2D Recettear as there is no haggling or shoppers in the game, it's an incremental grinder with RPG elements. There are Quests and a fairly funny story line though. Overall, thumbs up for this.

Like many of BioWare's well-done stories, this space-epic takes you across not a galaxy far, far away, but the galaxy we live in right now- wiping out a potential threat to it. Mass Effect has wonderful characters, fluid gameplay, amazing music, and beautiful level design (my favorite being the Citadel. It's just gorgeous to look at). The only downsides to the game are the occaisional lags in gameplay (like you feel like you've been shooting the same enemies over and over again), and the RPG elements stick out like a sore thumb, as you spend ten minutes getting everything situated after getting new loot from a shoot-out. But still an awesome game to the end.

It's hard for me to quantify in words what I liked about Mass Effect. Both back when it first released and upon retrospect.
Mass Effect was a huge turning point with video games and its influence is still readily seen to this day. It marked the shift toward cinematic based games becoming the norm and allowing you to interact with the events. It influenced dialogue driven protagonists with their own dialogue trees and progression systems. And it modernized concepts Bioware previously did in Baldur's Gate like party romances. Much of this was done before in games like Kotor or Metal Gear Solid, but Mass Effect tied everything up into a neat well polished package.
This was a game that blew me away when I first played it. It was truly the first 7th gen game that indicated to me where video games would eventually go. It looked amazing and I fell in love with the gameplay and all of the characters. It really was a game Bioware made in their prime.
Naturally playing it today will make you notice the game hasn't aged all that well. Bioware was still transitioning from mostly making turn based games like Kotor so they didn't quite perfect the gameplay til the sequel. I still highly recommend playing Mass Effect 1. It is easily one of the last great games Bioware made.

No one likes to display their closet nerd stuff out in public.
There are only about 4 types of game related shirts I come across that people seem okay with wearing out into public without getting massive wedgies from everyone.
Yes, the N7 symbol that comes from Mass Effect.  People walk around wearing this in real life with beaming pride.  The amount of respect for the symbolic designation of Commander Sheppard's training in interplanetary warfare (The N7 ranking) is huge amongst fans.  The distribution of Commander Sheppard's Jersey (N7) may very well rival the amount of wear and public exposure as some semi-popular professional athelete jerseys.
Mass Effect is here to stay...indefinitely.  With this first game a giant amount of gamers became life long fans.  It's amazing to see the sheer diversity of people who have become so attached to the universe and the characters.  People cosplay the characters and go to conventions even though the trilogy for Mass Effect has reached its conclusion long ago.  (No worries, there are definitely more Mass Effect games to come).
Along with Dragon Age, Baldur's Gate and Knights of the Old Republic, this would be another example of Bioware's dedication to crafting intense stories and deep characters that people can really dive deep into.
Mass Effect is a Space RPG focused on story and character development.  The conversation wheel is used frequently to allow the character to engage in discussions with other NPCs and teammates they encounter during gameplay.
In this game you play as the commander of an elite team consisting of the galaxy's most skilled interstellar fighters in a mission to save the galaxy.  It's essentially a
where you can issue commands to your teammates to strategically position them and to use special abilities on enemies.
You can fight with what is essentially Star Wars-esque Force Powers
Along with all manner of space guns: Rifles, Sniper Rifles, Pistols, Shotguns, automatics and so on.
If you enjoy Sci Fi and RPGs, this game is a no brainer.  You've probably played it already.  If you haven't...now's the time...

I genuinely love this game. It's as good, if not better, than the Baldur's Gate series (my favourite game series). I am amazed at how well they pulled it off. It has exceeded all of my expectations, and I was expecting a lot. It's the game I've waited 15 years for, and now that it's finally here I know that it wasn't just nostalgia - this is the way games are meant to be made. I'll be playing this game for many, many years.
If you liked Infinity Engine games, get this game. If you've never tried an Infinity Engine style game, but you like RPGs, get this game. If you hate RPGs... try this game! It might be the one to change your mind. It is truly a masterpiece and I really hope that it regenerates this genre, and proves there is a market for it.

This is one of those few gems in the huge pile of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ corridor shooters known as fps games during the call of duty era. I think this game was released just before single player campaigns of shooters became streamlined and boring. I have played Fear, the Half Life games, borderlands, some of the Call of Duty games. This game is somehow in between all of them.
Don't get me wrong, this campaign isn't free roaming or anything like that. You're bound to the areas the game wants you to go and you can choose not to and explore a bit before heading back to where the game wanted you to go. You are rewarded for exploring with currency and upgrades so there's no reason not to.
If I had to rate the gunplay in this game, I'll give it 3.5/5. But if I included the other mechanics, the gameplay would be 4.5/5. Now why is that? A bit into the game you get this device, the TMD. This thing is great, it helps you solve puzzles and aids you into combat with it's time altering abilities. There's no regenerating health which is a plus, and there are a couple of unique weapons to choose from. Some of them like the starting revolver feels like crap, but others like the time slowing sniper is amazing.
The story is genuinely interesting, and it keeps you hooked for the most part. But the locations you go to can drive you crazy, some of the places look so dull that you just want to get it over with. The gunplay is mixed for me, sometimes it feels great to fight unique enemies, but other times it doesn't feel good shooting them. There's no amazing feedback like Fear or other great shooters when you kill certain enemies, that's my only gripe with the gunplay.
In conclusion, great game with average locations and a good story. It has enjoyable gunplay but it certainly could be better.

The game may be old, but it is still a fun experience. There isn't anything impressive about the FPS aspects of the game. The unique mechanic of the game is where it shines. You take control of the TMD and have the ability to manipulate both time and age of your surroundings. The campaign is quite short. Took me six hours to complete the game. That includes exploring and reading into the games lore in the form of notes and audio recordings. Solid game and great visuals for its age. Prepare for some jump scares though, unless you got nerves of steel. I don't.

Read the full review on Gamer's Almanac:
While it would make sense to focus a review on the game’s creation aspect, there simply isn’t enough content currently there to talk about. Combined with MyWorld’s poor combat and the lack of harmony between the game’s reality and how it is advertised, It’s not something I can recommend. For now, ambition seems to have gotten the best of The Game Creators. The concept certainly has potential and it’s a game I’ll keep my eye on throughout the next seven months of its development, but unless The Game Creators can produce enough content to give the player the story and combat that are so key to the most successful RPGs, MyWorld might never make it out of the long shadow it cast for itself.

Note: This review reflects the April 28, 2017 loot update.
MyWorld has great potential within the RPG making community in my opinion. If you are looking for an RPG-making program that has a Steam Workshop – based environment, along with more in-depth 3D options than other basic RPG makers out there, then this is something you should look at. It’s not going to be Witcher 3 levels of graphics and features, but there truly is a good thing going on with MyWorld. Just keep in mind, it is Early Access and that general feeling of something missing is still prevalent throughout level testing.
Right now, after the loot update, I’m enjoying myself substantially more than before. Suddenly, I have an urge to fight as many skeletons, wraiths, and bosses as possible just to see what loot drops so as to level up my character. It really transformed the overall enjoyment of the game. Additionally, the ability to change the difficulty and new class options for the main character fill the gaps that were previously there. Since it is still so early in development, I feel that this game can become an RPG maker of substance once it’s matured, assuming it is updated regularly.
Start up the game and you’ll find a large portal in the middle of an open field, with more portals arranged in a circular manner. This is a 3D menu that is physically manifest within the game: a pretty neat concept overall, though sometimes I found myself wanting a regular menu. It’s called the Hubworld, and is the main area you use to access both the RPG worlds you create and other worlds created by the Steam community.
There are some pre-built worlds you can access through the central portal to get an idea of what you can accomplish using this software. That’s exactly where I headed, though I suggest watching the combat tutorial first, as I had a bit of trouble once several bad guys started showing up. The tutorials are on the left at a giant TV with red candy-colored buttons. It’s actually quite well arranged. You can also change out your character with some decent-looking hero choices, and the abilities of these heroes vary slightly across the selection.
There is currently no controller support in the game. I used my Steam Controller and rebound some of the keys from the options menu — I was very glad to have that key-bind option, to be honest. One critique is that the shift and tab buttons are used in the keyboard control setup and I had to reassign those to new keys because I kept accidentally activating Shift-Tab on my steam controller when fighting. Not exactly the best thing when I am stuck between a wraith and a skeleton and I suddenly have my Steam overlay pop up. I also don’t have the ability to jump, which is a little aggravating when I fall down and get trapped within some geometry.
My first pre-built world was the Blight; my guess is that this is a nod to Dark Souls. Anyway, exiting the portal, I arrived at a quaint farm with green slopes, a chicken pen, and a small house. There is a fetch quest to finish here by collecting eggs. This is actually a prime example of how fetch quests work within the game. It’s easy enough: run into the items and they are automatically given to you. After that, I had to kill a skeleton soldier. Again, this an effort at an introduction to game mechanics more than anything else. However, it’s worthwhile checking the controls for special power ups to avoid quick deaths.
The skeletons with clubs are two-hit kills, so be very careful when dealing with them until your armor levels up. My advice is to use the lock-on attack when confronted by just one skeleton and keep health flasks ready. If you die, you respawn at a campfire with full health and a temporary shield. The skeletons I killed stayed dead even if I respawned, which I think is great for those that prefer not to repeatedly kill the same baddies in order to proceed to the next checkpoint. If overwhelmed, remember to use special attacks, as that may be your only method of winning against multiple enemies.
This is the nitty-gritty of the ‘game’: creating a new world from a fresh canvas. The builder provides a medium-sized assortment of buildings, mountains, enemies, NPCs, and the like. Early on, you are introduced to a very neat feature: you can link these little worlds you make together in sections or join in with someone else’s world to play co-op. That alone stood out to me because here I can link worlds together to form a cohesive set of RPG chapters if I wanted to.
With the new update, heroes now have some moderate class definitions between each other: a new and frankly much-needed change. I generally preferred to play as a tank, and managed to get an armor loot drop right away that helped with this. There are now several levels of difficulty, so I can play as hard as I like or at a casual pace. The game really shows some marked improvement with that, allowing the end user to be as hardcore or easy going as possible with combat. It would be great if there were some attributes to set here so I could make a custom difference in abilities from one hero character to the next. I’d also love to see some options when picking outfits or skin tones. While the main characters you choose are animated, the NPC’s are almost like statues and that keeps them feeling quite basic. If there was an animated rest-state for NPCs it would add a lot to the atmosphere of the villages and quests. Hopefully, there will be an upcoming patch down the road that addresses some of these issues.
It’s a daunting task to tackle an RPG maker such as this. From what I can see, there is some rather personal interaction within the community among the players, as well as with the developer. That type of feedback is essential if MyWorld is to succeed. The tutorials are very helpful and give you some direction in terms of what kind of RPG you may be able to make. I do see a lack of system compatibility with Linux or Mac, but perhaps that will be worked out in the future.
Most importantly, I see an RPG maker that has the possibility to shine on Steam. All the basic assets are there; the game only needs time and updates to move beyond its initial Early Access criticisms. With online gameplay including up to four player co-op and eight player-vs-player options, it even allows for battles and some serious swordplay. The ability to chain worlds together with portals, and an appealing game world to build with, strikes me as a good starting point. After the April 28th loot update — a major content addition — you get quite a lot to play with for the $14.99 price tag. While I can’t wholeheartedly say go buy this game right now, I can definitely say it’s worth trying if you enjoy RPG makers, due to the prospective future it has. If you want to be part of a gaming community and help shape an Early Access game, it’s a good choice.

Note: I had just beaten the game, so it is still fresh in my mind.
You play as a character named Captain Nathaniel Renko. A U.S. Soldier that had a mission on the island Katorga-12. A strange island housing an even stranger element, E99. Crazy time manipulation technologies involved, but definitely an interesting way of going about them. Throughout the game you fight a mix of soldiers, and strange infested creatures. Boss fights are at a minimal but they are there and not very difficult.
Personally, the gameplay is a top-notch part of this game. It was fun, fast-paced, and definitely entertaining! They had two big boss fights, and a few more mini-boss fights / high-risk enemies. The game is definitely not an incredible horror game, either, but it is very scary at some points of the game for people who aren't very good with horror (me). The biggest downfall is ammo, and scarcity with weapon lockers. To be honest, I found weapon lockers when I didn't need them, but they were no where to be seen when I DID need them. It made some parts of the game difficult, but other parts of the game not so much.
I loved the story! Loved it, loved it, LOVED IT. It was interesting, took on time manipulation
well. Even had an insane plot twist. I'd have to say the biggest downfall of the story is the ending. I wish that depending on who you chose to kill (barisov/demichev), you could leave the other and continue on with a little more of the game. Sadly you have to kill them both.
Overall, the game was great. I'd give it an 8.5/10 because of the small issues that did make the game a tad bit more annoying than it really had to be. But other than that I'd definitely recommend this game to people who are into incredible stories, and time manipulation.

Singularity has some great thoughts to it but ultimately the circa-2007 graphics & lack of multiplayer kind of kill the fun for me. The graphics are reminicent of the classic FPS called Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, which i've racked up several hundred hours on, but, Singularity is essentially Single-player only at this point in time (multiplayer is dead). Much like Quake4, the graphics are actually too chintzy to forgive & look past & the gameplay doesn't make up for it enough to be worthwhile to slog through. Doom3, even though it is of the same era, has an immediately engrossing 'scary horror thriller' type storyline going on that really takes you into the action. Doom4, of course, is a new classic, but that is unfair to mention since that game came out in 2016 so it has all the razzle-dazzle special effects that are possible in this day & age.
The story is just too lacking in feminine influences to me.. are the guys homos or something? where are the broads... Anyways, what really put the nail in the coffin for this particular "scary FPS thriller" is the recent purchase of the remastered Metro 2033: Redux, which basically solved the things I thought were annoying about the first game of that series & it is a fun game again. In that game, there are both male and female characters who are active participants in the gameplay, & that makes it WAY more fun. No offense, but no chicks after a while just seems like a sausage-fest. just sayin'! The main protagonist is a guy & this isn't Tomb Raider or anything but it is a little more even-handed & there are couples flirting with each other & people trying to settle down & all that. Oh, and the storyline is excellent & you really get a feel for the events going on. It really takes you into what seems to be post-apocalyptic Russia of the year (you guessed it) 2033 in the future.
Rating: 5/10 there are better sci-fi / scary FPS's out there to play instead. OK for it's time, but pretty bad graphically by modern FPS standards. Oh well. The Chipotle burrito & NOS soda I had with the game was good! That's gotta count for something. It was more fun to travel by ZX6r to the fast food restaurant & back to get some food while waiting for the game to load than the actual game.

I was actually very excited to try this game, i loved tinkering with little big planet and diablo 3 on the ps4 is one of my most played games, I went into this with high hopes, great expectations, and sadly they were dashed.
Let me state now though that this is as of 25/04/2017 an early access game, there is time and hope for the game to improve (before you dismiss that comment, Space engineers started early access as nothing more than a tech demo and evolved into a massive and awesome game, and it is not alone….and yes i am aware that for every game like that there are also ones abandoned, this feels like it is more likely to go the space engineers route)
What is available at the minute is not particularly good (i hate being negative, i really do) when compared to the games in the slogan “where Dark Souls, Zelda & Diablo meet Little Big Planet”,
I have not played Dark souls or zelda but can say this is nothing like Diablo or Little Big Planet,
You have 4 special attacks, your normal attack and roll, as far as i could see you could not change your attacks, and all the character class models i choose had the same 4, watching the tutorial videos ingame (neat touch there!) i saw the level 50 guy with the same 4 skills and just a larger health bar. So compare that to Diablo and you can see it is immediately lacking in the kill area….ok what about the loot? Diablo is a loot em up, forever getting new cool loot!...this however has no loot, it does not even have an inventory system (NOTE in the key binding page is an inventory button, while it does not work yet it does however tell me one is coming...see my space engineers comparison above.)
So what about the rpg creator bit? I found the editor very good, it is simplistic in its approach and i was very quickly making a little scene, but is hampered by the lack of gameplay mechanics,
* and the quests you can make consist of one of two options “kill” or “collect” (with luck the developers will add “go here”, “activate”,”protect”,etc etc as time passes to allow for more robust quests.
*I was wrong on this, you can indeed add waypoints

The controls are pretty standard, your wasd affair. However there was no support for gamepad, this can be overlooked however as they have bigger issues to focus on.

It has a quirky graphic style that works really real for the game, i really did like it and the fact that the enemies and you are destructible (well when you or they die bits can fly off) it ran really well too, The graphic style may not be everyone's cup of tea but i have a particular passion for voxel based games, which although this is not fully one it does remind me of that style.

When I first started up the game, seeing the poorly translated dialogue scrolling up my screen gave me that sense of dread one gets when they spent their money on a bad product, and you're not sure you can get it back. The tutorial was peculiar; it scrolled too fast and I had no idea what it was trying to tell me half the time.
But I didn't give this game a thumbs up because I'm a masochist.
The dialogue is genuinely funny, and by the small movements and attention to personality in not only the main characters but the staff as well shows a lot of love went into this game. There's a lot of variety put into everything, from zones to fight in to upgrades to characters; and in an industry where devs tend to just re-color existing sprites, this attention to detail is quite refreshing.
And then there's the all-important game play. This is definitely a time-management game, and you have to be ready to keep your eyes on just about everything; you can't jut set and forget the staff you send out, or they'll die; but you have to pay attention to the quality of items the rest of the staff churn out as well.
And then there's the goal system. I expected all quests to be achieveable from the get-go, easily accomplished to move on to the next one. This is hardly the case; while some are instant satisfaction, there are many you have to genuinely work towards to accomplish, giving the player long term goals and lengthening gameplay.
When I finally came out of my weapon-making stupor, three hours had passed without my notice and my hand was screaming from the carpal tunnel I hadn't noticed creeping up the wrist. I enjoyed playing immensely, and I look forward to playing until I pay back that pesky 5 million.

Even since this software was first revealed to the public as a crowdfunding project, I've seen it to be this massive pocket of potential just waiting to happen. I tried it myself and found it rather disappointing (for reasons detailed below), but I still have not changed my mind about the fact that it has a lot of potential. It is a shame because I actually wanted to purchase the Pro license so I could broadcast with FaceRig.
- Most facial features (eyebrows, chin, forehead, etc.) on most avatars tend to jitter like crazy, rapidly and haphazardly fluttering even with my face up-close and perfectly still. I have a good camera, and I did try to play around with the "Smoothing" options that were designed to get rid of this facial capture anomaly, but to no avail. This may sound like a minor issue, but it really hinders performance when I encounter it. I looked in the website's forums for this issue and found only one other user who had it, and his query is yet to be answered.
- Some characters severely lack certain expressions. For example, the "wisdom" guy seems to be unable turn (not tilt) his head sideways, except through manual controls.
- Sort of related to the above issue: It is very difficult to have a character shake its head "yes" or "no" without anomalies. For example, the ghost in the Halloween DLC is almost incapable of doing a coherent head shake. He is also unable to nod "yes" without his eyebrows erroneously registering a series of scowls and raised brows. This was especially discouraging because I liked this character most.
- I noticed some characters completely lacked customization options, such as the aforementioned ghost.
It seems to be all these issues may eventually be solved while this software continues to be developed and improved. However, in the state in which it is now, I find it almost unusable at worst, experimental at best. My refund request is pending.
If you really like what this software offers and don't care about the technical issues listed above, then I see no reason why you should hold back. However, I personally recommend waiting until it is at least in a better state, especially if you plan on going professional with it.
