Not bad, just bland.
EDIT
People seem to like lists, so here's a list:
The Good:
- A CRPG
- Writing presentation (few mistakes, decent tone, little cheese, though avoid graveyards at all cost)
- Decent sound (Good voice acting, music seems fine, just okay)
- Quality of life additions (Speed up time, infinite stash)
The Bad:
- Writing is 90% Exposition, 10% story and character development
- Companions are bland, mostly silent with little banter
- No romance, no alignment (do whatever you want with no consequences)
- Lore npcs are basically walking tomes that you can't even speak to normally
- Combat balance (Poor wizards, RNG lets even the worst strategy win eventually)
- Environments (Tiny maps with little going on in them, low res backdrops)
- Graphics are quite poor overall
- Group stealth?
- Stretch goal fodder
- Bugs, bugs, bugs
The Good:
So let's get some of the good stuff out of the way first. So far, the writing seems decent. Not the actual content mind you, but the style so far isn't gratingly bad, or overly cheesy, or filled with mistakes you so often see in other imitators.
The music seems fine so far, not obtrusive and seems to fit the mood most of the time. The voice acting is also pretty good, though never great. I only experienced one or two technical issues with sound, but mostly it's quite dependable.
The Bad:
My biggest gripe is probably quite petty by most people's standards, but I really hate the companions in this game. None of them bring even the slightest bit of levity to the proceedings, and they have very little personality to go around. This is not helped by the fact that there is no alignment system, so they care very little what you do either way, just fading into the background. No romance options either, though I don't see myself caring as much seeing how little I like any of them in the first place. To add to the problems, it seems like only about 30% of their dialogue is actually voiced.
The lore, though it seems pretty competent, is delivered in massive exposition dumps. I've read entire volumes on the history of this world, yet I have no idea what is going on in the actual story. No villain so far, and no reason why I should personally care about any of this. My companions seem equally unmotivated, most of them seemingly in the middle of some fetch quest that they really don't care so much about after all.
The Ugly:
Environments are utterly disappointing thus far as well. Theoretically, the 2D backdrops could be as detailed as they want, but why does everything look like it was designed in Blender 15 years ago? The forests are particularly ugly, the same few trees and shrubs copied over and over again. Some interiors also seem rendered to a far lower resolution, and only stop looking pixelated after you zoom out as far as possible. 3D models are low res too, which makes the occasional "hidden" wall stand out like a sore thumb.
In conclusion:
I was so desperate for a good CRPG, that I was willing to lap up any scraps they threw at me. But in attempting to resurrect a classic, it seems we have been left with little more than a walking corpse. The parts are all there, but with the passage of time, it seems stiff, and unnatural. We've seen bigger and more detailed worlds in 3D (Dragon age, Skyrim), and even isometric games have shown they can look good and still deliver deep tactical experiences (Divinity: Original Sin).
Now none of those games delivered the classic Baldur's Gate experience, and I am hopeful that there is still a good, no, great game waiting to be made. But this bullheaded belief that changing even the smallest part will somehow taint it with the bane that is the modern casual RPG, is foolish to say the least. Is this really all Baldur's Gate was to people? Throw enough text on screen, add some RNG, tons of pausing and reloading, make sure the backdrops are dated, and there you go?
Those games were, and still are, so much more to me. The stories, the places, the characters, everything just worked. These are the things that mattered, and these are the things that seem to have been most neglected in Pillars of Eternity.
Some people will enjoy this, a lot. All the more power to them. Maybe I just have my nostalgia goggles screwed on so tight I don't even know anymore, in which case sorry for the rambling.

Ok - I am reviewing MyWorld in its current state of being in Early Access.
I know a few people are saying that there isn't much to do, only one class at the moment, not enough mechanics etc, BUT it is in EA, so what do you expect?
Surely the whole point of EA is to enjoy a product during it's development/lifecycle up to being released?
Anyway, on with my review.
I can see a hell of a lot of potential with MyWorld. It is very easy to get to grips with and the tutuorials provided are excellent.
Everything can be done from your hub (where you start when loading the game), such as viewing tutorials, hosting games, joining games, Steam Workshop, creating a new world, settings and more.
The world editor is very easy to use and whilst there may not be many objects to use at this moment in time, more are on their way.
Designing quests is also very easy, although will be better as more enemies/collectables are added in game to give a wider range to use.
At this stage I prefer to think of it as having a bare bones set up which allows me to master what is available, so that as more content is added I will find it enhances what I already have/know at my disposal.
As well as designing PvE world you can design PvP - simply place PvP spawnpoints!
For the price I personally feel they are giving this away!
I would say try it and within 30 minutes you will already be playing testing your own little world!
Have fun!

A non-cover based shooter that is pretty decent.
One complaint I have is that the power ups and upgrades aren't very relevant until late-game, and running out of ammo is a serious problem (especially when your standard melee attack gets replaced with an attack which uses another set of ammo). Considering how tough the enemies are until late game, this can be frustrating.
Another complaint is that the characters are flat. The only one who has any sort of depth is the villain, so the ending is kind of a non-issue (or it was for me anyway). The entire world could have ended and I wouldn't have been upset because I wasn't invested in any "reality" over any other, honestly. And yet, the ending was still better than the ending of Tyranny, which is a huge mark up in my book.
The graphics are good, there are a few jump scares (one very effective one) and a lot of the combat is fun once you get used to how spongy everyone is. Throwing explosive barrels and such at enemies or destroying cover and taking advantage of the battlefield yielded me some fun results. The atmosphere in some bits is pretty oppressive, though I think they could have taken better advantage of that than they did.
The voice acting is pretty good, the animation is decent, and overall the game is fun to play through. You can see that I have ~5 hours of play time as of this review, and that's about how long it took me to play through it. It's a bit short, but then, it didn't need to be longer.
Overall a very solid game, if imperfect. It's 7 years old at this point, so don't hold that against it. Pick it up on sale if you have an afternoon's worth of free time.

Really good campaign FPS. The game overall reminds me of Hard Reset mixed with Half Life 2.
It's got an interesting story, not spectacular but as far as FPS goes, it ranks up there. The shooting is solid, a bit bland with some weapons, the revolver and shotgun in particular are not very good but the rest of the arsenal feels pretty good to use. The weapons are quite aesthetically pleasing as well, they have that retro mixed with futuristic look.
The best part about the game though is the powers, you get to slow down time, age and reverse age objects/people, you can turn a person into a monster and have him battle other humans for you, there's telekinesis, you feel badass basically.
The monster/level variety is good as well, it doesn't get boring and you're not stuck in the same place constantly fighting the same enemies, it keeps switching it up which keeps the game entertaining. I finished the game in one sitting and I never found myself wondering how long is left in the game and that's something that happens quite often with me.
The game does have a few drawbacks, for one it's quite short, I finished it in 5 hours only. The graphics are a little bit outdated, especially with some of the texture work but models and whatnot are mostly fine. Another thing I really didn't like was that you are only allowed to carry two weapons at a time, that means you don't really get to shoot some weapons as much unless you decide to play multiple times.
The performance was surprisingly good too, constant 120+ fps for me (keep in mind I was playing on GTX 580), no drops or anything like that, not a single bug encountered, quite impressed with that.
Definitely recommend for FPS fans.

Quick notice I played this game after patch #36 so I have no previous knowledge on the games state and problems previous to the patch.
Pros:
Good Graphics
Well placed and used foliage (especially when incorperating architecture into the foliage)
Decently smooth gunplay (Still leaves some to be desired in custimization aspects)
Great lighting and shading
No draw distance settings (you wont get shot by someone who isnt even loaded in on your screen)
Smooth vehicle controls
Smooth character control (Nothing is overcomplicated, just good old WASD with some jumping and free look)
Clean UI (Could be more appealing but is simple to understand and use)
In depth crafting system ( Especially when it comes to structures)
Great map design and amazing architecture
World is full of "Volume" (Not alot of empty space, theres always something to be admired or appreciated)
Building models (Huge variety in shapes and colors, and when they do re-use a model they'll have a different interior layout)
Cons:
Mutant AI are lacking in responsivness (Sometimes they stutter due to connection problems, and are unresponsive to being shot or interacted with in any way)
Graphical requirements (The graphics are good but I feel the requirements for them are a smidge high, nonetheless good graphics)
Some "querky" animations (Characters disform from holding objects or going up a ladder, also pulling out weapons doesnt always have an animation which in a game with hostile people in it, the devs should make sure it's easy to tell whether someone is hostile based on weapon animations/sounds)
Footsteps are extremely loud and overprojected (Very easy to hear someone come for you especially if theyre on wood floors)
Jumping (Jumping can be spammed and the jump hieght is pretty high for a man carying 60 pounds of gear, the gunplay is ruined by the gun who runs around with a pistol bunny hopping his way through your bullets)
Character customization (Theres is none as of patch #36)
Again all of my experiences are from patch #36 so I don't know how well the games previous state is and this review does not include proper judgement of future patches.
But overall it's a fun game full of depth, a must have for the ten dollar sell it's on right now :)

if you are unfamiliar with BioWare then i suggest you play through Baldur's Gate and the sequel; as well as KoTOR (Knights of The Old Republic). if you are, then you're in for perhaps the best game they have ever put out. since their beginnings with Baldur's Gate, BioWare has managed to add a level of world, character and story depth unlike any other Game Dev. This has only grown more and more true while the rest of the Game Devs have seen fit to regurgitate garbage. BioWare's Mass Effect series is perhaps the pinnacle of modern day gaming with a complex and deep world along with gameplay that merges the best aspects of traditional RPG statistic/attribute/skill/feat progression and leveling with a shooter in a seemless experience.
a personal note about RPGs is an RPG is a Role Playing Game. i think this is generally well accepted; however this acronym has come to mean statistic simulator with regurgitated content and a story on a rail. BioWare, since they started, have never succumbed to this and have added more complexity and freedom to the idea of an RPG to truly make it a Role Playing Game and not just a skill tree with some♥♥♥♥♥♥story. but don't take my word for it; play it and see what i mean.
Gameplay:
one thing BioWare has been good at is finding a solid ground of gamplay even when they pull from ADND V2.0 like in their early Forgotten Realms games (i.e. Icewind Dale); and this only improves. While traditional DnD style rpgs rotate around a top down or third person non-realtime sort of abstracted turn based Mass Effect opts for a tactical shooter that includes the RPG aspects but still expects you to handle the combat. This may seem clunky and for those who played through the end of the Trilogy it may by comparison to the truly smooth gameplay of the third game; however it's a unique experience BioWare effectively pioneered and has yet to be cloned.
I will talk about this in Depth as well but it is worth noting that Mass Effect is one of BioWare's unique games that does not pull from a pre-existing platform. note that Baldur's Gate - Icewind Dale were based on ADND V2.0 with minor tweaks; and KoTOR is based roughly on ADND V3.5. Mass Effect is unique and it does not suffer for this.
Depth:
If you played Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn you know what BioWare can do and you will, yet again, be blown away. if you haven't... well you're in for a hell of a game. but i won't say too much, other than this game will feel more real, have mroe story, and more unique characters than any other. i will also say that while BioWare has used pre-existing universes (Forgotten Realms and the Star Wars Universe) this one is new and quite frankly more complete and interesting.
Romance:
i wonder what inspired BioWare to put romance options into their games when they made Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn; but whatever the reason it adds something unique to the story telling that few others have tried and no other has succeeded at. but one thing i think we all can respect is, while BioWare certainly knows what they are doing, they look for input from their fans and actually accommodate what they can while maintaining their own unique and truly fantastic style.
Cons
- none

Like exiting from a grueling dungeon of unspeakable terror onto a windswept coast as the sun sets bringing the promise of nightfall. As the last light fades the beautiful music starts up. You equip your lantern and head out into the wilderness towards the far off light of the castle hoping not to get jumped by some goblins. It's moments like those the somber and unnerving ones that really makes me see why people love it.
Verdict: Combat is fun and super fast paced if you pick an assassin. You can climb giant monsters and stab them to death like the Arisen has just played Shadow of the Colossus for the first time. The story is not good at all really and the pawn system while neat didn't do the same for me as a whole cast of supporting party members with their own personalities would have.

I think the community puts too much of an emphisis on the difficulty of this game, It's not that hard, you just need to know what your doing.
First off, they put a lot of work into this games lore, they really know how to build the world and make it feel real. (You do need to go looking for it though, read item descriptions)
The voice acting is iffy for some characters, and absolutly increadible for even more
The combat is amazing, it teaches you to balance dodges, blocks, parries, attacks, kicks, and healing. I've gotten sick of games where you just have to walk up to an enemy and press buttons to win. Dark Souls: Prepare to Die is a game of skill, not luck.
If you have friends who play this game, don't listen to them most of the time. A friend of mine told me I'd have such a hard time fighting the "Four Kings," and I beat it on my first try. The game is about intimidation, and it does a very good job at it, just use your brain to guide your hands, not your hands and nothing more.
There are several moments in the game where it becomes outrageously unfair, but the rest of the game outweighs such parts
You will die many, many times, but a lot of deaths does not point to impossibility or unfairness
This is a very polished game, and I recomend it to you 100%

If you are a fan of CRPG's from the 90s into early 00's, then you will likely enjoy this game.  I have not had this much fun playing a CRPG since Planescape: Torment.
The game feels like a classic Infinity Engine game (Baldurs Gate, Planescape Torment, Icewind Dale), but revised with modern graphic capabilities.   Some of the best gameplay improvements are:
* Half Speed Movement
* Double Speed Movement
* Inventory Stash to remove inventory management mini-game (easy access can be disabled for the truely hardcore)
* Removal of need to monster grind for levels by eliminating XP from monsters after a certain amount of kills of that monster type.  The XP focus is now on initial kills of a monster type and Quest experience.
Here are some other gameplay change that you may or may not like. I find that they streamline the game over D&D type rulesets:
* Trap Detection / Trap disarmement / Picklocking all covered by same skill: mechanics
* Mechanics is a skill that any class can learn, so it is no longer mandatory to have a rogue in order to cover the above thief like actions.
* Some spells/skills can be used a certain number of times per combat
* mage/priests can cast a certain number of spells of each level per 'rest'; mages can only select 4 spells per level
* AoE spells have 2 ranges, an inner range that can target both friend and foe, and an outer range that only can target foes.  In addition some AoE spells are listed as foe-only and can not harm friendly characters.  Stats can increase the radius of an AoE spell.
I highly recommend this game for anyone who was a fan of the RPG classics from the 90s and early 00's.

Pillars of Eternity is a fantasy role-play game developed by an amazing group of people.
The game represents a natural evolution of the 90s Infinity Engine games such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale.
Developers succeeded to merge the old style gaming and atmosphere with a totally new graphics and features. Although the game mechanics are clearly inspired by previous titles, developers succeeded to rejuvenate and improve every single aspect of the game, without ruining the player experience. In fact, when playing PoE everything feels natural and meticulously calculated.
I was blown away by the level of immersion of this game. Pillars of Eternity succeeded to bring me back in time to my youth when I was playing BG and ID, but it went much further, every single feature perfectly fits the game, the story is great. Sincerely this is exactly what I wanted PoE to be.
This is a real spiritual successor, probably one of the best games I have seen in a long long time.
Despite the recent trend were developers are making games graphically appealing but empty in contents, unimpressive, oversimplified, and boring I am overwhelmed to see that still we have some hope to get great games!
Also I would like to thank all developers for their efforts. I followed this project since the very beginning after pledging on kickstarter. It has been a long ride but it was worth it!

Owned it on Xbox at release and can easily say that it is the best RPG/Sim zombie game I have ever played. Recommend it to any and all zombie lovers.
- - - - - - - -
Edit: Proper Review : November-29-2013
- - - - - - - -
State of Decay (SoD) by Undead Labs is a 3rd person RPG/Sim where the goal is to scavenge for supplies for yourself and your group of survivors and survive the zombie apocalypse. The gameworld is an open world with a linear storyline.
You do not play as a traditional 'Lone Hero' but as a group/community of survivors which you can switch to as long as your relationship is set to 'friend'.
There is no character customization as it is not that kind of game, but the characters in the world are randomly generated from appearances to traits/skills/abilities and past lives except for the starting and story driven characters (Marcus, Ed, Maya etc...).
The game's focus is survival and scavenging as well as base building, supply and group management. Because your fellow survivors have personalities and in the real world, personalities crash... you may find yourself breaking up arguments or fights if your survivors don't get along.
Your doctor who patches you up and keeps your group healthy and going is an alcoholic and tends to belittle everyone in your group. This tends to start arguments frequently and your Mechanic (tool expert) finally had enough one day.
Your mechanic repairs your weapons and your cars since these are limited in the world and quite valuable. It is what allows you to keep the zombie hordes back. The mechanic and the Doctor get into an argument. Who do you support and back up?
While I personally don't know how far the consequences may go if you don't resolve them or talk /calm them down, they may simply leave, leave and take a portion of supplies or maybe even kill each other. All possabilities but I never allowed it to get that bad personally, so may need to ask others for confirmations or possibilites.
Back to the game overview!
The zombies have poor eyesight but good ears, so anything loud can have big consequences. You need to decide when to sneak around and go stealthly and when it is appropriate to go guns blazing. Too much noise can attract more zombies or hordes and put you in a tight spot pretty quickly.
You can easily take out zombies in melee, especially with a leveled up character, but there is always a risk with larger numbers and especially with rookie characters. There is
with each character... don't go thinking your invincible or you may lose a favorite character.
There are a variety of melee weapons with different catagories such as: Blunt, Edged, Heavy/two handers. Each with their own perks or properties such as decapitate/slice limbs, knockback or insta-kill.
There are also special Insta-kill moved your character can learn (depending on traits) as he levels up. There is guns, but they have a risk and ammo is very valuable. The latest Loot update/patch improved the randomness and receiving the same items for long periods of time and allows you the ability to collect more guns.
Some guns I have managed to acquire are (don't remember specific names): LMG's, assault rifles, various pistols and revolvers, shotguns, submachine guns or 'uzi' type weapons. Considering I am picking up grenade rounds, I am assuming there is some sort of grenade launcher as well.
Again, there are weapons, but I refrained from using them due to their risk of noise and making matters worse. I used them more as a last resort.
This is a single player game with a continuously existing game world...even when offline. This is a core and big feature to this game that not only adds a new element of gameplay, but simulates the game (this is the Simulation portion).
Basically, if you left your group with high morale, no one in danger or felling depressed/suicidal and have sufficient supplies with no immediate danger (infestations close by)... you'll come back to a happy community with little issues and may even find new items that the survivors found while they went out scavenging for supplies while you were offline/gone.
I must make sure that it is clear that you are NOT required to play this every day. The simulation will slow down considerably after being offline for 48 Hours and continuously slow down for X amount of days until reaching a complete 'paused' state. It will then resume the simulation once you log back on.
Game's story is approximately 15 hours. This is if you simply rush through everything not paying attention to your base, ignoring anything other than basic/needed story missions and not scavenging...may even finish sooner (like 10). The average is about 20-25 hours and those who take their time have about 30-40+ hours in.
The DLC released on November 29th 2013 which adds the ability to play as you'd like without the need to worry or focus on story missions. The side missions, base building and everything else still exists, but the mode is like a 'How long can you survive' type of mode.
Completing a round by finding the RV and moving to a new location in a refreshed version of the map increases the difficulty. You may find yourself sneaking around and being much more tactiful in this mode than in the base game. There are also new weapons and 'hero' type characters available for use in this mode that will need to be unlocked.
I have only played State of Decay: Breakdown for approximately 4.5 hours and cannot judge it fairly at this time (especially since I am still in the first round and haven't moved on yet. But the base game comes highly recommended to any and all zombie lovers.

Even though you need the 360 controller... it's still playable using the common set up (WASD for movement, left and right click for weapons, tab for inventory and ESC for the game menu) enjoyable but still in progress, even though this is an early access it's a 7.5 (so far I haven't played much so I bet the number will rise)

Wooooooh, it's been some time since my last review on the game huh? 360 controller, we're talking about early access times, even then this game was great, catching characters without much depth into their history, now we can use w/e we want (keyboard+mouse, joystick, head or knees if you're drunk) ANYTHING to kill the zombie menace... hah I say kill the zombie menace but honestly you'll be running and sneaking them so you can kill them in silence while you keep on training your stats until you're decent enough to last against several.
Back to the features, the game establishes well one thing, get surrounded by zombies (which is pretty much most of the time) and you're dead meat, make too much sound and yep, dead meat, go guns blazing and yeeeeeeep, dead meat (unless you have a silencer which is pretty useful), use cars a lot and yeeep dea... well you won't be dead meat then but it's still interesting when your car gets assaulted by ravid zombies aching for your earlobe (that's the appetizer).
Weapons are abundant and well made, random too so you'll never find the same each time you play, the combat and moving systems are what one would expect, well done, interesting and kind of realistic (mind you I haven't been in a zombie apocalypse yet but I reckon if I were I think this is pretty much how it would be), you need to get to a safe zone (your and the survivors home) and keep on checking them, remember that your character isn't just the two dudes and the girl you'll find, it's pretty much everyone you'll find and end up convincing to go to your home, some may take some convincing, others may take haggling and assistance (yep, you can help other settlements, if you can call them settlements).
Which brings me to a new point, homes, you'll be able to move between several places, each with its own strenghts and weaknesses, the bar at the corner may not be enough for 10+ ppl, but it sure has easy settings to defend it; the truck stop may be able to gather a lot of ppl but you need to have capable ppl and enough to fill the place so you can defend it (remember there's always a chance of a random horde going to your home), you'll have different areas in your home, gardens so you can produce your own food, beds (ofc you always need those), places to make ammo and fix things, storehouses, libraries, well you get the idea, pretty much a a fort and convert it into a place where your survivors can... well... duh, survive.
The system also includes this neat thing in which every person has weak and good points, while your some characters may not be the best in gardening or cooking they'll be handy when it comes to a fight (melee weps and shooting) others are just better at playing house and casually going out to get some stocks.
Well I'll keep on playing it and change this review since I STILL haven't finished lifeline (yep, the dlc in which you're the army.... awesome set up people, if you don't have it yet get it and check it out)

At it's core, this is not GameGuru, Multimedia Fusion, or some other development program. It is Mario Maker, or Little Big Planet, etc. The only real difference is that, instead of making platformers, you're making Dark Souls.
Do you like stamina-based combat? Do you want Soulsborne-style gameplay with a near infinite amount of content, which is even more important now that Miyazaki, the creative force behind that franchise, is done with Souls after The Ringed City? Then you will like MyWorld. You don't need to use the creative tools to enjoy this game, and I can't emphasize that enough.
Have you wanted a make-your-own-souls with an easy to use drag and drop interface? Did you enjoy using tools in the past like the Aurora Toolset for Neverwinter Nights? Then you will enjoy this game. You don't need to be a skilled Souls veteran to partake in the creative aspect of the game, and your creative freedom enables you to tailor a world for less tryhard combatants if you so wish.
Do you enjoy cooperatve/competitive play? Because MyWorld has that too. All worlds are cooperative with up to four players by default, and the map creator can use special spawn points to create team-based or free for all pvp. If you use a pvp spawn pad, you can even play cooperatively in a world with the addition of friendly fire!
The game launched in a private beta six weeks ago, and in that six week time period the game's creative content has close to doubled, in addition to new features and fixes being added at a consistent rate with no signs of slowing. The developers have been incredibly responsive and communicative during this time, and I have nothing but praise for what they've achieved. This is an Early Access from a reputable company, the creators of GameGuru, and not some indie basement-dwellers who don't know what they're getting into. I would say that in its current state, beyond being a playable game, MyWorld is a safe Early Access bet.

Where to begin? Diablo meets Disney, Never Winter Nights meets Legoland. This game is great on so may levels.
Whether you like playing action RPG's or you like to craft worlds/scenarios for your friends to enjoy, Single player, multiplayer, PVP, World editor.
I can honestly say I've not found a game that appealed so much in a long, long time. Mostly it is FUN. Fun to build, fun to play. Challenging if you're a serious mayhem seeker, entertaining if you just like to explore.
Since I wrote the above the game has received a steady stream of upgrades in terms of new buildings,props, collectables, choosable theme music, new npcs and enemies, a brilliant character creator so you can build your own npc's and enemies from a huge range of body parts and AI's, upgrades to questing making it much easier to control the flow of play. The dev's have been seemingly tireless in their dedication to fulfilling the game's early promise.
Now we have a big free DLC offering a whole new steampunk game style with buildings, props, npc's and enemies. Put together with the earlier release of mine decor - tracks and waggons - and big, town style buildings we have the opportunity to step away from the classic Tolkeinesque fantasy scenario into a mad, imaginary machine/robot world.
I'm up to over 800 hours now playing with this most excellent of software toys and it's still FUN.

I really enjoy the amount of options available to make your world in this game. Big variety that I would like to see expanded in the future as well. There is a huge possibilities of worlds to be created and specially with the Steam Workshop connection and being able to share your worlds and experience other people's worlds, I think the game nails the main focus of the game. The creation and exploration of worlds is really good. Apart from characters, the customization in the game is extensive.
I don't like the combat system, all characters only seem to have heavy attacks with big windups, that put you several seconds vulnerable to opponents, that style doesn't seem to fit this game very well, the character do have abilities (spin attack, stun, shield, and "power-up"mode) but all of them have the same abilites.
The camera is awkward to move, the wasd move the camera, and the scroll wheel zooms in or out, althought "w" and "s" also control the zoom, which makes it hard to adjust with you want to keep the zoom you can only use "a" or "s". wasd shouldn't interact with the zoom.
There is no snapping into place while creating the world, so aligning walls is a hard if you want them perfect. The rotation is also lackluster, you can only rotate with "r" and only rotate in one way, so if you rotate too much you will need to go all the way across to come back to the original position, which is boring and frustating.
And I think that's all, I still recommend this game, the world building and exploration seems awesome specially with other people and using the Workshop, plus it's in Early Access so I expect that some of the problems to be fix and improved, can't wait to see what other people can build.

Whenever I think of epic-scale RPGs, my first thoughts turn to the Mass Effect series, and usually after that, its first title that set the stage for one of the most enveloping and immersive gaming experiences that Canada can offer.
The structure of the 3 games is akin to that of the original Star Wars trilogy.
Though dated and still a bit clunky, the first title in the series of Mass Effect games did a beautiful job of serving as the exposition and rising action for a seemingly limitless amount of story potential. After 3 major games, 4 handheld games, 4 novels, 10 comic books, and a
in the works, BioWare claims that there is still quite a bit of this story that has been left untold. The next title in the Mass Effect series, though enigmatic at the moment, will likely reinvent and redirect the game series as a whole.
This game has the player character's customized hero, Commander Shepard, embarking on a galactic quest to catch an elusive rogue agent seemingly working to further his own goals, and to uncover the true hidden meaning behind the possibility of a threat that this galaxy was in no way ready for.
The combat system had certain enjoyable aspects that weren't revisited until the third game in the series, such as weapons that don't use thermal clips and the distance and speed covered whilst sprinting.
Though I usually have trouble discerning which game of the trilogy is my favorite, most of my thoughts are with its first title, which has imprinted on me as well as many thousands of other players a gaming experience that will never be forgotten.
Its visual style and gameplay are something that is only bettered by its successor, Mass Effect 2.

Many of the negative reviews mention that the port is bad.  “It’s only 30 FPS which means it’s literally unplayable”, and stuff like that.  This is not one of those reviews.  I usually like to add something humorous in these intros but, like Dark Souls’ gameplay, there’s nothing fun or humorous here.
Let’s start with what the game is, and does well: hack-and-slash.  You press one button for a weak attack and press another for a strong.  You can combo them into each other and there're your directional based attacks, as well.  It’s got that part down quite well.  You make your character (that’s kind of limited in options but it’ll get covered up with armor in due time) and, over time, pick your weaponry and armor.  Over the course of the game, you get a wide range of gear.  From the regular broadsword to a two handed claymore.  Several types of daggers, to axes, scythes, a dozen polearms, swords too big to actually wield, a few fist weapons, katanas, hammers and fancy swords.  There are also whips and bows but...uhh...yeah, don’t use those.  There are also three types of magic: Sorcery, black magic-esq; pyromancy; throw fire at people; and miracles, white magic and support.  Those descriptions aren’t the best and there’s a bit of crossover but it’ll work.
Armor comes in three types, light, medium, and heavy.  The difference in the three is the type of evasiveness and speed.  Lower weight = longer roll and more invincibility frames during the roll.  If you’re too heavy, then you can’t roll and your movement speed is terrible but absorb more damage.
The weapon and armor types allows for a good amount of customization.  If you allocate stats correctly, you can build however you want. Berserker, Dragoon, thief, a tank who specializes in magic.  Everything is possible - although it might not be viable but, hey, you bought the game.
As you search for gear you travel across the mountain called Lordran and kill dead things.  Lots and lots of dead things; and of varying types.  There are also rats, dogs, demons, egg-heads, dragons, gods, and the occasional actual living, person.  There’s a few more but that’s the jist.  I’d say why but I’m not totally sure why.  One day you get locked up in prison and someone lets you out for reasons never mentioned.  There’s a lot of reasons never mentioned in the game.
It also looks nice.  Visuals are appealing, although if you get too close it starts to look pixelated.  If you’re not happy with it all then head over the
and download some HD textures.
Music is wonderful but it only exists in boss battles.  It’s a wonderful assortment of orchestral and ethereal sounds.  Motoi Sakuraba has always been of my favorite, lesser known, video game composers and I’m glad to see he still has it.  I can’t find any official sources so here’s a

And, sadly, that’s all that the game does well.
While you traverse the land of Lordran you are in constant danger of dying.  Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty and there’s a reason for that.  There is no plot, there is no direction, there is no character development.  The camera will fail you, the auto lock will fail you, and the terrain will fail you.
I say there’s no plot but that is, technically, a lie.  You see the fire’s dying and someone needs to keep it lit.  What happens after you relight it?  Dunno.  What happens if you don’t light it?  Dunno.  There’s not a lot of closure in the game and it all just feels lazy and a waste.  You went through all of that for what?  Why did I kill this person?  Why couldn’t I talk to this guy?  Why are these guys so upset?  Who was this NPC person I summoned?  I have more questions than answers because the game provides no answers.
I also lied about character development as it does exist but only for a few NPCs who die.  You find various NPCs throughout Lordran, free them from their hardship, they show-up in your base of operations, and that’s it.  Sometimes they sell stuff but otherwise, they just sit there until something triggers them to leave and you have to kill them.

From a technical aspect, the game has flaws.  The camera hates when you turn and it’ll let you know by having you walk off a ledge.  The auto-lock works only when it feels like it and will fail to work when you need it.  You often have to be right in your enemies’ face so it’s hard to put yourself in proper position in boss fights.  Hitboxes come and go.  Sometimes they work, often they don’t.  For a game that is built on difficulty, the technical unreliabilities often make the game less challenging and more outright not fair.  There’s a difference between being hard and cheating.
The gameplay is just boring.  Because of the unforgiving difficulty, you’re going to die.  A lot.  Because of that, you’re going to be doing the same thing over and over and over and over and over again.  Killing/running from the same guys.  Walking long distances.  It’s a lesson in tedium.  You’ll learn quickly that walking for 3 minutes to die in a fight that takes 10 seconds isn’t fun.  And when you are in battle, it’s mostly just holding a shield or dodging for a while and only occasionally doing damage.  You’ll be looking for openings to heal more often than not.  Dark Souls is a game about patience, not aggression.  Punish your opponents or else they punish you.  That’s great but strafing for 10 minutes isn’t my idea of enjoyable.
Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty.  Had I only realized that sooner, I might have enjoyed it but I thought a modern game would have some semblance of story and finality.  Instead, I get a grind that never feels worth it.  Killing bosses never made me feel like I accomplished something: it was all luck based.  The hitboxes screwed-up again or the boss just didn’t use THAT move.  If you remove the difficulty, then you have no plot, you have no reason to care about of the characters you’ve saved, you have no reason to feel like it all meant anything.  It’s a poor hack and slash that feel devoid of reason.  Dark Souls could have good but the devs didn’t feel like adding plot and what little they did add is vague and might not mean anything since “Time is Messed-up”.  What’s there is nice though.
I wanted to like Dark Souls but too much of a frustrating grind and it just feels empty.  And I didn't even mention the controls and the terrible jumping mechanics, or accidental kicks.  There’s plenty of length but there’s just no depth.  It’s a hard game for the sake of being hard an that’s what you get.

Where do I begin, to put it simply this is one of the greatest RPG games I have played in my entire life.
Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen, for those who don't know, is the same as dragons dogma, practically. But containing all the Downloadable content. Now Dragons dogma itself came out in 2012 and is still regarded to this day as one of the top of the hierarchy rpg games.
You begin your journey as a colossal red dragon comes to your miniature shoreline village and ravages through the area, you quickly take an attempt at felling the beast only for it to take your heart; but you survive.
Although the idea is, well, a little monotonous for an RPG; they almost always include dragons and the like, it still creates a really well developed game and provides some beautiful gameplay.
Dragons dogma is well known for its learning curve, this is like a combination of Dark souls and skyrim. It can get tough and you will actually need to level. You cant do it like skyrim and breeze through as bethesda holds your hand, you will learn to fear or fight or you will die, especially at night. Capcom said they had wanted to develop a game that really made you feel vulnerable, and at night time in dragon's dogma you really feel that. Monsters roam everywhere and all you have to guide you is a puny light coming from your lantern, the rest; black.
Another major feature I love about this game is the combat; at first the combat can seem pretty bland as you have to level to unlock skills and such but once you've gotten to said level you can pull off amazing looking combos and leave your enemies pretty much trembling with trepidation as you slay their comrades.
Something I love most about this game (Yes I'm devoting a paragraph to it) is the fact that you can climb your foes, yes. Climb them. Capcom threw in a Shadow of the colossus feature into the mix that REALLY kicked it up a notch, and im not even exaggerating. Roam around on youtube and watch the game trailer and you will see what I mean. You can climb onto a dragon WHILE IT'S FLYING and hack the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it with your sword, daggers or whatever (That's how you do it skyrim, get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together). With huge bosses this mechanic is just so fun to play with, it feels so thrilling to be climbing up the back of a cyclops desperately trying to reach its eye, or scaling a golem to destroy that last amulet.
Now unlike most, if not all rpgs, there are two major functions of this game that really mix things up; the first being the pawn system. The pawn system is something completely original and it's that you have 3 "pawns" as followers, 1 main pawn (who you create and all that) and 2 support pawns that you can obtain from online friends or just people anywhere. Through entering the rift with online connectivity you're able to easily hire other players' pawns and transverse between them quite simply, and when you're done you can even send a gift to the pawn's owner and rate them depending on how well they look, how well they fought, and how helpful they were.
Another large feature of the game is something else completely original and unthought of, and that's NG Plus (New game plus). Pretty much what NG Plus is, it's a mechanic that lets you almost infinitely level your character. So once you've finished the main story most games would just, end, right? Well not Dragon's dogma. If you load your game after finishing the main story you can restart the story all over again, but you'll have the same level, same stats, same equipment and everything. allowing you to play through the game as many times as you please to get your Arisen to the level cap (200), which in itself takes a fair amount of time.
Dragons dogma is something I will always carry in my heart with me, no matter how much I play I can always seem to come back and feel some enjoyment off it. I mean, who doesnt love hacking at a griffin while it's flying off somewhere? I would recommend this game to any RPG fan or someone who just really likes to kill♥♥♥♥♥♥ It is the most fun I've ever had.

Going to give this a positive review, because I think it deserves it, though personally, I do not like the game and probably should have refunded it.
The art is lovely, slightly cartoonish but not in such an overly saccharine manner as to put people off. It is actually quite lovely in appearance.  The 'quests' per se are pretty much just listening to the narrator and doing what he tells you, so listen well.
So why didn't I like it?  Well, I had a hard time not falling off the edge of the map.  Some of the pathways in the beginning were narrow and (to me at least) way too easy to fall off of.  It is similar to games like Torchlight or Fate in appearance, battle, items and movement, but with a persistant chance of falling into the void, which I tended to do far too often to find the game enjoyable.  A lot of little things aren't explained.  Like what are the little purple things you pick up?  Only played a tad over half hour, but they were never used or explained which left me wondering if searching for the hidden chests and breaking stuff to find them was worth my time.
So if you are a clutz with lousy reaction speed and difficulty adapting cardinal direction movement into diagonal movement on the fly, this might not be the game for you.
If you are good at hack, slash & shoot while trying to figure out whether pressing up or right with move you diagonally without rocketing off the edge of the world, I think this is a good game and would be very enjoyable.  I just lack those talents.  I wanted to like the game, it runs good, looks good, sounds good, and felt 'clean' and finished, it was just not within my ability to play it without the frustration of repeated unintentional suicides.

I got this on sale with Transistor as well as both games' soundtracks - and I gotta say they were pretty good. I love the soundtrack for this game and the narrative great too - leaving you with ever more questions about the story.
That being said, it took me about half a year to finish this game, not because it was hard, but rather because I lost interest in it for a while. The story does pick up a bit later on in the game, but I only found the first part of the game interesting because of 1) the hype that you feel as a game starts, and 2) a friend of mine told me that the game is worth it.
So, do I recommend this game? Yes. The narrative was a step away from the usual, and Supergiant really tried to flesh out the characters for this game (even if some of the challenges that give you this background info are a bit harder than I'd like). That being said, if you'd rather a faster-paced or more immersive game then by all means, check out Transistor.

Mass Effect
For those who don't want a long review here's the short version: Is this game good? Yes. Is it as good as the second one? No. Should you still play this before getting the second? Absolutely.
In my opinion that is actually one of the most compelling reasons for getting this game, for the sake of the second. For those of you that don't know Mass Effect is a trilogy of games where you play the same character every time. Commander Shepard (the character you play) can be personalised with gender, first name, class and personal appearance along with some minor backstory options. In the game you recruit a crew of intriguing and likeable squadmates in your mission to (What else) save the galaxy. Each time you start a later game in the trilogy you can import a character you completed in the previous game, along with all the decisions you made. This means that if you're thinking about getting Mass Effect 2 I can't recommend this game enough. Not that Mass Effect 2 isn't a great game in its own right but as I mention this series is a trilogy, meaning they feature a lot (and I mean A LOT) of recurring characters). You'll meet a lot of these in Mass Effect 2 and the decisions from Mass Effect (if you import) can and will noticably affect the experience. Combine that with the emotional connections you'll form with the characters in Mass Effect and I'm not exaggerating that you'll only be getting half the experience you could if you played through this game even once.
There's some bad stuff of course, in my opinion the biggest is probably the combat. It's honestly rather clunky and seems to play rather similar no matter what class you choose. Going into and out of cover is difficult and frustrating, and on harder difficulties squad AI has one hell of a death wish. Combat is easily the weakest part of the game, to the point where I'd actually recommend just turning difficulty to easy, ignoring cover and going run & gun like Rambo; it's actually surprisingly entertaining. Another weak part is the vehicle sections where you drive a space tank called the Mako. The controls are unintuitive to say the least, a few minutes wrestling with them and you'll understand why so many people make jokes about Shepard's driving. Also, you frustratingly cannot save the game while driving, though to counter that you're also ridiculously over powered so you should be fine as long as you don't drive into any lava pits (which you will do sooner or later, just accept it). Also: Stay away from Thresher Maws; they are not worth it.
But seriously, don't let all that put you off; there is more than enough good stuff in this game to balance it out. To go over it in brief:
1. Story & Character. This is Bioware so expect good stuff here, the game is probably more story than character driven but the people you meet are still interesting and (for the most part) likeable.
2. Music: There are blockbuster sci-fi movies out there that don't have soundtracks as good as this one, this music is worthy of orchestral performances.
3. Cutscenes & Graphics: Mass Effect is getting on in years but I think the graphics still hold up, and the cutscenes are fittingly epic. Facial movement is well done, especially on th alien characters though the humans are still prone to some scary smiles.
4. Voice acting. Superb, nothing more can be said.
I could go on a lot longer but I think you get the idea, Mass Effect is a great game. If you're a fan of space opera, or even just sci-fi and RPG's in general, and have been looking for a new game to obsess over then this is for you.

If you are reading this review, you probably have already bought the game and passing time until it is ready, or wondering if this type of game is for you. Dispite most reviews, Dark Souls is not difficult, in a certain sense. The game is built on punishing you for not being observant. Running across an area to the next bonfire, or a checkpoint in other games, will get you killed. Enemies and bosses are programmed to be unique in design and attack pattern, learning how each enemy moves, and their varieties of attacks will even make some of the more difficult bosses a walk in the park. This game is loved by a massive community, so of course you will find people to only cause you suffering ingame, but you will also find plenty of people ready to help your Dark Souls experience. Their are plenty of YouTube videos explaining lore, boss strategies, game mechanics, and much more if you want to be invested in the game. All this being said, you will die, as it is the most important part of the Dark Souls series. Each death will contribute to your expirence, as you memorize enemy combos and move damage, grasp the fundamentals of when to block, and when to dodge, this game has much in store for the observant player. If that sounds appealing to you, then I say buy this beautiful game, and maybe you will love Dark Souls as much as many other players of the series. At the time of writing this review, I have slain almost all bosses of Dark Souls, minus Priscilla, and one or two DLC bosses. Knowing what I know now, I can easily rerun through these bosses on my second run. If you are looking for a beginning point in the Souls series, I say to start here, with the original Dark Souls. It only gets more challenging from here on out.

BEFORE YOU BUY
You need to ask yourself a few questions.
Can you deal with stress?
Can you spend lots of money on broken controlers?

The terrible port aside, Dark Souls is an action RPG with a heavy emphasis on patience and actual RPG elements. You roleplay a character of your own making, choosing his/her’s class, homeland, and starting gift. You’re promptly given a brief cutscene which really doesn’t tell you anything, then you’re on your own.
You find yourself in Firelink Shrine, a desolate yet homey location to call your camp. This is where you will spend most of your time talking to NPCs or purchasing equipment from merchants. Your newfound camp resides in the land of Lordran, a grim, depressing, and often times creepy environment. The characters follow suit, very few seem trustworthy, and even fewer seem genuine when talking with you, and all of them will regularly end their conversations with an unpleasant psychotic laugh. What you’re doing in Lordran, and where you’re supposed to be going isn’t clear, as the residents of this world try to help or hinder your adventure. It feels like the land is going through some kind of apocalypse, as hollowed-out humans and creatures wander about, prepared to mawl, crush or stab you on sight.
When it comes time to fight the hollows of Lordran, you’ll find the combat is rather slow and simulates real weight to your weaponry and armor, heavily punishing you when you try to rush or run past enemies. In most cases you’ll be standing in front of an enemy with your shield up, waiting for an opportunity to finally strike. This sets the pace for Dark Souls, being slow, meticulous, thoughtful and careful will often times bring the best rewards. This doesn’t just go for the combat either, if you’re aware of your surroundings you can often times see an ambush or trap ahead, which would otherwise feel unforgiving and difficult.
The story to Dark Souls isn’t very obvious, and much like the rest of the gameplay requires you to be thoughtful and aware to actually notice most of the stories being told. If you don’t have the patience for lore presented in a non-direct fashion, ignoring the overall story won’t really hamper your enjoyment either, as the lore of the world and characters are really just icing on the mechanics already there. If you’re interested in the lore, but like it being told in a more direct way, there are a plethora of quality videos online which showcase the story and lore.
You’ll see a lot of people saying “Dark Souls doesn’t hold your hand, and it will kick your♥♥♥♥♥” and that’s largely correct. You will be dropped in this large, relatively open area and unless if you pay very close attention to characters dialogue or contextual hints, you’ll be very lost. That’s precisely the experience you’re getting into when you play Dark Souls. If you go into this game with patience, wanderlust for a grim and sad world, the acceptance that you’ll probably die a lot, you will enjoy your time with Dark Souls much more.
Dark Souls captivated me back in 2012, and has since remained one of my favorite games. Although the PC port was terrible, the DSfix makes it bearable and the experience is worth the trouble in my opinion. If you haven’t already jumped into the series, Dark Souls Prepare to Die Edition goes on sale pretty regularly, and I highly recommend the game if anything I’ve said sounds enticing. Just remember, take it slow, be patient... and be prepared to die.

This game was and still is a very ambitious attempt to combine everything that people love about RPGs.
1.) It attempts to replicate climbing on monsters to fight them the way you would in Shadow of the Collosus.  It does this pretty well and will have you doing it a lot within the first hour of the game.
2.) It trys to replicate the kind of difficulty you would find in Dark Souls or Bloodborne.  It started out really difficult for me but after awhile I got into the swing of things.  Atleast with the main story that is.  The Dark Arisen DLC that is incuded with this game is where the difficulty spikes.
3.) It has a custom follower system that I haven't seen done anywhere in any game.  The game gives you a follower called a "pawn" that you can customize with the same kind of depth as your custom character.  This follower is then sent to a server where other players can employ this pawn.  The only place I have ever seen this done even remotely is the Skyrim modding community that is filled with custom follower mods.  It is very nice to see this implemented as an actual feature that you need.  When you employ a pawn or someone else employs your pawn, they might have quest knowledge or knowledge on how to defeat an enemy you haven't seen before.
4.) You will be presented with a multitude of tasks for quests.  You do have the option of doing cliche quests like fetche quests or escort quests but this is optional and is mostly done to gain money or experience.  Main quests are a lot more interesting.
Now to address some flaws.
1.) The most common complaint I hear in reviews for this game is that the story is awful.  That is not an incorrect statement.  The story starts out very cliche and the ending is disappointing to say the least.  I'd go as far as to say that it has to have one of the worst stories of any game I've ever played.  But the gameplay alone makes it one of the best games I've ever played on any console.  Not THE best, but AMONG THE best.
2.) The monsters are just really generic monsters.  you have goblins, wolfs, ogres, and direwolfs and other things like that.  No original monsters, just another take on some old ones.  I have seen this game before and I remember not thinking much of it because the photos were just of people with generic weapons fighting generic monsters.  The only reason I tried it out was because it was at a discounted price.
3.) There are game dynamics it doesn't tell you about when you start playing.  In fact you can play through the story without knowing there is an affinity system or a pawn inclination system or major quests that could have really helped you.  You will need to read a wiki or a guide sooner or later or you will miss something cool.
4.) This is a small problem, but I don't find the menus to be very navigatable.  Going from quests to maps to inventory to equipment just seems like a longer process than it should be.
The most important thing you need to know is that the advertising and reviews for this game doesn't do it the slightest bit of justice.  CAPCOM kind of shot itself in the foot because of that.  This should have been a big deal game like Skyrim or Dark Souls.  I definitly think it's better than those two anyway.

*Update* 7/17/2016 *Thumbs Up*
I'm Changing this review from a pretty firm thumbs down to a massive thumbs up.
This game has a lot of bang for the buck now, and the devs were taking peoples comments to heart, CLEARLY.
I'm a bold guy so I'm just going to give the highlights, followed by the downsides.
*Highlights*
The Devs are listening to the playerbase without compromising the integrity of their games focus to acomidate it. *This is very hard to find in dev teams anymore, its respectable*
The game has a hardcore survival feel to it with added survival elements like warmth, disease, poison and food you need to keep an eye on. There is even a dragon that is out to get you constantly throughout the game. *more on dragon in downsides*
The game has rich combat, you can and will have to use strategy to outwhit your enemies and defeat them. Its not used in a frustrating way though. Each fight becomes rewarding and enemies become simple to kill after learning their weakness. You essentially level by learning *Really want to stress here, this is not a darksouls learning curve, its managable for anyone*.
The graphics are not bad, their right around skyrims general area and feel. *More In Downsides*
There are bossfights with actually strategy needed to defeat them.
You can build houses, walls, repair broken villages and make lockable chests to protect your loot! *More in downsides*
The game has progression. You need to beat one island to get to the next to get to the next. This is not to be mistaken with step by step, you could spend your entire life on one island, its open ended survival. No linear storyline to mindlessly follow here.
The game has a wide verity in weapons, gear and houses to make and use.
The game runs on a PTP system, there are no servers, you essentially join other peoples games and play together or with friends. It runs smooth for a PTP which leads me to believe it has low bandwith consumption *Did no research on this, but i have a 5mb/2mb shared connection and it worked fine hosting for 3+ people* *Way more in downsides*
These are just the highlights, there are plenty more, but this is what stood out the most to me.
*Downsides*
The dragon is a little much for new people, its hard to survive to begin with, add a dragon shooting fire down way too often and you have a scenario that can cause frustration. A feature to press a button to show the dragon respect so it leaves or a hide system where if you hide long enough it just flys off is needed.
Graphics are way better than they were, but still need some work. Some of the monsters are a little stiff looking still *boar especially*. The snow storms some times look like smoke they are so thick. *I havent tested this on other systems, but it was downright hard to see in places, i could not see through the blowing snow that looked like smoke.
There are very limited ways to store your loot, between people in your game snooping and the small lockable chest that your extreamely limited with placement. Your going to get frustrated. the crafting system needs a crazy amount of resources to build what you need to craft and the stuff you need to craft it is almost impossible to safely store.
*Gamebreaking Downsides*
There are no female options....this worked back in the day, not so much anymore. Good luck getting you'r female gaming friends to play this, their not accomidated. Yes its a big deal to them.
The PTP system is cool....but when they can come in, farm all your games buildings and destroy the bosses you need to progress without you even being aware of it. THAT IS NOT COOL. In any way or form, be prepared to get really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at random people for screwing up your worldsave to the point you lose all your progress. No wonder there are no games to join, between them messing your saves up, looting your needed stored resources for crafting and just being rude. Why would people host a game you could join. A big boss respawn after an hour or so or limiting the reward for tearing down a building is needed.

2) Sense of Progression - This is what drives the player to keep playing, and they've done it well.  Collecting resources to craft better weapons and armor, build bigger buildings, and make larger packs to increase carrying capacity.
3) Variety of Enemies - Skeletons, wolves, plagued wolves, forest giants, dire bears, furies.
4) Size of Island - The size of the world is quite large.  After 60 hours I can't say that I've explored the entire thing.
NEGATIVES:
(Keep in mind that many of these negatives may very well be resolved as the game develops)
1) Grinding - Collecting resources can become a chore, especially mining.
2) Limited Resources - The resources in this game do not respawn, but that may change in the future.
3) Cost of Repairs - Many of the higher end weapons and armor are so expensive to repair and the resources required to repair them may be scarce, especially if you have several players on your server.
4) Base Building - Right now, it's so easy to strip an area of usable resources that there is no reason to spend time and resources on base building since you'll just have to move on anyways.
5) Map Reloads - Once you've stripped most of the island of resources the only way to keep playing is to load a new map.  Fortunately, you get to carry your character to the new map, but anything you've built is gone forever.

Baldur's Gate in Planescape drag, alas. Well worth playing if you want more of the former, but does nothing for people who want to see more games following the path of the latter.
Planescape: Torment became a cult classic in large part because it was put together with a good movie's ruthless economy rather than the flabby kitchen-sink approach of most CRPGs. No doubt owing largely to a limited budget, Planescape wasted neither space, time nor characters. Where RPGs most often send the player on a half-hour wander through a generic hometown before giving them a sword, a motive or the MacGuffin that reveals them as the Chosen One, Planescape began with a strong scenario—the player waking from the dead in a steampunk mortuary—and kept going at this pace, introducing characters with established (if hidden) relationships to the player and strongly themed maps that each contributed to the strangeness of the overall setting. Focused on story and theme rather than combat, it offered few spells, items and abilities, and tied many key advances in avatar strength to understanding the players' allies. By departing from the RPG tradition of blank slate protagonists, Planescape was able to launch the player into complicated relationships and create real feelings of guilt as it revealed its hero's past. 10-20 hours later (the blink of an eye in RPG terms), the game ended, having conveyed a strong story and wasted very little time.
Five (sorry, 12.5!) hours into Pillars, I've seen four forests, three boilerplate dungeons and a city with such distinctive locations as a shipyard, a palace and (daringly) a brothel. My allies have politely introduced themselves and their gimmicks, and then drip-fed personality in occasional speeches (oddly, after an introductory section it takes about 10 hours before one meets a female ally). A few side quests have touched on grey moral areas—and then forced me to pass judgment on them by deciding whom to kill. Some interesting plot threads have emerged, but it seems I will not be able to follow them further without hours of trudging across empty, generic maps and repetitive combat. In short, Pillars of Eternity does nothing wrong but nothing new with the genre. It colors within the lines.

This is in some ways a very interesting game, in other ways a horribly annoying one.
Let's start with the interesting part: A Zombie Survival RPG is something I always wanted to play, and the implementation is good; sneaking into houses, looking for resources and using them to improve my compound is fun. Recruiting more survivors, growing as a community, learning skills... all great. Considering the scope of the game and the fact that it's early access, there are also very few bugs, and none serious (well, I had that one amazing car jump of about 200 m length...). Fighting and shooting mechanics are ok, though why anybody would choose a controller for the latter over mouse+keyboard is beyond me. The Influece system for trading favours for equipment and other things is a brilliant idea for the zombie apocalypse.
Concerning the mechanics, the idea of having a persistent world for a single-player game is a mixed blessing. It creates a pressure and involvement in the world, but at the same time, casual gamers will be scared away. Personally, I didn't notice much of it, because I finished the game relatively quickly. I think the resource usage from it is far too high - it makes scavenging tedious, and limits base building due to high demand on some resources. Also, more importantly, it precents me from saving my game. This may be for some people, but I hated it. Luckily, the game is not all that hard if you pay attention to it.
And now for the annoying part: The endless, repetitive "side quests" the game sends you on. I hardly had time to gather a single resource before one of my poor, helpless fellow survivors needed rescuing. Again. Generally from something they clubbed to death all by themselves before I could even get out of the car. There is, of course, time pressure, since they may die if you don't take care of it. Add to that the fact that you can only carry one resource, car or no, before you have to return to base, and the quite quick onset of fatigue, resource gathering is no fun.
The story is clearly secondary for the game, but even so, I would have wished to have it explored a little more. Can't really tell much about it here without spoilers, but several threads just peter out without getting a decent ending. This was somewhat disappointing.
Things I'd have liked more of in the game: Base building (didn't really do anything with mine beyond making sure that there are enough beds + medical area), base management (my AI companions are USELESS - can you tell that this is a theme here ;) ?) and value in sneaking (I usually just drove everywhere and killed the two zombies which were still following me).  Also: Interaction with my fellows beyond "let's go club zombies".
Overall, 7/10. Good value for your money if you like zombie games at all.

In the grand scheme of things, this is a fairly unique offering. It is not one of the latest releases, but the graphics do not look dated as they have a fairly cartoon type quality. Firstly, the story - this was uninteresting and therefore quickly becomes nothing worth following as you simply don't care about it. Secondly (and lastly), the gameplay - very repetitive, just doing the same thing level after level with different (or upgraded) weapons and different enemies.
Would I recommend this? A difficult one to answer. If you can get this very cheap (which I did) it is probably worth "experiencing" as it is something different from the norm. TL/DR: Irresistible classic with story, soundtrack and voice-over that transcend its already brilliant gameplay to yield one of the great isometric RPG-lite classics of the 2010s. Score: 11/10, must play twice. This one will go down in video game history.
In detail:
Damn, what a beautiful game-- from an art-design, musical (!!!), voice-over and gameplay point of view.
is over 5 years old, so there may not be a lot new to say... but let me just tell you, this game is a classic for a reason. Or rather, several reasons:
- Unbelievably beautiful look
- Astounding voice work and sound design
- Not especially hard but a good sense of challenge/gradual improvement. The game seems downright easy up until the turning point when the Survivor figures out what's "really" going on (at least in his mind) and takes bold steps to completely screw things over, at which point the difficulty jumps sharply... bringing it up to a serious level of challenge that any hardcore gamer will appreciate.

This game is filled with challenges, and lets you add more by tacking on Idols (= extra XP-boosting gameplay restrictions) in the Shrine, but what's most fascinating to me is how the toughest levels are tied to the Kid's biggest psychological blocks (Who Knows Where levels and similar). This game is about coming to terms with our own responsibility for the Calamity that made our wonderful world go wrong... a perspective that just about anyone can appreciate from where I'm sitting in May 2017.

If you like
,
and the like, you'll be blown away by
's Western tone, from the acoustic roots/country/sitar-fusion music (surely among the top 3 soundtracks of the past 10 years) and the Stranger's narration to the old-timey weapon inventory and wild, overgrown environments. Even the noblest heroes are filled with regret. Nothing is ever perfect. Even the darkest suffering is beautiful.

This game shows off everything that made its Supergiant successor,
, the great game that it is, but it's anything but a mere precursor.
stands on its own as one of the all-time greats. It doesn't get much better than this.

Mass Effect is a must have.
Simply because it kicked off the most sophisticated Sci-Fi IP of the past 30 years. The richness and depth of the Mass Effect Series' universe is easily on par with Star Wars and Star Trek. If you are a Sci-Fi Fan you can not help but get sucked in and swallowed whole by this beast.
As a game the strength of Mass Effect besides it's lore is a superb story within that lore, believable Charaters to interact with, choices over choices that impact not only the current game but reach forward into part 3 and some of the best written and performed dialog of all time.
Within the series this is the game featuring the most Exploration opportunities and the strongest classical RPG elements (VERY stat and skill dependant down to a limit in inventory space, lots of loot).
The weak points:
Bugs. It's a problem with the whole series. There is nothing gamebreaking, but some Bugs are just plain out annoying and stupid but never got fixed. My guess is that this is in no small part due to the fact that the Mass Effect games are made for consoles first and foremost and are from a console era when patching wasn't really an option.
While the Exploration possibilities are quite big it sadly isn't done very well. Most of it consists of driving a vehicle with crazy physics through randomly generated height maps that had a few prefabs placed in them. That is litterally something that a hobbyist just learning how to make maps can put together in an hours work or less.
The list of weak points could be made longer.
But in reality they do not matter. Because the story and how it is presented not only makes up for the weak points. It lets you forget them. I am just in the middle of another series playthrough just because I have finally gotten all DLCs for part 3. And this probably is the strongest pro going for the series: Even though you could play just part 3. When you pick it up again you wanna start at the beginning again. With Part 1. Because seeing a new Shepard evolve and change over the course of three games is just awesome. It is just like those Lord of the Ring or Star Wars weekends when you watch all the movies in succession. Only better because it lasts for weeks. Hell a 100% completion playthrough of all three games is worth easily 150 hours of playtime.
Last but not Least: Another important reason to get the Mass Effect Series is that part 4 is rumored to hit us next year at the latest and you absolutely will want to know what all the fuss is about when that happens.

Surprisingly good game, thanks to its well crafted atmosphere, its convincing settings in an abandoned Russian scientific base where things went wrong, and a couple of original gameplay mechanisms, but unfortunately not great FPS due to its lack of rhythm, intensity and challenge, Singularity is overall a very decent experience if you manage to turn your brain off on all the little and bigger discrepancies of the game.
- Nice atmosphere, intriguing and slightly oppressive
- Decent variation of the enemies
- 1 good boss fight
- No save/load, but decent placement of the checkpoints (with a couple of exceptions)
- Decent time to beat the game : around 12-14 hours, without speeding :)
- Time based powers offering unique gameplay possibilities
- Nice story, but...
- ...But a lot of things in the story don't make much sense, especially the ending(s)
- The time based powers have 0 reality logic, it's only game logic (eg: you can make environment older, but only the specific parts designed to do so)
- FPS gameplay really lacks of impact & intensity ; it's significantly less engaging than the best FPS games
- In Hard difficulty, the game is globally very easy for the average hardcore gamer, except for a few hard passages (which are welcome)
- 1 small mini-bomb enemy is really painful (painful isn't same as hard ;-) ), especially coupled to the next point
- Our character doesn't run fast enough, can sprint only for a very short time, and is easy to get stuck in crumbles or crate edges while doing so
- Loot is somewhat random but it doesn't bring anything (except made me want to load the last checkpoint on a couple occasions)
- There are 2 or 3 times more health-packs and ammunition than required to beat the game
- You can upgrade each weapon point by point, which means you're very encouraged to always use the same weapon, especially as you'll never lack ammunition for it, which brings some lack of variety in the fights
- No subtitles for the numerous video and in-game audio-logs
- It misses a couple of special (and usable) weapons... eg: where is my plasmagun ?!? ;-)
