The mid to late Double Aughts is a era of semi generic saturation. Not only were there a bountiful number action/FPS games but they all had extremely similar vibes. Not to mention the few that were literally about the same subject. Time Manipulation and/or some sort of physics manipulation.
Singularity is one that got completely buried, even more so on PC than the much smaller number of titles available each console generation. Just remember for a moment. Resistance: Fall of Man,  TimeShift, FEAR, Half Life 2, Project Snowblind, BLACK, Dead Space, Mass Effect, Timespltters, Psi Ops, Fracture.. Hell for the sake of brevity let us not forget the other end of the spectrum -- Darkest of Days and Legendary; and the list goes on. I list all these just to reiterate how incredibly saturated the market was. There was no one to save Singularity from itself. Keep in mind this list is omitting however many iterations of Call of Duty, Battlefield and Medal of Honor there were at the time.
This game still holds up. Granted, it is not as old as some of those others. The guns feel good. The powers feel good. They integrate in ways you may not expect from initial inspection. I only played this once on PC and have indeed played it back in the day so I admittedly have some nostalgia.
You collect E99, a fictional substance required to power the TMD or Time Manipulation device. This has two types, one to power more effective means of dispatching enemies and one to spend on upgrades. These are however separate from weapon upgrades. The game also has some lite puzzle solving which will task you from throwing stasis fields, rapidly aging and restoring objects that have E99 present within them usually to remove some sort of blockage.
There are a lot of elements from other games I still yet did not mention. It feels little like BioShock at times. Only in it's
. There is a weapon called a Seeker which allows you to in slow motion control the path of an explosive bullet. I'd mention Heavenly Sword here but I feel the power of referential definitions is starting run out. There is also a grenade launcher that allows you to roll a grenade on the ground under and through obstacles should you wish.

Many of the negative reviews mention that the port is bad.  “It’s only 30 FPS which means it’s literally unplayable”, and stuff like that.  This is not one of those reviews.  I usually like to add something humorous in these intros but, like Dark Souls’ gameplay, there’s nothing fun or humorous here.
Let’s start with what the game is, and does well: hack-and-slash.  You press one button for a weak attack and press another for a strong.  You can combo them into each other and there're your directional based attacks, as well.  It’s got that part down quite well.  You make your character (that’s kind of limited in options but it’ll get covered up with armor in due time) and, over time, pick your weaponry and armor.  Over the course of the game, you get a wide range of gear.  From the regular broadsword to a two handed claymore.  Several types of daggers, to axes, scythes, a dozen polearms, swords too big to actually wield, a few fist weapons, katanas, hammers and fancy swords.  There are also whips and bows but...uhh...yeah, don’t use those.  There are also three types of magic: Sorcery, black magic-esq; pyromancy; throw fire at people; and miracles, white magic and support.  Those descriptions aren’t the best and there’s a bit of crossover but it’ll work.
Armor comes in three types, light, medium, and heavy.  The difference in the three is the type of evasiveness and speed.  Lower weight = longer roll and more invincibility frames during the roll.  If you’re too heavy, then you can’t roll and your movement speed is terrible but absorb more damage.
The weapon and armor types allows for a good amount of customization.  If you allocate stats correctly, you can build however you want. Berserker, Dragoon, thief, a tank who specializes in magic.  Everything is possible - although it might not be viable but, hey, you bought the game.
As you search for gear you travel across the mountain called Lordran and kill dead things.  Lots and lots of dead things; and of varying types.  There are also rats, dogs, demons, egg-heads, dragons, gods, and the occasional actual living, person.  There’s a few more but that’s the jist.  I’d say why but I’m not totally sure why.  One day you get locked up in prison and someone lets you out for reasons never mentioned.  There’s a lot of reasons never mentioned in the game.
It also looks nice.  Visuals are appealing, although if you get too close it starts to look pixelated.  If you’re not happy with it all then head over the
and download some HD textures.
Music is wonderful but it only exists in boss battles.  It’s a wonderful assortment of orchestral and ethereal sounds.  Motoi Sakuraba has always been of my favorite, lesser known, video game composers and I’m glad to see he still has it.  I can’t find any official sources so here’s a

And, sadly, that’s all that the game does well.
While you traverse the land of Lordran you are in constant danger of dying.  Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty and there’s a reason for that.  There is no plot, there is no direction, there is no character development.  The camera will fail you, the auto lock will fail you, and the terrain will fail you.
I say there’s no plot but that is, technically, a lie.  You see the fire’s dying and someone needs to keep it lit.  What happens after you relight it?  Dunno.  What happens if you don’t light it?  Dunno.  There’s not a lot of closure in the game and it all just feels lazy and a waste.  You went through all of that for what?  Why did I kill this person?  Why couldn’t I talk to this guy?  Why are these guys so upset?  Who was this NPC person I summoned?  I have more questions than answers because the game provides no answers.
I also lied about character development as it does exist but only for a few NPCs who die.  You find various NPCs throughout Lordran, free them from their hardship, they show-up in your base of operations, and that’s it.  Sometimes they sell stuff but otherwise, they just sit there until something triggers them to leave and you have to kill them.

From a technical aspect, the game has flaws.  The camera hates when you turn and it’ll let you know by having you walk off a ledge.  The auto-lock works only when it feels like it and will fail to work when you need it.  You often have to be right in your enemies’ face so it’s hard to put yourself in proper position in boss fights.  Hitboxes come and go.  Sometimes they work, often they don’t.  For a game that is built on difficulty, the technical unreliabilities often make the game less challenging and more outright not fair.  There’s a difference between being hard and cheating.
The gameplay is just boring.  Because of the unforgiving difficulty, you’re going to die.  A lot.  Because of that, you’re going to be doing the same thing over and over and over and over and over again.  Killing/running from the same guys.  Walking long distances.  It’s a lesson in tedium.  You’ll learn quickly that walking for 3 minutes to die in a fight that takes 10 seconds isn’t fun.  And when you are in battle, it’s mostly just holding a shield or dodging for a while and only occasionally doing damage.  You’ll be looking for openings to heal more often than not.  Dark Souls is a game about patience, not aggression.  Punish your opponents or else they punish you.  That’s great but strafing for 10 minutes isn’t my idea of enjoyable.
Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty.  Had I only realized that sooner, I might have enjoyed it but I thought a modern game would have some semblance of story and finality.  Instead, I get a grind that never feels worth it.  Killing bosses never made me feel like I accomplished something: it was all luck based.  The hitboxes screwed-up again or the boss just didn’t use THAT move.  If you remove the difficulty, then you have no plot, you have no reason to care about of the characters you’ve saved, you have no reason to feel like it all meant anything.  It’s a poor hack and slash that feel devoid of reason.  Dark Souls could have good but the devs didn’t feel like adding plot and what little they did add is vague and might not mean anything since “Time is Messed-up”.  What’s there is nice though.
I wanted to like Dark Souls but too much of a frustrating grind and it just feels empty.  And I didn't even mention the controls and the terrible jumping mechanics, or accidental kicks.  There’s plenty of length but there’s just no depth.  It’s a hard game for the sake of being hard an that’s what you get.

I'm still new to the game but i pretty much learned about the basic stuff.
The game is played on a single lane with 1v1 or 3v3 matchups. Each team has 3 turrets defending their side of the lane and a command center. Losing the command center means losing the game. There are 2 resources; Essence to buy units, and Gold to cast "commander skills". You get Essences over time and Gold by killing enemy units. Essence production rate can be increased by upgrading your mine, but this will halt the current Essence production until the upgrade is complete.
To destroy the enemy command center, you send units which will battle their way through the enemy's own units and turrets to reach and attack their command center. However, you can't control these units so you must rely on the best unit composition and a bit of luck to win the game. To send the units, you assign what kind of unit you will deploy from 10 kinds of units but you can only assign up to 5 to send. Once assigned, these units will spawn in waves to attack the enemy. On 3v3, players on each team take turns spawning their own units between waves(only 1 player on each team will spawn units in a wave). If the command centers are not destroyed after about 48 waves, the game ends when one team loses all of their currently spawned units.
-Game is fun once you get the hang of it
-Requires some strategy and team cooperation to win
-Matches last about 20 minutes at most
-Neutral community (neither friendly nor toxic. Good enough for me)
-Some units needs a bit of balancing
-Most games will have one guy afk(don't know if this is actually a bug as i've seen an AI afk too)
-Needs a lot of grind to unlock units
-Lightly broken translations

Hiveswap Act 1 is definitely worth a play if you're a fan of Homestuck. The art and soundtrack are fantastic, and I found the scattered bits of lore interesting and worthwhile. The writing and dialogue were inoffensive and generally pleasant. There were, however, several issues I took with the game and think are important for the potential consumer to be aware of:
1) Volume inconsistency—the second track on the soundtrack is nearly twice as loud as the first, and this isn't an isolated example. Some sound effects were terribly quiet, while others made me temporarily mute my computer volume.
2) Length—the game is wayyyyy too short; while I understand that this is only the first episode, it felt more like a demo than an actual game. It took me about as much time to play through as it took me to play the Undertale demo when it came out, and here I was trying nearly every combination of items and interactables I thought to try.
3) Combat—the strife system was poorly paced and made no sense. I found myself really struggling to understand what I was supposed to do half the time. I think the game would have been better had the strife not been included at all.
4) Puzzles—The puzzles had quite a bit of handholding, and the next objective was often spelled out very explicitly. Where this wasn't the case, there wasn't any satisfaction in figuring out what to do next because the solution was a little bit contrived, and not in a clever way. If you're looking for good puzzles, maybe give this title a pass.

This is an RTS game for people who suck at RTS games (like me). It's a low pressure RTS game with no micromanagement, watered down, simplified mechanics. When you first start out, you can practically AFK and still do decently. Sounds bad right? Well, it is a bad game. It's basic, it's unpolished, the Engish localization is poor, and yet... I would still recommend the game. Why? Because it's fun. Even bad games can be fun sometimes.
Once you start going up against better players, the game is very challenging. You need to make important decisions which could be the difference between winning or losing. You need to work with your team. You need to constantly analyze the enemy. You need to think quickly because timing is important and the flow of the game can change quickly. You need to be on your toes at every point in the game, from wave 1 to wave 45.
But what is the game exactly? You can think of it as a turn-based RTS game, or a one-lane MOBA game where you control what minions spawn. But there is a huge amount of units, so you can only guess as to what your opponents have up their sleeve. It's 3v3, so you only spawn 1/3 of the waves, the others are spawned by your teammates. You need to play units with synergize with your ally's and counter your enemy's.
The game is very well balanced, and due to the nature of its mechanics, even if you have poor internet connection, or a teammate goes AFK (a very rare occurence, by the way) you can still come out on top. I like it.

TL/DR: Irresistible classic with story, soundtrack and voice-over that transcend its already brilliant gameplay to yield one of the great isometric RPG-lite classics of the 2010s. Score: 11/10, must play twice. This one will go down in video game history.
In detail:
Damn, what a beautiful game-- from an art-design, musical (!!!), voice-over and gameplay point of view.
is over 5 years old, so there may not be a lot new to say... but let me just tell you, this game is a classic for a reason. Or rather, several reasons:
- Unbelievably beautiful look
- Astounding voice work and sound design
- Not especially hard but a good sense of challenge/gradual improvement. The game seems downright easy up until the turning point when the Survivor figures out what's "really" going on (at least in his mind) and takes bold steps to completely screw things over, at which point the difficulty jumps sharply... bringing it up to a serious level of challenge that any hardcore gamer will appreciate.

This game is filled with challenges, and lets you add more by tacking on Idols (= extra XP-boosting gameplay restrictions) in the Shrine, but what's most fascinating to me is how the toughest levels are tied to the Kid's biggest psychological blocks (Who Knows Where levels and similar). This game is about coming to terms with our own responsibility for the Calamity that made our wonderful world go wrong... a perspective that just about anyone can appreciate from where I'm sitting in May 2017.

If you like
,
and the like, you'll be blown away by
's Western tone, from the acoustic roots/country/sitar-fusion music (surely among the top 3 soundtracks of the past 10 years) and the Stranger's narration to the old-timey weapon inventory and wild, overgrown environments. Even the noblest heroes are filled with regret. Nothing is ever perfect. Even the darkest suffering is beautiful.

This game shows off everything that made its Supergiant successor,
, the great game that it is, but it's anything but a mere precursor.
stands on its own as one of the all-time greats. It doesn't get much better than this.

I backed this game but it's a massive mess. It requires far more system resources than it should. Visuals are low quality and look about the same as the old classic games from which it's inspired. For as much system spec as it demands I'd expect far higher renders for the backgrounds/maps and what little 3D is in the game is also low quality. It looks like the game was actually made in 2004 at best.
The need for 4+ gigs of ram and a Radeon 4850 for a game like this is beyond absurd and screams laziness on behalf of the development team. Many are quick to blame UNITY but there are tons of games on UNITY that are far more amazing visually and full 3D (like The Long Dark) and do not require such ludicrous system spec. The game is basically a large jpg/png for the “world” and some tiny♥♥♥♥♥3D characters and faked lighting. There is no way this game should be so demanding. Anyone playing on a laptop is sure to feel the pain as it will cook your CPU and GPU and drain your battery running the fans faster than you can say “Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥my balls are on fire!”
From there countless game breaking bugs and the more I tried to play the more I seemed to encounter every one of them. Save losses, crashes, lockups, visual glitches. The game is unplayable for me on Windows, ran on Linux with some issues until it decided to corrupt all my save data. Incredibly disappointing for a "gold" launch title. I'm no stranger to bugs but this is easily one of the worst game launches I've ever seen. I'm sure there has been worse issues on games I've never cared to play/experience but for me I've played early access and beta tested games in a better state than this!
From what I have been able to see the game does have a great number of positives but they are overwhelmed by the problems. Maybe I'll play next year and see if they were able to make the game worth while, I've already been waiting over 2 years...what's another year to play a game requiring a super computer to look like it was made 11-12 years ago...
As a backer you take a risk and a risk this was. I know this game could have been great, the team is seasoned but the lack of quality control descimates this release into something awful. My first Steam review. This game earned it, even in it's current state. I tend to be a bit longwinded, so bear with me, or skip this review.
(Note: I've NEVER played any of the other "Survivor Simulator" games out there, so I have nothing to compare it to)
Saw that the game had really positive reviews, was on sale for around 11$, and a game that was essentially the playable version of Cast Away seemed like something I need in my life. MMO's are getting stale, Shooters are getting stale, in fact most games being released these days, just aren't holding my interest for more than a few hours. So I picked this game up because the premise is so different from what I typically look for.
It was a short download, which was sort of expected since it's early release and 98% of the game world is water. Took about a minute to download. Loaded the game up, very simple interface, no flashy intro, no endless logos being cycled. Straight to the point. Clicked Start Game and I'm suddenly in a small airplane enjoying some light turbulence, just relaxing. After a well deserved drink which must have destabilized pressure in the aircraft, a massive hole opens in the side of the plane- we're going down! I wake up under water and swim around trying to find that convenient hole that got us into this mess. Noticed clouds of blood in the water and glanced into the cockpit of the plane to see that both the pilot and co-pilot did not survive. I frantically swim out of the wreckage and up to the surface for an overdue breath of air. There was a life raft waiting for me, so I didn't ask questions- I crawled up into it and passed out. I woke up, I'm assuming, the next morning floating in the ocean, and look around to get my bearings. An island lay not far, so I grabbed the paddle at my feet and started rowing like a madman.
This game is beautiful, even in these early stages. The light reflections on the water, the reef environments in the shallows, the moonlight dancing on the gentle waves at night, the humid haze, the sharks- It is very nice on the eyes. It runs like like butter down the sides of a hot biscuit. Great framerate at max settings with an aging rig (best thing I got is a GTX 750 Ti, everything else is due for an upgrade). I hope this doesn't change much as assets/ game mechanics are added over time.
You have three vitals that you must pay attention to in order to survive: Health, Hunger, and Thirst. You keep those levels up, obviously, by eating and drinking, sleeping, and avoiding injury, from say, falling off a palm tree. Or getting mauled by sharks. It's a very simple game in this state, but its crazy addicting- I played for 4 hours straight the first night, far past my bed time, and I couldn't wait to play it the next day.
After a few weeks of being nervous about paddling through shark infested waters to one of the islands in the hazy distance, I needed more materials if I was to make survival more comfortable, so hesitantly, I paddled off to a random island to scavenge what I could. There are shipwrecks both above, and below the surface of the water, and some smaller boat ruins that contain an item here and there- a flashlight here, a knife there, maybe some vitamins. There are no magic bullets to find, just small things that add up to slightly more comfortable survival. I love it.
This game is wonderful, even though it's incomplete. It's a breath of fresh air that I desperately needed. It's a break from the monotonous horde of shooters, MMO's and other games that are seriously lacking these days.
This game however does have some issues, which based on it's current quality, are surely going to be fixed. I'll start with the cons, many of which others have mentioned.
_Cons_
-You can literally sprint right up a palm tree, but if you go down the wrong boat hatch, you cannot climb back out,      even if you can jump halfway out. There is no climbing mechanic for ledges at this moment.
-There is no tutorial explaining the functions of your watch, or even telling you that you have one in the first place. There aren't any tuturials in fact, save for the one telling you how to make a martini at the beginning.
-You have 8 item slots. Not a big deal, but you can only carry stacks of 4 items in each slot. So 4 large stone hammers consumes a slot, or 4 whole coconuts, or...4 small pocket knives? You can carry 32 sledge hammers maximum, but you can also only carry 32 small shards of rock, max. Smaller items should have larger stack sizes, and larger ones should have smaller stack sizes.
-You can only have 1 saved game file. 1. So, currently, my girlfriend cannot try this game out because she would have to overwrite my save, and I CANNOT under any circumstance allow that.
-There is very little wildlife in the game currently- a few species of small fish, tiger sharks, great whites, a whale, and sea urchin, at least thats all I've seen. No birds, reptiles, rats (which are found on nearly every island in the world), bugs, etc.
-Traveling from island to island in a life raft with a single paddle is soul crushing. You have to paddle for what seems like days. I get it, it's a simulator, but you have to click for every paddle stroke, you can't even hold the mouse button down to paddle. I do not want to wear my mouse out for more sticks, rocks, or the off chance of finding a high quality axe.
There are some minor glitches here and there, nothing game breaking though, and I haven't experienced a single crash the entire time I've played. Now for the Pros:
_Pros_
-Beautiful game setting. Water looks nice, reflections are good. When you dive under you really get a feeling of being under water. Lighting and environment effects are realistic and easy on the eyes.
-Very immersive. You feel like you are really there. There is no HUD, you simply have a watch that you can look at plus a simple inventory screen. It's just you, and nature.
-Seeing sharks swimming around your boat when you venture out really puts you on edge, especially when they bump your raft with their tail and nearly knock you into the water.
-Building your own little paradise out of crude materials is good fun, and though incomplete, is a strong foundation to keep me playing until I build a metropolis out of sticks, rocks, and lashings.
-This game really taps into your navigational skills. If you don't pay attention when travelling away from your base camp, you can be lost and wandering for hours. Pay attention to the sun. Paddle in straight lines, and lay a stick on the ground pointing to your home island next to your raft. Even if you manage to find a compass, it only makes it a bit easier.

Solid shooter. I liked the plot and the atmosphere. Had some good jump scares and some genuinely creeeeepy moments. A decent take on time travel story-wise. The only negatives I would give the game are the following:
1. It has a BAD case of "consolitis". Meaning that you can tell it was primarily designed for game consoles not PC gaming. This is NEVER a good thing.
--You can only have two weapons which is stupid and really restricts the fun as you often don't have the weapon you need for a certain situation and keeps you from experimenting with new weapons when you've settled in on two you find useful.
--You only have save points in the game and can't save when you want to. This keeps you from exploring and trying different things. On top of that you only have one save so once you hit a save spot, you can't go back to previous spots. At least there's plenty of them so you hardly ever have to replay large sections of the game when you die or have to quit in the middle of an save chunk. Also, the game immediately closes off any area you've been to so there's no going back for any reason.
2. The ending is, iffy. There are four total endings and while it does let you go back and do each one without restarting the game, none of them are particularly satisfying. Not bad just not satisfying. It appears that they left it pseudo-open for the sequel that's never going to happen now that the company has been disbanded.
All in all a fun ride with some slight flaws. Don't know if I'd play through it again, but I'd certainly recommend it.

Singularity is a game developed by Raven Software and published by Activision. Singularity is singularly good (#cleverwording)
This little-known title is a cracker of a game which, even though it borrows from several other games, does so in it’s own idiosyncratic and original way rather than simply ripping them off. There isn’t a dull moment in its five or so hours of gameplay and the always enjoyable combat is backed by a solid story, good voice acting, some cool enemies, and a decent A.I.
There’s a wide variety of weapons available and every one of them feels good to wield and most of them produce very satisfying results. However, it’s the Time Manipulation Device (or TMD) that’s the star of the show and this weapon/tool is impressively designed and implemented. It allows the player to manipulate both time and matter in a number of ways every one of which is great fun to use
Graphically the game is acceptable enough, although some of the textures leave a little to be desired, some people have experienced glitches but I had none, and you get to fight your way through a reasonably varied range of well-designed environments
As a story-driven, linear FPS, Singularity hits the nail on the head and does so with a refreshing streak of inventiveness and individuality. I just wish it had lasted a little longer, as I was having so much fun!

Many of the negative reviews mention that the port is bad.  “It’s only 30 FPS which means it’s literally unplayable”, and stuff like that.  This is not one of those reviews.  I usually like to add something humorous in these intros but, like Dark Souls’ gameplay, there’s nothing fun or humorous here.
Let’s start with what the game is, and does well: hack-and-slash.  You press one button for a weak attack and press another for a strong.  You can combo them into each other and there're your directional based attacks, as well.  It’s got that part down quite well.  You make your character (that’s kind of limited in options but it’ll get covered up with armor in due time) and, over time, pick your weaponry and armor.  Over the course of the game, you get a wide range of gear.  From the regular broadsword to a two handed claymore.  Several types of daggers, to axes, scythes, a dozen polearms, swords too big to actually wield, a few fist weapons, katanas, hammers and fancy swords.  There are also whips and bows but...uhh...yeah, don’t use those.  There are also three types of magic: Sorcery, black magic-esq; pyromancy; throw fire at people; and miracles, white magic and support.  Those descriptions aren’t the best and there’s a bit of crossover but it’ll work.
Armor comes in three types, light, medium, and heavy.  The difference in the three is the type of evasiveness and speed.  Lower weight = longer roll and more invincibility frames during the roll.  If you’re too heavy, then you can’t roll and your movement speed is terrible but absorb more damage.
The weapon and armor types allows for a good amount of customization.  If you allocate stats correctly, you can build however you want. Berserker, Dragoon, thief, a tank who specializes in magic.  Everything is possible - although it might not be viable but, hey, you bought the game.
As you search for gear you travel across the mountain called Lordran and kill dead things.  Lots and lots of dead things; and of varying types.  There are also rats, dogs, demons, egg-heads, dragons, gods, and the occasional actual living, person.  There’s a few more but that’s the jist.  I’d say why but I’m not totally sure why.  One day you get locked up in prison and someone lets you out for reasons never mentioned.  There’s a lot of reasons never mentioned in the game.
It also looks nice.  Visuals are appealing, although if you get too close it starts to look pixelated.  If you’re not happy with it all then head over the
and download some HD textures.
Music is wonderful but it only exists in boss battles.  It’s a wonderful assortment of orchestral and ethereal sounds.  Motoi Sakuraba has always been of my favorite, lesser known, video game composers and I’m glad to see he still has it.  I can’t find any official sources so here’s a

And, sadly, that’s all that the game does well.
While you traverse the land of Lordran you are in constant danger of dying.  Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty and there’s a reason for that.  There is no plot, there is no direction, there is no character development.  The camera will fail you, the auto lock will fail you, and the terrain will fail you.
I say there’s no plot but that is, technically, a lie.  You see the fire’s dying and someone needs to keep it lit.  What happens after you relight it?  Dunno.  What happens if you don’t light it?  Dunno.  There’s not a lot of closure in the game and it all just feels lazy and a waste.  You went through all of that for what?  Why did I kill this person?  Why couldn’t I talk to this guy?  Why are these guys so upset?  Who was this NPC person I summoned?  I have more questions than answers because the game provides no answers.
I also lied about character development as it does exist but only for a few NPCs who die.  You find various NPCs throughout Lordran, free them from their hardship, they show-up in your base of operations, and that’s it.  Sometimes they sell stuff but otherwise, they just sit there until something triggers them to leave and you have to kill them.

From a technical aspect, the game has flaws.  The camera hates when you turn and it’ll let you know by having you walk off a ledge.  The auto-lock works only when it feels like it and will fail to work when you need it.  You often have to be right in your enemies’ face so it’s hard to put yourself in proper position in boss fights.  Hitboxes come and go.  Sometimes they work, often they don’t.  For a game that is built on difficulty, the technical unreliabilities often make the game less challenging and more outright not fair.  There’s a difference between being hard and cheating.
The gameplay is just boring.  Because of the unforgiving difficulty, you’re going to die.  A lot.  Because of that, you’re going to be doing the same thing over and over and over and over and over again.  Killing/running from the same guys.  Walking long distances.  It’s a lesson in tedium.  You’ll learn quickly that walking for 3 minutes to die in a fight that takes 10 seconds isn’t fun.  And when you are in battle, it’s mostly just holding a shield or dodging for a while and only occasionally doing damage.  You’ll be looking for openings to heal more often than not.  Dark Souls is a game about patience, not aggression.  Punish your opponents or else they punish you.  That’s great but strafing for 10 minutes isn’t my idea of enjoyable.
Dark Souls is known only for its difficulty.  Had I only realized that sooner, I might have enjoyed it but I thought a modern game would have some semblance of story and finality.  Instead, I get a grind that never feels worth it.  Killing bosses never made me feel like I accomplished something: it was all luck based.  The hitboxes screwed-up again or the boss just didn’t use THAT move.  If you remove the difficulty, then you have no plot, you have no reason to care about of the characters you’ve saved, you have no reason to feel like it all meant anything.  It’s a poor hack and slash that feel devoid of reason.  Dark Souls could have good but the devs didn’t feel like adding plot and what little they did add is vague and might not mean anything since “Time is Messed-up”.  What’s there is nice though.
I wanted to like Dark Souls but too much of a frustrating grind and it just feels empty.  And I didn't even mention the controls and the terrible jumping mechanics, or accidental kicks.  There’s plenty of length but there’s just no depth.  It’s a hard game for the sake of being hard an that’s what you get.

I can't recommend this game highly enough.
PROS:  Open-world play.  This game has some fun zombie-stomping action along with a heavy survival element.  You have to establish and maintain a base, various supplies, ammunition, food, and personnel.  People dying is permanent and realistic.  Much of the game is spent exploring the world and various buildings looking for supplies.  There are several random side-quests that pop up that are optional, but beneficial to do.  Characters don't level up per se, but their skills improve as you use them, making them more capable of fighting and surviving.  You also have to build a base, decide what add-ons to put on it, and maintain it.  There is a lot to keeping up with this game.  Even when you log off, the next time you play it passes the time since you last played and tells you what has occurred in that time.  If you left your people or base in a bad state, bad things can happen!  The graphics are good, voice acting excellent, and sounds are very well done.
CONS:  Very short, unforutunately. The main story is about 30 hrs give or take if you do as many side quests as possible.  Breakdown adds an infinite sandbox mode, which is much longer obviously.    Graphics on the PC are good, but very dark.  I have to bump the gamma up right off.  There is some rather foul spoken language that you can't censor.
Overall, this is one of the best new games I've played in a long time.  highly highly recommended!

I can honestly say, this is the first game to truly rival the feeling I had when I booted up my first PC RPG more than 15 years ago. The incredibly written dialouge, the intricate character creation and wonderful supporting cast are just icing on top of a wonderfully crafted cake of exploration and combat that place this game amongst the RPG elite. Job very well done, Obsidian.

So, it's exciting to see this genre of RPG come back, but I felt like PoE had a lot of problems. When I started, I would have reccomended this game, but a couple of dozen hours in have changed my mind. I agree with what a lot of the negative reviews have written, the game is buggy. Holy cow is it buggy. I've duped and destroyed random items; I've lost racial abilities because I double clicked something; I've entered into a room that caused the entire game to crash every time I left it so I had to return to an earlier save.
Combat feels grueling to me. In many areas, you're encountering a group of mooks every few steps and sneaking isn't wholly reliable. About 12 hours into the game I found myself wishing that there was something to do other than fight through this never-ending wall of guys to get from Point A to Point B, where I talk to an NPC who will turn aggro and force me into another fight. There is very, very little in the way of crowd control for your tanky characters. No way for them to reliably pull hate off of your overly squishy wizards, chanters and ciphers. The aforementioned caster-types have abilities that are largely AOE and the AOE will affect allies, making many spells extremely situational. You will often be fighting in cramped passageways that preclude using a lot of the wizard damage spells if you don't want to kill your first line of defense.
Also, why does might effect magic abilities? That's goofy.
Food, scrolls and traps feel like more effort than they are worth. Traps, especially, since I've yet to reliably use stealth in a fashion that would allow me to lay traps effectively. Crafting also feels a bit half-realized. After a while the stronghold mostly feels like a chore.
Story-wise, this is pretty standard fantasy fare. I find myself seeing a LOT of parallels to the original BG which at first felt referential and now just kind of feel derivative. There are some neat concepts thrown in, but a whole ton of worldbuilding concepts and terms whizz by and for me only a few concepts really stuck as important; sort of reminded me of playing Final Fantasy XIII. I find myself having trouble keeping This Fancy Sounding Noun and That Proper Name apart, and had difficulty caring about Such-and-Such-Important-Event.
Quests often involve going to some place and talking to some dude who either turns aggro or sends you off to a third place to kill some other dude; at the third place, you can either kill this dude or go back and kill the first dude.
I did find myself entering into each new town grimly wondering how many &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or battered woman" quests I would encounter; I think it averaged around 2 per town/city hub. Seriously, guys, the trope is exhausted. If you can say 'some guys stole my artifact' or 'so I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my neice and impregnated her an then some guys kidnapped her and are committing further attrocities on her' to get me to go to the same place and either would work interchangeably without altering the plot in any meaningful way, I would vastly prefer the first option because at this point going to retreive a shiny rock as a quest feels fresher than going to retreive the♥♥♥♥♥♥victim. They're both just treated like objects, anyway, right? So how about using the one that doesn't make me roll my eyes so hard that they literally never stop spinning? Effectively, Obsidian's tired use of the good ole refrigerator trope has created a perpetual motion machine from my eyeballs. Gratz on that, guys. Maybe you should kickstart some research into this phenomenon.
Bringing it back around to bugs, I seem to have gotten myself into a corner with my current save. I can't progress further in the main plot because my standing with the three main factions of the city in act 2 is too high to get an offer from faction #4, but I also cannot get the offer I need from the other 3 factions. My understanding is that if I go in and slaughter every NPC in each of the three main factions that I can get an offer from the fourth faction to continue to main plot, but at that point I'm not really roleplaying anymore so why not just trash 30 hours of gameplay and start over again? I think I'll pass.

Bought this game for me and my girlfriend, expecting something along the lines of Terraria and it was just a mind boggling mess.
Firstly, the game has some nice things, the combat is OK, the music is wonderful and the sprite art style is amazing, but all these things were just buried under the awkward gameplay, convoluded story and odd game design decisions that make you scratch your head.
First of all, the game is blatantly anti co-op and discourages teamwork. Why do both players have to complete every quest, and the quest items and progress is not shared at all? At one point in the game, we came across a quest that had us fetching 10 copper bars for whatever reason, and when I turned them in, we didn't realize that my girlfriend had to do it too, and she didn't have enough, so we had to backtrack to the planet again to find some. It's such busy work and makes no sense.
Secondly, there's no MAP screen (or atleast we didn't find one) which is so aggrevating, because it's so easy to get lost, especially underground which can be an endless maze full of tunnels and canyons.
Also, they got really, really lazy with the quests. We came across a village where 3 NPCs had exactly the same quest, where you go running around smelting silver ores, making us run around the village stupidly. It's busy work. It got even worse when we came across an NPC that told us to deliver a message to another NPC that was standing RIGHT NEXT TO HIM. It just makes no sense.
Other gameplay flaws are for example, the movement is so slippery, regardless of the surface you're on, that it's so easy to fall down platforms, and it feels like you are standing on ice constantly. There's no friction whatsoever.
Sometimes the quest objectives are also super confusing. One of the first quests you get is retrieving 20 crystals from a mine so you can fix your ship, but you can't retrieve the BRIGHTLY glowing crystals scattered around the mine, instead, you get ONE crystal in the end that counts for those 20 crystals. Why does the game trick you? It's just aggrevating and misguided.
Starbound is an example of game that tried to achieve too much, and just collapsed under it's own weight.
It's ironic that the main theme of the game is aliens, when the game itself feels like it was designed by one.
Not worth it.

I'm not generally driven to write reviews here, but this game has impressed me so much I felt it was owed another gushing review.
I've played various WRPGs and JRPGs for many years now, including most of both the Final Fantasy and Elder Scrolls series. In my opinion, this game offers a perfect mix of the two. It's quirky and unexpectedly humorous, with an attention to detail which makes it both endearing and engaging. Wade too far in some water and you'll be drenched - and this is relevant in combat. Had your lantern out when you did it? It'll go dark.
One thing which I feel is an unfortunate feature of open world gaming is prioritizing size of the environment over quality of the environment. I love to believe that the world which I am playing in is a living, breathing one which I can be immersed in. This is a large open world, but every bit of it feels relevant, either for the purpose of storytelling or gameplay.
Currently taking on the challenge of Bitterblack Isle, and the combat just gets better and better. Yes, it's challenging, but it's so much fun that my motivation to learn more never wavers. The difference in gameplay between classes is quite vast, so the option to change at any time is a welcome choice when wanting to change things up a bit.
Also, renting other player's pawns is awesome. I had my very own Princess Mononoke!
Repetitive quests, difficult travel system, and poor monster scaling to level. Do like the NPC use, but is not enough to make me want to play beyond level 10.

This could have been a great game, but the developers don't give a care about unit balance. Commandos one-shot almost any unit in the game with their active, and hit tank-type units for 3/4ths of their HP anyway, and Grenadiers trade the cloaking ability for the ability to 1-shot any unit ever with their active, in an 8 yard diameter to boot. Commandos aren't available till level 26, and Grenadiers cost thousands of gold.
Arhats and Sentinels make playing air-based armies impossible in any game they're present in, in addition to being the strongest midgame grunt unit of their faction, and despite being basic units anyone can access within the first few levelups, they make low-tier play a monotonous chore broken up only by the occasional use of commander skills by choking out pretty much any specialist unit. So if you're willing to spam the same units over and over again, then grind to spam the same elite units over and over again, this is the game for you.
Arena provides little respite, because although everyone is given a random selection of units, someone out of the six people in your match will inevitably be randomly given one of the "OP" units, and proceed to spam it the whole game, with whichever randomly arranged team having more randomly-assigned OP units winning. Ranked provides a ban system, but each team only gets a single unit ban, making it impossible to completely eliminate unbalanced units from the game. Ban Arhats and everyone will play Terran Commandos, ban Commandos and everyone will play Atlac Arhats, both teams somehow ban both, and then you get a rare game where you actually have room to experiment, strategize, and play rock-paper-scissors instead of rock-paper-scissors-sniper rifle... Assuming nobody is playing rock-paper-scissors-grenade.
*Sigh*
I really wanted to find a deeper layer of strategy, but most steam guides can be summed up in a paragraph or two thanks to the essentially broken unit balance. The community is also toxic as heck thanks to the violent clash of primarily American and Chinese cultures, and so much as asking for a simple change on the forum will summon a hate squad in whatever language you choose. So the game is beta, I can get over that. So the English localization is far from perfect, I can get over that. So the game is unplayable if you refuse to use one of four OP units? I can't get over that. Sorry.
/rant

This game is a underrated FPS gem. Singularity is a 2010 FPS by the legendary developers Raven Soft. The game is set in two timelines. One in 1950 and one in 2010. There is obviously some time travel involved and the TMD. TMD stands for Time Manipulation Device. This device gives you varying abilities, including but not limited to deploying  a stasis field and rapidly aging and unageing objects. Using this abilities is a lot of fun and very well implemented. The game has a unusual difficulty curve in the sense that it stars out hard and becomes easier as you get more abilities. The is one of the best FPS games I played this year. The only problem I have is that the game is short at 9 hours per playthrough. Definitely recommend.

So Singularity is a game made by Raven software back before they were just another call of duty studio. This game did not sell very well and thats why they just help with call of duty games now.
This game is fairly unique taking place in a world were the soviete union never fell, it doesnt really go into why it never fell but insteads it takes place on a single island that the USSR abandoned for an unkown reason. The US government sends you  and others to find out what this island is. Then pretty much in the first 10 minutes everything goes wrong. The helicopter you are riding in goes down and only 1 other member survives. You make your way thru the island which has tones of lore and stuff to click on. You find out this place was to test an element called E-99 that was suppposed to beat Americas nuclear power.
This element E-99 has some crazy powers to it and you find out it could be used to alter reality like making plants grow or even reverse aging. But with all things it was used as a weapon and thats were things went really wrong on this island because it mutated people and multiple other things.
So a little while later you enter a building after seeing an amazing bust of Stalin ( most likely made of Stalinium)  and soon after you get sent back in time right when the facility went defunct and exploded. It takes a weird turn when you rescue a random person. It terns out rescuing this person had weird affects on time.
This is all about the first 30 minutes of the story.
Lets talk about gameplay.
It starts out has a horror game with spooky parts and jumpscares ( really there is jumpscares thru the entire game).  The gun play is pretty close to call of duty. If you remove the monsters and just have weird time stuff this could of easilt been called Call of duty:  Singularity thru time or some other name.
Besides the random monster encounters you are shooting at generic Soviet soldiers, the only real change in these soldiers is basically juggernauts like ion call of duty. This game is really similar to call of duty.
The monster designs are pretty unique rather then just simple zombies. There is a tall stretched out one, mutated soldiers that have electrical powers and can teleport and more I dont want to spoil all the monsters.
Besides the generic shooting you have several weird weapons that rely on E-99 they are mostly useless and I just found the shotgun be good for 95% of the game. The other 5% I used the minigun.
Then finally you get a time device that goes on your wrist. It has several uses like fixing broken things, braking working things, aging monsters and creating time bubbles. YOu can also kill enamies with it but it was just easier to unload on enamies with the shotgun.
There was one part that I thought was pretty unique. The way it put you into the stealth section instead of just disabling your weapon or punishing you for using it in said part the game slowly made ammo more and more scarce leading up to this part so by the time you got to the stealth section you had little to no ammo.
The best thing about the game are the endings. Yes endings plural and they are all amazing. Honestly the endings blew me away. Now I only did one ending but I watched the others.
The game has multiplayer but I dont think anyone is playing it.
This game is great but has some flaws. 7.5/10. Get it during a steam sale.

Singularity crossed my radar back in 2012, someone from a gaming club i was part of suggested it. Apparently it didnt do so well upon release and im not surprised since i didnt even know it existed.
I bought it for the Xbox 360 and i really liked it, it seemed like a cross between Fear 2 and COD4 and i was pleasantly surprised by this.
The games' plot is rather thin and rather cliche, but i like it none the less. It has an engaging plot (although the "twist" is revealed to you in the fist 30 minutes so i wouldnt really call it a twist) that held my attention all the way until the end. The A.I. is competent enough and there are some interesting mechanics at play, namely that the player can use time travelling abilities. The use of time travel has been done before in games but the game keeps the idea fresh by introducing some cool puzzles and making the game challenging while fun.
The game isnt terribly long (about 8 hours or so) but considering the price these days that seems like an okay deal.
The issue i have with it is that the graphics options are non- existant. You can choose between a handful of resolutions (although there are not nearly enough choices in my opinion) and a few other bits but there are no advanced settings like shadows, lighting, or even textures. The game looks okay in general but the textures look awful in some areas and the lighting effects have aged terribly.
Desipte these issues the game does run like a dream!
There are a few other minor issues: The hit- detection seems flimsey at times, there is no navigation indecator or mini- map, and you basically trip over health kits and e99 which detracts away from the challenge somewhat (although this is negated slightly by the puzzles).
All in all it is a good game, but my recommendation depends on price. If you can get the game for less than £10 then i'd say its worth it, if not then dont bother.

The game that started one of the biggest sci-fi adventures in gaming history. It's got everything required to make it a classic; interesting and fun characters with unique cultures,  philospohical questions and moral dilemmas, all wrapped around a well-paced and intriguing story (in my opinion the best in the series). Throughout a lot of the game, characters will spend a LOT of time explaining things to you, like how cultures work and such.  The story, as I mentioned earlier is great, but the gameplay is not. Combat is fairly clunky, cover system is awkward, every gun feels the same, a lot of enemies are braindead and just run up to you with no regard for their own personal safety. Not exactly the highlight of the game, to put it mildly. The Mako, the vehicle which you use for explo-ration as well as a lot of missions, isn't much better either. It's awkward, handles very poorly and is very boring in use for combat, it's generally used for padding outgame length.
Still, it is all in all an amazing game, and gets a 9.1/10 from me.

Bought this game for me and my girlfriend, expecting something along the lines of Terraria and it was just a mind boggling mess.
Firstly, the game has some nice things, the combat is OK, the music is wonderful and the sprite art style is amazing, but all these things were just buried under the awkward gameplay, convoluded story and odd game design decisions that make you scratch your head.
First of all, the game is blatantly anti co-op and discourages teamwork. Why do both players have to complete every quest, and the quest items and progress is not shared at all? At one point in the game, we came across a quest that had us fetching 10 copper bars for whatever reason, and when I turned them in, we didn't realize that my girlfriend had to do it too, and she didn't have enough, so we had to backtrack to the planet again to find some. It's such busy work and makes no sense.
Secondly, there's no MAP screen (or atleast we didn't find one) which is so aggrevating, because it's so easy to get lost, especially underground which can be an endless maze full of tunnels and canyons.
Also, they got really, really lazy with the quests. We came across a village where 3 NPCs had exactly the same quest, where you go running around smelting silver ores, making us run around the village stupidly. It's busy work. It got even worse when we came across an NPC that told us to deliver a message to another NPC that was standing RIGHT NEXT TO HIM. It just makes no sense.
Other gameplay flaws are for example, the movement is so slippery, regardless of the surface you're on, that it's so easy to fall down platforms, and it feels like you are standing on ice constantly. There's no friction whatsoever.
Sometimes the quest objectives are also super confusing. One of the first quests you get is retrieving 20 crystals from a mine so you can fix your ship, but you can't retrieve the BRIGHTLY glowing crystals scattered around the mine, instead, you get ONE crystal in the end that counts for those 20 crystals. Why does the game trick you? It's just aggrevating and misguided.
Starbound is an example of game that tried to achieve too much, and just collapsed under it's own weight.
It's ironic that the main theme of the game is aliens, when the game itself feels like it was designed by one.
Not worth it.

The goal for Pillars of Eternity was to recapture the essence of old RPG games like Balder's Gate or Icewind Dale.  This game not only succeeds at this...it triumphs.  Character creation is very easy to follow with excellent descriptions and explanations to help you understand your stats, spells, etc.. In-game controls and UI are also easy to master; and with a multitude of options for customizing what you see, how you see it, and when the game will pause itself, you will feel comfortable playing in no time.
While all of that is a major plus, making the game fun to play, the best part of Pillars of Eternity is the story.  The developers could've easily just have done a simple fantasy trope and put the Baulder's Gate skin over it.  Here though, we have a very interesting and engrossing story, one that I instantly fell into and became obsessed over.  Some of the descriptions are down-right poetic.  The music is very well done as well, really captuing the fantasy spirit.
This game will not be fore everyone though.  If you do not like reading a lot of text or if you don't like a lot of point and click dialogue; Pillars of Eternity will not appeal to you.  There are no fast-paced combat maneuvers or CGI cutscenes.  Most of the cutscenes are simply displayed like a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure Novel and combat is really simply picking an attack or spell and unpausing the game to see what happens.  If such a notion doesn't appeal to you, then I would pass on this.  If you have played/enjoyed Balder's Gate or Icewind Dale back in the day or now on your mobile device...then you really will love this game.

A contender entering the RPG arena against such classics as Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Icewind Dale - such a game in 2015 was considered risky - but with nostaglic thoughts of the afformentioned games in full effect, Pillars of Eternity pulls it off competently.
8/10

Overall, a good game for a newcomer, and an amazing nostalgia-filled experience for a Homestuck fan, at a surprisingly fair price.
8/10, 9/10 if you're a fan of Homestuck.

It's ok. It feels like it lacks some polish, but it worked and I didn't run into any issues which is more than you can say for many games these days. The resolution felt a bit weird. I'm not sure why they made the screen so wide or fixed the aspect ratio but whatever, that's nitpicking.
The way the game starts throws you directly into the action, which is nice, but the way they presented it is a bit jarring. Apart from that, it's nice. The puzzles are neat, although I wish they'd made some things a bit more obvious, like explaining properly what your weapons do when you get them. I had to figure it out for myself and it was a bit frustrating. When I got the hang of the system, though, it was pretty cool.
I'm not a big fan of the battles. They're not much more than puzzles, and the way you go about solving them just doesn't seem to fit the idea of "I'm locked in combat with a deadly monster". There weren't too many of them though, so while they felt kind of weird to play I didn't get hung up on it for too long.
Generally, the story was good. I could immerse myself into what's going on. My only complaint is Jude's dialogue. As a character, he's annoyingly obtuse about telling you what to do and they made the choice of putting it in all-caps too. Not the biggest fan. The later conversations between Xefros and Joey are much easier to read and more pleasant in general. Another thing to note is that so far things seem increbibly linear. The game isn't choice-based.
This episode was short. I think a little too short. That said, the story did cut off at a good point; it didn't feel like it ended abruptly. Would I say it's worth it for the price? Honestly, not really. $7.99 is a bit steep for something that only took 2-3 hours to play through. But we'll see whether future acts deliver on being more worthwhile.
If you're a homestuck fan, it's nice. If you think you can happily enjoy 2-3 hours of homestuck stuff as an actual game, rather than a webcomic about a game, for the price it's being sold at, go ahead and buy it. It's not bad, and I certainly don't regret getting the game. Just keep in mind its strengths and flaws.
If you're not a homestuck fan, I'm not sure it's worth getting, especially at the current price. It has in-jokes and familiar terminology and mechanics that would be lost on anyone not at least slightly familiar with the homestuck universe. It's clearly geared to those already familiar with the source material. If you're interested anyway, try reading Homestuck first. It'll help you understand what's going on.

As a long time Homestuck fan, I loved everything about this game, and I am already counting down the days for Act 2! (god bless) Very cute, fun puzzles, and beautiful animations and scenery, not to mention funny, but that's a given when it's made by Hussie. I feel as though it would be confusing for someone who hasn't read Homestuck to play this game, but hey, it has plenty of positive qualities on its own!! It DID have problems running on my computer, such as glitching animations and freezing, but nothing that ruined the experience, and nothing I can't watch footage of on Youtube anyway! Summary: Loved it, and looking forward to more!!

This little-known title is a cracker of a game which, even though it borrows from several other games, does so in it’s own idiosyncratic and original way rather than simply ripping them off. There isn’t a dull moment in its 10 or so hours of gameplay and the always enjoyable combat is backed by a solid story, good voice acting, some cool enemies, and a decent AI. There’s a wide variety of weapons available and every one of them feels good to wield and most of them produce very satisfying results. However, it’s the Time Manipulation Device that’s the star of the show and this weapon/tool is impressively designed and implemented. It allows the player to manipulate both time and matter in a number of ways every one of which is great fun to use. Graphically the game is acceptable enough, although some of the textures leave a little to be desired (some people have experienced glitches but I had none), and you get to fight your way through a reasonably varied range of well-designed environments. As a story-driven, linear FPS SINGULARITY hits the nail on the head and does so with a refreshing streak of inventiveness and individuality. I just wish it had lasted a little longer, as I was having so much fun. 4/5

This game out of all the games I have played from Half-Life 2, to PORTAL 1 (& 2), to Time Rifters is one of the more interesting but odd FPS game I have played in recent years, with a great concept that had a good execution in the conclusion, let's start off with the basic main setting, you are a soldier in what I think is either the Russian Military, US Army, or Marine Core, going to investigate a abandonned island near Russia to find a small town near the docks in ruins, to which, as you explore to see what happened, a big wave of energy then came towards you before you are transported into the past, which was the same area, except newly developed & on fire, but as you are running through the burning down facility, you come across a man trying to get out of a burning room to which you save him, & after so you are transported back to your time... But wait, there's more, the man you saved, has changed the world drastically, negative or positive? Not gonna spoil it, you have to play it.
Now onto the gameplay, & mechanics, the hit detection always seemed okay, all my shots hit the enemy I was aiming at in  the right way, the guns are fairly different from real life guns, making them look interesting & new, but in all reality, they handle the same as real life guns, but this isn't a modern shooter as it includes medpacks, the sound effects of the guns don't sound all too impactful, but it isn't too bad, now onto the other mechanics, later on in the beginning you recieve this device known as the TMD, which can do many things, such as making objects age to new, or age to dust, but this doesn't exactly do this to everything, but it is still used while not feeling too much like a gimmick as you will come across new safe's that you have to age so you can get whats inside, or find a aged crate you can bring into modern age so you can get whats inside of it, & along side this you get whats called the Deadlock, to which you fire out an orb that expands on contact, & inside this orb time is slowed down, basically it's bullet time but only for a specific area, so it isn't too special, but it still is an interesting gadget incase there is a group of enemies, never gets old deadlocking a bunch of enemies in a area before blasting all their heads with a shotgun.
My overall conclusion, the story itself is intruiging, but what always scratched my head is how under developed some characters feel like, to which, there are pretty much only four characters in this campaign you really meet, now as for the overall gameplay, it is non-stop action, & even when the game takes a break to tell story, it is usually short & fast, one thing I wish they did in this game is to maybe make it more challenging, there are some frustrating areas, but this game is overall easy, & if your an experienced FPS player, I'd highly suggest playing it on Hard mode, cause even on hard mode for me, a player who beat DOOM, & QUAKE, only beat this game in 5-6 hours, & yes, this game did needed length cause it is a short game, but for a short game, it is damn worth every penny (Atleast, on the sale, buy it on sale), as it is so fun, I overall give it a 7/10 Great Fun, but a few short ends that keeps this game from being "Game of The Year" Great.
But to me, it is "Underrated FPS of The Decade" Great.

Another Perspective is quite an interesting game to say the least. There isn't really a story. The game more or less tries teach the player about a way of thinking, which explains the title. "So... The title is a spoiler?" you'd might ask. "Exactly." would be my reply, but the game tells it in quite an intriguing way,  a way I personally didn't see coming. It takes, the whole there's someone else who sais and thinks diffirent thing, what you've seen in the trailers and takes it few steps further. This, in turn, gives the story a little more weight to it, and, in my books, makes it a little bit better. The game really tries to make you think, but after a while it will be a little more brunt with its message, and you will notice that. That's quite the shame though, because at one point it really was making me ponder and this just made me lose the immersion it created.
Now for the mechanics and design.
Lets start with the art design:
The art design is pretty good. The levels look boring, just brown and grey brown. The character though, that's what I really liked. The drawing style was just a breath a fresh air for me, since I've gotten used to the standard triple A level of charachter creation.
Next up, the mechanics:
The mechanics are fine, great even. Mechanics are introduced and reused. The mechanics are varied and work as they should. And there's one more thing, a very big and important thing. Gameplay work together with the "story". Seriously, this game does things better than most triple A's out there.
And lastly, design:
The levels are good enough. For me at least. I haven't got that much experience with puzzle platformers so I was surprised at the difficulty of this game. Other won't have this problem, because they have superbrains or something. The difficulty ramps up to almost at the end, but it never overstays it welcom by presenting levels that look very much alike over and over again. It is really short because of this, which is a shame, but I can't hate it for that little flaw.
In conclusion. Some people might like it for the message, some for the mechanics and some for the challenge. In my opinion is the design not something which will hold it up, but it did help me in the decision making.
I hope you do buy this lovely little game and have fun.
A very clever self-aware 2D puzzler.

This game reminded me of some other beautiful indie games like Closure, The Misadventures of PB Winterbottom, The Swapper and Braid. Yes, its gameplay is similar to those games, but Another Perspective is still an original work. The puzzles are not much challenging but not as easy as to make the game boring. I really liked the humorous narrative, funny details, hidden places and achievements.

Another Perspective is a quick, fun puzzle platformer with interesting game mechanics.  While on the short side (I completed the whole thing in less than 4 hours), its simple, well-designed structure makes it fun to play.  The levels tend to range from easy to moderate difficulty, which keeps things interesting without getting frustrating.  There are only a few difficult levels, including one that actually requires taking advantage of a 'glitch' in the game mechanics, showing some extra creativity on the designer's part.
The Steam achievements are appropriate and keep the player looking for a few rewarding easter eggs within the game.  It also has an amusing "story" intended to make a player think, but not too hard.  It is obviously a game someone took pride in creating, and I would recommend this to any puzzle game enthusiast from beginner to expert, especially if it is on sale.

Decent little puzzler/platformer that borrows heavily from two indie darlings,
and
, and features not so much a story as a stream-of-consciousness exploration of self in a "conversation" between the player and the creator of the game. It's a bit challenging towards the end (I had to resort to watching a Youtube walkthrough for one of the puzzles) but for the most part not the kind of thing that'll make you want to tear your hair out.
It's enjoyable enough, though quite short. My playtime shows about 4½ hours because I goofed off a bit, but you could easily complete it in 2 hours I imagine. There is an extra game mode called "Mystery" that I haven't tried yet but which has bonus levels that are supposedly trickier than the story levels, and there is an achievement for a speed run of the main story mode, so there is a bit of replay value.
If I had a gripe with the game it would be that the story is rather meandering and slightly plagued with filler-itis, and while it tries to be thought-provoking and deep, it unfortunately reminds me of something you might see posted on
or
. It does, for me, bring to mind the concepts and ideas in the play
, and it's not something you often think about while playing a game, so it's an interesting thought experiment all the same. Still, I would've liked it better if the writer had kept the tone a little less informal, and perhaps broke the fourth wall a little less obviously. But these are just personal peeves, and you may not care so much.
Bottom line: short, sweet, a bit of a head-scratcher but not a scalp-bleeder, an interesting enough little diversion.

Bastion is such a beautiful game. From the beautiful visuals to the heart-melting music to the innovative storytelling... it's just perfect. You play as a 'kid' whose world seems to have been destroyed in a calamity. You group the survivors in the safe haven - the Bastion and you look for ways to undo the damage. Most of the time the only person whose voice you'll be hearing is the Narrator Rucks, another survivor. He's telling the story of him and the kid to someone else, and so he describes each of the kid's actions. These are not scripted sentences and they change according to how you play. You can screw around breaking a few crates with your hammer and the Narrator says "kid just rages for a bit." You beat a boss without taking damage and he says "Kid didn't let a scratch land on him." This kind of narration is employed to reveal the whole story and the game universe to you and it's a very refreshing way of storytelling, and you quickly become attached to this old gruff voice.
Gameplay consists of shooting and hitting stuff with your ranged weapons (bows, muskets, carbines) or melee ones (machete, hammer etc). Enemies are varied and you can't just run through the game with a single set of weapons. You have to adapt and advance. Weapons can be upgraded as you level up and there are puzzle rooms where you have to use them in unconventional ways to unlock prizes. Another interesting thing the game does is how it enacts a dynamic difficulty level. There are "idols" you can find in the game which you can use to unlock different penalties. These idols alter different aspects of enemy effectiveness but also nets you more xp. I find this way of doing things more engaging than the standard difficulty sliders. In fact this risk-reward mechanics is built into much of the game. Potions allow you to gain more max health but might make your attacks weaker. I love this approach. In fact I love the whole game to death. A piece of art. Do yourself a favour and get it asap. Did I say how great the soundtrack is?

I was looking forward to playing Dragon's Dogma, I've spent quite a number of hours on it but am ultimately dissappointed by this game.
It does many things very well. The class system, being able to scale large monsters, being able to share your party members with other players. These are very nice features.
My dissatisfaction is with the hack-and-slash dynamic of the combat system. In particular fighting large monsters has never come close to the sweet spot.
- Early in the game fighting a troll or cyclops is ten minute ordeal, I had several experiences of getting them down to the last quarter of their health only to be killed (from full health) in a single blow.
- Later in the game fighting a cyclops is a four minute spamming of the same attack pattern. Because the cyclops can hardly hurt me and I can hardly hurt it.
For me the game never hit the right balance between challenge, accomplishment and difficulty. So I can not recommend it.

Singularity had the potential to be something truly great. A promising concept (time manipulation) combined with an interesting sci-fi plot, Singularity instead doesn't use its chosen gimmick to its fullest, relegating it to mild puzzle solving (with some occasional gigantic logic holes - why can't I just climb over this collapsed door instead of crawling through yet more sewer pipe to get to the same place?) and some moderately useful combat abilities, most of which can only be used a handful of times per engagement; I ended up forgetting I had them. In addition, the game has only one proper boss fight and basically gives you God Mode near the end, making the difficulty not so much peak as plunge. You can get through practically the entire game with the assault rifle and the shotgun (the game conveniently provides a nearby sniper rifle whenever the situation calls for it).
That's not to say Singularity is a bad game. It isn't. The shooting feels tight and the ability to upgrade the damage, capacity, and reload times of your weapons is neat. It just could have been so, so much better if they had used their tools more effectively, given us more to do with the time manipulation mechanic, and hadn't tried to crowbar in some Bioshock-esque "twists" near the end. Missed opportunities, but still worth getting on sale.

Man, what can I say... this game quickly became one of my favourites ever!
It's fantastic how deep the whole system of the game is. You're always learning something new and improving on your gameplay abilities.
The multiplayer component makes for an amazing experience. It's fantastic learning tactics or hidden secrets by watching the other players playing (be it summoned by you or watching their souls). In therms of world building, the structure and design of the levels is magnificent. One of the best build worlds I ever saw.

Exploration. Discovery. Development. All present in this beautiful game. An interesting and exciting central quest thoroughly introduces you to the races and types of planets this game has to offer. This game is what No Man's Sky should have, could have been. The resource gathering in Starbound isn't boring, slow, or overly simplified. You can explore the surface of planets for your ores; or dive into the mantle and discover more than just repetitive cave systems found in similar games such as Minecraft. The crafting system is great as well, and there are a lot of mechanics in this game to explore. From basic armor and weapons crafting, to decoration and storage systems, to advanced wiring of electronic systems to create an epic end-game base, this game has something for everyone. There are tons of unique weapons in Starbound as well; a knome that shoots rainbows, an eyeball that shoots lazers and crystal grenades, and even a lightsaber-katana that can can hurl energy kunai at your enemies! There is something for everyone with this game. It is a combination of exploration, questing, mining, crafting, technical gameplay, and boss farming found in many popular titles all wraped up in a nice little indie game package. I definetly recomend this title for anyone who wants to have a nice, relaxing, single-player experience (Although the multiplayer is definitely a blast too) that takes place in a vast and fully explorable universe with unique life and biome types.
Who needs No Man's Sky when Starbound is so much more for 1/4 of the price.
