This is perhaps one of the best zombie survival games that is currently out there. The developers sort of tried to "test the waters" to see what players would like and wouldn't. The game has its fair share of bugs / glitches and the ending is a weak one, but think of it like a Bethesda title; full of bugs and glory at the same time. It's a definite must-try if you're an apocalypse or zombie fan; don't over look it for it's "indie-ness" (which is a horrible analogy because there are some butt-spankingly good indie games out there).
The game is worth about 20$, and for a relatively short game (it's free roam with a main quest that is relatively optional past a certain quest that allows you to establish new homes) it has quite an impact on replayability. The only thing missing; the option to skip the first section of the game (like a tutorial) or an option to spawn as a random survivor somewhere in the game, so you start from scratch and make your way around doing what you want.
Generally, the AI lacks depth. Your companions do nothing but cannon-fod and sometimes provide some helpful attacks (such as holding a zombie in place, then moving out of the way so you can get a clear shot on the head). Beyond that, they're almost useless; they can however, save you from a nasty blow by special infected such as the feral or the big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (both of which inflict severely heavy damage, especially the feral). Just short of that however, they can be killed relatively easily if you don't support them. A little bit of babysitting is required; but they aren't tedious - if you decide to hoof it during a fight, they'll back out and follow you instead of fighting to the death.
When not on the field, your AI companions can be called in to loot a place that you've discovered supplies at (if you can't carry any more) and you can help escort them as they do that "mission". Building trust and maintaining character integrity is important; otherwise you'll be spending more time dealing with in-house feuds than with the zombie hordes out there. Of course, you also need to scavenge for supplies, or witness your people fall to illness and in-house insanity where they kill each other or even suicide. Building your own homes and such is satisfying; however late-game things take a bit too long. This is due to the real-world timer system.
Everything is subtracted (supplies) and changed according to real time, so when you shut your game off, expect to come back to see less supplies, some survivors in trouble and in the worst case scenario (like what happened to one my forts that wasn't properly supplied with defence equipment) witness your fort fall apart as people die left right and centre. The positive side to this is that quests still pop up and disappear whilst you're away, so you can come back and see a few quests awaiting your doing. Survivors also come randomly in the world, each with their own (sometimes useless) professions; from TV trivia to Video-Game expertism, everyone has their own merits and demerits. With that in mind, everyone has stats (though everyone shares similar stats, some come with their own special personal skills) that you can level up as you play the character more and more; providing you with 1 or 2 specialisations when you reach maximum level for that stat (or weapon and personal skill).
It can be a little daunting at first when your "main" character is about to be ripped into two by a zombie horde or a mighty big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (which, is actually quite graphic) but rest easy, for if you have just one other survivor you're capable of playing, you can continue your game without issue. This is one of the coolest features, but the execution of it leaves quite a lot to be desired.
The game is truly impressive for such a small game. If State of Decay 2 comes out with more depth and more expansive territory and zombie scenarios, expect it to be the next "skyrim" (but not as an ocean with the depth of a puddle). Definitely worth paying 20$ to play this game - I've enjoyed it thoroughly even without a controller during early access.

Honestly, this is one of the best free games where I've had the most fun and time wasted.
An exceptional FPS, with a great community. Gameplay almost never gets repetitive, with numerous maps and unique players. Visuals are what you'd expect from a Source mod. Teamwork can be very critical depending on the map, such as requiring zombies to work together in specific strategies or survivors sticking together to heighten the chance of survival.
Lag compensation is quite horrid and the hit boxes can be also which makes me deduct a point on the score.
The game is quite easy to get started in, but has the typical motto of "hard to master". Some servers also offer modifications such as models, trails, stats, infection cure, and more. The community is still very strong, with hundreds of players still each day.
Some maps may be well balanced, or very survivor/zombie sided. Survivors can use various weapons including melee and explosives. Survivors can also use voice commands, "panic", flashlight, and many other actions.
Zombies must attempt to kill all the survivors before running out of time, lives, or the survivors reaching a point. The carrier is basically the 'alpha zombie', having more strength, health, and the ability to infect and 'roar'.
Modes you can play are objective mode (ZPO), survival mode (ZPS), team arena (ZPA), and hardcore (ZPH). There are also some deathrun maps. Some maps may require you to barricade. Some may require you to dodge blocks fired at you. The maps are very unique.
My overall score of this spectacular game/ Source mod is: 9/10

It's hard not to look at Another Perspective and be immediately reminded of another indie puzzle platformer, Braid. From the wavy hair of their similarly drawn lead character, to the general look and feel of the experience, and the fact they both inhabit the same genre allegations of plagiarism wouldn't be entirely off base. Setting that aside, the biggest thing keeping them both distinctly separated is that Another Perspective is little more than a poor imitation of Braid and so many puzzle platformers; like an off brand toy you buy because it's cheap, only to see it fall apart a day later from the shoddy craftsmanship.
It's a shame because the basic idea behind Another Perspective sounds really cool in theory. Essentially there are two (sometime more) copies of yourself, but only one can ever interact with the world at any given time. The others remain frozen in space, becoming makeshift platforms as you switch between them rapidly to get around the alternating level designs to grab all the keys and make it through the door. And, that's basically it.
My biggest issue with Another Perspective is it takes this one idea and tries to build an entire game around it. Before I'd even gotten halfway through the hour or so long story, I was already tired of constantly repeating the same tedious puzzles which seemed to be repeating themselves with but minor alterations, wishing that I'd come to the point where they would evolve and show the potential of the neat switching mechanic. But that moment never came, and I was left with an unsatisfactory ending that almost seemed to demean itself for the repetitiveness of its design, and the lack of any real point to its narrative which might as well not exist, being entirely comprised of random observations and overblown hogwash.
There were basically two possibilities for how I thought Another Perspective could turn out, the first that it would surprise me despite its nearly stolen art style with clever use of its mechanics and inventive puzzle designs, and the second being covered in the paragraphs above. It's a hollow experience and a miss opportunity, devoid of anything remotely impressive or memorable for me to latch onto. Near the end of the game my character began to question if there was any point to all of this, if it was ever going to amount to anything, which I can answer easily with a disheartening "no".

Another Perspective is a puzzle platformer that follows the different perspective of a confused character looking for something.  In each level you are challenged to obtain the key or keys, get to a door and unlock it to move to the next level.   While the game is graphically basic and relies on fairly simple mechanics, the simplicity is a strength to this game rather than a detriment. The music is well done, and propels the story and atmosphere of the world. The theme and story of the game is challenging, enticing you to continue going forward.  The different characters and their perspectives tie into the layout of the game very well.
While I feel it could have benefited from voiced narration by adding an emotional connection to the character, overall I found this game entertaining for the short time it took me to play it, and for its' price point I can gladly recommend this game.

is a very well crafted 2D puzzle game in which the protagonist - designed as an homage to
's Tim: he kinda looks like him (having that BIG head that literally takes half his body), moves like him (thanks to Siha for noticing), and he even has Tim's little insecurities that led him to be the self-inquiring little bloke
taught us to love in a game - acts like a message carried back and forth between the player and the developer. Wait, isn't this the case with gaming in general? Maybe, but very few games are actually aware of it. This game is and the fact that its developers built it around these design philosophies already makes it a very clever little game.
But what makes it truly shine is the fact that it is another fine game that turns gameplay into a very appropriately creative way to convey meaning. And what it conveys is a very well staged metaphor for conversation, for dialogue. Remember how you always take turns in conversation and its dialogical nature means that there are always at least two sides to it? And that means that there's always
involved. And, as the developers so keenly put it: "To change perspective is to change reality!"
Also, remember how in conversation you often take leaps of faith throwing in an argument that you don't exactly know where it'll land, but it kinda fits together with what was said before or may prove a standing ground for something to be said later? This little game managed to turn this into gameplay and it's obvious they put a lot of thought and talent into this because they also built the little "story" it tells around it. It's not uncommon for 2D puzzle games to turn a gameplay mechanic into a narrative technique (although, as seen in
or
that usually requires a lot of art work and concept design to fill the gap between the two), but here this is done so effortlessly and with so few resources that it's obvious the developers really mastered this art to perfection. And it's not a small feat to turn a minimalistic 2D game into a Socratic experience. I loved it to bits. NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Molemen Must Die! is a frantic falling platform shooter from new indie developer, Mokomoto.
Each game starts with King Moleman assaulting the American president and the president replying immediately by releasing a huge bomb down into the moleman tunnels. You play an unnamed female soldier whose task is to accompany the bomb downwards, fending off moleman defenders until, presumably, the bomb reaches the bottom and destroys moleman civilisation forever. (I haven't got anywhere near that far yet.)
Graphics - The graphics in Molemen Must Die! are pixel graphics with a good dosing of personality, although they can be somewhat hard to discern on occasion; I wasn't sure of the protagonist's gender until she was killed for the first time.
The molemen come in a number of shapes, sizes, colours, and abilities, and generally look cute, if deadly. And weapons and special effects are nicely done, with pixels flying everywhere, though bullets are rather large in comparison to the characters.
There are no graphics quality settings; full-screen/windowed mode, resolution, and a 'VHS' filter that makes the game look like it's played on an old TV are all that is included. (I turned this filter off immediately.)
Sound - Sound is repetitive, but good. There are only two music tracks, I think, but both of them fit the frantic game play. Weapon sounds and explosions are good and normalised for volume, and the protagonist's scream when she dies is a fine end to the game's action.
I'm in two minds as to whether less is more in this case, or whether the game would be better if there were a lot of crazy, gibbering, mole-men sounds as well. Regardless, what's here now works well.
Gameplay - Molemen Must Die! is played as a side-on two-dimensional action platformer. The giant bomb that you are protecting falls continuously down the screen, keeping the action moving downwards. If you touch the top of the screen of fall off the bottom then you die. If a moleman hits you (once), you get shot (once), or you're caught by a mole device or explosion (once), then you die. The goal really is to last as long as you can before the inevitable happens, amassing points for dealing out crazy moleman death as much as you can.
The molemen aren't just gunning for you, though. If you don't kill them quickly enough, they'll jump onto the giant bomb and flail away at it, gradually decreasing its health. If that gets to zero then you guessed it: you die.
Controller controls are simple, with left stick moving you around, A button jumping, X button shooting, and RT to use your rare super bombs, that destroy all moles on the screen. If you're insane (or you don't have a controller, I suppose), you can play with the keyboard, but controller is definitely best.
In a stroke of genius, the developers added an element of randomness in the form of active effects. You have three active effects at any one time (once you've played your third game, at least). At the start of each game the oldest effect drops off and a random new one takes its place. Each effect thus lasts for three games. You have no choice in these effects, and they range from truly excellent (a gun that shoots both left and right at once), to the weird (a rainbow trail that does nothing useful), to the downright annoying (huge molemen, or faster spawning molemen). They can thus change the difficulty significantly between games, and add a good dose of variation to what is otherwise a fairly repetitive game.
Each game you start off with your trusty semi-automatic pistol. Stay with this too long, though, and your thumb will get very sore and tired from pressing the 'X' button. Luckily, random weapon drops are fairly frequent, although somewhat limited in choice, at least to begin with.
As you kill molemen, they drop little XP orbs. Pick up enough of these and you gain a level, which seems to have only one effect: unlocking a new weapon. So the more you play, the more variation you'll see in weapons when you play again. I don't know how many weapons and thus levels are in the game, but so far I've seen machine guns, miniguns, rocket launchers, firebombs, homing missiles, shotguns, and mines, I think.
Pros:
+ A good sense of humour
+ Good controller response; I didn't often feel that the controls were to blame for my failure
+ Mostly nice pixel graphics and good sound
+ The three random active effects add some variation and replayability
+ Leaderboard and silly messages displayed after each game
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Not enough weapon variation, at least in the early game
- It's sometimes hard to see what's going on
Molemen Must Die! is a great first entry for Mokomoto on Steam. It has just the right amounts of addictiveness and randomness, and its gameplay is very frantic, but lots of fun. It's a simple game, but therein lies its appeal.

If you like the combat, exploring the world, and doing alot of managing of your inventory, gear, and supplies then you will like this game. It has a open world thats a fine size though not the biggest I have played in... but the combat is completely and utterly unique and there are 9 vocations(classes) and each one changes how you engage enemies and what you might want to bring with you as far as your party goes.
You have 3 other pawns (NPC party members), one of which you have direct control over their skills, gear, inventory and even the choices they make in combat like between grabbing loot or helping an ally, or going after mages/archers instead of the fighters in front of them.
The real main stay is the combat, any enemy bigger than you, you can scale and stab at their weak points. Any enemy smaller or equal size than you, you can grapple for your teammates or pick them up and throw them. Literally had an expierence where I was attacking what would be named a gargoyale. Hit it twice, saw its health bar barely move so I just picked it up and chucked it off a cliff. Was a hiliarious and great moment.
Also, something utterly unqiue is that character creation system. You can make yourself be like 7ft tall or 4ft tall. As well as being anywhere from 100 pounds to over 400 pounds. And these stats matter. The heavier you are the more you can withstand being knocked over and how much you can carry. The taller you are the easier you are to hit but your weapons scale with you so your weapons have an easier time hitting. Your staminia is linked to your weight smaller characters regen faster but bigger characters go throught it more slowly. Even simple stuff like how tall your character is effecting how deep the water needs to be to get you drenched/put out your lantern. (and this matters, the nights in this game are almost pitch black.
Really where this game falls on its face is the cutscenes and non-combat animations being janking and cringy as ♥♥♥♥. They are probably some of the worst non-indie animations I have ever seen. Also the last stage of the game is called "post-game" which is a vary poorly worded version. Its not where you beat the main story line and just simply run around dicking around in the world. You dont beat the game till there is a New Game Plus option. This is something that threw me when I played it on the xbox 360. I thought I had beat it so I stopped playing being a little upset because I wasnt big into the exploration aspects.
Oh yeah, this game runs amazing though it does get bugged somethings. Like after the first time I launched it the sensitivity changes I made to my mouse in game transferred over after I closed the game. Also there was another time where it just bugged out and was running at 20-24 FPS for some reason. Both of these issues were only fixed by restarting my computer. I still havent beaten the game either.

Have you ever wanted to cling to the inner-thigh of a cyclops and hack away at its unmentionables with a cutlass?
Well now you can.
So, I was pretty leary of this at first, suspicious that Capcom was trying to sneak a JRPG into western markets wearing the skin of a WRPG, but I was more than pleasantly surprised.
This might be one of my top five favorite fantasy RPGs that I've ever played. The game really stood out in several ways.
The World/Style: While the world feels a little confined and less open than most other games like this, the setting is unusual in that everything has a very southern-european/mediterranean feel, which doesn't show up often in fantasy games (which spend a lot more time in scandavian mountains or germanic woods and farmlands) and it was weirdly refreshing. The variety of different options you have when customizing your character is insane. Want to play as a waifu midget wizard? Go for it. Want to play as a giant fatty with male pattern baldness? Rock on. The fact that big, bulky, late-medieval armor is a thing is also fairly unusual, and something I was pumped to see. The ability to mix and match your armor load-out is scary addicting, and I'm not proud to say I spent more time trying on breastplates at Caxton's Armory than most girls do at a dress shop right before prom.
The Combat: The combat in this game is smooth and fun. You have three main combat trees, but all three are easy to learn, visually pleasing when in action, and have a variety of neat moves. You're not left with the robotic chopping of Bethesda games or the weird "heavy/light" attack wheel from the Witcher. PLUS, YOU GET TO CLIMB THE MONSTERS. I know this isn't a "first," and the directional controls are wonky as balls as you cling to the back of a Chimera like some sort of weapon-wielding koala, but it's fun! Instead of hacking endlessly at something's shins, you can clammer up it's body and beat it in the face like God intended.
The Pawns: Who doesn't want a mindless drone to follow them around, carry their stuff, and assist them in monster-face-beatings? Nobody. Being able to tweak a dedicated NPC to compliment whatever playstyle your main character happens to be using is pretty cool. Being able to check out and recruit OTHER players unique NPC's to build a small party of adventurers is ALSO pretty cool. I've never seen something like this before. With enough searching, you too can compose a party entirely of 7ft bearded men wielding clubs to help save the land.
While the final conclusion to the game itself was pretty dumb in an overly trippy, introspective sort of way, and a lot of the shop dialogue is skull-poundingly repetivtive, it was still a very fun game to play overall.

When everything comes together and works perfectly,
is a wonder to play, with top-notch sound design and satisfying combat. The problem, however, is that these moments are so few and far between that the lifeless monotony warrants the question of whether this is worth the purchase at all.
As the Arisen of legend, you are tasked with tracking down and defeating the Dragon that seeks to bring about the end of days and thus reclaim your stolen heart. With the world of Gransys nearing its end, the return of other beasts amidst the chaos will bring you up against the worst that the harsh and wild lands have to offer.
A textbook example of how to properly port a console title to the PC platform,
is, from a purely technical standpoint, superb. With 60FPS/4K support, quick load times and plenty of customisation options, the remastered version of the dated console release works like a charm, (short of the occasional stutter or pop-in), putting the other cash grabs to shame.
It's a good thing too, as the slick and intuitive gameplay relies on fast-paced, heavy-hitting action. Whether scrambling atop a chimera or holding on desperately as a griffin takes to the skies,
features some fantastic boss fights; reminiscent of
and
as you grab and climb up onto your foe for better locational damage.
With the ability to change and augment both characters with ease, the vocation class system is, for the most part, well thought out with similarities to the dual/multiclass mechanics of
Abilities are varied, giving player stats a decent boost and pack a satisfying punch on all difficulty levels.
Aside from the fairly standard character customisation and rudimentary crafting, the main drawcard of
is in the pawn system and custom companion mechanics. Allowing you to create a sidekick/minion to complement your class setup (and act as a packhorse for gear), your main pawn can also be sent out into the Rift, an online player hub where they can be recruited by other Arisen. It’s a neat little feature, if a bit of a gimmick, but the added interactivity is interesting nonetheless.
Unfortunately, that’s just about where the few positives end, as
excels at basic gameplay but not a whole lot else.
Progress is saved automatically through poorly implemented checkpoints and there are no manual slots for different saves either. While it is understandable that the developers wished to prevent players circumventing difficult scenarios and reflect the consequence of these choices, an RPG of this scope should have some form of backup, rather than simply restarting entirely or returning to the previous hub.
Speaking of difficulty, I often found myself wondering whether there was any at all; the AI is average at best and even the strongest of foes suggests a mere change in damage and health, rather than actual dynamic growth or progression. The thrill of taking on a Cyclops for the first time quickly loses its charm as they are spawned in more and more yet easily defeated. Having played as a Strider/Ranger, it wasn’t long before boss fights and entire battles could be carved through with ease, stuffing the party with a tonne of curatives to compensate for the drawn-out (and scripted) grind.
Thanks to repetitive level design, muddy textures and a clear enthusiasm for grass, rocks and trees, the world itself is remarkably bland and uninteresting to explore. With the same enemy types spawning in the same locations over and over
again, the monotony further detracts from any possible interest that one could’ve had in exploring the landscape. You’ll start to simply run past the groups of harpies, bandits and goblins you’ve defeated ten times before, or bypass them entirely thanks to the lore-appropriate fast-travel with port/ferrystones—a feature that wasn’t viable in the original release.
With barely any loot that’s worthy of note, experimenting with weapon types and enhancing your gear quickly loses its appeal as well, with other gear filling up your inventory to sell for gold you won’t spend. The camera also clips through objects, spinning out of control in close quarters and with no option to lock-on to enemies, melee combat can decline into a flailing mess, with targeting abilities dependent on pure luck.
It often feels as if the developers have gone out of their way to negate any sense of the grand and epic scale the narrative could have, leaving both the campaign and world feeling confused and hastily put together. Nothing you do matters; the main campaign is completely linear and major events either have no impact or are ignored entirely. The few plot twists can be seen from a mile off, with heavy exposition treating the player like an imbecile.
Without a single interesting character in the entire game, most of them are shoved in with no context or prior explanation for the sake of filling an archetype, fodder or one-dimensional tear-jerking. Cutscenes are robotic with clunky and looped animations and the voice acting and writing isn’t any better, laughably cheesy and full of clichés.
There’s no investment or connection with the player; the very thing that a role-playing game seeks to create, and what
fails so spectacularly to achieve.
is a completely forgettable experience, lacking any depth or interest outside of the combat sections that quickly become repetitive. Featuring a dull and empty world with practically non-existent role-playing elements and a painfully average campaign, Capcom has a long way to go for delivering a follow-up that's worthy of the open-world RPG title that it aspires to be.
It’s a shame, considering all the little touches that have been put in to indicate just how great the game could’ve been. As one who has always loved role-playing games and went into this with high expectations, the disappointment of this ultimately lifeless and uninspired action/MMO imitator is certainly not worth a second playthrough, let alone the first.
Save yourself both the effort and money and try the
series,
or
instead. A far from overrated thumbs down.

I was monumentally disappointed with this game, even after paying $10 on Humble Store.
Let me start with the positives:
- Combat is suprisingly intuitive after the first hour or so and you begin to familiarize yourself with the controls and abilities. This is particularly true when fighting monstrous, towering beasts.
- Customization is deep and there are options aplenty if you're into that.
- The class system (vocations) works really well and I was pleased with the variations of playstyles the game panders to.
- You can frequently get it on sale.
The overwhelming negatives:
- The storyline is pitiful. Narrative is practically nonexistent and what attempts they make and creating a cohesive plot is absolutely laughable. You go in, maybe, expecting a deep and lengthy tale but you're given this stale, shallow introduction before being presented with enough story to hardly fill a mobile game. There is more narrative in my criticism of the game than the entirety of Dragon's Dogma.
- Pawn AI is atrocious. What the ♥♥♥♥ were they thinking?
- Everything rendered in the game. Character models are sometimes questionable, lip-syncing to speech is like a bad lip reading video, EVERYTHING clips (this is particularly bad when fighting monsters).
- Washed out colors, awful textures, some seriously bad lighting, etc.
- Combat, again, while intuitve, becomes repetitive very fast. When you jump onto certain enemies, they recycle the same (clipping) animation and it never gets any better.
- The UI is frustratingly annoying to navigate. Think Witcher 2's map.
- Localization is altogether poor. This is a minor gripe and to be expected in some lower budget JRPG's.
In summary: if you get it cheap, it might be your style if you can surpass some glaring defects.

Easily one of the more fun & ACTUALLY f2p games on steam in ages.
FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
-I downloaded it with an "eh why not" mentality, and found myself playing for a solid 2 hours.
It's very simple but you get hooked on trying new strategies, unlocking new units, and being decently rewarded for playing the game. When you level up, you unlock new armies and new units for FREE as it should be: not to mention you get credits after each win and the daily quests give you a significant amount of credits for getting blueprints for advanced/alternate units.
GAMEPLAY:
- You get 3 different modes of gameplay. Arena, Ranked (3v3, 1v1), and Quick Match (3v3, 1v1). The game is still fairly new so there was no expectation of having a large diversity, though i feel that there will be more options in the future.
- There are 3 total factions in the game at the moment, The Terran, The Atlac, and The Yaoguai, each with their own unique units for your army. You start the game with only The Terran unlocked, but after a few matches you will unlock The Atlac, and The Yaoguai respectively. It doesn't take days worth of grinding to unlock any of this. Huge thumbs up from me!!
- The mechanics are incredibly simple and easy to get the hang of.
- You select the faction you'd like to play as and start up a game. The main goal is to defeat your enemy's armies and destroy their base. You accomplish this task by accumulating resources and spending it on units, slowly building your army with your teammates to overwhelm the enemy forces.
- While you don't get to "control" your units, you do have to use your brain quite a bit. You can't simply spawn 50 minions and expect to defeat your foes. You really need to adapt to what your team AND your enemy is spawning into battle.
Complaints:
- Nothing that would make you quit the game because it's broken or non-functional but there could be a few improvements. My main issue is the pathing of the units. There have been many times my units just aren't attacking because they're trying to figure out how to move around one of my own units and them doing that interrupts certain unit's attack, causing a pause in DPS which can make a difference in winning and losing a wave.
Overall the game is pretty fun and reminescent of older RTS games, but with a more modern mechanic to make the games about 10 minutes long every time. It's great to hop on and play a few games before you have to ahere to your real life responsibilities!

Although getting through the first 7 levels might be a seriously pain in the behind, it's definitly worth it when you destroy the enemy mothership. Can't wait to see what promise it holds when it's fully released!

Synopsis:
Considering this is still in Open Beta, Balancing are still an issue with the units in this game, obviously. The best way I can put this game, is the Starcraft II Desert Strike custom game mode that was created by another person. The units/race have almost the same concept when it comes the Starcraft II units, but slightly different. You play 1v1, every 15s you send your "army wave" to the enemy base, but there are a total of 3 turrets. (MOBA aspect) - this was inside of Desert Strike as well, but I don't think it was 3. If 3v3, you have you own opponent to fight + whatever was left over from the previous army battle. Ironically, after playing it and saying it's like SCII's Desert Strike, they brought out *Desert* Storm arena, which is a "Pick your race, and select 1/3 units provided to you at random." The game also has runes as you level up, you unlock more rune slots, like LoL's rune system, but you have to obtain X runes of the same type to level it up.
Cons:
The only complaint is that there is a cap on "In-game currency" This cap is 10k/week. The reasoning behind this as posted by the developers is to prevent people from getting far ahead of the game for those that can't play every single day for 24 hours. Keeps the rune/unit system balanced in a way.
Pros:
Pretty much love the game because it's like Desert Strike from StarCraft II or even Nexus Wars as someone else put it.
There are very similar units to Starcraft II, but it's still a fun external made game.

A polished free to play tower defenceish multiplayer game where you send waves of enemies at the opponoent. In 3v3 mode its the same as 1v1 except you take turns with two other teamates (which isnt as much of a drag as it sounds but maybe 2v2 would work better). Doesnt seem pay to win (as far as i can tell) as you can purchase all the units with credits you achieve. Seems they plan on making money on extra arena purchases (you get a free entrance every 5 days and can purchse more) (you play till 10 wins or 3 losses) and you pick units kinda like hearthstone. All in all nice time waster and very polished. I do not understand how people think there are balancing issues but im still kind of new. However seems fine to me so far and it seems they are making balancing adjustments in the updates. Its a good game but it does kinda seem like a cell phone game concept brought and evolved to PC.

universe that consists of the same repeated 10 planets over and over and over again.

Doing quests, whether the main ones or any others, does nothing! There is no point in
doing any quests -- sure you need to do some to unlock various things -- is it the
first story quest, so you can take your ship to other planets ? That is it. After
that you will notice that the universe of Starbound is entirely static, nothing you
do has any effect, there is no point in doing things.
So there are like 4 things you can do in this game. A - mine, B - run, C - farm, D -
quest.
A - mine, well yeah making your first mine is mildly engaging as you first explore
the art assets, after that you would need to make another mine on another planet,
because different planets have different ores. You would need to make about 4 mines
in total I think.
There is almost nothing to see underground, so mining gets boring fast. The mobs are
merely just annoying, with boring attacks and no drops. There is NO MINING
advancements, so apart from getting a stronger mining tool and 2 devices, ore
detector and cave detector, mining is a pretty boring endevour.
B - run, well yeah that is a way you can play this game, probably the most efficient,
but it is also probably the worst way to play it. Because of its efficiency you will
tend to mostly. You just beam down to a planet and run across the surface looting all
the boxes you find on your way and then leaving to repeat this on another planet. You
quickly see the three or four different surface structures IN THE ENTIRE UNIVERSE,
and collect enough ores, pixels, useless weps, upgrade modules etc... to progress
your character. This is also a fast way to notice how similar the planets are, which
again is a bit depressing. Each beam down becomes really drab, you know you wont see
anything interesting and just wish you could find that matter manipulator module you
need, so you can build a farm or something instead of this boring laggy borefest.
C - farm, well yeah making a farm is something different, you can play the game like
a farmer, to progress, since you can buy most ores you need. However you cant buy all
the ores, so your farmer will have to actually do running and maybe mining as well.
So although it was claimed you can be a farmer purely, you cannot. Well anyway so
lets say you did enough of the other things, so you have the seeds you need to make a
farm. You plant them seeds, they grow, you run over the plants, "havesting" them, and
put that produce in your terramart for pixels (game currency). NPCs wont do any of
this for you, so forget making a farming type colony, colonists don't actually do
anything - but that is the next point. Lets make it clear; Farming is this :-
1. wait for plants to grow.
2. run through all your plants that are ready to be havested, havesting them (press
e)
3. Put produce in terramart machine to pixels.
You can play this game (to an extent) like that if you want. There is NO FARMING
advancements, so that is it. Needless to say it is terribly boring.
D - quest, well yeah, so when you come across these handful of populated structures,
some of the NPCs there will offer you quests. The quest generator is apparently
stupidly complex for what it actually does. It will generate a sequence of
interrelated quests for you. These might be gather resources, then craft something
with resources, then give to someone, who gives you something to place in the NPCs
home. Pick up some stranded NPC. Save some NPC who is held by a few hostiles. Plant
seeds, grow produce, give produce to NPC... maybe a couple more. Firstly, the quests
are all boring as hell, secondly and more importantly they do nothing whatsoever! The
universe is entirely static.
Actually I recently read on the dev blogs, that the quests are really super cool and
do all sorts of changing things to the world. And the reason I didnt notice that
quests are super cool and have real consequences are because the quests are boring
and the changes are cosmetic or trivial -- so a NPC in some town now wears a funny
hat, because you did some quest! Or one NPC now can generate quests pertaining to
some other NPC, because you did some quest that made them friends! Who cares ? I
didnt even notice.
Doing these quests have one effect, you get various items, which you might need to
progress your character, albeit at a greatly slowly rate than just surface running
across planets will get you.
2) Nothing much to do. Well yeah, above ive described the entire game, that is it,
that is all there is to do. Sure you can spend time creating various structures,
which is nice, but you can also do that in paintbrush, or whatever... You can use the
wire mechanics to make interesting automated things in your structures, but again,
with nothing much happening or to do in the starbound universe, it is a bit
anticlimatic, since you spent all that time making some cool base structure, but it
serves no purpose at all. The one reason to make a cool base structure is to protect
your stuff, since there is no form of protection for player made stuff, even on your
own ship, you have to make a secret base in MP to store all your stuff in. Otherwise
other players can just mine everything from your ship. Making MP itself a really bad
experience. Enemies dont get harder depending on number of players nearby or
anytyhing, and you still only get loot for 1 person. So MP doesnt work, for anything
other than a IRC replacement. I mean don't get me wrong, I had fun making pass coded
doors for my ship, although it was a continuous feeling of depressing for me, knowing
I couldnt ever use them, since people could just mine through them anyway :/
3) Horrifically badly programmed. Well yeah, the engine of this game has been
horrendous since it was released on steam. I thought, well yeah of course that will
be sorted out, after many updates I started to worry about that, but remained hopeful
for the actual 1.0 release. Well it's here now and the engine is the same or worse.
This is just the fact of the matter; Starbound is horrifically coded and this makes
modding for it depressing as well, why make a mod for a game engine that is very bad?
There is no point, there are plently of other game engines out there. Anyway what we
have is that the game is basically a trivial and shallow program for showing off art
assets. The best of these are probably the NPC towns etc... But the engine cant
handle them and whenever you come across some cool town that you should be happy to
find and explore, its a double edged sword. Yeah its nice to look at, but its game
breakingly laggy to engage with in game. The engine doesnt even cut it as a simple
program to show off art assets!
It might be important to realise the priority the game engine should have. If you
want to make a game that features immersive NPC towns, yet the engine you have
created to do this, cannot do it; then the engine is a failure and without fixing
that, your game is broken. This is really important!

Starbound is a solid procedurally generated sandbox/survival/crafting/building/exploration game, with the primary focus on exploration and combat.
Unlike most games in this genre, this game has a complete story with instanced missions and boss fights that (loosely) ties into the procedurally generated galaxy. The story is servicable, but nothing terribly special. The instanced boss-fight missions are fun, but there's only a handful of them and they're quite short.
The bulk of the game takes place on procedurally generated worlds. The different world types are interesting the first time you visit them, but all the worlds of the same type end up looking more or less the same. Biome transitions on the worlds are abrupt and don't always make sense (I dug straight down on a hot volcanic world and found a frozen biome...) and the worlds are tedious to traverse, even with a fully upgraded character.
The upgradeable starship is a neat idea, but is hamstrung by the need to complete annoying randomly generated quests to recruit crew members to upgrade the ship. These quests have a very low "drop rate" for recruiting NPCs, and the regular rewards are generally pitiful for the time and difficulty involved in running back and forth from one side of the planet to the other.
Combat and exploration is a strong point. There's a nice variety of weapons, and they're satisfying to use. There's some neat items and upgrades for traversing the environment as well (I like the spike ball since it can climb pretty much anything). Weapon crafting and progression is quite weak however, unlike the armors the craftable weapons are very weak compared to the random drops, and entire weapon classes (guns) are unavailable to craft for much of the game. To me, it doesn't really make sense to make all the armor tiers craftable but force the player to have to deal with the RNG to get good weapons.
One huge plus for this game is official mod support. Many of these issues have been at least partially addressed already by mods. The devs also plan to continue working on this game, so hopefully it will continue to improve with time.
While not necessary a shining example of early access done right (like pretty much all early access games, the devs appear to have overpromised and underdelivered), this is a complete game that is quite fun as-is at a reasonable price, despite some of the unpolished and not quite finished features.

The story is deep, serious ♥♥♥♥. You like galactic, cyberpunk stuff that reminds you of swtor? Play this, it's so precise, voice acting for every moving thing, storyline has so much attention to detail, especially the characters, they DIFFER so much from each other, and it continues to develop and evolve as the series continues. Music is so nostalgic, everything is ace, the film-grain effect for that retro look... People don't pay respects to these little details that the bioware team throws in. They are aware of every aspect of good storytelling, and they exploit it well in this series.
Summarising stories is the worst way to fish someone into what you're selling, won't want to make them play it for ♥♥♥♥. If I summarized the storyline it would be; 'you are commander shepard, goal is to save the galaxy with a team' But the storyline isn't what it is about, otherwise there would be so much of the same ♥♥♥♥ in both the gaming and film industry, what really matters is how you execute it. Play this game, it will hook you in the first 3-4 hours, if it doesn't, then it isn't your thing. It's a game that isn't open-world yet offers so much freedom.
PROS:
+ Definitely one of the most interesting, yet complex plots out there
+ Gameplay is dynamically shaped by your actions and dialogue selections
+ Can go around as a total ♥♥♥♥, or an ethical and universal role model
+ Epic protagonist
+ Great model designs
+ Fluid game mechanics
+ Does a decent job getting your emotions a little worked up
+ Viable for replayability
+ Most maps are impressively immersive
+ AI is actually pretty good
+ Different alien species can be fun to learn more about
+ Gives the player the option to play strategically with the eccentric specialties of each squad member
+ Fun side quests, with some being humorous
+ Even after understanding the plot 100%, there are still unresolvable mysteries that leave the players to assume for themselves
+ Awesome voice acting, but Shepard's can start to sound monotone after a while
+ Textures are a little meh, but are enough to keep you immersed
+ Lotsa lens flares
+ Optional and unintrusive romance
CONS:
- Had a few issues with characters models dissappearing randomly
- Citadel is large and can be too confusing to navigate through
- Too many useless elevators
- Walking/jogging speed is kind of slow
- Inventory system is really annoying to use
- Sound sometimes, but rarely, started acting whacky for me
- Exploring ("landing on") planets that are extraneous to the main plot can sometimes be rewarding, but are mostly "cookie cutter'ed"
- Music is very sci-fi'y, but sometimes annoyed me due to the short loops
- Gun model variation is pretty unexciting (maybe 2 models per type, with about 3 colors per model)
- No free-roam after completing game, so make sure you do all the side-quests you're interested in and explore BEORE you begin the final quest
Leaves you thinking for nights after completion :D

If you've ever played the awesome free indie game Super Crate Box, Molemen Must Die! will be immediayely familiar. It takes that general idea - 2D platformer, survive as long as you can against waves of enemies, collect a variety of guns - and turns it up to 11. For one thing, it's always on the move: you have to escort a bomb down toward the centre of the earth, and its slow progress ensures that you're never fighting on the same set of platforms for very long. Every time you die, a random modifier is applied, so the game gets very chaotic very quickly. And the guns! Oh, the guns. So many guns.
If you want a genuinely pulse-raising game experience you can enjoy in just a few minutes, or play for hours on end without ever seeing the same scenario twice, buy this game NOW.

I've been a Homestuck fan ever since I was 10. I always thought it was the coolest and funniest thing ever, and it brought joy and smiles to me for all the time I read and watched the whole thing from page 1 to 10,000, and even though I was too young to make a pledge when this came up as a Kickstarter, I was hyped.
Has the 7 years, the tension, the pain, all been worth it?
...Heck yeah! Even though it was only the 1st part, I absolutely love this game to bits. Make me feel like the dumb geeky preteen I used to be when I first saw Homestuck.
Hiveswap, in my opinion, isn't just a game for the big fan of the original webcomic: it feels like a great way to segway yourself into it, shows fans of things like Undertale their original roots and also have a great and fun story to play with all the charm of Toby Fox's music and character, or you can just play it as it is; a great adventure game that has style, some neat ways to solve puzzles, and a lot more, for a pretty low price too!

I beat the game in a little less than 3 hours and I loved it! I'm not a huge fan of the point and click genre, but I thoroughly enjoyed it as a Homestuck fan: I got to appreciate that good old Hussie sense of humor while learning a bit more of the Troll lore.

Well, that was a trip down memory lane.  I backed this game on Kickstarter five years ago, back in the height of the Homestuck craze.  So much has happened since then, both in the webcomic and with my life, but playing Hiveswap reminded me of the magic of that time, sitting on my new college friend's dormroom floor at 3AM devouring surprise updates.  If you're like me, an old Homestuck fan, I think you'd be pretty safe in picking this up and enjoying it.
The overall writing quality is fantastic. Though Hussie did not write this himself, his trademark slightly dry, tongue-in-cheek narrative voice is wonderfully prominent in the object descriptions and interactions.  There also is unique text for many, many, many strange combinations of objects, as you would hope in a point and click adventure. However, I feel that the character dialogue was a little different stylistically than I was expecting.  It wasn't bad per se, just not quite as "Homestuck" as the rest of the writing. This is especially noticable in the later parts of the game, where two characters are interacting much more frequently.
Though it was quite short, I believe that Hiveswap stayed for about as long as it needed to for this Act. I finished it in my 2.5 hours of playtime and I did quite a lot of random clicking and combining, though I do read much faster than the average person.  What Pumpkin kept the zones pretty small, which kept the time spent getting stuck to a relative minimum.  I am admittedly a point-and-click philistine, but this more confined space allowed me to finish without feeling frustrated, or looking up a solution, which has happened other times I've tried to play games in this genre.
Other users have reported some debilitating bugs and graphical glitches.  In my playtime, I had no crashes or game breaking bugs, though there were a few minor UI blips.  Hopefully these issues get patched soon, but it isn't 100% broken.
If you're a Homestuck fan, I don't really see any reason not to pick this up.  If you're not a Homestuck fan, it's still a solidly written, beautifully drawn short adventure.  As long as you're not expecting some gigantic Joycean epic, it'll definitely be an enjoyable afternoon of attempting to tapdance at every clickable object in vicinity.

Really awesome, well worth the money! I had a bit of a problem finding the batteries, and there were a few graphical glitches, but otherwise it was really fun. I enjoyed clicking on and combining everything for the flavour text, and enjoyed the cutscenes, and I had fun with all the little references to various things! I'm just worried the next act will take forever to be finished, but I know making video games takes time, and I'm certain it will be well worth the wait!

When everything comes together and works perfectly,
is a wonder to play, with top-notch sound design and satisfying combat. The problem, however, is that these moments are so few and far between that the lifeless monotony warrants the question of whether this is worth the purchase at all.
As the Arisen of legend, you are tasked with tracking down and defeating the Dragon that seeks to bring about the end of days and thus reclaim your stolen heart. With the world of Gransys nearing its end, the return of other beasts amidst the chaos will bring you up against the worst that the harsh and wild lands have to offer.
A textbook example of how to properly port a console title to the PC platform,
is, from a purely technical standpoint, superb. With 60FPS/4K support, quick load times and plenty of customisation options, the remastered version of the dated console release works like a charm, (short of the occasional stutter or pop-in), putting the other cash grabs to shame.
It's a good thing too, as the slick and intuitive gameplay relies on fast-paced, heavy-hitting action. Whether scrambling atop a chimera or holding on desperately as a griffin takes to the skies,
features some fantastic boss fights; reminiscent of
and
as you grab and climb up onto your foe for better locational damage.
With the ability to change and augment both characters with ease, the vocation class system is, for the most part, well thought out with similarities to the dual/multiclass mechanics of
Abilities are varied, giving player stats a decent boost and pack a satisfying punch on all difficulty levels.
Aside from the fairly standard character customisation and rudimentary crafting, the main drawcard of
is in the pawn system and custom companion mechanics. Allowing you to create a sidekick/minion to complement your class setup (and act as a packhorse for gear), your main pawn can also be sent out into the Rift, an online player hub where they can be recruited by other Arisen. It’s a neat little feature, if a bit of a gimmick, but the added interactivity is interesting nonetheless.
Unfortunately, that’s just about where the few positives end, as
excels at basic gameplay but not a whole lot else.
Progress is saved automatically through poorly implemented checkpoints and there are no manual slots for different saves either. While it is understandable that the developers wished to prevent players circumventing difficult scenarios and reflect the consequence of these choices, an RPG of this scope should have some form of backup, rather than simply restarting entirely or returning to the previous hub.
Speaking of difficulty, I often found myself wondering whether there was any at all; the AI is average at best and even the strongest of foes suggests a mere change in damage and health, rather than actual dynamic growth or progression. The thrill of taking on a Cyclops for the first time quickly loses its charm as they are spawned in more and more yet easily defeated. Having played as a Strider/Ranger, it wasn’t long before boss fights and entire battles could be carved through with ease, stuffing the party with a tonne of curatives to compensate for the drawn-out (and scripted) grind.
Thanks to repetitive level design, muddy textures and a clear enthusiasm for grass, rocks and trees, the world itself is remarkably bland and uninteresting to explore. With the same enemy types spawning in the same locations over and over
again, the monotony further detracts from any possible interest that one could’ve had in exploring the landscape. You’ll start to simply run past the groups of harpies, bandits and goblins you’ve defeated ten times before, or bypass them entirely thanks to the lore-appropriate fast-travel with port/ferrystones—a feature that wasn’t viable in the original release.
With barely any loot that’s worthy of note, experimenting with weapon types and enhancing your gear quickly loses its appeal as well, with other gear filling up your inventory to sell for gold you won’t spend. The camera also clips through objects, spinning out of control in close quarters and with no option to lock-on to enemies, melee combat can decline into a flailing mess, with targeting abilities dependent on pure luck.
It often feels as if the developers have gone out of their way to negate any sense of the grand and epic scale the narrative could have, leaving both the campaign and world feeling confused and hastily put together. Nothing you do matters; the main campaign is completely linear and major events either have no impact or are ignored entirely. The few plot twists can be seen from a mile off, with heavy exposition treating the player like an imbecile.
Without a single interesting character in the entire game, most of them are shoved in with no context or prior explanation for the sake of filling an archetype, fodder or one-dimensional tear-jerking. Cutscenes are robotic with clunky and looped animations and the voice acting and writing isn’t any better, laughably cheesy and full of clichés.
There’s no investment or connection with the player; the very thing that a role-playing game seeks to create, and what
fails so spectacularly to achieve.
is a completely forgettable experience, lacking any depth or interest outside of the combat sections that quickly become repetitive. Featuring a dull and empty world with practically non-existent role-playing elements and a painfully average campaign, Capcom has a long way to go for delivering a follow-up that's worthy of the open-world RPG title that it aspires to be.
It’s a shame, considering all the little touches that have been put in to indicate just how great the game could’ve been. As one who has always loved role-playing games and went into this with high expectations, the disappointment of this ultimately lifeless and uninspired action/MMO imitator is certainly not worth a second playthrough, let alone the first.
Save yourself both the effort and money and try the
series,
or
instead. A far from overrated thumbs down.

I was monumentally disappointed with this game, even after paying $10 on Humble Store.
Let me start with the positives:
- Combat is suprisingly intuitive after the first hour or so and you begin to familiarize yourself with the controls and abilities. This is particularly true when fighting monstrous, towering beasts.
- Customization is deep and there are options aplenty if you're into that.
- The class system (vocations) works really well and I was pleased with the variations of playstyles the game panders to.
- You can frequently get it on sale.
The overwhelming negatives:
- The storyline is pitiful. Narrative is practically nonexistent and what attempts they make and creating a cohesive plot is absolutely laughable. You go in, maybe, expecting a deep and lengthy tale but you're given this stale, shallow introduction before being presented with enough story to hardly fill a mobile game. There is more narrative in my criticism of the game than the entirety of Dragon's Dogma.
- Pawn AI is atrocious. What the ♥♥♥♥ were they thinking?
- Everything rendered in the game. Character models are sometimes questionable, lip-syncing to speech is like a bad lip reading video, EVERYTHING clips (this is particularly bad when fighting monsters).
- Washed out colors, awful textures, some seriously bad lighting, etc.
- Combat, again, while intuitve, becomes repetitive very fast. When you jump onto certain enemies, they recycle the same (clipping) animation and it never gets any better.
- The UI is frustratingly annoying to navigate. Think Witcher 2's map.
- Localization is altogether poor. This is a minor gripe and to be expected in some lower budget JRPG's.
In summary: if you get it cheap, it might be your style if you can surpass some glaring defects.

Dragon's Dogma is what happens when you smash Monster Hunter, Skyrim, Dark Souls, and lots of heart into one.  It's rough around the edges, and there are certainly a lot of small flaws, but it remains as my favorite game of all time even after playing hundreds of hours on the Xbox before.
Graphic/Animation/Immersion:
For an old game, this game has some of the best physics/animations you can find.  Graphically, it's aged fairly well even before modding.  The sounds are all great, and the immersion is awesome.  You need lanturns in the dark, and they will go out if you are wet.  You can throw crates or barrels at enemies... etc.  I told you this game had heart.
Gameplay:
Oh boy, here's where the game really shines.  From fighting the smallest goblin hordes to the largest Dragons, this game does not disappoint.  It is challenging, yet reward.  The gameplay is complex with lots of skills/builds.  Each class also plays completely differently.  The game features the best portrayal of two handed weapons along with the most badass sorcerery spells.  Enemies react interestingly such as a Cyclop being tricked to remove his helmet if you climb on its head... etc.  Oh and there are the pawns...
Pawns:
This game has the most extensive and interesting RPG Ai system that I have ever seen in the form of "Pawns".  Each player gets a companion "Pawn" that is fully customizable and will learn to "play" the game from watching you.  Those that complain about dumb AIs are not training their pawns correctly or hiring smart pawns.  Training and finding smart pawns just to watch them solo the entire game on the hardest difficulty is rewarding in itself.  Though they can be annoying in how much they repeat the same lines when faced against a large group of the same enemies: "Wolves are weak to fire!"  I told you the game was rough around the edges.
I'm gonna have to cut this review short, because there are so many unique and interesting things done right in this game.  Is the game as polished or streamlined as AAA titles like Witcher 3?  No.  However, if you can look past the rough exterior, the game is one of the best in the action RPG genre, and you are more than likely to get your money's worth.  Give it a shot!

Really boring game, nothing much to do, horrifically badly programed.
1) Really boring game: The game is just so shallow it is really a bit hard to believe
that it would be even possible to make a game so shallow. There are a few (like 20)
nice things to look at. That is all well and good for a small art gallery, but not so
much for a game.
Don't be fooled by the supposed "procedural generation", there are only a handful -
what 10 or so? different types of planets, and the "generator" does nothing to mix
things up. Two planets of the same type are so identical that you often think you
have ran into exact same planet. Maybe theres one more tree between the spawn point
and the hill on the left... who cares... What you have in reality is a massive
universe that consists of the same repeated 10 planets over and over and over again.
Exploring to notice this really is an anticlimax.
Doing quests, whether the main ones or any others, does nothing! There is no point in
doing any quests -- sure you need to do some to unlock various things -- is it the
first story quest, so you can take your ship to other planets ? That is it. After
that you will notice that the universe of Starbound is entirely static, nothing you
do has any effect, there is no point in doing things.
So there are like 4 things you can do in this game. A - mine, B - run, C - farm, D -
quest.
A - mine, well yeah making your first mine is mildly engaging as you first explore
the art assets, after that you would need to make another mine on another planet,
because different planets have different ores. You would need to make about 4 mines
in total I think.
There is almost nothing to see underground, so mining gets boring fast. The mobs are
merely just annoying, with boring attacks and no drops. There is NO MINING
advancements, so apart from getting a stronger mining tool and 2 devices, ore
detector and cave detector, mining is a pretty boring endevour.
B - run, well yeah that is a way you can play this game, probably the most efficient,
but it is also probably the worst way to play it. Because of its efficiency you will
tend to mostly. You just beam down to a planet and run across the surface looting all
the boxes you find on your way and then leaving to repeat this on another planet. You
quickly see the three or four different surface structures IN THE ENTIRE UNIVERSE,
and collect enough ores, pixels, useless weps, upgrade modules etc... to progress
your character. This is also a fast way to notice how similar the planets are, which
again is a bit depressing. Each beam down becomes really drab, you know you wont see
anything interesting and just wish you could find that matter manipulator module you
need, so you can build a farm or something instead of this boring laggy borefest.
C - farm, well yeah making a farm is something different, you can play the game like
a farmer, to progress, since you can buy most ores you need. However you cant buy all
the ores, so your farmer will have to actually do running and maybe mining as well.
So although it was claimed you can be a farmer purely, you cannot. Well anyway so
lets say you did enough of the other things, so you have the seeds you need to make a
farm. You plant them seeds, they grow, you run over the plants, "havesting" them, and
put that produce in your terramart for pixels (game currency). NPCs wont do any of
this for you, so forget making a farming type colony, colonists don't actually do
anything - but that is the next point. Lets make it clear; Farming is this :-
1. wait for plants to grow.
2. run through all your plants that are ready to be havested, havesting them (press
e)
3. Put produce in terramart machine to pixels.
You can play this game (to an extent) like that if you want. There is NO FARMING
advancements, so that is it. Needless to say it is terribly boring.
D - quest, well yeah, so when you come across these handful of populated structures,
some of the NPCs there will offer you quests. The quest generator is apparently
stupidly complex for what it actually does. It will generate a sequence of
interrelated quests for you. These might be gather resources, then craft something
with resources, then give to someone, who gives you something to place in the NPCs
home. Pick up some stranded NPC. Save some NPC who is held by a few hostiles. Plant
seeds, grow produce, give produce to NPC... maybe a couple more. Firstly, the quests
are all boring as hell, secondly and more importantly they do nothing whatsoever! The
universe is entirely static.
Actually I recently read on the dev blogs, that the quests are really super cool and
do all sorts of changing things to the world. And the reason I didnt notice that
quests are super cool and have real consequences are because the quests are boring
and the changes are cosmetic or trivial -- so a NPC in some town now wears a funny
hat, because you did some quest! Or one NPC now can generate quests pertaining to
some other NPC, because you did some quest that made them friends! Who cares ? I
didnt even notice.
Doing these quests have one effect, you get various items, which you might need to
progress your character, albeit at a greatly slowly rate than just surface running
across planets will get you.
2) Nothing much to do. Well yeah, above ive described the entire game, that is it,
that is all there is to do. Sure you can spend time creating various structures,
which is nice, but you can also do that in paintbrush, or whatever... You can use the
wire mechanics to make interesting automated things in your structures, but again,
with nothing much happening or to do in the starbound universe, it is a bit
anticlimatic, since you spent all that time making some cool base structure, but it
serves no purpose at all. The one reason to make a cool base structure is to protect
your stuff, since there is no form of protection for player made stuff, even on your
own ship, you have to make a secret base in MP to store all your stuff in. Otherwise
other players can just mine everything from your ship. Making MP itself a really bad
experience. Enemies dont get harder depending on number of players nearby or
anytyhing, and you still only get loot for 1 person. So MP doesnt work, for anything
other than a IRC replacement. I mean don't get me wrong, I had fun making pass coded
doors for my ship, although it was a continuous feeling of depressing for me, knowing
I couldnt ever use them, since people could just mine through them anyway :/
3) Horrifically badly programmed. Well yeah, the engine of this game has been
horrendous since it was released on steam. I thought, well yeah of course that will
be sorted out, after many updates I started to worry about that, but remained hopeful
for the actual 1.0 release. Well it's here now and the engine is the same or worse.
This is just the fact of the matter; Starbound is horrifically coded and this makes
modding for it depressing as well, why make a mod for a game engine that is very bad?
There is no point, there are plently of other game engines out there. Anyway what we
have is that the game is basically a trivial and shallow program for showing off art
assets. The best of these are probably the NPC towns etc... But the engine cant
handle them and whenever you come across some cool town that you should be happy to
find and explore, its a double edged sword. Yeah its nice to look at, but its game
breakingly laggy to engage with in game. The engine doesnt even cut it as a simple
program to show off art assets!
It might be important to realise the priority the game engine should have. If you
want to make a game that features immersive NPC towns, yet the engine you have
created to do this, cannot do it; then the engine is a failure and without fixing
that, your game is broken. This is really important!

Starbound is a solid procedurally generated sandbox/survival/crafting/building/exploration game, with the primary focus on exploration and combat.
Unlike most games in this genre, this game has a complete story with instanced missions and boss fights that (loosely) ties into the procedurally generated galaxy. The story is servicable, but nothing terribly special. The instanced boss-fight missions are fun, but there's only a handful of them and they're quite short.
The bulk of the game takes place on procedurally generated worlds. The different world types are interesting the first time you visit them, but all the worlds of the same type end up looking more or less the same. Biome transitions on the worlds are abrupt and don't always make sense (I dug straight down on a hot volcanic world and found a frozen biome...) and the worlds are tedious to traverse, even with a fully upgraded character.
The upgradeable starship is a neat idea, but is hamstrung by the need to complete annoying randomly generated quests to recruit crew members to upgrade the ship. These quests have a very low "drop rate" for recruiting NPCs, and the regular rewards are generally pitiful for the time and difficulty involved in running back and forth from one side of the planet to the other.
Combat and exploration is a strong point. There's a nice variety of weapons, and they're satisfying to use. There's some neat items and upgrades for traversing the environment as well (I like the spike ball since it can climb pretty much anything). Weapon crafting and progression is quite weak however, unlike the armors the craftable weapons are very weak compared to the random drops, and entire weapon classes (guns) are unavailable to craft for much of the game. To me, it doesn't really make sense to make all the armor tiers craftable but force the player to have to deal with the RNG to get good weapons.
One huge plus for this game is official mod support. Many of these issues have been at least partially addressed already by mods. The devs also plan to continue working on this game, so hopefully it will continue to improve with time.
While not necessary a shining example of early access done right (like pretty much all early access games, the devs appear to have overpromised and underdelivered), this is a complete game that is quite fun as-is at a reasonable price, despite some of the unpolished and not quite finished features.

As of right now I'm only at 90 minutes of play time but that has been enough to inspire this review for three main reasons.
1. The atmosphere of the game is amazing.
2. Playing with other people and helping each other out in such a well done atmospheric setting is an experience that leaves a very good impact on the feels.
3. None of the reviews I've seen so far seem to have touched on the atmosphere of the game much.
My time in this game so far was spent in an online hosted game where I started out knowing little but was quickly brought up to speed from asking questions to the other people in the game. They helped me figure out some things I needed to complete the tasks assigned by the game when you first start. At the same time I helped collect resources to continue the development of our little village that was forming and scouting any nearby enemies, mainly wolves and skeletons. Once I finished all my tasks initially assigned by the game (basic ones I'm assuming to help you get into the game and to know what you're doing) I thanked my fellow adventurers for the assistance and logged off.
During the above in game actions I encountered a few more things that honestly helped me to fall in love with this game's atmosphere rather quickly. Here is a short list of things I enjoyed:
- Standing next to the other players near a fire to keep warm.
- Hearing the fire crackling and popping.
- Hearing the cold winds howling around and sounds of nearby animals/creatures.
- Hearing my character breathing heavily in the cold air as well as almost a sniffling sound during this process.
- Witnessing the scenery during the different times of day, especially in the evening/during sun set.
Honestly, if you play games for their immersion and emotional interactions, this game is priceless (Especially with a good pair of headphones, as well as a headset as you can hold Tab to talk to other players). Content and basically everything else will come in time and can be added in the future but the atmosphere is something that has to be done right early on. In this game, it is, and the developers seem loyal to producing more content and considering good feedback and suggestions from the community.
On another note (and I'm sure this is because the game is in early access) I can see where you can run out of things to do in the game currently, however I have obviously not made it there yet due to my 90 minutes of actual play time. I don't think this will be much of a problem for me though, because I've already found great enjoyment in doing simple things such as the events described above.
I look forward to playing this game a lot in the future and as of right now I'm hooked on it!

This is like the next installment of BG, with 4E-style rules (per-encounter, per-rest abilities) and a few changes, like being able to build up your own fortress and take prisoners in it.  There's plenty of reading if you want it and yet you can skim the parts that don't interest you.  Also, there will be no rerolling chars endlessly.  You get a set number of points and no more.  No savescumming to min/max any more.
If that's what you wanted, you will be very satisfied.  If that's not what you want, this isn't the game for you.
The only real problems so far are some really dumb pathing during combat, but then I learned to pay more attention to whether my cursor had little feet on it to see if my mage was going to wander into melee to cast that spell and this has informed my spell selection.
A few hints for people starting out:
* Even Mages need MIGHT.  MIGHT == damage.  I don't get it either, but it does make this clear at character creation.
* Use fast mode + sneak.  Why?  So you can find the hidden stuff (and not be too slow).  Sneak around suspect areas.
* TAB highlights the goodies... but see above.  Hidden stuff won't appear via TAB until detected via sneaking.
* There's hidden stuff everywhere, even in the middle of the wilderness.
* Cast range is an important spell attribute.  Look for little feat on the cursor to see if you need to be closer.
* Guns are OP.  There's no reason your wizard can't shoot one.
* Always geek the mage first... and the priest.
* If you sneak up to enemies then unload on them with a lot of powerful ranged weapons, the fight may end immediately.
Good spells (I forget the silly names, so will just describe the effects):
* Ice fog - long range + blind
* Magic missile - range + single target damage
* Confusion - especially good during some bounties
