Another Perspective starts out as an innocuous indie-platformer, like so many others. Only the intriguing part is this parallax view that is the gameplay, where you view an object from two - or a multitude - of different perspectives and the object, in this case the level, changes its appearance. The gameplay itself is reminiscent of how some of the levels of The Swapper plays out, in the interplay of the “clones” or in this case just arbitrary copies or resized models of the same Braid look-alike character that we, the player, are in control of.
You get the feeling of Another Perspective's metanarrative quite early on in the game. Where the narrator seems aware that this game is, in fact, a game. The player is set out to find the objet petit a or the “unattainable object of desire.” The same object that later turns out to be something completely different.
We have many metanarrative games these days, games that poke fun at the derived nature of most game genres. It happens so often that these metanarrative games become this type of derived, iterative, easy way out for delevopers that lack “real” creativity in their storytelling. I struggle to figure out if this game is one of those games, or not. To break the parallax here I would say it's somewhere inbetween. It, almost, seems like the metanarrative in Another Perspective manifested itself qua lack of ideas. But in that process, what actually manifested itself turned out to be rather enjoyable, albeit mildly mawkish, but to be honest I've never felt as appreciated for playing a game, so I'm okay with the overly sentimental parts of this game. I was smiling during some portions of the game, due to its narrative, or to this self-aware developer/player interaction commenter guy.
And on the subject of derivation, this game borrows its tone heavily from Braid. Not the melodies themselves, but the undertone, the brooding, surreal hum of the strings that plays throughout the game reminds me of the same undertone in Braids OST. The character animation is also something that, along with games like The Bridge, seems to be a not as iconic ersatz of the character in Braid. But that's something ubiquitous in the indie-2D-platformer-scene.
The general artstyle is rather simplistic, almost minimalistic, not to the level of Thomas Was Alone, but still very simple. This gives the player all their time to focus on the puzzles themselves. And in a metanarrative, the gameplay surely suffers(?), as in the case of Spec Ops: The Line and The Stanley Parable? Not in this case. The puzzles in Another Perspective range from simplistic, puzzles that are there to make the player happy (KEYS!!!), and mind-bogglingly complex puzzles that turns into a gradual understanding of the complete picture. As in The Swapper, and as mentioned before, the copies' interactions is what the majority of the puzzles are based upon, but in a deeper sense than what The Swapper provides, since in that game these are only one of multiple different ways these clones interact and solve puzzles. Here the focus is on different types of perspective and the interplay between these perspectives and entities. The way you had to think between different screens and positions really made the game's more complex puzzles very satisfying to figure out. And despite the narrative being self-obsessed it managed to, rather creatively, explain the games mechanics to you.
The narrative, narrator, commentator, the supposed player thoughts, does at one point in the game break down, due to the meaningless of it all, and pleads the game to stop, the player to stop, just for this madness to end. At this point I wondered if this was supposed to mirror the player's thought on a game where there is no discernible goal, or meaning. What that did instead was to bring down my overall thoughts on the narrative, the text on the screen, the conversations, that even though it's a short game, it starts repeating itself in a slightly annoying fashion. But at just that point of annoyance, it switches things up and the end draws closer, relieving not the player of meaninglessness, but the narratives' inertia.
Another Perspective is a short, cheap game, and it's worth your time. It's clever at points, in both level design and narrative, and even though there is no real outstanding visual or auditory style to the game, it has enough style, to not make it completely bland. As mentioned before, I've never felt so appreciated for playing a game. And just for that, I feel this game is worth something. Its humility despite its skeptical narration is admirable, and the final moments of the game are fairly cute and lovable, depending on how cynical and bitter you feel that day. I would give this a shot if I were you.

When you start Another Perspective one thing immediately becomes clear. And that’s how much it looks like Braid, another puzzle platformer from a couple of years ago (which, to this day, is still mighty brilliant). Not only that, but you also have to use clones. So in a way it’s also very similar to The Swapper. Again, another amazing game. The puzzles, however, are what make it different and unique from these other games and overall they're pretty good.
And wow, this game made my brain hurt sometimes, and I mean that in the most positive sense possible. Some of the puzzles are pretty hard and require patience and dedication. Once you ‘see’ the solution it’s actually very obvious, like most of the puzzles out there. Now, not all of the puzzles were difficult. It varies greatly in its difficulty. That’s also partly because of its narration, which basically consist of text lines shown during the levels that try to explain the ‘story’, or the general idea behind it. At first I thought it was shallow but the further I got the deeper the narration became and by the end I was truly intrigued by the lesson it tried to ‘teach’ me.
As I said, the graphics are reminiscent to those of Braid, so it has a style that looks like everything’s made with watercolor paint. It looks pretty, but it’s also very dark at the same time. The lighting is done very well, and gives the game a bit more style. It would’ve been nice if it used some variety in its backgrounds instead of just showing black but I can’t argue with the developer here as it’s an artistic choice.
There’s only music; there is no voice acting here. The game doesn’t need any and the music is relaxing and fits the genre. It doesn’t want to push you forward but wants to let you play at your own leisure, which is absolutely a good thing. Especially if you want/need to think things through.
There were some typos in some of the narrated lines. I don’t think these were intentional and I suppose they could be fixed with a patch. It didn’t break the game or anything, but it did pull me out of the experience, even if it was for just a little bit. A minor problem, in any case.
Another Perspective isn’t a very long game, depending of course on how good you are at solving puzzles. It will take roughly between 30 minutes and 2 hours to complete the story. After that you can start the Mystery mode which gives you even more puzzles and apparently a different, real ending, so I guess there must be even more to the story than I originally thought. I have to be honest and say that I haven’t completed the Mystery mode (yet) but I think it’s safe to say that you can add 30-60 minutes to the total playtime, maybe even more.

Well, well, well, time to wrap things up:
If you enjoyed Braid and The Swapper you really shouldn’t have to think twice. It might not have the same narration or complex puzzles as those games have but it still manages to stand on its own two feet. And even if you haven’t played those games – or as long as you enjoy puzzle games in general - this is absolutely a fine experience to begin with.

Average shooter that possesses exceptional atmosphere, detailed backdrops and a decent story. Worth a purchase at $5 or less, but it’s shortness (6 to 10 hours) creates value issues at higher prices (the multiplayer is dead).
Total size on my hard drive: 7.7 GB.
You can
.
A large EMP pulse from an island blinds a United States satellite, so the US sends a team to investigate. The pulse originated from Katorga-12 – an old Soviet research settlement founded around the mines of a mysterious mineral, E-99. Even traversing the initial level, pulses occasionally appear, creating “time spikes” that suddenly take your character to a different time; then another “spike” sends you back to the present. The truth becomes clear: the Soviets were able to utilize E-99 to create a time-travel device (among other uses). The device and the two scientists who would control it become the centerpiece of a journey through multiple time-lines to prevent the alteration of history. Like in any good time-travel story, preventing one disaster makes other disasters possible. While the story is linear, there are multiple endings; none of them are specifically “good,” each requiring an element of sacrifice. A decent sense of closure, but it’s bitter-sweet because there was clearly the possibility for a sequel (which has never materialized). Decent voice-acting and character models only add to the experience. The soundtrack is serviceable, but not exceptional.
If time-travel isn’t something you care about, and you just want a cool first-person shooter, well, you’ll get it. The fps part, anyway. The coolness isn’t really there. The game is linear. The combat mechanics work, there is a decent variety of weapons, and there are some upgrade choices to be made, too (remember to equip a perk, not just purchase it). The enemies comprise Soviet soldiers and strange creatures that mutated from all the E-99 radiation (contemporary timeline) – some of which are truly gigantic beasts. But the character movement feels heavy and slow, there is no cover mechanic, and chaingun + sniper rifle means you can handle all situations with little need to bother with other weapons. Some of the other weapons are really good – the grenade launcher which can launch a grenade that you then guide forward to the target was my other favorite – and the E99 weapons (where available) are over-powered as hell, but except for specific situations, there is little call to use them. And these “specific situations” usually have a weapon locker nearby, so it’s easy to switch to what is needed, then switch back when done. If you find yourself overwhelmed, pulse the wrist-mounted TMD (Time Manipulation Device). It’s got decent knock-back that can give you a breather when you need it. Multiplayer is dead.
But the primary attraction of Singularity is the atmosphere. It reeks with it. Every area is incredibly detailed, whether exploring an old Soviet barracks in the current timeline (rust, dirt, cracked glass, smoke) or traversing a laboratory in 1955 (bright, clean, apparatus everywhere). The graphics help in this department: though occasionally low-res, Singularity is one of the best uses of the Unreal 3 engine I have seen. And because it is Unreal 3 (and highly optimized), it runs great at maximum settings on moderate equipment (I easily hit 120fps @1080p on an R7 260X).
Singularity is a fun ride, no question, but you’ll have to really love the atmosphere and story to play it more than once, which hurts its overall value. Singularity rarely drops below $7.50 when on sale, but if it does, go ahead and get it.
Notes:
- A 3-button mouse is REQUIRED. Without the game-play mechanic tied to Mouse Button 3, some sections will be nearly (if not entirely) impossible to complete.
- Frame-rate is capped at 120fps.
- There are no subtitles for any language.

So you'll just end up wandering in to a place that is going to kill you over and over again while you try to find a place to rest and replenish supplies. The game says to follow the blue quest indicator if you're not sure where to do, but this just takes you to a place that tells you to return later once you've leveled more.
A few other things that led to my inevitable rage quitting: there is no load feature. The game only holds 1 save at a time, and the only way to load that one save is to quit the game, then load from the main menu. If you press the "Return to last checkpoint" option, it doesn't take you to the last time you saved, but to some arbitrary check point that I assume only activates when you rest at an inn. My companions killed themselves multiple times by just jumping off of cliffs or in to water and drowning. Resummoning them requires you to travel a considerable distance out of your way to a certain kind of stone in safe areas.
I really wanted to like this game, and it does have some interesting ideas behind it. Climbing on top of monsters a la Shadow of the Colossus was fun, the pawn system is interesting but the game could have done a little better of an idea explaining how it worked. Simple and Fun multiplayer game! The goal of the game is pretty straight-forward .... make it to the goal without becoming a zombies meal! The two game modes I have played so far are "Survival," (don't die within the time limit) and "Retrieval," (Retrieve an object, such as anti-virus). There are two teams, "Survivors" and "Infected."
Survivors typically start off the round with a pistol (with 1 clip) and melee weapon. If you want to increase chances of survival, you will need to search for more powerful weapons (sledgehammer, ak-47, etc.); But watch out! You can only carry so much weight and so many items. TO win the round as survivors, you must: Live longer than the time limit, Reach the Goal, Retrieve an item and reach the escape point. If you die or become infected, you will respawn (or turn) into an infected and your new goal is to eat your former comrades. ;)
Infected goal is pretty simple, eat all of the survivors! There are two types of infected, Commons and Whitey. "Whitey" has slightly more health and has the ability to infect survivors and act as a spawn point, attack coodinator (he shines bright yellow signalling all other players where survivors are).

I absolutely love this game, and so do my subscribers! I stream it at least once or twice a week and never get bored. I love leveling up and seeing what awesome weapon I unlock next! Playing with your friends makes this 100 time more fun.

I noticed that most people reviewing this game have previously played similar games. I don't have much experience with CRPG'S at all, thats why I thought my view of the game can give another perspective on things. That means I have not played games like Dungeons & Dragons, Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale or Neverwinter Nights before playing this game.
Pillars of Eternity starts of with a character creation. The amount of options that you have here is absolutely crazy. You can probably spend hours here, changing every little detail. You pick your sex, race, class, attributes, culture, appearance and finally voice.
This game have many difficult settings and are obviously made for replayability. Pillars recommend that you start on easy difficulty, so I did. I most say that easy in this game isn't that simple!
Loadscreens while you rest are pretty and some other environments in the game, like dungeons and forests. I like the details on the characters, it's very sharp, even when you zoom in. The only complaint I have is that some backgrounds are a little blurry and low res, which looks a little bit silly when it's next to a very detailed character. I get that they went for an "old-school look" but I still think that doesnt really match. But when you zoom out that won't really bother you.
I recommend that you crank the volume up for this title, because background noise and sounds, in the dialogue and in combat, are great. It will help you get into the story and atmosphere better.
Ventors in the cities and villages will buy all the trash you loot from enemies. You can buy camping tools, weapons and potions from them. If you have many followers you can carry more items, and all items can be transfered over between anybody in your party, which is great. So if I find a staff as barbarian I can simply open up the inventory and equip in on my mage.
You will have to read most of the dialogue yourself, although some story related things are read for you. I still wouldn't recommend this game if you hate reading, because there's a lot of it. You can right click on items and spells to read everything about them as well. Some are just lore stuff, others are actually useful information.
The story is dark and mysterious. Combat in done with real time and pause. You can also use slow motion in fights to make things more manageable and easy. As you level up your character and possible followers, you gain points which you can spend on things like sneak, survival, etc. You also get to pick spells.
You can create really silly partys if you want. You can combine all the races and even have animal followers like bears. It's entirely up to you who you bring along the quests and you can choose how they will look like, what weapon they will use and what role they will have in combat.
Options menu is very good. You can customize everything they way you like it in terms of controls. The graphics options are not as good, but for this type of game I wouldn't say its needed.
The replayability is obviously insane when you think about how many races, followers and difficulty levels this game has. You can play the entire game solo, or you can choose to bring mages, dwarfs, godlikes, wizards, humans...and so on, with you. You can also create different kinds of humans, elfs, etc. It's fantastic.
Obsidian Entertainment has created a great game overall, that even new CRPG players like me can enjoy. I have barely scratched the surface of this game, but I can already see that amount of work put into this title.
It's fun, dark and mysterious and im having so much fun playing and learning new things everyday.
Highly recommended title, if you don't mind reading of course.

Once you "beat" the game, which only took a day or two of playing, there was just nothing to do. And by "beat" i just mean aquire the best armor and weapons really. There wasn't really any story at the time.
Fast forward to now. 1.0 is released and the game has changed drastically. One day, a few weeks back, I decided to try this game out once more. It was all over the home page of Steam and it really made me want to give it one more chance, at least to the point where I felt like it was worth the buy. Well, I can honestly say that, after playing for another 20 hours or so and beating the main story, it isn't a bad game. The story progression is decent, the game mechanics are smooth, and it is overall an enjoyable experience. Before I explain any more in detail, I will list a few of my personal pros and cons.
Pro:
-Fun with friend (Multiplayer)
-Good sense of completion/accomplishment after completing main story quests
-Plays well (Good weapon/tool mechanics)
-Has a lot more potential
Cons:
-Quite boring alone (In my own opinion)
-Story is a bit too short
-Story missions are a bit too repetitive
-Final boss is the main one that doesn't feel very rewarding (also too easy and quick)
-Has a lot more potential
The reason I put "Has a lot more potential" on both is because it really is both good and bad. It's good that the developers have room to make the game better, but it's also not too good because at points, the game still doesn't feel fully complete. There also needs to be more variation in the main story. Every mission is just (spoiler warning possibly) scan (race) objects -> teleport to (race) location -> defeat boss. It just feels too wash-rinse-repeat. Anyhow, on a better note, the game is actually enjoyable with friends. Mining and building with others is fun, and upgrading your ship and EPP provides a fun feeling of progression. Exploring the various environments and fighting the different enemies is both exciting and annoying, but hey, I think those feelings combined make these type of games good. If it's never a little annoying, it's probably not challenging, and cake-walk games aren't generally as fun. The weapon/armor progressions/tiers were a bit confusing. It was a bit tricky to figure out when you really had the best things in the game, and the wiki wasnt much help. It seems to still be in the progress of being updated. Anyhow, let's wrap all this mess up into a conclusion.
Starbound is a fun game if you have another person to play with. If you are looking for a game that has a lot of replayability, I do not believe this is a game for you. It's fun to play through the main story once, maybe twice, but much more it just feels to overdone and boring. If you are okay with that, this game is a good buy. I was pleased with the newest update. If they add more to the story, I will consider playing again, but for now, once was enough. Like I said, there is definetly more that this game could be, the question is, will any more come of it?

This game..... I so much would like to love this game. All of the elements of a good game are there, everything that should make this game great can be witnessed through the turgid veil of garbage that covers its surface.
I bought this game YEARS ago, when your starting sword was overpowered and there were no quests of any kind. It was filled with bugs and horrendous performence issues, along with having nothing to do. These days, there are still bugs and horrendous performance issues. But at least there's something to do, right? Quests, bosses? Yeah. Sure, they're something you can do. None of it is fun, though. The bosses are all way too easy or damn impossible to fight thanks to the game needing to freeze every couple of second during a fight. And the quests? In my hours playing this game with this most recent update I have yet to find a single generated quest that was not some variation of; "Get me X" or "Take me to Y" or "Kill Z".
One of the longest awaited features of Starbound was a story. A cohesive plot told beyond vague npc coversation bits, or overly-long and poorly written codex entries. A little while back, they finally added a main quest. Guess what? The story is boring. It's dull, and unoriginal. It's basically a compilation of all generic space-mythos. Giant ancient tentacle beast coming to destroy everything and all that.
But, the story is forgivable. The quests, too, are forgiveable. At least they're trying to add content, right?
While I can look past all that, one thing I can't look past is how god-awfully this game performs. Every time I play I discover a new bug. Huge chunks of the world go unloaded for extended periods of time, entities glitch back and forth so frequently that I was convinced it was a feature. During combat, when you're really trying to get in there and attack, the game will just spontaneously freeze. It's almost as though it's trying to calculate the damage values with a ♥♥♥♥ing abbacus.
One of the main features of a Mineclone game is BUILDING and MINING. Building is unsatisfying, as it just doesn't mesh well with the exploration elements of the game. You make a huge, magnificent base on your first planet's surface, fill it with everything you could dream of, and revel in its beauty.... Then you realize you need more materials and have to leave. You never find the planet again. There's no point to build, as you're just going to leave it all behind anyway. The mining is one of the most frusterating parts of this game. Everything in this game leans towards the vertical over the horrizontal, in terms of how you traverse the world. Now, this wouldn't be a problem, if you took less fall damage. It's at this point that I must compare Star man's Sky- I mean Starbound, to Terraria, so, please forgive me for that. Terraria excells in the 2D Sandbox elements because of the inherent factors that compose its world generation. Caves are sparce, but grandious, always giving you just enough natural structure to not feel overwhelmed, but they still feel like your digging straight down had a point. Starbound, on the other hand, fills its subterranean layers with oversized caverns, fit only for you to die in. Cave systems are absolutely massive, and getting lost in them is far too easy. I couldn't really put into straight forward words what makes the caves so frusterating, so, allow me to use an analogy.
Imagine you come to a crossroads. Two paths branch off on either side of you. Both paths offer something you want, but you can only choose one. Easy answer, I hear you saying, go down one, then return to the other. Yes, that is an option. The only problem is, once you get to the end of the road you've selected, you fall into a pit where the world has yet to load and die.
Sorry for the poor analogy, but I couldn't be bothered to write any more hyperbole.
"But, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game has SPACE." I hear you shouting. Yes, I know, it has a massive universe to explore, with millions of different procedurally generated planets to interact with. Sound familiar? Like a certain flop of a game that has become a well-recognized meme? Well, much like said game, exploration in this game loses its luster fast, once you realize that all you'll find on the planets are an assortment of pre-made, unimpressive structures. Towns aren't fun to find, since there's no interaction with its denizens, apart from the 'randomly generated' quests they offer. (All of which are just fetch quests or kill that guy quests, might I add.) And random vendors are basically pointless since anything they could offer you can be found for free in the wilderness.
I want to like this game. The music is fantastic, the lore of the universe is facinating to read about, and to be entirely honest the pixel art is rather appealing to look at.
But, having bought this game about two years ago, and watching as the developers simply try to shovel more content into it, instead of fixing what they've already added, I simply cannot stand to recommend this game to anyone.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Totally, asoblutely, recomended. Giant enemies mechanics are just awesome. It's an open world action RPG with surprisingly fun and flexible class system. It'll take you a long time to finish new game plus and/or hard mode and, once you do that, you can always change your main class for variety and fun. On top of that, the mechanic for giant/boss mob fights are awesome. You climb atop giant mobs to access weak points, or to limit their movement and expose the mentioned weak points to your party.
I've been a gamer for over 20 years now (though I shouldn't admit that in public makes me feel old lol) and tbh, making an almost impossible jump to get to the top of a giant Beholder, then crawl to its weak point and stab it to death while it tries to shake you off is probably the most satisfying boss kill I've ever experienced.
It doesn't offer much in the sense of choice/consequence but as I said, it's a really awesome game regarding the boss fight mechanics. Can't believe it took me this long to try it!

A phenomenal game, particularly for early access. As long as it doesn't get abandoned as is the case with many games in this stage of development it could be one of the best games on the F2P market.
Styled like a traditional RTS and a MOBA had a baby. This game is simple, but still extremely enjoyable. Not many english speaking people have picked it up yet but they seem to be increasing steadily as the translations get improved. One of my favorite things about this game is that the online matches are relatively short, so I'm not stuck in the game for 25 to 30 minutes at a time.
There are some issues but they're typical to this sort of game, some units are somewhat OP. Pretty much any unit that attacks air units, as it can attack both air and ground, is more useful than units specific to ground combat. The Terrans antiair units are really easy to spam and devestate with. I have a pretty high win ratio because I figured this out early on. I'm sure that won't hold but it's a fairly simple tactic. I feel like the Atlac and the Yaoguai are maybe a little to similar. Comparatively to the Terrans who are nothing like either of them. Maybe a 4th more unique race will come into play later.
There does seem to be a pretty effective exploit that involves spamming Arhat troops in the Atlac tree, which have both a high range and damage and will eventually stack up into the hundreds overwhelming your enemy. I'd suggest nerfing either their damage or range.
There is also a pretty irritating issue with Idle players. If you get one on your team it's a guaranteed loss. I've had them on my team 3 games in a row before.
Overall it's well worth trying, especially considering it's free.

This game has a great deal of potentional and is already very fun for its current state.
I cant wait to see how this game develops/translates over time.
The developers are taking alot of care with unit balancing and adjustments, Just to make it better they post very detailed (%'s/values) in patch notes when there is tweaks and such.
Its pretty much a "creep/minion" management game, For those familiar with the MOBA genre, You'll generally think of pushing a lane with allied monsters. However here you control the monsters to push the lane. Which has a great relaxing tug of war feel to it.
Theres 4 modes in this game currently, Quick play, Ranked, Vs Bots/Ai, and Arena (Arena is like hearthstones layout, Longer you go the better stuff you get, Unfournately 10 waves/matchs is the max currently.)
This game takes alot of inspiration from starcraft units, and even some of the more popular starcraft modes. Such as desert storm. Now to the good stuff! Units :D Which are all amazing and developers have outright said more will be added. Which most would suspect, But its nice to hear it from them.
Currently there is 3 factions in this game, All of which have thier own strong points and commander abilities as well as passive skills.
(Your regular "human earth force") - 20 unit trees(default units), consisting of default verisons and another 20 variations spread throughout the faction. A very marine-y type feel. A great deal of heavy machines and such.
(A alien-y protos type race) - 18 unit trees(default units), consisting of 19 different troop variations/augmentations.
Alot of laser beams pew pew, Shield based race (They are great damage soaks with approriate setups) A very solid energy based race.
(Your typical raging beasts. Easily looked upon as a swarm, If underestimated beyond deadly)
- 18 unit trees(Defaults units), consisting of 23 troop variations/mutations.
These guys are just amazing, From thier exploding sheep to thier braincontrolling spiders. I love the units, I love thier synergy.

(Best part about sound is the faces you can make during battle. They are quite amusing and are often over spammed, Thats your warning :P, Loses points for lack of ambient music variation. But will most likely be added in future.)
(Theres not really any overly aggressive talk going on in this game, Theres usually not much talking at all in fact. Which i find better then constant flaming :D)
(I love everything thats in-game so far with the expection of the weekly gold-cap, Which is currently 10k. Developers said this is subject to change)
(This is often a huge deicider for people, I'm happy to say i regularly feel matched accordingly. The worst thing about the match making, Is the afk/purposely timing out.)
Would i recommend it? Yes. If you look over the game/screenshots/discussions/reviews and find yourself interested,
Why not give it a shot? I've defintely had alot of fun, and a new gaming addiction :P, Keep in mind there is a wipe coming.

I'm really late to the party, but I gotta say: This is a gem that, in hindsight, I wish I would have played sooner. It's got a great story that sucks you right in, features characters that aren't simply cardboard cut-outs, and features a very immersive game universe with loads of backstory and potential for spinoffs, even.
If you're completely new to Mass Effect like me, the game can feel a little overwhelming at first. So many places to go, so much gear to collect, weapons with modifiers of which you have no idea what is useful or not. Even picking your class can be a tough decision - I went with sniper, only to gun through the game with a pistol most of the time.
The battle system is actually much better than most make it out to be. It takes a little getting used to, but I found myself increasingly enjoying it the more I played. Turning this into an FPS would have made for an easier learning curve, but also a less memorable gaming experience.
There's not much to say in the way of complaints. Of course, the inventory is a major pain in the neck. And the ending was something I wish I had more control over, though I understand compromises had to be made so the story doesn't completely go off on a tangent. And the game balance is a bit off, too. When you first start out, most enemies on assignments can make you throw your imaginary controller at the screen. But after a while of sidequesting, you mop the floor with them and it becomes too easy. Something in between would have been nice.
Usually I only play JRPGs on consoles, but this one of the very few 10/10 games I've played on the PC. Highly recommended.

It feels weird to give Mass Effect a negative review, given its reputation, but I really didn't enjoy it much.
Pros:
Visually appealing, especially environments.
Good atmosphere and story.
Cons:
First and foremost, this is a pretty bad port. Getting it to work without constasnt crashes involved uninstalling my graphics driver and reverting to a driver from 2007~. There is also no controller support, which is odd for a game that was ported from a console.
Armor textures look terrible whenever there is a closeup on someone's face, which is 50% of the game. It's petty but it was really distracting for me.
The action elements are boring and just feel like something I have to get done with to progress the story.
RPG elements aren't a lot better. While Mass Effect is good at story telling and creating interesting characters, It fails with basic RPG elements like items and skills. Leveling and skill point allocation are uninspiring. A standard skill tree approach would have worked better in my mind. Items were terrible. All guns look the same, getting new ones is just a small stat boost so it isn't very exciting. Money is easy to come by so buying new gear is also easy and not a difficult decision. All the loot is so similar that looting is actually a bother, and I ended up just looking for the number at the end of the name to see if something is actually worth examining. Even weapon mods, which is something I'm usually excited about, are very boring, and since 80% of enemies are mechanical, there is no reason not to use the mods that improve damage against mechanicals on all guns.
Side quests were all thrown at me at such a pace that they looked like an overwhelming chore list. I tried one because it involved going back to the solar system which I thought would be cool. It was boring and involved clearing the same room three times.
All in all, the only thing that kept me playing to the end was the story, but at times I really had to make myself keep playing.

SINGULARITУ is a first person shooter with some time manipulation elements made by Raven Software (who's previous works include Heretic, Hexen, Jedi Outcast and Quake 4)
The story starts with you investigating some abandoned soviet island before discovering some mutants and science experiments gone terrible wrong, and you're pulled back in time where you accidentally ♥♥♥♥ things up royally. You spend the rest of the game trying to fix your mistake, traveling back and forth between two time periods, all while shooting mutants and commies and solving an ocasional puzzle.
The gameplay is pretty much your typical modern first person shooter - you have a decent variety of guns (about 10) which you can only carry 2 of. Most of the weapons are actually pretty fun to use, and you can upgrade each weapons's damage, magazine capacity and reload time. Apart from your guns you also have your Time Manipulation Device (or T.M.D.) which gives you additional combat options (freeze time in a certain radius, age oponents quickly, some telekinetic abilities). You also use the T.M.D. for solving some puzzles here and there and I never really had much trouble with them. The T.M.D. can also be used to age and de-age some items like stairs, safes, fuse boxes, barrels etc. It's not much but it is pretty fun.
You'll mostly be fighting soviet soldiers who shoot at you, and mutants who try to melee you. The soldiers have different guns but pretty much all of them will be shooting at you. The mutants have a bit more variety - some of them can phase in and out, some of them are kamikazes (aka annoying as ♥♥♥♥), and some of them are big guys who take a lot of punishment before going down.
Now let's talk about the problems. First off this is a very lazy console port. There are barely any video options, the FOV is really low and can't be changed without a separate program (I used Flawless Widescreen) and there are no subtitles, which is really unfortunate because everyone talks with a russian accent in this and it's hard to hear what they're saying sometime. Another issue I have is that the game took me 4 hours to finish on Normal, which was way too forgiving. So I feel like 20 euros is a pretty steap asking price.
Overall, Singularity is an okay game. It doesn't do anything amazing but it's pretty solid all around and I can't find too many things to complain about. Pretty fun, would recommend.

I noticed that most people reviewing this game have previously played similar games. I don't have much experience with CRPG'S at all, thats why I thought my view of the game can give another perspective on things. That means I have not played games like Dungeons & Dragons, Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale or Neverwinter Nights before playing this game.
Pillars of Eternity starts of with a character creation. The amount of options that you have here is absolutely crazy. You can probably spend hours here, changing every little detail. You pick your sex, race, class, attributes, culture, appearance and finally voice.
This game have many difficult settings and are obviously made for replayability. Pillars recommend that you start on easy difficulty, so I did. I most say that easy in this game isn't that simple!
Loadscreens while you rest are pretty and some other environments in the game, like dungeons and forests. I like the details on the characters, it's very sharp, even when you zoom in. The only complaint I have is that some backgrounds are a little blurry and low res, which looks a little bit silly when it's next to a very detailed character. I get that they went for an "old-school look" but I still think that doesnt really match. But when you zoom out that won't really bother you.
I recommend that you crank the volume up for this title, because background noise and sounds, in the dialogue and in combat, are great. It will help you get into the story and atmosphere better.
Ventors in the cities and villages will buy all the trash you loot from enemies. You can buy camping tools, weapons and potions from them. If you have many followers you can carry more items, and all items can be transfered over between anybody in your party, which is great. So if I find a staff as barbarian I can simply open up the inventory and equip in on my mage.
You will have to read most of the dialogue yourself, although some story related things are read for you. I still wouldn't recommend this game if you hate reading, because there's a lot of it. You can right click on items and spells to read everything about them as well. Some are just lore stuff, others are actually useful information.
The story is dark and mysterious. Combat in done with real time and pause. You can also use slow motion in fights to make things more manageable and easy. As you level up your character and possible followers, you gain points which you can spend on things like sneak, survival, etc. You also get to pick spells.
You can create really silly partys if you want. You can combine all the races and even have animal followers like bears. It's entirely up to you who you bring along the quests and you can choose how they will look like, what weapon they will use and what role they will have in combat.
Options menu is very good. You can customize everything they way you like it in terms of controls. The graphics options are not as good, but for this type of game I wouldn't say its needed.
The replayability is obviously insane when you think about how many races, followers and difficulty levels this game has. You can play the entire game solo, or you can choose to bring mages, dwarfs, godlikes, wizards, humans...and so on, with you. You can also create different kinds of humans, elfs, etc. It's fantastic.
Obsidian Entertainment has created a great game overall, that even new CRPG players like me can enjoy. I have barely scratched the surface of this game, but I can already see that amount of work put into this title.
It's fun, dark and mysterious and im having so much fun playing and learning new things everyday.
Highly recommended title, if you don't mind reading of course.

Bastion has solid gameplay.
Bastion has a gorgeous aesthetic.
Bastion has great music.
Bastion has great narration.
So why did it feel like a chore to finish the second half?
I think my main issue with Bastion, was that the story really didn't show itself enough to keep you motivated to play. The motivation to keep playing was "Gotta get all of the cores and shards to fix the Bastion".
I get that you are supposed to pick on world details by listening to what the other two have to say about the items, but it just results in a lot of back story, but yet no actual immediate story whatsoever. It just really started to hurt the game once things started getting a little more repetitive. The weapons usually offered a good mix-up, but they all seemed to situational, so I found myself switching back to Cael Hammer/Scrap Musket most of the time.
All in all, there's a lot to love about Bastion. The subtlety can be a strong point at times, but the COMPLETE lack of immediate progressing story does hurt the pacing of the game. It's a good game, and the story could be deeply analyzed to probably invoke some deep meaning. But at normal value, the story lacks.
I still recommend this game, because it just barely overstays it's welcome, and the gameplay is really nice. Also, the songs that are actually sung, are incredible.

Pros:
- Expansive universe to explore, with dozens of different species of flora and fauna to find and interact with.
- Infinite replayability with the creation of new universes.
- Integrated Mod support allowing for dozens of mods which completely alter the game, or just add in new features to tools within the game already.
- A multitude of weaponry, from Rocket Launchers with homing missiles to Swords which allow you to helicopter your way to victory, there are tons of ways to cut a swath through to your destination.
- An expandable ship that grows as the size of your crew grows.
- An overly abundant amount of materials which can be used in building. Do you want your house to look as if it's a rusted, run-down apartment building? You can do such! Do you want a giant scientific complex? You can do such!
- Impressive in-game civilizations which can be found almost anywhere, regardless of planet type, just have to do some exploring.
- Intriguing, yet simple crafting system. It just.. Works.
- Colonization features allow you to colonize a planet, resulting in the construction of massive cities, or small primitive civilizations.
Cons:
- Extremely lackluster storyline.
- Crew members recruited to your ship often die when exploring new planets, resulting in their existence becoming a moot point. This, bundled with the fact you can't recruit JUST ANYONE (without mods), results in quite a large headache.
- Crew recruitment missions essentially devolve into escort missions and fetch quests.
-
. What I mean by this is, the game is a breeze to just jump from one tier to another in regards to exploration. The storyline isn't required to progress planet tiers, and most planets don't actually present a valid threat until several thousand feet underground. Highly recommend modding the game to get more playtime out of it, as well as more exploration as well as a multitude of worlds (Might I suggest Frackin'universe?)
- A soundtrack that is both great, but also extremely annoying due to how unecessarily repetitive it is. Biome changes do not trigger soundtrack changes, thus resulting in the same serene exploration soundtrack to trigger during a rather tense situation where you're trying to survive underground.
- Bosses are inconsequential, unfun, and not very challenging.
- Legendary weapons are extremely laughable, to the extent of some of them being actually detrimental to use. Primarily used white-blue rarity weapons to explore planets.
-Extremely obvious balancing issues (Noticeable in certain areas of the game. I need not say more, as it's obvious later on).
- Poorly optimized in certain areas due to an overall massive amount of effects (I have a PC which can run any game nowadays on ultra, this should not be happening in a 2D pixel sidescroller. It is a minor complaint, but definitely does exist.)
- No discard hotkey, resulting in a frustrating amount of time being spent stacking rotten food and other things to throw away.
- Monetary values are arbitrary in that at endgame, they are essentially equivalent to nothing.
- The inability to resize the matter manipulators selectable area. You'd think this would be something in the game from the get go.. Yet it is not.
Overall score: 7.5/10. I'd suggest anyone play the game, however whilst it is very obvious that the game takes some of its inspiration from Terraria, and succeeds where it never has (replayability), it also falls flat in some areas that Terraria delivers with aplomb. Upon the release of 1.0 the developers removed a multitude of features, including mechs, and other features which gave the game a more interesting take upon planetary exploration. Starbound is not an entire game without mods, which should be highly considered by anyone who is playing for the first time, as well as anyone who has played a multitude of hours.
Mod suggestions:
- Frackin'Universe. Adds a relatively large new endgame as well as being bundled with other mods which allow for some interesting tinkering.
- Frackin'Music. Adds new music for the biomes of FU.
- Matter Manipulator Manipulator. Toggle liquid collection on/off, or set your matter manipulator cursor size from 1x1 to 5x5.
- Earth's Finest Crew Improvements. Actually makes your crew a tangible force to be reckoned with, also allowing for the recruitment of merchants and so on>
- XS Corporation Mechs. Introduced mechs into the game once more. Gives off a lost planet feel as you explore the planet in your giant mech, disembarking to explore buildings and dungeons.
- ZZ Mech Customizations. Allows you to customize mechs to a certain extent. Need I say more?

Not sure why I'm writing this since it'll probs just get lost but anyhow, here's my review of this game.
I originally purchased this game around it's initial "Early Release" release over two years ago. The game back then seemed too vanilla. The concept was very intreguing. Being a huge fan of Terraria, the idea of that game on a much bigger scale really held my interest. To my disappointment, the game didn't have much to offer. Once you "beat" the game, which only took a day or two of playing, there was just nothing to do. And by "beat" i just mean aquire the best armor and weapons really. There wasn't really any story at the time.
Fast forward to now. 1.0 is released and the game has changed drastically. One day, a few weeks back, I decided to try this game out once more. It was all over the home page of Steam and it really made me want to give it one more chance, at least to the point where I felt like it was worth the buy. Well, I can honestly say that, after playing for another 20 hours or so and beating the main story, it isn't a bad game. The story progression is decent, the game mechanics are smooth, and it is overall an enjoyable experience. Before I explain any more in detail, I will list a few of my personal pros and cons.
Pro:
-Fun with friend (Multiplayer)
-Good sense of completion/accomplishment after completing main story quests
-Plays well (Good weapon/tool mechanics)
-Has a lot more potential
Cons:
-Quite boring alone (In my own opinion)
-Story is a bit too short
-Story missions are a bit too repetitive
-Final boss is the main one that doesn't feel very rewarding (also too easy and quick)
-Has a lot more potential
The reason I put "Has a lot more potential" on both is because it really is both good and bad. It's good that the developers have room to make the game better, but it's also not too good because at points, the game still doesn't feel fully complete. There also needs to be more variation in the main story. Every mission is just (spoiler warning possibly) scan (race) objects -> teleport to (race) location -> defeat boss. It just feels too wash-rinse-repeat. Anyhow, on a better note, the game is actually enjoyable with friends. Mining and building with others is fun, and upgrading your ship and EPP provides a fun feeling of progression. Exploring the various environments and fighting the different enemies is both exciting and annoying, but hey, I think those feelings combined make these type of games good. If it's never a little annoying, it's probably not challenging, and cake-walk games aren't generally as fun. The weapon/armor progressions/tiers were a bit confusing. It was a bit tricky to figure out when you really had the best things in the game, and the wiki wasnt much help. It seems to still be in the progress of being updated. Anyhow, let's wrap all this mess up into a conclusion.
Starbound is a fun game if you have another person to play with. If you are looking for a game that has a lot of replayability, I do not believe this is a game for you. It's fun to play through the main story once, maybe twice, but much more it just feels to overdone and boring. If you are okay with that, this game is a good buy. I was pleased with the newest update. If they add more to the story, I will consider playing again, but for now, once was enough. Like I said, there is definetly more that this game could be, the question is, will any more come of it?

This game...has totally dominated my life like no other game since Oblivion (Yes, I liked ES:IV better than Skyrim).  Having just beat a New Game Plus, I am finally satisified that I have done at least 85% of the quests and can let it sit for a while.
As a lot of other people have said, the combat system and companion or 'Pawn' system are incredible.  You can change your vocation - class - at any point after hitting level 10 so the combat never really gets old.  One hour I'm clinging on an ogre's♥♥♥♥♥ smacking it with a sword, the next hour I'm hiding behind my minions casting (very visually pleasing) epic spells in fabulous flowing robes.
The one real downside to this game - the lack of any real character development.  RPG's are the one game genre, in my opinion, where character development is, if not required, absolutely expected.  Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen does not deliver.
That being said, the story is original, but not anything really great (no Oblivion or Skyrim for sure) but definitely hooking enough to warrant at least one enjoyable playthrough.
The monsters and enemy AI are pretty solid - even after I began really understanding attack patterns I still found myself dying when I wasn't fully paying attention.  As for the minions, I found them to be pretty solid AI allies, I know a lot of people didn't like how they play (and constantly chatter) but I enjoyed them (and found their chattering rather endearing).
If you like epic RPG's, DDDA should be on your computer.
Here's to hoping for Dragon's Dogma 2!!

Even if Singularity is not very long (8h) and the storyline is linear, it's a very pleasant shooter.
It is obvious that the title borrows many ideas from predecessors, both in mechanics (Half Life), player progression (Dead Space) and setting (Bioshock, Metro 2033), the game manages to have its own identity and is very satisfying to play : once you got the Time Manipulator, it is possible for you to approach each encounter with a very distinct style, ranging from classical shooter up to combos like : deactivate barrel, carry barrel, lock enemies in time, reactivate barrel, throw barrel, shoot barrel - and wait until every single enemy is blasted off.
The game features three endings, that you could just explore by reloading the last scene. Replaying the game is still interesting since the progression system allows you to use knowledge of Time Manipulator augments to adapt to your playstyle.
So even if Singularity is not a "great" FPS, it is a decent one with a very good execution. Raven still got it !

The Mass Effect series is the greatest work of entertainment I have ever experienced. Sometimes memories of the game come flooding back to me in a way that can only be compared to the nostalgia of summer camp or late night bike rides with neighbood friends as a child. There is an uncomfortable poignance in knowing that none of it actually happened, the friends you made don't actually exsist, and perhaps the harshest truth: there are only a few real-life memories I wouldn't trade for Mass Effect.

Things I liked:
+space based 3rd person SciFi cRPG (big plus, my favoured game type).
+storyline in general.
+combat system.
+exploration of solar systems.
+ability to mod items (weapons, armour).
+ability to replay game with the same character again.
Things I disliked:
-too short storyline (it ends way too quickly).
-exploration limited to usualy one planet per system and unfortunatelly VERY repetative (the same crashed probes etc). It's getting boring quite fast.
-lack of non-lethal weapons (BIG minus for me)

So far, this game is amazing. It's like a lot of survival games, but at the same time, it's nothing like anything else. This survival game puts you on an island with a story. It's not just some random place where they tell you to cut down a tree.

I recommend this game only to veteran survival sandbox game players. It is simply too hard for 96.7% of average game players. I have made it to day 89 of 7DTD solo without dying. I have played other games hardcore, as well. But this game was almost unplayable. The learning curve is wicked hard. Almost none of the people posting game videos online have made it past 4 videos. They simply cannot remain alive.
PROS: Great looking game visually even on lower video settings.
CONS: The repeated use of the same trees that can be harvested gives it a christmas tree farm look at times.
PROS: Great weapons and armor
CONS: You can have an Ebon Steel axe or Ebon Steel Armor. You only have enough gem shards for one or the other due to fairly horrid constant repair costs.
PROS: The game has a relentless feel that drives you to goals related to survival, such as warmth and food.
CONS: The game is developed by devs who are like frustrated teenagers who inexplicably took viagra. The warmth and life bars lose 1 life per second at times. The devs are like the boyfriend who is premature, and the players are the girlfriends who have a moue.
PROS: The crafting although basic is doable and has a need to do it to survive element to it.
CONS: There are only a few abandoned buildings to stay in, requiring you to make camp fires every couple of minutes as you travel at the beginning. Also there is only one forge in an abandoned town I found to use at the beginning, and it is camped by a patrolling red eyed skeletal warrior. They are instant death at the beginning, but by the time you have chainmail and an Ebon Steel Axe, they are simply annoying, as they cause damage to your armor that is horrid to fix.
CONCLUSION: Love the game, love playing it. But it is going to fail in commercial release, as it is simply too hard. Even if they put in a do this, then do that tutorial, the game is simply too hard for the majority of gamers. I had to delete my first 8 games, since bears and wolf packs camped my bodies making them unretrievable. Great game. Too hard. Loses all but the very most stubborn veteran sandbox players. Would have made it a negative review, except I enjoyed it too much.

Savage Lands is brutal, if you don't work out in time how to survive you are dead. It's a simple formula.
Join a server for the first time you play at night, and you'll probably die through starvation and/or cold. That is if the inhabitants don't butcher you for all your worth before hand.
I really like the games potential, it does borrow some ideas from the likes of Skyrim, but with a much steeper learning curve. There is no world map, no fast travel. Can't use a compass? You'll never find home again.
I think as the updates come, this game will only get better, there are some basic elements that would make the game better in the future, and it needs to delve deeper into a story line or at least more 'objectives' so once you have completed the initial survival tasks and murdered a few of the heavier enemies/survived to a basic sustainable level there is more to do.
When I started I didn't have a clue where I was going, or what I was doing. I won't spoil the fun and tell you, but you do have a ureka! moment when you finally start to survive and craft some essential items.
The start of the game sees that you build/craft some essential items for survival - nearly all of them have a purpose or a function with exception to building a "Leanto" - it offered me no obvious cover, warmth or protection as you cannot crouch or go prone, which in turn is a waste of time and resource - which being almost naked, half freezing to death on a beach is a luxury you cannot afford.
In the latter stages of the initial game you can build stone houses, and eventually a Town Hall, which in my opinion is vastly under-used at the moment as it offers no viable enhancements, except for a visual claim on a piece of land, and perhaps a gathering point for the community. It should have an upper floor which serves as a lookout, or something similar, and offer some other benefits - perhaps have a throne in it and then appoint a ruler of the territory/land.
Improvements the dev's could make:
I want the game to essentially turn out like a first person "Banished crossed with Skyrim" - it would be great to be able to build more in the village, like a mill, a farm and a baker - a market place and then if the resources were scattered around the map, for example corn only grows on certain locations on the map, this could lead to a trade system, as well as a transportation system, kind of like protect the flag, except its corn. (or a territorial war all together) and the building of market places, and larger towns (Even CASTLES!) (Imagine a castle siege by warring factions!) where everyone has a purpose and a house.
The creatures could still attack as normal, and there would need to be dedicated watch men/women to alert the rest of the village. The dragon, could at any time attack said village and potentially destroy buildings which would need to be re-built.
There could be basic paths and roads added, signposts would be a massive win, and potentially horses, leading to knights, and an armoury.
I think that there also needs to be a cull on 'server hopping' and dropping high level items to new players - this spoils the fun.
We learned that the players of Skyrim yearned for a sense of ownership, and thus the ability to build your own house was introduced. This kind of starts to fill that void, but once the building plans have been improved, the storyline expanded on and more challenges added I think we are onto a winner.
Overall, I would recommend you buy this game for it's potential, but at the moment it does have limited playability based on the objectives you need to complete and the 'bosses' you need to slaughter. Once you have survived whatever perils await you and built your kit up high enough so you and some friends can murder the dragon, that's pretty much the main challenge sorted.

As one of the original backers for this game wayyyyyyy back in the heyday of Homestuck, it's certainly been a wild ride waiting for Hiveswap. And after 5 years of delays, hiatuses, and a mess of a fandom constantly reeling at the idea of a video game being *somewhere*, I can honestly say that not only was this worth the wait, but I'm already excited for Act 2.
A word of caution that's been thrown around for quite a while about this game: If you haven't read Homestuck, it's *very* recommended that you do so beforehand. It's not necessarily required, but it definitely will help you quite a bit in terms of understanding the backstory to this game. Plus, it shines a lot of light onto the universe you're diving into here.
In terms of gameplay, this is certainly a 90's-style point-and-click in every sense of the term. There are the occasional puzzles here and there, but you're not going to be constanly fretting over them like say, Myst or Secrets of Monkey Island. They're quite simple, and don't take too much thought. Your inventory will have at most 10 items, and only 5 or 6 things can be combined to solve the puzzles. Still, that doesn't discount the game in my eyes.
If you're playing this, you're doing it for the experience. The game itself looks stunning, with the beautiful background sets, incredible sound work by James Roach and Toby Fox (Yeah, *that* Toby Fox), and the occasional interlude of animation, very much styled in the form of Homestuck's flash panels.
If you're taking your time and reading all the flavortext, checking out everything in your environment and taking the experience in, this game will last you around 3-4 hours per playthrough, and on my first playthrough I only got about half the achievements, so there's room for replayability.
It's hard to say if I'd recommend this for someone who hasn't read Homestuck, just because you'll be diving into an integral part of the story's universe in this game, but if the game does interest you, I'd say the source material is worth the read. It'll take you a little while, but the art and music that spawned from the webcomic should definitely get you excited to delve into this adventure.
At this point, all I can do is wait excitedly for the next entry, which hopefully comes sooner than later.

If you've seen the Angry Joe Review, then you've seen the game and heard his remarks about the state of the vanilla game. Now the updated version has come to the PC and nearly every complaint of his has been entirely addressed, meaning this is the best possible version of the game that you can purchase.
I've always wanted to be the director of a game that was the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of Dark Souls and Shadow of the Collossus. Did Capcom beat me to making just such a game? Well, no, at least not the exact game that I want to make, but this comes pretty close, just add a dash of Skyrim and this is what I feel their recipe for DD:DA was.
Combat and enemies are pretty generic for what the genre as a whole has to offer: spiders, skeletal knights, cyclopes, etc. I haven't seen a mimic in this game though, but I'm glad for it.
The most exciting aspect of the game is the bosses, where you'll use the climbing mechanic to reach a cyclopes' eye or chimera's tail. There actually is a mechanic where you can use the weight of your party to keep a griffen grounded, preventing it from flying away before dropping its phat loot.
The biggest negative aspect is the pawn rental system. This is the way you create your party, and what Yahtzee called 'Pimping the mentally subnormal' in his video was a pretty apt description. The biggest cause for pawns not behaving the way they should be, is you the player, or the player that created the other pawns, not knowing the mechanics behind the pawn's AI protocols.
Pros:
+ Vibrantly alive community whose DEMANDS for this game finally brought it to PC, with the upgrades included
+ Controller support, tons of options for video and sound for low-high end PC's
+ AAA production value shows through writing, voice acting, etc.
+ Offers choice in difficulty, both easy and hard modes, and speedrun mode.
Cons:
- 'Wiki difficulty' as information about the game is obfuscated, you will have to regularly visit a wiki to uncover it
- Story informs gameplay, not the other way around*
- Mechanics are less than perfect. You have to learn certain skills in order to properly grab enemies to set them up for your team, otherwise you'll just throw them over your shoulder fireman style and become encumbered. I wish you could grab large things and just push them, but there's only grappling or climbing.
*Capcom have a story to tell in DD:DA, so you can't just go Renegade like in Mass Effect. I ambushed a castle guard at the top of the tallest tower in the castle, and chucked him down to the ground below where he exploded into a cloud of bloody chunks. Then he got back up again, and everyone ran around to arrest me. Some characters do not have the same benefit of 'Plot Armor' and they are arguably the more important NPC's actual questgivers, that if they die, you will miss out on the quests they would have offered for the rest of the playthrough. Mundane soldier? Invincible. Traveling Merchants? Dragon sucked their soul up.
Final Verdict:
9.5/10 - I was a fan that was anticipating its release onto PC for YEARS. The game shows its cracks, but is worth not only the money but the time input.

I waited since 2014 for this game and I feel completely underwhelmed at the lack of diversity and depth of lore. It doesn't feel much different than from two years ago, except now it feels like little grinds were put into everything to make it seem like there's more content.
It's an interstellar open world space game yet I can't scan a planet to see if there's a Glitch village or a mini-biome present and the game forces me to explore one planet after another in search of them.
Housing? Hoverbikes? Fossils? They have little to no reward for the effort of completing them. Money (pixels) is easy as crap. Farming sucks because food won't stack and rots, making complex food items not worth making anymore. I farmed tons of rice and coconuts and just carried around a kitchen station to surpass the food rotting and stacking issue (rice and coconuts stack but need to be "cooked" into food).
Cosmetic armor, trophies, dumb crew members (except engineer). Useless in a single player game. My ship is my base... which makes building a base or anything on a planet completely optional. It shouldn't be - it should be needed, to get NPCs for needed items, but instead it's all optional and a grind at that.
Back in the day you were a badass if you went to a cold planet and placed torches to keep warm instead of making a suit of leather armor. Now it's just an EPP backpack that grants you access to a type of planet to get a resource to make the next EPP, and so on.
Lore is just bland. Where's the Novakid lore they said they'd put in, or Novakid towns/cities? Each race is stuck in its stereotype and I brought that up years ago only to be argued by fanboys who said it would be better. They were wrong.
Doesn't take long to progress and finish the vanilla game at all. Frackin' Universe, however, kept the game alive for me. What would have taken two days and complete disappointment turned into 90+ hours over two weeks of content that the game should have in the first place.
This game should have been $10 and creators of the mods that make up Frackin' Universe should make a deal with Chucklefish as a DLC for $5.

This game has been out for a while, but it doesn't stop people from calling it an Assassins' Creed clone. There are a few interesting points to note regarding this comparison.
- This game has a weaker narrative and a much shorter story. (Nonetheless enjoyable for LOTR fans.
- The fundamental design of the combat system is, of course, a direct imitation of the Assassin's Creed series. The interesting part is that Shadow of Mordor does it *better*. Much better. Attacks and counter killing is executed much more smoothly than the Assassin's Creed counterpart. There is a greater variety of approaches to defeating your enemies. Stealth killing is here and better than ever. As a guy who liked Assassin's Creed Syndicate, Shadow of Mordor does it a whole lot better.
- Now, I mentioned before that the game's story is short. IT IS. I'm not joking. It's over really fast. That's where the real problem lies. With such a well developed and fleshed out combat system, there's only a few hours of story before it all comes to an abrupt halt. It hampers the potential that exists in such a great combat system and they should've found ways to let you enjoy it to the fullest.
Still, if you liked Assassin's Creed and/or Lord of the rings and if its on sale, get this game. Don't rush the story and enjoy the hell out of it.

The game takes place right after the second Hobbit film with a "What If?" scenario.
If you are are a hard-core LotR fan, this game might rustle you a little; but this game takes an interesting perspective within Middle-Earth.
Although the game focusses around the main character, Talion, who becomes a half-wraith, this game is really a setup for Sauron's origin story via lore objects, and looking at things that are touched upon in the older books.
The gameplay is not as complex as orginally advertised in the earlier reveals / discussions, but overall the game turned out well, with interesting combat tactics.
The addition of having the equivalent of a mini photoshop tool in the game, is also a bonus; allowing screenshots to be taken at any time, and allowing the user to edit them in-game.
In the end of the story though, it becomes obvious that the budget was running low, or something occured, because the game is greatly rushed at that point, and boss battles are very simple, or even cinematic.
As for DLCs, they contain cosmetics, runes, specific orcs, challenges, and expansions. One epansion, Lord of the Hunt takes place in-between a story arc in the game, which honestly doesn't make too much sense time-wise, and is sadly its own separate instance. The other, the Bright Lord, is a flashback expansion set in its own instance, but sadly just reuses the current maps, which make literally no sense (due to it taking place thousands of years earlier).
I do not know if a sequel will actually come ot fruitation, but the ending of the main story intrigued me greatly.
I would say to try this game out, even with its flaws; there are plenty of steam sales, and many users who are interested in Lord of the Rings could probably find entertainment within this game.

There is a bunch of quests and they really put a effort to make a good variations of type of quests, even the sidequest are not that boring to do, like the most games, i even collected all the collectables :D and it rewards you with runes, xp, upgrades to use in your skill tree.

Avec Zombie Panic Source, on oublie un peu tout, on met sa cervelle de côté et on prie pour être du côté humain.
...
Est ce que ça vaut le coup de passer 4 heures à télécharger ce petit mod ?
Et bien pour se faire, je vais vous citer tous les bons côtés de ce mod, ainsi que ses défauts.
Côtés positifs :
1)On a le droit à un jeu accessible : il est gratuit (c'est ce qu'on attend pour un mod après tout). Le jeu est aussi accès casual, franchement, c'est plaisant et ça pose aucun soucis (exemple lambda :"You are dead ! [.5 minutes later.]You've spawn as a zombie !Kill them all ...". Mais garre !Le jeu est, comme aujourd'hui 102% des jeux de zombies, très coopératif, autant du niveau des humains que des goules.
Mais, ne nous égarons pas. Le jeu est avant tout très plaisant, et on n'en demande pas plus. De plus, on sait à quoi s'attendre avec ce jeu, ce qui est un élément à prendre.
Côtés négatifs :
2)Comme tous ces jeux gratuits, la communauté ne suit pas vraiment. En fait, le jeu est pollué par des pyjamas sans être à cours d'insultes russes. Et oui, pour nous, pauvres français, la majorité des gens sont russes. Si seulement. Des fois il vous arrivera d'entendre des battles très virils entre enfants. Passionant ... Plus sérieusement, créer une stratégie avec vos collégues demandera patiente et persévérance !C'est un peu le revers de la médaille...
Mais, à ce que je sache, le jeu n'a pas beaucoup de problèmes comme de bugs.
Il est temps de répondre à cette question : est- ce que ça vaut le coup de télécharger Zombie Panic Source ?
Et bien oui ! Même si la communauté de ce jeu peut parfois décevoir, et qu'il est difficile d'établir une stratégie, le jeu vous procurera une bonne dose de fun pendant une petit heure, le temps de se mettre dans la peau d'un mort-vivant.
Je vous recommande ce mod.

Simply a great RPG. I haven´t had that much fun in a PC RPG in a long time.
Graphics 8.5/10 - This game is a videogame port from a game that is a few years old. While the graphics are pretty good and still hold up well, they do not have the same level of detail as a newer game like Witcher 3.
Sound 9.5/10 - Great music from the beggining until the end. The reason this game does not get a 10 is due to lipsync issues.
Gameplay 10/10 - Great combat. There are 9 classes to choose from, it is easy to play with any of them and the game even encourages you to change class from time to time. The pawn (helper) system is very interesting and allows you to get help from other players and lend your support character to help someone else. Beating a Cyclops, hydra or Cockatrice is incredible.
Story 9.5/10 - The main story is interesting, even if a few missions are escort or fetch quests. You will be thinking about the meta ending. This game also comes with the Dark Arisen DLC with its own interesting story. Two games for the price of one, and two good games.
Overall 9.5/10 - I had so much fun playing it, more than playing Witcher 3, that I had to play it twice. Do you like Dark Souls? Buy this game. Do you like Witcher? Buy this game. Do you like Dragon Age? Buy this game now!!!
