Starbound is a game that had a monumental premise thrown about when first being shown, which it has fallen short of to a certain extent. Starbound is a great game, but is lacking in very many ways in regards to its actual OFFICIAL release (Coming out of early access). With all of the above said, the game is still extremely charming, and worth getting for a singular completion of its main storyline, then the installation of mods.
Pros:
- Expansive universe to explore, with dozens of different species of flora and fauna to find and interact with.
- Infinite replayability with the creation of new universes.
- Integrated Mod support allowing for dozens of mods which completely alter the game, or just add in new features to tools within the game already.
- A multitude of weaponry, from Rocket Launchers with homing missiles to Swords which allow you to helicopter your way to victory, there are tons of ways to cut a swath through to your destination.
- An expandable ship that grows as the size of your crew grows.
- An overly abundant amount of materials which can be used in building. Do you want your house to look as if it's a rusted, run-down apartment building? You can do such! Do you want a giant scientific complex? You can do such!
- Impressive in-game civilizations which can be found almost anywhere, regardless of planet type, just have to do some exploring.
- Intriguing, yet simple crafting system. It just.. Works.
- Colonization features allow you to colonize a planet, resulting in the construction of massive cities, or small primitive civilizations.
Cons:
- Extremely lackluster storyline.
- Crew members recruited to your ship often die when exploring new planets, resulting in their existence becoming a moot point. This, bundled with the fact you can't recruit JUST ANYONE (without mods), results in quite a large headache.
- Crew recruitment missions essentially devolve into escort missions and fetch quests.
-
. What I mean by this is, the game is a breeze to just jump from one tier to another in regards to exploration. The storyline isn't required to progress planet tiers, and most planets don't actually present a valid threat until several thousand feet underground. Highly recommend modding the game to get more playtime out of it, as well as more exploration as well as a multitude of worlds (Might I suggest Frackin'universe?)
- A soundtrack that is both great, but also extremely annoying due to how unecessarily repetitive it is. Biome changes do not trigger soundtrack changes, thus resulting in the same serene exploration soundtrack to trigger during a rather tense situation where you're trying to survive underground.
- Bosses are inconsequential, unfun, and not very challenging.
- Legendary weapons are extremely laughable, to the extent of some of them being actually detrimental to use. Primarily used white-blue rarity weapons to explore planets.
-Extremely obvious balancing issues (Noticeable in certain areas of the game. I need not say more, as it's obvious later on).
- Poorly optimized in certain areas due to an overall massive amount of effects (I have a PC which can run any game nowadays on ultra, this should not be happening in a 2D pixel sidescroller. It is a minor complaint, but definitely does exist.)
- No discard hotkey, resulting in a frustrating amount of time being spent stacking rotten food and other things to throw away.
- Monetary values are arbitrary in that at endgame, they are essentially equivalent to nothing.
- The inability to resize the matter manipulators selectable area. You'd think this would be something in the game from the get go.. Yet it is not.
Overall score: 7.5/10. I'd suggest anyone play the game, however whilst it is very obvious that the game takes some of its inspiration from Terraria, and succeeds where it never has (replayability), it also falls flat in some areas that Terraria delivers with aplomb. Upon the release of 1.0 the developers removed a multitude of features, including mechs, and other features which gave the game a more interesting take upon planetary exploration. Starbound is not an entire game without mods, which should be highly considered by anyone who is playing for the first time, as well as anyone who has played a multitude of hours.
Mod suggestions:
- Frackin'Universe. Adds a relatively large new endgame as well as being bundled with other mods which allow for some interesting tinkering.
- Frackin'Music. Adds new music for the biomes of FU.
- Matter Manipulator Manipulator. Toggle liquid collection on/off, or set your matter manipulator cursor size from 1x1 to 5x5.
- Earth's Finest Crew Improvements. Actually makes your crew a tangible force to be reckoned with, also allowing for the recruitment of merchants and so on>
- XS Corporation Mechs. Introduced mechs into the game once more. Gives off a lost planet feel as you explore the planet in your giant mech, disembarking to explore buildings and dungeons.
- ZZ Mech Customizations. Allows you to customize mechs to a certain extent. Need I say more?

Not sure why I'm writing this since it'll probs just get lost but anyhow, here's my review of this game.
I originally purchased this game around it's initial "Early Release" release over two years ago. The game back then seemed too vanilla. The concept was very intreguing. Being a huge fan of Terraria, the idea of that game on a much bigger scale really held my interest. To my disappointment, the game didn't have much to offer. Once you "beat" the game, which only took a day or two of playing, there was just nothing to do. And by "beat" i just mean aquire the best armor and weapons really. There wasn't really any story at the time.
Fast forward to now. 1.0 is released and the game has changed drastically. One day, a few weeks back, I decided to try this game out once more. It was all over the home page of Steam and it really made me want to give it one more chance, at least to the point where I felt like it was worth the buy. Well, I can honestly say that, after playing for another 20 hours or so and beating the main story, it isn't a bad game. The story progression is decent, the game mechanics are smooth, and it is overall an enjoyable experience. Before I explain any more in detail, I will list a few of my personal pros and cons.
Pro:
-Fun with friend (Multiplayer)
-Good sense of completion/accomplishment after completing main story quests
-Plays well (Good weapon/tool mechanics)
-Has a lot more potential
Cons:
-Quite boring alone (In my own opinion)
-Story is a bit too short
-Story missions are a bit too repetitive
-Final boss is the main one that doesn't feel very rewarding (also too easy and quick)
-Has a lot more potential
The reason I put "Has a lot more potential" on both is because it really is both good and bad. It's good that the developers have room to make the game better, but it's also not too good because at points, the game still doesn't feel fully complete. There also needs to be more variation in the main story. Every mission is just (spoiler warning possibly) scan (race) objects -> teleport to (race) location -> defeat boss. It just feels too wash-rinse-repeat. Anyhow, on a better note, the game is actually enjoyable with friends. Mining and building with others is fun, and upgrading your ship and EPP provides a fun feeling of progression. Exploring the various environments and fighting the different enemies is both exciting and annoying, but hey, I think those feelings combined make these type of games good. If it's never a little annoying, it's probably not challenging, and cake-walk games aren't generally as fun. The weapon/armor progressions/tiers were a bit confusing. It was a bit tricky to figure out when you really had the best things in the game, and the wiki wasnt much help. It seems to still be in the progress of being updated. Anyhow, let's wrap all this mess up into a conclusion.
Starbound is a fun game if you have another person to play with. If you are looking for a game that has a lot of replayability, I do not believe this is a game for you. It's fun to play through the main story once, maybe twice, but much more it just feels to overdone and boring. If you are okay with that, this game is a good buy. I was pleased with the newest update. If they add more to the story, I will consider playing again, but for now, once was enough. Like I said, there is definetly more that this game could be, the question is, will any more come of it?

This game..... I so much would like to love this game. All of the elements of a good game are there, everything that should make this game great can be witnessed through the turgid veil of garbage that covers its surface.
I bought this game YEARS ago, when your starting sword was overpowered and there were no quests of any kind. It was filled with bugs and horrendous performence issues, along with having nothing to do. These days, there are still bugs and horrendous performance issues. But at least there's something to do, right? Quests, bosses? Yeah. Sure, they're something you can do. None of it is fun, though. The bosses are all way too easy or damn impossible to fight thanks to the game needing to freeze every couple of second during a fight. And the quests? In my hours playing this game with this most recent update I have yet to find a single generated quest that was not some variation of; "Get me X" or "Take me to Y" or "Kill Z".
One of the longest awaited features of Starbound was a story. A cohesive plot told beyond vague npc coversation bits, or overly-long and poorly written codex entries. A little while back, they finally added a main quest. Guess what? The story is boring. It's dull, and unoriginal. It's basically a compilation of all generic space-mythos. Giant ancient tentacle beast coming to destroy everything and all that.
But, the story is forgivable. The quests, too, are forgiveable. At least they're trying to add content, right?
While I can look past all that, one thing I can't look past is how god-awfully this game performs. Every time I play I discover a new bug. Huge chunks of the world go unloaded for extended periods of time, entities glitch back and forth so frequently that I was convinced it was a feature. During combat, when you're really trying to get in there and attack, the game will just spontaneously freeze. It's almost as though it's trying to calculate the damage values with a ♥♥♥♥ing abbacus.
One of the main features of a Mineclone game is BUILDING and MINING. Building is unsatisfying, as it just doesn't mesh well with the exploration elements of the game. You make a huge, magnificent base on your first planet's surface, fill it with everything you could dream of, and revel in its beauty.... Then you realize you need more materials and have to leave. You never find the planet again. There's no point to build, as you're just going to leave it all behind anyway. The mining is one of the most frusterating parts of this game. Everything in this game leans towards the vertical over the horrizontal, in terms of how you traverse the world. Now, this wouldn't be a problem, if you took less fall damage. It's at this point that I must compare Star man's Sky- I mean Starbound, to Terraria, so, please forgive me for that. Terraria excells in the 2D Sandbox elements because of the inherent factors that compose its world generation. Caves are sparce, but grandious, always giving you just enough natural structure to not feel overwhelmed, but they still feel like your digging straight down had a point. Starbound, on the other hand, fills its subterranean layers with oversized caverns, fit only for you to die in. Cave systems are absolutely massive, and getting lost in them is far too easy. I couldn't really put into straight forward words what makes the caves so frusterating, so, allow me to use an analogy.
Imagine you come to a crossroads. Two paths branch off on either side of you. Both paths offer something you want, but you can only choose one. Easy answer, I hear you saying, go down one, then return to the other. Yes, that is an option. The only problem is, once you get to the end of the road you've selected, you fall into a pit where the world has yet to load and die.
Sorry for the poor analogy, but I couldn't be bothered to write any more hyperbole.
"But, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game has SPACE." I hear you shouting. Yes, I know, it has a massive universe to explore, with millions of different procedurally generated planets to interact with. Sound familiar? Like a certain flop of a game that has become a well-recognized meme? Well, much like said game, exploration in this game loses its luster fast, once you realize that all you'll find on the planets are an assortment of pre-made, unimpressive structures. Towns aren't fun to find, since there's no interaction with its denizens, apart from the 'randomly generated' quests they offer. (All of which are just fetch quests or kill that guy quests, might I add.) And random vendors are basically pointless since anything they could offer you can be found for free in the wilderness.
I want to like this game. The music is fantastic, the lore of the universe is facinating to read about, and to be entirely honest the pixel art is rather appealing to look at.
But, having bought this game about two years ago, and watching as the developers simply try to shovel more content into it, instead of fixing what they've already added, I simply cannot stand to recommend this game to anyone.

More levels grant you better weapons, better weapons grant you even mightier ways to conquor your enemies. Some of the singleplayer missions are so difficult it's almost completely up to luck and repetition to pass (Fiesta Forever, I'm talking to you!). On occasion the game glitches out and you lose your progress in a mission/game that you were currently partaking in, seemingly with no explanation at all. This problem is actually what prompted me to write this review, I was almost done defeating the final singleplayer mission when I was whisked away back to the homescreen to join the charade of protests from the other players. Even excluding the listed problems, sometimes this game just gets too annoying to handle. If you perservere through all the pain and agony though, you'll eventualy unlock amazing weapons like the bouncy ball. This game may have it's share of brain-bashing, I'm-about-to-jump-off-a-cliff moments, but it also has it's enjoyable ones. After dedicating countless hours to this game, even getting kicked out of my final boss battle (as previously stated) I'm still going to go back and finish it. I have that undescribable need to finish what I've started, even if It'll be my eventual downfall. So if you are also willing to invest in this game, be prepared to get mad. Be prepared to get angry. Overall though, be prepared to never hit anyone with that damn bouncy ball.

Amidst a crowded market of early access post-apocalyptic survival games, Miscreated distinguishes itself as one of the greatest. It positions itself among giants in the same genre, DayZ and Rust, and even surpasses them in some areas.
Jumping onto a server, the first thing you will notice is the beautifully broken world that is Orca Island. The foliage, grass and mountains are breath taking. Walk into a town and you have no doubt this is the apocalyps. Broken down buildings, overgrown with grass. The environment feels much more 'home" than DayZ, as the style of architecture and items within buildings are very North American. Appliances (tvs, computers etc) laying around the world indicate that the apocalypse started sometime not very removed from our day and age.
The atmosphere of the game can range anywhere from hopeful (in the bright sunny mid-day, hearing birds chirping gleefully as you stride through the forest) to spooky (in night's grips as you can see nothing other than what your flashlight illumines in front of you). The grey fog that spreads accross the land at times during the day is my favourite weather effect, as it ushers in a very foreboding and chilling atmosphere as you loot around Orca Island.
The mutuants and wolves are sure to keep you on your toes, as you stealthily search for that which keeps you alive.
Basebuilding is mature. It takes a group of people to build a base, and near impossible to build anything substantial alone. There is a new inventory system in the game also, where you can store your precious loot.
Combat mechanics are a bit clunky. Melee combat is satisfactory, as there's some allowance to dodge blows and maneuver in a fight. However, it is the aiming system that is unsatisfactory. It can be very "shaky" feeling, and is something that takes practice and getting used to.
As for the community, there are 7 unfriendly players to every 3 friendly (in my personal encounters anyway). Of course this is part of what makes the game fun. Albeit, when people start shooting at you with no quality interaction, it can become wearisome and negate some of the joy you experience in playing. My wish is for more roleplay servers wherein it is a requirement to have adequate interaction before "going to war".
Personally, this is my favourite survival game. I love it.
9/10. Keep up the good work, devs.

As a gamer who thinks Baldur's Gate-games, and in lesser extent the others created with Infinity engine,  are pretty much the best RPG's ever created, I am jubilant they finally got the offspring we have been waiting for.
The fact that it is no longer based on the D&D system was a concern of mine, but the new system works brilliantly. The classes, leveling and talents are solid and fairly easy to understand. Giving up on certain classic D&D rules is a good idea in my opinion. Now you can have your Cleric wield a crossbow, making it a deadly sniper from the back. However, the lack of specialization classes is a flaw IMHO. Also the lack of Party AI (behavior) is a really silly. A lot of micromanagement needed at times.
Graphics are very solid, beautiful, yet paying homage to the original games. 3D characters look very good an blend seamlessly into the background. Sounds are also good and the music made me think of old Baldur's immideately. The game feels sublime and finished, and there seems to be very few bugs to encounter.
However, the story seems a bit vague compared to the original Bioware games and characters lack charisma. They are not as interesting as say Minsc or Edwin, but still are interesting enough to keep you company.
All in all, I am giving this game a strict 8/10.
If the party AI is added I would raise it to 9/10.
There is plenty of content, but I do hope there will be a substantial amount of extra content in DLC-form in the future.

The game takes place right after the second Hobbit film with a "What If?" scenario.
If you are are a hard-core LotR fan, this game might rustle you a little; but this game takes an interesting perspective within Middle-Earth.
Although the game focusses around the main character, Talion, who becomes a half-wraith, this game is really a setup for Sauron's origin story via lore objects, and looking at things that are touched upon in the older books.
The gameplay is not as complex as orginally advertised in the earlier reveals / discussions, but overall the game turned out well, with interesting combat tactics.
The addition of having the equivalent of a mini photoshop tool in the game, is also a bonus; allowing screenshots to be taken at any time, and allowing the user to edit them in-game.
In the end of the story though, it becomes obvious that the budget was running low, or something occured, because the game is greatly rushed at that point, and boss battles are very simple, or even cinematic.
As for DLCs, they contain cosmetics, runes, specific orcs, challenges, and expansions. One epansion, Lord of the Hunt takes place in-between a story arc in the game, which honestly doesn't make too much sense time-wise, and is sadly its own separate instance. The other, the Bright Lord, is a flashback expansion set in its own instance, but sadly just reuses the current maps, which make literally no sense (due to it taking place thousands of years earlier).
I do not know if a sequel will actually come ot fruitation, but the ending of the main story intrigued me greatly.
I would say to try this game out, even with its flaws; there are plenty of steam sales, and many users who are interested in Lord of the Rings could probably find entertainment within this game.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a action-stealth open world game that steps up the Lord of the Rings Games to a new level. The game is solid and satisfying to play, and its open world with bunch of sidequest, collectables to collect and more stuff.
You play as Talion, a Captain of the Black Gate (Rangers) that saw hes family slaughter and then banned from death and here enters, his curse, Celebrimbor, the ring-maker ghost, but with this curse, both can fight the evil in Gondor, and bring down those who torment the land and Talion's family assassin's.
Now, the story is not bad, i believe its pretty good, but far from marvelous. The characters are just a few, the deserter, the old laddy, the hot daughter of the old lady, the bad guys who kill your family, your family, you and your shadow, and if my memory dont fail me, thats pretty much it. ahhhh. GOLLUMM, man, it only shows up like 2, 3 times in the game, and sincerely, i felt like it wasnt necessary, the appearance of this character sound like a bit force, just to reinforce the refference of the LOTR. but otherwise, the characters are decent ... i liked the the daughter of the old lady pretty much :D ... and the voice acting its GREAT, for real, it's really good.
Putting aside the combat that is practically a copy of Batman series style of combat, though its very satisfactory, the animations and skills, the stealth systeam, hands down, 5 stars.
The Nemesis System is a Masterpiece, its like a hierarchy composed by Warchiefs and Captains, and more in the middle-end game you will be able to dominate them and have them in the palm of your hand. You will be able to dominate Captains to obey your will, and one of the ways to take down Warchiefs is Betrayer, if you branded their bodyguards, you can make this to betray the warchief and they will help you in the fight, the same applies to the normal Uruks, in a normal fight they are yours. Like a Army all around Gondor. Damn Son....
Of course the system allows you to do more, the captains murder eachother, warchiefs making riots to a captain, etc...and that gives you a great freedom.
There is a bunch of quests and they really put a effort to make a good variations of type of quests, even the sidequest are not that boring to do, like the most games, i even collected all the collectables :D and it rewards you with runes, xp, upgrades to use in your skill tree.
One thing that dissapointed me in the game... The Boss Fights... not the warchiefs, because those,,, man some are pure rock, the more you hitted them the more they like you ( ♥♥♥♥ingg LORM, i got your head in the end .... ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ uruk), back to business, they boss fights and the story ending are a dissapointing and taste little.
The first boss its like fighting almost a normal uruk or a captain, the second you just need to caught him with the guard down and brand him a few times and thats it... but now, when you face Sauron, guess what, a quick-time event battle, NOOOOOOOOOO, the ending boss must be a brutal fight, with you low health low focus and suddenly you find the strength inside your heart, your fingers stop shaking and thats it, kill or be killed, not a goddamn quick-time event where you cant feel the thrill of battle. MAN, here they blow it.
GORGEOUS VISUALS, and that is enough.
From all the experience i had with this game, the story, the gameplay, the visuals, the battles, the pros and cons, i give it a 8.5/10
If the characters were more charismatic, im not saying Talion is not a good character, Attention, hes a badass, but the rest if more charismatic, if the ending was better, and the rewarding was a bit more present i would give this game a 9.5 or even a 10/10.

Mass Effect:
+ A very narrative centered game filled with decisions which impact the way your character is perceived and how the world develops around you.
+ Lots of dialogue explaining the background and plot of the title, so you become immersed in the story.
+ Interesting array of weapons, with modifications which can increase weapon stability, damage, heat absorption and more.
+ Mass Effect combines RPG and shooter elements to make an interesting action packed game. Level up your party by gaining experience from quests, killing enemies or decrypting locked cases. You can spend talent points to upgrade your skills in firearms, combat armour, health, electronics and more.
- For an RPG it isn't the longest game, taking around 45-60 hours to finish. I explored a lot of the galaxies and the main questline is sort of short. I didn't see everything the game had to offer but for the most part I did.
- Graphics are really dated for a game released in 2008. In comparison, the Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion which hit the market in 2006, looks far superior. Nevertheless, you'll get used to it the more you play.
- Inventory system isn't streamlined and a bit clunky, room for improvement here.
Overall Score: 8/10

The concept of playing lands on a hexagonal board makes this game like no other CCG. A number of factors make drawing extra cards far less important than other CCGs. It's really nice to be able to focus on things other than card drawing when building a deck. The board is just the right size where you have some room to manuever, but nothing seems too far away.
Collecting cards goes fairly fast for commons and rares, but it takes a long time to get many of the higher rarity cards. Though even with the low rarity cards, you can still build fun decks.
The single-player content is decent. The generic versus AI parts aren't that interesting, but the puzzle mode, and boss modes offer compelling, if limited content.
Battle mode (vs players) is fairly fun. Trying out new decks is my favorite part. My problem with Ranked mode is once you climb the ladder a little, it seems like every match is intense, and lasts a bit too long. Pandora mode feels like a waste of time, so I just avoid it.
The recent addition of a co-op mode is a neat idea (though it takes a lot of gold to unlock if you aren't willing to buy it). You can have an AI player as your ally, but they seemed pretty bad, so you probably need a human ally.

Such a fun and relaxing game with quite a bit of indepth strategy. I'm constantly building and editing new decks while earning new cards. Definitely a game worth playing if you take the time to understand deck builds.

Though it says I have put about 20+ hours into Pillars of Eternity it is more accurately something like 12-15, but I suppose leaving it on pause while you build pc would do that. This game was kind of a mystery to me before I put some time into it, and I was not sure what to expect. I know that it looked similar to the baulder's gate that I played in the past, and if you have not played any of those titles then let me say it is a good thing to be compared to. Let me say after 10 hours of gameplay and some reading and experimenting with the class and gameplay this game is growing into a new favoirte, now let me tell you some of the reasons why:
First of I am a fantasy nerd, I read fantasy all the time, and when I am not reading series like "Malazan book of the fallen" or "Legacy of the Drow" then I am listening to audio books or playing games that delve into that genre. This game so far can be classified as fantasy rpg, and has a rich story so far that keeps me wanting to progress. The story in some areas is very original and in other's does what many other totl fantasy novels do. I would have to say as far as going off the story, the game is worth play thus far.
Some games that are good do one of a few things right well enough to keep people interested and playing till the end of the story, something like story rich, great gameplay, stunning graphics and soundtrack, etc. Well, I am happy to say that this title gets 3 of those 4 things I just mentioned, Story, which I mentioned up top, next is gameplay, and though this game is not completely originaly with it's mechanics but what it does it does very well. First impressions, for myself, were so-so and I decided that I hd to keep playing to get a better judge. I am glad I did the game play very fun once you decide on which function and role you want each member of your party to play in each battle, It is also important to know the character's in party stregnths and weaknesses so that you can pause in fight(yes you have the choice to pause in the game and set your characters up for  which spell or ability they be doing next and to which enemy, or something like weapon change and or party buff when endurance is low. It is a nice feature that you do not see in many games. There is still things I am sure like different abilities and higher leveled skills that I have yet to learn which even improve on the gameplay.
So far, this game is kind of addicting I like the ability to get caught up in events in the npc's lives things that could definitely happen if this game was taking place irl, and have the end choice that has impact on not just your character but the lives and or well being of a town or individual npc is a really nice if not sometimes frustrating feature. I really do feel this game is a must try to those that like the more old school rpg's and enjoy fantasty, but I do not think only diehards would really enjoy this game. This game can be for any gamer that takes the time play past the tutorial.
As far as cons on this game I would most lilely say the worse things I have experienced in this game is probably the fact that I have not been able to rotate the camera(not sure if it is just something I have not set right) so that I can spin the camera 360 degrees and see better in some instances. The graphics  are fine for this type of game but I do think they good of added some better textures. Other than these two things I have not had qualms with this game and have nothing but positive thoughts and hopes for it's progression, I hope others take a chance on this title because it is very much worth it.

In the BG series you could set the ai to use certain types of spells/items, in PoE you have to micromanage with pausing every fight, unless I missed something? The game as is may be fun but not for the current price. that's my opinion :) I'll probably play a few playthroughs but then I'd bet I'll be playing one of the older rpg's again...
3/31/15 now That I've played even more I thought that I would expand on my review. Another example of how I think that it's dumbed down is traps. Any class with the skill can disarm them and place them, there is no penalty for failing to disarm a trap, no explosion in the face or anything like that. There is very little variety between the races/classes. Everyone can use everything, There are no weapons or armor that are class or race restricted and no extra penalties for any class to use something that would normally be considered odd, like a caster in armor. Everyone builds up and at high level your wiz and my wiz will be the same regardless of race, your fighter and my fighter will be the same etc. The stronghold improvments are all set, just pay for repairs, no options to pick something over something else etc that would make it unique. Everyone will have the exact same stronghold. Events at the stronghold are based on game time, nothing random. Every time you play you'll have the exact same experience. You say I can change my main guy? Well that'll make a difference if you play solo and take no followers. As is you micro manage the entire group so it's pretty irrelevant which is your main character. Even the portraits lol, can't import, the portraits don't even look like the 3 head choices that you get, forget hairstyles etc. Make a Godlike of any class and try to get it to look like a portrait, that's just a very minor example of cutting corners on this game. Pathing, omg, good luck if you want a complete party of 6. Bugs = I've had very few and they were minor, I've read some horror stories here though.
People are loving the game tons now because a game similiar to this was badly needed but once the honeymoon effect is over I think that many more will see the things that I see.
All of that said, I am loving playing the game right now. I see very limited replayability unlike it's predecessors that have much more customization even with more linear plot lines than this one. They made a ton off the kickstarter, profits and not just costs, the game come out and costs a ton for the type of game that it is. It should be much better imo. BG2 blows this away. I hope that they make many improvements in patches and don't start churning out expensive dlc's for stuff that should be a part of the game now.
I really hope that they make some additions and changes and I'd love to rewrite this in the future as a positive, now it's fun but not worth the price by a long shot.

Pillars of Ethernity is a masterpiece, a game that shows what developers commitment and crowsourcing love can do. The game is a spiritual successor of Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale/Planescape: Torment but it also improves most of the aspects, like graphic, sound, the combat system and the character customization. The main difference between those games and PoE is the fact that PoE is not a D&D game and doesn't use any of the D&D settings. I was a bit worried about this because D&D 2nd edition is very rich and recreating something even similar requires a lot of time, but the PoE team surprised me: the game mechanics are good, sometime even better than old games. The strategy is dominant in every battle and the game is challenging even at lower difficulties. The non-linear progress of the game can be a pain for people used to games with linear progression, but the result is a realistic world in which you must be careful and wise.
Graphics and sound are amazing. In particular I find the soundtrack inspired and well placed.
If I have to find a problem in the game, probably I would point out that the story is not completely original; sometimes it resemble a certain game about past lives...but honestly that could be considered a feature of the game, considering that the other game is another masterpiece.
I recommend this game but not to everybody: the game is challenging, story-driven and sometimes slow, e.g. when reading dialogs. You have to like this kind of games to love this game.

The combat is, essentially, the same as Bioshock Infinite. The story is similar as well, but no further details on that (spoliers). Finally, the monsters and areas are similar to Silent Hill. Strange, twisted monsters vaguely human, ruins of a town with blood, but few bodies. WhIle sometimes a bit lackluster, this game is fun and memorable.

I actually spent 20 hours in this game in the last 4 days in Steam offline mode, so ignore Steam playtime.
Mass Effect was a pleasant surprise for me, because of two reasons: I'm not a fan of space opera and sci-fi, and I couldn't get into one of Bioware's well known title - Dragon Age: Origins. But screw them, let's talk about Mass Effect. The game has messy inventory system, clunky animations, pretty straightforward weapon upgrades and doesn't allow progressing after finishing the main story, aaaaaaand... that's it, that's all my criticism for ME. What can I say more about it? Mass Effect is a well-crafted game from head to toe, with nearly all aspects perfected.
First, I freaking love the narrative. In the first 30 minutes, I thought it was some typical pretentious sci-fi piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that overcomplicates everything, but nope, the story really hooked me in, even it was just a standard good-vs-evil story filled with cliches. I can't tell exactly what I love about ME's story, but it gave me a sense of real progression, and pushed me forward through each events in the game. Sometime intense, sometime emotional and sometime even silly (especially in romance subplots), and of course it doesn't lack "epicness" for a sci-fi saga.
Next, the dialogues. There's no such thing as illusive choices. In ME, every choice matters, and not all decisions lead to a good end.
. Tip: Spend your points in Charisma or Intimidate, they're very important, don't ignore them.
Teammates. Uhuh, this is not your standard companions, your squad mates are TRUE human (or alien) beings with their own unique personality. You know what? I found it more interesting to wandering around the Normandy, talking to my squad mates, rather than exploring the galaxy. And I've never, ever, felt so much difficult in deciding between 2 squad mates' fates. There was no game that made me care so much about my team mates like Mass Effect. Why? Because ♥♥♥♥ you Bioware, you created some of the most memorable and well-developed side characters in any game I've ever played. If I don't see Garrus, Wrex, Liara or Tali in the sequels, many tables will be flipped.
Gunplay hasn't aged well, but it's certainly enjoyable. Tons of weapons, upgrades and special biotic abilities. You don't need to be a strategist to play the game, but it certainly helps if you can order your squad mates to assist you on the battlefield.
Aargh. why, why did I spend the last 7 years without giving a damn about Mass Effect? Why didn't I know about it sooner? Why did I pass on this masterpiece? And why does Garrus's face look low-textured? Anyway, Mass Effect, 10 ♥♥♥♥ing out of 10, heavily recommended. If you are a fan of RPG or sci-fi, play it already. If you don't give a crap about RPG or sci-fi, then still give it a try, because you might like it as much as I do.

Overall Rating: 9/10
Gameplay Rating: 9/10
Accessibility Rating: 7/10
The first in a series from BioWare, Mass Effect was designed to be an open, choose-your-own-adventure type game within a relatively loose storyline.
You play as a Human Alliance Navy Commander named Shepard.  You're quickly embroiled in a fight to save not only yourself and crew, but humanity and all races in the universe from extinction at the hands of the Reapers.
The story for Mass Effect and the effects between games that your decisions have makes playing the whole series on occasion quite enjoyable.  The games can be long, so they can be daunting to try and replay.  Make sure you have time!
Mass Effect opens to the main menu, so you can set subtitles before the game begins.  Sound controls let you adjust music, sound effects, and dialogue volumes independently.  For gamers with mobility issues, you can rebind all keys to suit your needs.
In gameplay,
The bullet animations are fast, and you may miss them until your shield is gone already.  I often did not know I was being shot until my health was critically low, which is the first major visual indicator of damage.  This can make the game frustrating at times.
Pros:
- Subtitles are large and easy to read with light blue text and black border.
- In conversations, you see who is talking and subtitles at the same time.
Cons:
- Most subtitles are shown because you trigger them, but some come from nearby people and they are not named, so you may not know who is talking.
Mass Effect is single player; no chatting available or required.

Stranded Deep is by far one of the best games I have ever played. It combines the random generation and crafting of Minecraft with the ambiance of Journey, as well as the visual graphics and lighting graphics of The Last of Us. This game is an amazingly well done game. It both looks and feels beautiful. It has a vast and large exploration factor that is some of the best in gaming. It includes many amazing features such as:
*Amazing graphics
*Vast and open enviroment
*Great ambiance and sense of adventure
*Dynamic day night system
*Dynamic lighting system
*Complex yet simple crafting mechanic.
*Sense of both danger and peace
*Very detailed enviroment
*And many more that you have to play to enjoy
Stranded Deep is a very ambitious project, and yet it delivers excedingly in its promises. Playing it you will definitly get a mix of The Forest and Rust vide. But that shouldn't deter you. Those were great games, and if you enjoyed them at all, then you will definitely have fun with this. But despite this there are a few flaws. the main ones are:
*Glitches that make it when you stand on something you are carrying, you fly upwards slowly
*Sharks occasionly swim through the island like they got the no clip mod
*Certain ships will have a door that leads to the bottom, while there is valuable stuff, you very likely will either need to glitch to get out, or you die
*Sometimes the water effect is shown on land for a brief time
*The raft will sometimes completely dissapear in the middle of the ocean.
These are just some glitches that have shown up in my game. A few things I would hope to be improved upon a little better are:
*It takes to long to get to other islands, maybe shorten it a little bit
*The islands will sometimes appear close, but then will all of a sudden look much farther away, maybe keep them at a static range so it is easier for someone in a hurry to know which island is closest
*Despite being needed in a lot of crafting, on many islands rocks seem to be on short supply, making it hard to build the neccassary equipment, maybe ad the mechanic of being able to break bigger rocks into the normal ones, or just add more rocks to the islands
Overall these are sometimes prominent in the game, it does not ruin the game. I would suggest this game to almost any gamer. It is beautifully crafted and holds up in pretty much every way imaginable.

Simultaneously endearing and addicting, Starbound is one game capable of providing innumerable hours of enjoyable gameplay. Whether you wish to explore strange new worlds and civilizations, or battle a space mobster penguin in a flying saucer, the adventure is there awaiting you.
By and large Starbound is a stressless, carefree, and charming sort of game. While some of the bosses in the game can be somewhat challenging, it is not the sort of game that invites much frustration. Others may comment that the controls can, in some instances, feel a little clunky; I wasn’t too pleased I could only use my weapons while standing still… but overall, I cannot complain, and I cannot say that minor nitpicks like that have ever bothered me. There have only been two areas in which I have experienced minor frustration.
Number one cause of minor frustration: some of the modes of the game, such as Survivor, cause you to lose pixels (currency) and drop all of your current items upon death… and if you drop your items in an out-of-the-way, hard-to-access location (like a cave on the far side of a planet), it can become rather irritating to attempt to regain your lost inventory (you might die SEVERAL MORE TIMES in the process, only worsening your situation). However, players can choose to use the Casual mode instead, in which no pixels or items are lost upon death in the game.
Number two cause of minor frustration: while Starbound provides a lot of in-game teaching to help you learn how to use various items and equipment, there were a number of instances in which I had to Google how to do something I thought would be intuitive – how to plant and grow crops, how to build blocks with the matter manipulator, how to eat food, how to craft certain items, etc. Maybe this is solely my problem, caused by obliviousness, and others find these actions more intuitive. However, for me, at the start of the game, I often found myself fiddling around, confused about how to proceed with what I thought should have been simple tasks. But – that said, that was only a minor frustration at the start of gameplay. I have come to realize that Starbound is a lot about exploring options and discovering things on your own – and with that mindset, learning how to do new actions in a casual exploratory-sense became a lot of fun, and I lost all such taskmastering concerns about how to do things.
And that really is what makes Starbound so enjoyable: exploration. Exploration of planets and planets and planets and planets. Exploration of desert biomes, frozen mountain biomes, jungle biomes, ocean biomes, even flesh biomes. Exploration of various alien species civilizations. Exploration of worlds with one-eyed cat ghost alien creatures, fire-breathing bird alien creatures, hopping carrot alien creatures. Exploration of how to cook rice or build rope or construct shields or upgrade your space vessel. I will admit I haven't gotten too far into the story, even having done about 36 hours of gameplay... but I don't mind. It's just too fun to explore. I'll casually mosey my way through the story eventually.
I suspect some people could get bored of the biomes available on Starbound alone, or of the quests, or of the music, or of the general overall “feel” of Starbound. The game carries with it a sort of simplicity. For me, though, and the other individuals I know who play Starbound… it is carefree and addicting.
Mods for this game are definitely worth checking out, as they provide new layers to Starbound, and many more different types of things to explore.
Starbound is a game I would recommend to many people. Again, it is charming. It is endearing. It has a smile-evoking, amusing, uplifting sort of atmosphere to it. It is a game I have already spent many hours playing, and plan to spend many, many more.

I was not prepared for the awesome quality of this game. I knew the history of the devs and played all their previous games and I was a bit worried that this would not make it past the rose tinted glasses, I reserve for those older games.

3/31/15 now That I've played even more I thought that I would expand on my review. Another example of how I think that it's dumbed down is traps. Any class with the skill can disarm them and place them, there is no penalty for failing to disarm a trap, no explosion in the face or anything like that. There is very little variety between the races/classes. Everyone can use everything, There are no weapons or armor that are class or race restricted and no extra penalties for any class to use something that would normally be considered odd, like a caster in armor. Everyone builds up and at high level your wiz and my wiz will be the same regardless of race, your fighter and my fighter will be the same etc. The stronghold improvments are all set, just pay for repairs, no options to pick something over something else etc that would make it unique. Everyone will have the exact same stronghold. Events at the stronghold are based on game time, nothing random. Every time you play you'll have the exact same experience. You say I can change my main guy? Well that'll make a difference if you play solo and take no followers. As is you micro manage the entire group so it's pretty irrelevant which is your main character. Even the portraits lol, can't import, the portraits don't even look like the 3 head choices that you get, forget hairstyles etc. Make a Godlike of any class and try to get it to look like a portrait, that's just a very minor example of cutting corners on this game. Pathing, omg, good luck if you want a complete party of 6. Bugs = I've had very few and they were minor, I've read some horror stories here though.
People are loving the game tons now because a game similiar to this was badly needed but once the honeymoon effect is over I think that many more will see the things that I see.
All of that said, I am loving playing the game right now. I see very limited replayability unlike it's predecessors that have much more customization even with more linear plot lines than this one. They made a ton off the kickstarter, profits and not just costs, the game come out and costs a ton for the type of game that it is. It should be much better imo. BG2 blows this away. I hope that they make many improvements in patches and don't start churning out expensive dlc's for stuff that should be a part of the game now.
I really hope that they make some additions and changes and I'd love to rewrite this in the future as a positive, now it's fun but not worth the price by a long shot.

Pillars of Ethernity is a masterpiece, a game that shows what developers commitment and crowsourcing love can do. The game is a spiritual successor of Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale/Planescape: Torment but it also improves most of the aspects, like graphic, sound, the combat system and the character customization. The main difference between those games and PoE is the fact that PoE is not a D&D game and doesn't use any of the D&D settings. I was a bit worried about this because D&D 2nd edition is very rich and recreating something even similar requires a lot of time, but the PoE team surprised me: the game mechanics are good, sometime even better than old games. The strategy is dominant in every battle and the game is challenging even at lower difficulties. The non-linear progress of the game can be a pain for people used to games with linear progression, but the result is a realistic world in which you must be careful and wise.
Graphics and sound are amazing. In particular I find the soundtrack inspired and well placed.
If I have to find a problem in the game, probably I would point out that the story is not completely original; sometimes it resemble a certain game about past lives...but honestly that could be considered a feature of the game, considering that the other game is another masterpiece.
I recommend this game but not to everybody: the game is challenging, story-driven and sometimes slow, e.g. when reading dialogs. You have to like this kind of games to love this game.

Beautiful and vibrant atmosphere, EXCELLENT job by the narrator (really carried me through the whole game), alright combat system and there's quite a few challenges for the hardcore gamers out there. The soundtrack was awesome as well and really helped set the tone.
The story itself really might not make too much sense right away, but I definitely picked it up piece by piece as I went along. The moving mechanics were a little frustrating at points (mainly talking about the dodge roll) where I would roll right into a gap trying to get away, but the nice thing is the game doesn't make falling off the stage very punishing; you just fall back down from the sky and take a little bit of damage.
Finding new weapons was pretty fun and you could carry two of them at a time which put a little bit of strategy in the game. Although whenever I found a new weapon, in most cases it was the best weapon in slot to use so I really didn't take too much time upgrading old weapons. The enemies you encounter all have different mechanics and you really have to strategize and you figure out that you can't just hack and slash through everything.
Overall it was a pretty weird game, but in a good way I think. I would definitely recommend picking this game up if it goes on sale.

Bastion is, mechanically speaking, an action RPG. But it's different than pretty much any other aRPG I've ever played, and that list is decently long . . . and Bastion stands out as having the best story I've ever seen in an aRPG.
Unlike most aRPGs there's no real feedback loop of "better loot" (somewhat akin to Jade Empire in that sense). Items you get are paradigm shifts, not incremental upgrades, and there's no such thing, really, as an item that is superior in every way to another. That makes it more of a "which style do I prefer" than "which stats are better".
There's probably two mechanics in the game that stand out: the first is the narrator. There's a narrator talking over things that you do, and it actually works. There was only . . . once? I think? that the narrator repeated something he shouldn't have, and otherwise it added immensely to the immersion of the story. Definitely play the game with headphones or speakers turned waaay up so you can hear the narrator fully, because whoever voice acted him was amazing.
The second mechanic is the shrines --- you can basically add multipliers onto each mission, which makes them more difficult but gives correspondingly higher rewards. It's a great way to make the game more interesting, particularly since if you've played a bunch of aRPGs before the higher levels tend to get a little easy. (Blocking OP plz dont nerf)
But Bastion realllly shines with its story. The story is delivered almost entirely through cutscenes and the narrator, and despite the main character never actually talking (or named, he's referred to as "the kid") there's a surprising amount of depth to the story. I won't spoil it here, that would just be sad . . . there's some choices, but it's mostly linear. As a big fan of games with branching storylines, I wasn't sure about this. But it actually really works in Bastion.
Overall, it's a pretty decent aRPG wrapped with a very good storytelling engine being used to talk about what happens when you survive an apocalypse. (Spoilers for the first 30 seconds, sorry.)

Welcome to a top down apocalyptic cartoonish survival game from german developer vidiludi who can be found here
Most of the negative reviews on Steam can be summed up into three major spits...
1) A mediocre survival game based on the fact that there is currently limited longevity for many people because there are very few achievements, it has an easy levelling up system, and a low amount of rare and super rare resources. Granted its not early access, but the single developer/team have by no means finished with it adding more and more content in fairly frequent allotments throughout each year. Currently they are working on money quests among other assortment of goodies. So why would you give a game a negative review based on the fact that it's current state is mediocre when there is beyond a shadow of a doubt a huge potential of fun for gamers, especially those who like to make video's? It seems the real problem is some gamers lack imagination and how to have fun.
2) The game was once free and now it is not. This is true, the developer made a risky move to try and get more people to look at his game by making the content free for a period of time. He also added hat and skin cases which are obtainable by doing quests in game and through a micro transaction of a dollar be unlocked, or sold on the steam marketplace instead. However he soon realised that making the content free had a two edged sword about it, on the one hand while it made people more aware of his product, it also allowed in a huge herd of immature trolls that flourished at the expense of others. These trolling kiddies were equally demanding in the discussion board and on the developer himself voicing in a nearly temper tantrum fashion there every whine and lame brained 'I want it now' requests. One therefore can quickly sympathise with the developer why he has wisely moved the game to a very affordable customer bracket who are more likely to appreciate the hard work that the developer has already placed in the game. Also why would you criticise a game for being a dollar when you can clearly just keep collecting hat cases and sell them on the market?
3) I was trolled. My body was driven over several times as a speed bump and my back pack of goodies was stolen and used against my body in a most ungodly fashion, then they blew up my car and placed meat where my dead body was to encourage dogs to come and lick the ground. All I can say to this is toughen up cupcake, its survival dammit. The developer can hardly be blamed for your thighs being too flabby to run from impending danger. Stop eating all those candy bars frequently scattered in all those apocalyptic loot crates.
However, it is true your experience with this game and whether it will be an overall positive or negative one is really more dependent on you and how smart you play. The story of the game is simply survival. You the player are immune from the virus, but the zombies and the gun totting NPC's with gasmasks are not immune and are quickly designed to attack you as they also want to survive. It's not actually easy for another person to kill you. Oh sure they can drive over you, but that's not as easy as it may sound. They can't actually just shoot you either. Each person has a 100% Karma level, only if your Karma level goes down can they start firing at you. Your Karma level will start to drop as soon as you start attacking someone's wall or base, then it's suddenly opening firing range. This means you can defend your base quite easily if your base is being attacked, but they can't shoot you as you haven't been destroying anyone's walls.
Unlike other survival games which demand constant logging in daily, this one has a mechanic which allows a person to leave the game for a long period without the need of again having to start the whole thing from scratch. While it is true that your structures dilapidates with time, items that you have buried in game remain there unless someone uncovers them with a shovel. As long as you keep count of the secret place you have buried your stash, unless discovered by someone by accident it should remain where you buried it, allowing you again to start off with the items you have thus far accumulated. Even with the developers constant upgrades to the game your hidden stash remains safe. It is therefore this mechanic of not having to start the whole thing again from scratch and its relatively stress free nature that makes this apocalyptic game seriously attractive and a fun romp for many.
There are many things to learn, here are a few good hints to get you started.
'Get in the habit of accumulating stuff and burying it. Carrying all your good stuff with you in your back pack is just asking for trouble when you die'.
'If you have steak in your backpack a wandering dog may in fact eat your whole backpack making you lose everything. Fish, drinks are a great alternative'.
'Always make sure you have bandages on you and antibiotics, cloths make bandages quickly.'
'Never bury your good stash within your base. If people break into your base it will be the first place they look. Instead make sure it’s outside a relatively good walking distance from your base to make it harder to locate'.
'If you place a steak underneath a car and wait a while a collection of dogs will come scavenging for the meat they can't reach. Feed each dog individually and you will be rewarded with an army of dogs.'
'Tesla coils can be sniped through windows, make sure your windows are boarded up too'.
I could go on and on about various tips and tricks you could do. Below is a fairly long play through of the game which I intend to add to over the upcoming weeks. We go about trolling other bases and players to show what and what not to do. What’s up so far should be enough for you to see if you would enjoy this game. Have fun, stay safe, and be friendly...

The first in a series from BioWare, Mass Effect was designed to be an open, choose-your-own-adventure type game within a relatively loose storyline.
You play as a Human Alliance Navy Commander named Shepard.  You're quickly embroiled in a fight to save not only yourself and crew, but humanity and all races in the universe from extinction at the hands of the Reapers.
The story for Mass Effect and the effects between games that your decisions have makes playing the whole series on occasion quite enjoyable.  The games can be long, so they can be daunting to try and replay.  Make sure you have time!
Mass Effect opens to the main menu, so you can set subtitles before the game begins.  Sound controls let you adjust music, sound effects, and dialogue volumes independently.  For gamers with mobility issues, you can rebind all keys to suit your needs.
In gameplay,
The bullet animations are fast, and you may miss them until your shield is gone already.  I often did not know I was being shot until my health was critically low, which is the first major visual indicator of damage.  This can make the game frustrating at times.
Pros:
- Subtitles are large and easy to read with light blue text and black border.
- In conversations, you see who is talking and subtitles at the same time.
Cons:
- Most subtitles are shown because you trigger them, but some come from nearby people and they are not named, so you may not know who is talking.
Mass Effect is single player; no chatting available or required.

The original Mass Effect is a game I've played to death. I played through it at least 4 times when it was originally released on the 360, and again on Origin when I bought the ME Trilogy.
Mass Effect is a re-imagining of the typical Bioware game design of making choices between being a good guy (Paragon) or a d-bag (Renegade). You will travel the galaxy visiting very interesting and well-designed worlds. You will be led on an epic quest to hunt down your enemy, while playing a respectable third person shooter.
The inventory system becomes very overbearing, as every enemy drops an item and it is often in your best interest to check if something better has dropped. Also, native controller support is not included, even though this was originally a console game (though mods can fix this).
Overall, Mass Effect is still a fun game, and it's worth playing through the beginning of what is generally considered one of the best science fiction universes created.

This is a truly excellent strategy game. The living board is a unique idea, which stretches your mind in some new directions, and it is implemented extremely well. Strategy is both deep and fun, and there is just the right amount of RNG for the genre: you are expected to manage risk and opportunity, but games rarely come down to RNG alone. Your decisions all matter.
Additionally, the game minimized pat-to-win aspects very nicely. Some of the most competitive decks are very easy to afford and build. Expanding your collection (which is also integral to the genre) mainly gives you more options, which is nice, but it really isn't necessary to win.
Some of the main criticisms that have come up lately relate to the Oversky expansion, claiming that the new cards are overpowered and imbalanced. I think these critiques can be safely dismissed. Top players and tournament winners continue to play older styles of decks, and the newer cards are integrated nicely here and there without breaking the core identities or gameplay. There were some balance tweaks made as the expansion was rolled out, and overall I'm impressed with how quickly the developers responded to the issues and adjusted the game.
A core part of the game's balance is rooted in low-cost rush decks, which keep game-breaking cards from ever getting completely out of hand. Insofar as there's a solid critique of the games meta, it is that rush is consistenly very powerful and plays a key role in balancing the game ... but it certainly isn't unbeatable. Overall, I appreciate the role it plays in the meta.
Hopefully, this game will get the audience and attention it deserves, once it launches on mobile. It is very, very, very good.

Scratches that Action RPG sweet spot that rare games like Dark Messiah of Might and Magic have reached, and further. Takes the best parts of the typical Elder Scrolls gameplay and makes the open world fantasy experience even more enjoyable with many varied enemy types and player classes. It's quite possibly the only game I've played that makes this happen with a useful party system, too.
It isn't flawless though - the characters and animations throughout the cutscenes can be a little wonky (mainly camera work and too much gesturing while talking, voice acting is also spotty in some sections). The main character seems to spend pretty much every cutscene dumbfounded at literally anything that is happening, despite being able to command powerful allies and take down eldrich abominations. Those are small gripes though for a game this solid.
In terms of visuals, the world is clearly a product of a well researched team. The majority of armors and equipment resemble real world pieces from the middle ages, and most of the combat options for non-magical classes are grounded in real-world techniques. The magical classes themselves do use a system that is believable, with spells taking time to prepare and more effective combinations taking time to set up, but they do pay off. Although there are only two main cities, they are both large enough to concievably be functional cities. Dungeons FEEL like dungeons, and this game is the first game since Dark Messiah (for me) to really give that kind of a strong atmosphere. The first time you encounter an undead just lingering in the darkness of a hallway is simply magical. Few games ever do bring that uneasy feeling of finding another human-shaped being in an abandoned place. Although perhaps the world is a bit small compared to other titles like this, the development team clearly chose quality over quantity and I would take that any day.
Here's hoping for a sequel.

Undead Labs have delivered.
An Immersive open world:
-You can go inside EVERY building.
-Zombie hordes parade around roads and other areas that attract human attention.
-Clear zombie infested locations.
-You're not alone, other surviving groups are out there.
-Your survivors go out on missions of their own volition.
Scavenging:
-Hey image that...people collect more than tape and scissors in the apocalypse! -Scavenge things that matter; food, medicine, fuel, ammo, weapons, bombs, noise makers, etc.
Building:
-Have your group of survivors make and upgrade a garden, a library, workshop, medlab, kitchen, etc.
Fortifying:
-Barricade your windows.
-Create and upgrade a lookout tower.
-Assign a sniper.
-Plant mines around your stronghold.
-Need a bigger base? Find a new potential homestead.
Character Development:
-Each character has their own psychological traits.
-Characters can die, there is no respawn. That goes for everyone.
-Quests in general are well written, meaningful, and carry lasting changes in the world. -Voice acting that doesn't make you want to stab your best friend.
-RPG development of skills as you continue to use them.
And there you have it, if that isn't ambition, I don't know what is. Yes, it's buggy and no, it's not perfect, but it's a massively huge axe-cleaving step in the right direction. A direction aimed towards battling zombie fatigue and saturation with a meaningful, immersive and an all out fun experience! I like to think of State of Decay as the fully functional, feature rich rough draft for the best of survival games yet to come, not just those set necessarily in a zombie apocalypse.

I started this game next to a medical building. It was an early morning and you could hear the birds chirping. I began to search this building only to find a few food rations and a bottle of water. I noticed many sleeping bags inside and thought of all the people that were living in this building, using it as a shelter, before all of this happened. I continued to explore the rest of the town. By the end of the day I had found a backpack, a hunting knife, and a few food items. I spent my night hidden away in an abandoned house that was slowly being taken over my rats and moss. It started to sprinkle a little bit that night and my body temperature was slowly lowering. By morning the sprinkle had turned into a thunderstorm and rain was beginning to get into the house. I quickily decided I would need to find a new place to go. I ventured out onto the puddle covered street and instantly was covered in water. I was getting very chilly and was nervous I would catch a cold. I ran along the road for a very long time seeing others in the same boat as me. Many were in short sleeve shirts and some had no shirts at all. As I continued, I spotted bases where I imagined experienced survivors lived. Sitting next to a warm campfire, wearing coats, and eating warm food. I finally stumbled upon an abandoned bus that had a dead survivor in it. I took his coat and cargo pants and instantly felt more secure. As I sat in the bus eating my lunch and listening to the rain. I heard a gunshot. I glanced down at the dead survivor and imagined the gunshot brought someone a similar fate. I looked around the parking lot and found a tarp and some other essentials and build a small tent. I fell asleep listening to the thunder roaring. All of this in my first day of the game. This game is far from perfect. But it has so much potential. The immersion you feel while playing is crazy. This is easily one of the greatest games I have ever played. And if the developers continue to stick with it, this game will easily beat any other survival game.

If you've played both before, you will really see what I mean. That aside, they picked a good game to mimic, because this came out really well.

Singularity is one of those "old" FPSs that still sort of works. The graphics are good for the era they were made in and still holds up pretty well, the story while barebones works, and the weapons (while a bit vanilla but with a few interesting new ones) are satisfying to use. There is a fair bit of enemy variety, and you get a few neat time powers to kill them with. You can upgrade these powers using in-game currency, but the upgrades are pretty much just power boosts. You can also upgrade your weapons using kits found around the game, but again it's pretty basic, increasing stats but nothing else (the guns don't look any different). Once you get the ability to freeze time in a big bubble thought the game kind of gets really easy.
Overall, this game is essentially Bioshock, only using time manipulation instead of genetics, but a fair bit less intricate.
The Good
- Story works
- Nice graphics
- A barebones leveling system
- Explores the idea of alternate timelines pretty well
- Interesting level design
The Bad
- Fairly short
- Very little replay-value
- Can only carry 2 guns at a time
- Fairly easy
Final verdict: I'd recommend this game if you're just looking for some quick shooting time with some time powers, but you might want to wait until it gets discounted.

The original Mass Effect is quite the game. This is a series I really enjoy, and would contest it's sci fi setting with the likes of other great sci fi's, like star wars and star trek. It's world is very realized, a trademark of many Bioware games, and it manages to stray away from some of its other games flaws. One nice thing is your choices matter more in this game than many other choice based games, even if the choices are black and white. Where this game falls short however has been support for newer PC's over the years since it's release. It is in no way an ugly game, and there are mod's that you can install to increase the texture resolution, their a tad harder to install than some other mods I've done before but it's worth it as it doesnt change anything to the game, just increases the immersion factor. There is a major bug on two story levels that has to do with certain graphics cards, your characters will all be covered in a black pixel blob, and the only work around is to activate the command panel and disable the shadows all together making the game look much worse, if more playable. I still recomend Mass Effect, despite its few flaws. A solid Sci fi RPG with a few third person shooter elements, and a decsent 20 hour story.

Why is it that in sci-fi themed RPG's it's always called a "mission" and not a "quest" and spells are always psychic powers?
It may seem a bit of a late autopsy; mass effect having been released some time ago now, but I maintain the veiwpoint that a good game is timeless.
So is mass effect a good game?
Obviously, I think so because I've reccomended it, but there are some elements of mass effect which others may find harder to ignore than me.
Mass effect plays like a blend of western and japanese RPGs. Heavily story driven, with an in-depth level of combat customisation just like a JRPG, but with the freedom and choice of a bethesda game.

The combat isn't too bad either, although the "spells" interface could learn a thing or two from WoW, and some abilities should have just been made automatic - I'm looking at you, shield recharger!  instead, you have to hold the space bar, select your spell (Sorry, SKILL)  then hope you had the camera facing the right way before releasing space.  All a bit much for someone to do when they've just been shot!
But as with JRPGs it's not so much the combat, but the story that compels us to play - and this is where mass effect shines. It starts off generic - but under the sci-fi clichés (And they're pretty much ♥♥♥♥ing compulsory it seems) lies a truly original and inventive plot. The alien races have personality and variety and it looks fantastic.
Unfortunately, immediately after completing mass effect, it struck me that the gameplay had been like hoovering a mansion. Having to repeat the same dull task over and over in a succession of very beautiful rooms. Sure, you can change the clothes you're wearing - use new and exciting skills to aid you in your task, and meet and chat to the various characters that live in the mansion. And you might even be so wrapped up in your surroundings that the hoovering becomes fun for a while, but in the end, when everyone's said their piece, it's still just hoovering, Perhaps that's why the game bangs on so much about "doing ones' duty" and "doing what needs to be done". Words normally spoken before housework if i've ever heard them.

There is definately room for a few playthroughs (which is good because it only took me a measly 35 hours to complete despite doing all the side-quests - MISSIONS, sorry, MISSIONS) So you can get someone different to hoover the mansion (yes, i'm
labouring that metaphor). For instance - I picked a grizzled, white haired male - the sole survivor of a catastrophe - to hoover the mansion in my first game. In my next I may well get a sassy, pert woman to do it. And you know what? I'll probably have fun.

I wrote back in Febuary that this game was "A great concept, but desperately needed more content."
Its now July and sadly Im updating my review to repeat that statement - but sadly on a less  possitive note.
The amount of content added in the past 5 months is really minimal, development and progress has been coming down the pipes, but at a woefully slow pace, granted the Dev team is only two people, but updates have been few and far between and havent really contained all that much given the time span.
new content seems to be the devs teams lowest priority. They are more concerned with bug fixes, UI mechanical, engine and graphical tweaks.
In most cases this is understandable, get the game in to a stable state first then add new stuff, but I really believe Standed Deep is a bit of a rare exception to the rule, and devs should probably adjust their road map.
Here is why, for an EA title, the game actually looks very nice, has a great atmostsphere  and even upon release the game play was quite solid. As of 0.03 there are still some bugs, yes, but very little which is literally game breaking.
But the area were this game falls flat is not Graphics, UI, bugs or Mechanics, ITS LACK OF CONTENT and that was pretty much everyones complaint when it came out, and it still hangs over this game like a black cloud.
There is simply not enough to craft, not enough to see and not enought do to keep you going for the long haul.
Once you have built a house, looted a seafort and built a motor raft, you have hit the game worlds climax, there is really nothing more the world has to offer you after that, besides repetition.
Suddenly you find your self on Day 40, grilling your zillionth crab and wondering... why am I still doing this? :(.
You the player are indeed 'Stranded deep' but ironically in a rather shallow world:(  And this sadly IS the single biggest problem, as a crafting/survival game, the game world and the players interaction with it, is just not rich enough :(
Of course as with any EA or even the biggest AAA title, the devs need to tackle bugs, but WHY do they insist on so much tweaking, sometimes even overhauling various mechanics or graphics that were really not so terrrible to begin with?
I wish they would stop trying to fix what aint really broke and realise that its not really any of those things that are hurting this game. The formula is ok, there just needs to be more of it.
Co-Op is coming soon, which is great and will please many - but again, with so little content, will it be enough? I really dont know.
My recomendation is: reseach this game well before you buy, The Quality is there, but only you can assess if the quantity is enough to hand over your money.
