Day 2, 13th August
I awoke blinking and almost blinded by the sun and overwhelmed by the heat. I had only forgotten for a brief moment my current situation. After gathering my senses I set out to start creating some crude tools with which to hunt, cook and craft. I do not yet know how I am going to make a spear, as there appear to be very few rocks around the shoreline on this barren hell I now call home.
I managed to somehow scrape enough stone together however to make a crude yet effective axe. Again, night time beckons and I have already eaten my fill of crab for the day.
Day 3, 14th August
I awake to yet again be smacked in the face by the damning reality of my current predicament. With no-one to socialise with, I feel I may become more and more like the crazy stranded hermits I had seen in motion pictures before the crash, talking to coconuts and dancing around fires during the middle of the night. I will not let myself succumb to this.
I had spotted just off shore a small sunken vessel, browned with metal decay from the salty waters of my surroundings. I waded out to the vessel to search the cabin and to my surprise, found a woodcutting axe, a lantern and some bandages. Whoever was stranded here in the past or whoever left these supplies clearly perished. I feel their misfortunes are now my savior.
Day 4, 15th August
After yesterday's apparent success I have made a formal decision to abandon the idea of living the remainder of my time out on this sandy, dusty hell and I have chosen to gather the supplies I have and make for land...or at least just somewhere else.
So far I have not encountered any other wildlife, aside from crabs and sardines just off the shore and continue to rely on that to be my main source of survival. I managed to open some coconuts in order to drink the succulent milk from within. It was like nectar as I had used the remaining fresh water I still had yesterday. Night has dawned...dreamless sleep awaits...
Day 5, 16th August
Rising early, I made for the raft and paddle and begun pushing it out to sea. My pack is filled with cooked crabs as I realised this may be a long journey. After eating some food I set out for new horizons, not fully understanding what I was about to run into. I had believes my solidarity from living things had been my great advantage so far, however things were about to change very quickly.
Paddling towards a small speck I could see in the distance and at this point could only determine to be another god forsaken island I stopped for a moment to observe the scenary. There are many of these barren wastelands dotted all over the sea and I do not know how far I am from the main land at this point. I think to myself, where could I possibly go to be safe? At this very moment the raft moves from underneath me. Startled by the feeling of what was a fin I could only look over the edge of my raft slowly, trembling with fear and anticipation of what may arise from the depths. In this moment there was silence, only the sound of the ocean's waters lapping against my raft. Still trembling I waited, with bated breath, when suddenly a Tiger Shark appeared from the side of my raft and began swimming quickly towards me. Panicking, I swung wildly with my axe, however this made no difference. The shark knocked me into the water and sent my raft veering away from me. I am now officially in hell. With the shark slowly circling me and moving ever closer I feel the need to get back to the raft, so I do. Quickly I swim towards it and manage to board it. With my hands now shaking uncontrollably I reach for my paddle and begin frantically paddling towards the shore of a nearby island.
On arrival I come to an understanding that it was my lack of preparation that caused this inevitable scenario.
Day 6, 17th August
It's raining. It hasn't stopped raining all morning. All throughout the night it continued to pour as I had spent all night hacking away at the local foliage, in order to gather enough resources to construct a crude dwelling. From my watch, it says it is 7:30am. I am now squatting uncomfortably in my shack, wondering where I go from here. Over my breakfast of crab...again...I come to the idea that perhaps the best way to survive is to hunt the very thing I have now learned to fear. Perhaps this will be my downfall. Now, it seems like the only option.
Using a rock I smashed earlier this morning and some sticks found lying on the beach, I have managed to make myself two crude, yet sharp spears to combat my underwater foe. Climbing into my raft with my paddle, spears and axe I make my way to open water. Whilst paddling, I notice a brown pipe breaking the top of the water. This can only be the top of a mast of a ship sunken underwater. After gathering my bravery, I took the decision to dive into the water, completely unaware of any danger in my immediate surroundings. Diving deeper, I open the door to the ship, just touching the sea bed and make my way inside. After opening a couple of lockers I have found a torch, a propeller and a jerry can and within a chest in the main room of the ship's interior I have found some flares. Making my way to the surface to find my raft, I then paddle back to shore and deposited my loot into my shack and waited out the rest of the day. It's now too late to go hunting sharks and I do not wish to do this at night time.
Day 7, 18th August
The days are starting to blur together, it feels like a week has now passed and I am still no closer to rescue. My idea to hunt sharks is my objective today, so with spear in hand I make my way to the open ocean once more in my trusty life raft. Here I sit, waiting for my prey...or demise...
After no longer than 3 minutes on the water I see a dark fin making it's way towards me. With a steady hand I waited until my prey moved closer and then delivered a short, sharp stab with my spear. A solid strike. The shark twitched in irritation. This has clearly angered the beast as he quickly circled back and begun heading towards me once more. Another few strikes as he passed the raft, he is clearly now extremely angry and has begun attempting to ram me from my raft, diving after each attempt. However, during each attempt I manage to land a few blows here and there, wounding the shark. He makes his way for deeper waters and just as he begins to swim away, I land the strike that kills him. I had done it. I had done the impossible. My predator has been vanquished and I have dragged his carcass aboard my raft. With my paddle in hand and my prey laying on my lap, I make my way for shore swiftly, so the beast has no time to foul from the wounds suffered.
Upon arriving on shore, I drag him towards my crude hut and fire and begin to butcher him for the meat. I realise now I will be eating shark soon and will not go hungry for a number of days. As I begun to cook the portions of shark, I could not help but feel elation at my victory and began to laugh uncontrollably. After a brief moment of insanity I regain my composure, only to look across the ocean for a brief moment to spot another two fins...
It would appear I won't go hungry again for a long time yet......

Ok so as you can see I've racked up nearly 160 hours on this game. Addicted? Possibly!
So where to begin. I don't think its worth me providing you with a "good" & "bad" list because a lot of that will down to personal taste. The game to me is delicious and is best played via the Breakdown DLC. The storyline is ok, but it's merely a filler. The game is all about survival and you don't need a plot for that. The Graphics are decent enough and while I'm sure someone with attention to detail may be able to point out some issues with them, they do the job well and you feel immersed.
Unlike a lot of Zombie games I've played, this isn't all about melee. There are tons of weapons too but like everything in this game you have to find them, and the ammo too. By far one of my favourite things about this game is that more or less every building can be entered and the loot from each is completely random every play through. Sure there are hotspots fo some of the loot in the game, but it doesnt detract from the fact that you have to hunt them down, carry them home and do it with zombies crawling all over you.
I've had the chance to play with mods too and found one which gave me the ability to disable the "special" zombies. While these present a decent challenge and are great additions, they can at times be a bit overkill with 2 out of the 4 able to kill even your highest level character in just a few hits.
I could go on and on about this game... I'm still playing it and expect I'll be close to 1000 hours before I tire of it, if not beyond. There is a new DLC on the way too with a new map (sweet) so this will just refresh the game for me. The forums are also alive with both friendly players and staff so you are never far from help.
If like me you want a survival challenge, want it with Zombies and on a reasonably large map (we always want bigger and better Undead Labs :P) then don't look anywhere else. I've searched long and hard for a game of this type, and this ticks most of the boxes for me. I'd be really surprised if you were disappointed.
Hope this review was useful and if you buy the game... enjoy!

State of Decay is a good zombie game for an early-access game. People have tried to compare it to Dead Island, the DayZ, the WarZ, and Dead Rising. Somehow in its own way, it carves its own niche and offers a cross between a survival game and a management game.
You can access different characters if you befriend them. Once a character is dead, they are permanently dead. Once a car is out of commission, it's permanently out. With that and the numerous home bases, the game ensures you take the time to plan out accordingly. You have to make sure your resources are well-invested, your characters are in tip-top shape, and recruit others that would be good for your group of survivors. The zombies act as they should. They are not intelligent but they come after you as they should. There are freak zombies that require a bit more strategy to take out.
As it's an early-access game developed by a small company, there are some growing pains involved. There are bugs, although they don't detract from the overall feel. There is no support as of yet for the keyboard and mouse, although you can still play with them - you'll just need to find a guide for the mapping. There's also not going to be any multiplayer due to certain constraints the dev team must stay within.
In a nutshell, if you like management games like Tropico or Sim City and you also like survival games like Dead Island or the DayZ, you will like State of Decay. Just remember it's not quite a finished product yet.

QUICK SPOILER FREE REVIEW:
UPSIDES: It was a fun journey, and the world was alive. Every tiny thing was filled with details and Hussie's signature humor style. The music is fantastic and the characters are really well made. You can tell how they feel about things by their words and surrounding. The story has a lot of potential and I can't wait to see more. The puzzles are fun. And for 8$, it’s a fantastic game.
DOWNSIDES: With a 4 hour game time if you just do the essentials, it may leave you unsatisfied. You really have to take your time and not rush the story. Enjoy the small things. If you breeze through, you’re not going to have a lot of fun.
CONCLUSION: All and all, a great game, really delivered with the content it had, which wasn't much unfortunately. I'd recommend waiting until all the games are out, then buy and play through them all to get the most out of it. If you don’t want to wait, be sure to take your time and enjoy the world.

Honestly, this is one of the best free games where I've had the most fun and time wasted.
An exceptional FPS, with a great community. Gameplay almost never gets repetitive, with numerous maps and unique players. Visuals are what you'd expect from a Source mod. Teamwork can be very critical depending on the map, such as requiring zombies to work together in specific strategies or survivors sticking together to heighten the chance of survival.
Lag compensation is quite horrid and the hit boxes can be also which makes me deduct a point on the score.
The game is quite easy to get started in, but has the typical motto of "hard to master". Some servers also offer modifications such as models, trails, stats, infection cure, and more. The community is still very strong, with hundreds of players still each day.
Some maps may be well balanced, or very survivor/zombie sided. Survivors can use various weapons including melee and explosives. Survivors can also use voice commands, "panic", flashlight, and many other actions.
Zombies must attempt to kill all the survivors before running out of time, lives, or the survivors reaching a point. The carrier is basically the 'alpha zombie', having more strength, health, and the ability to infect and 'roar'.
Modes you can play are objective mode (ZPO), survival mode (ZPS), team arena (ZPA), and hardcore (ZPH). There are also some deathrun maps. Some maps may require you to barricade. Some may require you to dodge blocks fired at you. The maps are very unique.
My overall score of this spectacular game/ Source mod is: 9/10

The storyline has insufficient context to make sense of anything major going on in the world. For instance, why do these pawns follow you at all to start with? They just show up out of nowhere and everyone just acts like that is normal. It's obviously not, but hey, lets go on a quest.
Which brings me to the next rant. You're some badass, so you go looking for some quests. First one available? Pick flower. It's exactly as fun as it sounds.  Then, found a notice board. Great! Something else to do.  Kill 10 mice and 6 rabbits. Not mutant rabbits, not terror rats. Just the fluffy little critters wandering around.  Way to go hero!
Tough that out a bit more and next things you know, you're fighting goblins. Great! Oh wait, after 5 shots, you're out of stamina and just sitting there, catching your breath for 5 seconds while the punk stabs at you over and over.  And while I'm raging about shooting, the controls for this are also the next thing that'll make your vein pop out of your head with anger.  Line up a shot, fire.. nope, draw a damn arrow instead.  So you miss that shot, out of a sense of realism (fine) but there was no indication you needed to do that, and then when you can finally take a shot, you fire 3 at once. Pop pop pop. Bows do not work this way. If you're going to be realistic, fine, but don't go half way.
Then the first major boss. You're in some camp, with some schlep demanding you take a trial to prove your worth (no choice here mind you, or explanation as to why you should care what a talking rock thinks or says, just do it or no more story for you).  The mission starts and you get some cutscene of a big monster beating up the whole village. Off I go to be a hero.. except there's no-one in sight, only one guard standing against a gate waving his arms.  Ok I think, time to go over and investigate this, as he's probably signalling that this is the way to the quest (because there's nothing on your minimap of course, that'd be useful).  I walk up, and I kid you not, he yells at me "DO SOMETHING!" and that's it. The camera points me into the wrong direction, and I wander around aimlessly until I find the right exit.  Get out, and then proceed to fight a monster which I have no idea how to beat short ot just button mashing until I win, thanks to the fact the tutorial ended early. I won, and everyone walked around like it never happened.
I'd hit my limit.  I cliked the required 8 times to exit the game (going through 3 layers of menu) to finally quit. A final insult to the gaming kick to the nuts that s Dragon's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥e: Dark Arisen.

When I first started playing this game, I thought it was rather enjoyable. Then, after a few hours enjoyment began to fade as some flaws were growing more and more obvious. As I carried on playing, these flaws really got on my nerves and frustration started to take over, especially when I realised how stupid the quest system is. Yet, I kept playing. I'm not really sure why, perhaps because I thought it would get better and also because I paid for this piece of entertainment. Fortunately, the game DID get better as I progressed through the main story and got to level 20-ish. From then on, I was hooked and I actually started to properly enjoy the game.
If you didn't guess it already, Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a very difficult game to review. There are so many flaws in this game yet so much potential, it's hard not to see it...
-
Your character is very agile, you can climb buildings, double jump, grab things and throw them and climb on giant monsters and so on. This is a great change from your typical RPGs because you usually end up playing characters with brooms up their arses.
-
You can switch from one vocation to another by simply talking to an NPC. So you can basically try any gameplay you like. You can also take advantage of augments from different vocations in order to make a very overpowered character.
-
It's not Skyrim big but you'll actually be thankful it's not since you're mostly on foot. The monsters always spawn at the same place unless you've progressed very far into the main story, which can be either convenient or repetitive, depending on your mood.
-
You can create your own pawn and you get to enlist two additional ones. Your pawn will learn from you and behave according to their inclinations, which you can technically choose. You can also borrow your friends' pawns, which can sometimes make your life way easier.
-
a dungeon with far stronger enemies than the ones you get in the regular game, which will still keep you interested if you're above level 70. On top of that, this dungeon has some Dark Souls vibe and some decent difficulty.
-
I won't spoil it for you but the whole concept around the condition of the world is original.
-
Capcom did a really good job there, I really love the design of some of the monsters, they make the scenery look way less dull.
-
Some vocations are arguably really unbalanced, though the game doesn't care. You need to do a specific amount of damage in order to even hurt some monsters. This will force you to grind because this game is above all a numbers game and not a skill game. This can also make some fights really frustrating, especially when you're playing a vocation mainly dealing physical damages against a Ghost.
-
You have a stamina bar that you will consume when you run or use physical attacks. While this seems very logic, the developers thought it'd be a good idea to add an animation when you run out of stamina. This very animation prevents you from doing anything until your character has recovered a few stamina points. As long as you're running, it might just make you wish you were just forced to walk more slowly, like in most RPGs. However, the animation remains the same even during combat. This often creates ridiculous situations where your character will suddenly get an asthma attack after firing an arrow, which will more often than not, get you killed.
-
The weight limit is based on your character's weight, which of course depends on your height and fat/muscle ratio. However, if you planned on playing a very average person, like I did, you'll constantly be between average and overcumbered. This is really annoying since the amount of items you carry changes your running speed. This will force you to transfer any piece of material you'll find to your main pawn, which gets annoying very quickly.
-
Most players will give up before they even get to know it exists. This will make the first playthrough quite painful unless you look it up on the internet. But I shouldn't complain really, the original version of the game had only ONE portcrystal on the first playthrough. That's what I call sadism.
-
There are some inclinations that will determine how your pawn will behave during combat. Unfortunately, these are very poorly documented and counter-intuitive. The guardian inclination is glitched and renders your pawn completely useless since he will just stand right next to you and do nothing. The worst thing is, even if you take some potions to reset your pawn's inclination, it will slowly revert to guardian unless you absolutely avoid ever pressing the "help" command. My advice: always check your enlisted pawn's inclination, always.
-
Some side quests will cancel themselves if you progress too further into the main quest with no warning. This will prevent most people from accessing some areas along with some really nice other side quests. On top of that, some of them are incredibly obscure and almost impossible to accomplish without looking at some wikis.
-
You can't easily compare one piece of equipment with another because you'll only get the basic statistics if you keep your item equipped. To properly compare X to Y, you'll have to unequip it, press the details button and remember what gives what. This is unacceptable.
-
When you'll get to the end of the Bitterblack Isle, you'll be left with nothing else to do but to grind in order to get the best equipment of the game. This of course is optional, but the loot system over there feels really unfair due to the predetermined list of items you'll get solely depending on the "colour" of your vocation.
-
You get one piece of information at a time but you'll often ask yourself why you're even doing what you're doing. There's almost no character development, the main quest does not make much sense and by the time you understand what's going on you'll no longer feel involved.
-
Even when you reach a very high level, some monsters will still be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥because of the poor camera and "climb detection". You will often find yourself rolling your eyes because you can't see a thing while climbing a Firedrake. On top of that, some enemies tend to make your character glitch/teleport to random places while you're climbing them.
I know my review might seem mostly negative but that doesn't mean I didn't enjoy the game. It's just that things are not that simple, because I've been oscillating between hate and love many times while playing it. This game could have been a hundred times better if Capcom fixed  these issues. So bear in mind, this game IS good, but you've got to be really determined to keep playing sometimes.
Therefore, I think you should give this game a try if you enjoy playing RPGs such as Dragon Age: Origins, and already knowing the game has these flaws should set your expectations low enough to actually be surprised by it.
So, get it on sales. You might regret it at first, but if you keep playing, you'll know how satisfying this game can be.

Dragon's Dogma is an Action RPG that was released back in 2012. It definitely still holds up, and with the addition of an optimal PC port, it makes a great game even better. Let me just say that this game has the best combat in any fantasy game I've ever played. Skyrim, Dragon Age, Witcher, though superb games on their own right should definitely learn from this game. You can pick up and hold enemies in full nelsons, climb onto giant monsters, throw people off cliffs, cover enemies in oil and set them ablaze, all in real-time combat. The fights in Dragon's Dogma feel like real battles, something that I don't get the impression of from other fantasy games I love. The music is epic, booming, something just right for a high fantasy setting. It’s also particularly amazing when you get the upperhand on a difficult boss, and the music matches your actions makes you feel like a heroic badass.
The combat and music is superb. The loot and armor are also pretty cool. Great. Now onto the bad….
The game isn't the best written or particularly engaging in other fronts outside of combat. The quests and lore, although they can be interesting at times, are rather boring, with most quest having the player do little more then go here, and kill these bandits, monsters, find this item, etc. Sure, many games do this as well, but in those games your task has consequences or at least context. Outside of the main antagonist, I don’t really remember the names of many of the characters in the world, which is a shame since I spent over 100 hours on this game. The world is also boring and drab, and outside of some cool locales, have little interesting things to discover. In fact, I would go as far as to say the huge open world hurt the game moreso than helped it. I feel like if this game really tightened its belt on this end and gave us interesting, varied quest and world building, it would easily make a great game essential.
One of the game's primary gameplay mechanics is the pawn system. In it, you create an NPC that will follow and support you on your journey. You pick their class, appearance, and attributes, and as you level they will level. Where your pawn goes, they will go. As you adventure, other people will hire your pawn, and as your pawn ventures with other players, they will come back with items and tactical knowledge regarding many of the games enemies. It is a rather unique concept.
The problem though Pawn AI. Unless you raise your pawn a certain way, they'll always start gaining traits that make them more of a hindrance than a help. My mage pawn Faya, would always join me in the fray even though her role as a squishy wizard is to stay as far from the carnage as possible. So many deaths were because I had to save my pawns when they weren't doing their jobs right. Renting high level pawns does seem to address this complaint, as I found around the mid 60s and 70 leveled pawns, pawns seemed to get their crap together and actually fight like a player would. The pawn chatter is also a common complaint, but I didn’t feel that it detracted from the experience too much, and it can easily be turned off if it annoys you too much. I have to say though, it is annoying when the pawns repeat dialogue as if the player character had just stumbled onto a place of enemy, like they have a case of Anterograde amnesia.
The Bitterblack Isles is also included in PC release. Definitely for the hardcore who found the regular game easy. I feel I enjoyed it much more than the base game. In fact, it seems like its creation was for the purpose of rectifying many of the criticism that the game received. As you explore the bitterblack isles (You know, as you're getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked), you learn how such a vile place came to be. It provided more exposition and character development then I felt the huge open world base game did.
All in all, I enjoyed my time with the game. No matter how annoying my complaints got, the game really is fun to play, and the combat almost makes up for any criticism I can muster. It would be an absolute sin if this game didn’t get a sequel, and when (or if…) it does, I hope these complaints are taken into account. Some things I would want in the sequel are
-More detailed, varied, and interesting world building and locales (Ex. Elder Scrolls, Witcher Series)
-Quest with consequences (Ex. Witcher, Dragon Age, Mass Effect)
-Fix Pawn AI and comments ( Ex-Skyrim Mod Companions like Vilja, Inigo, Bioware companions)
-Additive content (More monsters/variations, more classes, weapons, loot, items, bigger world)
My suggestions, with slight refinements to the combat system (The game’s combat is almost perfect) would easily make this game close to my ideal rpg. I highly recommend you check it out, but take the criticisms against the game to heart. But for $30, it’s easily worth it.

Singularity is a game that can be summed up in one word: Adequate.
Some quick pros and cons before I go in-depth:
+ No regenerating health. Use medkits to heal
+ Terrific pacing
+ Doesn't overstay its welcome
- Can only carry two weapons at a time
- A lot of corridors, few open spaces
- Really easy
Everything else can simply be described as adequate. The story is decent, there are audio logs and notes that you can observe if you're into it, otherwise they can be passsed. Minimal cutscenes, story is mostly delivered via gameplay. However, the environmental storytelling doesn't really make a lot of sense. You'll see some messages written on the wall that leave you wondering things like "Why would a person write that?" The pacing is great, at least. The ebb and flow of tension is right on. Which is something that a lot of games like this underestimate the importance of and subsequently flub. But Singularity nails pacing.
The shooting is fine. There's an alright variety of weapons. Pistol, machine gun, shotty, sniper rifle, plus some more heavy artillery. But you can only carry two weapons at a time. Which is not a mechanic I'm fond of. I know it's unrealistic that a person could carry a dozen weapons on their person, but this isn't a military simulation kind of shooter. Very much an arcade kind of shooter. Let us carry more guns please. That being said, there is a particular weapon that is seriously overpowered and makes the rest of the game a cakewalk. Not that it was ever particularly difficult to begin with. So once you pick up that gun, you really don't even need a second one.
There's an upgrade system for both yourself and your weapons, which is adequate. A simple Damage+ and Reload Speed+ kind of upgrade system. Health+ and Stamina+ for your character, etc. I found myself purchasing a lot of upgrades simply because I had nothing else to spend the currency on. A lot of the upgrades just make an already easy game easier.
Enemy variety is fine. All the humans are... well, humans. All the mutants are mostly interesting. Not always the most imaginative designs, but at least there are some diverse attack patterns to deal with. Unfortunately, the game tends to only throw one kind of enemy hoard at you at once.
This game's unique mechanic is your ability to control the time of certain objects. And it's alright. You can move certain objects backward and forward through time, like taking a decayed, broken bridge and restoring it to new so that you can continue. And some interesting puzzles and gameplay are borne of this interesting mechanic. Unfortunately, there's only a couple interesting puzzles the devs came up with and they repeat them pretty frequently. So, it's a really fun gimmick the first time, and then a bit ho-hum for the rest of the game.
It's a very linear game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Sometimes linear is alright. I can appreciate a tight, focused narrative/gameplay experience, which this for the most part is. And there is slight (very slight) exploration. The most typical kind of exploration you'll be doing is entering a room with two exits. One exit is the way forward, and the other exit turns out to be a closet with resources in it that you spend two seconds in before moving on to the other exit. My major gripe is that there's a lot of surprise locking doors that prevent you from backtracking to the previous room. Very frequently, you'll get locked out of a section of the map before you expected to. The F key will illuminate some footsteps showing you the correct way to go, so often I'd light up the correct way, and then go the opposite way so that I know I'm going down some brief explorative path before I continue. That all being said, linear games are fine, but this one might have been slightly too linear.
Graphics and sound are, you guessed it: adequate. The game looks fine. It's detailed and interesting to look at. The graphics aren't mindblowing, they're just as good as they need to be. Not distractingly pretty or distractingly ugly. Just right. Audio, same story. Voice acting is fine. A bit generic. I hope you like token Russian accents. Monster noises are believable. Good ambience. The gun sounds are a bit anemic, however. I really wish the weapon sound design was stronger, because it really did detract from the experience a bit. But, y'know, it's not bad. It's just... adequate.
All in all, I enjoyed my time with the game. It's good for about 7-8 hours, which is just right for this game. It doesn't feel padded or drawn out, nor does it feel rushed. It lasts exactly as long as it needs to, and it never lets itself get stale. I played it in two sittings. The second sitting was the majority of the game, and in the middle of that, I took a break to eat lunch. And all throughout that lunch, I kept thinking to myself, "I really want to finish eating so I can keep playing." Not a lot of shooters give me that experience. It's a combination of good pacing, good story, and not-exhausting gameplay that really makes that happen.
Nothing is absolutely spectacular about this game, but nothing is boring, dull, or just plain bad, either. It's not earthshattering by any means, but I don't think anybody making the game expected it to be. They set out to make just a pretty good shooter, and that's exactly what they've done. So, as long as your expectations are in the right place, you'll probably have a good time.

Singularity is ambitious. Singularity wants to play all sides of the field. Singularity wants to create an engaging and comprehensive FPS experience. Unfortunately for Singularity, it seems far too hollow to be great.
This game isn't just a FPS. It is THE FPS. It is quintessential in all ways. Everything that embodies modern first person gaming is here and accounted for. The only notable exceptions are  chest high walls and turret sections. If you've played half life, or call of duty, then you've seen all this game has to offer. Nothing at all will surprise you here. You're better off looking elsewhere if you want an interesting first person shooter.
Everything is just so standard. Singularity doesn't take any risks with the formula we're all familiar with. In fact, it seems proud of its influences. The protagonist is silent but gifted soldier who must save the world from countless monsters, the big bad guy, and droves of opposing soldiers. But wait, this protagonist has the power of a magic doohickey that can grab objects and alter the environment to solve basic puzzles. And also there's a scientist, and a secondary female character that shows up sometimes.
Nothing is interesting about this game. It seems unable to make up its mind. Its hard to give complements after braving the constant, and I mean CONSTANT audio logs & mundane written notes lying around, the enemies that repeat the same two battlecries, a myriad of jumpscares; (or what I only could assume were supposed to be jumpscares,) a handful of unique enemy types, and a story that left me confused and annoyed. The game tired, I guess. But how many times can I see ghostly scenes of generic russian man #34 screaming, running away from something, or dying randomly before I just get bored and play something more effective at horror and a first person shooter experience. By the end of the game, I just wanted it to end. Not only did I stop paying attention to the plot, I had taken to throwing myself head first into enemies, which was just about the most significant source of fun this game has to offer. There are many better first person shooters to play.

This game is amazing. The concept is phenominal and the execution was nearly flawless. However, knowing it's in Beta, you'll forgive me for saying there are things needing fixes. And forgive me if there's something I suggest that is already in the game or a control I wish for that is already there, for I haven't played the full extent of the game.
For those looking for a review to tell what the game is:
This isn't a regular RTS where you build a base and make troops to send at the enemy's base. This is not a C&C game. You select troops and those get sent in every wave (Or every third wave if you're playing 3v3, every wave is one of the three players on your team, going in a certain order so you guys technically take turns) You have abilities which cost gold which you get for getting kills with your troops. You can purchase more than one of each troop you have (essentially have an army of one troop) this kinda works in the whole MOBA category, with your troops being the "Creeps" of the game. However, there aren't heroes you can play as, as that would ruin the game. There are three towers on each side. Three you defend, three you destroy. Simple as that. Then attack the main base. As you progress you'll gain access to new armies and new troops.
Things to fix:
Bombing Runs. They're good on tactics and it's good it costs more gold each use, but it's still possible (in a 3v3 match) for someone to send out troops and get them automatically obliterated by a bombing run. (Yes, this happened to me for 6 waves straight)
Frame drops. This may be my computer just being bad, and it doesn't happen often especially when lowering the details of the game, but occasionally all the combat will drop the frame rate or freeze the game for a few seconds. Normally it won't matter but there may be times you need to purchase a troop before your next run but can't because the game has frozen.
Connection. This is not a big issue but it can get frustrating when seeing everyone stop for a few seconds then shift forward in one way or another. While again this may just be my system (My computer was poorly repaired by cheapskates and I have a hard time holding a connection) it wouldn't hurt to bump up the servers a little bit.
Targetting. I've seen reviews complaining about targetting and thought they were just overreacting, but the targetting really is a problem. Perhaps add our own targetting (Give the "RTS" tag a run for its money) or set certain things to priority, while still of course having a massive warfare on the battlefield.
Things to add:
Optional health bars. This obviously isn't a big request but it would be nice to be able to turn off the health bars above the troops so that we can just see the troops fighting.
Voice chat. Voice chatting is far more convenient and accessable than text chat for obvious reasons.
(I'll update this review the more I play this game. That is all for now)

- Good worldbuilding and setup, I can see future acts having a really good plot.
- Very, very good characters. I wish Jude could have been fleshed out more, but I guess that's for Hauntswitch so I can't complain!
- Music transitions are buggy, especially around strifes. Volume is also extremely inconsistent across rooms, even compared to sound effects. Seems more of a programming issue than anything related to sound design, however.
- Weird "hitboxes" for items, and a few "conflicts" between movement and interaction. Particularly, having to use an item on a door was unexpected, considering the icon didn't change from the regular movement icon when you hovered over it with the item, and the fact using items on transitions was unprecedented.
- ANY button skips stuff, even the screenshot button. A nitpick, but an annoying one.
- Relatively short, took me three hours while taking my time. I would have vastly preferred a bigger amount of interactions between the characters over item combination/interaction text, which I enjoyed, but wouldn't deliberately seek out. That said, this is no big deal: I have to remember it's only Act 1.
- It's just too easy. I got stuck one time, and that was with the door incident I mentioned above. I definitely don't want an obscurely frustrating experience like with some old adventure games, but I feel like the only times the game made you use your head were ruined by the fact you got unasked hints for them right afterwards. Maybe make the hints optional in future acts?
Conclusion:
. A very fun adventure game, and a great Homestuck experience (if you're into that), but a bit too easy and too short to be perfect. I hope future acts make you think a bit more often.
I can recommend it to everyone who enjoys adventure games, and it's definitely a must-play for Homestuck fans.

Dragon's Dogma is an Action RPG that was released back in 2012. It definitely still holds up, and with the addition of an optimal PC port, it makes a great game even better. Let me just say that this game has the best combat in any fantasy game I've ever played. Skyrim, Dragon Age, Witcher, though superb games on their own right should definitely learn from this game. You can pick up and hold enemies in full nelsons, climb onto giant monsters, throw people off cliffs, cover enemies in oil and set them ablaze, all in real-time combat. The fights in Dragon's Dogma feel like real battles, something that I don't get the impression of from other fantasy games I love. The music is epic, booming, something just right for a high fantasy setting. It’s also particularly amazing when you get the upperhand on a difficult boss, and the music matches your actions makes you feel like a heroic badass.
The combat and music is superb. The loot and armor are also pretty cool. Great. Now onto the bad….
The game isn't the best written or particularly engaging in other fronts outside of combat. The quests and lore, although they can be interesting at times, are rather boring, with most quest having the player do little more then go here, and kill these bandits, monsters, find this item, etc. Sure, many games do this as well, but in those games your task has consequences or at least context. Outside of the main antagonist, I don’t really remember the names of many of the characters in the world, which is a shame since I spent over 100 hours on this game. The world is also boring and drab, and outside of some cool locales, have little interesting things to discover. In fact, I would go as far as to say the huge open world hurt the game moreso than helped it. I feel like if this game really tightened its belt on this end and gave us interesting, varied quest and world building, it would easily make a great game essential.
One of the game's primary gameplay mechanics is the pawn system. In it, you create an NPC that will follow and support you on your journey. You pick their class, appearance, and attributes, and as you level they will level. Where your pawn goes, they will go. As you adventure, other people will hire your pawn, and as your pawn ventures with other players, they will come back with items and tactical knowledge regarding many of the games enemies. It is a rather unique concept.
The problem though Pawn AI. Unless you raise your pawn a certain way, they'll always start gaining traits that make them more of a hindrance than a help. My mage pawn Faya, would always join me in the fray even though her role as a squishy wizard is to stay as far from the carnage as possible. So many deaths were because I had to save my pawns when they weren't doing their jobs right. Renting high level pawns does seem to address this complaint, as I found around the mid 60s and 70 leveled pawns, pawns seemed to get their crap together and actually fight like a player would. The pawn chatter is also a common complaint, but I didn’t feel that it detracted from the experience too much, and it can easily be turned off if it annoys you too much. I have to say though, it is annoying when the pawns repeat dialogue as if the player character had just stumbled onto a place of enemy, like they have a case of Anterograde amnesia.
The Bitterblack Isles is also included in PC release. Definitely for the hardcore who found the regular game easy. I feel I enjoyed it much more than the base game. In fact, it seems like its creation was for the purpose of rectifying many of the criticism that the game received. As you explore the bitterblack isles (You know, as you're getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked), you learn how such a vile place came to be. It provided more exposition and character development then I felt the huge open world base game did.
All in all, I enjoyed my time with the game. No matter how annoying my complaints got, the game really is fun to play, and the combat almost makes up for any criticism I can muster. It would be an absolute sin if this game didn’t get a sequel, and when (or if…) it does, I hope these complaints are taken into account. Some things I would want in the sequel are
-More detailed, varied, and interesting world building and locales (Ex. Elder Scrolls, Witcher Series)
-Quest with consequences (Ex. Witcher, Dragon Age, Mass Effect)
-Fix Pawn AI and comments ( Ex-Skyrim Mod Companions like Vilja, Inigo, Bioware companions)
-Additive content (More monsters/variations, more classes, weapons, loot, items, bigger world)
My suggestions, with slight refinements to the combat system (The game’s combat is almost perfect) would easily make this game close to my ideal rpg. I highly recommend you check it out, but take the criticisms against the game to heart. But for $30, it’s easily worth it.

Only in this game can you vomit clusters of water baloons that explode into rings of homing blood lasers...
...and that's only one of the numerous different combinations of items, without even taking the massive number of mods available on the Workshop into account.

It's a standard JRPG as far as the story and most gameplay mechanics go, but this game has a unique combat system; you can grab onto big monsters and slash them away! Really fun. Also love little details like your lantern needing to be maintained and goes out if you underneath a waterfall.
Another unique feature is the companion system. You create your "pawn" from their looks down to their profession, who will permanently follow you and can also recruit other pawns that other players have created. Your pawn can also be recruited by others and can come back with items and new knowledge of quests or enemies.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to any who love role-playing games.

Combat is definitely fun at first, and the mechanics for jumping on/mounting larger adversaries and attacking different bodyparts to achieve differnt effects (blindness, hobbling/rooting, etc.) is pretty cool. Spells feel impactful and varied, too, and focusing on any of the magical vocations feels powerful in ways that many RPGs fail to achieve. The ability to switch vocations and still keep certain spells/abilities/passives across all classes is also a nice mechanic, and encourages a more subtle kind of multiclassing.
The pawn system starts off as a nice addition when you get to design/create your permanent companion, and the idea of your companions adventuring and getting XP, money, and items while you're offline is pretty cool. The pawn system admittedly gets stale fast, but there are some great ideas in there that I'd love to see other devs appropriate.
The soundtrack is also well done, and I find myself coming back to it despite having given up on the game itself.
Unfortuantely, there are just too many deal-breakers here:
Despite fun combat mechanics, the lack of variety in baddies greatly reduces the novelty and fun factor after only a few hours. And although combat feels weighty and meaningful for both martial and magical vocations, the extremely limited number of skills you can effectively equip during combat greatly reduces your spread of actual options. It isn't long before every engagement feels the same -- a tedious, formulaic, and unsatisfying slog to another drop of garbage items.
The inventory system itself is a tedious and disorganized mess, even by the admittedly low standards set by console ports. Mods that increase carrying capacity are a virtual necessity if you want to spare yourself the frustation of constantly needing to sort, combine, and otherwise dump all manner of assorted crap.
Despite the world's apparent size, it is frustatingly empty and devoid of meaningful things to do. Enemies constantly respawn, forcing repeated zone clears just to get anywhere, and the "story" -- if we're being generous here -- is a cliched, nonsensical mess that quickly loses what little momentum and coherence it had once you exit the initial area.
I love epic SPRPGs and bought this game after reading through many of the overwhelmingly positive reviews here, but this just didn't do it for me.

Considering how late I am to this party, I doubt my review is going to matter much to many people.  Still, I enjoyed this one too much not to say something about it.  I picked this up at the Steam holiday sale.  I'd never given it much of a look since I thought of it as basically just a shooter, and I generally much prefer strategy and roleplaying games.  I had seen the sci-fi theme and the shooter genre tag and just sort of written it off as the next Doom.
I was wrong.  This is an immersive, addictive masterwork ... a strategic, tactical, and roleplaying epic.
The RPG (character-building, dialogue) elements and strategy (squad building and destination selection) elements are simple but immersive, and they matter enough to be engaging. The world-building is genuinely impressive: history, races, economics, industry, politics, they really thought about a lot of elements.  But the moment that really hooked the open-world RPG fan in me was the first time I opened the galactic map on the Normandy (the spaceship that you ultimately explore the galaxy in) and saw all the different possible destinations. That level of non-linear, open-world (open-galaxy!) freedom reminds me much more of RPGs like Skyrim, or at least Dragon Age (the latter perhaps moreso, since they’re even by the same studio).
The voice acting is absolutely excellent, and I both the male and female voice actors for Commander Shepard (the primary protagonist, whom the player can choose to have be male or female) are outstanding, and if anything, I'd give the quality nod to Jennifer Hale playing the female commander.  Her voicing of the Renegade dialogue options (the less heroic, more Machiavellian morality path of the two that players choose between) are convincingly badass.
I finished this a while ago and have already imported my character into Mass Effect 2 and am a little more than halfway through that, and I'm impressed by the amount of story continuity BioWare worked into the series: when you import a character, choices made in this game don't just affect the rest of this game, they affect the next game in the series as well.
If, like me, you're not much a fan of the shooter genre and prefer to have more story, setting, and character development in your games, you should still definitely have this one in your library.  This one lived up to the hype and more.

First and foremost I'd like to say that while they look similar, it's difficult to compare this game to Terraria. In terms of scope, I don't believe it's unfair to say that Starbound has a lot of content in comparison to Terraria, which to be fair is also a massive game in its own right.
Then again maybe that's just me, but being able to explore the stars and visit various planets feels fresh, and Starbound simply succeeds at building a fun and inviting universe.
While I feel that vanilla Starbound is lacking in a few areas, mostly in terms of minor details, Steam Workshop really polishes the experience. I probably use close to 100 mods on my game, and honestly, the ability to have the freedom to refine the experience and tune it how you'd like is one of the best aspects of Starbound. You can change so many aspects of the game to fit your liking. Added content, added races, different zoom options, extended UI options, the list goes on.
My favorite feature, something that Terraria lacks, is a zoom slider. To be honest, Terraria’s sprites are a bit small for me, and the game can be hard on my eyes at times. Starbound alleviates that issue by providing different fields of view. And perhaps I'm ignorant of a mod for Terraria that fixes this, if there is one, somebody link, please!
The bookmark and flag system for teleporting to previously explored areas really helps make travel less of a chore too. The universe never seems SO large that you cannot comprehend it. Being able to beam to party members (friends in Co-Op) is also incredibly useful.
The only aspect of the game I don’t like is the fact that you lose 30% of your pixels (currency) upon death. I’d rather they have used a scaling option similar to Borderlands (losing a small fraction of your total credits upon death), rather than a large flat percentage.
At any rate, if you’re looking for a comfy, cozy experience of travelling the universe either solo or with friends, Starbound is certainly worth the $15 price of admission.

Short: it’s like Skyrim with swords and multiplayer.
It reminds me a lot of mine craft alpha, but without as much building.
Long: In the 11 hours I have played I have managed to build all the different buildings currently in game. I have not seen some things yet (like bears), but I am impressed with the game.
Keep in mind it is early access, so it has things it needs to work on.
Buildings- the only one worth actually building is the forge. It is the only house that acutely has a permanent light and heat source, and it is relatively easy to make if you can mine up some ore and rock. It needed to make armor, better gear, and repair some stuff. The town hall I not worth it, although it is the only other one that seems to have a floor- it looks like it should be multi story but its jest a box like the rest and takes up a lot of wood. Despite what the description on it says, the forge offers more heat (or at least seems to. Spent most of my time there). There are torches, but something smaller like candles would be nice, that last longer but provide no heat. The only current furniture you can put in a house is a box, which is useful but I hope they expand to include chairs, beds, tables, etc. Or even fur rugs that bring up the warmth of the room. Fences would be nice also.
Terrain- it’s a lot like getting lost in a forest. There’s rocks, trees, and sometimes abandoned buildings or towns. Also a lot of things want to kill you. There is also a tower (towers?) that has a dragon at the top. One of the things missing from the landscape however seems to be water in the form of pods, stream, or rivers. There are also no cliffs or caves, its jest hills. Due to the fact that you cant dig your own mines or whatnot, it would be nice to see mines you can use at some point.
Mining/logging- One of the things that I do dislike is the fact that ever tree and rock is a finite resource. There is no way to grow back trees and rocks get mines out after a bit. Without the ability to create a mineshaft or other resource gathering things, this means you will always have to venture further and further out. Not that big a deal, until you get to the higher tires of crafting and more so with high tire repairs. I don’t know if items held on a character travel with them to other maps, but there is a point where you could clear the map of all trees/rocks. There are mini spawning points near rocks for some of the things you can get form them, but for large scale crafting it won’t sustain you. That said, it’s kind of fun to look for things and be able to make where you have been before with if a rock is taped out or not.
Enemies are hard. The only thing that doesn’t attack you is deer. The damage system could use work, but it’s like mine craft alpha where there was no knockback. A damage indicator as in what direction things are hitting you from would be nice. Low health gives you the blood eyes thing and makes the screen grayer. So far, I haven’t had much trouble with anything other than one enemy. I found a tree giant at some point, but not knowing what they looked like (and because they don’t move) I thought it was a resource… that went well. I lived but he broke all my armor (it would be nice to be able to repair broken gear by the way!) and he went back into the trees.
All in all, it’s fun. I think it would be better with people, as I have been playing until this point solo.

Found this game by accident and ended up playing it for 10 hours straight.  If you've ever played a "Creep War" type game (like the ones from Warcraft 3 custom games) it's like that with MOBA elements;
You don't control your units except for the few that have activatable abilities, you purchase units that fight with the goal of destroying the enemy's command center in a tug-of-war-esque 3v3 or 1v1 game modes.
You'll probably see a majority of Chinese players but with preset emotes communaction is fairly simple. All I can say, is:
+Art of War: Red Times is incredibly fun
+it's free
+fairly balanced
+ranked play that doesn't wreck your progress with losses
+it's free *(*Possible Micro-Transactions but none as of right now*)*
+every unit is unlockable with earned currency
+vs ai, quick play, or ranked play
+fairly short games (15min avg)
+Increadibly well done and well made for only being in beta. Very poslished, with very few bugs.
+matches are usually even with the last few minutes being crucial
-Lot of non-english speaking players (not a bad thing, just hard to communicate outside preset emotes)
-addicting
-Tutorial is only for 1 of the 3 playable races
-ai intelligence can be a little slow
Give it a try, you won't be disappointed.

This is the most engaging online tcg that I've played. Even early turns have a lot of decision-making to be done, and the skill cap for the game is very high. Play this game if you like to think a lot, analyze board positions, and build decks.
The devs are very responsive to the meta, and the latest balance patch speaks to this, as they have nerfed some dominant cards from the last meta without driving them into the ground, and they even buffed several underplayed cards, which is helping the meta feel fresh despite the low number of cards compared to other ccgs.
One of my favorite aspects of the game is that it has very few cards which are truly outclassed by others; while of course there are dominant archetypes at any given time, they can often be built in many ways, and if there's a card you really want to build around, and you're good at deckbuilding and playing, you can make just about anything work.

This game would be so much better if you didn't have to pay to play the only mode that is any fun.
----------
AI Missions - Good for new players to learn mechanics. These missions quickly become easy to dominate with nothing but the starter decks you are given. Unfortunately, you have to grind out 14 of these at a time just to get 5 new random cards, or to grind gold for daily missions. *yawn*
----------
PVP - Don't. 75% of decks you come up against either abuse DLC card mechanics ("Swallow") that eliminate all skill from the game by essentially erasing your cards from existence from anywhere on the map with literally no way to prevent, or are the rush deck meta flavor of the month. I guess you could enjoy that, but the whole point of a card game, developing and building custom decks, is sort of null and void due to the huge power imbalance between cards.
----------
Boss Missions - Absurdly unfair battles against cheating AI (fixed opening hand, fixed turn order, double max health, starting with 3 special lands on the battlefield, starting with a creature on the battlefield, generating 5 energy per turn instead of 3, and dealing 20 [OHKO] damage to random targets every turn past the fifth - and that's all ONE boss). There's no point to this other than to unlock vanity items; the challenges you face here are totally irrelevant to normal gameplay, and they almost all require abusing specific game mechanics or legendary cards to complete.
----------
Pandora - Genuinely fun and truly enjoyable; you are randomly given access to 3 of the 4 colors in Faeria and you draft a 30 card deck from random components of those colors. You use that deck against other players for a set number of matches and then get to draft a new deck.
Unfortunately you aren't actually allowed to play Pandora mode. Every 24 hours you get 1 "practice coin" that let's you play 2-4 games for no rewards. If you want to play for real you have to BUY the entry coins. So either be prepared to start handing over cash OR grinding gold on daily missions for a week just to get a single entry to play.
----------
I would still recommend, because there is enough early game content to enjoy for 10-15 hours before you reach the point of grinding for days just to play one series of fun matches. The game also hands out free cards like candy in the beginning, which makes for some fun deck building when learning to play.
Just don't expect to be able to use those decks in matches against real people though until you buy the DLC cards. And also throw your personalized deck away in favor of either the Meta flavor or the Counter-Meta flavor.

I found Faeria while browsing for a fun strategy/deckbuilding game and Faeria's vibrant art caught my eye. I downloaded it and gave it a go.
To start off, you are given fairly simple little missions and puzzles to teach you the basics, and how the game is played. They were pretty explanatory, and tell you what you need to know.
After that, you are gifted 1 Pandora coin, an item used to play in a draft-style environment. Unfortunately, you only get one, and after that you've got to purchase more, and they're rather expensive - twice the price of a 'Battle Chest', which contains 5 cards. You do get one 'practice coin' per day, but the rewards are minimal.
Unfortunately, after you finish the first missions, you must pay 500 gold (half the price of a Battle Chest) to unlock each new set of wild (random) missions, or pay 4,000 for a larger, themed set.
The graphics are very nice overall, and they really spark my imagination. I dislike the yak art though, because it just feels like a different style of art. That's just personal opinion though, and it is still cute.
The gameplay is rather strategic, and enjoyable, but it can feel repetitive after a while. Certain AI (I'm looking at you, Sharra and Khalim) can be very frustrating, as they are far more agressive and difficult to beat. Especially when none of the 4 starting decks beats them reliably. The bosses are worse - they are extremely tough, because they get huge starting advantages. Multiplayer would probably be wise to steer away from early on, because you won't have the cards to really compete.
While in-game purchasing is a thing, it's impact is greatly reduced by Pandora and singleplayer, so it's not a big deal.
Now, ratings out of 10:
Graphics: 8/10
Singleplayer gameplay: 6/10
Multiplayer gameplay: 6/10
Overall: 7/10
Verdict: Cute and visually appealing, but best to play for a bit each day - grinding gets old fast.

Singularity is a game about war and time travel, but it isn't a generic rebrand on the story like a lot of other games centered around war and time travel in the genre are. The game is centered around an American soldier who gains control of a time manipulation device, more commonly known as the T.M.D. and changes the history as well as the future in his mission to save the world from a rip in time called a singularity.

Of course, you already know what Singularity is like: it's like a hundred other games. You slow down time. You freeze time. You have a highly advanced piece of kit that allows you to break things and repair them again (not a spanner). Press a different button and you can lift things, use them as shields and throw them at bad people. Did you say Gravity Gun?
Graphics are courtesy of Unreal 3 for the last console gen, which means bad. Hardly any detail and lo-res shaders like everything is smeared with vaseline. There are no settings to turn up.
The plot is also gibberish. You go forward in time, you go back in time. You shoot a man in the head then he starts having a conversation about causality, so you have to shoot him again. It's almost as bad as Bioshock Infinite. Almost.
Still, the big spiders were nice, the guns were alright and it was £2.50, so that's a thumbs up.
5/10.

Even in its early access state, State of Decay is one of the best and most enjoyable zombie "sims" i have ever played. If you are fans of the zombie genre and love sandbox mode games, do yourself a favor and pick this title up.

State of Decay is the open-world third person apocalyptic survival game that I have waited for this whole generation, Day Z and Dead Island were close for me but they both lacked a few things here and there. While DayZ had survival, Dead Island had the world and mechanics, State of Decay have both of these aspects, and pull them off very successfully.
You quickly realize that the game push a lot of information at you the first few hours, like every home base can only have so many structures, do you want more sleeping areas to keep the characters in the camp rested? Or maybe you want a library to research some better medical aid for when someone get hurt? From this point on the game becomes very dark, it will test your moral. And rightfully so.
Every now and then you stumble across new survivors, complete strangers in need of help. What are you going to do? Do you help them and risk running out of food? Or do you save them in hope of finding a few food supplies?
This also takes us back to the base aspect, you could build a garden instead of a library or sleeping area, as this will give you food daily. Because food each day must be good right? Yes, it is, but if you don't have enough beds for everyone, each character will slow but sure get tired, fatigued. This goes for your playable characters as well as NPCs in the camp.
If a player character don't rest after a while of exploring, the stamina will decrease, making you worse in combat and increase the chance of dying. Death is permanent, and there is no save/reload feature to abuse. The game autosaves after each finished mission, and that is it.
The less playable characters you have available, the harder the game gets, because you have less to pick from when the others need a few hours in the bed to rest.
Keeping a character alive and well will not only serve as a jump option, but they also gain skills and level up depending on what they do. Melee combat? Increase the fighting skill, making you more efficient with melee weapons. Same goes for guns, looting etc.
However should you be unlucky and die, the items you got on you can be retrieved with another character, so don't panic!
You will meet tough situations where people you know get infected, and we all know how to "fix" that problem. It can be a hard call, depending on the connection with each individual character, the NPC can get overrun while on a supply run you called in, and if you don't help them, may they RIP.
The game consistently keeps throwing missions/tasks at you, you have to prioritize, which is more important? Save this guy? Or scout this area to call out locations of meds, zeds or maybe you want to find out what the Army is up to.
The story is also pretty well put together, i keeps you interested, and makes you feel connected with the characters living in the world, making you feel the need to help (most) of them. Helping other survivor outposts will also benefit resources like ammunition, food, construction material etc. But how you play in the world also affect how everyone in the world watch you, reckless driving is negative and will make everyone look at you in a bad way, same goes for reckless shooting. But in the end, it's all about survival, keeping morale up, food on the table and killing the zeds!

A captivating RPG which really lets you make your own choices that carry through the whole story. In Mass Effect, you don't play as Commander Shepard; you are Commander Shepard.
The first installment of the series boasts an immersive plot that makes you want to learn the rest of the story right away. Mass Effect world is based on amazing amount of lore, available in game in form of 'codex entries', creating a complex and self-consistent universe almost comparable to that of the Star Wars saga. Add to that extensive dialogues, literally dozens of explorable planets and exciting combat, and you get the glimpse of why ME is so compelling.
It's a game enjoyable for both die-hard RPG fans and newcomers. The equipment system with its stats and the sheer amount of items might be a bit overwhelming at the beginning, but it's easy to get used to; same goes for the leveling system. Fight itself is not very complicated, but those who seek a challenge will definitely find it on higher difficulty levels. Mass Effect power system makes enemy encounters more than just simple firefights, and you can choose from several squadmates with unique skills to tackle different kinds of enemies.
Still, the power of Mass Effect lies mainly in dialogues and player decisions. This is why ME (and the trilogy as a whole) holds such a big replayable value - by making different choices, you can complete several playthroughs and still encounter new parts of the game. By completing side quests (or, in Mass Effect terminology, asssignments) you get some 40 to 50 hours of the game, even though the main storyline can be completed pretty quickly. But that's not the point, is it?
Don't forget to download the free 'Bring Down the Sky' DLC and enjoy! This might well become your favourite franchise, as it is mine.

What can I say about Mass Effect? It is one of my all-time favorite games. The story is really good and the replay value is high due to the fact that you can create different characters focusing on different abilities. Want to be a soldier with all the toys of destruction or a full biotic with limited weapons, or a technician. You can play a character as these types and some in between.
One of the greatest things about the Mass Effect trilogy is that you can import a completed game character into the next installment of the franchise and get bonuses for completing the last installment and pick your character up where you left off. You of course can always just start a new character as well, but it is the carryover of the character that makes the series really unique.
The only strikes against it is some of the tedium related to exploring planets and inventory wrangling.
Definitely a must buy.

This is a fairly impressive over-the-shoulder 3rd person RPG with action/FPS elements. It plays alright on the PC but it's console roots are clearly exposed which give it an amateur feel at times. Given that it is now around 7 years old there are some elements that have not aged so well but overall this is a classic game that deserves a play through. 8/10
Pros
+ main storyline is quite good
+ codex library contributes to a very deeply detailed world (though at times it can be a lot of reading)
+ combat cover system is quite good which makes this feel more realistic ( and less like an overpowered shooter)
+ weapons and armor variety
+ side-quests are numerous
+ Normandy starship offers a phenomenal atmospheric setting
+ dialogue engine offers high variety and allows for personality shaping
+ exploration area is seemingly huge
+ some character models are brilliantly designed
+ companions are well thought out and offer interesting background stories
Cons
- console-based "look and feel" very much short changes the combat and gameplay
- RPG elements are weak
- in-game menus (such as the inventory) are poorly designed
- size of the game is artificial as most locations and mini games are repetitive and quickly become tiring
- character models are inconsistent with some being horrifically bad (certain scenes show out of proportion body parts which kill immersion)
- elevator travel was poorly designed sacrificing efficiency for immersion (who wants to watch the characters stand still for 30 seconds listening to elevator announcements!?)
- squad combat design is a neat idea but the execution falls flat
- reuse of levels and building design is abundant and tiring by the end of the game
I appreciate the producer effort but however some of the things are not meant to be changed.....

I've played this game duing early access, played it all the way through, played the nightly builds, played through the game all over again when 1.0 released, and modded the hell out of it to make the expansive universe more expansive. Seeing this game go through the phases of development was a wild ride, from Beta to 1.0. I got emotional when this game went out of early access, seeing a game that you've been watching for years and watching it bloom with it making an appearance to the front page of the Steam Store. Playing it through the end made me feel that as well, knowing that you finished this complete game that didn't normally have an ending. I had a great time with Starbound, with the constant feeling of wonder with every hour I put into the game. From getting lost in the caves and surfaces of the planets, from gathering the materials for getting better gear to progress the story, and from experiencing the main missions. I do wonder if my experience with the game could've been better if I had a better computer, but with that aside, I still enjoyed everything about the game. If you love travelling through space, getting lost in exploring, progressive gameplay, and the other things that make sandbox games fun, I recommend this game to anyone of the sort. But, if you don't like the repetitive tropes to sandbox survival games, I wouldn't, but one review shouldn't affect someone's interest to try it out.

To this day, Dragons Dogma is one of my favourite RPGs. It features a somewhat large open world, interesting combat and great classes and skills.
There are 9 vocations (classes) that are all wildly different and interesting and thus deserve detailed descriptions
-Fighter (basic vocation, sword and shield, good allrounder)
-Strider (basic vocation, typical dagger/bow user, agile and quick)
-Mage (basic vocation, staff user, low armor but strong spells as well as healing and support capabilites)
-Sorcerer (advanced vocation, uses archistaffs and casts spells with extremely long casting times which leaves him vulnerable, but upon casting devastates large groups of enemies with giant tornadoes, earthquakes and meteors)
-Warrior (advanced vocation, wearing two handed weapons and capable of quickly destroying large groups with broad swings. Can be a force to be reckoned with when left alone due to very strong charge skills)
-Ranger (advanced vocation, uses daggers and longbows, has several strong bow skills that allow to quickly kill targets from afar with strong and charged shots and snipes. Lots of utility, like sonic arrows that distract enemies as well as special debilitating arrows)
-Assassin (advanced hybrid vocation, master of weapons - has skills for swords, shields, daggers and bows that make him useful for any situation. Also capable of invisibility when using daggers as well as excellent single target damage and countering)
-Magick Knight (advanced hybrid vocation, uses maces and magick shields. Can counter foes easily with his enchanted shields that he can enchant with all sorts of elements. Also a lot of utility and surprising aoe damage as well as excellent defense)
-Magick Archer (advanced hybrid vocation, uses magick bows and daggers. Capable of hitting even spread out enemies with magick bow shots as well as sporting a lot of utility like an illuminating arrow that lights up even the darkest of caves)
As you can see all the classes are varied and dang fun to play. Fighting in DD is the most fun you will ever have with a battle system in an RPG - that alone is reason to buy it. If you need more, here are the pros and cons:
Pros:
-fun, active real time combat - hitting and evading enemies is very satisfying and the combat is largely skill based
-visually and mechanically very impressive skills - every class feels like it really gets more powerful. Sorcerer has the best and most destructive magic spells ever seen in any game, for example
-huge enemies which can be climbed and have several weak points (for example breaking off tusks when fighting a cyclops or attacking his eye)
-very "western" design with castles and ruins
-pawns are a unique mechanic - the game is singleplayer but you can rent companions designed by other players as well as sending out your own that other players can rent which gives you rewards
-tons of items in the game that can be combined in many ways
-lots of stuff to do, all held up by the great combat
-enemies all behave differently and your pawns will employ different tactics based on what they learnt either when traveling with you or other players (also applies for quests - pawns can help other players in quests and then share their knowledge with you once you embark on the same quest)
-good character creation with plenty of choices
-excellent voice acting
-Dlc "Dark Arisen" sports a new interesting area with difficult challenges
-big world...
Cons:
-...that is sadly not visually appealing and very samey (mostly grassland,dark arisen area not included)
-fast travel is convoluted and only works to big cities and crystals you set up yourself, making it so that you always have to travel to some areas on foot
-pawns wont shut up and it gets annoying - while there is an option to turn it off, that also disables their helpful tips
-the story isnt anything special and largely uninteresting
-pawns are often stupid and don't do what you want them to - the only way to somewhat control them is to set their behaviour on a knowledge chair but even that doesn't always work and then you die without getting healed
- the 100th time you will hear "Masterworks all, you can't go wrong" from the weapons merchant in the capital, you will want to murder someone - generally very repetitive dialogue not only from pawns
-inventory weight limit is annoying, as is losing stamina when sprinting and having to catch your breath - I HIGHLY recommend using two mods to get around this as the game is so much more fun without inventory weight management and only being able to sprint for 5 seconds (also some texture mods make the game look very beautiful, otherwise it just looks servicable)
All in all DD is an excellent and different RPG with amazing combat that will keep you entertained way past the 50 hour mark. Trying out differnt vocations is fun and you can even go for stat min maxing if you want to. It is an RPG that might not be for everyone but in my eyes is a hidden gem with tons of depth, especially in the combat.
Personal Score: 8.5/10
