I bought this game with the ever so tempting theme of fantasy monster encounters meets the forest or what have you. Unfortunately I rode the steam preview hype train right into disappointment station.
Bearing in mind that this is an early access game, I won't go into polish aspects of the game, like animations, sounds, gui and what have you. Those are easy to fix and I'm sure one day they will be nice.
These game design factors are what turned me off after about 3 hours of gameplay:
1: The progression system is terribly odd. By the end of the first night I had built a blacksmith's forge (a huge building built by one person in the middle of one night) I was in what I assume is the third tier armor set, the other two being made of leather and pelts and this one being made of metal. If this is "gritty survival" then this is outright bizzare and completely jarring. If this game is more about starting from nothing into an epic style fantasy, then I suppose it's on par, but the jump from barely making it to being eligible for medieval footsoldier status is a near instant jump.
2: The game gives you a huge checklist of "survival tasks" to undertake, but the end result of this checklist (buildings, etc) can be found along the coast not ten yards from where you spawn. So I assumed from the beginning that you had to make camp, approach these other camps with caution cause who knows what you'd find. I then realized there was no real danger and no sense in wasting time building these things on the checklist.
3: The biggest problem I ran into, however, was it was utterly boring after the first 30-45 minutes. I had to endure a painfully long night cycle with no real threat other than the possibility of freezing to death, and then setting out the next day into a world that isn't very hostile or interesting. I couldn't find any monsters other than wolves. There are no complex recipies that require maticulous searching to find components that would warrant such a huge world and if there are I never found them. Again, it may be because there are plans for expanding the wilderness in the future, but right now it's more lifeless than a no-npc Skyrim mod.
As for co-op, it all becomes somewhat more tolerable, but then the issue is you and a friend are so powerful nothing is a threat to you at all.
All of these aren't deal breakers in and of themselves, but with no real roadmap from dev(s?) and an incoherenent theme presented by the "meta" of the whole thing makes me a bit apprehensive. Maybe later down the development road it will be fleshed out and labeled correctly and coherently on the tin, but as of right now it is a mess.

Pillars of Eternity is, hands-down, the best game in its genre since Baldur's Gate II.
So, yeah. Anyone who ever played any Infinity RPGs for fifty hours straight knows what I'm talking about. Huge, isometric, story-driven games which emphasized immersion in worlds where your choices mattered, your mistakes were painful and the story was engaging. Sure, you had to read giant blocks of text and fight uphill battles that you could lose at the roll of a die, but both of these activities were immensely rewarding in themselves, because the writing was top-notch and the tactics you had to employ against your enemies had to be both creative and abide by Gygax's Tome of Neverending Rules to succeed. This was obviously before they slapped the RPG label to streamlined generic space operas or sandbox Bethesda countryside crawlers with bad writing and worse design.
Pillars of Eternity takes place in Eora, which might seem as a garden variety fantasy world at first, but quickly establishes its own identity as you discover that souls can be seen and interacted with and are considerably more palpable than the metaphysical malarkey you normally use to pick up drunk hippy chicks at pretentious parties. Add the political intrigue of separatist colonies and the invention of gunpowder into the mix and you get a uniquely deep universe in which you will have to use cunning, diplomacy and brute force in equal measure to stand a chance.
While both the classes and mechanics are basically modernisations of the D&D archetypes and rulesets, enough has been built on top of them to improve the overall experience: you have an infinite inventory for junk, craftable food, potions and enchantments provide secondary activities that enrich your arsenal and there's a really clever compromise between streamlined gameplay and the typical Dungeons and Dragons downtime which separates your encounter health pool (called Endurance) from the general health pool (which you can only regenerate by resting). The cherry on top is the stronghold you get to conquer and own fairly early in the game, and investing into its various buildings not only beautifies the initially decrepit keep, but also provides bonuses, NPCs and a recurring supply of gold.
The graphics are gorgeous, giving a painterly feel to the backgrounds and overcoming the technical limitations the Infinity engine had 17 years ago (dynamic water, convincing particle effects and modern resolutions being just the obligatory minimums), while retaining the general feeling gamers had exploring Faerûn. Even the classes and spells are pretty much the same, with occasional renames (presumably to avoid copyright infringement), though their efficiency has been tampered with and itemization is much less restrictive than it used to be.
If what you read appeals to you, then, by all means, buy this game. It's worth every penny and you'll get your money's worth in gametime, guaranteed. If you're like me, which is to say an absolute loser with no future and zero qualifications, you'll probably have the time to run through it within a week, but if you spread your doses responsably enough you'll probably be playing this a few months from now. Regardless of how immersive and brilliant this game will seem three hours in, don't forget to walk your dog, hang out with your friends and bang your girlfriend 'til she smiles.

Pillars of Eternity is essentially a fairly faithful remake of the first Baldur's Gate. The setting and the story are different, but the gameplay and gameflow are almost identical.
+ The Infinity Engine is back!
+ Pillars of Eternity is solid on the technical level, with crisp pretty graphic, good music, solid voicing, a deep D&D-ish RPG system, a reasonable story with good writing, and everything else one's heart desires.
+ There is plenty of content. In particular, there is a massive dungeon completely unrelated to the main game that you can clear at your pleasure. (I beat the game without even entering that dungeon.)
+ The ending cinematic - a pictorial summary of the consequences of your actions in the tradition of Fallout - is extremely satisfying. You get to hear of what happens to the places you visited and to the NPCs who accompanied you.
+ Pillars of Eternity is a labor of love, and that shows in the little details that catch the player's eye once in a while. For example, at one point you search for a guy who's being chased by the law. When you find him, he says he isn't guilty, etc, etc. I gave him a bag of gold and told him to beat it and be a good boy. Some time later, I ran across him in a random inn in a nearby town. Now this is attention to detail!
- Loading times can be frustrating. For me, loading times became longer as the game progressed. Might be due to my playing on a laptop. Toward the end, it took me about a minute to transition between areas. I gave up on questing and just rushed to the end.
- Pillars of Eternity compares favorably to BG1, ID2, and maybe even PT; but it's inferior to BG2. How? The thing is, BG2 just had more of everything. More quests, more classes (with kits and whatever), more and cooler spells, more boss fights, more loot, more quality across the board. BG2 was the pinacle of the Infinity Engine, and one of the 10 best-rated games of all time. Pillars of Eternity is not quite that.
- Many areas feel  bland. They are sort of empty.
- The dungeons tend to feel slightly unrewarding. This is because items in PoE are a bit boring. I acquired many of my best items from the vendors (and enchanting) rather than through questing. And many of my best items looked like: Dagger +5 +to hit +% damage. That's not a fun item. It's useful but not cool.
- The main story's end-game dungeons felt too easy. I beat the last battle on my first attempt, without trying too hard. (Of course, you always have the big dungeon under the Stronghold if you want a challenge.)
- In some instances, the game demands too much reading from the player. I like reading, but if I want to read, I'll lie in bed with a book, or open up a pdf on fullscreen. Reading a long rant sentence by sentence in the little dialogue box the game has is painful.
- One feature the game sorely misses is AI scripting of the kind BGII had. I just want to tell my Priest to spam the same spells in every fight. But I can't. I have to order him to cast every single spell every single time.
* I played Paladin, but the class I liked the most was the Cypher. You get to take a Cypher NPC a few hours into the game; and mine became a beast! The Cypher is also the class that feels the most native to PoE - whereas all other classes have D&D parallels, the Cypher is unique.
* Another class I liked was the Chanter (a.k.a. Bard).
* The Stronghold is all right.
* You get to use your reputation and skills once in a while.
* The next PoE game has the potential to be truly great.
Conclusion: Pillars of Eternity is a welcome ressurection of the old Infinity Engine isometric RPG's, and a great game in its own right. It's not quite Baldur's Gate II, but it does compare favorably to BG1.

Believe me when I say that this game used to be incredible, and my play time should speak for itself... but the fragile balance of each playstyle was obliterated with 1 single decision.
Elaborating on my experience playing this game, I used to enjoy the monthly ladder resets because it motivated me to switch up my decks to try different strategies and playstyles which the developers encourage. typically getting caught between the 5-1 ladder rank and occassionally breaking through to the god rank ladder (my record was #221 in the world). Before oversky the only multicoloured card was the famous three wishes. I remember playing decks built around this card and loving how powerful the late game was but also it wasn't overpowered because it took a while to gain momentum.
After the oversky update the game was suddenly flooded with multicoloured card types to encourage playstyle similar to three wishes decks of previous metas. Now this would have been a welcome edition and quite frankly most of the new cards are very cool and allow multiple new options that at first breathed new life into my decks. However, the single game ruining decision that I previously mentioned was the decision to add the new "swallow" mechanic. Ironically they named it pretty perfectly because it absolutely does swallow... all of the fun out of this once great competitive and unique game I had grown obsessed with. Anyone playing with 3 or more swallow cards in their deck, no matter the skill level will almost always have the upper hand on someone without. It is essentially a handicap that encourages less thinking and more luck based wins because it basically gives you at least a 2 turn advantage over your opponent but usually even more.
To put it bluntly, I quit the game 2 weeks after the introduction of oversky. This was a game that I could not stop playing and genuinely put multiple daily hours into. The developers pretty much did me a favour breaking my addiction by breaking the game.
They acknowledged balancing issues and released a patch for certain overpowered cards but it wasn't enough in my opinion, so I decided to wait and occupy myself with another game in hopes they would come to their senses and realise how awful this mechanic was. A month later, I gave it another shot and ended up playing for another week and I can safely say that nothing has changed. People at rank 15 on the ladder (basically bronze) are winning games against me that I would've otherwise done away with easily had they not filled their decks with 3 crystal flowers and 3 skywhales. In the span of 2 turns I had 4 of my 5 minions swallowed when they were surrounding my enemy's orb. Obviously I rage quit because multiple turns had been cancelled out, and you can argue that maybe I'm not so good at the game anymore and wasn't able to adapt to the new update... but I believe this disease is rampant throughout the game now.
In conclusion, without swallow cards in your deck you are essentailly risking a loss from the start because 8/10 games you play at least 1 of your minions is getting swallowed.
Anyway, my rant is over and I understand that some people may disagree but personally with this many hours put in to this game constantly striving to better myself and beat my record of #221 on the ladder my motivation is completely lost. At least 400 hours of these 430+ I put into the game were enjoyable so at least I got my money's worth! Sad to see it come to this so quickly but at least I no longer have to deal with the many apparent bugs and broken coding issues you will experience every so often. Thank you for making such a fun game Abrakam, it's just a shame it was short lived for me.

Wonderful game.  It feels like a combination of chess and texas hold-em.  Some people complain that it's pay to win, but that isn't remotely true.  I'm fairly highly ranked, without having bought anything.  I eventually bought something just to help out the developers, but I've received at least 10x more stuff without paying a cent.  The game is quite generous, and you can dominate the game without buying cards very quickly if you know how to play.  Look at cappucino's cap to hero, where he went from free to play to god within 12 hours, without buying anything.
Watch some of the better players like luuu and jok3se if you are getting thrashed and do not understand why.  The game has a lot of depth, and if you don't understand it you may think you are losing because other people have better cards, but that is rarely the case.  Generally good players have good cards, but that is because they have more experience, not because they have the cards.  A great player with lousy cards will consistently thrash a strong but modestly weaker player with every card in the game, and that is how it should be.  The deck at the top of the meta right now is extremely cheap in decks amd cam be quickly completed without paying a cent, and there are a number of very strong competitive decks that take very little work to get.  The decks that are expensive are generally fun decks that aren't at the top of the meta.
As much as I love this game, it can be a little less than obvious why you lost unless you take time trying to play some decks that are beating you.  For instance a lot of people complain about yellow rush.  If you want to understand yellow rush, try watching some guides on it and how to beat it, and play it for awhile.  After getting good at playing it, you will find it much easier to beat, because you will understand it's weaknesses.  Most of the apparently very strong decks are not really all that strong, they are just played well and you do not understand their win conditions.
Anyway, this is a fantastic game, and I encourage you to buy something to support the devs.  You do not need to buy anything to win, many if not most of the top players are F2P, but buy something to help the devs anyway.  I recommend goki the gold miner, he is by far the best deal and the best use for gems.

Fantastic game, despite its age. There's nothing quite like anihilating a room full of soldies with a sniper rifle that lets you steer bullets.
The game has a really creepy atmosphere. Dried out corpses are all over the place, and once in a while you get a time shift into back when they were still alive and see their suffering. You fight against monsters who used to be humans but got messed up by time radiation. You also fight against modern day soldiers. You also fight against 1950s soldiers.
You have a TMD, a special device that lets you age things (or soldiers) or revert old things back to new, among other things, like shooting time-slowing bubbles. There are quite a few "puzzles" where you have to think how to age or unage containers and power boxes, among other things, to get further.
The story... I wasn't really following it. It felt like some scientist was just telling me what to do (similar to Half-Life) and I just trudged along. I kept thinking he was about to screw me over the entire time. But the impact of what a time-altering technology in the wrong hands can do is tangible throughout the game.
So if you can handle feeling the dread of inexorable death waiting for you around the corner as you watch things decay, this game is for you!
P.S.: the game is ancient, so for obvious reasons the multiplayer is dead. You can't even start it up and wonder around the map alone.

This is a very solid port to a good but flawed console game that I wished by never expected to get a PC release.
The game has a fun combat system, with a real sense of weight and physicality to the player, pawns and enemies. Not just from good animations and sound effects, but from hitstuns, the physics engine and smart immersive game mechanics. Your clothes get wet and your latern goes out if you are in water, being a fire will prevent Griffons from flying, being douse in oil makes you slick and take more fire damage, damage parts of enemies fall off when taking enough damage and turn into loot drops where the part fell. Being able to grab unto larger enemies is fun, and not just a gimmick, as there is strategdy to holding on, letting go and positioning. You can even prevent the griffon from flying if you throw your pawns unto it all at once. Special attacks are flashing and useful, though some are too easily spammed they can still fun to use and abuse. The only time combat is not fun is when the player or enemies are caught in stunlocking combos, which make the fights either frustrating or too easy, depending on which side of the stunlock you're on. The stagger mechanic could use more balancing IMO.
The character customization is prety robust as well, and being able to make your PC and main companion is nice for creative/expression-oriented players. You also get to recruit the companion of other players and see what they made.
The game has 9 classes, which have unique weapons, passive abilities, active abilities and armor restrictions. They play fairly differently from one another and are all fun to play in my opinion.
The game has a cool crafting system for items, and you can use materials to upgrade gear, but it would be nice if crafting went furhter IMO.
The enemies are varied for the most part, and stronger reskins tend to come with their own attacks and new mechanics, like turning invisible or using magic.
The game has a nice world, and a good number of distinctive dungeons. However, the overworld is fairly sparse in many places and not as large as I'd want it to be.
The game also has a bad habit of becoming too easy if you take your time to explore and level up a lot. If healing items couldn't be used in a menu, I think the game would be more difficult, but it has the same problem that skyrim does in that healing can be done virtually whenever with no penalty beyond the depletion of the item.
The plot isn't great, but its not too important either. Though you only get one save file, which is supposed to make choices more meaningful, but it will bother some players and it can be inconvient to some if you dont' care about the story choices all that much. I didn't mind it too much, but it will be a bugbear for some.

If you have played survival early access titles, like Stranded Deep, Long Dark, or The Forest, you will figure out the angles a little faster. I spent less than $10 on this, it is early access, and I am 2 hours in at this time.
In the first 2 hours, if you stick close to the (safer) beach spawning point like I did, you will likely:
- Build your first fire pit, which doubles as a crafting location
- Gather resources (stones, chop trees etc.)
- Learn to create and repair weapons and some clothing
- Fight and kill your first boar or deer
- Build your first house structure, which offers a little protection and warmth
- Begin to starve, which forces you to venture into the interior before you are fully ready
- Die, either by cold, starvation or creature... as you realize too late you need more food
- Respawn, and live again, wiser this time (and better equipped, if you can find and loot your old body)
During all that time, there was a constant feeling of being watched by creatures that lurked further into the island - and a sense that sooner or later survival and wunderlust would force you toward those dangers. If you have played The Long Dark, this game likewise will not let you get comfortable for long.
Crafting is on the whole is satisfying so far (multiple things to make to achieve the same purpose). Artwork, physics, and performance seemed quite good for early access. I have not tried multiplayer, but I assume that will add layers of fun.
At $5 per hour (so far, and that number will go down) easily one of the better purchases I've made. Looking forward to seeing this one develop further.

Savage Lands seems to be one of the new type of breed of games, the early access hell style of games never reaching completion. You lack your music, your content, your story, your smooth difficulty progression, your construction technology progression, your engaging fight sequences and your respect for your players' time. It could have been a passable gaming experience, but right now there's no game to go with this aged game engine. It's mediocre packaging with nothing inside it.
In its current state, you have your huge island map to explore, with the caveat that there is nothing TO explore.
They say there are ruins, there's a small pillar with a bit of a wall in like three places on the map, and there's nothing to do there. There are three tall towers you can use as landmarks for orientating yourself, but you can't do anything with them. There's a unique area in one place of the map that at first seems to have some significancy, but it doesn't. There's just nothing added in the game to make it just that. A game. At the moment, it's more of a walking simulator.
The game wastes your time alot when it comes to just getting yourself around the world. At first I was excited by the prospect of no fast travels, but in a massive barren landscape without mounts, with limited running and no autorun, no map, no music, nothing to explore and with annoying enemies you can't get away from, you're spending a good 90% of the game bored to tears. I can't stress enough how boring the game's traveling is!
You sometimes encounter enemies that can spawn around you, but sometimes you can go literally hours before meeting a second living/undead thing. It's really killing the mood when you're on your own in a vast, dead world for hours and just want SOMETHING, ANYTHING to happen. There are stronger enemies that drop stuff you need for your next tier crafting, but there's no way to know where their unique spawn locations are. combine that with the uneven way spawns work, and you could literally walk past that one spawn location a dozen times and never notice.
Combat is at its most basic form. You run close, hit hit hit until it or you are dead. You can't escape the faster monsters, so it's fight or die. The monster AI is also in its absolute most basic form, where you can easily outmaneuver it by walking behind a stone, a tree or if you encounter more than one enemy, you can run rings around the one you're fighting and completely avoid having to fight more at the same time. Combat with something you shouldn't be able to take down becomes a tedious dance around the closest tree, because you can't get away and you don't want to die and have to spend the next ten minutes running back to your corpse, so you strafe around and hit the monster the 20-30 hits until it keels over, and hope to thegaming gods that you don't get another one of those monster spawns while you're fighting.
You can shoot arrows too, but there's no hit detection other than a big square hitbox. I've fought the biggest monsters in the game and shot and hit the air between their arms and body, between their knees and under their arms, all being counted as hits on the monsters.
You'll also go the whole game building yourself up to fight the biggest baddie, only to find you can't actually fight it when you want to.
The list of recipes in the game is sorely lacking content, firstly in the sense that it's got huge progression holes between tiers of items you can create, and secondly because most of the stuff you can make is obsolete or simply useless from the start of the game.
For instance, you've got achievements to make a couple of buildings, and that's about the only reason to make those buildings. Why make a stone hut when you can make a smaller wood hut more easily? No reason. Why make a hut at all when you can make a blacksmithy that works both as a hut and as your only crafting station? No reason. Same with most of your armors, weapons and tools, completely useless and too expensive material-wise to be worth ever making. After the initial two hours when you're setting up your base to survive and learning everything about the game, you'll hit a lull where you'll need certain materials, and after that point you'll have hours of walking around to look forward to before you stumble upon what you need to make stuff you have no need to make, since there's no more game for you to experience.
All in all I'd recommend you DON'T waste your time with this product, not even if you get it for free. It's no fun, it's not exciting or challenging. It's got nothing in terms of content. It's a dead, empty husk of a product that the company managed to sell as "early access". Abandonware.
Had it been an actual game, with content and/or a story, it'd been a middle-of-the-road survival type game, nothing special but perhaps worth a good ten hours and a 50-75% off purchase. Now, however, it's worth literally less than nothing.
If all you want are fast and easy achievements to boost your stats, if that matters to you, then pick this game up when it's 95% off. You could get everything with a guide and user-made map in like 3 hours.

Pillars of Eternity is, hands-down, the best game in its genre since Baldur's Gate II.
So, yeah. Anyone who ever played any Infinity RPGs for fifty hours straight knows what I'm talking about. Huge, isometric, story-driven games which emphasized immersion in worlds where your choices mattered, your mistakes were painful and the story was engaging. Sure, you had to read giant blocks of text and fight uphill battles that you could lose at the roll of a die, but both of these activities were immensely rewarding in themselves, because the writing was top-notch and the tactics you had to employ against your enemies had to be both creative and abide by Gygax's Tome of Neverending Rules to succeed. This was obviously before they slapped the RPG label to streamlined generic space operas or sandbox Bethesda countryside crawlers with bad writing and worse design.
Pillars of Eternity takes place in Eora, which might seem as a garden variety fantasy world at first, but quickly establishes its own identity as you discover that souls can be seen and interacted with and are considerably more palpable than the metaphysical malarkey you normally use to pick up drunk hippy chicks at pretentious parties. Add the political intrigue of separatist colonies and the invention of gunpowder into the mix and you get a uniquely deep universe in which you will have to use cunning, diplomacy and brute force in equal measure to stand a chance.
While both the classes and mechanics are basically modernisations of the D&D archetypes and rulesets, enough has been built on top of them to improve the overall experience: you have an infinite inventory for junk, craftable food, potions and enchantments provide secondary activities that enrich your arsenal and there's a really clever compromise between streamlined gameplay and the typical Dungeons and Dragons downtime which separates your encounter health pool (called Endurance) from the general health pool (which you can only regenerate by resting). The cherry on top is the stronghold you get to conquer and own fairly early in the game, and investing into its various buildings not only beautifies the initially decrepit keep, but also provides bonuses, NPCs and a recurring supply of gold.
The graphics are gorgeous, giving a painterly feel to the backgrounds and overcoming the technical limitations the Infinity engine had 17 years ago (dynamic water, convincing particle effects and modern resolutions being just the obligatory minimums), while retaining the general feeling gamers had exploring Faerûn. Even the classes and spells are pretty much the same, with occasional renames (presumably to avoid copyright infringement), though their efficiency has been tampered with and itemization is much less restrictive than it used to be.
If what you read appeals to you, then, by all means, buy this game. It's worth every penny and you'll get your money's worth in gametime, guaranteed. If you're like me, which is to say an absolute loser with no future and zero qualifications, you'll probably have the time to run through it within a week, but if you spread your doses responsably enough you'll probably be playing this a few months from now. Regardless of how immersive and brilliant this game will seem three hours in, don't forget to walk your dog, hang out with your friends and bang your girlfriend 'til she smiles.

Pillars of Eternity is essentially a fairly faithful remake of the first Baldur's Gate. The setting and the story are different, but the gameplay and gameflow are almost identical.
+ The Infinity Engine is back!
+ Pillars of Eternity is solid on the technical level, with crisp pretty graphic, good music, solid voicing, a deep D&D-ish RPG system, a reasonable story with good writing, and everything else one's heart desires.
+ There is plenty of content. In particular, there is a massive dungeon completely unrelated to the main game that you can clear at your pleasure. (I beat the game without even entering that dungeon.)
+ The ending cinematic - a pictorial summary of the consequences of your actions in the tradition of Fallout - is extremely satisfying. You get to hear of what happens to the places you visited and to the NPCs who accompanied you.
+ Pillars of Eternity is a labor of love, and that shows in the little details that catch the player's eye once in a while. For example, at one point you search for a guy who's being chased by the law. When you find him, he says he isn't guilty, etc, etc. I gave him a bag of gold and told him to beat it and be a good boy. Some time later, I ran across him in a random inn in a nearby town. Now this is attention to detail!
- Loading times can be frustrating. For me, loading times became longer as the game progressed. Might be due to my playing on a laptop. Toward the end, it took me about a minute to transition between areas. I gave up on questing and just rushed to the end.
- Pillars of Eternity compares favorably to BG1, ID2, and maybe even PT; but it's inferior to BG2. How? The thing is, BG2 just had more of everything. More quests, more classes (with kits and whatever), more and cooler spells, more boss fights, more loot, more quality across the board. BG2 was the pinacle of the Infinity Engine, and one of the 10 best-rated games of all time. Pillars of Eternity is not quite that.
- Many areas feel  bland. They are sort of empty.
- The dungeons tend to feel slightly unrewarding. This is because items in PoE are a bit boring. I acquired many of my best items from the vendors (and enchanting) rather than through questing. And many of my best items looked like: Dagger +5 +to hit +% damage. That's not a fun item. It's useful but not cool.
- The main story's end-game dungeons felt too easy. I beat the last battle on my first attempt, without trying too hard. (Of course, you always have the big dungeon under the Stronghold if you want a challenge.)
- In some instances, the game demands too much reading from the player. I like reading, but if I want to read, I'll lie in bed with a book, or open up a pdf on fullscreen. Reading a long rant sentence by sentence in the little dialogue box the game has is painful.
- One feature the game sorely misses is AI scripting of the kind BGII had. I just want to tell my Priest to spam the same spells in every fight. But I can't. I have to order him to cast every single spell every single time.
* I played Paladin, but the class I liked the most was the Cypher. You get to take a Cypher NPC a few hours into the game; and mine became a beast! The Cypher is also the class that feels the most native to PoE - whereas all other classes have D&D parallels, the Cypher is unique.
* Another class I liked was the Chanter (a.k.a. Bard).
* The Stronghold is all right.
* You get to use your reputation and skills once in a while.
* The next PoE game has the potential to be truly great.
Conclusion: Pillars of Eternity is a welcome ressurection of the old Infinity Engine isometric RPG's, and a great game in its own right. It's not quite Baldur's Gate II, but it does compare favorably to BG1.

I've spent a bit of time in this game exploring all side missions and goofing off with my friend and yes we've had great times on this game but as of now I cannot bring myself to recommend Starbound and here's why :
Pro's:
- Sandbox, you may alter the environment and lay waste to procedurally generated neutral towns as much as you desire
- The tech system eventhough there isn't a whole lot of options in it currently (9 upgrades) adds some great secret areas that can only be traversed with the upgrades
- The randomized challenge portals are a heap of fun and actually are very diverse from platformers, to trap challenges to actual arenas
- Unlocking the markets in the Outpost gives a good sense of progress in a similar way where in Terraria you receive new NPCs
- One of the two vehicles in the game are very fun to play around with (the bike), leap over terrain at will!
Con's :
- Becoming landowner and building a village for rent has the most mundane rewards imaginable. we built a town in a volcanic planet for the higher rewards there and we ended up with incredibly rare and low amounts of pixel payouts and absurd quantities of food, bandages, seeds, ... which didn't seem like much of a reward at all
- Random planet generation isn't all that random with each terrain of planet having a gauranteed type of one civilization and slightly different organised village of said type of civilization (Floran, Apex, ...) you'll want to find a neutral and hostile type of each civilization
- The main storyline quest is repetitive always following the same recipe: Scan 5-10 objects of the next race, then visit that race's capital in a special 5 minute mission. Do this 5 times, congratulations you have completed Starbounds main "story"-line.
- There are other things being omitted from my review for the sake of not listing the entire contents of the game (such as limited armour, weapons, ...)
P.S. If you haven't tried it out yet, Terraria, Craft The World, ... have a LOT more content than this game!

Faeria is simply amazing.
- Easy to learn hard to master.
- A lively community and supporting devs.
- Little to no RNG.
- A real competitive scene.
- No p2w at all, you can get the entire collection with ease compared to other card games.
- A very unique and interactive board provides a very strategic game-play.
- Even has a co-op campaign.
If you like card games, give it a try.

Faeria deviates from the cookie cutter CCG in several respects, most notably including the dynamic Catan-style gameboard onto which your creature cards can be played. This opens up an entirely new dimension of strategy not present in many similar card games - battling for board control and opportunities to subtly outmaneuver your opponents using card effects and positioning. Furthermore, Faeria supplies a refreshing modification to resources used to play cards, in that the resource doesn't disappear after the turn ends, which allows players to stockpile it and unleash huge plays later when the time is right. In other games, not using this resource each and every turn results is wasteful, and makes those games vulnerable to repetitive and forced match mechanics. Finally, Faeria is quite F2P, at least it has for me in the 60 hours I've played and remains enjoyable with excellent multiplayer options including a card drafting mode (great for new players who don't have a huge collection) and a seasonal Ladder mode which is reasonable to climb and doesn't feel like a grind or chore at all. Some downsides: the player base could be bigger, as could the card pool, but the game will likely have new expansions in the near future and this will improve both of those aspects almost immediately.

Comparing to some other free card games, I think this one has a long single player campaign. Which can reward you you with other cards and xp so I strongly recommend this game for people who like the campaign style in card games too.

Singularity is a pretty solid FPS game, though it's not worth its asking price. If you can get it at 75% off, then it is well worth your money.
To me, Singularity feels like a blend of ideas and influences from other FPS games, but it is done very well, and the end product does feel like a game of it's own, and it makes this multiple directions work well.
You play as a US soldier sent to investigate an energy surge on an island off the coast of Russia where secret experiments were performed with the fictional mineral E-99, until a massive explosion destroyed the island in the 50's. Once there, another energy surge sends you to the past, and once you return, you realize that you changed the present and that Russia rules the world. From there on, you try to fix the present by once again changing the past.
The story wants to be complex, but ends up being relatively simple and kind of falls flat, with the twist not really being a twist(and can easily be deduced 5 minutes into the game), which is revealed a moment before the final decision which leads to 3 different endings which all felt rushed and cobbled together, and none felt like a satisfactory end to the story. Still, I did enjoy it most of the time, especially when it hinted at something more intruging that the straightforward route it ended up taking.
Graphically and visually, the game felt a lot like Bioshock to me. It doesn't resemble the environments of Bioshock, but the overall atmosphere of you in a place where something bad happened prior to your arrival and the way it uses environmental storytelling with audio recordings, notes, and movies you can find felt a lot like how I explored Rapture. The HUD is almost a direct copy of Bioshock's, the best way to describe it would be to call it "Bioshock with a slightly different skin". The island design is pretty good, and I enjoyed exploring it for upgrade materials almost just as much as I did in Rapture.
Also the game frequently sends you back in time, so you get to explore the environments both now and in the 50's before the xplosion, similar to the principle used in Prince of Persia Warrior Within.
In terms of gameplay, this is where the game shines, and again, feels a lot like Bioshock, with a pinch of FEAR in the mix. You have a decent arsenal of guns, all of which can be upgraded with tech found on the way. You can also upgrade yourself, gaining increased health and other perks, some of which are very unbalanced and can potential break the game flow.
You can carry two guns at a time, and can pick up weapons and ammo from fallen enemies, as well as change your loadout at predestined locations. Some weapons offer you the ability to slow-down time while you aim, though this does not last long and has to recharge before being used again.
You are also given a TMD(time manipulation device) which grants you a small array of time powers used to solve simple, yet clever puzzles and aid you in combat. You can age your opponents to dust, freeze everything in an area, or create a large energy pulse to knock them back. Also, the TMD has all the capabilites of Half-Life 2's gravity gun, allowing you to throw explosive barrels at enemies or catch their grenades mid-air and return them.
The gunplay feels great, and the powers add enough variety to keep things interesting as you gun down russian soldiers and various mutants, though there were some enemy types which were really annoying, which is the only issue I have with the gameplay.
Overall, the game is relatively short, lasting about 3-5 hours depending on you speed, but very enjoyable experience. I do feel they could have done a little more with the game, especially in terms of the story and it rushed ending, but still, I would recommend buying the game if you can get it at a discount.

I haven't really looked into it, but I assume that they didn't beta test this game. there are a lot of flaws. a LOT of flaws. it had promise but they screwed it up.
First issue:
Capcom doesn't know how to make carrying capacity fun, appearenty. only how to make it realistic. In skyrim, you're able to upgrade your carrying capacity everytime that you upgrade your stamina. in this game, carrying capacity is based off of the weight of the character you made. so if you want carrying capacity that is actually beneficial to you, you have to make a REALLY heavy character, like a giant or something. and nobody wants that (I think). the only other way to get better carrying capacity is to get a certain augment that is specifically for only one of the different types of vocations (classes). so yeah, if you made a small character, you're stuck with 20kg for the rest of the game. you have no idea how many times i've had to pause my game and discard 50% of my things just because both me and my companion are filled to the brim. Things that I want and need might I add.
Second issue:
Stamina. the stamina is absolutely crap. In many other open world games, you can level this kind of thing up. but here you can not. whenever you sprint, you can only sprint for like 15-20 seconds and after you run out of stamina you have to stop and rest for like 3 seconds. it might sound like a small amount but really, in the middle of battle its kind of an issue.
Third issue:
The game is really slow paced. I dont know about you guys, but the thing I like about RPG's is the feeling of improving my skills and leveling up to eventually become a really strong and really unique player. but that sense of progress is non-existant in this game. you can quickly get all the classes (or vocations as they're called) and switch between all of them whenever you want, so the only sense of progress after that is either leveling up (which doesn't give you a sense of progress at all) or getting new gear. and let me tell you, getting new gear is RARE. I mean REALLY RARE. 99.99999% of the time all the gear you get is bought from someone else, you cant find anything really useful outside.
Fourth issue:
throughout the game you get items that say things like "can be used to craft weapons" or stuff like that. but let me tell you, there is NO way to craft weapons. you can only improve them. you can craft things like potions and stuff through combining materials but thats it. No blacksmithing, no woodworking, no nothing.
fifth issue:
Fast travel? more like, uhh, NO travel. the only thing you can do to quickly go from one side of the map to the other is to get consumables (called ferrystones or warpstones or something like that) and I mean there was one time that I found (I say found, it was just in my inventory one day, could have been there from the beginning) a stone that could be used infinitally, but then theres the issue that you cant really fast travel everywhere. there has to either be a special stone monument in the area that you want to travel to, or you have to find an Item and place the monument down yourself.
This game had a lot of promise. a LOT of promise, like you have no idea how amazing this game could have been. but they screwed it up. they should have had a lot of beta testing done, because thats the only way I can think that they actually left such an incomplete piece of trash out onto the market. if its remade and has good reviews, get it. if it isn't, its not worth your time.

There is one major problem with the original Dark Souls: Input Lag. There is a fundimental lack of responsiveness to inputs that, combined with input buffering and high difficulty, can result in a great deal of frustration and deaths that don't always feel fair. However, as the issue lies with input and not the game itself per se (unlike the terrible Dark Souls 2), I would still recommend this game for purchase as you can adjust somewhat to the input issue. If you do adjust, you will find an extremely compelling fantasy adventure buried under these dated graphics.
However, if you're really worried about your ability to play there's nothing wrong with skipping to Dark Souls 3.

Still that's part of the game and you as the player have to overcome the challenges and that's what makes this game so amazing. Dark Souls 1 was my first Souls experience ever, and oh boy did I die a lot. Still I never gave up and now I consider myself a very good PvE player (I suck at pvp)
I recommend this game to everybody who wants a true challenge and is not afraid of dying again and again :3

I've played this game duing early access, played it all the way through, played the nightly builds, played through the game all over again when 1.0 released, and modded the hell out of it to make the expansive universe more expansive. Seeing this game go through the phases of development was a wild ride, from Beta to 1.0. I got emotional when this game went out of early access, seeing a game that you've been watching for years and watching it bloom with it making an appearance to the front page of the Steam Store. Playing it through the end made me feel that as well, knowing that you finished this complete game that didn't normally have an ending. I had a great time with Starbound, with the constant feeling of wonder with every hour I put into the game. From getting lost in the caves and surfaces of the planets, from gathering the materials for getting better gear to progress the story, and from experiencing the main missions. I do wonder if my experience with the game could've been better if I had a better computer, but with that aside, I still enjoyed everything about the game. If you love travelling through space, getting lost in exploring, progressive gameplay, and the other things that make sandbox games fun, I recommend this game to anyone of the sort. But, if you don't like the repetitive tropes to sandbox survival games, I wouldn't, but one review shouldn't affect someone's interest to try it out.

Before I get to my personal view on this game I'll say this
- My experience has been bug free. I know some people have reported bugs and I don't doubt their stories, but I think this is a small minority. All accounts point to this being an extremely polished game.
- This game is tough. Even on easy and normal the combat doesn't hold your hand and you will, at some point, most likely get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked....stick with it, mastering the combat is its own reward.
- Hope you love to read. Like...a lot. I love to read. I love my lore laid on nice and thick and they do that here, right out of the gate. Some of it is voice acted, but a good chunk of the text is not, so it will require you to read. Skipping through is no good, you'll miss a lot and, I think, missng all of that would render the game a rather hollow experience.
- The soundtrack is gorgeous. Part of it was recorded with a live orchestra.
- Best character creation I've ever seen in an RPG...ever. The various back stories you can create are simply awe inspiring, the fact that each piece of your creation tweaks the game in some way is even more incredible.
- Choices, choices, choices. Who doesn't like their RPG to react to their choices? Character tuned narrative, it's here in grand style. This stuff isn't just black and white...good and evil...there are so many situations here with shades of gray, stuff that will make you think before you act. Make sure you act carefully, there are consequences.
This game...such beautiful nostalgia. I honestly never thought I'd be able to play a game like this again, something that truly captured the essence of games like BG and Icewind Dale--the RPG's I grew up on.
Don't get me wrong, the resurgnence of the isometric CRPG has been wonderful in games like Wasteland 2 and Divinity: OS, I love both of those games, but they don't quite capture that old school BG D&D feel, at least for me.
Pillars of Eternity does.
If you grew up on the Black Isle games (BG, Icewind Dale, Fallout, Planetscape: Torment) this will be like coming home. Skyrim and Mass Effect are good fun, but for me, nothing sucks my life away like this sort old school RPG.
If you're new to this genre, there's no better place to start than here. Who knows, you may find a new obsession and find whole new realm of games waiting for you.

I'm not normally a reviewer but I thought I should for others that are on the fence about getting into this game. I'll start by saying I'm a complete newbie to card games similar to Hearthstone but I wanted to get into one, it wasn't an option, so I gave Faeria a go. It's a very easy to pick up and play game and has a unique way of presenting itself as something more like a card/board game. When you first start you're gonna have to do a little grinding for your first battlechests containing cards but at least it gives you a chance to learn how the game plays. There's a lot of single player content and chances for gold to buy a chest now and then with and sometimes you'll get one as a reward but unless you're lucky you're not gonna be getting all the cards you need to put up a fight with more aggressive players. I found the only way you're gonna stand a chance in pvp is when you have a decent deck by buying battle chests. It's a great game and you can play for free but I can't see you getting anywhere far without at least spending a little on it and getting lucky with what you draw. It's certainly not pay2win as there's a lot of stratagy involved with even a good deck but before you got all the cards you want it's gonna be rough because a lot of players go straight into rushing overpowered cards and buffs and if you can't defend yourself from that initial assault and hang on long enough to set up some control or counter it somehow then you already lost just because you were over powered. So all in all it's good game with a lot of ways to play but it's not going to be the most enjoyable game in the world if you aren't buying some chests.

Introduction
After my journey with Hearthstone (which i've gotten to legend and several 12 wins in arena) and Shadowverse (hit "master" which was the preveiously highest rank), I came to faeria as i was wandering on steam, and I immediately invested myself into the game as I realized the game is actaully more skill-driven or say has more potential for players to display their skill than the other OCG i played. Through thorough tactics and planning, each moves (position of creatures, location of lands, land type etc) can matter the game, and in certain matches if you make one single mistake, it can literally cost you the game.
After hitting God ranks and serveral months/patches of playing, I can no longer say I enjoy the game to it's fulliest as I have experienced the "broken" side of the game which has only become a larger problem during my time of playing. Besides the many problems faeria is currently facing, I will address two of them below which I found most relevent to me
Issues:
1. Meta (Expansion release)
Yet, I must say every card games that I played with have this issue (Yu-Gi-Oh, Vanguard, wowtcg, hearthstone, shadowverse, and then faeria), but the devs definetly made it way too far with the newest released expansion: Oversky, although it's been several balance pathces, some of the card in the games are still remained broken, as a result, most players on the ladder (ones that didn't rage quit because of the expansion) are forced to use oversky cards or build very specific decks and can counter the oversky cards.
To go into specific with the issue of the release of expansion/new cards, it's what I call "High-tech abuse", which basically means abusing your opponent with far superior card (High-tech) or a series of cards that can combo/synergize into a massive power play that your opponent will have abosolutely no answer. (If you are reading this comment and have played a lot of card games then I believe you'll have a clear understanding about this.)
The new "swallow" mechanic realeased in oversky fits exactly into the category. When the expansion first came out, "swallow" decks were dominating on ladder, you either have to use extremely aggresive deck to kill these swallow decks before they can even establsih an advantage or play the other decks and watch youself slowly dying from your opponent's power play. In this expansion the devs are pushing too fast to add new game mechanis but they didn't realized the original cards are no match to the new mechanic's power level. (Or as I knew they didn't recognize the problem during the test phase) And swallow is not the only unfixed mechanis that made faeria a "half-broken" game at the moment.
And most unfortunately, the charm point of faeria - thorough tactis and planning, are negated by the overpowered cards (both pre-existing cards and ones from new expansion), sometimes you simply just need to play your hand within a certain sequence to win the game without much consideration, this is what i found most frustrating of the game each time when a new expansion/ new cards are released or when the meta is dominated by certain archetypes
2. Fun deck?
It's hard to define "fun" as card game players have different way to gain enjoyment from playing the game itself, however, I personally like to surprise people with unexpected tactics as to share the "fun" with my opponent. Singularity is a fun little romp about time manipulation and travel on an old WWII Russian island base.  It has overtones of Bioshock (scientific utopianism), Fallout (1955 environments and retro-tech) and a good chunk of Resident Evil (monsters).
The music isn't anything fancy, and there are no subtitles.  The graphics hold up very well for a six year old game.  I did run into a couple of bugs, but nothing bad or a simple reload didn't fix.
The game is labeled as survival horror.  This is not correct.  It's action horror, simply because it is almost impossible to die unless you're just bad at games.  By no stretch of the imagination is the game difficult, as it practically throws medpacks and boxes of ammunition at every available opportunity.
This is, of course, not including the Time Manipulation Device and its various abilities.  With it, an otherwise average corridor shooter is spiced up with some simple time puzzles and incredibly overpowered battle mechanics.  It pretty much breaks the game, but it's enough fun that you don't really mind.
I didn't play any multiplayer.  From what I understand, it was great, but dead seeing as how old it is.
There are reasonably large upgrade systems for both the TMD and your guns.  Unfortunately, there is no NG+, which is kind of a bummer seeing as how there are technically four different endings.  From reading the other ones, I hesitate to call any of the endings "good", with the primary choice being kind of a letdown.  There's room for a sequel, but it'll never happen because Activision liquidated Raven Software as soon as the game was done.
Don't pay more than $15 for it and you won't regret it.

Dear sir/madam. I am writing to return the enclosed 'Time Manipulation Device' I purchased as part of your first-person shoot-them-up 'Singularity'. I had looked forward to using the tool to rend the fabric of spacetime like a cheap hooker's tights, but was confused by the results. When assailed by a spindly mutant, for example, I found my TMD simply caused him to turn red, inflate, run towards me and explode – at some cost to my constitution. How is this related to time manipulation? I fail to see how the mutated gentleman could have been an about-to-explode gentleman at any point preceding our encounter – nor destined to become one after it.
Furthermore, while I see consistently good results using the device to age crates and staircases, it has no effect on doors. I did read your helpful disclaimer that the device could only affect objects infused with Element 99, but this only raises further questions. What benefit did the Soviets imagine the most lethal chemical known to man would bring to the humble stair?
I hope for a refund and that you will rename the device The Certain Things Manipulator to save future customers the same confusion.
Yours faithfully,
Your Future Self Or Something Trippy Like That
In Singularity you're an American captain sent to investigate a remote Soviet outpost. What happens there changes history to put a powerhungry lunatic in charge of the world. His empire is based on the Singularity, a power source derived from dangerous new element E99. Ostensibly, E99 is the explanation for both your time manipulation abilities and the mutants you fight. More honestly, they might as well have called it Unexplainium.
The joke is that this is Raven's first original game in a decade, and it's comprised entirely of parcel tape and borrowed ideas. It's as if they've been collecting tropes to rip off: when they couldn't find a way to fit time travel into a Jedi Knight game, or exploding alien bugs into Wolfenstein, they put them into this. I don't mind the borrowing – more games should learn from what the classics do well – but the unfocused jumble they've ended up with makes a lot of the coolest ideas arbitrary or useless.
The Certain Things Manipulator is a perfect example. It's supposed to age things or renew them, which in most cases means bending spacetime to perform menial maintenance work, such as repairing decrepit staircases. It's used for one good puzzle, where you wedge a collapsed crate in a narrow space and renew it to widen the gap. But rather than build on that puzzle type, they simply repeat it four or five times and never come up with anything else.
Even true time-travel isn't used for anything interesting. I thought for one exciting moment that I had to use a crate to jam a bulkhead door open in the past, so it would remain open when I hopped back to the future. But no. You just have to take the crate itself to 2010 and stand on it to reach a higher ledge.
Then you start using the CTM on enemies, and the jumble of random mechanics you find is almost funny. Some enemies it ages. Some it swells to twice their size. Some it turns into zombies who vomit acid on their friends. And some, as mentioned, simply turn red and explode.
The thing is, turning people into projectile-vomiting zombies is awesome. If the device always did something along those lines, it'd be a fun and inventive cornerstone of combat. Instead, even towards the end of the game, it takes a second to remember which arbitrary effect your CTM will have on the enemy type you're facing.
One idea that's close to working is the stasis field: you can throw out an orb that pauses everything in a generous sphere of influence. It's awkward, thanks to using the same key as your rudimentary gravity gun, but it offers some interesting options. Lacking any long-range weapons, I was about to give up fighting a sniper when I tried firing a freezeball at him. It hit some cover between us, but every shot he fired was caught in the field and held there, while I slipped round it and shotgunned him at close range.
More commonly, it provides breathing room to fuss around with the game's tactics. You can pick up and fling both exploding barrels and freeze canisters that turn enemies rigid and brittle. You can pump bullets into a stasis field and they'll all hit at once when it collapses. And you can manually roll grenades around in a murderous game of Marble Madness. None of these things are quicker or more efficient than shooting people with guns, but stopping everyone with a stasis field gives you time to do them anyway.
You can eventually level-up your abilities, including the size and duration of your stasis field. But 'eventually' is a dangerous word in a seven-hour game. You get enough E99-themed experience points to make customisations, but most of these are locked until you find certain scraps of paper. It's only in the last hour or so that you have any real freedom to upgrade yourself and, shortly after that, you're given infinite energy for your CTM. I'd specialised in maximising that, so all my upgrades were a waste of time. Sulk mode activate.
The other problem with the level-up stuff is that you get a lot of experience points by exploring. This isn't a nice game to explore. Apart from dragging you through some miserably drab takes on Ruined Lab, Anonymous Warehouse and Thing That Might Be A Sewer, it's riddled with invisible barriers. Can you jump on that? NO. Can you get through there? NO. Can you get across- NO.
The scenery isn't helped by a problem where low-detail versions of most surfaces don't get sharper when you get close. It looks like the world's been hosed down with a number of increasingly beige flavours of soup. That the developers missed this hints at something gone badly wrong behind the scenes.
What did happen behind the scenes, surprisingly, is a whole lot of effort, love and intelligence on the multiplayer. A feature that's so often rushed, in a game that clearly has been rushed, yet it's packed with far more ideas than it strictly needed – all done well. It's a class-based humans vs mutants deathmatch, with an objective-based mode to focus the action. So having a random jumble of unrelated abilities actually works here: each human class has only one or two of your singleplayer powers, and each mutant has a radically different way of fighting.
My favourite's the Phase Tick: a tiny insect that can walk on walls and ceilings, explode on people, or jump on a human's face to take them over. At that point you simply become the player you face-hugged, only with lethal friendly fire. Great fun to do, and even oddly fun to fight against: as a human, I respawned once to face my tick-possessed doppelganger – who promptly killed me with my own carefully chosen loadout.
I'm not optimistic that there'll be many people to play against in the long run – there's no server browser, and already the matchmaking is struggling to find me a game. But it's another aspect to Singularity that makes me sad the overall game was bungled. It just needed someone to say, halfway through development, “Good work guys, now pick three or four mechanics that really work, make them consistently useful, design a few more puzzles around them – and cut everything else.”
It would have given them time to do something interesting with time travel, the space to give each ability its own key (currently four keys double up), and scope to make the combat creative and satisfying throughout. What we've got instead is a desperately muddled game that's routinely frustrating to play, but one that copies enough cool stuff to be fun every ten minutes or so. If it drops to a pittance on Steam, it's worth your time.

I haven't really looked into it, but I assume that they didn't beta test this game. there are a lot of flaws. a LOT of flaws. it had promise but they screwed it up.
First issue:
Capcom doesn't know how to make carrying capacity fun, appearenty. only how to make it realistic. In skyrim, you're able to upgrade your carrying capacity everytime that you upgrade your stamina. in this game, carrying capacity is based off of the weight of the character you made. so if you want carrying capacity that is actually beneficial to you, you have to make a REALLY heavy character, like a giant or something. and nobody wants that (I think). the only other way to get better carrying capacity is to get a certain augment that is specifically for only one of the different types of vocations (classes). so yeah, if you made a small character, you're stuck with 20kg for the rest of the game. you have no idea how many times i've had to pause my game and discard 50% of my things just because both me and my companion are filled to the brim. Things that I want and need might I add.
Second issue:
Stamina. the stamina is absolutely crap. In many other open world games, you can level this kind of thing up. but here you can not. whenever you sprint, you can only sprint for like 15-20 seconds and after you run out of stamina you have to stop and rest for like 3 seconds. it might sound like a small amount but really, in the middle of battle its kind of an issue.
Third issue:
The game is really slow paced. I dont know about you guys, but the thing I like about RPG's is the feeling of improving my skills and leveling up to eventually become a really strong and really unique player. but that sense of progress is non-existant in this game. you can quickly get all the classes (or vocations as they're called) and switch between all of them whenever you want, so the only sense of progress after that is either leveling up (which doesn't give you a sense of progress at all) or getting new gear. and let me tell you, getting new gear is RARE. I mean REALLY RARE. 99.99999% of the time all the gear you get is bought from someone else, you cant find anything really useful outside.
Fourth issue:
throughout the game you get items that say things like "can be used to craft weapons" or stuff like that. but let me tell you, there is NO way to craft weapons. you can only improve them. you can craft things like potions and stuff through combining materials but thats it. No blacksmithing, no woodworking, no nothing.
fifth issue:
Fast travel? more like, uhh, NO travel. the only thing you can do to quickly go from one side of the map to the other is to get consumables (called ferrystones or warpstones or something like that) and I mean there was one time that I found (I say found, it was just in my inventory one day, could have been there from the beginning) a stone that could be used infinitally, but then theres the issue that you cant really fast travel everywhere. there has to either be a special stone monument in the area that you want to travel to, or you have to find an Item and place the monument down yourself.
This game had a lot of promise. a LOT of promise, like you have no idea how amazing this game could have been. but they screwed it up. they should have had a lot of beta testing done, because thats the only way I can think that they actually left such an incomplete piece of trash out onto the market. if its remade and has good reviews, get it. if it isn't, its not worth your time.

The dialogues are good and the few people you can speak are very interesting, the music is adequate, so you can get that immersive feel. But that's all.
The side quests are pretty lame, the maps on the side quest are repitive and lame. Generally there is not much room to explore in any map except for the main quest maps. They are talking about how big this planet is or how big this space ship is and you can only run in some linear tubes, where scripted events will trigger and only a hand full of people and aliens are. The Items are pretty lame, there is nearly no crafting. You just play the same mini game over and over to open a chest, loot it all and swap if there is something with a higher level than your current item. And repeat.... boring. Everybody has so much to say, i nearly spend half of the game (maybe more) time hearing people talk, although i even skipped some stuff.
The RPG system is quite lame and not really vital for your progress as the combat system (combat is lame because there are items missing). There are just 4 different gun types and a grenade. Of course you can upgrade them, but it nearly doesn't matter or adds some kind of weapon diversity.
I'm pretty disappointed, but i just paid 2$, so it's okay.

Before playing the game, I was expecting something different than it delivered.

-There is arena, casual and ranked games.
-Game is based on achievment system which grants game currency which is needed to buy better units.

But it's f2p, and the download was 700mb. so I kind of recommend it if you don't have anything better to do.

most of the negative reviews are from people who either got it during the f2p time, before which it was paid as well, or just ragequit after getting killed.
One thing that you need to know is that the game is so much easier when you play with friends as the bandits can be very difficult in groups.
There aren't many people on say, North America, but Russia, for example, would have 8 people on.
There is a form of reward for peaceful players, which is the karma system. If your karma reaches 100, you cant take damage from other players and have a gold nametag. Green nametags are good, red is bad. If your karma reaches 0, you will have a red name and a skull next to it. New players start with 100 karma, so you cant get killed when you start unless you've attacked someone
Players are friendly, but usually interaction is minimal. You can get a ride somewhere pretty easily due to the cars spread out around the map and the players driving them.
Another form of spawn protection would be the many safezones located around the map, marked green in the map. You also spawn in these locations and they are trade posts as well.
One thing to note is that missions are usually very simple and not much fun. They are mainly a stop in a road trip or a way to earn quick experience towards a rank up.
Art is more of a personal preference matter.
This game does have more content than you would expect, even before the full map was released, there was more than enough stuff to do on half the map. For example, there is a maze of rocks which isnt marked on the map. Many lootboxes are found in unexpected places as well.
One thing that would help people playing by themselves, is the explanation of how stealth works in this game. Zombies are very good at detecting you, but are very weak compared to bandits. Bandits however, are basically deaf. They rely on line of sight. Ive gotten into the best protected areas by just walking behind them. The ai also isnt very persistent and will either stop chasing you after it is off of your screen for a while, or after a certain distance from where it was stationed.
Moving on to the tutorial, the most broken part of the game. The tutorial island is separated from the main land and acts as a wilderness survival guide. The problem comes when you stay on the island. Pigs and sheep respawn so that there is always at least one on your screen. Trees also regrow very fast. I have gotten to rank 5 from crafting and killing animals on the island. Not only is it an easy way to grind xp, i came off of that island with 3k gold worth of steak.
Movement lag is purely because of internet lag. On the russia server, it can become noticable at times, but in no way would stop you in your tracks unable to move.
With one exception, i havent seen a single hacker. I went on europe one day to see that the most popular town (A, aka hometown) was coated in metal doors and tesla coils. The person who built that must have needed more than 4k metal for the tesla coils alone. I did try to mess around once with CheatEngine, but of course the items arent stored locally. One interesting bug that you can force is when your camera gets locked onto the middle of the safezone at A. I forced this to happen by increasing the game speeds, but my friends have had this happen regardless. More bugginess is when your inventory doesn't load in, which can be fixed with a simple reconnect, like most problems.

Pillars of Eternity is a brilliant throwback to rpgs like Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale, faithful to it's roots, but at the same time clever and innovative. I love seeing the biography of my hero develop as the story progress, and I love the mechanic that allow me to create hirelings for my party using the character creation tool whenever I need some specialist that I don't happen to have in my party already.
There IS a lot of exposition, but I see that as a plus, not a negative.  My only complaints are minor - the pathing is rather basic, you have to watch out for characters getting stuck on terrain, and they aren't smart enough to rerout on their own. There is also one minor annoyance in battle, where if a character can't repeat the action they just took, they just stop and do nothing, instead of using a default attack on nearest enemy which might seem natural, but that's just not how combat works in this game. Other than that, I find very few problems with the game.

If you miss the 'Old-school' Rpg's eg; Fallout 2, Planescape, Icewind, Baldurs Gate, this is definitley for you.  VERY similar in atmosphere and style to Baldur's Gate 2, VERY enjoyable so far.
Some minor sound 'clicking' issues at the start.  Sorted with simply disabling Tutorial/Combat tips, for now.  Imagine this will be fixed in early patch.
Solid game, great atmosphere, brings back alot of memories.  It's very hard for me to dedicate time to games these days, I tend to get bored or dissatisfied.  This however holds my attention and is truly captivating like only a few others eg; Skyrim, Baldurs gate, Fallout / " 2 / "3 / N Vegas, Icewind dale, and great RPG's.
Brilliant thus far in my personal opinion, already excited at future proscpects, expansion, and content, future releases with same flavour etc.

I first saw a preview of this game a few months before it launched on Xbox Live Arcade.  Got it at launch and immediately loved it.  The two main problems I had with the Xbox version are already solved: resolution and framerate.  The Xbox version was horribly jaggy and it could be really bothersome.  On top of that the framerate could be pretty low and chuggy.
Despite the careful assurances of the devs, this game is already fantastic on the PC.  It runs extremely smoothly and looks great in high res.
As for the game itself, it's a post-zombie apocalypse survival game.  It's open world and has a story/mission progression, but like other open world games it is a nice big zombie filled sandbox.  You can explore, meet other survivors who will have all sorts of interesting random traits.  You build up your base, scavenge for supplies, fortify outposts, and keep your group working together.
Some caveats for this early access version: as the devs warn, it's very beta.  Xbox controller only for the moment, and UI and control is idential to Xbox version. An amazing zombie survival Action-RPG that gets most of the important or even crucial aspects of zombie survival absolutely right and delivers them in a captivating and satisfying way. Those being:
-Building and managing your base (you can change between several different locations ,attract survivors,build stuff,create outposts...)
-scavenging for supplies while avoiding to get overrun by too many zeds or tiring out your characters
-keeping your "crew" in check (essentially the people who live in your base,different personalities which can often clash and require you to take actions...)
-dealing with all sorts of  problems and randomly generated missions and infestations
-Permadeath. (no,this doesn't mean you'll have to restart if one of your survivors dies,stop whining! :3) Wounds may take ages to heal and if your survivors get some,it's because you screwed up. This is essential for zombie survival games and has nothing to do with "roguelike". You can recover from mistakes and find more survivors,but if you screw up too often and charge into too difficult situations you will probably have to restart. This is good. Also,playthroughs won't be the same,because:
-Random generation of all sorts of things: quests,survivors,personalities,locations of loot,loot tables,zombie hordes,infestations...
-Visceral,brutal combat: It's satisfying to smack the brains out of zeds,and that's what you'll be doing. Finishing moves that are absolutely devastating, each blow has a weight to it that can knock zeds around and down and stagger them or blow their bodyparts to pieces (detachable bodyparts similar to Dead Island). you can "combo" up different swings,grapple,kick and shove zeds around and unlock moves like legsweeps.
-RPG elements that don't feel too "magical". You'll improve cardio,weapon skills with different weapon types,leadership skills and so on as you play and unlock moves and "traits" that don't feel out of place. (you won't be getting fireballs and lmgs that don't use up ammo every 3rd shot or something stupid like that,but moves and traits that actually make sense)
-Different breakable,non-respawning vehicles. If you waste too many cars you won't have any more cars. Driving over zeds also feels as satisfying as the melee combat,they can grapple on to your car and will try to get in and eat your brains out,so a car isn't a safezone or tank.
There's so much more that I could talk about here,but what it boils down to is: this is an amazing zombie survival game for a ridiculously low price for the amount of content and quality you'll be getting. If you like zombie survival, get this game. It's good. really good.
