Let's keep it short, no Spoilers no anything:
You like shooter ? Buy it, but on sale, like for 5 bucks it is almost impossible to be disappointed.
For 20 ... well let's say, I played for 8.5 hours and I turned every ♥♥♥♥ing Stone around.
Seriously if you don't mind the short playtime you literally can't go wrong with this.
I'm talking about the gameplay here, the story and the other stuff, we'll it's best if you see for yourself.

Gratuitous Cyrillic is bad, mkay? It can be understandable if you put it in the title for style (though I still grimace at that), but you really shouldn't put it all throughout your game, to the point where you objectives are, "Fiиd Katheяiи aиd escape." Every time, through the entire game. It gets old really, really fast.
Now that that little grievance is out of the way, Singularity is fun. It's an interesting tale of the Butterfly Effect and the instability of time travel. The story itself isn't exactly groundbreaking, and some of the narration-particularly the end sequence, which talks for a minute or so and just sort of ends-is poor, but it gets the job done. You're an American military spec ops dude who goes to a Russian island for something they never really specify, and find the island was an old Soviet research facility for an element called E-99 that has time changing properties.♥♥♥♥♥♥goes wrong real quick and you're sucked into the past, where you change history by accident, and come back to find a world run by a brutal dictator who was formerly one of the researchers on the island, which is now overrun by strange abhuman beasts. Now you gotta fix it. There's a sort of twist at the end, too, and while I didn't really see it coming it wasn't exactly M. Night Shyamalan levels of "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥" Still not a bad story by any means, but you really aren't playing Singularity for a riveting tale.
What you're playing for is the action. In a similar setup to Bioshock's plasmids, you acquire the TMD (Time Manipulation Device), which allows you to age/de-age objects and people as well as do some other neat♥♥♥♥♥♥ like telekinesis. There's really nothing quite like snatching an enemy RPG out of the air and throwing it back at him. You also have guns. You're honestly going to use the guns a lot more, but the TMD is very useful in interacting with the environment. There's a particular puzzle involving age-crushing a box that the developers really, really, really like. The TMD can one-shot human enemies, instantly aging them to mummies, and has various other effects on the time warped monsters throughout. It takes a lot of energy to do those, though, and while you're constantly swimming in ammo for both your guns and TMD, having to reload after every 2 agings when there's a billion dudes around kinda puts a damper on the useability. So you'll be using your guns a lot, which you can find "weapon tech" to upgrade and get larger magazines, faster reloading, and higher damage.
This is where the game makes its biggest mistake. It gives you the Autocannon. It's basically a minigun, and you get it maybe halfway through the game. This isn't a mistake in that it's a bad thing-in fact, quite the opposite. The autocannon is so good I almost only ever used it after getting it. For about half the entire game. It's useful against any enemy, it's high damage, high rate of fire, and the ammo is plenty. Towards the end of the game, **Mild Spoilers** you even get a TMD upgrade that eliminates the use of energy, allowing unlimited use of the TMD's aging attacks against the Russian hordes **/end spoilers** I still used the autocannon anyway. It's just that good, and you feel like a Terminator implacably advancing towards the enemy and cutting them down in a hail of gunfire. Especially with damage reduction and max health upgrades, you feel unstoppable.  There's also the Seeker, an E-99 powered gun that lets you control the bullet mid-flight and is probably the coolest gun in any video game ever. Sadly, you don't get to keep it since switching weapons drops it and the ammo only appears in select areas, but it's always fun while it lasts.
Singularity is a good game. The story is feasible enought to provide a backdrop for the action, the gameplay is solid, and autocannon autocannon autocannon. Would recommend.

'Singularity' is an FPS that I would recommend to anyone who likes to have FUN when playing this genre, as it is the second most enjoyable shooter I've played in a long, long while (and I play pretty much all of them - 'Wolfenstein - The New Order' is the only one that's better IMO). That was my opinion at the time of it's release in 2010, and it hasn't changed since.
You know how (whisper it) some of the "classics" like 'Halflife 2' / 'Bioshock' actually have slightly crappy gunplay (despite other great gameplay mechanics), or titles like 'Halo' have great shooting but little in the way of exciting setpieces - wouldn't it be good if there was a game with great shooting, great gameplay mechanics and exciting setpieces?
That's where 'Singularity' comes in - I would say it has it all, but, um, I'd be lying if I said the story was all that....Everything else is superb.
Funky weapons? Check!
Perhaps you'd like a sniper rifle that slows down time, and makes for super satisfyingly gory headshots (the game is an 18 rating for it's violence) - it's a gun nicked from 'Resistance' on the playstation, but that's a moot point for pc owners.
Perhaps you'd like a gun that allows you to steer it's bullets, and also does it in slow mo, so once again the effect is rather brutal as limbs gets separated, and heads explode - nasty!
Maybe you'd prefer a railgun that lets you shoot through walls? Like most of the weapons they aren't totally unique (Red Faction had a gun like this, for example) but rarely has a game had such delightful "toys" all under one roof - or at least a game that doesn't have 'Wolfenstein' in the title......
Then there's the standard weapons - pistol / shotgun / machine gun / heavy machine gun, that are all very satisfying thanks to a slick, hefty feel to them, and the afore mentioned viceral results.
Then 'Singularity' adds in even more - in the form of a device called "The TMD" (time manipulation device) which does the obvious thing of, err, manipulating time.
Would you like a time dilation barrier that stops projectiles and enemies in their tracks? Or to rapidly age enemies, or cover in the environment, into dust? The TMD also has a blast effect that knocks down enemies to provide a bit of breathing room, and can also pick up objects / enemies and launch them.
And, yes! - that is exactly like the gravity gun from Halflife2.....I'm not gonna lie and pretend that 'Singularity' doesn't crib from just about every decent FPS ever made, but it does so with a skillfulness that many games lack. All those weapons and gameplay mechanics are beautifully executed, and the pacing and the feel of the game is flawless.
It has spooky setpieces, blazing gun battles, and tense wave based standoffs - the only FPS staple it doesn't do is onrails vehicle sections, and I don't suppose many fans would miss those bits. The boss battles aren't hugely epic, but are satisfyingly tricky, and there isn't too many throughout - maybe four at most. There's also little puzzle bits, which whilst not especially taxing or varied, are nice enough diversions.
Storywise it's all quite competent, and the voice acting / performances are all well done. But it lacks a little something in that department  to elevate it upto the likes of HL2 / Bioshock / New Order. Overall it's certainly much more fun to play than the various COD's / Battlefield's that have been released over the years. I already played it on Xbox 360, and was just going to have a quick look at the pc version to see how the graphics were - 6 hours later I had to make myself stop playing it!
My previous playthrough clocked up around ten hours on the hardest difficulty, so it's not hugely long to get through - but there's no filler or duff bits, so for me the quality makes it worthwhile. At around £15 (when not on sale) I'd still say it's a bargain, and it looks fairly reasonable too - there's not many graphical options, though I doubt it would tax most modern graphics cards anyway.

I've spent a bit of time in this game exploring all side missions and goofing off with my friend and yes we've had great times on this game but as of now I cannot bring myself to recommend Starbound and here's why :
Pro's:
- Sandbox, you may alter the environment and lay waste to procedurally generated neutral towns as much as you desire
- The tech system eventhough there isn't a whole lot of options in it currently (9 upgrades) adds some great secret areas that can only be traversed with the upgrades
- The randomized challenge portals are a heap of fun and actually are very diverse from platformers, to trap challenges to actual arenas
- Unlocking the markets in the Outpost gives a good sense of progress in a similar way where in Terraria you receive new NPCs
- One of the two vehicles in the game are very fun to play around with (the bike), leap over terrain at will!
Con's :
- Becoming landowner and building a village for rent has the most mundane rewards imaginable. we built a town in a volcanic planet for the higher rewards there and we ended up with incredibly rare and low amounts of pixel payouts and absurd quantities of food, bandages, seeds, ... which didn't seem like much of a reward at all
- Random planet generation isn't all that random with each terrain of planet having a gauranteed type of one civilization and slightly different organised village of said type of civilization (Floran, Apex, ...) you'll want to find a neutral and hostile type of each civilization
- The main storyline quest is repetitive always following the same recipe: Scan 5-10 objects of the next race, then visit that race's capital in a special 5 minute mission. Do this 5 times, congratulations you have completed Starbounds main "story"-line.
- There are other things being omitted from my review for the sake of not listing the entire contents of the game (such as limited armour, weapons, ...)
P.S. If you haven't tried it out yet, Terraria, Craft The World, ... have a LOT more content than this game!

A fun game that's a mix of Hearthstone and a land building game. Set up lands across the playing field to attack your enemy directly or draw cards to use and attack from a distance, while building lands with deserts, mountains, lakes, and forests. Very enjoyable and the free to play aspect is done very well. Great options if you want to pay money but it doesn't feel like it's a necessity. Coins are earned well enough based on leveling up, winning matches against other players, and completing events and quests, which will allow you to purchase card packs fairly easily.

A single and multiplayer CCG where you play cards onto a hexagonal grid. You use 30-card decks with a limit of 3 copies per deck and a starting hand of 3 cards. It starts out as a grid of neutral ocean and you takes turns placing land tiles where you can summon creatures/structures and make your way to their half of the map to attack them directly. Single-player includes missions and puzzles, the Oversky (pay for a harder set of 4+ co-op missions that custom decks are useful in), and World Bosses (very hard missions that require specialized decks), and the regular skirmish vs AI. Multiplayer includes the Oversky (2v1 vs AI co-op), casual/ranked VS games, and Pandora (the main multiplayer mode for me; you play a deck you create from randomly generated cards).
Progression rate is decent enough and you get decent amounts of gold for logging in daily and doing the daily quests/daily Pandora mini-run. It's nice that it lets you reroll rare/legendary cards that you get in the booster packs (chests). It means that you can reroll if you already own too many copies or if you want to try for something else. There is a disenchanting system to fill in your collection if you want to convert cards to dust. However, after 100 hours and 130 levels I'm nowhere near close to owning all the specialized cards needed for a top-tier deck. It was still enough for me to clear all the Oversky islands (with enough retries) and more than half of the World Bosses (with enough retries). To be fair, I do have 500 dust from excess copies to craft cards with (it takes around 80 for most rare cards but hundreds for legendaries) but I was saving for the 'shiny' cards which cost 5-10x as much). And I've never disenchanted anything because I like the option to play many different kinds of decks (which is useful in single-player missions).
Like all CCGs, RNG is a pretty big factor. In an extreme example, if they rush you down and you don't draw any answers so you lose by turn 5, that's too bad. On a less extreme example, if you spent a lot of mana and cards pumping up something for the opponent to draw a Frogify (transforms into a 2/2), that's also too bad.
Play long enough and you get 'Amazing!' moments like someone about to lose drawing 2 shards, opening Pandora, and winning that turn (or just afterwards). However, it's two sides of the same coin so there will be just as many moments where you receive the bad end of the deal.
It's worth a try if you like CCGs and are fine spending time in single-player modes. If you don't pay, you're limited to one Pandora mini-run a day (get 3 wins before 2 losses and earn 1/3 of a real Pandora run). I was fine with that because the runs take a good chunk of your time anyway (often over an hour). I haven't played Hearthstone in a while, but this seems like a good enough F2P alternative with better gold gains (via Pandora/daily stuff).

*Note: This is a copy of the review I posted on Wildlife 2*
Okay I'm gonna say it... this game is better than Zoo Tycoon 2
*Immediately changes name and goes into hiding to avoid assassination from the ZT2 mafia*
Before I explain why let me say that I spent countless hours growing up playing ZT complete collection and ZT2 complete collection, and for this comparison I'm referring to Wildlife Park 2 + all expansion packs and DLCs
Things I like better about WP2:
1. Animal designs are so much more realistic than in ZT2, and many are unbelievable adorable because of it (the otters!!!)
2. Animal's needs and behaviors are more realistic (i.e. needing it to be hotter or colder, interacting with the natural parts of their environment for food, water, shelter, and entertainment)
3. More animal and plant species to choose from (including oddities that can only be achieved through breeding and certain species that have color options when you purchase them)
4. Zoo IS NOT set up on a grid system which allows more design options.
5. Environmental challenges such as weather changes and temperature challenges
6. You don't have to make a zoo, ZT2 made you have a zoo entrance and guests would show up and complain no matter what you did. WP2 gives you the option to make a zoo, nature preserve, farm, ranch, animal shelter, or just a natural environment for the animals to exist in.
Things I like better about ZT2:
1. Terraforming controls are much more user friendly in ZT, however those in WP2 are more realistic in terms of how one would actually landscape and form lakes and deep water tanks
2. The sorting system, WP2 has no sorting system for anything and that can be overwhelming before you know where everything is and tedious once you do.
3. Staff didn't need their own individual buildings, nor did they have a limited range
Really in the end it all comes down to what you are looking for in a zoo game. In my case, I wanted realistic animals more than anything and a wide variety of them on top of that. However, if you want a more user friendly, child safe (I've seen multiple posts in the discussion boards from parents who aren't pleased with the realistic mating in WP2) zoo game, then perhaps ZT2 is better for you.

Great game. I played it out in one sitting, which should say enough on its own. Singularity is basically a mix of Wolfenstein and Half-Life with an obvious flavor of Timeshift and some distinct Dead Space aftertastes.
It is a linear game, but it shines and confuses just enough to actually give you the ability to miss things because you wander down the corridor that you think is the 'side room' and it turns out to be the next section which prevents you from heading back. (The save points are killer for us completionists in that way.) The huge amount of world-building, be it through notes and projectors of varying kinds, or even the outright 'experience' as only a time-travel game can.. it all makes for a highly enjoyable and engaging experience.
My biggest complaint is probably the fact that whenever the game tosses you a special weapon with a 'you will need this', you know that you are in for a lot of pain. Not because of the crazy battles, but rather because those special weapons tend to be so damn awkward compared to more conventional stuff that I just keep dying when using them. Having been trained by those moments to love my regular weapons, I ended up specializing in my two favorites and avoided everything else like the plague. (I liked one or two other weapons too, but you can only carry two weapons with you, so why waste time and effort upgrading those other weapons?) Regardless, there is plenty of variety in the terrain allowing most of those weapons to find some times to shine, although actually having the right weapon in the right situation is a rarity outside of those moments where the game literally feeds you the gun in question. Pretty fun game. If you have played any "Tug of War" custom maps from the games that support them, you won't see anything new (except maybe ranked). That doesn't keep this game from being really fun.
+ Amazing graphics (Starcraft 2 Quality)
+ Decently Optimized
+ Quick games
+ Easy to get into
+ Hard to master
+ Somewhat decent balance (Still needs tweaks, but its a beta)
+ Lots of Custimization
+ No method of paying in (So you can't pay to win)
+ Farming caps are decently high (Gives you about 6 hours of play time a day for a week before you stop gaining, then it resets)
Negatives:
- Some strategies take a while to unlock, and are REALLY strong, while matchmaking is decent, you won't always get a good game.
- There is no alert system when a match is found
- Penalties for not accepting a match are severe (3 times in 1 day is a 30 minute matchmaking ban, 2 times is 5 minutes, it must be on a 24 hour timer because I got hit with a 30 minute wait after quitting the game for 6 hours and missing 1 queue. The queue misses weren't all in a row.)

I guess this is one of the games you hate and love at the same time.
The pawn system (traveling in a group of up three other NPCS), the dynamic fights against the bosses and big monsters like cyclops and the level design are just a few things that make this game outstanding in my opinion.
On the other hand the bad save system (no f5 quicksaving), the dull inventory overlay (console adaptation, what to expect) and the lack of actual numbers on the attacks suck quite a bit.
Luckily there are mods out there to help you out at least a little where the game might otherwise tick you off. Increasing your carry weight, adding a hotkey for quicksaving or just reducing the damn glow of almost everything at night are just some examples you might want to consider.

Actually a really solid game, if rather short (story takes about five-six hours).  That said, it's a story mode that is well worth paying, especially if you get it on sale.  Some people say that the "twist ending" is stupid and predictable, but I say, without spoiling anything, that they're not seeing the actual plot twist.  I wish I could say more about the story because it's really good, but praising a story like this without giving it away is almost impossible.
Gameplay is above average, with a variety of enemy types and physics puzzles that, while simple, require actual thought rather than "insert otherwise pointless obvious puzzle solution object A into otherwise pointless item slot B using otherwise pointless magic puzzle solving tool C" like some other games use.  Enemy AI is not brilliant, but for a 2010 game it's not bad by any means, and the different kinds actually require different approaches without resorting to weirdly specific damage resistances to throw you off your game (Looking at you with both middle fingers up, Destiny).  It isn't boring, and the parts that are hard are because they require skill, not because the enemy has five hundred health bars (Seriously, up yours, Destiny).
There are a variety of passive abilities you can get and basic character upgrades, whose utility ranges from "Why did anyone program this into the game" to "Literally might as well be turning on god mode", but all in all they balance out.  You also have several active abilities, most of which are less convenient most of the time than just shooting your enemy, but which can really be useful in a pinch or as part of a clever tactical approach.  They all play into puzzle-solving, as well, so you don't have any abilities that fall into the "weirdly specific puzzle solution" category I mentioned earlier.
The weapons are something of a weak spot, in both a literal and metaphorical sense.  There's a pistol that really wants to be a .44 magnum but has all the impact of a child's BB gun, an assault rifle and semiautomatic shotgun that you'll probably end up sticking with through the entire game because of their plentiful ammo and endless utility, a sniper rifle with a time dilation effect on the scope that makes long-range enemies a joke, a minigun with a totally pitiful magazine size that's essentially a "kill me" sign, and the worst railgun and grenade launcher in the history of gaming.  You can upgrade stats on all of these, but most of the time you won't bother because they'll fall under the heading of either redundant (with full upgrades, the minigun is almost as useful as an un-upgraded shotgun) or not enough to make a difference (I don't care how fast I can reload the railgun, it's still a time-delayed hand grenade that does less damage than my sniper rifle, is less accurate, and has less ammunition, and is generally a pointless waste of inventory space).  With all of that being said, once you accept the Holy Trinity of assault rifle, shotgun, and occasionally sniper, you'll stop thinking about the weapons at all and the lack of variety will not really matter.
All in all, I absolutely recommend Singularity.  It isn't necessarily the greatest game of our time, but it's fun, it's different, and it's a lot more worthy of your time and attention than most of the shooters out there lately.

Better than most CCGs. Living board is unique and adds another element of strategy. Game is generous in allowing players to earn free packs. Good variety of modes.
Only downside is there aren't a ton of cards, so the deckbuilding aspect isn't as strong as other CCGs. I'm a pretty casual player, so I mainly play CCGs to scratch that "collect em all" itch. That said, because there isn't a ton of deck variability, PVP requires a lot of strategic thinking. Since decks are well balanced, it really comes down to how you build your board and how you deploy your units.

Polished game with engaging gameplay and an extremely generous reward system even for F2P players
-The fusion of board-building along more traditional CCG systems adds a new layer of depth
-Coloured-land system is reminiscent of the colour pie in MTG, in both theme and ability to combine colours together
-Meta is quite diverse, even though like in any other game there will be a handful that feel a bit oppressive at times
-The faeria (mana) management and the board-building mechanics are often more important than card management, which makes for a novel experience for anyone who's used to treating pure card advantage as the #1 priority
-Draft mode is super fun with a surprise twist. If you just enjoy the experience of drafting a deck and trying it out, they even give you free daily runs (which can earn you real runs for increased payout)
-The game is extremely generous to F2P players. Daily quests, login bonuses, and level up bonuses. I've gotten 3-4 solid legendaries just for leveling up
-Pack system in general is the one of the most forgiving I've seen as you can reroll the rarest card in the pack if you don't like it
-There are a plenty of budget decks that perform solidly on ladder and by the time you're done with all of the free puzzles, missions, and draft mode plays, you'll likely have enough to start building towards a more expensive deck
-Lots of very good value purchases if you do decide to put money into the game
-A bit infrequent between card releases since team is pretty small
-Balance is sometimes off the mark, though every game has this
-People are nice and community manager Aquablad makes tons of videos on decks and other topics to help people learn new strategies
-The only real issue is that it's relatively small since the marketing budget seems pretty low. Matchmaking and game times are a bit long
-Despite being a relatively small team, the game looks and feels very polished with a unique aesthetic
-Yaks

I know I only have a few hours on record, but I'd like to state that my current review of the game is based on level and current observations, and is bound to change. Currently, as mentioned, the state of the game is in Early Access, which means it has much to change before the official release, hopefully the problems I state here in this review will be rectified by that time.
My first issue is that the English that is used in the game is not well translated, it makes it hard to concieve what units to use, or how to use them effectively, even the voice overs are poorly done when it comes to the language barrier. For example, the game asks if you are losing," Are you sure your commander has an apropriate skill to be here?" Instead of," Are you sure you're good enough to be playing here?". Or so on, and so forth. Honestly, the voice overs aren't that big of an issue, but the unit descriptions are.
Next, is the fact that the servers are clearly not seperated by continent, leading to lag spikes due to the connection to server. This can cause drastic changes in the battle. It may be in Alpha/Beta, but the Devs could at least try to host an American/European server.
The races are poorly balanced, I don't think I saw any of the beast race played once, meaning their either hard to unlock, are unaccesible at the moment (which they're not, I got some in a drop), or are simply terrible. Most users play either the Atlac or Terran factions, both being extremely similar to Starcraft II, basically Protoss and Terran. However, the Terran commander abilities are by far more effective, have large areas of affect, and superior damage to the Atlac. The best thing an Atlac commander can do is petrify an area of soldiers, leading to an extremely dissappointing mass building up.
Many of the units within the races have too low health and damage to be considered, and the stealth units are extremely ineffective at any stage of the game other than the first two sets of rounds, as you can see the units quite clearly, and sensor units are cheap to deploy.  Terran units are exponentially stronger, and cheaper than Atlac units, and are able to kill larger portions of units per capita. Their unit variatians are also stronger, sporting AP crossbowmen that can kill nearly any Atlac unit provided you have 2 or 3 units verus their one, and with the cost it is entirely possible. Terran units are also effective against most of the Atlac unit types, leading to mass slaughters. Bombing runs from the Terran side wipe out an entire opposing force, leading to spam of it to build a mass of troops. Units labeled "Anti-Air" on the terran side also attack ground units with high powered weaponry, leading to mass-slaughter.
Honestly, I can say with certainity, this game has great potential, and it is fun. I will keep playing it, but I don't feel as if I could reccomend this to anybody, as it grows repetetive and borish to play more than 3 games. The same units are spammed, and the spam meta always wins. However, they did nail most of the other features, except for income, as you can't gain more of it, which leads to issues when cheap, and strong units are available.

Been playing for a couple weeks now and love it.  Finally got the last achievement today.  I'm excited to see what additions and changes will come about. Great game!  I love it.
Pros-
It's a big island.  Lot's of space to roam and get lost.
Other than the coastal area, there are easier places to survive and harder places, with no clear lines on the ground to tell you which is which.  So there is always a sense of danger as  you explore that something bigger and badder than you will face you down.  I was pretty confident in my high end gear, strutting around like I owned the island.  Then got taken down by a large pack of wolves, and another time by a pair of bears.
In most cases there are a lack of cheat features that trivialize the intended difficulties.  No map that would instantly make the world smaller if you knew where you were, where you wanted to go and how to get there.  A compass that makes you re-learn how a primitive compass actually works.  No pause feature (at least not one built into the game for that purpose).  No instant health potions.  I appreciate the limited hand holding.
Cons- Which are more like personal suggestions on what might improve the game.  I thoroughly enjoy the game as it is and have 230 hours in the game already.
A limited array of building options with no discernible difference between them other than look and material costs.  And no ability to customize, design your own, or furnish them. It's also difficult to build where you want to build.  So you end up wandering around while turning in circles to find just the right position where it will allow your building.  This means it isn't turned the way you want it or positioned in relation to your other buildings how you want it.
Several of the beasts/monsters have movement limitations that allow you to exploit them and avoid danger (low level skeletons and bears).  Packs of wolves can't always attack all at once.  Some of the wolves get stuck behind the others.  so you can take them on a couple at a time, which is significantly less dangerous.  When it works correctly they surround you and add orifices to your body.
Some of the high end gear doesn't seem to last as long as the cost to maintain them is worth.  So I use a stone axe to chop trees and bushes because the higher end items seem to deplete just as quickly, can't be maintained out in the field without building a forge, and require a large amount materials that are very time consuming to gather.  So what I gained in chopping the tree down in two swings rather than the 8 it takes the stone axe, I more than lose when I have to mine for hours to get the materials I need, and either run to a forge or build one.  The other high end weapons are needed against the higher end monsters (or if you don't want to chase deer down to be able to kill them in one swing) so you are forced to do a lot mine grinding.  And that can get old.  I keep a set of high end gear in my bags while I use the mid grade gear that I can maintain in the field and without large amounts of mine grinding.   I understand the idea of keeping it more realistic by including wear and tear.  And that is needed for the low end beginning gear experience.  But part of achieving the high end gear should be either significantly more durable gear than it is, a drastic decrease in the materials needed to repair, or doing away with upkeep altogether.
No way to lock up your items.  You want to invite people to your world, but you don't want them to have free access to everything you have spent hours gathering.  Let me put a lock on my chest.  And if the world is set to hostile give them the ability to bust it open with some effort.  And in the same vain of thought, let me build defences for my buildings.
All in all, great game!

After doing 5 walkthroughs and reaching over 150 hours with Mass Effect I have to say this is one of the best games I have ever played.
Game mechanics are mediocre at best - the cover system is not the best and managing your inventory could have been much better. But this was released for consoles back in 2007. We have come a long way in this genre since that year so let's just accept these issues as well as the somewhat dated graphics and focus on the story instead.
Well, the story is all about a commander called Shepard who is tasked with capturing Saren who goes rogue and by doing so endangers the lives of many. He is from a race called Turian and is an agent of the notorious group called Spectre.
Along the way Shepard discovers Saren is just a pawn in this game. He continues to uncover who exactly is in the background and the findings are interesting enough to have two more sequels for this game.
The sequel focuses more on the action and the third and final episode tries to combine both. At this point you have probably heard of the controversy in connection with the ending of the trilogy. It is always nice to start with the first where there were no expectations and this is where you meet the Commander and the various races living in the galaxy.
There are tons of side missions and you have your own ship to control to be able to reach the planet you desire. You meet new characters who'll join you as during each mission you control a squad consisting of 3 people.
What makes Mass Effect really great is its depth! How the story unfolds and not just the main story but the story of each and every character important to Shepard's quest. From time to time you get to make decisions and these decisions can seriously affect the storyline.
The personality trait you have is also very important: going with the good choices makes you a paragon in the eyes of your comrades while sticking to the darker side (you see what I did there?) renders you a renegade. A 2nd walkthrough is the minimum just for the sake of seeing what could have happened if you'd gone the other way.
Mass Effect is a great game: Its storyline, music, voice acting (the female Shepard's voice is equally good), characters, art design are all top notch. You didn't like the casualness of the second part and the ending of the trilogy was a letdown for you? Grab the 1st where it all started. But this time, pick a different line in a conversation or a different class for Shepard at the beginning. Or a different background for him. Or simply complete some side missions in a totally different order. One thing is for certain: you'll find something new in your next walkthrough.

Bought this game during a weekend sale and was completely blown away by the gameplay style of this RPG. Usually when I play RPGs, I pay attention to the story as the main measure of how good the game is. Dragon's Dogma started out confusing af. The game starts out with a random tutorial intro, then character creation, then more tutorials, then all of a sudden: "Hey guess what you're the chosen one. All hail you." I was ready to give up within the first 30 min because of how badly the story was introduced. But it was the gameplay style that saved this game for me and makes it one of the best rpg I've played so far. Here's the pros/cons breakdown summary for me:
Pros:
+ Character class system was very well-implemented. The game allows you to switch between 2-3 classes based on how much experience points you earn as you play. Pretty cool to be able to experience the game using different combat styles during one playthrough.
+ Combat is balanced and satisfying. You will feel like a total badass yet can't just dive into battles button smashing. You and your team can still get owned by a simple band of thieves if you don't fight methodically.
+ NPC followers are AMAZING and feel alive. They're aware of the world around them and will adapt attacks/defense tactics during combat to best aid you.
+ Plays smoothly as a PC ported game.
+ Decent storyline but nothing unique.
+ Huge open world that's ridiculously beautiful (on high everything).
+ Plenty of pretty badass-looking armor that's still very lore-friendly.
+ Teaches you to think with your head and not with your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Cons:
- Poor story presentation
- No player conversation choices
- Can't romance your NPC follower T_T
Would definitely recommend. 9/10

An amazing sucessor to the epic story telling of Baldurs Gate and the narrative depth of Planescape Torment. This combines the best elements of tactical dungeon bashing and high fantasy adventure.
The Bioware crown has been lost to Obsidian and Paradox.

-The hand-drawn environments are stunning, gorgeous and filled with details. Additionally, clicking on certain objects or landmarks comes up with well-written descriptions that further give you a sense of place.
-It is a game that involves reading some text. But it's highly interactive - I would think that even some who don't enjoy reading on a regular basis would be hard to deny that it is a very engaging experience.
Character dialogue is found to be further engaging with descriptive texts of what your characters or NPC's are doing, whether they are making facial emotions, gestures, or drawing weapons ready to fight. The writers and developers really wanted to make you feel like you were being pulled into a intense stage drama.  Even the music seems to be scripted to play at certain dialogues creating even deeper atmosphere and mood rather then just looping over randomly.
-Character models are detailed, I've so far found a wide varieties of different looking helmets, armors, cloaks and clothing. You have your standard fantasy buffet of humans, dwarves and elves but Obsidian adds a few unheard of races that not only fit well in the world but are interesting looking to boot.
-And lore, I have to mention this. If you enjoy RPG's like the Elder Scrolls that have a tremendous amount of in-game lore and history to explore through then you will be absolutely giddy at the abundance of information on the fictional world in Pillars of Eternity.  A completely fresh world with it's own history, it is clear before you even leave the character creation screen that Obsidian took great pains to make this world as rich in it's history, maybe even richer, then games like the Elder Scrolls.
You are not only going to be spending your hard earned dollars on a great, fun and entertaining RPG game but also interactive storytelling at its finest.
9 Boos out of 10.

I was looking at the wrong things before. Left here to prove that even idiots like me can change their mind after finding the game I wasn't looking for buried under my stupid complaints.
Updated Review @ 4 hours in
It's not a positive review, and for that I apologize to the Devs. I wanted to like this game, especially after seeing it described as open-world survival Skyrim. That certainly sounded fun...and I guess the base mechanics are there for that description, I just could not personally find any real enjoyment in actually playing the game.
I am NOT saying this is a bad game, I am simply explaining here why I personally did not like it.
You should try it yourself as you may have a completely different experience.
:
4 hours in, half the achvs done (all basic ones), killed a lot of deer, boar, wolves & a Dire Wolf, explored a lot, mined a lot.
:
It's always the graphics that keep me from really enjoying this game. They look so dated to me. Even on the highest settings I just can't feel any love for the way the game looks.
Granted, graphics & art style are very subjective, and as many 8bit games on Steam (& Minecraft) can prove, graphics do not make the game. The art style here is just not one I like. The animations feel strange to me. The overall feel of the game, graphics-wise is not one I personally prefer.
Also SP feels extremely lonely. I could see MP being more enjoyable just for having other people to interact with and break up the tedium.
I know this isn't a voxel game, so no terrain deformation, but mining really annoys me. Mining consists of whacking large rocks while said rock spits out loot. Nothing ever actually changes visually on the rock you are mining. You just eventually stop getting loot spit out at you then move on to a new rock to whack.
:
Combat is fine. Things work as you would expect for every weapon I've tried.
:
The amount of items you can craft is fine, though I find the crafting menu very unintuitive. There is no search function and finding out what you need that decayed pelt for requires leaving the game to do a search. I prefer games that let you stay in game and give you hints about what you can use items for, to let you know what you can eventually make with said pelt, etc, so you know what else to gather.
*Below are my original comments after only 40min in. They were a bit harsh, but I really didn't like what I was seeing then*
1) Graphics are insanely bad. I got my hopes up from the really nice screenshots, & I love survival games, so I took a chance when this went on sale.  First thing I did was try to get the graphics to look just "nice". Anything other than "fabulously craptastic" would suffice. Alas, no luck. There is nothing I can do to make the graphics in this game look anything other than truly terrible. Plus there is some weird wobbly thing going on that is headache inducing. No clue what that's about.
2) Crafting. It's bad Jim. Granted, I didn't spend much time here, but what I did experience was unintuitive. The interface, to me, just did not make sense. Not like in 7 Days, where everything feels natural & easy to figure out. Again, just my opinion based on a limited amount of gameplay.
I may come back to this after some future major updates to see if things have improved any.
Just be aware that although my comments on crafting are strictly my 2cents & not even worth that, my comments on graphics are true. They really really suck (at least imo), especially compared to the shots featured on the store page, which I have never actually seen ingame.

I've only played 27 hours and I find the game to be a handful at first, but playing with others makes it ten times easier. In the 27 hours I've played, I managed to craft the best armor and get the best weapons in the game. It's rather dissapointing to be honest. Food is easily manageable so long as you find a deer or what have you. The cold is easy to manage as well, all you need is wood, stone and flint and voila, campfire. I can see how it would be difficult at first for some, but I found it rather easy, like I said, I have the best of everything in the game after 27 hours. It's a bit boring now, I've killed all the bosses barring Kur, the dragon, and there's just not much to do to be quite honest. The game is worth 50 hours of gameplay max right now if you know what you're doing. There are no quests other than killing the 5 or so skeleton bosses. Combat is rather plain as well, but can be difficult when fighting bears or forest giants or any of the bosses. Other than that, if you're well equipped, you'll mow down everything without losing any health. Resource gathering is easy, but tedious, most of my time playing was spent gathering materials for armor and such. Back to combat, like I said it's rather plain and the attack animations are nothing to right home about. There are no shields and you cannot block whatsoever, the archery isn't all that great and there is only one bow as it stands, no crossbows, spears or the like. You're limited to mostly one handed swords, especially the high end gear; it's all one handed swords. There are a few axes and maces, but the weapon variety could be more varied. Shields and a blocking mechanic would definitely spruce up combat, perhaps. Now that I'm thinking about it, theres so much disparity between being well equipped and not being equipped as such. For example, the savage wolf armor I wear for the most part allows me to take on huge groups of wolves without losing any health, but when I first fought a wolf with just basic clothing and a primitive axe I almost died. Now, I know you want to rewarded for your efforts in getting good gear, but the disparity from fighting one wolf and almost dying early on to easily spanking ten or more without getting hurt is a little much. Overall, the game has a lot of potential just as others have said and as of right now, if you go in alone it will net a player around 50 hours or so of gametime if I were to guess, which isn't half bad. There just needs to be more to do, combat could be made a little more interesting and more difficult when at higher levels of gear, crafting could possibly be a little more difficult as well. Through and through it's a solid game to invest a little time in so far.

I should put a giant BUT on this:
I wouldn't recommend it AS IT IS NOW, but the game has a lot of potential.
Quite simply, there are better games with more stuff for your money.
The concept is cool, and with a bit of time and work this game can be great but currently, once you've got yourself a decent set of gear/food/tools/weapon etc. (which, with good luck - takes no time, but with bad luck - never) - you basically beat the game and will be bored. I mean sure you can go play cat and mouse with the treant, but... why.
Give this another few months or however long it takes to get some real stuff to do and it might be worth truly selling.
EDIT: as per the developer feedback, here is what I was thinking for 'more content':
- there is already a concept for dragon/bosses in the game - expand on that with dungeons, epic loot, etc. The towers can be endgame dungeons perhaps
- Deepen the crafting/gathering system so you're not finding about the ebonsteel recipe an hour in and thinking 'so like I'll never get that at this rate' having just found your first leather.
- mining is silly - maybe use minecraft as a guide for how to color-code and lead the players to find ore. refining is currently a huge PITA, with coal being the limiting factor and no reliable way to get it.
- add random maps? or enlarge the current one. I love the prefab concept and the ruins especially, but having them as more of a dynamic element would be cool (also see point 1).
- dynamic difficulty - as time goes on and you get more powerful, add more powerful enemies (and more of them)
- ranged weapons - include better bow upgrades/versions and arrow varieties for fighting things like the treants
- I love the housing crafting concept - but the actual housing is so ... bleh right now. Like one room? Ugh.
- Treasure hunting, with shovels and everything, maybe with some puzzles too
- a bloody map
those are just the few off the top of my head.

I played this game for many hundreds of hours on PS3. I loved it so much, I figured I would check it out on PC since the framerate difference looks like night and day.
The game is 500000x better on PC with the proper mods. Good lord. First of all, the game can look absolutely stunning with the right ENB configuration. (It takes the bland color palette away and makes it much more lively).
My opinions on the game stays as it's always been. Dragon's Dogma has the best combat of any RPG hands down. Each strike of a sword feels weighty and satisfying, but light enough for you to feel like you can jump around like an acrobat and swing your weapon to your hearts content. The combat is "Free" in that regard. Some of the melee skills are absolutely amazing. Arc of deliverance, a skill for warrior, has you charging up your strike for a few seconds and then you strike down with the power of a colossus. The feeling of one-shotting a Chimera with it is astounding. Another favorite of mine is Dragon's Maw. It is a fighter skill that has you throw out a whirlwind of sword lashes, each with amazing power and knockback capabilities. The great thing about this skill is that you are grounded like a true fighter for the duration. No beast can knock you out of the animation.
Non-melee combat is amazing, too. As for magic - Sorcerers are ungodly powerful, but require mindful positioning due to them being very vulnerable when charging up their spells. These spells are probably the coolest ones I've seen in any game. High/Grand Gicel has got to be on of my favorites. You conjure many spires of ice to thrust into your enemy. Looks very cool.. I one-shot a gorechimera with that bad boy.
Archery vocations are a ton of fun. Ever want to shoot 10 arrows at once with each arrow having an explosive at the end? You can do that. And it's deadly. (It can melt Death itself in a matter of seconds, credits to Karathrax) Ever want to draw your bowstring ALL the way back and unleash an arrow so terrifyingly powerful, it makes a GUNSHOT SOUND? You can do that. The only thing I don't like about bows are that shortbows sound like little nerf toys. No big deal, though. Longbows are where its at.
Now for mounted combat. Oh boy. The bread and butter of this game. If you're reading this review, you probably already know that the coup de grace that this game has against all others is that you can climb on your enemies with the likes of shadow of the colossus - and it is executed beautifully. This feature makes those big boss fights feel epic with an extra bit of grandeur. Most significant enemies have weak spots, and it is a ton of fun to climb them and slash the hell out of whatever weak spot that is. The game has truly set a precedent with this feature that will rival all new RPG's to come out. It's that good.
I adore the pawn system. Many find them to be too chatty, although I disagree. I love having that feeling of my team being there and them telling me useful bits of knowledge or helpful advice for a quest. It really does feel like an organic experience. Most people fail to understand how useful pawns can really be, though. Their inclinations mean a lot, and it determines how efficient they will be to you. That is one thing that can be improved upon; Making pawns more efficient needs to be less shady/confusing. All in all though, I love love love pawns. I also love torturing them by throwing them off cliffs and hearing their spines snap when they hit the ground. They still get up and brush it off every time while still being ever so loyal to their master Arisen. Love you guys <3
Anyways, what can I say? Many of the cons that were made about the game have been solved in this PC release. The eternal ferrystone makes it so traveling isn't so much of a hassle anymore. (I never quite had that problem on PS3 anyways.) Outdated graphics can be EXTENSIVELY improved upon with mods. The lack of being able to have multiple saves can also be remedied on this PC version by following the right online tutorials.
A big gripe about the game that can't quite be changed with mods or anything is that quests are mostly lack luster. I don't necessarily agree with this - most of the main quests are a lot of fun. However, I believe a big part of the game is making your own quest by exploring and discovering new things in the huge game world. The quests are merely there to progress story and introduce you to new places you haven't been to before.
With that being said, I'll conclude my review by saying that this is one of the top games I've ever played and will probably stay that way until they make a sequel. (Come on Capcom, stop with the whole Dragon's Dogma MMO shenanigans)
And remember folks: They're masterworks all, you can't go wrong.

It's God Damn Mass Effect. It's hard not to give this game great praise; it is simply a great game. Ten years from now, when people reminisce about old games they played when they were younger, they will bring up Mass Effect. When people come up with new story-rich sci-fi games, they will compare it to Mass Effect. When players look through their library and stumble on the words "Mass Effect," a short smile comes across their faces.
There are many reasons why Mass Effect is remembered so fondly, most of which surround story-telling and character interaction. However, I'm going to start with the negatives:
Mass Effect, at least the first, does not succeed incredibly well with gameplay. It's hard to call it a tactical TPS/RPG because of how little it actually requires tactics to win. It's not that the game is incredibly easy (the hardest difficulties give you a run for your money), it's just that the tactical options available are too weak to make a difference, relegating the game to more of a third-person shooter with somewhat bland combat options.
The levels you actually fight on are either hallway-esque or open-but-empty. You find cover, shoot what's in front of you, keep going. Dying just means returning to your last save. You'll find yourself trudging through a few of the duller levels.
And you'll trudge because what happens between missions is where the fun really happens. The citadel, your 'hub', is a multi-layered open area where you'll do everything from upgrading gear to negotiating with alien races to engaging in barfights. Your ship, which houses all your crewmates, is free to explore, and your companions always have something new to say. Speaking of your companions, the list of characters is short-but-sweet; any character you decide to favor will talk and act as if they were an integral part of the ongoing story and they will have many things to say throughout the series.
But the part where Mass Effect shines is this: Mass Effect is not simply a game, it is a trilogy. What happens in one game affects the future ones. Mass Effect 2 may be regarded as the 'best game in the series', but it's only great because it built on top of Mass Effect 1. A decision made way back in ME1 might have an effect on ME3. Characters may not stay by you the entire series, but the ones that don't have a tendency to make themselves relevant in other manners.
The plot is interesting and unpredictable, the lore is expansive, the characters are charming, and the 'game' stretches 3 titles for an incredibly thorough adventure. While ME1 is starting to get a bit dated now and its mechanics weren't the best, it is recommended to play the whole series from the beginning, as it will help make ME2 and 3 more impactful. And what an impact it is.
Ah yes, beware the DLC; since ME3 is not available on Steam, but only on Origin, you probably will not be getting it at any kind of discount. ME1 has no significant DLC, and ME2 has only a bit (some of which can be acquired by simply confirming your copy of the game), but ME3 may require going through Origin to get the 'full' experience.
The Mass Effect trilogy will leave you wanting more; that much is sure.

I waited a long time for this game to go on sale and I should have waited longer.  It wants to be Bioshock but fails on so many levels that I've just about given up on it.
The story is decent and has some interesting concepts, but the mechanics are entirely inconsistent.  In the beginning you are given a knife, as you are given in all modern FPS's, but a few hours in the knife is removed and replaced with an Ironman style repulsor hand thing.  Sounds cool, right?  Not if the repulsor has a recharge delay and can only be used 3 times.  WIthin minutes of losing the knife I wanted it back. Really enjoyed this game tonnes of potential, I've listed some points below about it thus far...
SURVIVAL: Its an issue when you start, but if you don't faff about standing on player made houses throwing rocks at each other, its easy to get the hang of, and only really becomes more intense when you start to venture far from your homebase, especially at night. I really hope they add some sort of crop growing system in future, as it'd at least provide a break from slaughtering the islands natural inhabitants for sustenance (Plus seriously its an island = limited supply of game to chew up).
COMBAT: Pretty simple really, like Skyrim, using a bow is satisfying when you get the hang of it. No shields, or parry, so you just have to dodge by stepping backwards etc. I hope it gets a bit more advanced in future as I expect it will, as this would also be a bonus for PvP when/if anyone decides to engage in that sorta stuff.
MOBS/BADGUYS: Like in every game they can get a bit dull a bit quickly, plus, aside from the odd wolf pack, duo of bears, or party of heavily armed skelebobs (who only spawn in certain locations) I wouldn't say the mobs are hard, more a nuisance, that if you let your guard down will hurt you. Though very interesting, and certainly more is planned, I'm hoping that mobs become far more threatening to the player in future. By that I mean, they actively hunt players, and not just spawn in place and randomly patrol about. It'd be awesome if the game would occasionally send a large pack of skeletons, or even new deadlier creatures to haunt/attack player camps. Perhaps even have it so some use stealth to pick players of, whilst others just lay siege to villages. Perhaps other events/happenings where something emerges from outside the island etc at random points, just to keep us on our toes.
ONLINE: Game is best played this way IMO. When persistent servers needs to be added, alongside greater controls for hosts (say prevent players griefing/stealing others buildings or belongings) it would be excellent. When I first hosted my own server it became full pretty rapidly, and people began building their own shacks/houses next to mine to the extent a sizeable village had sprouted up. Coming back to a busy camp with people coming and going was just brilliant! We often traded, brought in goods from other servers etc, and went out to help newbies at night find their way their. Its also why I hope in future bands of mobs will attempt to rush and kill players in their camps, it'd definitly develop a new dynamic survival wise.

Disclaimer: With this game being in Early Access, there's a good chance that a lot of the "cons" I list will actually be rectified.
Mind you, I have done about 9 hours so far into this game, two of which were done with a friend on co-op mode. So far, there have only been a few graphical glitches (i.e. when my friend put on a helmet his head disappeared), and a bug where if you drop something like leather too close to a chest, it will disappear. I have been enjoying this game quite a bit, and expect to spend a lot more time in it over the next few days.  For now, I will list the pros and cons I see so far.
Let's begin with the CONS so people who are skeptical can see these first-hand. (Warning, there are some spoilers here.)
Cons:
1. Not a lot of information provided on how you can actually learn new recipes. It's all based off of what you loot/pick up (which is semi-standard), but small hints would be useful for new players.
2. While the game has a lot of procedural generation/localized generation of mobs, it appears that if you are moving quickly through an area, only the deer-based spawns actually will show up. I've spent over 6 hours in one game, even going so far as to run all night long while dropping fires here and there for warmth, and saw no dire wolves, no dire bears, etc...just deer and random skeletons (none of the elite-ish ones either).
3. The world is HUGE (this will also go into "pro"), so it can be a bit overwhelming and difficult to try to go off and explore and make it back to home before dark. If you don't have a large inventory through bags to help you gather things, while holding materials to make fire pits or lean-tos, and if you don't have a compass, things will be quite rough.
4. No actual stats on armor other than durability. From what I can tell, when you're armored from head to toe, you CANNOT take damage unless your armor dies. This makes the armor differences only really matter in the manner of how much durability it has, as opposed to a combination of durability and resistances. - Edit: 23 August 2015 According to dev comments, this is by design. I don't mind it at all, just something some would see as a "con".
5. Too many "helpful" random spawns. If you run up and down the coastline from your spawn point, you'll find multiple lean-tos and fire pits just begging to be used, and next to them are randomly RESPAWNING goodies. Everything from food and materials, to weapons and crafting tools. There's even a village you can see as you head inland toward the dragon tower, and in that village is a forge, as well as several buildings that will have randomly spawning goodies on the floor. I've even gotten higher-end weapons from these spawns just as I passed through, then came back an hour later to find a bunch of other goodies. Like I said, while it's nice and helpful (to a degree), it also makes the game seem less like a survival game, and more like an easter egg hunt. - Edit: 23 August 2015 According to devs, this is normal for the starting area, and I can confirm that as you go "deeper" into the territory, you get a lot less "help".
6. No floors. Seriously, it's all grass floors. Even in the stone houses. Please add floorboards or have a dirt floor cleared when you place something like a house. Also: It snows indoors! Who knew?
7. If you can make a blacksmithing forge, you don't even need a house. Since there are no beds and no restrictions on how many chests you can drop on the ground (other than size of the blacksmithing forge building) you can stay warm and toasty without even needing to use the torch on the wall.
8. Wood houses and torches just don't work. The heat generation amount is so low that it takes an entire night to warm up if you were below 30 temperature.
9. No furniture/other customizing options or option to set a fire and actually sleep. It's like I'm a super-human who only needs food and warmth, and the rest doesn't bother me unless I take damage. This kind of dovetails into the whole more simplistic level of survival mechanics. I would like to see some other things needed to help stay alive (e.g. drink mechanic, sleep requirement mechanic, etc...).
10. Very little direction other than "stay alive, craft uber-stuff, then try to kill the dragon". More content, random raids on your home by skeleton hoards or wild animals, possibly dynamic NPCs that may pop up and try to ask for help or something would make this game a lot more fun-especially given the before-mentioned limited building options.
Okay, as I said in my disclaimer, there's a good chance this is just because of the nature of Early Access, and there's a good chance a lot of my Cons will be rectified. If that happens, I will edit this review.
Now for the Pros.
Pros:
1. Stable multiplayer hosting and use without needing to set up an actual server instance.
2. Characters can be used on different worlds, even if you had a multiplayer character.
3. Combat is fun!
4. Deer are blind-ish, so you can sneak up and whack-em! (I feel like this is just a stopgap until they get more animals in, but it's fun going all ninja on a stag.)
5. Scenery is quite pretty, if not hyper-detailed. Not bad for an EAccess game!
6. Setting is really cool and you definitely get the sense of "bleakness" that they were going for.
7. Most of the game is fairly intuitive and isn't hyper-complex. While this can detract from the challenge of it, it's still enjoyable.
8. Nighttime is SCARY! Don't go out at night unless you have a weapon with at least 20 damage, and armor on...Bad things come at you at night if you wander out too far!
9. As said in the cons, the world is HUGE! This is fun, but daunting, and without a lot of direction, or being able to carry a lot, many players won't want to travel too far away from base-camp.
10. Lots of choices for crafting of armor/weapons! It's actually really fun to see what happens each time I pick up a new hide, bone, gem, etc... and see what unlocks.
Overall this game is really fun, and if they can address the cons I've listed, this could actually become one of my favorite survival games. It is MUCH less complex and group-heavy than games like RUST and Life is Feudal, without being SO simple as to make you feel like its holding your hand. If they can flesh out the environment more, add better graphics for higher-performance machines, make the AI a bit more dynamic and maybe add some other content to up the challenge, this will be a damn great game!
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
23 August 2015 Edit:
Having played a few more hours, and explored a lot further, I have found the game to be a lot more challenging for survival purposes. It is especially difficult to recover if you've taken your best equipment, bags, etc... out and been...say...stomped to death by a forest guardian. >.<;; Trying to recover from that, especially if you don't have backup sets of gear and weapons at your home base, makes things exceptionally painful.
I would like to list another suggestion/improvement idea. As much as I know there's a LOT more stuff the further inland you go, there's very little actual draw (from what I can tell) to actually get away from the coast and try to venture inland. Other than the possibility of getting an achievement for taking out the Forest Guardian mob, or trying to complete the "They only come at night" Achievement, there's not a lot of draw to go inland unless you're simply curious. Things like puzzles, maps, found journals that spawn missions, etc... would go a long way to helping provide that extra bit of motivation to venture away from the general safety of the coast. IF these things are already in the game, I haven't found them.

Oh my god the references! There's so much nostalgia here for me. I grew up in the period this game is set, so there's so many toys and other junk that I recognize. That aside, this game is, SO FAR, fantastic. If it keeps this level of quality that I've had in the first hour, then it's going to be one of my all-time favourite point/click adventure games.
The music, the visuals, the humor! And the hidden achievements! I just got an achievement for trying to feed the Bubsy poster a pet treat. The result was hilarious.
EDIT: I've just finished ACT 1, which is currently all that's available. Here's my thoughts on my experience:
I'm sure if you only spent your time solving puzzles, you could beat it in about 20 minutes. But that's not what I did. I spent as much time as possible using every object and action on everything else even to the point where I got an achievement for trying to use a pigeon on 30 different objects.
3 hours later, I was very satisfied with the experience, and I will probably play through it again tomorrow to try different object interactions. I hope ACT 2 doesn't take too long to release.
If you're looking for reviews of specific things or whatever, then here you go.
Visuals: Very familiar to Homestuck fans. Some camera errors that don't impede gameplay that I'm sure will be fixed soon.
Audio: The soundtrack is stuck in my head.
UI: The top bar can get in the way of some puzzles, so if you're stuck, maybe try minimizing it while you look around. On the subject, there is no highlight on the interactable objects (aside from your cursor changing when hovering over), which I feel was actually a good choice. When you discover some funny writing by doing something like, as a previous example, feeding a pet treat to a Bubsy poster, it feels all the more special by the knowledge that the game didn't explicitly try to tell you there was stuff you could do with it at all.
Stability: Well, in all the time I played it, it didn't crash. That's something.
Story/Writing: Top quality writing. The story definitely seems to be accessible to people who have never read Homestuck. In fact, I think it will make those people go and start reading it.
If you've got any specific questions, leave a comment on this review. I don't write reviews often so maybe I've missed something you want to know.

A robust action RPG with a wide selection of very different weapons and other customizations to suit a player’s desires, Bastion is the simple story of a kid caught in the middle of an apocalypse that turns the world into small floating pieces, and his quest to scrape together whatever survivors and hope he can find.  The game drips with a fantastical Old West flair (both in visual design and music), tied together with the expertly-voiced dialog of a single old man, who narrates everything from the backstory of the world to the tumble off the cliff the kid just took.  A few flaws do set the game back:  The locked isometric view can be difficult to navigate and perceive, making walking off ledges a common occurrence, and the difficulty of the main game leaves much to be desired (though the “dream” challenges more than make up for it).  Nitpicks aside, the game oozes atmosphere and focus on the “feeling” of the story, rather than the story itself, making for a very interesting and refreshing experience.

Thematically, I don't think that this should've been a Middle Earth game.  The protagonist is seeking revenge, gives in to easy power, and repeatedly dominates his enemies, removing their free will.  None of this is in line with what a hero should be based on Lord of the Rings.
That said, it's a damn fun game.  The orc social structure is interesting and provides many angles of approach when you're deciding where to go and what to do.  The combat is similar to the Arkham games or Hand of Fate, and expertly executed.  The leveling system and unlocked powers are fun and interesting, and really offer new ways to play as you level up.  The powers really do turn you into a superhero by the end, and it reminds me more of Infamous or Saints Row IV, but with the Arkham combat system at its core.  If you're looking for a more grounded experience, this won't be it.  Personally, I thought it was right up my alley, but I'll admit that it's a bit of a niche.
