UPDATE: the devs have finally added some metal walls AND activated durability for the melee weapons. Now it takes something like 10 hatchets to tear down 1 metal wall. No more losing your loot to freshspawns with a common knife... well unless said freshspawn knows how to dupe items, which from player reports seems like there is still a way to exploit. Still can't recommend the game, as all the other issues I mention in the review below are sadly still present. Will keep an eye out for changes and adjust my review appropriatly. There is hope yet :)
I wish I could semi-recommend this game, but unfortunately the score is either recommend or not. So I'll have to go with a not recommended. The deathmatch part of the game where you run around in forests and deserted cities are quite entertaining and feels, and probably is, not far from being realistic. I would rate this part of the game 8.5/10. Also the graphics are pretty sweet, and the rural atmosphere and feeling mixed with the occasional city is spot on. Performance has also improved alot during development, especially considering how nice the graphics are. Graphics in games like Rust, Ark and H1Z1 is not very good in comparison. On the other hand there is a number of gamebreaking issues in Miscreated that ultimately prevents me from enjoying the game the way I like. These issues are primarily to do with basebuilding and vehicle storage in bases; something I only after playing for hundreds of hours finally could experience fully: that's how long it took me to collect all the base plans for bases (I also lost my first character after 200 hours play due to the server I played on suddenly disappearing, so had to begin anew. So there's another gripe: you can never be 100% sure to keep your character progression because the server might close some day, which is out of your hands. I suggest playing on an official i3d server since they seem fairly consistent (first server I lost my character was not an dev run i3d server, but I didn't know this at the time since the game made no mention of it, and still doesn't btw. My current character is on a server called "Official Miscreated -
- UK3 #2018", so pick any server that has that format. Country code and number may vary. afaik these servers are run by the devs, so should be as safe as it can be. Someone please correct me if Im wrong though).
Here are those issues:
- Vehicles suddenly disappearing from base, even if you interact with them every day (according to devs interaction must happen before 48 hours, but too often vehicles just disappears for no reason, even if it the was boxed totally in behind multilayered walls and platform ceilings with zero openings or cracks to shoot or throw pipebombs/molotov into, so that no players could have destroyed them. Sucks extremely to lose your car + contents all worth many hours worth of scavenging to the disappearing bug).
- Fuel and oil missing from vehicles after server restart (incredible that the devs have not fixed this issue, it happens very consistently upon server restart, why is it still happening?!).
- Jerrycans and tires able to be stacked on trucks and busses to easily jump over +6m high walls, this is one of the major gripes I have with the game. Completely unessesary with these items physics such that players can stack them on vehicles and stand on them: there's is no other usage for this other than exploiting to bypass walls.
- Base structures used to being ridiculously easy to tear down (~5 min to destroy a wall with a commonly found hatchet), but no more. Melee weapons now have durability and a new metal wall have been introduced that takes something like 10 hatchets to destroy, so very huge boost to defense right there.
- There's also the odd design decision to only allow two storage boxes, one small and one large and it took AGES for the devs too finally implement. I don't know why they are so much against people gathering tons of ressources... why is that a problem at all? Apparantly large parts of the community are fiercly against more storage, seemling with the reason that it "prevents hoarding". Why is hoarding a problem? If it's a performance issue I could understand it... but come on, we are taking about totally static inventory items. The data storage need to store the info about these items can simply be stored server side and loaded easily and very performance friendly upon opening the box. The engine should be able to support almost unlimited item storage with basically no performance issues, and if it isn't, well it's a sad engine then :/ There's no reason really to stubbornly limit the storage like that.
- Most of these gamebreaking issues have been around for years and years without ever getting fixed. And I didn't even mention the floating bases! Mostly because I can appreciate the fact that implementing some sort of physics for structures is a tremendously hard task to solve, I wouldn't let that issue detract from the score unless the issue persists into the completed release version. To be fair there is also a good thing to say about basebuilding: Miscreated allows the use of up to 250 small individual baseparts to be rotated around the vertical plane (y-axis) and placed with no snapping. This really allows for a very wide array of different and unique bases. While this can allow for better base defenses for creative players (not indcluding the floaters or impossible to reach types) the other issues I mention with basebuilding unfortunately cancels out way too much of the advantages to the freedom of creative building design. The lack of any form of terrain alteration also creates a number of build issues unless you strictly build on flat terrain (again not including floater bases, and I also I wont let lack of terrain alteration detract from my verdict as it would most likely require huge rewrite of the game engine which is unrealistic to expect for what the devs set out to do; although it would most certainly be absolutely fantastic to have it included. a better solution could be implementing foundations like the ones used in Fallout 4, that'd be a really good idea imo. So why haven't they made some foundations already? why does it take years and years without end in sight to implement solutions for these very crucial core issues? it boggles the mind.).
So bottom line:
If you like a continuous deathmatch without end playing soldier with realistic weaponry and damage models, and darker nights, especially inside buildings and forests making it possible to really play hide and seek: go buy it already, this part of the game is pretty fun and unique, albeit not worth the 20$/20euro asking price.... I'd say 50% off would be more reasonable. If you value the basebuilding/management this part is unfortunately severely lacking as evident of the issue list I made in my review.

Mass Effect games are always fun to talk about, never sure if I love or hate them more.
The 1st game in the series undoubtedly plays most like an RPG of the 3 games, though even then, it would stand as a rather odd RPG when compared to others.
For those that have played BioWare's best work: Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic, you'll notice some similar sub-stories, characters, and styles. I mention this only because the influence is strongest in the 1st game, when the series hasn't really defined itself completely.
Anyways, it stands as the black sheep of the trilogy for its odd mix of RPG and 3rd person shooter mechanics. It does, however, possess strengths the others lack. The Lovecraftian horror influence is pretty clear in some of the side quests that take you to remote planets -- the fear of the unknown, the ominous music all play into this.
The vehicular sections on the remote planets are a bit clunky, but they do a good job of establishing mystery -- you don't know quite what you're going to find. This works well in both reinforcing the trilogy's whole narrative and the general style the narrative embodies: the unknown, powerful threat, the dirty/dark sci-fi.
Of course, one has to forgive the incessantly repeated interiors and textures for the side quests, this game lacks polish. If one can get past it, one will find a series of stories that help add to and fill in Mass Effect's universe, even setting things up for the sequels well.
If one does everything, the game will take roughly 45-50 hours. If one moves through the narrative alone, you can complete it in 10-15 hours.
The main story narrative has the strongest KOTOR infuence. KOTOR was a campaign across a series of planets, not an entire galaxy. Mass Effect too, is composed of fairly long missions on a small handful of planets -- each a sort of individual story that connects to the larger narrative. Or there's the fact that in both KOTOR and ME1, the player follows the antagonist, or rather retraces their steps, to discover their motivations and goals, across different planets.
This is contrasted, then, with Mass Effect 2 and 3, where the meat of the games is composed of much more compact and exposition heavy missions with a lot of tight, polished shooting across many locations.
The shooting mechanics seem to, in principle, be based on what many call a Gears of War or GTAIV cover based system. Player pops in and out of cover. However, it's pretty clunky, the player doesn't stick too well to cover and cannot navigate it very well.
Add in the fact that weapons, armor, and upgrades are doled out in a traditional RPG manner, with damage stats being compared, unique drops, the skill point based system of character leveling. and a huge inventory to sort through, and one will begin to notice that things seem out of place.
It is not so much that these elements are bad in and of themselves, but more that they don't belong together. As if the developers were unsure of what kind of game they wanted Mass Effect to be.
After several replays, I've come to realize that they don't do a very good job of leading up to what is supposed to be the central twist of the narrative, the big reveal about the focus of the whole trilogy, the thing to make the games all connect. Avoiding spoilers, I mean the event with the 'virtual intelligence' on Virmire late in the game.
Anyone replaying will notice that the game will go so far as to basically tell, through other characters, the player directly what the narrative reveals later in a manner obviously meant to be climactic. It is again, odd, unpolished, and atypical of BioWare, much like the entirety of the game.
**SPOILERS AHEAD**
Besides feeling out of place and sometimes unpolished, the game has a lot of content, has mechanics that work even if feeling awkward, and manages to present an engaging narrative -- I still get rather excited when Joker commands the fleet upon Sovereign in one of the final scenes. Mass Effect's cinematic presentation is fantastic and never fails to make me feel invested in the story.
(If, again, one can forgive some of the cliches like checking the body of the villain to make sure he's dead only to discover him alive or thinking the hero is dead only to have him reemerge triumphantly. I think it is possible to view these little storytelling sins sympathetically, cute little mistakes of young Mass Effect)
I spent around 150 hours (100 on my Steam copy) on this game over several playthroughs. As I said at the beginning, I have a lot of issues with the series and it definitely isn't perfect. I can't deny though, that they do some things so well, and are so unique that they are games we can conclude are worth playing, worth discussing, worth evaluating.
Despite the game's flaws, odd qualities, and weird inability to define itself, I have to recommend it for all it does well, for starting a great trilogy and for leading into the best game of the series: Mass Effect 2.
Controls aren't the greatest, but it's one of the best games I've ever played.

Singularity is a pretty fun little game. But the biggest flaw that the game has is that is REALLY REALLY easy, even on hard.  I mean your character starts cartoonishly overpowered. I never once felt in danger of dieing in straightforward gunplay / monster combat. Ammos and full healths in  abundance in every room (both stackable and on the spot full health pickups). Enemies are predictable and weak, but boy there sure are a lot of them. Even the boss monsters die really easily under the thrall the extreme powers weild ( and you're given really early in the game too).
Powers like a indestructible bullet Shield, a melee weapon that literally blows the limbs off of people and send them flying 20 yards back  (fun a hell to use and never gets old by the way)  and the guns that you are so very powerful and accurate so it doesn't take long to feel like an unstoppable one man army. I almost feel bad for the guys that are in your way because they have ZERO chance of killing you unless it's some kind of cheesy scripted jump-scare moment (there are a few of them along the way) where a monster leaps out.
One thing that's kind of cool about Singularity is that it's just plain fun game. It does not require a whole lot of thought to play it you just turn it on: Let Yourself have, fun and basically when you're done playing you turn it right off and you're on to other things in your life. There's no level system there's no crafting there's no super huge skill tree that you need to be worried about hitting the finer points of so your guy can be sweet enough to beat a particular boss and or pack of enemies.  For some people that might sound like a real big turn-off; but for me I actually enjoy a good pure no BS first person shooter.
This review is being written in spring 2016 and just so you know the online portion of the game is a ghost town. So you're basically buying it for the single-player only.
In the final review I give it a nice solid B minus (83/100),  Good but not great. Nice graphics and shoud, lots of fun and cool weapons, and powers, some neat enemies, in the challenge department the game is flat as hell, but at the end of the day is a solid, well-made, and enjoyable game.
If you just casual gamer or a novice first person shooter (some one without any hardcore MP triger time) or a fan of games like bio-shot and there ilk, the you'll want to pick this one up and.
Start to finish the game will take you about 12 to 15 hours to complete, if you're slow and steady in your progression. I would suggest buying it on sale during the next winter or summer sale when it’s marked down 50 percent or more.

What was one of my most anticipated games of all time many years ago. When the early access beta released back in 2013, I finally got a chance to play the hell out of this game. Obviously, the game didn't have a lot to stand on in that state, but was still reasonably polished and had a functional progression system, with long hours to be spent getting to high tiers.
Somehow much of the game's content that was present back then was simply cut from the game. Even closer to the game's release, there was far more content. Weapons are a joke now, very little randomisation from the procedural generation, no procedurally generated armors, racial armor bonuses were oddly never implemented (in fact much of the racial exclusive stuff was simply removed. why?), biome generation is, incredibly, rather stale and similar, all the cool movement techs and mechs were removed, and to hit the final nail on the coffin, the main story was awfully implemented.
Let me tell you, the 150+ hours that I have on this game are very misleading. Around 140 of those hours were spent in the early access versions of the game. I spent probably around 20 hours with version 1.0, and within 10 of those hours I had the best armor and weapons for my specialization (melee/tank), and almost 5 hours later, I had the best sword in the game, as well as two pistols that were boss drops that are highly overpowered when coupled with a staff that can place an energy field (otherwise every gun in this game is pitiful because of the energy consumption). The rest of my time I spent just standing around on planets because this game has the redeeming quality of being absolutely gorgeous.
tl;dr I can't recommend it, because so much of the old content has been stripped, and it feels hallow and bare. Only mods and future content patches will save this game really. If you never touched the beta, you might enjoy it.

This was probably one of the best $15 dollar gaming investments I have ever made. I have played through every major installment of its beta testing and have completed the released game. The starting storyline and added polish makes the released game fresh and appealing even to those that have played earlier versions. The central technology initially awarded to the player, if you consider its full span of upgraded uses and symbolic nature for a sandbox game, rivals a Jedi's lightsaber for awesome utility. The player(s) have a near complete freedom to go (or attempt to go) where they please. Understandably, early characters struggle against difficult terrain and the player may occasionally die to inadequate preparations before more lengthy exploration and gathering efforts. It should be noted there is a casual mode but I played on survival (which introduced hunger and a real reason to farm - or at least hunt).
A multiplayer dedicated server is the same world as the server host's single player universe. The player's ship is actually part of the character profile, so whatever modifications you do to your ship are taken with you from server to server - or single player to multiplayer. Additional players do not increase the difficulty of boss fights, but may generate more overall monsters on a planet as they spawn near players (assuming the players are spread across the planet - which by the way, there are unfathomable numbers of planets). Each planet ranges in size and gravity, with variances in weather. More difficult planets require special enviromental pack items (which can be hidden by other items), but you CAN go their without the environmental packs if you really want to (you'd live for a couple seconds at least lol).
In the released version, doing NPC quests will lead to them asking to join your crew. You may have up to 2 NPC crewmen with you at a time. They teleport as necessary and respawn at no penalty (other than you need to go back to your ship to get them again). If they are getting in your way, you simply tell them to stay on the ship or stay where they are (and they will mill around the local area). NPCs can be found across the universe or summoned with player purchasable spawners.
You don't need to upgrade your ship to its full size or build a super town to beat the game, but you WILL want some place to store your loot and a handful of crewmen are nice to have around to keep monsters off your back while you are busy trying to get that hard to reach ore.
Other observations...
- Rope initially seems less useful than in Terraria but it is much more fun to use.
- Weapon type variety keeps most items useful (line of fire geometry differences, dps, range, effects).
Even lower tier weapons are useful because you can shoot them for longer periods of time when your armor (and corresponding energy capacity goes up).
- The 2-person hovercar is cool but can't really handle non-starter planet terrain that well. There is that Explorer vehicle mod though... ^^
- The cooldown time when switching weapons or recharging guns is painfully slow and frequent. You will have to hop around once or twice waiting to fire the gun salvo again or swing the sword you just switched to. This forces good timing and slightly better split-second planning in combat, but it does admittedly make combat feel slower than it should be.
- Released Starbound (non-modded) block variety is super impressive and amazing structures can be made. The look and design can easily surpass unmodded Terraria and Minecraft. Terraria boss fights seem more epic but Starbound boss fights are more meaningful.
- Oh, based on certain bits of content that was occasionally available in beta, leads me to believe more content may come in the next few months.

Castaway : The game!
Yes, thats right! This game is very similar to the film Castaway (with Tom hanks), a bad thing? Not at all, the game is actually pretty good.
The story -
Well, like any survival game, there is no story to it apart from 'DON'T DIE'. This game is in the same topic of as, but of course with a different area.
You are left to defend yourself on basically sea and little islands spreaded around a HUGE sandbox, collecting and crafting items along the game.
When time passes, I feel that it was slightly getting boring! The only reason I say this is due to I've done nearly everything within the same at this moment in time.
The Performance -
The game runs really well on a AMD chip and GTX 600 series, 60fps without any drop. I feel that the distance render lacks highly, for example; You build a house / shelter, make a fire and you just haven't got enough crafting items to build another shelter or whatever, so you go on your travels to another island to find these items. When trying to head out to your main island, you will not be able to see your house, nor fire! There are several islands to choose from and a slight turn will tae your off course.
Items and crafting -
Crafting with items is a must have in these kind of games, but making them work well is another thing. Stranded Deep makes crafting easy, even knowing what items to get is very simple. I know its in alpha and all but at the moment, the crafting is limited and rather boring at times when done it several times.
Little annoying twerks to the game -
Yes, there are annoying things about this game which does affect how I feel about the game, here is a list on what I've found annoying -
Rendering at distance (as descriped above)
Distance to one island to another is not correct (you will know when you head over to another island)
Island to island is far (isn't a bad thing) but maybe a auto swim / raft as my finger and eyes get tired of doing nothing
Storage for items is way to low - The maximum capicity you can have is 8 slots, maybe a craft of back packs? or maybe even find them?
Maybe an indication of where you've been or something to add - Maybe a map which you can add your location on or something.
Bigger islands please! Small islands are great but they are samey.
So, would I recommend this game?
Yes!
Its a brilliant game, can't wait for the updates and hope the game grows to something big!

This game definitely lives up to it's name, in that is both Savage, and has tons of Land.
In all seriousness, this is a fun game, if you aren't looking for a cake walk. You will fight for everything. You will die. Repeatedly. Then you will crawl across the stretching miles, buck naked, to pillage your own corpse. You will be savaged repeatedly by packs of wolves, bull dozed by bears, harassed by skeletons and be frustrated as a deer flips you the bird and disappears into a bush.
You will spend AGES bashing rocks with your tools, breaking them repeatedly. Every swing hoping to get a decent gem drop. And when you do, you'll rejoice, for you earned it.
Then, through the blood, sweat, and tears, you will find yourself at the top, looking down.
Don't buy this expecting a huge in depth crafting system.
Don't buy this expecting a quick victory.
Don't buy this expecting the world handed to you. You're just a piece of meat in this world.
Do buy this expecting to get lost in the wilderness, praying you don't starve to death, or freeze to death, or get mauled to death.
Do buy this expecting to spend a literal hour trekking across the island. It's that large.
Do buy this expecting a good time.
Or don't buy this. But you'll never git gud.

Dark Souls is like a slow, strategic, punishing, survival horror hack n slash story and multiplayer hybrid game.
For starters, It has engaging enemies and bosses that have interesting design.
Secondly, immersive exploration and great level design as the whole world is cleverly interconnected and the shortcuts are well placed and can surprise you .
To add to that, there is a huge variety of play styles and weapons/magic/miracles to choose from and it's an added bonus that you can not only forge weapons from bosses, but also forge them from tails of certain bosses if you manage to cut their tails off.
Last but not least, the ambiguous lore really adds to the experience as well since it's intriguing not quite knowing the answers but having to imagine yourself what's really going on. You're given fragments of information through item descriptions and and clues through all sorts of details when you're playing. There are barely any cutscenes.
Nevertheless, there are some problems - level design starts to suffer in the second half, one boss sucks so much A S S that you'll question if you want to touch this game ever again (but makes up for having some of the best and most intense at least), and poor framerate at times.
Overall, this is one of my favourite games of all time and I'm glad I got to play this. You'll die a lot and at times question why you're playing a game where you die so much. But trust me, it's worth it. Overcoming the challenges of certain areas and bosses or even discovering things yourself are incredible sensations of joy that Dark Souls emulates so well.

Few things you must do after installing
1. Download and install DSfix
2. Disable Steam Overlay for the game
3. Lock the game at 59.9 fps (at 60 fps and up you get fewer i-frames when rolling)
4. (Optional) Install HD Texture Pack
The game should run normally after this. There are a couple of areas (Blighttown) that are just badly optimized, but my computer isn't that powerful, and I at least 25-30 fps in those areas.
Debugging aside, Dark Souls is an absoulutely amazing game. Rather than telling the story like most are used to, it relies heavily on indirect storytelling such as atmosphere, item descriptions, etc. Of course, the real reason this game is heralded is for is the infamous difficulty. It's true that Dark Souls is one of the hardest games that you will ever play at first. However, after that period of adjustment, you will find the game to be much easier. Don't let it go to your head though. You can and will still die easily on very high levels if you get cocky. All in all, this is a game that is worth every cent, and you will not want to put down your controller after buying it. Yes, the game will feel frustrating and cheap at times, but all hardship in the game can be overcome with skill and the correct strategy.
Buy this game. NOW!

This game feels kind of like Skyrim and Dark Souls child. It is an open world action-RPG that relies most on atmosphere and gameplay.
The atmosphere feels Skyrim's in villages, and like Dark Souls's in the dungeons/caves. If you do not choose to play the easy difficulty, the game can be almost as hard as Dark Souls, but much more forgiving about death and mistakes in general.
The storyline is meh, "you are the chosen one blah blah" you have heard it about a billion times if you play video games on a regular basis.
The atmosphere is awesome,the sound design is great everywhere, the few towns and settlements there is feels quite realistic and lively. Exploring dark dungeons, caves, and Bitterblack Isle with a lamp or a torch as your only source of light, while having to be careful not to get it switched off by water gets you completely sucked into it.
The gameplay is a mix between arcade and reality : You can pull off moves that are sort of like MMORPG skills (like shooting 12 arrows at the same time) but you cannot jump 10 meters high or long, you cannot sprint forever, you die when jumping from too high, you get the point. It may seem weird when described like this, but it is very enjoyable and satisfying.
By the way, you and your companion can switch your classes as much as you want.
Speaking about companions, this game has a companion system that is quite unique. You create a "Pawn" which is basically a servant controlled by the AI. You cannot get rid of this Pawn as long as you dont start a new game, you are linked. What's interesting is, you can hire up to 2 other Pawns, which actually are themselves the unique Pawn of other players, the one that are linked to them. You are free to separate from them anytime to hire others. Other players can hire your unique Pawn as their secondary pawn too, and your Pawn will communicate everything that he learned with other players with you : which way to go during a quest, how to beat a certain monster... I had never seen such a system in a videogame and I must say it is quite awesome.
Well, as a conclusion,I probably forgot to say a lot of things since this game is deeper than it looks, if you are after a RPG with an emphasis on the storyline, this is not for you. If you want good gameplay and immersion though, it is really good, even at full price.

Before i say anything, i just want to point out that this game kicks butt of ALL bigger title RPG's that have been made recently. I cant believe that Obsidian was almost on the verge of shutting its doors, and then they came up with something like Pillars of eternity. In my opinion, the brightest star of RPG industry currently and the best possible tribute anyone could have done for Baldurs gate's, Icewind Dale's etc. PC D&D rpg games.
If baldurs gate's 1/2, icewind dale's 1/2 were you thing back in the days, i can tell you Pillars of eternity just brought the genre back! Beautiful hand made graphics, orchestral music, top notch plot etc. brings me back to the days when games had just the right amount of difficulty and the player wasn't lead from the hand in every turn.
And dont worry, the game isnt stuck to the early years of rpg's. The UI is very well made to the modern standards, as is many other things such as possibility of "hiring" a companion wich is basically creating a filler character in your group by yourself.
The hiring system is a genius idea honestly, as you want to have a full group as soon as possible early on in the game. Later on you can also of course find groupable NPC's that have a personality, opinions and own agenda wich you can choose to proceed if you will.
So now you get to make a group with every other npc character in game, as you can simply fill the empty spots with the hiring system. Smart.
As you play the game a bit further, you get your own stronghold where you can build stuff, switch your companions, get buffs after sleeping there etc. Its a great idea, because you start to get overflowing with money at some point eventually. You need to hire guards wich take weekly payment etc.
Also you can send your overflow hirelings to do your bidding in case you get a writ. Usually a smart move too.
One thing i really loved, was how the inventory was made. Can't tell you how many times i almost lost my nerve (except in bg2 with bag of holding :) when i had inventory full of stuff and no idea where to put all that junk.
So yes...
You can indeed carry as much items as you wish. You have an option to drop stuff to stash whenever you want, and your inventory will never be stuffed of hundreds of "junk" -items, wich btw are worth collecting and selling to vendors as you get back to town.
Also i've found out that all the items you find (mushrooms, jewels etc.) are in fact useful and worth keeping instead of selling. All books, papers etc. include tips if you read them carefully and use your imagination.
If you find jewels and herbs etc. you can use them for enchanting/crafting. I even found vendors selling crowbars, climbing hooks with rope, torches etc. All these items that i found useful eventually. Every now and then you gotta pry some bars aside, climb a wall, or possibly torch something up possibly.
AND yes! You can craft anywhere! You can select the item you want to "enchant" and just do it on the spot without finding a forge and flapping thru useless junk in your inventory for hours. This makes the game much more straightforward (in a good sense) and you dont get stuck at inventory for ages.
Also no grinding is involved for crafting. Theres no skill's or such required from what i've seen, no farming etc. You simply check what enchants, foods, potions you want/can make and just hit craft. Sometimes you can learn a recipe or such, but overall ive found crafting ever so deliciously simple.
Obsidian clearly has realized that spending time in inventory instead of playing has been a fun killer for ages. Theres a lesson to be learned from this for all the big budget RPG -maker's.

To get this out of the way, the PC version of DaS1 is a horrible mess, and if you PCfriends plan on playing it, I strongly recommend you have the patience to fiddle with mods.
If you don't like messing with that sort of stuff, be like me and play on console instead. I hear the NoGaemsStation3 has gotten pretty cheap recently.
But yeah, Dark Souls 1. What about it? It's a pretty good game, well deserving of its status as a modern classic, but some aspects just feel a little wrong.
Gameplay in general is pretty good in my book. Not for everybody, but if you've ever played a game like Monster Hunter and enjoyed it (like me), Dark Souls is right up your alley. It's slow and methodical. However, coming back to it after about 200 hours in DaS3 (on PS4, I sincerely believe that console is the best way to play these games, but hey you do you), DaS1 feels a little too obtuse and clunky at its worst moments, but manages to use its clunkiness to its advantage. Compared to bosses in later installments, a boss fight in DaS1 is more a test of who's the better duelist, instead of trading hits simulator 2k16. A perfect example of this is
, a particularly difficult boss who moves fast and hits hard, but is also pretty squishy. This means that being swift enough to avoid his attacks and punish his retreat means a chance to get a hit in, and if you git gud, it shouldn't take long to defeat him. But let it be known that there's also a fair share of joke bosses. I recently played through this game with a strength build, and bosses (who I have no gripes spoiling because they're
easy) like the Moonlight Butterfly, Pinwheel, and the Iron Golem, are much funner to just spam taunts at and eventually hit for, like, a million damage. Also before moving on, Poise is an amazing mechanic and makes certain enemies a non-threat, so keep that in mind when you're playing.
Lore is pretty fun to piece together, but it's nothing to write home about. Sure, this story about [iconic boss/location] was fun to put together and speculate on, but it really kind of pulled me out of the game for a bit, and the resulting story isn't quite as grand as what fanfiction writers like Vaati make it out to be. Do read item descriptions, though, they actually do help a bit.
Performance is iffy, even on console. You've no doubt heard of Blighttown, a diseased hellhole with soul-crushing death literally oozing out of every crevice. Hell, it's so disgusting that even the framerate blows chunks just from having to deal with it. Every other minute is spent desperately fighting with your fps, and that's not good when swarms of mosquitoes rain down on you all the time. And if you're playing on PC w/o mods, every area feels like 10FPStown. Fun, right?
Lastly, know what you're getting yourself into, y'know? Patience and a keen eye is key, and a short temper is a death sentence for both your character and maybe your easily-broken personal belongings. If you do have the patience to git gud, you're in for one of the most unforgettable experiences modern vidya has to offer. A long game with a head-spinningly large variety of possible equipment combinations, and engaging combat that rarely gets boring. All in all, Dark Souls 1 is a fantastic game, easily a solid 8/10, and your vidya pallete will be all the richer for playing it.

It has one of the best combat systems I've ever played.  Climbing on Griffins, shooting Cyclopses in the eye, Magic as the Heavy artillery. It puts other combat systems to shame. The class system is fantastic.  You're level is independant of your class level and the stats you gain per level are determined by which class you're playing.  This means that you can get the cool class skills without waiting until the end game and you become more specced to play a certain class the more you play it.  You can focus on min-maxing or try out everything and you won't be punished for it. Each class has their own strengths and they all play very differently.  A warrior swings around a big♥♥♥♥♥weapon in slow but strong hits,  a Mage hopes to stay safe long enough to cast a massive spell, a strider moves quickly through battle, taking potshots with his bow and the Hybrid classes get unique skills like the Magic cannon, immolation or dire gouge.
Finally, 90% of the story may be nonsensical and generic but that last 10% is quite good.  Also, the DLC (which comes with the PC version) is very good. The system could've easily taken into account the charge factor for the railgun and decreased the amount of time that it took to charge, for instance, or it could've given the grenade launcher a higher range--different upgrades depending on the weapon, to overcome the respective weapon's weaknesses. Faeria is the first digital card game I've played in a long time. The last time I played a card game was probably over a decade ago on some online Yu-Gi-Oh! simulator. Yeah, it's been a while.
I was looking for a light game to add to my library to play during my "downtimes" while I worked. An "alt-tab" game, so to speak. After I installed Faeria and found that it had windowed mode, I felt that it catered to my need quite nicely.
---------------------------------
The game starts you off with a tutorial and some starter "missions" that gets you acquainted with the game. The initial deck that the game provides you after completing your tutorial missions kinda sucks, but everyone has to start somewhere when it comes to a card game. Oddly, the second deck you receive (a forest deck) soon after is pretty overpowered for the next several dozen missions.
It's not hard to learn how to play Faeria. After about three hours in, you'll get the hang of it and then it turns into what you'd expect: Play missions to farm money to buy more cards or do some other stuff.
---------------------------------
Would I personally recommend this game? It's hard to say. If Steam had a "Not Yet" button for that question, I would choose it. The reason for this uncertainly has to do with a small design flaw of the game itself.
Because the game was designed to be F2P, you have access to pretty much everything in the game without paying a single cent. That's great; it's wonderful to play a game with excellent graphics, smooth gameplay, and no P2W content built in. The only issue with that is: It becomes a massive grind because the devs have to force people to buy premiums if they want to make any money off of the game.
Another "issue" so far is the lack of cards; the game is new and there aren't that many cards released yet so there is a lot of repetition. However, I wouldn't put this against the devs. It's a new game and most cards have their own animations and special effects, so it takes them a lot of time to code them into the game. Maybe as time progresses, there will be a lot more variation.
I would say: If you can help it, start playing a year later when there is significantly more content. At the moment, I still consider it to be "Early Access", if only for the lack of content.
---------------------------------
Most of the "cool" features in the game after you've received the initial freebie offerings cost a ton of money, which takes a long time to farm. You can spend your money on "blue chests" to get more cards, but for new players, these chests pretty much only offer you garbage 80% of the time. You're better off spending the money on unlocking features elsewhere in the game, especially in the new "Oversky" exploration mode.
Because of the poor chest drop rates, I've pretty much given up opening the chests altogether because it's pretty much a waste of time to even click them. I get better cards just playing through missions and getting the rewards from them, and franky, the missions themselves regularly reward you with enough blue chests to warrant not even buying them.
The game has a few neat modes that are quite enjoyable to play and are very promising. They have a great foundation, opening the door for new content that can be added into those modes as time progresses.
---------------------------------
Aside the usual missions, which are basically individual 1v1 matches as well as some puzzles thrown in for you to solve, and the battle mode, which is multiplayer 1v1, there is a boss fight mode and an "Oversky" exploration mode, as well as a mode called "Pandora".
If you don't want to, you don't ever have to play against actual people. This is great for people who have any sort of "competitive anxiety." You can stick to playing against bots forever if you wish. The boi AI is pretty good, although they occasionally make bad decisions when they're near death.
The boss fight mode is a great concept but overly limited. You're only allowed to fight a boss once every five levels (IIRC) if they're not part of a mission pack (a set of missions), and five levels takes a few hours of non-stop farming to get. I wasn't particularly pleased about this.
The Oversky exploration mode isn't really exploration, but a sort of world map system where you fight against individual bosses with either a bot as your ally, or any real friend you choose to invite in (assuming they've played quite a bit and have built a decent deck, which would take new players a relatively long time to do). The ally bot AI is actually surprisingly good. Sometimes so good that they win the matches for you, making you feel like you're just enabling them. I'm not sure how I feel about this; I guess it's cool since it's an easy win.
Lastly, Pandora is basically a mode where you need to form a deck with cards that you pick from randomly generated sets of five cards. After the deck's formed, ou fight against waves of foes (up to nine). It's a somewhat challenging mode that tests your understanding of the game as well as impromptu decision making skills. Of all the modes available, I would say that Pandora is the most enjoyable and has great replay value. It's unfortunate that you only get a sample run once a day and it costs a decent amount of money if you want to play the full length run, though.
---------------------------------
In summary, I would say that Faeria is designed well. It's beautiful, sleek, and has great potential. Feel free to try it out if you're looking for a card game with strategy board game elements, but keep in mind that the game is still in its infancy. You might want to hold off for at least a few more months before trying it out.

Faeria: so much promise, ruined by greed.
Where to begin? How can I have a blue-based hand, that 15 matches in a row, has all 3 of my key card to take out strong enemies -- frogify --at the bottom of the deck, so that I didn't draw it once in any of those matches?
I construct decks based on the assumption of random dispersion. With Faeria, it became an exercise in futility, because the drawing was obviously loaded based on some calculation, relative to cards in the deck, and players in the match.
I'd know it when I'd face another player, I felt their frustatration as I watched the worst possible ordering of their cards cost them the match, cursing the stupid deck drawing non-randomizer  -- because it made my win feel empty and worthless. I didn't have to play well, I needed 0 skill to win, because the opponent couldn't draw anything helpful. I don't know if they suffered round after round, but for my match against them, I was rewarded with a meaningless win.
I stayed playing Faeria for so long, becasue I was really hoping they'd fix whatever it was in their card randomizer, which most of the time, meant 90% of my discards, redrawn as the same card, even if I only had 1 of them in my deck.
With the release of oversky, I can't deny that what they're doing is intentional, and done to encourage people to buy stuff so they can make more money. Ranked play between people, when one side of the match are all new specialty cards, with insane amounts of power relative to the traditional deck, and the oither side has no way to have those cards, is beyond ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
What exactly are you ranking? Players, or how much you're willing to tip the scales for money?
Some call it good business. I call it bait and switch when you're advertising free to play, and it's pay to win.
There are better models, that don't screw your playerbase, or turn your game into a whoring out of nuclear options to tip matches towards paying players, against gamers.   Gamers are players who have no desire for unfair advantage --unfair advantage compromises any claim to skill, which is at the core of gamer ideology and value -- doing your best, and then getting better. Buying your advantage, makes you a non-gamer, more interested in winning than developing skill.
For instance -- Digital Extremes might make mistakes with Warframe and their development of it, but I never felt like I was being cheated because I didn't pay money. Faeria, I can't say the same.
So, no real loss to the company, because I'm not paying, right?
Tell it to digital extremes, as my Warframe playing, has drawn dozens of new players, about 25% of which paid money because they wanted to catch up to where I was at, and money can help you catch up in Warframe... but doesn't create imbalance in the game.
I truly despise companies that pretend like they're free to play, when in fact, they're pay to win. I despite dishonesty being used on players. I appreciate that companies much make money, but they are ways to do that and still allow integrity to be kept.
Not recommended, unless you're a plebe that likes pay to win, because you're self esteem is based on win/lose ratios, rather than the experience of gaming, and getting better, so you're Win/Loss ratio actually means something.

Bastion is a really cool action game with some amazing environments, an excellent soundtrack, and a mysterious, but ever-so-intriguing narrator.
You play as a boy simply known as "The Kid." who lives in the world of Bastion, which had suddenly suffered a catastrophic event only known as "The Calamity." Not much is known about The Kid, at first, but later on in the game, you'll be able to access an area where your backstory can be heard and explained.
In the world of Bastion, during The Calamity, the world started drifting apart, and islands started breaking up.Suddenly, monsters started to attack these various islands, and every single person in the game's world has been turned to stone... or is everyone?
In Bastion, the ground comes up under The Kid's steps, or at least, the land that remains. You must visit these broken-up islands, eliminate the enemies that attack you, and collect shards of power, so that you can provide power to a large structure called "The Bastion," which becomes your player's home base. It also becomes the only safe haven, and the player's space for new buildings that can be built, which allow many different bonuses, utilities, and can provide different challenges.
The game's currency, fragments, can be used to purchase upgrades, make buildings, and improve weapons. Gaining experience also boosts the player's stats and gives them more health. Throughout the game, there are various weapons that you can collect, although you can only have two equipped at a time. You can also equip a special attack, and there are quite a few different types in the game. Enemies drop potions, that, when drunk, can restore some health or give you the special items needed in order for you to use your special attack moves. In order to change your weapons, you must use an arsenal at The Bastion.
The environments in Bastion are very nicely made and quite unique. Each one has a different look and feel to it, as well as different enemies. You'll often find structures and ruins, and places where life suddenly stopped; when The Calamity hit. You will come across many fun and challenging areas, as well as challenges that reward you with EXP and with other items.
Bastion's soundtrack, written by Darren Korb, is stellar. It's very fitting to the game, and very immersive. It's got its own unique style, and it's energetic, Western, and they've got some really catchy beats along with those awesome acoustic and folk-type songs, some of them with a vintage but breakbeat theme.
In the game, you will meet some new characters as well, but I will not spoil anything about them in this review. Their personalities are quite varied, just as the landscapes in Bastion.
I would recommend Bastion to anyone who loves action games with fun combat and with a really cool story! ^.^

Before i say anything, i just want to point out that this game kicks butt of ALL bigger title RPG's that have been made recently. I cant believe that Obsidian was almost on the verge of shutting its doors, and then they came up with something like Pillars of eternity. In my opinion, the brightest star of RPG industry currently and the best possible tribute anyone could have done for Baldurs gate's, Icewind Dale's etc. PC D&D rpg games.
If baldurs gate's 1/2, icewind dale's 1/2 were you thing back in the days, i can tell you Pillars of eternity just brought the genre back! Beautiful hand made graphics, orchestral music, top notch plot etc. brings me back to the days when games had just the right amount of difficulty and the player wasn't lead from the hand in every turn.
And dont worry, the game isnt stuck to the early years of rpg's. The UI is very well made to the modern standards, as is many other things such as possibility of "hiring" a companion wich is basically creating a filler character in your group by yourself.
The hiring system is a genius idea honestly, as you want to have a full group as soon as possible early on in the game. Later on you can also of course find groupable NPC's that have a personality, opinions and own agenda wich you can choose to proceed if you will.
So now you get to make a group with every other npc character in game, as you can simply fill the empty spots with the hiring system. Smart.
As you play the game a bit further, you get your own stronghold where you can build stuff, switch your companions, get buffs after sleeping there etc. Its a great idea, because you start to get overflowing with money at some point eventually. You need to hire guards wich take weekly payment etc.
Also you can send your overflow hirelings to do your bidding in case you get a writ. Usually a smart move too.
One thing i really loved, was how the inventory was made. Can't tell you how many times i almost lost my nerve (except in bg2 with bag of holding :) when i had inventory full of stuff and no idea where to put all that junk.
So yes...
You can indeed carry as much items as you wish. You have an option to drop stuff to stash whenever you want, and your inventory will never be stuffed of hundreds of "junk" -items, wich btw are worth collecting and selling to vendors as you get back to town.
Also i've found out that all the items you find (mushrooms, jewels etc.) are in fact useful and worth keeping instead of selling. All books, papers etc. include tips if you read them carefully and use your imagination.
If you find jewels and herbs etc. you can use them for enchanting/crafting. I even found vendors selling crowbars, climbing hooks with rope, torches etc. All these items that i found useful eventually. Every now and then you gotta pry some bars aside, climb a wall, or possibly torch something up possibly.
AND yes! You can craft anywhere! You can select the item you want to "enchant" and just do it on the spot without finding a forge and flapping thru useless junk in your inventory for hours. This makes the game much more straightforward (in a good sense) and you dont get stuck at inventory for ages.
Also no grinding is involved for crafting. Theres no skill's or such required from what i've seen, no farming etc. You simply check what enchants, foods, potions you want/can make and just hit craft. Sometimes you can learn a recipe or such, but overall ive found crafting ever so deliciously simple.
Obsidian clearly has realized that spending time in inventory instead of playing has been a fun killer for ages. Theres a lesson to be learned from this for all the big budget RPG -maker's.

Singularity had gotten my attention when it first came out, but I had to dismiss it because I lacked the skill to deal with the FPS genre. A few years later, with Borderlands 2 and Mass Effect under my belt, I found the game suggested in my steam queue, and purchased it the next time it went on sale. I was surprised to find that the game had aged well, and was solid.
The meat of the game is in the gameplay. Singularity takes a solid shooter base, and adds interesting time-manipulation mechanics to the combat. Enemies are varied and interesting, and different tactics are required to deal with them. The standard arsenal of pistol, machine gun, shotgun, and sniper rifle are augmented with a few other interesting and appropriately scifi weapons, which you can upgrade.
The setting is an island named Katorga-12, a secret soviet research facility. The levels are well designed, and full of personality. There are lots of notes to read, and audio recordings to give you a look into the history of the island. Little details all over the place create an immersive experience that encourages exploring every nook and cranny. Periodic puzzle sections provide a pleasant change of pace without being too difficult, and "thinking with portals" (as it were) provides access to extra goodies.
That being said, the game, like most FPSs, is extremely linear. Despite the themes of time travel and choice-consequence, you have no real say in how the story plays out, save for the 3-ish choices you have right at the end. This is frustrating, especially as you find messages all over calling your actions into question. I spent the whole game looking for a fork-in-the-road, and there isn't any.
Likes:
- Solid game-play, suitably varied
- Well-built levels that are both lovely to look at and fun to explore.
- Intriguing, timey-wimey lore
Dislikes:
- Linear levels
- Linear Narrative
- Spooky tutorial levels!
- Short length

What was one of my most anticipated games of all time many years ago. When the early access beta released back in 2013, I finally got a chance to play the hell out of this game. Obviously, the game didn't have a lot to stand on in that state, but was still reasonably polished and had a functional progression system, with long hours to be spent getting to high tiers.
Somehow much of the game's content that was present back then was simply cut from the game. Even closer to the game's release, there was far more content. Weapons are a joke now, very little randomisation from the procedural generation, no procedurally generated armors, racial armor bonuses were oddly never implemented (in fact much of the racial exclusive stuff was simply removed. why?), biome generation is, incredibly, rather stale and similar, all the cool movement techs and mechs were removed, and to hit the final nail on the coffin, the main story was awfully implemented.
Let me tell you, the 150+ hours that I have on this game are very misleading. Around 140 of those hours were spent in the early access versions of the game. I spent probably around 20 hours with version 1.0, and within 10 of those hours I had the best armor and weapons for my specialization (melee/tank), and almost 5 hours later, I had the best sword in the game, as well as two pistols that were boss drops that are highly overpowered when coupled with a staff that can place an energy field (otherwise every gun in this game is pitiful because of the energy consumption). The rest of my time I spent just standing around on planets because this game has the redeeming quality of being absolutely gorgeous.
tl;dr I can't recommend it, because so much of the old content has been stripped, and it feels hallow and bare. Only mods and future content patches will save this game really. If you never touched the beta, you might enjoy it.

This was probably one of the best $15 dollar gaming investments I have ever made. I have played through every major installment of its beta testing and have completed the released game. The starting storyline and added polish makes the released game fresh and appealing even to those that have played earlier versions. The central technology initially awarded to the player, if you consider its full span of upgraded uses and symbolic nature for a sandbox game, rivals a Jedi's lightsaber for awesome utility. The player(s) have a near complete freedom to go (or attempt to go) where they please. Understandably, early characters struggle against difficult terrain and the player may occasionally die to inadequate preparations before more lengthy exploration and gathering efforts. It should be noted there is a casual mode but I played on survival (which introduced hunger and a real reason to farm - or at least hunt).
A multiplayer dedicated server is the same world as the server host's single player universe. The player's ship is actually part of the character profile, so whatever modifications you do to your ship are taken with you from server to server - or single player to multiplayer. Additional players do not increase the difficulty of boss fights, but may generate more overall monsters on a planet as they spawn near players (assuming the players are spread across the planet - which by the way, there are unfathomable numbers of planets). Each planet ranges in size and gravity, with variances in weather. More difficult planets require special enviromental pack items (which can be hidden by other items), but you CAN go their without the environmental packs if you really want to (you'd live for a couple seconds at least lol).
In the released version, doing NPC quests will lead to them asking to join your crew. You may have up to 2 NPC crewmen with you at a time. They teleport as necessary and respawn at no penalty (other than you need to go back to your ship to get them again). If they are getting in your way, you simply tell them to stay on the ship or stay where they are (and they will mill around the local area). NPCs can be found across the universe or summoned with player purchasable spawners.
You don't need to upgrade your ship to its full size or build a super town to beat the game, but you WILL want some place to store your loot and a handful of crewmen are nice to have around to keep monsters off your back while you are busy trying to get that hard to reach ore.
Other observations...
- Rope initially seems less useful than in Terraria but it is much more fun to use.
- Weapon type variety keeps most items useful (line of fire geometry differences, dps, range, effects).
Even lower tier weapons are useful because you can shoot them for longer periods of time when your armor (and corresponding energy capacity goes up).
- The 2-person hovercar is cool but can't really handle non-starter planet terrain that well. There is that Explorer vehicle mod though... ^^
- The cooldown time when switching weapons or recharging guns is painfully slow and frequent. You will have to hop around once or twice waiting to fire the gun salvo again or swing the sword you just switched to. This forces good timing and slightly better split-second planning in combat, but it does admittedly make combat feel slower than it should be.
- Released Starbound (non-modded) block variety is super impressive and amazing structures can be made. The look and design can easily surpass unmodded Terraria and Minecraft. Terraria boss fights seem more epic but Starbound boss fights are more meaningful.
- Oh, based on certain bits of content that was occasionally available in beta, leads me to believe more content may come in the next few months.

Here's (outdated) gameplay as a zombie, you can see how many people I kill with ease:
Rather than let the game's community affect my perspective on this game like most others, I will primarily be reviewing the game itself.
Originating in December of 2007 and originally being a Source Mod for Half Life 2 Deathmatch, this game is on its final days of living unfortunately. It runs on the old Source Base 2007. It's very thrilling to play alongside your friends and have them fall to the undead, turning against you and eventually feasting on your flesh (hopefully not!).
The game is quite easy to get started in, but has the typical motto of "hard to master". It is difficult for starting players, but you get better at the game rather quickly, so do not feel discouraged if you lose a lot in the beginning! Find the right people to play with and they'll be glad to help you out! Some servers offer modifications such as models, trails, stats, infection cure, and more.

Teamwork can be very critical depending on the map, even mandatory to win, such as requiring zombies to work together in specific strategies or survivors sticking together to heighten the chance of survival, although teamwork is usually not present due to poor communication or stubborness.
When survivors die they turn into zombies, having the new goal of having to kill every survivor.
Survivors, depending on the map, must either survive, kill all zombies, or complete objectives, which usually ends in escaping the map.
Zombies must attempt to kill all the survivors before running out of time, lives, or the survivors reaching a point.
Visuals are what you would expect from a Source mod on the 2007 engine, running Direct X 9. There are numerous visual bugs and glitches, especially from minimizing and re-opening your game, but most of them are minor and won't disturb the game too much. Shadows and flashlights will show through several surfaces and walls. Hitboxes may also show through surfaces and can be damaged, although this is uncommon.
Lag compensation is quite horrid (zombies can hit you five feet away due to extended hit range). Players can have the same ping and one player will still be able to have lag compensation advantage. When zombies use their lunge ability (temporary speed boost), they almost always get extended hit range. Zombies may hit you even without looking at you. Even on LAN these things will occur. I've found the lag compensation to be the most bothersome when trying to enjoy the game.
There are up to seven survivors to choose from, all with their own unique voices and quotes, ranging from a waitress with weird breast implants to a bald police officer. They also have their own zombie counterpart. Voice acting is quite comical but sounds generic and awkward at times, such as the waitress having an odd moan when she attacks. Survivors can use voice commands as mentioned, "panic" which gives you a temporary stamina and speed boost,  a flashlight, and many other actions. The starting zombie will become a zombie known as "The Carrier". The carrier is basically the "alpha zombie", having more strength, health, and the ability to infect, highlighting targets, and "roar".
There are weapons of course, and unique melee weapons too. Some weapons include rifles, shotguns, chairs, IED explosives, grenades, and even props themselves. Accuracy and recoil are pretty meaningless on most weapons so you can jump around like a maniac and land headshots. You have multiple crosshairs you can select from, but you can't customize through console and you'll have to create your own VTF if you want a custom one.
Modes you can play are objective mode (ZPO), survival mode (ZPS), and hardcore (ZPH). An additional modded mode called Deathmatch (ZPD) is present, which pits survivors versus survivors. There are also some deathrun maps. Maps are very unique and creative, some requiring imaginative barricades or dodging giant blocks fired at you, adding to the endless replayability factor. Some maps may be well balanced, or very survivor/zombie sided, as well as grotesque-looking maps with poor designs and numerous bugs, which is usually the norm now.
Quite an enjoyable game to play with friends, albeit the small playerbase of today. It's free too, so it's worth a try.
- A large variety of maps, good and bad.
- Simple, creepy soundtrack.
- Co-op and teamwork is the main focus of this game for both zombies and survivors.
- Easy to get started in
- Simple, intuitive voice commands.
- Chill community.
- New dev team actively responds to players and is continuously updating this game.
- Rounds can become tediously delayed when fewer players are alive.
- May be a pro, may be a con depending on your tastes: there's a lot of unbalanced custom maps.
- A lot of people refuse to play zombie and will rage quit, harming the server population and flow of the game.
- You may encounter bugs since the major update hit recently, be sure to report them!
Replayability factor: Very high.
My overall score of this game/Source mod is: 8.5/10

I want to actually make a helpful review so here it goes. Lets start off with personal rating of 4/10. Now, on with the details of why I say this:
I hate it when people release games as early access. I remember back in the last days of my console plebbing (about 7 years ago) games would not realease as "Early access". Games were finished products, and then updated to fix bugs. Early access allows devs to make tons of money (Lets review starforge and rain of kings hmm?) and then leave the game without updates or any intent to bring it past the the starting line. Games like rain of kings and starforge have a 10-20 US dollar price tags, are fun for the first 5 seconds, and they die after a couple of days of gameplay. This game had me in a head spin. I bough it, looked at the trailers, I saw that every screenshot, and realized that every one was massivley editted to be higher quality and the videos more fake than Jessica Nigris boobs. I played the game for 43 minutes and automatically noticed the limits in the game, almost no crafting recipies, no animations, poor graphics (looks like the game is 8 years old), and above all, no point to playing it.
Lets go into further detail, no crafting recipis, this bugs me, you want 19.99 ( 7.99 on sale) but your game has around 20 items to craft. There are no animations, when i say "No animations" im not talking about cool cutscene like animations of picking something up eg. crouching over, anything like that, Im talking about, when i go to pick something up, my hand doesnt move, I cannot even see my body. When I smash a tree, it just bloop, breaks into 3 pieces and you magically pick up everything with telekenisis. There are no crafting animations/wait times this sorta bugs me, I like it in rust when servers have insta craft as an option, but I want to expierience what it is like to craft lets say a hammer. Is it less than 1 second? Can I solve a rubix cube before i have it in my hands? I know the game isnt going for realism, but not waiting to take raw cloth and turn it into mechanically sewn clothes is a bit rediculous in my opinion.
Lets break off from that noise and talk about the graphics. The graphics look like they are from around 2008, Im talking about first generation PS3 games, worse than fallout (sorry fallout, your graphics were not good back then <3) . Trying to make this short (failing so far) moving on to game mechanics, you hit a tree like I said before, 3 logs, smash into bits, if you are a timewaster and hatchet it once every 3 seconds, you will see the tree do a crappy animation of falling, its pointless to wait this long. I walk up to a bush (nearly bigger than me), I smash it with a hatchet, I only get ONE stick. The building reminds me of "The Forest" you can only build pre-fabricated houses/items, and when you do, just like the forest, it gives two you the icons of lumber and sticks, you collect them and press E in my opinion this is crap.
Do not buy this game, I bought it played it for less than the hour and already saw its worth. If you are going for a survival game pick rust, dayz (if you dont mind playing experimental gameplay that bugs), ARK:SE, the forest, so on. I spent 7.99 on this and was actually disgusted with spending more than 1 dollar. Call me cheap, but this game deserved no ones money. If you have a job at which you earn money dont spend it on this, this game doesnt even work hard for its money. Please, do not buy this game, this is a really well written warning.

The expansion has ruined the game. It introduced a new mechanic "swallow" if a unit or building swallows an enemy unit it is banished and returns only when the unit/building that swallowed it is destroyed. This is fine and all except the only two cards to feature this mechanic are neutral. Furthermore they are incredibly cheap to cast. The two of them did recently see nerfs and the crystal flower card is arguably balanced. However in spite of a 2 health nerf the Azure Skywhale is still completley overpowered. I have not queued into a ranked game (and I havent played in some time so I am rather low ranked too) without encountering this card.
Compare Skywhale to last Nightmare. The yellow spell is 6 cost destroy a minion. Skywhale the nuetral minion is 6 cost destoy a minion and gain a 6/6 flying creature. Technically skywhale has a higher land requirement but that is irrelevant when land ramping is so easy. Technically you can get your creature back if you kill the whale, but thats not so easy when it can move three tiles and any threat you do place will just get swallowed again. Its nice to see the devs nerf the card reasonobly quickly but the nerf is meaningless. Reducing the cards health does not change the fact that swallow as a mechanic is fundamentally broken. Since you can't swallow a unit with swallow it comes down to who can play their whale first.
I've seen that at higher ranks people do play decks without whale, but if you're reading this its likely because you haven't played the game and so won't have the cards to make such a deck and I can promise you getting ♥♥♥♥ed by this one card while you scrounge the cards you need to counter will not be worth your time.
I'm actually astounded that such a clearly powerful card could be released at all never mind as a nuetral card available to every deck, even more so that in spite of the concerns raised by the community the devs come out with such an innefectual nerf.
It's a cryig shame too since this game is so beautiful. The art is gorgeous, the music ambient, the core mechanics sound, the bosses fun and the coop features awesome. But ranked, the meat of the game, is simply not worth playing.

I've been playing for several weeks now. This will be my fourth online TCG I've played (or would have) long term.
I don't mind certain pay aspects of games. Especially in TCG games there is a certain expectation that if you pour some money into the game, you can get an edge. What I have a problem with is huge sections of the game completely walled off and sitting behind paywalls.
I loved this game at first. Nice aesthetics, cool stregegy based card systems, unique table dynamics. I burned through my free missions, which lasted a few days and started openening free card packs and feeling like there was a good balance to the collection system.
After I ran out of my free missions BOOM. Totally different game. The Pandora system is locked behind a paywall. The rest of the missions were locked behind a paywall. The Oversky "expansion"  offers a few missions and then extremely expensive "islands" you have to buy to get anywere. You can do free multiplayer for a little gold here and there but not enough to feel like you are progressing any more.
Ever play Clash of Clans? Like... you build for weeks and get really into it and then eventually realize if you don't start dropping $$$ on the regular you're not going anywhere anymore? It's kind of like that.
I wouldn't mind dropping like $30-40 to boost myself into some content. But based on observation that wasn't going to get me by for very long. The prices on the Mission locks are high and demand a lot of gold. They also don't renew so you have to keep buying mission packs. I have never played a game this greedy before... it was disheartening to say the least.
Then there is the matching system. For a long time, the matching system took a while because there wern't enough players in game. So they fixed it so that instead of being matched against similar equipped/skilled players, you are matched with anyone? The result being match after match of being slaughtered by players with very expensive decks.
I feel like there would be considerably more players in game if they were fairer to new players. Thus far, unless you got in early and committed to spending some dough on the regular, you're not going to get far.
Oh and the customer service email link didn't work. The first time it returned as failed so I used the built in customer service link about a potential bug I encountered and never recieved a response.
To summarize: A well built, pretty game that was implemented very poorly.

In this game you are Captain Renko, a US Army Operative who is sent with a team to Katorga-12. An island just off the coast of Russia. Whilst there events occur and you end up changing the course of history and finding a device by the name of the TMD, or the Time Manipulation Device (Creative. I know). On the Island of Katorga-12 a revolutionary resource used in many technologies throughout the island and is the basis of the island having any sort of presence at all, and that resource is E99. It is what powers the TMD. When E99 is applied to something, be it an object or a living creature/person, adverse effects happen and the TMD was created to channel that.
PROS:
The TMD (Time Manipulation Device) is something that sticks with you as an item all throughout the game. Occasional upgrade related to plot events means it always has a relatively fair balance against the enemies you will encounter at different porions of the game. You'll get to use it to turn back or advance time on an object in the world to do a number of things. One of those things is aging and then restoring objects to open shutter gates which are there halting your progress to continue the game, or (IMO) more importantly to find hidden goodies such as the fairly rare Weapon Upgrade Kits and also more of the much wanted E99 Technology.
Atmosphere Is pretty good, best in the first part of the game but it does end up being non-existent in some places but revives again eventually only to die out again. Atmostphere is worthy to be listed as both a pro and a con simply because of it's inconsistency.
Weapons are basic, and small in range but they offer enough variety to turn a linear experience in to something worthwhile I'd say.
Mechanics include the TMD to manipulate and manage the flow of time in real-time, which I explain more about in the original paragrapth about the TMD.
An upgrade system for the TMD, you as an individual via perks and also the weapons via upgrade kits. With E99 Technology as currency in this to be used at upgrade stations and weapon lockers to get health, ammo and upgrades as I just mentioned. The mechanics in this aren't very in-depth but they do exist and are pretty solid, solid enough to say they're a pro rather than a con.
CONS:
Characters, whilst thankful they exist they lack depth of any sort, they're stereotypical, sometimes useless, feels like they're was supposed to be more to them but no one bothered to add those things. The range of actual characters is very small and like most if not all other Linear FPS shooters, you don't actually "Speak" to characters but moreso you are simply told things by them, given instructions and then you go on your way.
Atmostphere (Refer to the Atmostphere paragrath in PROS for more info)
Multiplayer (When it existed) was okay but not really, it was really unbalanced because it was playable humans VS non-humans, and generally it was just bad at that because the maps made it more balanced for one side over the other, and naturally as time has moved on nobody plays the game online anymore.
OVERALL:
I'd give it a slightly better than okay 6.7/10
