This was probably one of the best $15 dollar gaming investments I have ever made. I have played through every major installment of its beta testing and have completed the released game. The starting storyline and added polish makes the released game fresh and appealing even to those that have played earlier versions. The central technology initially awarded to the player, if you consider its full span of upgraded uses and symbolic nature for a sandbox game, rivals a Jedi's lightsaber for awesome utility. The player(s) have a near complete freedom to go (or attempt to go) where they please. Understandably, early characters struggle against difficult terrain and the player may occasionally die to inadequate preparations before more lengthy exploration and gathering efforts. It should be noted there is a casual mode but I played on survival (which introduced hunger and a real reason to farm - or at least hunt).
A multiplayer dedicated server is the same world as the server host's single player universe. The player's ship is actually part of the character profile, so whatever modifications you do to your ship are taken with you from server to server - or single player to multiplayer. Additional players do not increase the difficulty of boss fights, but may generate more overall monsters on a planet as they spawn near players (assuming the players are spread across the planet - which by the way, there are unfathomable numbers of planets). Each planet ranges in size and gravity, with variances in weather. More difficult planets require special enviromental pack items (which can be hidden by other items), but you CAN go their without the environmental packs if you really want to (you'd live for a couple seconds at least lol).
In the released version, doing NPC quests will lead to them asking to join your crew. You may have up to 2 NPC crewmen with you at a time. They teleport as necessary and respawn at no penalty (other than you need to go back to your ship to get them again). If they are getting in your way, you simply tell them to stay on the ship or stay where they are (and they will mill around the local area). NPCs can be found across the universe or summoned with player purchasable spawners.
You don't need to upgrade your ship to its full size or build a super town to beat the game, but you WILL want some place to store your loot and a handful of crewmen are nice to have around to keep monsters off your back while you are busy trying to get that hard to reach ore.
Other observations...
- Rope initially seems less useful than in Terraria but it is much more fun to use.
- Weapon type variety keeps most items useful (line of fire geometry differences, dps, range, effects).
Even lower tier weapons are useful because you can shoot them for longer periods of time when your armor (and corresponding energy capacity goes up).
- The 2-person hovercar is cool but can't really handle non-starter planet terrain that well. There is that Explorer vehicle mod though... ^^
- The cooldown time when switching weapons or recharging guns is painfully slow and frequent. You will have to hop around once or twice waiting to fire the gun salvo again or swing the sword you just switched to. This forces good timing and slightly better split-second planning in combat, but it does admittedly make combat feel slower than it should be.
- Released Starbound (non-modded) block variety is super impressive and amazing structures can be made. The look and design can easily surpass unmodded Terraria and Minecraft. Terraria boss fights seem more epic but Starbound boss fights are more meaningful.
- Oh, based on certain bits of content that was occasionally available in beta, leads me to believe more content may come in the next few months.

This game is what you get if you combined Hearthstone with a tactics game, and added a small splash of Magic the Gathering. Personally, I find this game quite good, especially considering some of the strategies you can come up with, or have to defend against. I've also found the fantasy settings, along with the music/sounds and slightly cute nature appealing, especially after having played so many dark games over the years.
Even better, the game is free. Potentially, this could be a P2W game in some respects, but I've found that, so far, the game has been relatively generous (compared to some other games) at doling out gold and free booster packs, which certainly helps. That being said, I have mainly played Pandora (AI and PvP), as well as the solo missions.
I've tried my hand at regular PVP Ranked Battles and am absolutely terrible at it. It does seem as though the opponent has better cards, but also that they're veteran players. I'm hoping that as I accumulate better cards over time, and as I gain more experience, this will counteract that, but who knows. So...be aware of that aspect if you're thinking of playing. At first, you may want to stick to the Pandora mode (sometimes called Arena/Draft mode in other games) so that you'll be on even footing with other players, in regard to having the same equal-quality deck.
Another comment I'd like to make is that even though this game has a sizeable number of cards, divided between various factions (Red, Blue, Yellow, Green, Neutral), it would be nice if it had about 50% more, with more varied keywords in each faction. Perhaps, this is just my personal preference, but it would make the game even more engaging.
Overall, I give this game a thumbs up. If you're not sure about it, you could download it and give it a try. It is free afterall. Hope the review helps in your decision.

I'm going to say it here and now that this game is a work in progress with a load of content missing, and this review will reflect that as well so only read this if the game is still in its early access stage. (WARNING: REALLY DO YOUR RESEARCH WITH OTHER LETS PLAYS TO GAUGE HOW GOOD THIS GAME IS SO YOU DON'T REPEAT MY MISTAKE.)
For starters, the game's UI is clunky and still in need of a lot of work. Inventory is ugly, and hard to navigate, especially with initial starting assault of hints and tips windows, and also having to navigate back to key bindings for instructions. In game at the moment, you can definitely notice a significant difference in quality compared to what's seen in the trailer. Frames will drop often for you at medium graphics and I assume this is due to its early access build since my computer can run pretty on high graphics for most of the time.
In terms of gameplay, I've mostly got into building for the first three hours or so. The game likes to drop you in with a starter 'checklist' for collecting materials and building a fireplace and hut (which you cannot sleep in). Very similar to The Forest except in a winter landscape (even its building mechanics are the exact same thing), excitement only occurs when night is starting to fall where SOME enemies may start to spawn (my game has spawned about one wolf so far in and the dragon at the tower ignores me completely). As mentioned before, the game's trailers and screenshots are far from what it currently really is in terms of content. For example, fall damage has not even been implemented since I evidently survived jumping off the tower you see in its trailers.

However, updates are well schedules and it seems they've kept up those promises so far.
Do not buy this game unless you're in it to really support the developers, or you have the faith to entrust your money into its future developments. The game certainly has potential, but it also needs time to reach it.

This is my first review done for a videogame. I started playing back in Early Access. This was before dungeons and NPC quests. TBH the game was great before such content became available, I was content just being thrown into a unviverse with nothing to go on other than survive/explore/crafting. Since then the game has made so many great improvements!
A quick start guide for the newbies. Open ship locker before beaming down to planet and loot the useful items/torches/canned food. When you beam down immediatly cut down some trees. You can craft the wood into timber. Use timber to create crafting table and a wooden door. Night will come soon meaning more randomly generated baddies. Now is a great time to dig a hole and make your first shelter. I like to find an area with cobblestone to carve my shelter out of because cobblestone is used for crafting stone furnace. While digging keep an eye out for vines, sever them at the roof of the caves and collect the plant fibers, they are used for bandages and fabric. Also look for minerals such as iron, coal, copper. After you have cleared out a small space for a shelter, place your wooden door in the entrance of your space. Set up a campfire and you have your first mining camp setup! Wait out the rest of the night by finishing building your furnace and clothspinner. Build a bed if you have materials for one. Beds can be used to heal yourself. By the time the next day arises you should be ready to venture out into the world and explore!
One more helpful hint. By pressing Shift or Ctrl while using the Matter Manipulaor lets u manipulate background objects and change the manipulators point size, respectively. I did not know this for the longest time....

This is such a hugely underated game. It has taken a lot of elements from Half-Life 2, Dead Space, Resident Evil 4, and combined them really well into a game based on time travel and the Cold War.
Complete with character and weapon upgrades, the ability to physically pick up and move items, the ability to age certain objects around you, and special abilities (such as instantly aging someone to death, or mutating a soldier into a disgusting creature, which will instantly attack other enemy soldiers).
The engine is decent, it's clearly a console port, as the options are very limited, but it all looks fine and runs perfectly smoothly. The sound effects and music are great, and the weapons range from generic assault rifle and shotgun, to a sniper rifle that lets you move the bullet around in real time (like the Redeemer in Unreal Tournament). Which means you can snipe someone in the back of the head, despite being in front of them, and behind cover.
It also features a grenade launch, which lets you manually control the grenade, almost like a remote control car (that blows up!).
The plot is really impressive, with plenty of great time travel elements, horror, and decent characters.
I really highly recommend getting this game. The only downside is that the game is very short (about 10 hours), so you may want to wait for it to go on sale. It does have a multi-player mode though, which may extend the lifespan.

Singularity held up pretty well as an old-school shooter that has no cover-shoot, and no autoheal. What it does have is the TMD, a time manipulation device that you can deploy both in combat and merely to solve environmental puzzles. The setup is pretty cute... a major radiation event on an abandoned island near the Russian border lead to a special US response... a spec ops team moved in, but an EMP event have them crashed on the island and the team scattered. You, Renko, must traverse the island, attempt to reunite with your teammates, and figure out what's wrong with this island, as the singularity whipsaws you between 2010 (game's "present day") and 1955. You screwed up history in one of those whipsaw transitions, and you have to spend rest of the game trying to undo what you have done, as you fight your way through soldiers (both 1955 and 2010) and monsters, horribly mutated humans and whatelse left on the island also horribly mutated.
What really sets the game apart is how your special power, the TMD, can be deployed in combat. There's a "shockwave" command that blasts all enemies back, and by endgame it is upgraded to limb shedding slam power. Enemies that phase shift (blinks in and out) can be "blasted" by the shockwave back to the present for you to shoot. The device is also a personal tractor beam for grabbing and throwing. Grab an explosive barrel (either on the ground or in midair, such as one thrown at you), and throw it at the enemy.  Many objects can be aged (turned into ruined version) or deaged (return to pristine condition). You will end up de-aging a lot of things. Busted boxes that contain medkits and ammo can be deaged. Regular boxes can be aged so they can fit through gaps that they would not otherwise fit, like under a door, then de-aged so it acts as a jack to lift the door up, or use as a platform for you to jump onto other places. Enemies can be aged, safes can be aged (technically, just the safe door). The TMD can also throw a protective bubble shield to freeze time for a few seconds.
The game offers various upgrades for your TMD and your weapons, and there are a nice selection if a bit typical: pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, then it veered into the exotic, like a grenade launcher that alternately launches a guided "rolling ball", a spike launcher that launches explosive spikes, a sniper rifle with time-dilation (i.e. bullet time) when scoped, and the autocannon (a gatling gun, actually). You can discover "weapon tech" points that you can spend on upgrades (each weapon can be upgraded in reload speed, clip capacity, or raw damage) during your travels. You can also accumulate "E99" energy containers that acts as currency that you can spend on additional TMD upgrades (betware as you can only equip one TMD upgrade at a time), as well as other perks like "better projectile damage resistance", or "recharge health per kill".  You can access those at the various TMD upgrade stations and Weapon Stations.
Combat is pretty frantic as the game throws new challenges at you all the time, and some of the environment puzzles are genius. If you are stuck on where to go, there's always "chrono-ping" which tells you which way you should go.
The game involves time travel, so it should be no surprise that there are plenty of causuality loops, and there's a big reveal near the end that sets up for a sequel, which has yet to happen, but a tweet earlier in 2015 seem to suggest that the developer is working on such. And there are at least three endings (and two fail-repeat semi-endings) that you can attempt to get.
The graphics are quite good (you almost can't tell it's a 2010 game) and sound effects very well done (proper stereo effects as you turn the character around and the sound source does localize). Music tempo increases with combat and ends when all enemies are defeated.
All in all, Singularity is one of those games that few people have played, as it's so oldschool, but it plays fine today, which is a lot of praise for a 5 year old game (released 2010, reviewed 2015).

As I write this, I'm about fifteen hours into what is, the internet tells me, a 60 hour + experience.  However, barring a truly spectacular implosion in quality, I'm more than confident in recommending this to anyone who likes any of the following:
*Owning zombie cats.
*Resolving marital disputes with the use of bears.
*Quality RPGs in general.
because I'm pretty sure what we have here is the best RPG in well ove a decade.  In particular since Baldur's Gate 2 swaggered confidently into existence - giant miniature space hamster companion trotting along by it's side - and pointed out to the other RPGs that they were severely underlevelled by comparison.  For reference, I put $200 into the kickstarter for this game.  And I have got an absolute bargain.
In feel, Pillars of Eternity has totally succeeded in capturing what made the Infinity Engine games of yesteryear great.  If you played them, you can rush for the buy button immediately, as you know their quality.  If not, some elaboration:  The real time with pause combat system manages to successfully combine the tactical sense you get with turn based gameplay with the ability to react immediately that you would find in an ARPG.  The painted backgrounds are beautiful and will make you wonder why people ever thought switching to 3D engines was so important.  The companions will make you smile with their banter (or in some cases, make you wonder what you let yourself in for when letting them join) and I'm confident they'll start to feel like friends (Eder and Hiravias are personal favourites at this stage).  The huge number of richly developed side quests that have as much care lavished on them as the main plot will suddenly take you from "hmmm, a little bit of Pillars before bed" to "Well, it may be 1 in the morning, and I do have to be in work tomorrow, but why not just do another level of this dungeon?".
In addition to this, Pillars has added it's own things to the mix.  Reactivity and choice in quests was present in those old IE games (moreso Planescape than BG), but is much more a feature in Pillars (more akin to something like Fallout).  Quests have entirely different ways of resolving - back one side in a local squabble over another, seek justice on a criminal or agree that he was driven to it, make a frontal assault on a castle or sneak in through the sewers, almost every quest involves some degree of choice or moral dilemma and the game is the better for it.  Note that this doesn't mean you are choosing between two horrible options, as can sometimes be the case when choice is emphasised in an RPG, I'm definitely able to feel like a real hero who is achieving good in the world, but I'm doing it my own way, and I have to think about my actions.  Also notable are the cutaway pencil sketch illustrated sections that allow you to interact with the gameworld and give you choices of how to proceed (often with the aid of a trusty grappling hook or prybar).  These capture the experience of PnP roleplaying better than any other game I can think of.  Though sadly, use of the ten foot pole was cut during development.
Cons: These are really minor, but are here to show you that I am not entirely a raving fanboy (merely 90% raving).  So - there are a number of wilderness areas that are significantly less content rich than the other areas of the game.  Some people like the exploration aspects of this, I like areas to be stuffed with content like a battery farm chicken is stuffed with GM corn (the main towns are much more to my liking here and I don't think anyone could complain about them on this score).  Some of the dungeons have pacing issues (as with every other RPG ever made except Baldur's Gate 2) where you have one room with lots of story and then a lot of hitting things everywhere else (that said, the majority of them are brilliantly paced - there is an early abandoned temple that I thought was super well done).  There are, inexplicably, no romances, despite the fact that the companions are hugely talkative and as a rule rather interesting.  Um...that's about it, really.
All in all, if you like party based RPGs at all, if you like story based games at all and especially if you miss (or just want to know) what has been lost as games have pushed cinematic and accessible over literary and deep, then you MUST gather your party before veturing forth into Pillars of Eternity.

So I had an open mind when I started playing this.  I understood that it was early access, and that release fetures would not be present.  That being said, I really enjoy the game and look forward to what new material will be added.
I consider myself a completionist kinda guy.  I like to have the best armor, weapons, and materials to craft the biggest and best item in the game.  The diversity in the game isn't there...yet, but I can imagine an epic crafting tree with tiers of gear to explore the Savage Lands with.  The combat is pretty straight forward with a few enemies having the weakness of not turning fast.  You can cheese it for slow, lumbering mobs, but the fast moving wolves don't play by those rules...and I like it.
Now for the slight downside that I have for the game.  I spent about 3-4 hours one afternoon and mined, chopped, collected everything that my world could offer.  I found that after that was done, there wasn't anything else left for me.  So what did I do? I created another world and went back at it.  I personally feel that characters should be tied to a world, and not allowed to be used on different worlds.  My second drawback is the size of the map in relation to content to explore.  I've found 5 villiages, and a few "ruins" but nothing in those towns made me want to stay and explore the surrounding areas.  I would just check a few houses, and move on down the path.  Give me something that has some lore to it so I fully understand about the land.  The lack of reference of distance also hurts the exploring of the game.  I have seen the island from coast to coast to coast and I have no fathomable idea on how large that actual island is.  I know if take between 15-25 minutes to travel in a straight line from one side to the other.
All in all, the game is great.  Small tweaks over the next few months should be extremely pleasing for this game.  I can't wait for what this game truely has to offer.

This is a great game, and its free to play mechanics are not a detriment. The game gives out regular rewards for you to advance your collection (example: every 10th level you gain you get to pick between 3 cards you don't have a full set of already, and this can even be legendary cards). The rate of gaining in-game-currency (gold) is also at a pretty reasonable rate.
You also get rewards just for logging in, usually only a small amount of gold, but every 5th day you log in you usually get a pretty good reward (a larger sum of gold, a free chest with 5 cards, or sometimes you get a mythic chest, someting that you otherwise only get by spending real money on the game). Best of all with this log in system? You don't need to do it in a row to get the good rewards. You won't be punished by not being able to log in every day.
The Pandora mode (comparable to Hearthstone's arena or MtG's draft) is fun and changes some of the rules of the game, and you get one free practice run every day. Win 3 games in this practice run before you lose 2 times, and you earn 1/3 of a full run (win 3 full practice runs, and you get a free full run. A really good feature to make new players able to try out and learn this "gambling"-mode without feeling they are just wasting gold trying to get good at this gamemode.
Also, they are regularly updating and balancing the game, so if you were tired of Hearthstone's "we only do balance-changes every blue moon" then this game might have a developer team for you. I have bought the steam pack and their new expansion that is launching now, and I have been happy to use real money to support this game.

Bastion has to be one of the greatest( If not THE greatest) games I have ever played. Action RPG might describe the gameplay itself but it doesn't even come close to how much more there is to this
...
.
The gameplay is fast-paced and
satisfying to yourself chopping, shooting, and smashing your way through a multitude of different enemies each one of which uses a different tactic and game mechanics to try and stop you; And in each level these varying combinations made each single moment where you're shooting a turrent, slashing a Windbag, or pulverising an Ura feel like a tense and unique battle. I've played through it three times now and I haven't feel any kind of repetitive or tiring combat (which I haven't really even seen before with two or even one playthrough).
But the action isn't all this game brings. It comes with an absolutely amazing story(with enough depth to be interesting and spark investigation, while not burying the player in details) which starts In Medias Res. Meaning that it starts "into the middle of things" where you discover the past of what happend while you move forward with what will happend.
But the past story isn't just something that they hand to you on a silver platter. The Narration, Memento's, Dialouge gives you hints and clues (that you must notice) in the most balanced way possible so that you become invested in learning about the complex History of Caelondia and what caused the Calamity without feeling like your being dragged through an  incredibly confusing mess( i.e. Dark Souls (don't hate I love it too)). It's astounding to me how much of an emotinal attachment was cultivated between me and the characters with only a couple of lines of dialouge.
The sound track itself is also incredible. Darren Korb uses Guitars, Drums, Banjos, Accordions, Harps, the talented Ashely Barrent, and all sorts to create very enjoyable and quite quirky music.
The singular flaw( cause there's no such thing as a perfect game) is something which I didn't find personally a problem, but I noticed was a problem for others. In order to truly enjoy the game, it requires you taking a leap of faith and investing yourself into the story ( for at most an hour or half an hour); their whole plot and story-telling technique surrounds itself upon wanting to learn about what happend and what will happen. So far I haven't meet someone who didn't take this leap and enjoyed it but I understand that some people would rather the game draw them in instead of diving into the game on their own.
Over-all, I would highly recommend this game to anyone and everyone wanting an experience that will leave you begging for more. I bought it for 25% off (I think) But I would have gladly paid twice that for this game. Well worth your money, time, and attention.

So let me start by saying that this is A Very Good Game (tm).
I was a bit pessimistic about it -- after all, how many times has Obsidian come so close to releasing a truly great game, yet failed to completely deliver (granted, often through no fault of their own). I got to play a bit of Pillars at Gamescom last summer and was left feeling pretty meh about it. In hindsight this was probably more because the limited time I had to play it wasn't enough to really properly "get" the game from the very beginning.
The writing is very Obsidian, and the worldbuilding is deep and complex. After a few hours in, I can already see Obsidian's trademark moral choices everywhere, and they definitely appreciate the shades of grey that they always have. Some of the choices you're forced to make leave you seriously wondering if you're -actually- supporting the good/bad guys, and I think that's honestly really great. Pretty much exactly what you'd come to expect from Obsidian.
Now for some gameplay stuff: I'm playing on Normal difficulty, and as a vet of Infinity Engine games, I'm finding it quite challenging... though that could be my party composition. Being able to create adventurers to fill in gaps in your party is a great feature, but the writing on the companions is good enough that you'll definitely be missing something by using the cookie-cutter custom adventurers. That being said, one thing I'm definitely going to say now is HAVE A ROGUE in your party. The first hour or two of the game you can get by fairly easily without one, but I'm now running into a lot of areas that are laden with traps/lockpickable doors, and I really don't have anyone in my party that is adept at 1.) seeing traps before triggering them, and 2.) deactivating them when necessary. You can probably get away with a Ranger instead of a Rogue, with a bunch of points dumped into Mechanics/Stealth, but nothing is as good as the real deal.
All in all, I do not regret paying full price for this game. It's really great, and simultaneously scratches that nostalgic itch for a Baldur's Gate-type game while at the same time offering many current features that make it stand apart on its own as well.
I hope Obsidian makes bucketloads of money with this and then goes on to make spiritual successors to some other Infinity Engine-era CRPGs. Arcanum, anyone?

Now, here's some advice if you're new to half-life, or wondering if you should buy it! (you should)
The Source versions are a remake of the original games on the engine used by HL2. Half Life: Source is pretty much identical to Half Life.
The recommended playing order is pretty much the release order:
Half Life (Or Half Life: Source)
Half Life: Opposing Force
Half Life: Blue Shift
Half Life: Decay (skippable - PS2 only)
Half Life 2
Half Life 2: Episode One
Half Life 2: Episode Two
Half Life 2: Lost Coast is just a tech demo for graphics options that went into later Source games. If you want to be quick, you can skip everything but Half Life and Half Life 2.
Portal is also tangentially related to the Half Life plot, but isn't too important as it doesn't have much story of its own. Portal 2 may change this however.

This is a truly amazing game, I don't even know where to start.
PROS:
-Dev team updates often
-Gorgeous CryEngine graphics & textures
-Vehicles that are a ton of fun to fix up and drive
-Great combat, lots of different weapons
-Fun community
-Cool setting, feels like a zombie game but actually is about post-nuclear war survival with mutants (basically zombies)

CONS:

-Dying happens really fast. If you get shot in the head or chest and its a kill shot, you will instantly go to a death screen and not be able to see how you died or who killed you.  You almost never even hear the gun fire that killed you because it instantly turns to death screen.

Overall this game is a lot of fun.  The devs update a lot and the gameplay is awesome.  I wish they would make server files public and will continue to fight for that to happen. Join this community and help it grow, it deserves more praise than DayZ which is a barely functional ♥♥♥♥♥how of a game that will never work.

TLDR opinion; I would recommend The Light Empire as a nice little game if you are seeking a distraction. Worth a look if you are into sci-fi themed and / or rogue-like games but NOT if you are looking for an RPG.
Please note that this is a cautious thumbs up, the game is improving steadily but is still very rough and simplistic in some respects.
Now, what to say about The Light Empire?
The good:
This game is very open and honest about what it is; a rogue-like game based in a sci-fi setting in a randomly generated universe. It playes well to those classifications, offering some nice diversity in encounters and destinations. It also plays well on the rogue-like side of things, no two trips will play out exactly the same and so there is definite replayability here.
The RPG elements it claims in the description are definitely present but they are not that in-depth, aside from being able to customise the stats of your ship when you begin the game. There are some flavour texts in some of the events which is a nice touch and some unlockable ships but from what I have played there is no real overarching story or world development, being able to adjust the stats on your ship is the meat of it.
Some effort has also clearly gone into the presentation of this game, there are some good images and textures involved and a good amount of detail can be seen on the in-game assets. Sound-wise it is distinctive, having some strange and otherworldly sound effects and music choices that may catch you by surprise but help give this game a unique feel to it.
The bad:
Okay, yes, there are bad things I see in this game. First off is the UI which feels a bit clunky and unresponsive. It is also cluttered, presenting you with all of your stats and resources all of the time while not offering tool tips or explanations. There is, however, a small guide built into the hud that you can access at any time for a quick overview of things (READ IT!).
The game also feels a bit slow-paced overall and the interaction and feedback are not that good. There are many things you do that feel a bit drawn out and slow, listening to or watching things without needing any real action on your part as you wait for it to finish. This plays as part of the aesthetic design of the game but here I do feel like it gets in the way a bit. But I must admit, the sound when you set off a distress beacon because you have run out of fuel is the most unique sound for such a thing I have ever heard.
Lastly it feels just a bit repetative and slapped together. The former could be due to a lack of varieties in some of the sprites (like all planets of a certain type look the same) while how the galaxy exploration is handled is effectively random things popping up on a starscape. It feels a little like a flash game in that regard.
So. Conclusions?
Overall I would have to say yes, I recommend this game. Is it worth the asking price? Probably. If it continues to develop after release (which it looks like it might) then it can only get better and it does show a lot of potential. Will it provide a diversion and entertainment? Probably. If you are into sci-fi or space themed games and / or into rogue-likes trying to see how far you can get, then yes, this might be a game you would enjoy. If you are after an RPG game definitely look elsewhere.

It may not have all the bells and whistles it could have but it is fully functional and does have its moments. So it is definitely worth a look and I look forward to seeing what this guy comes up with in the future.

This is a game that Capcom released that didn't really take off on the consoles very well. The game originally ran at 30 FPS, and even that was a massive stretch. Massive fights would happen and you'd be lucky to get even 20 FPS during these fights. That being said, this game is absolutely amazing, and easily the best thing to make its way to the PC.
Being one of the few Level ∞(200) players, yo'd be surprised just how much content is actually in this game. The maps are extraordinarily large, and there's so much to see, fight, collect, and discover. Frankly, it didn't bother me at all having to start completely from level 1, with nothing because I absolutely loved this game on console and it really tugs at my heartstrings when I got to play the "Dark Arisen" DLC again and its final boss.
The gameplay is simple yet intricate in certain aspects, the story is very simple and straight-forward until you reach a certain point, where the game blows your mind over and over.
The combat animations are immaculate, I don't recall a game ever having magic look THIS good ever. The attacks are impactful, the animations are beautiful, the music is compelling, the pawns are utterly pestersome until you realize how lonely it gets when they aren't commenting on every little thing.
The only "downsides" this game has, is the little character development you see in virtually every character other than your own and Selene. The character bio for Quina on the Capcom website is infinitely more informative than anything else you learn in the game. That and the combat eventually boils down to playing a bow class being able to do everything faster than every other class in the game.
Many fans like myself, pray every day for another Dogma to descend on us from Capcom.
That being said, THE WIND IS PUSHING MEEEEEE

You will be requried to think out of the "select all, click target to kill" box, even though the difficulty setting description states otherwise. Examples: you might be required to KITE a boss around with a ranged dps character becuase the rest of your party is DEAD/MAIMED, you might be required to use tight spots (DOORS) to prevent enemies from overwhelming your party, you might be required to PULL monsters where you want them to be before actually engaging them, etc.

Singularity is a FPS game that takes place in a small Russian controlled island, where they conduct dangerous experiments involving a new element called E-99. This is triggered by their fear of America's knowledge of Atomic Energy and in that island they found an element that greatly surpasses that power. The problems arise due to the Russian's overworking everyone on the island and with everyone handling a potentially dangerous new source of energy, an accident inevitably happens. That is when you, an American soldier named Renko and a second team are sent in to investigate. Before you can land, a shock-wave causes both helicopters to go out of control and leaves you as the only known survivor. You land in a small abandoned dock village and make your way into a building full of old timey Russian propaganda, map of the island's facilities and a statue of Joseph Stalin's head. Another shock-wave appears and suddenly the room is full of people and on fire. As you try to make your way out of the crumbling building, you rescue a man from death. The shock-wave wave reappears and you are now by yourself and notice that the statue of Stalin's head is now replaced with that of the man you saved. This is where our adventure truly begins.
The environments are now off somehow, you can't put your finger on why but you know you are in danger. The opening scene has amazing atmosphere and a lingering sense of dread since you are unarmed. You go through quite a bit being unarmed and the tension of not knowing what is out there is used very effectively. Ghosts appear from time to time that show the last moments of the deceased and the stories of what happened to your surroundings. This game does a great job at pulling you in and getting you interested in the twisted world you find yourself in. Eventually you do get a pistol to defend yourself from the horrors that await, but it is very weak and there is limited ammo to be had. How I wish the game would have stayed this way, but atlas you run into both an assault rifle and a shotgun in quick succession, immediately destroying any fear you may have of what lurks in the shadows since you are now armed to the teeth with powerful weapons. That issue only worsens as you are granted more and more powerful weapons as the story goes on. You can only carry two weapons of any type at a time but ammo is very frequent and I never found myself lacking in ammo. Weapon kits are scattered about that allow you to upgrade your already powerful weapons. This game got very easy, real fast on the Normal difficulty. If you have decent experience with the genre or want to maintain the horror aspect, I would recommend going for hard the first time through.
Besides your weapons, you will also be able to upgrade yourself with E-99 to allow you to run longer, hold your breath underwater longer and much more. Well since the fact that you being able to manipulate time is the game's first selling point I suppose it's not a spoiler to say that you will have other-worldly powers that you can also upgrade. These are a very nice addition to the game and gives you many more options during fights such as aging people into corpses or tossing an explosive your enemies’ way to name a few. Your powers are not unlimited however and are reliant on energy which slowly refills over time. It does add to the problem of being an overpowered killing machine with no need to fear anything, but it is a ton of fun to freeze time around a group of enemies, shooting them all in the face and unfreezing time before they knew what hit them. Thankfully one feature that helps alleviate you feeling like you can't be killed is that your health does not regenerate. If you are careless in fights your health will whittle down and you will run the risk of dying by what is usually a laugh-worthy attempt at killing Renko the Space Wizard. Health is recovered via syringes laying around that are used on the spot or health kits that you can carry around, up to five at the start. Health kits do have an animation of wrapping your wound before your health is regenerated making you an easy target for enemies.
That is not the only old school feature Singularity has. Shooting without using iron-sights is a viable option for combat and allows you to immerse yourself in the environments instead of having your face pressed up against the iron-sights just in case an enemy appears. The levels are fairly open ended and with the combination of health kits, ammo, weapon kits and E-99 scattered about for upgrades, the temptation of exploring off the beaten path is great. This works far better to get us to explore creepy areas that will probably have something inside waiting to bite our faces off ,than having a random collectible that only completionists care about like most games coming out around that time would have had. Outside of useful items there are also notes and audio logs scattered about that add information to the events that have occurred in the game. The overall story of Singularity is fairly interesting but really lags during the middle of the game, it does pick up again near the end thankfully. For whatever reason this game does not have an option for subtitles, which is both very annoying and odd.
That brings me to the biggest issue with this game. It is very common for users (myself included) to have no sound whatsoever until you go through
workaround. That fixed the issue of there being no sound whatsoever, but cutscenes were still far too quite. With the lack of subtitles and being unable to hear what people are saying in cutscenes, even with my headphones at their loudest, I had no idea what happened in the ending of the game due to it. There are several endings and it is a shame that I had to go out of my way to search for mine on Youtube. Once you finish the game, there is no option to start the game over with any of the stuff you have unlocked and the multiplayer is also dead, which I sadly had no way of experiencing. There are no motives for replaying the game other than selecting a higher difficulty setting. It took me 8 hours to complete the game, so standard time for games of this genre and I left pleased with the experience but the lack of anything else to do may be a turn off to some. That aside, graphics are still decent considering the title is half a decade old and environments have a lot of cool yet useless interactivity like messing with phones, sinks and microphones. Enemy variety is decent enough and has you facing both humans and creatures that can be far bigger than you. Humans end up being far more dangerous than most creatures as they have quite an aim and effectively use cover.
Boss fights are tense and feature the aforementioned giant creatures that will quickly murder you if you don't discover their attack pattern and weaknesses. Best of all there are no Quick Time Events to be found here. Your movement speed does hamper the enjoyment a bit since like most modern FPS games you move around at a snail’s pace and are only able to sprint for a few seconds. It's not all fighting though, you will come across an occasional simplistic puzzle or two every once in a while. One other modern aspect is that you will not be able to backtrack, so if you leave a ammo crate hoping to retrieve it later on when you need it, you will be unable to since doors inexplicably close and seal shut behind you. When all is said and done however, it is a nice blend of both the old school health system & useful rewards for exploration, as well as newer features of the genre such as story and upgrade systems. While not the horror game it could have been, it is a fun journey with a interesting story to tell. Singularity is a game fans of the genre looking for a single player experience will more likely than not enjoy, as long as they don't mind fixing the audio issue that may occur.

I read quite a few user reviews before I bought this, like I always do. Some ppl call it hidden gem, masterpiece, etc. but to be honest it is somewhat average FPS with some interesting ideas here and there.
I'm not someone who would care much about graphics but I think they were not considered very good even when this game came out, as I mentioned textures are pretty bad.
The story, yes it has one, is vaguely interesting at least at first glance. But later on it slowly slips into swamp of time travelling bullcrap so I wouldn't say it's good. Maybe I'm just biased because I don't like time-travelling/alternate dimensions stuff. It actually features 3 different endings, none of them is particullary interesting and the one which could be considered a good ending doesn't make any sense due to involved paradoxes that are presented to you, Red Dwarf's ep. "Ouroboros" makes more sense and is more entertaining.
Shooting itself is ok, nothing to write home about. Your arsenal consists of standart pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, etc. There are few interesting pieces like rifle with homing bullets, which isn't standart arm since it is given to you only in certain parts of the game, or a grenade launcher with RC-like grenades (cool idea but sadly I didn't find it any good).
You can also upgrade your weapons as long as you find weapon kits, but the impact of said upgrades is hardly noticeable, well you will obviously notice increased clip size but you don't really need increased dmg or reload speed. And I almost forgot that you can only carry 2 weapons at a time, personally I ended up using AR and minigun, this fact makes gimmicky weapons like that grenade launcher much less desireable.
The game also has it's currency scattered throughout lvls, it's called E99 tech. It's spend on character upgrades, these are somewhat more impactful than weapon upgrades, or you can buy ammo with it but it's unlikely that you will ever find yourself low on ammo.
What else? Oh right, Singularity's signature TMD. You can use it on enemies with various effects. It's used to solve ehm "puzzle" for the lack of better description and you can also use it to trivialize every enemy encounter once you aquire ability to make time-slowing bubble. This leads me to the fact that the game isn't difficult at all. Enemy soldiers have potatoe aim and you can easily avoid almost any attack from creatures. There is just one part which gave me a bit of trouble, it featured suicidal bugs.
Overall it's slightly above average shooter, but only because few good ideas and the freighter level I really liked. It took me roughly 10 hour to beat on the highest difficulty.
Buy it when it's on sale if you want to play FPS and can't think of any better than this one. Here's my reserved recommendation.

I stumbled across Faeria while browsing some free games. What I expected to be a casual game for the evening quickly turned into one of the best and most addicting games I've ever played.
-
Faeria plays a lot like Magic: The Gathering, except on one of many board layouts. You take turns strategically turning the blank ocean slate into a battlefield to summon/move your creatures across, block your opponent's offensive moves, and even harvest extra "Faeria" (mana) each turn, so you can get the upper hand.
-
There are 4 elements to choose from, and each has a distinct playstyle. You can combine elements for some really wild plays, or stick with one and hone your strategy.
-
While I had hours of fun with just the free version, I loved it so much I bought the Adventure Pouch.. and now I love it even more. It unlocks nearly unlimited missions for you to test your skill and newly earned cards, adds World Bosses to test your abilities (with great rewards!), and so much more.
-
Building a deck is a cinch. Unlike many other CCG-like games out there, Faeria keeps it simple and focuses on what it does best. Winning is based on skill and strategic choices (instead of a pay-to-win model like Hearthstone), and even a basic deck can still be formiddable.
-
Try Faeria. If you like this genre of games, you're going to love this.

I'm getting all emotional over this game now. It's like Baldur's Gate 2 but way better.
This is like Baldur's Gate 3 with enhanced visuals and game mechanics to make it smooth and fun to play on modern systems.
The game is challenging, but it gives you multiple ways to complete your objectives.
What changed from Baldur's Gate 2:
+ 3D models
+ The stat system has been reworked (It got better)
+ There are multiple ways to complete your objectives while still keeping the game challenging (more immersive, better)
+ It's slightly harder. (I've only played the game on hard difficulty) (I like it)
An ogre for example looks more dangerous and hits harder too.
+ Classes and skills have been completely reworked to make every class viable. This is a huge difference and major improvement. The bard for example used to be a silly character running around playing his harp in battles. The chanter from pillars of eternity on the other hand is totally badass.
Obsidian has succeeded in making a game that gives you that same awesome look and feel you had when you were playing Baldur's Gate 2 on release day, and made it possible to enjoy this on modern machines with modern mindsets.
The only negative point I can think of in this game is that at some point in the future I will finish it, which is sad because I want this experience to last.
I've read some negative reviews to see what people could have issues with.
I'll comment on some of them based on my experience (Check my playtime)
Here are their gripes:
-  Game is bugged.
-> I have only encountered 1 bug, The game completely crashed once.
Starting it back up I was able to replicate the issue, but it was easy to get around.
For a game that has just launched it could be a lot worse IMO
- I'm stuck and had to go hire some toon to get my mechanics up
-> The  developer had apparently anticipated this problem and
they have actually implemented multiple ways to complete objectives.
This problem does not exist in the game in my experience.
Use your head and think of other ways. The game challenges you.
- The combat is slow and it sucks
-> It's not an action RPG. If you have never played a game like Baldur's Gate, I suggest perhaps watching a tutorial video, but it really isn't that hard.
That's it for my review. This is the best game that will come out in a long time still.

I'm into this game for about 4 hours now and I can clearly paint a picture of what I am dealing with here, and it is not pleasant. I will categorize my praise and critisism as far as possible - hopefully without losing focus.
- Skip if not interested. But it gives you an initial idea of how lazy this port was.
a) Graphics
In the graphics menue you will be surprised to find only a choice of resolutions which will all leave your view narrow. With no option to manipulate FOV, since it is not for you to change, this sensation intensifies and gives even me headaches. And I honestly never had problems with FOV before this game - never felt I needed a slider. Additionally, you are able to change minor settings (depth of field, bloo, "high quality decals" - I'll get into this later) which are merely cosmetic but the developers do not seem to trust you with relevant stuff like AA or filtering. You can change your Vsync option, though.
b) Audio
You will be faced by two possibilities: change your SFX and music volume. That's it. No way turning on subtitles, no choice of sound quality whatsoever. This is just poor!
c) Controls
While you are able to change certain buttons, you will find yourself in the situation, that *reload* and *use* are assigned to one and the same button. No way of changing that. I am asking: Why? We own keyboards with more buttons than only 12. Laziness strikes again! There also seems to be a rudimental port option featuring aim assist. Other than that, there is no way to lie down or to check a box if you want to be in ironsights permanently or while clicking the RMB.
First of all, I have to mention the horrible texture work all over the game,
. This and the fact that some textures are not in place at all makes me furious about the obviously lazy devs. I would, without joking, compare those textures to Half Life 1, which came out in 1998! Remember, that Singularity came out a few months after Metro 2033 in 2010. Neither from an atmospheric nor a graphical aspect I can't understand people who compare those games. They have nothing in common. In fact, it is an insult for the devs of A4 Games.
I mean, Singularity has its atmospheric peaks here and there (
) but they are immediately destroyed by following "level design choices". I am talking about absent dynamic lights or objects (not even a flashlight,
), washed-out sky textures, which look frozen and unreal and cheap weather effects (e.g. rain).
It's the same with the leveldesign. It is okay for the most part, nothing extraordinary. But there are so many moments where you will encounter unfinished structures and missing details (e.g. cut-off cables stop mid air and aren't modelled correctly). Unfortunately, there is some kind of physics engine, which is presented rarely. But when you encounter it, boxes will be flying around if you touch them or objects will get stuck and so on. It is super frustrating and happens at random! Other objects, like curbs, debris, bunsen burner nets, door handles, etc block you constantly. Mid-fight this is deadly and overall it is very disturbing to just get stuck in the middle of a room. You will get stuck randomly 1/3 rooms on average.
This brings me to the games linearity (LOTS of poorly scripted events though), which does not have to be a bad thing. But this games crams it so far down your throat, that you just want to spit out. Invisible walls every other step, you aren't allowed to jump simple obstacles (like railings), there is no back tracking (doors magically close, invisible walls appear, etc) and there is massive hand holding, when following a fellow NPC. Just terrible and annoying. Unexcusable. On the other hand, you might be allowed to wander off the trail for a few paces: Take a corridor with several doors and one additional opens up for you to have ammo, health or E99 (coming to that later). So, searching in a very limited fashion is rewarded and present.
The game is a FPS in a classic fashion which has a focus on arcade gameplay (lots of medipacks, ammunition, buffs, guns, loads of enemies) that reminded me of Serious Sam and Wolfenstein at moments (just the arcade aspect!). If this was executed well, I would not have a problem with that. But the main thing that is terrible, is the KI. Enemies move as slow as if they were in slow motion, they run into walls for seconds and can see you through same. Why
will stay a mystery to me. Many enemies (
) are literally bullet sponges, including bosses - this is just something you should avoid, except for boss fights. They spice up the gameplay!
At least there is variation in enemy design (at least optically), but fighting feels dull. You can wait in any corner you like for enemies to approach and pick them off one by one (dying animations do not vary a lot with most enemies) without being in real danger. It only gets dangerous when you need to heal, because you will slow down even more (yes, sprinting feels like you are dragging your boots through mud) and only heal 33% of your helath with a forevertaking animation, often leading to death by default.
Besides standard guns (shotgun, pistol, assault rifle, etc), there are specials. One of which is the time traveling glove (see below) nourished with
atoms (called E99), which also serve as a means of payment for upgrades. Yes, you actually can upgrade yourself (health boost, accuracy, etc - also from blueprints you find) and your guns, which is an admirable system, although it has been in games (Dead Space) before. But a nice feature nonetheless. Unfortunately, weapon sounds and animations are not at the technical level of 2010 when the game came out and sound/look just awful (again: HL1 like).
- pretty much a spoiler!
Now the tough question after all that what feels like negative superiority. Would I recommend it? There is just so much clunky mechanics and minor mistakes combined with visible laziness that adds up to an infuriating melting pot of emotions. On the other hand, if you are only out for mindless and average designed FPS action, this might be something for you. As I expected more of this game, especially because of its praise in magazines and by other players, I can not recommend it. There is just too much missing, which I saw in games like Metro 2033, Half Life 2 or other story driven experiences with a character of linearity. I am not gonna put points on this game, because interest of players might differ too much.

A wonderfully crafted card-based RPG, fans of old tabletop games like D&D, or Magic the Gathering will find much enjoyment in Lucadian Chronicles. Beginning the game as the green faction, you take the role of rebels attempting to defend their forest home against encoraching foes. As the chapters progress you'll eventually play as each of the different teams, white for air, red for fire, and blue for water. A black faction exists but they represent death and are the ultimate foe; they become so powerful that all of the other factions eventually put aside their differences to unite against them.
The storyline is good, if not a little bland but the game is definitely one that you'll complete multiple times for additional cards and coins: one of the most fun aspects is that with each new victory the game awards golden coins that may be used to 'purchase' booster packs of cards to add to your army. This allows you to have a truly customizable experience that will suit any play style. You may also play against online opponents in multiple ways, such as a four player match, or a competition of dozens of other live opponents from around the globe.
A fun, competitive game with artwork this beautiful and music this enjoyable a rich experience is to be had in Lucadian Chronicles.
+Complex and rewarding strategy game
+Novel 'booster pack' mechanic is exciting
+High replayability
+Fantastic artwork and sound
+Story could have been a little longer
+Option to play as the death faction needed

I'm 20 hours into the gameplay and enjoying it very much.  (The solo campaign demo, free, took about 5 or 6 hours and it was easier than the later stages.)  I normally play turn based strategy games like Civ 5, so this game has a much lighter and more casual feel, but it's still very intellectually engaging.   It's mostly a card game with a loose framework of a storyline and a fantasy campaign setting.  The gameplay where you will be spending 90-95% of your time is somewhere between tactical combat and puzzle solving.  I find myself saying things like "Well, that didn't work, maybe I will try deploying my berserker opposite that elven archer, so he will lose some HP and start attacking more vigorously, because I need their ghouls to die before their skeletons so they don't keep getting hit point boosts..."  and "Dammit, the fire tribe engineer can't be placed next to the air-aligned ballista to repair it."   Also, "I'm stuck on the campaign map, I just don't have enough 1-point cards to fill out a solid team after choosing my best vampire leader and the armor cracker and the druid.  Even after trying all the different spells I still can't bring down their healer fast enough.  So I guess it's time to go PVP to build up some more gold and buy more cards."   Some other reviewers have criticized the art; it's admittedly an odd mix of "old masters", anime, and classic dark fantasy art.  But, for less than $10, this is a great buy.  Lots of fun, thought provoking gameplay.   A very smooth, bug-free gaming experience, both PVE and PVP.  Check it out!

When I saw this, I thought "Cool a CCG!". Then I found out it's one of those where you don't interact during battles. And then I found out it's actually not a card game at all.
What is it though? It's a strategical combat puzzle game, where you place up to 5 characters with different stats and special skills in a specific formation in order to fight an opposing team. You don't interact during the battle, it automatically plays out following specific rules. So the gameplay consists of figuring out a good team combination and and formation to overcome your opponents. Thanks to pretty interesting mechanics and a good variety of very different characters this is a surprisingly interesting task.
tl;dr: This game is probably not what you expected, but it's actually pretty good at what it does.

Starbound...a game that seemed to be in development for an eternity.  Unfortunately, by the time it was released, I no longer cared about it.  Still, I decided to give the finished product a try, and I'm sorry to say there are more bad points than good points.
The new intro and storyline seem like an afterthought which was tacked on to the game because it "needs" a story.  I much preferred the simplicity of the early access game to the final version.
The combat mechanics, whilst they're supposed to be simplistic in a game like this, just don't work for me.
Melee weapons are, pardon the pun, hit and miss in terms of effectiveness.  I find myself mashing the mouse buttons and running away, rather than feeling like my fighting is effective.  Ranged weapons are useless for anything other than single targets.  Unless you get a ridiculously overpowered ranged weapon, you might as well not bother.
I find that the interface gets in the way all the time and halts the momentum of the game.  Moving an item from a container to my inventory shouldn't be a click fest.  It should be painless and the bread and butter of a sandbox game.
Starbound...A time sink, definitely, but unfortunately not an enjoyable one.

This is an open world action adventure brawler set in the Lord of the Rings universe with one of the most unique and interesting gameplay mechanics I've seen in a video game: the Nemesis System.
The world is populated with randomly generated uruks, each of which has different strengths and weaknesses, such as immunity to ranged attacks, or fear of fire.
You'll need to work around these strengths and weaknesses to defeat these enemies, as they can be tough, and killing them is the only way to obtain gear upgrades.
They also remember encounters with you, if you defeat a nemesis with an arrow to the eye for example, you may encounter them later with an eyepatch, and they'll have dialogue referencing this.
Each time you win or lose a fight with one of them, they'll grow stronger, gaining more strengths and losing weaknesses, which can lead to some really powerful enemies near the end of the game.
Gameplay itself is a mix between the batman arkham series' freeflow combat and assassin's creed's parkour.
Story is passable, but enough to keep you interested.
Visuals are very good, even for a 2 year old game.
In my opinion the game is worth playing for the nemesis system alone, however the other elements of the game mostly good as well, and it often gets heavily discounted in sales.
Overall I'd say this is an 8.5/10

The first episode is free, so take a look see. It has a classic plot of a crime drama, with some weird tie in with a British drama. It plays out in many ways as a classic 80's or 90's crime drama but the British drama angle, the plot ties in a "everyone has a secret". While I didn't expect the writers of Ten Days in the Valley to show their cards so early with the first episode, it may prove that later episodes add in a significant twist.
The plot has interesting parallels between the fictional story (or so it seems) that the main character is writing for a fictional TV series, and the one we watch play out through our "TV" episodes of Ten Days in the Valley.
It would also appear that the series wasn't cut out from a TV production, as it has no notable fades for advertisements. In many ways it does feel like it's an "Indie" series. Perhaps it could just be my comparison between a web series and series found on cable TV.
Anyways, give the first episode a try, it's free, and see if you come to the same conclusion.

Good god, if you're not playing this game, something is seriously wrong with you.

Ok, ok...details...
The interface is beautiful and very, very intuitive. It's the tiny details like when a small scroll rolls out in the corner of the screen for a few moments it's clickable; or when you scroll the map around the player portraits show along the edges..and are clickable; the inventory lets you select characters and equip items between them without having to perform tedious item management between characters; everything about the interface is well considered, and perfectly implemented - including resizing the dialogue box in the corner, and hovering over the combat commands that have been executed shows the calculations in a tooltip - it's a perfect.
The music is evocative, reminiscent of Baldur's Gate, Dragon Age: Origins, Icewind Dale etc.

This is a beautifully designed, emotional game. Along with an interesting story, gorgeous music, and dazzling artwork, this game has a ton of fun weapons to choose from and enemies to slay. Now I really want Transistor!

Maaaan, how come It took me over 5 years to find this piece of art in Steam Store? Oh well, alright, I'm getting to the review:
Story:
I do want to avoid spoiling anything, so I'll just leave a little bit of that here.
You play as a character that is being refered to as "The Kid", setting off on a journey to redo some things the calamity that hit your world has taken away. The whole story is being told throughout the game as you advance further.
Gameplay:
You move with the Kid throughout the levels as in the any other game, WASD keys, the levels are platforms set up in middle of nowhere, just high up in the sky most of the time. The platforms automatically build themselves infront of you when you get close. The combat system is what is really shining in this game, most of the weapons are equally powerful, there is not one being largely stronger than another, and you can wield 2 weapons at once. One weapon's attacks done by mouse 1, and the other's by mouse 2. Apart from that you can also use your special abilities, such as being able to go invisible, to throw a grenade, to shield yourself and deflect the damage...
Bastion is a 3rd person RPG that comes in with fighting some monsters, the monsters have various kinds of abilities and weaknesses, so a different weapon might come in handy against each of them.
There are 3 modes you can play at the beginning of the game, easy, normal, and no-sweat mode. Easy is easy, normal is normal, no-sweat makes you unable to die in the game, being infinitely able to stand back on your feet when you're defeated, I guess that's something for those that just want to play for the story.
There is a leveling system, allowing you to reach up to level 10. Each level unlocks you a new distillery slots, you can fill those slots with various brews that will give you buffs in the fights such as mitigating the damage you take by 15%, being able to carry 2 extra healing potions, guaranteed critical hits when your HP is less than 33% and so on.
You can also upgrade your weapons if you gain enough crystals that are gained from completing various quests, defeating enemies, or just breaking stuff around the map. You also need special forge materials that you can find across maps, buy for crystals in lost and found building, or gain in training grounds where you're supposed to see how good you are using that specific weapon you'd want to upgrade.
You can also activate some blessings of the in-game's gods in a place called shrine... You thought blessings would make you stronger? Wrong! Although you get extra crystal drop rates from every blessing (there are 10 blessings that you can have all active at once), your enemies also become stronger. They can get buffs like health regeneration base on the blessings you activate. The shrine is not there to help you, as the game without the blessings is quite easy. It is there to make the game more challenging/fun for you.
Game's art:
The graphics are well-made and fitting the game, there's nothing much to say about it. Visually, the game is doing right what it is supposed to do. And yet, even a rusty graphics card like mine can run the game without issues.
Bastion's music is a music that no other recent game has, although some of the tunes reminded me of Rayman 2 and similar older games a little, it still is different. I know many games like Bastion have great soundtracks, but this one is really compared to those other games.
But there's something else, that is abnormally good, and I've never experienced something this good at any kind of game before. The narration. The voice was really appealing to me.
Summary:
Pros
-Great, addictive story. Makes you want to finish the game on one playthrough.
-Perfect combat system
-Great graphics, yet even an old GPU can run the game with no trouble
-Idea of how the game's terrain is presented is amazing
-Best narrations I've ever seen in a game
-Amazing music
-Has a difficulty allowing you to play the game just for the story
-On the normal difficulty, with all the shrine idols involved, trying to complete everything in the game (achievements included), I can certify you'll have over 10 hours of fun.
Cons
-Literally nothing, unable to think of any
My final words:
I've bought the game for 2.99€ when it was on discount, and although I wanted to spend them on something else, I do not regret I did not do that. I'm pretty sure I've already expressed how much I love the game above in the review, so I don't think continuing to compliment it is neccessary. If you're fan of this kind of games, I don't think there's any need to hesitate about buying Bastion, especially if the game is on discount.

This is an open world action adventure brawler set in the Lord of the Rings universe with one of the most unique and interesting gameplay mechanics I've seen in a video game: the Nemesis System.
The world is populated with randomly generated uruks, each of which has different strengths and weaknesses, such as immunity to ranged attacks, or fear of fire.
You'll need to work around these strengths and weaknesses to defeat these enemies, as they can be tough, and killing them is the only way to obtain gear upgrades.
They also remember encounters with you, if you defeat a nemesis with an arrow to the eye for example, you may encounter them later with an eyepatch, and they'll have dialogue referencing this.
Each time you win or lose a fight with one of them, they'll grow stronger, gaining more strengths and losing weaknesses, which can lead to some really powerful enemies near the end of the game.
Gameplay itself is a mix between the batman arkham series' freeflow combat and assassin's creed's parkour.
Story is passable, but enough to keep you interested.
Visuals are very good, even for a 2 year old game.
In my opinion the game is worth playing for the nemesis system alone, however the other elements of the game mostly good as well, and it often gets heavily discounted in sales.
Overall I'd say this is an 8.5/10

Great start for an early access game, but I the game could be more dynamic. I've seen many suggestions for bigger islands, making the sharks more aggressive, and making the shelters and camp fires actually help you by keeping you from getting sick.

I think these are good suggestions, but the one big fix that would help, and be fairly easy to implement at this point, are disasters. There's so much potential, and it would make structures and rafts all the more essential. There would be tsunamis that swell up and cause you to abandon your stuff and get onto the raft, which might then cause you to be lost at sea for a day. There could be monsoons that knock your hut over, or scatter your store of coconuts into the shark infested waters.
Another awesome addition would be the opposite of disasters: the possibility of getting rescued. You may see a plane flying above, and unless you picked up the flare gun and shoot it within the plane's field of vision, It would just be a lost cause. You might also see a cargo ship if you're out at sea, and be able to track it down with a fire. Of course, these instances would be very rare.
These additions would make the game a lot more playable, and add more ups and downs to what ever narrative the player takes away from playing the game.

Perhaps one of the best zombie games of all time with different modes providing something for everybody. Unlike other zombie games, all zombies are player controlled, this removes the issues surrounding dumb AI and really creates the air that you
being hunted (but can create issues surround rage quitters/afkers). At the start of each match, a proportion of the players are assigned the starting zombies (assuming that too few choose to be), after this, any player joning will automatically be assigned as a zombie and any survivor who dies will become a zombie. This can lead to a snowball effect where, from a single zombie, a horde can decend upon the last few survivors as they make their last stand. Zombies generally respawn when they die unless the mode type is where they have a finite number of lives and the objective is to kill them all.
Survivors start each match with a pistol and a melee weapon, throughout the maps lay various weapons such as shotguns and automatic rifles (and the ammo) that can greatly help in taking out the zombies. A weight system keeps track of how much you are carrying and adjusts your running speed accordingly, you also have a stamina bar that lowers as you run and subsequently will also slow you down. These two mechanics are there to try and reduce gun/ammo hording, if you are slow then you are zombie bait. Staying together, covering each other and ammo sharing is a must though there is no mechanic that forces you to stay with the group.
Zombies have a simple melee attack, in each team there is a single special inffected that has slightly greater health, deals more damage and infects survivors (they then change into zombies after a while). Ambushes are the name of the game usually for zombies until the late game where a horde of zombies can simple rush the survivors.
The relative difficulty of playing either survivor or zombie varies greatly with each map and the mode of play, while you will inevitable gain more kills as a survivor (even though you have a single life per match), an experienced player can still rack up the kills as a zombie with each one giving you the satisfaction in knowing that your horde is growing.
Personally, my favourite mode is the objective mode where survivors are given a series of tasks to complete to attain victory, a good map to try would be Biotec. The survivor modes task you with surviving untill either a timer runs out or the zombies run out of respawn lives (which one of these two depends on the map), two maps that are popular are Cabin and Church. There is also a competitive mode for team warfare but this is played little.
This mod has been out a very long time, as such the graphics tend to be reasonble poor but this game isn't about staring over a well rendered valley. It is about getting out there and killing as much as you can, whether that is getting those headshots or feasting on your opponents brains, it is up to you.

Magic the Gathering's *better* half.
1. You can no longer be land screwed, for one, since you always have the option to put down land.
2. The living battlefield: There are actually quite a few games which are "M:tG but with a battlefield" type games out there.  Faeria's mana wells add interesting strategic considerations. If you rush, you give up extra faeria (mana) from the faeria wells. If you go for the Faeria wells, you aren't advancing on the enemy. You could go for a balnced route instead, sticking to either left or right field. In short, those Faeria wells actually add a lot of strategic depth to the game.
Very recommended.... but keep in mind it is still a collectible card game on an online platform! You can never trade cards with other players, and you are expected to fork out real money eventually if you want to enjoy the game fully and start building your own decks. If that doesn't sound like money you want to spend, walk away from this genre altogether.

Good "one-more mission" game. Imagine a Mount and Blade clone (open-world, go from village to village to hire new villagers or buy cheap merchandise to sell in the city, meeting and combatting bandits on the way, etc) but tactical turn-based and without your own character in the game. I like the art style, and each character has its own personality. Everything (or maybe almost everything?) is procedurally generated, so you won't have the same game twice.

I've never seen a game with this much RNG that is this boringly uniform and monotone. There are around 10 different fights you'll encounter in this game, and there is essentially one strategy to win that you rinse repeat until the RNG wipes your company in a situation you have little to no control over. If, however, you enjoy the kind of game where you constantly run into enemies that are either pathetically weak compared to you and therefor a waste of resources to fight (and also really boring), or wildly strong for you and close to unkillable (not to mention infuriating), then you should buy this game.
The bell curve is fun/interesting if you like mindless grinding, but the second you understand this game you may as well stop playing.

There's a bellcurve to the game. Once you figure out the XCOM on steroids level difficulty and get yourself into a decent position in the world, you realize that there's really not a whole lot of variety. There's only a handful of missions, most of which are basically just "hunt down that guy over there and kill em."
I didn't find any interesting pre-built combat maps like a cave or something obvious that they could've thrown in there for special quest battles.
Feels like a great all around concept game where they had like ten ideas and didn't see any of them to completion. Basic stuff like trying to figure out the stats of characters you hire before you hire them, weapon stats before purchase [I'm not spending four hours of gameplay gold to find out if that armor is really worth it] and the finicky morale system all feel unfinished.
Even the max level perks were very "Whatever". I understand there's 12-20 characters in your party, but the only actual story you get out of most of them is a paragraph once in a while about one character interacting with another.
I got my money out of it, but I wouldn't buy it again.

Far too difficult in the early game to recommend this clunker.  A casual player will not enjoy this game.  A serious gamer will also probably not enjoy this game unless they really enjoy grinding and saving the game before every action.  I am not sure who this game is for; it's frustrating, mission pay does not cover mission expenses, enemies will outnumber and outgun you, and your game will end quickly via violent death, starvation, or desertion.  The economics of the world are just bad.  Making a living via trade isn't possible, you will get lucky from time to time selling high, but it will never pay enough or be steady enough to make a difference.  You will spend 3000 to hire and equip a party for a mission that pays 300.  There is no game balance, it is almost a certainty that your party, even a brand new I-just-started-the-game party, will run into a random group of enemies that are two to three times their number and fully equipped with excellent armor and weapons.  A brand new player can, on his first day, absolutely run into an enemy that can kill a member of their party with each swing.  If you enjoy role-playing games where your level one warrior wearing dirty rags and wielding a rusty old sword can run into a ancient fire-breathing dragon and six of his larger friends just outside of Newbie Town on his first day, this is a game you will enjoy!  I would give this game a hard pass, absolutely not recommended.
