On the other hand if you are philanthropic and looking to support the vision of this game, or indie development then getting early access may be for you.    In it's present state it's not really a game at all and certainly not a $50 dollar game. I was part of the initial kickstarter campaign, and I'm gratified to finally start seeing some things come together now to they point you can see just what this game may actually be like when it's finished.     That being said there's no game here yet, just a lot of promise.

I love this project. And I believe that it will overcome a thorny path from idea to finished project.

You are moving from one cutscene to the next but in betwen you have to shoot a bunch of guys, and maybe press a special key at a special time.

Black Ops had none of that.  It is a traning exercise where the targets that appear out of nowhere happen to move around a bit.

If I were to pick one word to describe Bastion, it would be "quaint".
Bastion has everything it needs to be a fun, unique experience to kill the time- the definition of a good game- without anything else. One could argue that this is a negative, as it truly does just have the bare essentials, and at times the game feels a bit more like an interactive story than a game, but for me it's a positive. In a day and age where game companies are in the great graphics-race, tossing aside any focus on a game's actual mechanics and fun in exchange for trying to one up the competition on which "looks better"; and in a similar manner indie developers abusing the once great concept of early-access to put out half finished games without repercussions, all I ever really ask for is just a well put together game that I find enjoyable and isn't the same rehashed experience with a different style. Bastion delivered this for me.
I got Bastion on sale but I can easily recommend the game even at it's full price, to anyone that's not specifically looking for an action packed fast paced experience. Some notable things about the game are it's great sound track and use of stylization in it's visuals, so if you're a fan of soft, calming music or vibrant colours, that'll be a bonus for you.
Overall I'll give Bastion a 9/10. There were only minor things I didn't like, and I couldn't honestly say they actually bothered me.

If you can get this game on sale and you're a fan of tactical combat, go for it. But beware. The game is very repeitive, and very hard. Apart from the early game quest and end game crisis, the coregameplay consists of traveling around doing side quests and killing roving enemies, slowly upgrading your gear and characters as you go. It never really chagnes, and there are only a few enemy types, though fighting humans versus orcoids versus undead and various beats is very different.
The combat system is more restricting and far less forgiving than other turn base tacticals you may have played. With every strike aimed against even your most powerful fighters, there is a chance your well laid formation/plan will be outdone by an unlucky decapitation. Your troops are vulnerable and it requires planning and tricks to win even easy fights without losing large amounts of men.
There are slightly different ways of fighting different enemies, but every fight tends to devolve into the same; form a shield wall with spears in the center to intercept enemies. Put your archers behind your shields to send shots into unshielded enemies. once contact is made, pick off strong enemies with your two hander wielding men and use your hand+shield men to close the flanks. Sourround and cut down the enemy. Repeat. Almost every fight is like that.
If you are a fan of this genre of game, then this is worth it if you can get it on sale. Its good for a few weekends. If you are not a veteran of turn based tacticals games, you will not have fun with this.

Basically what all the other reviews said is true. RNG is stupid in this one. Like, really stupid. There are times when you will be missing over and over depite an 80%+ chance to hit. Here's the mindset I recommend you have going into this game: Don't worry about losing a guy or two, they come cheap and are easily replaced unless they're a super high level;  expect bad RNG, going in expecting the worst is your best bet for a healthy playthrough; be patient on learning how it goes, took me probably 10+ hours before I got the hang of it and started winning every battle with ease.

If you consider that this game is eleven years old, it's not that bad. Sure, the animations are a bit wonky by today's standards and the highest available resolution is 1024x768, but the game runs at  smooth 60fps at my crappy lappot with stuff going on in the background.
This game wins my heart because of its setting and story. There is no other game in which you can stealth around Charnobyl, Kremlin AND Lubyanka. The AI is good as well, it is not perfect, but enemies will seek cover during firefights instead of standing in the middle of the room like bunch of idiots. They are not pansies too, they were trained in the Glorious Soviet Union, so they hurt. Really hurt.
The crafting system is good, I have no idea how Carter knows how to make a mine out of a can and three bullets, but it works in the game and is balanced, so I won't dig much. Maybe he was trained by the CIA after all... The 'camera' is a great gameplay tool as well.
There are of course some bad things. Apart from a bit dated visuals, which do not look bad if you ask me, the missions in which you control Comrade Grushkov are in my opinion the worst. Sure, I get it, he's a soldier so he does not sneak around, but in one of 'his' levels the enemies literally spawn in front of you. This also happens in one place towards the end of the campaign. All in all, the final few missions are IMO worse than the rest of the game, but your milage may wary.
All in all, for the asking price of 5EUR, and possibly even lower if you consider buying this on sale, it gives you a solid campaign with very unusual setting and challenging gameplay. I've finished the story in 7 hours on normal, but I've played the game at least twice few years ago, so I still remembered what to do and where to go.
TL;DR: If you're not terrified of dated visuals and have few bucks lying around, give it a try.

I think it stands as testament to how many years I've spent playing first person shooters that I can pick out all of Singularity's techniques that have been lifted from other games. Singularity's first person shooting mechanics are by and large influenced by Call of Duty with a hint of old-school flair. The time powers are largely bits of Bioshock dressed up with a time-travel vibe. System Shock 2 did its ghosts the same way Singularity does its ghosts. But the problem is with all these lock, stock, and barrel 'inspirations' is that the developers didn't bother to see what made them work, and so the game turns into a ♥♥♥♥ing mishmash of things that don't really work well together.
There's all these cool weapons! But I ended up sticking with the assault rifle/shotgun duo because they are the most expedient at killing soldiers with guns/melee-focused brutes. There's an awful pistol, but I jumped away from that as soon as I got the assault rifle. There's a sniper rifle that acts like the one from Bulletstorm, but you can't store it in your weapon locker for some ludicrous ♥♥♥♥ing reason. There's a railgun with exploding rounds that's way less accurate than a standard railgun. There's a grenade launcher that you can secondary-fire to take manual control of the grenade, but Jesus Christ, I didn't spend all this time in Quake bouncing grenades off of walls and into ugly faces to be nannied by my own gun! These are all weapons with solutions in search of problems that never really materialize.
While this game tries to innovate, it drops the ball in areas where it really shouldn't have. The game is adept at giving you a bunch of help messages and then being completely useless at pointing out exactly where you have to go! Audio logs are 'revolutionized', in that you have to wait in front of an audio log in order to hear it all, which breaks the flow of the game quite a lot. For a game focused around fast-paced running and gunning, it sure has a lot of ♥♥♥♥ing long-winded memos strewn around the place! And they're all information-and-flavor-light variants on "Something weird happened, technobabble technobabble technobabble, ow a mutant ate my arm, humans are the real monsters", etc., etc. The game sure has problems telling its own story, burdening down the player with a half-hour's worth of boring, poorly paced and told exposition before the player finally gets to shoot something. But since nobody pays attention to the story, let's focus on the real problem: The difficulty curve. Bioshock, the game that Singularity is drawing little hearts around in its notebook at school, has a proper difficulty curve and it requires you to stay competitive by ingesting plasmids and upgrading them. And by doing that, you slowly become one of the lunatics of the underwater insane asylum. Singularity, on the other hand, has a flat difficulty curve and its upgrades are just token bonuses. You are still the same old American Kick♥♥♥♥♥SuperCool Super Marine that's getting all the MLG 360 NOSCOPE HEADSHOTS, but you can choose to shave a fraction of a tenth off of your reload time on your shotgun. But if you don't choose to, no biggie! Just plug away! No stakes to raise, you're doing good! Everything is fine, just plug away until your shift's over!
Singularity is a competent game, but it tries to be other games without understanding how those games became their own thing, and then subsequently fails to become its own thing. It's yet another plodding, mediocre mess from the fine folks at Raven Software.

If I were to pick one word to describe Bastion, it would be "quaint".
Bastion has everything it needs to be a fun, unique experience to kill the time- the definition of a good game- without anything else. One could argue that this is a negative, as it truly does just have the bare essentials, and at times the game feels a bit more like an interactive story than a game, but for me it's a positive. In a day and age where game companies are in the great graphics-race, tossing aside any focus on a game's actual mechanics and fun in exchange for trying to one up the competition on which "looks better"; and in a similar manner indie developers abusing the once great concept of early-access to put out half finished games without repercussions, all I ever really ask for is just a well put together game that I find enjoyable and isn't the same rehashed experience with a different style. Bastion delivered this for me.
I got Bastion on sale but I can easily recommend the game even at it's full price, to anyone that's not specifically looking for an action packed fast paced experience. Some notable things about the game are it's great sound track and use of stylization in it's visuals, so if you're a fan of soft, calming music or vibrant colours, that'll be a bonus for you.
Overall I'll give Bastion a 9/10. There were only minor things I didn't like, and I couldn't honestly say they actually bothered me.

This comes with a caveat, but I like the game for the same reason I like Terraria. If you play it without worrying about what it isn't, there is fun to be had in spades. Granted, there are gameplay elements I really wish had been included, but they aren't here, so meh. For what it is, which is nothing more than Terraria in space, the game works.
The caveat? Frustration is legion in this game. Starbound probably has more things potentially wrong with it than many games I've played, even though I'm enjoying playing it. There are graphical glitches galore, even with a decent computer rig. Some of the early gameplay seems dead-set on killing a new player at every opportunity. The most annoying element, however, is how long it takes just to get the main part of the game going, even if you already know what to do beforehand. Having to do five things first just to accomplish one thing is stupid and inefficient. Going on a fetch quest as a main part of what is essentially a tutorial almost killed the enjoyment for me. Just, dude, fix my ship first, and THEN I'll be happy to go do your scut work.
Anyway, I also rerolled my character four times before finding a starting planet that was worth the frustration. Lots of stuff to find and use, with the potential as a quite nice base of operations in the opening hours of play. Hopefully, my experiences will continue to improve from here.
So I recommend the game, but new players with no previous knowledge of this or any other game in this genre should be prepared for as much misery as fun starting out. Once you get some decent weaponry and such, the game does get much easier, and more fun. So enjoy...if you can.
Edit--after more than a year, I still love the main parts of the game, but there are still too many annoying parts to make the game an absolute must-play. It's fun in small doses (and the music is still some of the best I've ever heard), but otherwise, meh.

- Graphics are really good! Animations, art, everything feels better than most of the CCGs out there. Feels that there is actual care with what is put in the game.
- Stuff to do in game is huge and I only remember seeing 2 CCGs with something so extensive. Adventure Mode, Tutorial, Puzzles, PvP, Arena, they got you covered for a big time, buddy.
- Impressive number of cards and strategies! Game started very limited during the early access and even got a few strong and unbalanced cards but after some work they sorted everything and the game feels good. Even some cards that you scream right away
are actually very balanced when you try to use them because of the way the duels flow.
- They give you a ton of stuff just for playing their single player mode and actually finish it. The number is so impressive that not only you learn how the game works while doing it but also get a very decent number of currency and boosters to make a ton of different decks.
- Learning curve. It takes probably more than most of the players would want to spend to play the game. Players that comeback after a while also feel out of the game unless they spend their time in Pandora to learn the game again.
- PvP. It's already good, nothing against it because I love Pandora, but seeing how many unique single player modes the game has, I wonder what more could be done.

The perfect game for generals who always dreamt about commanding their own medieval mercenary company. In a mixture of Mound & Blade world map interactions and XCOM tactic fights, you lead your brothers over the continent and through all kinds of different challenges: From catching a few thieves to taking part in a full-scale war, while seeing them grow from simple peasents with pitchforks to shiny knights in impenetrable armor.
Just two things to consider for potential customers:
- The game is hard to learn, even harder to master and does not have a state-of-the-art tutorial (just a few youtube videos). But if you invest a few hours time to get into it you will be rewarded with an exciting masterpiece of a game.
- The game takes time. While you usually manage to build up a reasonable company within a few hours it will take you a long time to build up a really good team with the best equipment to finally face the three endgame crises. It took me ~80 hours to "complete" the game just in Beginner, without ironman mode.
For the developers:
I would like to see some more late-game content for upcoming DLCs or successor games. The seconds half of my 80 hour playthrough I just spent hunting for unique weapons and armor and fighting off endless hordes of orcs and undead while the speed in which my brothers became stronger decreased a lot compared to the beginning (unless they died of course). Some more interesting battle sites like the black monolith (but a bit easier, please!) or other opportunities to spend the money on (maybe an own castle for my mercenaries to build and improve?) would be really nice and tempt me on further playthroughs.

Important: MUCH RICHER STRATEGIC learning: Why is this important, because there is a method to everything in the game you must learn. Caravans leading to legendary items, Taverns gossip and great morale boost, How to switch weapons mid fight to earn great items, proper specific builds that use their job trait, like a Thief Dagger killer with high dodge, or HeadHunter w Flails, how to buy low and sell high, yes those copper and goat cheese matter. Proper trait allignment. Take notes, know your towns and cities and how to use your inventory. So much deeper than just roaming.
CONS:
1.	Sorry there are some, very complicated game with rules and a brutal learning curve. It will frustrate even the most expert player, and anger the beginners. You may start over again and again early if you don't learn fast. Why you ask, because of the lack of tutorial. Though I see there are more added, and discussion helps. You should not have to go to school for an hour before you play. Con for me, However, once you truly learn. You will go batty.
2.	Its simplistic strength is also its vast weakness. I wish this was more like Mordheim or Dungeons and Dragons in its modeling execution. The fact that its hex isometric and old style hurts its over all visionary outlook. As a player, you never feel fully engaged in the storyline and the lack of inner game beauty hurts the over all appeal. You want to draw the player inside the game. Not watch overhead. For example, the Hill up and down option is counter productive and annoying. A feature the player should never have had to worry about. Who knows, maybe BB2 will be vastly more developed in its look and appeal.
3.	The lack of voice overs, flashes, and story modes can make reading things for the vision impaired a nightmare. Would have liked to see a UI overall customization added to make small text and numbers that are so small more visual to the eye. What was that percentage hit number, 17? Make that huge man, wear are my mag glasses. The fact that you really do not see the traits in play hurt.
4.	There is a redundancy that plays too safe for this game, ok I got it, mission, walk over, slice-slice, collect, ok mission, walk over, hack-hack, and on and on that will eventually make players go elsewhere. Game needed more depth and story complexity.
5.	The inventory can get a little clunky and disorganized and even moving it into order can get tedious. Darn it I had all my food in a row. Why you! There is too much opening and closing of screens for my liking. Having a sort helps but takes away the organized gamer. That may not be a good thing when you accidently BUY something THREE times because you didn't know you already had it.
Important: It is a con for me. If any game has the potential for Multi player option its Battle brothers. I could have seen 4-8 player matches and the fact that it does not have a multi player option hurts. However, that could change in the future with additional content or the next version of the game. Some may not care about Multi player, not for everyone, but a nice option to consider.
OVERALL: Battle Brothers is a fun game. It has a lot of fun things that if you have the time will get you pumped. For a first-time developer a nice effort and a game that can be built on. I do think other developers will pick this up and even under another theme do it and execute it vastly superiorly, but Battle Brothers does get the blood going. I would recommend seeing the VIDEO above discussion to see the actual gameplay before you buy. Get it on sale, because the regular price is too high for the content.
I would also caution even if unreal and simplistic animation in its over all view. Battle Brothers is like going to the carnival, going to the whack a mole machine, except when you hit them they explode to goo. Something parents may get turned off on for their younger kids. Teens and Adults will not care, but youngies? Don't say I did not warn ya lads!.  A positive review, but I caution the cons.

If Assassin's Creed and The Batman Arkham games had a love child, this would be it.
The game takes place in the fantasy world of Middle-Earth, which is of course the same world in the Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit books and movies.
Firstly, if you're thinking that you need to have read/seen the material BEFORE playing this game, you needn't worry. There are definitely references, or characters you may not appreciate as much going in with no or little knowledge, but you won't mind as the story explains it pretty well, and you can of course just look something up if you want to know more.
The core gameplay is, as I said, like Assassin's Creed/Batman Arkham games. You'll be climbing, sneaking, avoiding detection much like Assassin's Creed, and the combat system is definitely like the Arkham games, but you're not knocking out baddies, you're here to kill some Orcs!
The world is semi-open world, by that I mean the map isn't HUGE (there are actually TWO maps in the game), but there always is something going on. The world also doesn't demand you do something right away, so if you want to begin just killing some orcs in a camp, or getting some collectables, you CAN.
When you complete quests, or get collectable, you get an in-game currency wherein you can buy upgrades such as more health or rune slots for your weapon (more on that in a moment). You will also earn XP from these things, or just killing orcs.
Now, as I mentioned the game lets you augment your weapons (sword/bow/dagger) with runes! Each rune varies depending on level and rarity. Some let you get health from a stealth kill, or have a chance to get some more arrows with a certain type of kill, and so on. You can sell them for money if you don't want to use them, and switch them out as you like.
One of the most amazing, if not THE most amazing thing, is Sauron's Army and the random generation of enemies. Throughout the world, there are regular grunt Orcs, and then there's higher level ones. Now, you may run into any of these at any given time, story missions not withstanding.
For example, you might be going after some orcs in a camp, and then suddenly one of them yells "MAN FILTH!" at you, followed by a mini-exchange where he taunts you, and you realize this is captain or general, and you had NO idea. Each special orc has their own strengths and weakenesses, which you can use to your advantage, meaning you can't always go in sword swinging.
For instance, one captain may be immune to arrows, so you can't snipe him off, so it must be up close...but he also be immune to stealth, so you can't sneak up on him either, meaning you'll have to confront him directly, and he mah not be alone. This is just ONE example.
I've had many times where I went after ONE captain, and suddenly THREE more appeared out of nowhere! Then this small fight you were starting turns into a massacre if you don't get away. These moments are both frustrating and exciting.
Another thing with this system is that if a grunt orc, with no name previously, kills you, he ranks up becoming a captain, and if a ranked orc kills you over and over, he becomes even MORE powerful, and his weaknesses get less, and he has more strengths, constantly making you want to kill him, he'll even taunt you over having failed to kill him!
The collectables are mostly backstory, or side stories to give you a bit of flavor for the world. You get about 50 monies for  each one you pick up, along with achievements if you're interested.
The game constantly challenges you, and the more you die, the more challenging it can get, but you also can level up yourself with new abilities so you can level the playing field.
There is certainly more, but even getting all the collectables, I have over 20 hours into it, and I'm not done with it either, and I haven't even begun the DLC.
So, if you're looking for a really amazing game where you can play so many different ways, and even replaying it will be different, Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is an excellent choice, one you won't regret.
If you know nothing about the world, you'll love it all the same, and if you enjoy Lord of the Rings or The Hobbit, you can appreciate references here and there as well. So, get out there, and to quote Aragorn: "Let's hunt some orc!"

Cold War is a 2005 made, parodic stealth action game. It is some kind of 3rd person view No One Lives Forever with hand-made gadgets which starring a journalist. It was really good first. I even planned to recommend it to you, but then, i got bored because of some problems and changed my mind. There are some summarized pros. and cons. below:
+ Story is interesting enough
+ Graphics are already outdated but it isn't ugly at all.
+ Some unique attractions like gadget crafting and X-Ray camera
No widescreen support. Control scheme a little bit weird and dull, but somewhat useful as well. Especially setting your walking speed with mouse wheel is a good idea. Music is OK but repetitive.
- Stealth is a little bit dull. You can't do so much actions for best stealth results. Furthermore, at the last half of the game, say goodbye to stealth.
- Characters you control can't run. They pretend to do so but they seems like they are taking a stroll on the park. Any NPC runs well though.
- Aiming is bad. You can't change shoulders while aiming, so, time by time you can't see the target properly.
- You're playing on same locations over and over again.
- Planting gadgets like mines is deceptive. You have to stop the desired plant location first, then you have to highlight the gadget on the menu and left click to insta-plant.
- Background sound effects are annoying.
- A frustrating bug on Meltdown level ( spoiler:
)
After all, it worth for $1,25 but don't expect too much. Especially after the last half, quality of the game started to decrease in my humble opinion.

Journal
Day 1 - Crash landed in the middle of the ocean. Paddled all night in that life boat until I reached an island. It looks like it has enough coconuts and even potato plants to keep me alive, and I still have my knife and lighter (I could really go for a smoke right now). It looks like it'll be night soon, and I could use some shelter. Time to gather what I can.
I don't remember if I even enjoyed that drink. I hope I did, because it looks like it's going to be a while before I get another. Boss is going to kill me when he finds out I'm alive and I lost my laptop.
Day 2 - Didn't sleep. Couldn't find a spot where I didn't sink into the wet sand, or have tiny bits of vegetation scratching at me.  I've managed to bind together some basic tools using sticks, rocks, and strips of a yucca plant (who knew being a Scout would actually come in handy one day); an axe and a hammer. With these I should be able to make... something.... I have cut down most of the trees on my island and I'm now sitting on a rather large pile of logs, sticks and leaves.
Discovered a small family of crabs, and a wrecked boat off the coast had some medicine in a cabinet and a compass in a box. I paddled my raft to it. Not brave enough to swim.
Day 3 - Still no sleep. I'm becoming irritated. No sleep and that DAMN sun! I was so angry I started chopping at a poor, innocent rock only to have it break into little bits. I bound one of the bits onto a stick and made a spear. Well, a spear-like object. I've also managed to make a fire. I cooked a few of the crabs. I ate like a king.
Day 4 - Began constructing a basic hut for shelter. It keeps off the sun and rain, if nothing else. Somewhat, anyway.
A shark has managed to swim into the sand under my island, somehow. He lives under my hut,  and gives me a bump underfoot here and there just to let me know he's there. I've named him Rick.
Crafted a basic leaf-cot to sleep on. It's no Tempurpedic, but it somehow feels like Heaven all the same.
Day 5 - Decided to brave the ocean to catch some fish. Growing tired of the diet of coconut and potato. I managed to catch an Angelfish before a shark appeared. I thought to flee at first, but quickly decided to use my new spear as a weapon. I don't know how many hours I fought that shark, but no matter how many times I stabbed him, he just wouldn't die. I began to use my axe after some time, but still to no avail. I'm ashamed to say I swam back to my island, tail firmly between my legs.
Day 6 - Ate the Angelfish. Turns out it was poisonous. Unfortunate. Medicine seems to be working.
Day 7- Getting homesick. I decided to leave my island and venture to one of those that seem close. I'm on a seperate island as I write this now. It seems lonely here without my hut and Rick to keep me company. I saw a sunken ship just off the island, and investigated. Inside was some medical badages, a bucket, and an engine for a motor. My father taught me a lot about boat motors when I was a boy. If my Scout training can pay off, maybe that knowledge can too.
Day 13 - Been some time since I've written in this. I've begun mapping out the islands with the use of the compass I found. Using the journal pages to draw the map. Sunken ships hold lots of shiny treasures. Still no other parts for that motor, but hey, you never know. I feel dizzy. Been out in the sun too long. Been diving too deep.
Day 20 - I've built a veritable mansion! When they find me, they'll beg to stay with me on my island paradise! Maybe I'll offer them a coconut, or a crab. But not shark meat. That is my trophy; THE FLESH OF MY FOES! Rick takes no offense.

This game has a lot of potential, but it fails for two primary reason: (1) it random number generator (RNG) is atrocious - you will hit your enemies about 30% of the time, and they will hit you about 70% of the time; it is maddening; and (2) there is no map or character editor for this game: everything is random, decreasing your chances of success greatly, especially in the early game.  I cannot recommend this game to anybody for more than $5.  If they patched-in a character editor, I'd probably value it around $7 or $8.  It's just not fun when you cannot win easy battles or advance in the game as a result of some off-balanced RNG.
That said, Battle Brothers does remind me of two of my favorite games: Ogre Battle and Final Fantasy Tactics.  It's different than those two, but that's what it reminds me of.  I like being able to customize individual troops in a large army, and I love turn-based strategy games.  You are able to equip individual members of your crew with armor, shields, and weapons and level them up when they gain enough experience.  You can specialize individual units for roles like ranger, tank, infantry, etc.  This is why I think the game has so much potential.
This game also reminds me a little bit of the trading games like Patrician, Tortuga, and those types of games insomuch as you can buy (or find) certain resources in the game at a lower price and then sell them in a big city for a higher price, making a profit and encouraging that town to do more business with you (like more and better mercenary contracts).  Potential.
Battle Brothers is a challenging game because you have to constantly be aware of the status of your troops.  Each one requires a daily upkeep with food, money, and sometimes medical supplies.  You also have to pay attention to them during the combat sequences because once they die, they are gone.  (You get their gear back, sometimes, but this is a perma-death game.)  This typically frustrates me, as customizing characters usually makes me care about them more; and the odds of success are so low in this game.
This game, in its current state, is a poster child for squandered potential.  It could be a great game.
I can't even think of a game that has a more fun turn-based combat system. This is a must buy if you like turn based games.

Battle Brothers is a really solid title for people interested in replayable sandbox games in a medieval fantasy world with a large dose of danger.  The game is quite difficult and the risk/reward of battle can lead to feelings of total disappointment or the utmost euphoria.
In this game you are the leader of a recently fallen mercenary band and your job is to build it back up.  The main gameplay loop centers around going to townships on a procedurally generated overworld map in search of gear, supplies, recruits, and contracts for a variety of tasks.  Many of the tasks you're hired for will end up putting you in a battle, which takes place on a tactical terrain hex map.
Battle strategy is a book in it's own right.  Turn based strategy with a strong emphasis on cohesion and falling back to plan B, I consider this the thrill of the game.  You might want to look at some Youtubers for help on this, as there are many variables that go into a battle and you want to be certain to tip the odds in your favor when possible.
In the overworld every 100 or so days a crisis will trigger and the game turns into an epic fantasy with a land in peril from one of three potential threats.  Upon ending the crisis another will spawn in 100 days, and all three crises can be experienced in one long, epic game.
The campaign has an OPTION for "Ironman Mode" and the game is NOT "Rogue-like" by default.  In a normal game you can save and load as in most titles.
When I had played a good many rounds of this I began to interest myself with more in-depth strategy and began to seek out what others had been doing via the internet.  What I found was a great number of potential strategies, all with people assuming their skill set had "must have" skills that I never even bothered with.  The amount of ways you can play this game and build your mercenary company are vast and the game is really a masterpiece of replayable procedurally generated strategy as a result of this.  Characters actually have character and you get to know everyone in your group pretty well after a time and you find that you really lament their loss when the time comes.

This is a well-made game, but be aware it's more roguelike than X-Com. NOTE: I'm reviewing this based off of the veteran combat difficulty.
This is an RNG heavy game from your starting world setup, to your starting companions, to future mercenaries, to encounters, to contracts, etc. etc. Despite this, it is unforgiving and brutal. Mistakes cost you your run. RNG costs you your run. Poor economy skills cost you your run.
**PROS**
*    Artwork is gorgeous.
*    Writing is much better than expected for a generated roguelike.
*    Combat is smooth
**CONS**
*    RNG Heavy - RNG can cost you a run which to me is a turn off. If you're a big fan of roguelikes, this may not be a big issue to you.
*    Poor Handling of Microfailures - To me, part of the fun of X-COM and other permadeath games is that you can have these microfailures where key members die and sometimes the potential of a team wipe. It provides consequence for failure but allows you to continue. In this, one death or wrong positioning has a decent chance to wipe your team or do a force retreat which injures all of your team for several days. Effectively making you useless. Might as well restart than spend 4 days draining yourself of bandages, food, and gold trying to heal up. That makes failure less interesting and more tedious. Again, you may like this if you enjoy a lot of roguelikes.
* Lack of Information - One thing that makes tactical games fun is that you have most of the information you need to understand what choices you're making. It's difficult to tell how dangerous an enemy is and whether you should flee or not. It's difficult to tell how dangerous a given mission is.
**Summary**
If you enjoy roguelikes and tactics/srpgs, pick this up right now. If you like roguelikes or tactics/srpgs and aren't sure on the other, pick this up on sale. If you hate the idea of dudes on a grid, the screenshots really should have been enough to dissuade you.

Kane's Wrath marks the end of more than one era. It is one of the last old-school RTS games where the designers had both budget and creative freedom, one of the last full expansions before the days of piecemeal DLC and probably the last great Command & Conquer. It also meant something new in C&C history, namely an add-on dedicated to the Brotherhood of Nod.
Those uninitiated in the lore would do best to start with Tiberium Wars and watching the preceding C&C cutscenes from Youtube. This is to ensure the plot makes at least some sense, not that C&C is meant to make one rethink ones life. The three chapters in the 13-mission campaign happen before, during and after Tiberium Wars thus completing the storyline. Joseph Kucan's Kane is still the greatest FMV villain in gaming history and I will never tire of his superhuman scheming. Carl Lumbly as Brother Marcion is an entertaining Evil Evangelist whereas Natasha Henstridge has blonde hair and says things.
All three factions (the alien Scrin made their entrance in the base game) are further split into three sub-factions all of whom get new toys to conquer the digital Earth with. Not all are equally interesting or receive enough playtime in the campaign but enough changes are made to give the gameplay new freshness. The gameplay itself has stayed the same, of course, with units being built and lost quite quickly. A typical campaign mission does not go past the 30-minute mark and mission design is varied enough to maintain interest throughout. Sights and sounds are good even today, despite all the advancements and changes in hardware, with the deliciously evil unit quotes getting a special mention. There is also the Global Conquest mode, with it's Risk-style metagame built around the skirmishes. It is not greatness but as an added amusement it is worthwhile indeed.
If you downvote this game you are an enemy of NOD, look forward to a knock on your door shortly heratic.

What would you do in a post apocalyptic setting? Be a lone hero, form a group to survive with or maybe hide and wait for the sweet release of death?
is here to help answer that question for you. With little more than the shirt on your back, you will be thrust into life or death situations along with other players trying to survive.
There isn’t much of a story to speak of in
. You spawn as a generic character and after a few hints on newbie island you’re left to fend for yourself in a barren wasteland. All player generated characters look the same, no option to customize or change the gender, and there are no backstories at all. "I don’t even know where in the world I am nor what happened." The non-playable characters also offer no help as all they do is offer to sell you  things, give missions or try to kill you.
Not having a story isn’t necessarily a bad thing. This game is an open world multiplayer game so  the game is what you make of it. If you can find people to play with, you can build up forts and take down tougher enemies. If you can’t find anyone to play with you’ll be wandering around aimlessly, freezing and starving to death. Then, once you die, you’ll lose any items you had on you and wonder why you even bothered. The controls aren't very responsive and you move very slowly, there is also a lot of empty space so expect to be slowly walking through nothingness a lot. Unless you find the car...which might crash because it’s hard to maneuver.
I didn’t get a chance to build anything, I had trouble finding material and even more trouble staying alive. I started the game with a stick that made a good weapon but lost it upon my first death, I couldn’t kill animals food because they moved faster than I did and all I had then was my fist. I finally found a new weapon but was then quickly killed by a nearby monster before I could even get the weapon into my inventory. I’m personally not the biggest fan of open world games but the amount of frustration involved with
plus the lack of other players really made it a chore to play.
Despite any issues with the actual game I might have, I can admit it looks pretty good. You play from a top down perspective and you wonder through the 3D rendered world that has day and night lighting. The screen also changes by adding different tints if you’re hungry or hurt, adding to the urgency of the situation. There just isn’t much to see in the game, however; there are a few safe areas and a few action areas and then empty brown space with maybe a tree or animal if you’re lucky. The game so far has no music, just sound effects but some spooky atmospheric tunes would certainly help players become more immersed.
+ The game is very cheap. You can buy the four pack for only $2.99 and drag your friends into the game.
+ Multiplayer so you can play with others even if none of your friends are around.
+ You can build structures in the game. Create your own fort and hide from enemies and other players.
+ Or you can just attack other players and see who lives the longest in the game.
+ Graphics aren’t bad and I like the day and night change.
+ It has trading cards.
- Unless you do buy the four pack you might not find anyone to play with, the servers are either barely populated or dead depending on which region you choose and the time of day.
- Hats are the only way to make your character look different from other characters and they cost money.
- Too much empty space with nothing to do or see and very little to explore.
- Depends too much on multiplayer, very little reason to play alone.
- Too easy to die and you lose everything unless you managed to squirrel it away.
This game is only in the Early Access phase so I do hope that the finished product will offer more to do and perhaps be more forgiving to players. A nice finished product will hopefully bring more people to the servers and unlock the true potential of this title. In its current state, however, I cannot recommend
unless you grab the four pack and try to make a go at it with friends.
4.5/10

This game went on sale shortly after I finished Splinter Cell: Blacklist, it was on sale for $1.24 and when I saw the video I figured it would just be a low budget version of splinter cell and bought it because it was cheap and mostly for the lulz.
When I actually started playing the game I was pleasently surprised, as it turned out to be a lot more fun than I expected it to be.  My initial impression was mostly correct, this is essentially a low-budget version of splinter cell, but it is done well and if you enjoy stealth games you will probably like this.
The stealth is handled well, you have a visibility meter which shows how visible you are, and you have 4 movement speeds.  The slowest movement speed moves very slow(obv) but the enemies cannot hear you even if you are right behind them and as you increase in speed the enemies will be able to hear you from farther and farther away.  Movement is easily toggled and as you learn the correct distances to which an enemy can hear you, quickly toggling your speed becomes second nature.
You also are kind of a MacGyver, you find junk lying around(cans, plastic bottles, etc etc) and you can use this junk to craft al manner of items which make being stealthy easier and easier.  You unlock blueprints as they game goes on and once you unlock a print you can craft that item if you have the proper junk for it, is is all easily done and very intuititve.  The gadgets overall are very cool, you can make a slingshot and craft all manner of silent ammo for it, you can lay traps for enemies(both quiet and non-lethal to loud and boomy) and you can even create luring devices that will make your enemies plod right into your mine, provided you lay the trap in a dark place.  If you drop a mine in the light the enemies will see it and disarm it.
You also get an x-ray camera weapon which is beyond cool, it lets you see through walls and locate enemies before they can see you, and it even damages enemies through walls, although ammo is limited for it, it is very cool to be able to just blast enemies silently through a wall.
There are only 2 guns in the game, the pistol and an ak-47.  The vast majority of the game is stealth but there are a few run n gun sections, and luckily the gunplay handles well enough, although it is easy to bait the enemies into choke points and just blast them as they walk through.
The story is good, and rather lengthy, the game took me about 11-12 hours to complete and there are several twists and turns as the story progresses, it is entertaining and mostly well done.  There is also a save anywhere function which comes in handy, just be warned the game only auto saves at the start of levels so make sure you use the save system because the missions are generally pretty lengthy.
At a sale price of $1.24 this game was a steal, but even at the full price of 5 dollars you are getting your moneys worth.  If you enjoy stealth games like splinter cell you should pick this up, it is not as good or polished as that game, but it is a good time and well worth the low asking price.

Singularity is simply a great game.
Raven's last real try at producing a stand alone title, Singularity is also one of their few IP-owned properties and it shows.  Unlike 2009's Wolfenstein, which was bland, drab and uninspired, Singularity is a vibrant game that shows love/thought in every facet of its construction.  Possessed of a *great* story that gives you several plot twists and a beautifully unique theme/aesthetic, Singularity beats most other FPS story elements hands down, creating a living, breathing and interesting universe.
Gameplay isn't to be outdone by Singularity's story, however, as the game runs on modest stystems, looks good, has genuine ambiance and great set piece design.  The game has a unique aesthetic and much like other games, including Deus Ex or Bioshock, creates a unique visual identity for itself.  Scary moments abound, of both the jump scare and creepy varieties and the game has excellent weapon variety with good punch/heft/feel.
The show-stopper, however, is the TMD (time manipulation device) which is a glove that allows you to do a variety of things.  Shove enemies back with a forceful pulse, age/de-age objects so that they change shape, age enemies to either kill or mutate them into monstrosities that fight by your side, open portals, levitate/hurl a variety of objects and other powers, all allow you to manipulate a physical world to solve a variety of problems.  Upgrade weapons, your TMD, and even yourself to customize your playthrough in the way that best fits your style.
The game has a staggering attention to detail in the campaign but the title is quite short, with most players finishing it in under 10 hours.  That said, the game has multiplayer!  While the community is dead, the multiplayer is pure gold and that's a shame.  Deathmatch or team deatchmatch seem like simplistic options but team deathmatch offers a Left 4 Dead  1/2 asymmetrical gameplay style that pits powered humans against Katorga 12 creatures.  Humans can wield a variety of weapons and employ a small handful of skills/perks but may also choose of one of four classes that confer either teleporational capabilities, healing skills, improved durability/melee or the ability to turn invisible.
The monsters are even better!  Played in third person, your options include a phase-shifting brawler, a crafty spiderling(phase tick) which can climb over almost any obstacle in the map(yes, he can run on the ceilings!) and detonates himself kamikaze style(or takes control of enemies) and a giant arachnid tank that fires grenades.  Perhaps the best monstrous class, though, is the Revert which is a slow but tough mutant that burps up mines and vomits a putridly hilarious and voluminous torrent of toxic sludge.
From every possible facet, this game is a pure winner.  Its lack of success is mostly attributable to Raven's lack of a reputation and its publisher's failure to advertise the game on release.  While it may not be worth 30 or 40 dollars, if you can get this game for half that, it's a worthwhile FPS classic that I would place on the shelf next to the best examples of the genre.
Highly recommended.

I wanted to play a game in which I shoot stuff. I also prefer my shooting games to have something quirky or fun or special to set them apart from all the other shooting games. I bought Singularity and it delivered, for the most part, at least.
Singularity is a very basic shooter. It's story is nothing really special (it's a very predictable time-traveling mess), the voice acting is standard, the guns are regular guns (except for the seeker, which the game occasionally hands you so you can have some fun) and the enemies are russians who shoot you and mutants that slash, punch and bite you.
So what sets this game apart?
The TIME MANIPULATION DEVICE! While the game occasionally seems to forget that the thing exists, and while the mechanics on which it operates (story-wise) are confusing as hell and while it's mostly just a gravity gun with a "kill enemy" function, it DOES set Singularity apart from all the other shooters. An enemy giving you trouble? Age him/it to dust! A bunch of soldiers giving you trouble? Revert a couple of them into feral mutants and watch the madness. The TMD also allows for some fun puzzle design, which is a bonus as far as I am concerned.
Singularity is not a long game and it's not the best game there is, but it's competent and well worth a few bucks and an evening or two.

It's not as great as people with 2hours on record make it out to be.
Starting out, the game in the first few hours is a pure delight. You'll start that first area thinking "Damn, this is better than Baldur's Gate! So much going on, so many companions... Oh cool, my first dungeon! My first puzzle! Amazing! So much fun and the enemies are challenging enough... kind of easy on Hard but i'm sure it'll get more
later on." Then you come across a single fighter that has the same mechanics as any fighter does: Regenerates "Endurance" during the fight which means you better have the damage to counter his regeneration or you're 1. At a stalemate or 2. Going to die.
Don't go into the bear cave.
The first thing you'll notice that's completely different is the stats points and what they represent. While it seems to follow the same D&D style of min and max points allowed to be allocated to a stat(3min, 18max) it's far from D&D. They tried to do something different here but made the whole stats process overly complicated where each stat has dual purposes. Might/Strength for instance improves physical damage but not only physical damage but spell damage and healing amount for spell casters. Out of combat it dictates how much you can intimidate NPCs in conversations if the option is available. This is pretty much the same for every stat and goes against everything you've ever learned in RPG character creation when it comes to stat points... What you end up with is a ball of confusion that no one really knows what to go with. The idea was to get rid of "dump stats" and avoid min/maxing certain stats or attributes but gives little to no context as to what is a good value and what isn't a good value to have. Is 13 acceptable in constitution and resolve for a tank? Should you max that? Should you spread your points among more than the three main attributes? You don't really know and will probably find yourself trying to max Constitution and Resolve then looking at Dexterity and quickly deciding against putting points into it(Again, it's not D&D it's their own take on stats and attributions... It just isn't great imo).
Combat is slow with a lot of chasing most of the time.... I don't know how they managed it but killing enemies is slower than Baldur's Gate even with the speed turned up. Each swing is slow but you can run like there's no tomorrow. Enemy aggro is completely random too so there's no more sending your tank in to soak up damage and then sending in your damage dealers. Instead you'll have enemies disengage your tank with no way for you to pick them back up unless you chase them(as a tank) and constantly trade attacks otherwise enemies will split off and chase down characters that would die/get knocked unconscious in three hits. It ends up being the perfect scenario for the Benny Hill theme song, literally. Your mage will be running in circles trying to outrun an enemy with your tank in tow chasing after the enemy to try get aggro on it.
Let me guess... you thought health was important in combat? Guess again. It's all about endurance. Once your endurance reaches 0 you're knocked out for the rest of that fight. You might have 300 health but only 50 endurance. If you run out of endurance with 300 health left it doesn't matter, that's you out for the fight. If everyone's endurance reaches 0 that's your game over. Reload and try again.
This is a really bad decision on Obsidians part. Spell use is the same as in Baldur's Gate: You have X amount of spells you can use before you have to rest to get those spell charges back. It makes sense in Baldur's Gate because you can rest whenever you want. In Pillars of Eternity you have a limited amount of times you can rest without stocking up on camping kits. On Hard that limit is 2. Not "20." Just 2. So you'll find yourself in a predicament: You're in a dungeon, you're getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you and you have a mage with 4 spells he can cast(Can be any spell as long as you have it learned unlike BG where it was memorised). You use all spell options you have to take down enemies... Well, you have to sacrifice one of your rests(A max of 2) just to get your spells back. What you end up with is a mage that's great but only for one engagement. The mage has an ability that recharges after each engagement but it deals so little damage it's not worth bothering with(Less than a melee swing in most cases).
Ugh... where to start. There's what was already mentioned and then there's the fact that you have to pay your mage to learn new spells? Picked up a Grimoire with spells your mage doesn't know? That's 100cp please. Why? You have the material there, you just got it off someone's corpse. You're not going to a trainer, you're not spending time studying it but hell, your mage just seems to be asking for 100copper for his own benefit in learning a spell? There's no sense in that! Maybe if you actually had to bring the book to a trainer and then learn it through a mentor but there's none of that in this scenario.
Let's put it this way: I've never seen so much use of the word "and" in all my life. It's pretty bad. Some parts are fine but then you have one sentence every now and then with "and" being used four times. Yeah, it's pretty cringeworthy to say the least. "He had golden locks for hair and a mustache, and a tunic, and a t-shirt, and yellow teeth, and, and, AND..." There's also bits, at least in the first few hours, that seem so out of place it's just a sin to commit. For one you come across a witch(Let's just call her a witch) who is fully voice acted. The VA does a decent job but the current situation does not fit the attitude the voice portrays what so ever. You also come to the realisation rather quickly that this "witch" is not important to the plot what so ever and you're not going to see much of her after the three or four lines of questions you ask her which begs the question: Why commit full voice acting for her dialogue and not others?
It's not bad... it's just repetitive. Every time you see an NPC you can ask questions it's the same first three questions over and over. You might think it's standard for an RPG to ask "Who are you?" but most RPGs try to mix it up a bit... here they don't. Every interaction has the same options: 1. "Who are you?" 2. "What brings you here/why are you here?" and 3. "Can you tell me about X." Then you have maybe one or two extra options if they have a quest for you or they're part of a quest you need to do.
I'm not sure but I think this is a bug(But there's those who would actually defend it). Essentially you have an unlimited "Stash" by default in addition to each characters individual inventory. One would think your stash is a static object, as in a bottomless chest in a specific area or areas you have to visit to put things in and take things out... Nope. Your stash is just there. You can access it freely, put things in it freely and take things out whenever you want. The option to disable universal access to your stash only disables you from taking things
but doesn't stop you from putting things in. Basically you don't need an inventory.
It's no Baldur's Gate. It looks pretty good but Obsidian decided to make their own rules up and the game suffers because of it. You won't notice at first but you'll begin to notice when you actually encounter the real parts of the game.
It's okay but not worthy of 95% it currently has. You will be more frustrated than entertained and drawn in with this game.

TL; DR: THIS GAME IS NOT TERRARIA! It's much more exploration and construction oriented, therefore many reviews are criticizing the story and PvE elements. If the words "colonization", "exploration" and "messinf about" interest you, read on. If you want the amazing boss battles and events from Terraria, THIS ISN'T THE GAME FOR YOU.
Now for the actual review:
I bought Starbound way back in the early beta. Back then, all it had were some basic bosses, a progression system involving hour-long mining trips interspersed with crafting for 5 minutes and flying to another planet. Since then, Starbound has grown and developed into a sandbox rivaling Minecraft and Terraria, and far exceeding them in variety.
The key difference between Starbound and most other sandboxes is the procedural generation of planets. Where in Terraria you were stuck with the world you generated once, Starbound lets you hop around infinitely, looking for that promised land with pink soil, eyeball trees and volcano crabs. And you will eventually find it, since planets are procedurally generated and no two planets are the same. This makes this game perfect for players looking for exploration, allowing you to enjoy randomized views without once going underground.
Another defining feature is the colony system. Whenever you build a house in Starbound, you can rent it off to whatever tentacle monster takes it, and the tetacle monster in question will be entirely determined by the building and furniture. This adds an incentive to building that other sandboxes lack, and makes construction in general more enjoyable. The best part? Remember how Borderlands promised its players 87 bazillion guns? Starbound has 87 bazillion chairs. This pretty much negates the chance of getting the same kinds of villagers, turning house-building into a catch-em-all minigame where you spend hours trying to get that fabled alpaca villager.
Starbound also features a procedurally generated quest system if you have nothing better to do, as well as fleshed out farming and archaelogy. Also you can have a one-tentacled floating octopus as a pet.
Every game has its flaws however, and here are the most annoying ones:
The story in Starbound is a means to an end, that end being telling you when you should probably upgrade your equipment. It's simple, dull and, though the boss fights can be fun and challenging, I once found myself impossibly ill-equipped to deal with a certain samurai, resulting in me getting repeatedly destroyed, using up all my healing items and finally succeeding only with the help of a friend's character.
For a game so reliant on collecting and farming, Starbound's inventory system is unfortunately lacking. While a "sort inventory" button unintuitively marked with two arrows has been added since the beta, there is still no way to sort chest inventories and I often find myself sorely missing the "quick stack to nearby chests" option from Terraria. Food items dont stack, and if you turn half your planet into fields like I did, you will find that it takes you 10 or so runs back and forth from the place where you sell the crops.
If you played Starbound early beta, you would remember the fun combat system where monster attacks were procedurally generated with the monster, there was no damage on contact and hammers were amazing. Unfortunately, this has been removed, so monsters once again damage by touching aside from their basic attacks, and hammers take several seconds to wind up before every swing. One can only hope interesting melee combat will return in future versions, together with the promised individual abilities for each race.
Overall, I loved Starbound and would sincerely recommend it to anybody who loves messing about with construction and farming. If you just finished Terraria and are looking for a second helping however, you will not find it here.

The combat is very satisfying, the sound design is on point and the general structure of the quests doesn't ever really feel tiresome. You'll notice that dialogue gets recycled after about twenty hours, but even though there's a serious lack of writing, there isn't a lack of things that could happen to you on any given assignment.
The three most common jobs are 1) Escort/deliver this item(carrier) 2) Go here and get this item and 3) Go kill  these dudes.
Despite that, I don't remember feeling *bored*. I usually end up giving this game a rest either because I get slightly frustrated with some bad luck (which doesn't feel unfair) or because things seem to be taking too long (which is now avoidable with new options.)
So long as you understand that this game is hard at the best of times and that you can't see the soldiers you hire as anything other than high-risk financial investments, you'll be fine. The team you assemble can feel super individual and alive, but if you lose too many guys it'll be difficult to remember everyone's name. People's faces tend to blur together after awhile, since there's only so much variance you can have with muscular white men.
But if you're in the market of muscular white men, this is a good game. Definitely worth the price, but it's got it's flaws. If you're unsure, buy it on sale.

I have to confess, this game was just a ridiculous amount of fun. It felt like I was interacting in a cheesy spy novel, and it did a good job at it. Well, this is a third person stealth/action shooter. The first six to eight levels are more stealth oriented, but once the Russion Special Forces, (spetsnaz) are sent after you, you can pretty much kiss stealth goodbye. It's all shooting from there. It implements a system where you can collect gadgets lying around like rags, alarm clocks, plastic bottles, cans, chemicles, ect. and McGyver them into cheep tools for temporary use. For example, you can use a plastic bottle and rag at the end of your barrel for a cheep, disposible silencer. You can also make explosives, paralyzing chemicle agents, and other completely implausible but fun innovations. But not to worry. It is a very easy system to pick up with very little learning curve. The story is told through a series of comic book-like cutsceens between missions with corny, voice-acted Russian accents that, (in my opinion) adds a lot of charm to this game. I found myself drawn into it and empathizing with the characters. Also I loved the ending! This game is cheep, the controls are very good, the graphics are great for 2005, there is a quicksave system as opposed to a checkpoint saving system, and I ask you: what other game allows you to have a shootout inside of Lenin's tomb? This game has a lot of atmopshere and I highly recommend it. Honestly, if there is anything even remotely negative I can think to say about it, it is that the character moves kind of slow, and has a lot of wide open ground to cover. The sprint system only works for a few moments before your character gets tired and has to rest, so traveling while sprinting isn't too much faster in the long run than walking. Traveling from one side of a map to another can be a bit tedious. But this is a very minor complaint. This game is a definite winner.

C&C3 became a frustrating slog for me, with a difficulty zig zag that wore me to the point of being kind of depressed at how many hours I put in to it all. I was extremely close to not bothering with Kanes Wrath as I assumed that the expansion would only increase the difficulty, frustration, my blood pressure, etc.
Instead Kanes Wraths campaign is done in a way that is far better balanced, far more open, and allows for more types of play than its predecessor. It does this largely by slicing up each level, if you are a skilled player slamming through things then youll go through the objectives rapidly with a more organic story feel and an exciting but risky play through. If you are like me and a bit crap then a lot of the missions youll hold off, take your time, stabilise, play a bit of sim city and build a huge army before hitting the objective and moving on.
As a result, it was so much more enjoyable, there was never a brick wall of difficuly I ran in to, and each level allows you to effectively play at the pace you want depending on your mood. Its a real shame, though understandable for an expansion, that there isnt more of a campaign in it. That said, they do throw in a bunch of interesting additions.
Skirmish and multiplayer have been given a boost with the different factions and such, and then there is Global Conquest. A more free flowing version of the old Dune 2 map where you could choose the way you expand.
Its pretty rough around the edges; even after winning a few rounds of it Im sometimes confused by what exactly happened on a bunch of turns and lots of play styles will mean you never actually need to play in real time even at harder difficulties. but its an interesting mode of play to try out, and it had a lot of potential. Its a shame this wasnt fleshed out, fixed up, and maybe made in to a fully fledged expansion/game in its own right, like Dawn of War did with Dark Crusade only with C&C game play and the more sophisticated Global Conquest map.
All in all there is a fair bit here to get through in this expansion and its really solid, varied, enjoyable stuff.

I have great difficulties rating this game, so I go against the trend and give it a thumbs down. It certainly doesn't deserve overwhelming positivity. Sometimes Battle Brothers is extremely frustrating and sometimes very rewarding. The exploration, management, event and rudementary story aspects are really neat and even the combat can be more than bearable at times. Unfortunately, combat is the game's focus.
My main complaint about it is actually that the battles are too difficult, even on Beginner/Beginner (and the devs say it is meant to be played on Veteran!). Now, one could argue that the challenge is part of the fun (and it certainly is for the hardcore crowd, to which I don't belong and the beginner difficulty kinda defeats the point), but there is more to this. Let me summarize:
- The game does a very bad job at explaining itself, so you have to find out what works on your own. Which, again, could be interesting in itself, if it wasn't so intent on punishing the player for every mistake.
- The types of challenges are very repetitive and turn into tedium after a while. Either you figure it out or you don't. There isn't much variance both in your enemies and your own customization options. This wouldn't be a problem if the game could be finished in 12 hours. It can't.
- Optimization is mandatory, which again limits any variance in experiencing the game. It also infringes on the enjoyment of the minor aspects: exploration and roleplay. Worse, the builds for your mercenaries are all extremely similar and a lot of abilities are completely pointless or very circumstantial. Character progression, of course, is linear. The heavier armour is almost always the correct choice etc.
- There is no coming back. If you screw up a run, you might as well start a new campaign. This relates to the next point:
- Horrible pacing and threat scaling. The difficulty indicators and monetary rewards for each mission are grossly misleading. You never know what will happen until you know the composition of the enemy forces. Battle Brothers also falls into the same trap as D&D with the release of 3.X, namely an inflexible challange rating. You simply won't get easy fights. And engaging something too far above your CR is suicide. This results in an extremely even pacing with few ups and downs. A first time engagement still feels like a climax, but everything in between is just the same.
That said, I enjoy Battle Brothers a lot when its not out there to punish me. Had it mod support it would probably be a phenomenal game by now.

Rating 8.5/10
Overview: Underrated First Person Shooter
The Good:
+ The story is about time travel and trying to change the past to affect the future. It doesn't provide anything new but it does make the game more interesting particularly when you travel between the past and present and see the changes in the environment.
+ Good atmosphere featuring a post apocalyptic setting
+ Creative weapons that feel great to use and can be upgraded by finding upgrade kits scattered throughout the levels.
+ In addition to weapon upgrades, you will find blueprints and experience to upgrade your character. It provides a nice rpg element to the game.
+ Good sense of pacing - The levels feel different, the gameplay changes up every once in a while, it never feels like you're doing the same thing over and over again despite shooting down hordes of enemies.
+ Despite the linear nature of the game and the levels, exploration is heavily rewarded in the form of experience.
+ The main premise of the game is that you are given a time manipulation device used to age/renew objects for some light puzzle solving. It's a good premise but I never felt like they fully utilized it.
+ Nice boss battles
+ Good buildup to the end of the game and a solid ending
The Average:
The graphics even for its time doesn't really stand out, textures are very bland.
The Bad:
- no sub title option
- audio bug that needs to be fixed (check forum for soultion)
- Multiplayer is dead
Conclusion
This game borrows different ideas from different games and puts it all together in one satisfying package. This is a very underrated game that deserved more success, too bad Activision thought differently and sent it out to die upon release. If you are looking for a FPS game and still haven't gotten Singularity then do yourself a favor and pick it up, you won't regret it.

This is the very first hidden object game that I've ever played. So when reading this review, please keep in mind that I have no frame of reference to other HOGs, and I don't know if this one is particularly good or bad in comparison.
So, in this game, you play as the well-known detective from 221b Baker Street, who is called upon by Sir Henry Baskerville. You travel to Baskerville manor to unravel the mystery of the curse that has been haunting the family for several generations. Breaking the curse involves finding the coat of arms for every family member and eventually face the beast itself. And since it's a HO-game, you do this by finding items, solving puzzles and progress room by room, location by location. And that's pretty much all there is to this game.
+ Sherlock Holmes :)
+ good game to spend a few hours on, nice time-killer
+ visually quite attractive, I liked the rooms and locations
+ use of the amulet as an extra game mechanic is a nice touch
+ the option to auto-travel to the correct room once you find all pieces of an item (the game prompts and asks if you want to travel to the according location)
- bad voice acting, bad animations
- the map travel option is virtually useless, since every location can be reached in two or three clicks anyway, and remembering where each location was is about as difficult as most of the puzzles in this game
- puzzles are too simple, with the exception of one near the end, which is (in comparison) waaaaaay too hard; I replayed the game on "Hard" mode to see the differences, but "Hard" mode is only marginally more difficult and still not really hard at all
- strays off from the original A.C. Doyle story a bit too much for my taste; time travel, magic medalions, whichcraft all seem to be real in this game, while Doyle's Sherlock would push for "the only logical explanation" and discover the truth behind the seemingly magical and supernaturalal phenomenons
While it's not a bad game, I still don't recommend it. If this game were more reasonably priced (around 3,99-4,99 euros), I would actually recommend it, but for the full price of 9,99 you just don't get enough bang for your buck IMHO. It's good to get on sale or as part of a Sherlock Holmes bundle, though.

Greetings Everyone!  So, I was very tempted to just copy / paste my review from the base game as I played them together.  However, there are a great many differences between Kane’s Wrath and the original game Tiberium Wars.  To begin with the campaign is shorter but this is expected as it is an expansion, not a stand alone.  You also get your typical new units but interestingly they actually divide each of the three factions into mini factions giving you more options and makes some difficult decisions on which ones you want to play each match.
Guess who’s Back:  Yup the coolest video game actor ever (Joseph Kucan) is back in an expansion dedicated to the forces of Nod.  One amazing part of this expansion is that it is told specifically from the point of NOD, specifically Kane and all the missions reflect that as NOD is the primary actor.  In addition it explains a lot of loose ends from the prior game of the series and the base game.  The story can be a bit jarring from time to time as it does skip around a bit and the game has a few small puns of ‘I feel like I’ve been here before’ which I enjoyed the breaking of the wall in the light hearted way it was given.
Where is that Unit:  One annoyance I had about this game during the campaign is the constant changing of your ‘faction’.  This may sound odd but in the expansion campaign you actually swap between a few factions within NOD (and GDI / Scrin for multiplayer) which really isn’t that big of a deal but more than once I was looking for a specific building or unit and discovered I was playing one of the other sub factions.  For better or worse I also found the game to be much easier than the original and like the original the AI has a tendency to forget to mine to the point of stalling their economy and if you just leave them alone and build up they won’t really do anything.
Risk Command & Conquer:  One really fun addition is the global conquest map, plays a bit like a board game where you are trying to conquer the world in a turn based map system.  You build strike forces that will attack enemy bases in normal skirmish battles.  One nice touch is that you can play as all three sub factions within your faction on the map which allows you to pick the best one to encounter that specific enemy base you need razed.  Overall it did kind of devolve into big strike forces just steamrolling the AI’s base before it could build up counter attacking forces but I enjoyed the addition.  More games should include such things (please SC2).
Overall, good game; if you have the original, get the expansion no real question there.  But if this expansion is being bought with the original does it provide addition value above and beyond?  I’d say yes, not only does it provide additional campaign (my primary reason for playing RTS) but the global conquest is a great addition above just playing AI skirmish.  You may want to wait for a sale as the game is so old that those sales tend to deep discount however, enjoy!

The campaign lasted about twelve hours for me, but that includes a lot of searching and backtracking for items, because that's the kind of player I am. Someone who just rushes through might only take six hours to finish the game.
The mechanics are solid, the graphics are nice for the time it was published, the sound is well-done, the levels are challenging, and the gameplay is fun overall. If you like third-person stealth-'em-ups then this is the game for you. Even if it is a bit over 8 years old, it's still worth the five dollars, or perhaps a tad more.

Faeria is ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant.

Back to the positive.. the FREE Arena is EPIC fun. I got so many great games out their arena, deep, thoughtful, 100% engaging until the timer runs out searching possibilities for more and better moves... It was an epic journey of strategy discovery... every game I lost I felt like I learned something. Skillful play is so critical. huge RNG of course (its a card game), but overcomable by knowing your deck and its probabilities, all the available strategies in a given situation.... its a card game so it boils down to luck at the top-top-top tier, but still has moments of brilliance and that feeling of discovering new techniques and layers is SOOOOO deep... sincerely puts a lot of other games like hearthstone to shame in the discovery of gaming depth level.... Doesnt mean I dont think very highly of hearthstone's depths, Im just saying PLAYING each turn in faeria is a much richer experience. Once the contenty-goodness of new cards ran out in hearthstone I felt fairly static with few and far between discoveries... here i felt a new dsicovery regularily. almost every game. It lends itself great to deep engagement yet forgives and educates less thoughful play. Incredible. I sure blabbed about that point but i find it super interesting and important to card/strategy games in general that turns are tight, interesting, deep, and full of learning from tradeoffs that arent buried behind too-too much RNG.
