This is one of those games where I wish Steam ratings allowed something like a star rating rather than a simple thumbs-up or thumbs-down; there are some things I like about the game and some things I don't.
In the short term, this is an excellent game, which is probably why it's gotten so many positive reviews. The tile placement for needed resource types along with the need to collect from and protect faeria (mana) wells makes for strategic play that isn't found in most other CCGs.
Early on, play is rewarded well both in the way of gold and new cards, however it doesn't take long for those rewards to die down.
On the other hand, the game suffers from many of the same problems other CCGs have, and it doesn't seem to have figured out a formula to reduce the frustration with those issues.
Like many CCGs, if you are paired up with another player who has superior cards, the chances are very strong that you will lose. Other CCGs such as Hearthstone seem to try and keep things fair by making sure that whenever possible you are paried up with someone at the same play level you are at. Faeria on the other hand, possibly due to the much lower player count, tends to frequently pair players together that aren't even close. It is not unusual, for example, to have reached something like rank 17, only to constantly get matched against someone several ranks higher, assuring you repeatedly lose badly and get knocked down again. Something like this should be expected in the type of game now and then, but in Faeria it happens so often that it gives you the feeling of constantly hitting a brick wall.
The primary way to get past this appears to be to get better cards - however those cards are extremely tough to come by unless you are willing to shell out a good chunk of cash. As an example I am current at level 60-something, with over 70 hours invested, and I *still* haven't been able to complete the "beginner" decks that you are given templates for when you first start playing. As you progress, the game over time will give you additional, more advanced deck templates - and of these I'm usually lucky if I have even half of the cards needed.
So I would have to say if you're willing to drop a significant amount of real cash on virtual cards, you might get extended enjoyment out of this game. For the others, I'd probably have to recommend either a different CCG, or for that matter just a better card game that isn't collectible and puts everybody on the same ground to begin with.

Welcome to After Reset.
I was a supporter of Mr. Nixon and his vision for AE since the Kickstarter campaign so this is not an unbiased review.
I am here to tell you why you should support this game, not why you shouldn't.
You should choose to support the development of AE because of vision. The vision that the devs have for the game.
To me it is the Fallout descendant that never happened. Sure FNV and F3 were amazing games in their own right, but they were not the desert land which we all come to love and cherish. The ambience is there, the feel is there, the story is there. You want to get excited pick up Fall of Gyes and give it a read. I was salivating in my frontal cortex as I was reading it, just thinking how good the full story is the game will be.
The graphics are breathtaking for an isometric based game. I understand its alpha at the moment and there is a lot they need to do, but the raw commitment to detail and level of quality is already evident. It had all those shiny polished edges we have come to expect of Mass Effect and Civilization visual levels.
The gameplay isnt there yet obviously, but that will hopefully soon come as updates roll hot off the presses. Poke around the website, drool at screenshots and so far it looks like it will be all the fun, explody, clicky bits that keep us happily poking away at Wasteland and Fallouts. And yes it has cyberdogs and lasers.
And of course I have to squeeze in a spiel on commitment and persevearance that the devs have shown so far to the game. Kickstarter, Fall of Gyes, Steam Greenlight and Early Access are all proof that they ARE working to get this game done. ON THEIR OWN TERMS. They could have sold out to any of the big boys to get the game done. There have been and there will be publishers coming to them to offer coin for their seat at the table, but so far Richard Nixon and his team have stayed strong to their vision for their game and their independence. I for one am tired of AAA massive budget title games that in the end feel like cookie cutter, vanilla, sexless clones. Let us finally have a game made by someone with guts, skill and spine.
Get the game, support the indie devs and have patience. The full release will be well worth it.

This is an alpha build for a very promising game. As of right now all you can do is create a character and explore a small laboratory so I will comment on the features that are implemented.
Character Creation:
The character creation is very in depth, there are many races to choose from although there is only one available in the alpha to try out. The way the skills and attributes are set up is very reminiscent of Fallout 1&2, Wasteland and other classic RPG games. This gives you the ability to completely tailor your play-style with great precision. There are also options to customize the physical appearance of your character’s height, weight, age, eye color, and many other options that are not yet implemented. Finally there is an open ended Bio editor so you can create meaningful and detailed backstories (if you are into that sort of thing)
Appearance:
The attention to detail in this game is superb. The menus are well crafted with a pleasant and interesting blur effect on the text (this effect was toned down significantly with the last update due to user feedback). The in-game graphics are excellent, far beyond what you would expect in an alpha, honestly better than I have seen in some AAA games lately.
The Development:
This game is alpha (more of a technical demo at this point) so if you are not interested in that sort of thing turn back now. What I can say is that the development team is HIGHLY active and extremely open/straight-forward. I have been following this game since I backed it early on in the kickstarter and the quantity and quality of the status updates from the developers have been phenomenal. As of now there have been 57 updates pushed out on kickstarter alone keeping backers updated and informed every step of the way. The website for this game has active dedicated forums and the developers seem to be taking the feedback on the game seriously. The content updates are coming at a steady rate and only seem to be increasing in frequency and quality lately.
Bottom Line:
Again this is currently alpha so if that’s not your thing than don’t bother with this yet, but keep an eye on it because it is shaping into something that has the potential to be amazing. If the alpha experience is for you and you wish to be an active part in shaping this game then this is the game for you, I recommend you join the forums and let your opinions be heard because the developers ARE listening.

TL; DR: THIS GAME IS NOT TERRARIA! It's much more exploration and construction oriented, therefore many reviews are criticizing the story and PvE elements. If the words "colonization", "exploration" and "messinf about" interest you, read on. If you want the amazing boss battles and events from Terraria, THIS ISN'T THE GAME FOR YOU.
Now for the actual review:
I bought Starbound way back in the early beta. Back then, all it had were some basic bosses, a progression system involving hour-long mining trips interspersed with crafting for 5 minutes and flying to another planet. Since then, Starbound has grown and developed into a sandbox rivaling Minecraft and Terraria, and far exceeding them in variety.
The key difference between Starbound and most other sandboxes is the procedural generation of planets. Where in Terraria you were stuck with the world you generated once, Starbound lets you hop around infinitely, looking for that promised land with pink soil, eyeball trees and volcano crabs. And you will eventually find it, since planets are procedurally generated and no two planets are the same. This makes this game perfect for players looking for exploration, allowing you to enjoy randomized views without once going underground.
Another defining feature is the colony system. Whenever you build a house in Starbound, you can rent it off to whatever tentacle monster takes it, and the tetacle monster in question will be entirely determined by the building and furniture. This adds an incentive to building that other sandboxes lack, and makes construction in general more enjoyable. The best part? Remember how Borderlands promised its players 87 bazillion guns? Starbound has 87 bazillion chairs. This pretty much negates the chance of getting the same kinds of villagers, turning house-building into a catch-em-all minigame where you spend hours trying to get that fabled alpaca villager.
Starbound also features a procedurally generated quest system if you have nothing better to do, as well as fleshed out farming and archaelogy. Also you can have a one-tentacled floating octopus as a pet.
Every game has its flaws however, and here are the most annoying ones:
The story in Starbound is a means to an end, that end being telling you when you should probably upgrade your equipment. It's simple, dull and, though the boss fights can be fun and challenging, I once found myself impossibly ill-equipped to deal with a certain samurai, resulting in me getting repeatedly destroyed, using up all my healing items and finally succeeding only with the help of a friend's character.
For a game so reliant on collecting and farming, Starbound's inventory system is unfortunately lacking. While a "sort inventory" button unintuitively marked with two arrows has been added since the beta, there is still no way to sort chest inventories and I often find myself sorely missing the "quick stack to nearby chests" option from Terraria. Food items dont stack, and if you turn half your planet into fields like I did, you will find that it takes you 10 or so runs back and forth from the place where you sell the crops.
If you played Starbound early beta, you would remember the fun combat system where monster attacks were procedurally generated with the monster, there was no damage on contact and hammers were amazing. Unfortunately, this has been removed, so monsters once again damage by touching aside from their basic attacks, and hammers take several seconds to wind up before every swing. One can only hope interesting melee combat will return in future versions, together with the promised individual abilities for each race.
Overall, I loved Starbound and would sincerely recommend it to anybody who loves messing about with construction and farming. If you just finished Terraria and are looking for a second helping however, you will not find it here.

The story has a lot of potential in this game, and I'd say they pull of the story about halfway into the game. After that a lot of things start to happen kinda without explanation. So I strongly feel that this game was rushed at the end and that the game kinda suffered for it, this is something I will come back to several times in this review.
You yourself is much like a Gordon Freeman, voiceless and even faceless in this game. I honestly think this is a bit of a shame, they could have made the story more intriguing and interesting if they character you were playing had feelings and thoughts on the situation. The other characters are pretty standard. There's the good guy, bad guy and the cute girl, these are the three NPC characters you interact with pretty much. They're not well written and you don't care about them but they do their part. Perhaps if the game wasn't rushed this wouldn't have happened.
The enemy design is really cool in this game, the monsters are scary, gross and challenging to kill. They do lack a bit of variety so you won't see to many different kind of enemies. But the game isn't super long so it's okay. In between fighting monsters you will be shooting at Russians, they are standard NPC's with guns, not much to discuss there.
The weapons in this game feel great, look great feel very balanced. The problem I have with them is that there are like 6-7 weapons in total at the end of the game, and I only touched the first three because the others were just introduced to damn late and you have already spent so much upgrade points on the early weapons that it doesn't feel worth it switching to the new ones, this might be a side effect of the game being rushed as well. The weapon upgrade system leaves a lot to wish for, each weapons needs 9 points to be fully upgraded. I'm not even sure if I find a total of 20 upgrade points through the whole game.
The powers are probably what carries this game, You have a device on your arm with lets you age specific objects in the world, stop time in an area, levitate and throw objects (kinda like HL2 gravity gun). It's just a ton of fun and the effects look fantastic. They come up with some interesting puzzles with it as well.
Much like most games this game lets you choose between easy, medium and hard difficulty. I tried normal on my first play-through and I honestly don't think I died a single time. I'm now playing it again on hard and I still have a very easy time. I can play through some parts without any problem and then die seven times in a row in the next area, so the difficulty level feels a bit unbalanced.
You can also purchase upgrades for you character and your "gravity gun" in this game, which I think is really fun, The bad part is that you have to find the blueprint for the upgrade in the world and they're sometimes a bit hidden. Meaning that you could potentially miss out on some essential upgrades for you character simply because you didn't look around the room enough. They also don't give you enough points here to upgrade everything but that's fine, it makes you have to choose what to prioritize and what you feel is more important to you.
This review might have sound really negative overall but don't get me wrong, I genuinely enjoyed this game a lot and would recommend it to anyone. If you play this game you won't get mad or irritated at all the bad traits I've pointed out, rather you will acknowledge them and perhaps, like me, realize that this game with a bit more time and polishing could easily have been a 10/10.

I think now that I now have completed the main campaign, the lord of the hunt compaign, and the bright lord campaign, I am now in a position to write a review for Shadow of Mordor. The game as a whole is fantastic. I got the game of the year edition for around $10 during a steam sale. This is a very good deal for what I was able to do in the game. The way I see it, if you can put the more hours in than the cost of the game, it is worth the purchase. I played the main campaign as a completionest, I did everything I could at leisurely pace and it took me at least 40 hrs. However, very little of that time was the story.
Pros:
-The story that is there is good.
-Lots of cool abilities.
-The nemesis system is great. It is a very nice way to punish the player without giving the player a serious disadvantage.
-The soundtrack is great.
-The Lord of the Hunt and Bright Lord campaigns will only take a couple hours to finish, but are still nice to play, giving new abilities definitely improves the gameplay.
-The graphics are also very nice, especially if you can run it at its best.
-The tests of power are also good, and are rather intense as your time left decreases.
Cons:
-After playing for ages, it feels too much like a hack and slash, it fails to be unique, but it's still none-the-less satisfying.
-The story is really short. Because of its length, the character relationships are a bit rushed an are cut off too fast. I would like to see more of that in the sequel.
-The controls are odd, but these can be changed. I think that this is a game to try with a controller as well.
-The final boss was a let down. It was merely a quick time event. If you want a good final boss, check out the Bright Lord campaign.
-The Parkour lock on is annoying. You can end up jumping onto the wrong wall or right over it if you're not careful. It doesn't always do you what you wanted it to.
All in all, I will recommend this game. It is a lot of fun and a very nice addition to the Middle-Earth saga. As I have listed, it isn't without flaws, but they don't break the game. It is very similar to the Assassin's Creed games, so if you like them and the Middle-Earth setting, definitely buy this game.

I believe most every game I've reviewed so far came from the same two companies, so it's interesting to have a bit of a change. Not too much of a change - HOGs mostly abide by the same basic formula - but a change nonetheless.
Some elements are fairly major fumbles by a company not used to making HOGs - the game takes forever to start, won't close in response to alt+f4, and the Russian version apparently won't work at all on computers running Windows 7 - and it's not like we're talking about particularly old game failing to work with a newfangled system, this came out in 2010. On the other hand, there are some ideas here I wish more prolific HOG makers would steal wholesale.
Homes, Watson and Sir Henry arrive at the
manor, to be confronted by a hall full of ancestral portraits. They must investigate the room (or set of rooms) associated with each ancestor in turn, collecting pieces of their coat of arms, and travelling into the past using a wolf-head with crystal eyes, to experience the moments right after said ancestor was murdered by the hound (an explicitly supernatural beast in this incarnation, obviously). As noted in the video link at the start of this review, everyone are terrible mellow about all the murders they've just missed, or all the spooky scares they encounter (actually, this bit is weird. We get 2-3 scare jumps as the game starts, and then... nothing else ever, as though someone flipped a switch) Once a coat of arms is assembled, the player receives a random supernatural power for the Baskerville family medalion - the power to smash♥♥♥♥♥♥ a flashlight, three arbitrary powers used 3-4 times each, and we ran out of ideas so the last two portraits just give you key pieces.
Interesting innovations (besides the powers, which, as noted above, can be mostly replicated with a visit to the hardware store):
Your clicks in Hidden Object Scenes are limited - after 4 or 5 misclicks, Holmes grabs your mouse and gives you a short lecture. This is frustrating but not as amazingly annoying as I might have thought, as the HOS' are actually well laid out, in consideration of the fact that your clicks are limited.
When you're confronted with "Collect 5 butterflies" style puzzles, you are generally told exactly what you need to proceed, have a little "X/Y collected" counter, and the game will
to the spot when you have everything you need to open an obstacle. Better yet - not only is the backtracking limited and helped by the fast travel map, but the game will even tell you when you have "completed" an area and will never need to go back to it again. It's even removed from the fast travel map, which is kinda fantastic. The "skip this puzzle" button takes longer to charge than any HOG I've tried so far, but most puzzles were just about the right difficulty to be challenging but not frustrating.

Wow, this may be the most frustrating, cognitively challenging game I've ever played... And I love it! Most other games allow your characters to be sponges for absorbing hits, bullets, or whatever the game throws at you. That's great, but totally not realistic. This game takes ALL of that into account. Food, tools, aummunition, healing supplies, payroll. Not to mention if you put your best, most highly-trained man on an island in the middle of a bunch of baddies.... HE WILL DIE. (Don't do that) I did that with one of the first men the game gave me, thinking, he's good with an axe, he'll be armored and fine. Nope; that poor soul died on like Day 2. Then there was the case of my Sergeant, who was formerly a homeless man. I told myself not to get attached to him, but after a few clutch crossbow shots I felt like I knew him. So, in a classic story of redemption, he became the Sergeant for my group. He lost a nose, ear and almost died in battle. I considered retiring him just to make sure he didn't die. In my mind I envisioned him retiring to a life of comfort. Alas, I didn't do that; he was killed by a stupid orc who seemed hell-bent on taking him out. No randomly-generated video game character ever made me cry, but I had a moment of silence for him. Not on purpose; I was so saddened I didn't want to continue. When a game makes that happen, makes me think like that, it shows how amazing the game is. Buy this; you won't regret it.

Not as great as expected, yet still solid expansion - apart from standard for Real Time Strategy game expansions campaign and new units and overhauls for all factions, this one introduced subfactions, and a new Global Conquest mode. While that's quite a nice selection of goodies, it is quite apparent the expansion was rushed by EA, and the lack of polish reflects on both quality and stability of new additions.
Now, the campaign, you play as LEGION, Kane's another AI creation, which he activates soon after defeat in Second Tiberium War, and the first chapter tells the story of Kane covertly recovering grasp over divided Nod without alerting GDI. Unfortunately, while taking place soon after Tiberium Sun events, it doesn't feel any more close to it atmospherically. The second act has LEGION reactivated right before the original game's events and add some more plot details. Third act takes place quite some time after the Scrin invasion and has you retake the Tacitus for some reason which is totally not Tiberium Control Network as CnC4 is totally not canon and no way it ever existed in the first place. Anyways, one thing that gives off the expansion was made in a rush? Quite some campaign maps are in fact repurposed and more or less altered skirmish maps, and others are rehash of vanilla maps. In general camapign mission design is OK at best. Also there are just two missions where you fight Scrin, and a few featuring Nod, the rest are all GDI, even if you do get to fight different subfactions with different own subfactions.
New units in general are pretty cool - superunits like Redeemer, Hexapod and MARV in particular, even though they're the same "super large strong unit infantry can garrison for specific bonuses and with one special gimmick", just their designs are enough to make them feel different, not to mention the extra hardpoints occupied by infantry can make them super versatile. For more conventional units, while some like GDI dedicated anti-air slingshot are pretty generic and just patch up the hole in balance and serve their purpose, meanwhile some others like Zone Raiders or Reckoner have interesting special qualities that make them fun to meddle with. Some old classics make a return too, like Wolverine and Titan mechs and Nod cyborgs. By the way, some new features may cause desynchronisation (connection loss due to diverging data, pretty much) problems in multiplayer - such as fourth turret addition Nod has, or the landing pads for aircraft, which is really unpleasant as otherwise balance is great.
The Global Conquest mode also falls prey to the lack of polish, but it's quite an interesting take on those turn-based metamap modes like Dark Crusade campaign. The armies can be harmed outside of combat, so can bases, using superweapons and special abilities, and all three factions have different resource collection methods. Oh and you get to use all three subfactions, that's really cool, you may end up with really unusual scenarios like MCV getting knocked out and you being forced to take out the enemy force without ability to receive any reifnorcements. Problem is, sometimes you may end up waiting out for map and stealth to reveal as enemy leaves one last unit hiding, and the melee maps get very repetitive fast and in general kinda break the immersion.
It's a pretty solid expansion, as I said, though could have been so much better if developers didn't have to rush it. By the way, unfortunately, it seems TibWars has way more community-made mods than Kane's Wrath, which is pretty sad and makes it less of a must-have.

I will preface this by saying that I haven't really played any of the Infinity Engine games before this one.  The closest that I've gotten to real time with pause combat is Neverwinter Nights 1, 2, and Dragon Age: Origins back in the day.  So, given that I have experience with this type of gameplay, I set my difficulty to Normal.  And I will say that I am having a blast!
I think the story is genuinely interesting throughout the game and up to the 14 hour mark.  For me, this isn't a game that I can binge play over a weekend since there is a lot of information throughout the main story line and the myriad of side quests.  I'm the type of person that initially sets off to read everything, but then gets burned out after too much dialog.  In the early game, PoE does a good job of mixing combat with dialogue, but it started going dialogue-heavy on me once I got into the first major city.  I know this is what most people playing cRPGs like, so I won't dock the game for doing that.
The reason why I play cRPGs is for the combat and tactics.  The combat in PoE is quite fun with normal difficulty giving a fair number of challenges.  There were a couple of times where I felt that I was doing quests in the wrong order, because my party would wipe several times in a row on the same fight.  To solve this issue, I simply left the area, did some other quests, and came back with better gear and stronger characters.  Those difficult fights became much easier and I could steamroll through mobs with limited micromanagement.
I do have one criticism though...  My main character is a rogue (built like an assassin), and he spends a lot of time on the ground.  This is because of the stealth mechanics and their interaction with backstab.  If I move my rogue up into backstab range, that usually means the rest of my party is lagging behind because their stealth is not on par with my rogue's.  This usually ends up with everything charging after my rogue and the rest of my party moving to intercept.  However, my rogue usually gets caught in melee range which forces me to choose whether to tank or disengage.  Both usually mean that the rogue is dead.  I am tempted to start the game over as a different class since the rogue feels very limited.
Overall, the game is pretty good at what it does.  It's definitely a labor of love, and is absolutely worth the asking price if you love cRPGs.  If you don't play them often, maybe wait for the Christmas sale and see if you can get a discount.  However, all fans of RPGs should play this game!

This is one of the best and most challenging time management games I've ever played.  The concept is pretty simple: you have a conveyor belt with things on it (burger parts, fry boxes, drink cups, and so on) and have to assemble items for customers that come in.  As you progress in levels new items are added to the list of things you can make, power-ups are unlocked to help you in tight spots, and new customer types with various tastes and quirks are introduced.
The pace is quick, the controls are simple, the story is presented with a fun sense of humor, and the way the game introduces new stuff is fun (you can choose what new item to unlock next in each stage, until you've got them all).  There are 160 levels in the main game (80 levels in the main story and another 80 in the expert story once you've beaten that) which can all be replayed to try for perfect ratings, along with a couple extra modes to try out, so there is a lot to do.  (There are 96 in-game achievements to earn but unfortunately these aren't implemented as Steam achievements.)
If you like this game be sure to check out Burger Shop 2 too!  It adds all kinds of new fun and crazy things to the formula.  The planned third game, Burger Shop 3, has been in development hell for nearly a decade and sales of the first two games on Steam might help nudge them towards finally finishing it.

I know that this game is based on Cthulhu, but I'm really not into that literature genre and most of all it's been years that I don't read books so I enjoyed this game without basic knowledge xD
It's a casual action game with simple beautiful graphics, in which you can choose two different modes (normal campaign, and endless mode - which can be a little bit boring if you go for the campaign) with increasing difficulty.
Basically, you control smoothly your boat which is influenced by tides and the moon, you have to collect money and to avoid missiles and other obstacles in a classic arcade side-scrolling game.
Plus, apart being fully controller-supported, you also can mess with the moon in the sky and so after the first few levels it gets quite challenging (although never impossible) - of course, the moon influences tidal waves so it's up to you to combine the moon and its waves with your boat and the directional keys or the gamepad (i found the game completely playable with keyboard and mouse).
Anyways, it's short for what concerns the number of levels (there's only 10 of them) but long if you're never been into arcade games since your childhood ahah XD So, it can be a little bit frustrating but it's super smooth, created with Unity at its best, and the moon-placing is a very nice addition!
The only bad thing is that I don't know anything about Cthulhu and you don't get much information in the game (in fact, your boat is actually a simple boat and graphics are nice but simplified) but who cares about the story in a free arcade side-scrolling game? :)
Get used to the controls and the moon-placing system in order mainly to avoid obstacles - the "temp goals" I referred to at the beginning, of course, are the usual Flash/Unity temporary goals: destroy X missiles, travel X kilometres, don't take damage for x, and upgrade your ship of course! That's why it took me like, I think, 15 or 16 hours all.. ahahah
It's a casual indie funny arcade game, so don't expect lots of replayability (especially for the levels are quite the same apart from the difficulties), but given for free (I'd love to pay something since it really deserves support and unfortunately has no DLC, the soundtrack is nice too!) is really recommended if you're into arcade games, or if you played them in the '90s like me every day XD

Another Hidden Object adventure involving Sherlock Holmes in one of his famous stories from the homonymous original novel. This time Frogware is just a publisher not the developer and this choice is evident in many ways inside the game.
This short adventure starts With Henry Baskerville asking Sherlock Holmes to help him to break the curse of his family which involves a big Hound that brutally kills all of the Baskerville family members from generations. Now, for those who are familiar with Sherlock Holmes and the original novel, yes: this is not exactly a faithful transposition but it's more like an interpretation... Which works good and bad at the same time. Good beccause the adventure in a big mansion where a Demonic dog is supposed to be is quite a good idea giving the game a good dark atmosphere. Bad because this interpretation involves magic and time travel (without any particular consequence, so it's just an excuse to have another room with riddles with a few minor graphic differences), which really don't belong in a Sherlock Holmes adventure.
As a Hidden Object game The gameplay doesn't need much explanation. You need to explore rooms or other ambiences, pick up items, interact with various objects and when you focus on determined zones you will be requested to find a long list of items very well hidden in the screen. Besides that you can find a very long list of puzzles and riddels, some of them are quite easy, but there are few VERY TOUGHT ones that forced me to get some help to deal with them.
This title can count on a good soundtrack most of the times trying to give a tense atmosphere, maybe even more than necessary. Besides that Holmes, Watson and Henry Baskerville will often talk during the adventure and not just with captions as already happened with the persian carpet, but we can hear the original voice cast for our two protagonist, which is really appreciated.
The worst side of this title I believe is the menu and game system, where you don't save because it's an automatic progress but you can't start a new game befor you completely finish it first unless you erase and create a new game profile... An operation that will delete your (ingame) achievements, which is the reason that took me 5 runs instead of just 2 to fully achieve the game.

I have played COD for many years, but I lately, I have been disapointed in both the single player and mulitplayer experiences —especially when compared to titles like Battlefiled.
The story is great, but the gameplay for singler player is exactly like it has been in the past. There have been few changes to make the gameplay better. Perhaps one could say the weapons are different in Black Ops, but is that really an improvement? No... The graphics are improved in this version of COD, but are nothing to the physics of Battlefield or Ghost Recon. I am not impressed.
Gameplay for multiplayer is great for COD, but my primary dissapointment with COD has always been the lack of dedicated servers hosted by the publisher. While Black Ops solved the issue with MW2 (where one random player became the host computer —therefore opening the door right up for hacking) by allowing one to rent a dedicated server, you still have to pay money to rent a server! Seriously?! You mean me and the many other players have to pay $15/mo for servers? Nice move.
Overall, I would not reccomend this game: you deserve better. COD is meant to be a console game and is downgraded for PC/Mac. Spend a few extra dollars and get Battlefield, a game designed for computers and downgraded for consoles.

I wish that the review system for Steam had a "meh" option; because this game is by no means bad, but it isn't really that good either.
Let me explain.  I bought this game 3-odd years ago, and it was a totally different game.  It was buggy and poorly-thought out, but you could see that the core concepts to make an amazing game were really there.
I got bored after a week of playing and didn't play again until a year later.  By then, the game was entirely different.  Each race had cool abilities and unique weapons and armor bonuses; which is still kind of in the game, but not as varying.  The story was subtle, which made it even more fun to be whoever you wanted to be.  You weren't "The Last Protector." You were whoever you wanted to be.
My big problem with the game in its current state is it's unrewarding loot and crafting system, the generic "in your face" story, and the general homogenization of unique features.  Like why did they get rid of the cool, unique S.A.I.L. avatars in favor of the generic humanoid ones?  Why make the loot and weapons so ♥♥♥♥ing hard to find, but not offer a way to create a crafted equivalent?  Why drop the subtle story and replace it with the current boring♥♥♥♥♥version.
Not to mention, the problems and things missing from the game have to be modded in.  There is actually no system in place to accurately tell when your food will rot.  But you'll have so much of it that your food rotting doesn't do anything but make the game that much more annoying to play.
And with all of this, you'd think I'd give this game a negative rating.  But since they included Steam Workshop in the final build, most of this stuff is forgiveable.  Just keep in mind that you'll be installing a fair bit of mods to make the game truly enjoyable.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED. This is a fantastic game.  Great fun, great developers, great community. And it's free, so there's no reason not to give it a try.
Some of the things I appreciate:
-It's a really interesting combination of a collectible card game and a tactical turn based strategy game, so it really hits both of the things i like about those genres at the same time.
-It's one of the most free-to-play friendly games I have encountered. You can definitely play competitively without spending any money, though you may have to be willing to play solo mode and pandora (the draft format) for a little while at the beginning to build up your collection a bit. But those are good ways to learn the game anyway.
-Unlike most CCG's I have played, RNG takes a backseat to player skill. Of course what you draw matters, but you can compensate for bad draws with good board positioning and can even draw extra cards on your turn to get what you need if you need to.
-Lots of cool mechanics that make the matches/decks varied. There's no class system (unlike Hearthstone) so you are free to construct a deck with any cards in the game and have it viable - it's more like MTG's color system.
-Multiple game modes - you can play solo, friendly matches, ranked, limited, and they are adding cooperative multiplayer modes like world boss mode in a few weeks.
The only thing I can think that is really lacking for me is more attention to the lore like you would find in a more developed world like the MTG planes. The art style is great, but I think it would be great if there was a little more attention to the stories behind the characters and creatures.
Other than that, I have no complaints!

After 354 hours on this game, and 5 seasons of getting the highest rank possible, I have finally given up on excuses to like this game. I believe the other reviews tell you the pros of the game: most of them I don't dispute. Here are all the reasons why I cannot recommend this game over Hearthstone of GWENT to any of my friends: and the reason why you, dear reader, should also invest your time in something else.
Community: Dead. The subreddit (r/faeria) is completely barren. The main discord has had 30 messages in the last 24 hours.  I estimate 3/4 of the active community is in god rank (a cheap marketing tactic to encourage people to keep playing, "since they're so good at the game"), and the only people who talk about the game anymore are a tiny group of maybe 15 people who have been around too long to quit. And even that group is dwindling: recently there has been a wave of high-profile players quitting because of perceived meta issues. The wait in queue times is 5 minutes. This is the loneliest multiplayer game I've ever experienced.
Metagame: Holy jesus christ. In the highest tier only two decks are played: bjump and crackthorn. It has been this way for a long time now, and while stale meta is something every card game will occasionally experience, this really is something else. Last monthly cup, a player literally forfeited on turn 3 of the game because his opponent was playing bjump and drew a perfect opening. TURN 3. Every game you play at 1700+ elo is decided by turn 5 with 90% certainty. Literally Hearthstone has less RNG than this game.
Gameplay experience: There is a list of around 20 bugs. Here are a few that I find the most aggravating: Can't see health when flying creature is placed next to hero (seriously???), no sound on land placement, game crash on disconnect, iona taunt interaction, structures completely bug out if you click on them too fast when played, double clicking on placing dash creatures cancels the dash. Developers don't care.
Here's the deal. This game is several years old now. It's done all of the growing it can do. It's gotten a totalbiscuit feature, it pumps in however much money to try and make it an "esport" (grand finals tops out at around 100 viewers on twitch, laughable). The community isn't getting any bigger (and it really is that terrible), the developers show no sign of fixing the underlying issues that plague the game.
Sorry, Faeria. I can't make any more excuses for you.

Place hex tiles, play cards. You get 3 mana per turn and can play either 2 neutral lands or one special land (forest or desert etc.) Cards have two requirements - a mana cost and a number of special lands of that colour. Damage to creatues and structures is persistent (a la Hearthstone) and extra mana can be retreieved from the wells at the corners of the board.
Faeria deserves to be MUCH more famous than it is. The hex tile board necessitates skillful land placement and solves several problems that games like Magic and Hearthstone suffer from, such as over-powered game starts (you need to get a creature within striking distance of your opponent).
The requirement of both mana and special lands owned to play a card gives this another dimension either lacking or shoehorned into other games.
This early into the game, card variety is low but that is countered by the myriad ways you can build a deck (any colour combo is possible from the start) and more importantly the same deck can be played with differing tactics due to the dynamics of the board.
So much fun is there to be had throughout the solo missions that I felt it my duty to support the game with a couple of purchases. It's not really pay to win either, I've seen plenty of whizzbang players with the flashiest avatars and wells bumble over their choices.
The crafting system is similar to Hearthstone - extras can be trashed for 25% of their value towards making new ones. Mythics are the 'foil' versions of cards and are prime candidates for trashing early in the game.
The mythos is dilute, yaks seem to play a large part and I'm not all sure of any background story - this to me is unimportant.

Battle Brothers is truly a labor of love from Overhype Studios.
You are basically running a mercenary business, doing this for the money and not for the greater good! So don't get too attached to your guys, because the game is challenging and losing brothers is part of the fun. You will lose, you will learn.
The art style is detailed and unique, not to mention varied, for every item and character in the game. Special shoutout for the facial details. The writing is also great.
The gameplay is extremely varied:
- Many types of weapons with their own ability sets, you have so many options to play with and adapt to enemy types
- Party formations and backup slots for recovering injured guys or rotating them
- Mercenary backgrounds offer a lot of variety and random events associated to them
- An economic system that fluctuates according to demand, events and relationship, providing trading opportunities or scarcity
- Contracts allow you to help a town, make money and befriend them to get better prices
- Weapons and armor variety in shops and as loot include different tiers, up to unique types
- Replayability is insane, every map is generated according to seeds so no playthrough is the same (unless you want it)
- 3 end game crises makes you feel part of a world that is suffering and changing around you, forcing you to adapt to new challenges, encounters and raids
- Skill tree for leveling up your mercenaries helps you to specialize their roles in your band
The game is not without flaws, mostly quality of life improvements and saving optimization, but in-game bugs I have not encountered any.
If you like turn-based tactics you will not be disappointed by this gem, unless you like them easy and braindead.
The only thing I would wish for is that the devs would continue adding content even if slowly, but in some way. There is so, so much potential here.

Bastion is a really compelling and very memorable top-down action/RPG with lots of heart. It has a unique tone, great music, and style to spare. It isn’t perfect by any means – the combat is slightly awkward at times and there are a few other mechanics and features that aren’t great - but the pros outweigh the cons, in my opinion. Long story short, I’d say that when it comes to art style, mood, music, and so on, the game is a strong A, while the actual mechanics are a B. Ultimately, I think that the game is stronger than its individual faults, and that the whole project as a sum package is captivating and really worth playing. If you like adventure games and retro stuff, I’d recommend Bastion in a heartbeat.
+ The art style is fantastic. You know when you see great concept art for a game, and then the actual in-game graphics don’t even begin to capture that concept art? Bastion is the rare case where the in-game graphics actually achieve a large part of the wonder, scale, and mood shown in its concept art. The imagery will definitely make people stop and say, "Whoa, what are you playing?" The mission maps are filled with lots of lovingly-rendered clutter and little details, and the character designs run along this really interesting thin line between being cute and charming but also kind of rugged and tough. The visual tone does a great job of setting the mood...a little sad, a little lonely, a little dangerous. It's just an all-around striking and oftentimes stunning visual package.
+ The story is actually quite solid. It seems simple at first, but it's got some unexpected depth to it. I found myself growing unexpectedly invested in the story of the Kid and his comrades. The narrator is awesome, and his voice gives the game such a unique flavor. There’s also quite a surprising amount of lore and little anecdotes that help to create the world and its backstory. By the end of the game, this feels like a truly fleshed-out and real universe with an actual history. I would love to play a full-fledged RPG set in this world, so that I could explore these environments and interact with these characters in a more thorough and in-depth way.
+ As many others here have said, the music really is amazing. It’s got this electronic Western/folk vibe that is extremely evocative and works well with the visuals to produce a very cool effect…a bit lonely, a bit bittersweet, a bit exciting. The music is a huge part of why this game succeeds. The vocal songs are especially great and even beautiful. I definitely think that the original soundtrack is worth buying, some of these tracks will really stick with you for a long time.
+ You've got tons of weapon variety here. I was really surprised by the number of options. You start out with a hammer and shield, but you’ll eventually get a machete, pistols, a flamethrower, a mortar cannon, a spear, trip mines, and several other weapons. You’ve also got a wide number of available super moves, some are which can be unlocked through completing special challenges with each weapon. I really loved having the ability to switch up my weapon loadout to try out different combinations; the weapons are so different that each loadout almost makes you feel like you’re playing a completely new game. If you go through most of the game using the hammer and bow, you’re going to have a very different experience from someone who swears by the calamity cannon and musket.
= The combat is largely satisfying, but the ultimate effect is kind of a mixed bag.  There are some amazing, nail-biting moments of action, and there are some frustrating bits where your attacks clip through enemies or you just slog through a bunch of monsters without anything interesting happening. Some of the enemies are great, some are boring. There are some stunning highs that will make you sit up and play for another hour, and there are some lows that will make you shrug and stop playing. It can be thrilling at times and repetitive at others. The combat and mechanics ultimately average out to being simply good but not spectacular.
I know that this sounds like a pretty big knock against the game - you might be saying to yourself, "Wait, so the combat is just decent and not extraordinary? Why should I bother with this game?" Despite what I'm telling you about the combat, and despite the flaws that I'll talk about in the next few points, I really believe that the overall experience of the game is very worthwhile. If you're willing to accept that this game will give you incredible atmosphere and mood alongside gameplay that is solid but occassionally flawed, I don't think that you'll be disappointed.
- The platformating aspects aren’t very good…the ledges and walkways are extremely narrow and it can be way too easy to fall off the edge of a platform by mistake. This is by design and it's an obstacle that you're expected to overcome, but it’s annoying instead of dynamic or challenging.
- The game is definitely rather short, and levels are all way too linear. You won’t be doing any real exploration or digging for lots of hidden treasures or alternate paths. There are a few collectible items that you can pick up, but they're not even remotely tucked away...they're all just laid out there right in front of you so that you can get them at your ease. I would have liked at least three or four additional missions, some light exploration elements, and a handful of boss battles. Really, why aren’t there any boss battles here? I think that a few bosses would have helped with the pacing and would have just given the missions a bit more focus and pay-off.
- The ranged weapons have an auto-aim function that you can manually adjust, which sounds straight-forward enough, but the whole experience of aiming and adjusting was kind of clunky. Some weapons are better about this than others; the bow is pretty smooth, but others, like the mortar cannon or throwing weapons, are pretty stiff.

I'm going to assume you've read the description of this game before you read this review, so I don't have to explain the premise of the game.
Your task is to travel to various levels and collect Cores to restore main hub. (The Bastion) After each time you collectone you can build a shop where you can buy upgrades, passive buffs etc.
To get Cores you need to travel to all kinds of monster-infested areas, kill every thing that moves and make it to the end of the level, where you'll be rewarded with a core and a fast-travel back to the Bastion.
Combat is pretty fun. You have an array of different weapons to choose from. Guns, bows, a hammer, a mortar etc., so there's bound to be something that works for you.
It can get a bit cluster♥♥♥♥y at times, and it's pretty easy to not see where you're walking and fall off the level. Whenever that happens you get smacked back onto the ground and you take some damage. The game is also isometric, which makes it even easier to fall off.
I highly recommend playing this with a controller, since trying to navigate the small levels using the keyboard while 13 different monsters are beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you is like trying to play Expert TTFAF in Guitar Hero after you've had your hands immersed in icewater for 10 minutes.
When you get the hang of it, the gameplay is pretty fun and it's satisfying as hell to turn 12 bloodthristy birds into pâté with a single shot of your shotgun.
The story merges seemlessly with the gameplay, since all of it is narrated while you play by a man with a sexiest voice on earth. Most of what's told is lore about the world got ♥♥♥♥ed. The story focusses more on the Calamity rather than what's going on between you and the other characters. (Which is not necessarily a bad thing.)
This might be because there are barely any other characters. It's you, the narrator and 2 other survivors, and you never really interact with any of them that much. Most of the story events happen while you're off slaughtering the local wildlife and you only hear about them when you get back to the Bastion. Still, the story is good at drawing you in and the characters that are there are likeable. Also the premise is solid and the story nice builds on it. The ending is a bit of an anti-climax though.
The game is over in about 5 hours, and there's not that much to do afterwards except achievement hunting. There's NG+ but it doesn't really add anything new.
In conclusion:  Solid gameplay, solid story. Bit short, but that doesn't make it any less fun.

Unlike most of the other Sherlock Holmes games on Steam, this is more a classic Hidden Object type game rather than Point & Click or FMV. It's a perfectly good game for its genre with good HO scenes and logic in puzzles. The puzzle type and difficulty varies greatly throughout the game; most are doable without guide or hints.
The story follows Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson as they go with Lord Baskerville to his mansion to find out why his bloodline has apparently been cursed and his ancestors all died to this curse by being attacked by the creature known as the Hound of the Baskerville.
As a Sherlock story it's a bit... blasphemous; the story has heavy focus on supernatural theme and there no logical solution is found (this is not really a spoiler),
The game has good visual progress with throughout the game you complete "badges" to unlock powers to get into new rooms. Not really sure if this is good or not as it reminded me a bit too much of the much more child-friendly Princess Isabella games.
All achievements are easily earned; the one it says you get for "completing the game" is actually earned for Easy mode only, and as it has an achievement for completing Hard mode, you'll have to play it through twice to get all achievements. All dialogues can be skipped and as I accidentally clicked away a sentence said by a character, I can only assume that the "do not skip" achievement is only messed up if you click "skip" on dialogues entirely and not for normal left-click for skipping the sayings individually.
I didn't have too much problem with the voice-acting; Sherlock is a bit more enthusiastic in this game than he is in the later P&C games Testament and Crimes and Punishment. The sound effects and music is pretty good, but if you play League of Legends it might annoy you that in one musictrack there are sounds almost identical to "found a game" and "game invite" in LoL.
Buy more for the Hidden Object genre than for it being a Sherlock Holmes game. You may wanna buy it on a discount as it's getting a bit old, but it's a very enjoyable game.

This is honestly one of my favorite HO games, not the least because I'm a Holmes fan and Hound of the Bakervilles is one of my favorite books.  However, I will warn the Sherlock purists that this game has only a very passing relationship to the book so if you're looking for a HO-version of the classic, you very well might hate this.  The story is really very different.
In terms of general gameplay this is a pretty standard game for the genre, with HO scenes mixed with minigame puzzles and the usual inventory-based puzzles.  Where it departs from the norm is with a handful of special "powers" unlocked throughout the game that add to the puzzles; while in some cases it's apparent what you have to use and when, other times it took some thought and I appreciated that.
Puzzles and minigames themselves are average difficulty, not hard but not too easy, with the exception of one or two of the minigames that were just obnoxious; however there is a skip button or if you're intent on getting a no-skip achievement, there are solutions online (I confess to being guilty of looking up one or two solutions for that reason).
Sound and voice acting is nothing stellar but definitely better than the average, if you consider that most HO games have extremely poor voice acting.
All in all, a great game with some unique aspects that make it stand out.  Worth it if you're a fan of this style of game.

Now I've been following Daniel Remar's stuff since ye olde Game Maker days, so I kind of know what to expect from the guy and his team. And Ittle Dew 2 certainly delivered on all expectations and exceeded them in many places. I started playing, couldn't put it away and beat (almost) the entire thing in two sessions. This is a really good game, and a really good sequel to the first one.
Where the first game was mostly puzzles with a side dish of combat, this one balances the two out a bit more. Combat is faster and more dynamic, and there is now a clear distinction between combat rooms and puzzle rooms in the dungeons, both of which start out very easy and get absolutely fiendish as you progress in the game. The fire & ice wizards in level 8 in particular come to mind; there's a part where you have to beat two of them at once - easily one of the most difficult combat rooms in the game.
The main bosses are all rather easy to beat once you figure out their pattern, and if you have some of the optional powerups you find in secret areas all over the game, it makes your life even easier than that. The optional bosses (and dungeons) however are pretty demanding and kind of expect you to have as many powerups as you can get.
Speaking of the secret areas, that's where the game really shines in my opinion. I'm a huge sucker for secrets and exploration in videogames, and the fact that there are so many hidden rooms and even mini-dungeons in this game delights me to no end. There's even some secret rooms within other secret rooms, where you won't find an item but mysterious encoded messages instead (which I haven't been able to figure out yet). All of the secret rooms have a hint on how to open them, you just have to recognize what the hints are talking about when you come across it. So in summary, the game hugely rewards curiosity and exploration by hiding useful optional powerups in secret areas. I can't think of many recent games that do this - encouraging players to stray off the main path and including content so well hidden that most players probably won't even see it - but it has been a staple of Remar games since Iji and the magic moment that was Sector Z.
Bottom line: This game is a delight, and if you're an adventure fan and don't shy away from the more difficult enemy formations the late game throws at you, I absolutely recommend picking it up, at full price even.

Kane's Wrath, or the C&C3 games, are very good in my opinion. I always loved the C&C games, and like the others this game has good campaigns, movies, maps, skirmish, graphics etc.
There's only two negative sides with this game, and that is the multiplayer laaaaaag and desync. I have made a lot of custom maps for this game, because I really like the game and wanted to give the game some new gameplay modes with my custom maps, like Tower Defenses, Survivals, Missions and more. Unfortunately, the multiplayer usually lags and you never know if a map (usually custom map, but also normal maps) will desync.
What I have learned so far is that NOD Quad tower upgrade and Air Support Towers may give desync in multiplayer, and I also think some kind of "bad" scripts done in the worldbuilder may cause desync (maps work fine in single player, but they desync in multiplayer). When I say "bad" scripts it doesn't mean that there's something wrong with the scripts, it's just something wrong with the network programming in the game, cause the maps are fine in solo games. Only way to fix desync is to debug the custom map and remove the issue.
Overall, the game is old and is not getting any updates/patches from EA any moment soon, so I can't blame the game when it's nearly 10 years old. I loved the game in the past, I had much fun and I still llove it, despite the negative sides :)

I am playing and reviewing Frogware's Sherlock Holmes series in chronological order of the games. This game is considered a casual adventure game and it is unclear if this game is considered cannon or not. This game is made and could chronilogically be after Sherlock Versus Jack the Ripper.
The issue is that at the end of Sherlock Versus Jack the Ripper the Sherlock told Dr. Watson to cover up Jack the Ripper's story with a story about magical hounds refering to the story The Hounds of Baskerville. Playing this game could have easily be "fiction" in the Sherlock universe to cover this up, however during the game Watson refers to the Jack the Ripper case in this game thus putting this game in a type of limbo within Frogware's Sherlock Holmes universe.
After playing Sherlock Holmes: Mystery of the Persian Carpet, I was cautious to play another point and click adventure game by Frogware. I was happily suprised immediately when I start the game that all my worries were for not. Frogware fixed everything that was wrong with the Persian Carpet. There are slight animations instead of still frames, voice acting, and unique setting and puzzles. This game is worth full price and should be in, any fan of Sherlock Holmes, gaming library.

Child Phobia: Nightcoming Fears is an adventure game currently in Early Access. I can easily describe it as a psychological horror game featuring very mature themes such as child abuse, in a surreal/abstract way.
Gameplay:
Your character is a young child and at least the part of the game that is currently available evolves around a house. Gameplay looks kind of linear, at least so far, as you explore the house and the different rooms, following certain objectives that trigger the story to move forward.
I must say that I was not too excited though about the movement speed of the character you are controlling.
Graphics:
The game features hand-drawn artwork in a very interesting style. Extra points for that!
Music/Sound Design:
In this department the game also does well, with the sound contributing a lot to the atmosphere.
Pros:
-Hand drawn artwork
-Interesting themes
-Great atmosphere
Neutral:
-Mature themes that may make some people uncomfortable.
-Game is rather short but it's still in Early Access and there's more to come.
Cons:
-Character moving speed is a bit on the slow side which makes walking through the house, something you do A LOT, a bit tedious.
Conclusion:
The game looks good and has potential. Still in EA so we can't be entirely sure how it will evolve or where the story will ultimately go but for 1.99 it's not really a risk.
Score:
Gameplay:		7/10
Graphics:		        9/10
Music/Sound:	        8/10
Concept/Story:	8/10

My hours here aren't real amount of hours I got in this game. I had CnC3 and KW both on a CDs since 2009, and since the CDs are long dead I decided to get it here on a same. .
If only this was the last game in the C&C franchise, we'd all be able to happily say that the C&C went out with a hell of a bang. Sadly that's not the case, but I won't go and mention that Tiberium Twilight abomination anymore.
I'm just going to list some stuff here, and won't go into much depth:
Nod focuses on stealth and hit and run tactics. But... Then comes the Black Hand faction which reminds me of Sisters of Battle, they completely drop the stealth and hit and run stuff, and go for the complete
. Who needs stealth when we have god damn purgatory flames which cut through buildings... And everything like butter. But that all comes at a cost, a cost of still being squishy and not having air units. They're the glass cannon faction. Oh and the Black Had has the Mantis, which can lay waste to entire fleets of air units.
- The strongest superunit in 1v1 fights against the others without units - it's a crazy looking walker with tri-laser gun and the Enrage ability which can cause chaos to the enemy.
GDI is more of like TANK power. They've got the most tough (ground) units out of all factions. Highest armor and a great amount of damage by default. + They got some really good bombers (which can switch to anti-air rockets and turn into the sky gods) and choppers. And of course the Apocalypse tank spin-off the Mammoth tank. Their tanks focus on railguns - except for the ZOCOM faction which focuses on sonic emitters. Also there's a Steel Talon faction which focuses on walkers. Instead of the default vehicles most of their units are walkers. Each faction has different types of upgrades, be it for vehicles, units or air units. Some add more armor to their air units, while some add more ammo.
- Amazing looking tank with sonic shells. And can be garisoned by the most units: 4 infantry units. On top of all that, when you drive it over the tiberium fields it automatically gathers resources for you - dope, isn't it?
- My favourite faction! Scrin has similar armor values on their vehicles as Nod, but no stealth. Instead they get tankier by getting shields on literally every vehicle they can produce.... And ships. Scrin differs from the others with their air superiority. While others have the ground artillery, Scrin uses Capital Ships as artillery, and their damage is far greater than anything the other two factions have. Then on top of that, they have the Planetary Assault Carriers which are pretty much the most powerful non-superunit in the game in my opinion. They release small fighters to kill stuff for them, and can produce storms that increase combat effectivness for all air units.
But... there's always but, isn't it? There's a Reaper-17 faction, which completely focuses on ground units - they're completely unable to produce air units. However their Tripod is way more powerful than the one from the other two Scrin factions.

- Doesn't matter how you look at it, it's a giant spider, no more, no less. It can be garissoned by 3 units. It's somewhat funny looking, especially comparing to the other two superunits. Have you ever played Terraria and thought "Man, I don't wanna keep on making worlds to find other stuff." or "I like this game, but there's no story." Well, do I know the game for you. The closest thing I can relate Starbound to is Terraria, with it's 2D-survival based gameplay and it's stellar (pun intended) combat. However, I find it to be so much more than space Terraria. You've got quests, and instead of having pickaxes and axes, you have a single tool that you can do just about anything with, and it can be upgraded as you go on. Yeah, you can build a pickaxe, but it breaks over time, and the only benfits it has is that it mines faster and has a larger dig area, which can be fixed with only a few missions in-game. They also have pets that can actually fight, crew members that you can hire, goblin darts, moon ghosts, 8ish playable races, procedurely generated planets, and probably some things that I haven't reached yet, most of my hours are from Pre-release.
tl;dr Fun game, buy it
Also, you can play as Space Cowboys made from Stars, that's pretty cool.

an interesting take on the ccg format. Reminds me of the early days of games like poxnora or dungeon dice monsters.
For those who are already familiar with ccgs, you build the battlefield as you go, selecting different types of spaces (fire, water, earth, air, and non elemental) and rather than simply placing cards on a table and attacking, you summon them to the board as you build it and move around the field, attacking enemy monsters and the opponenet themselves.
The map building also acts as a secondary resource in that elemental lands that you create are also necessary to summon elemental creatures both in summon locations and in how many needed to summon each monster. Each player is building the terrain so you not only have to build a path to your enemy, but as players can summon monsters onto any space they have created, you also have to try and stop your opponent from building paths right to your front door.
The creatures are your garden variety mythical monsters, but the artwork is fantastic, and the game (while having an in game store because it's a ccg so of course it does) is not shy about giving non paying players a fair shake and a good number of ways to earn free packs of cards.

All right, will sound harsh but the main reason I am not recomending this title is the fact that people were trying to hail it as the next Baldur's Gate. It isn't.
While it sort of looks and feels a little like Baldurs gate, its just not. Here are my basic complaints.
1. Messing With the Stats
The creators of this game decided they wanted to get creative with the stats. So they dumped everything you're familiar with (Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Etc.) And put in brand new stats. So if you are hoping to just jump right in and know whats going on from other RPGs, the answer is no. You're going to have to re-learn all the stats
2. Absolutely Zero AI
In Baldurs gate, you could give custom scripts to your characters. Things like "Hey, you, you're a cleric. Cast healing spells when we take damage." "Gotcha Boss" So you could focus on watching health, positioning, spell casting, all that good stuff. There is NO AI IN THIS GAME. If you have six party members, you are micro managing six party members. Otherwise they will just stand there and pick their nose.
3. Small Maps
I've been running through for a while and.... well these maps feel really small. I can discover well over half a map in like..... 2 minutes. It feels cramped over all. They look nice don't get me wrong but.... I imagine even while finding secrets I can blow through an entire area in five minutes.
4. Yak Yak Yak, Yak Yak Yak Yak Yak Yak.
So.... much..... talking. I've started to just skip it. You can see I've been playing 16 hours, but I've only gone through 4 areas. THERE IS SO MUCH TALKING. I'm all for story line but don't write me a damn novel all at once here.
5. What the hell am I doing?
They have little pop up windows to give you advice but.... lets be frank here. A whole damn tutorial explaining stats, skills, daily abilities, encoutenr abilities, the fact that you can flank, what survival does precisely, all would have been very useful.
So there's my gripe. People kept screaming "OHMYGOSH ITS JUST LIKE BALDURS GATE" And its just not. Saying its like Baldur's Gate is like saying Clue is Just like Monopoly. You move pieces around a board right?

I'm not a fan of CCGs in general. I've tried several and I find that it's nearly impossible to play many of them without spending money, and I'm not one to spend real money on digital cards, and on top of that, as a long-time Magic: the Gathering player, I find most of them to be rather bland and non-interactive in comparison. However, I am enjoying Faeria quite a bit.
It isn't too hard to build up to a new deck as long as you're a decent or lucky player - that is, as long as you can consistently make it to 4-5 wins or more in Pandora (the "sealed" deckbuilding, like Hearthstone's Arena). The rewards you get are fairly generous for a CCG, and most decks have a pretty healthy mix of commons, rares, epics and legendaries.
The added depth from not only having a field to play your cards on, but actually building the playing area as you go, is what keeps me around I think. It adds like 3 new layers of complexity to a genre that generally doesn't have very much of that. Not only does placement of your lands matter, but timing (do I need these two forests right away, or can I hold off and just play prairies to get board control?), and the types, based on your deck. This system is familiar to me as a MtG player, where certain spells require a certain number of like-colored lands in order to cast them. Unlike Hearthstone for example, where you're locked into whatever class you chose, plus neutral cards, in Faeria you have every card available to you in deckbuilding, and the only thing restricting you is whether or not you can play enough of the right colored lands to cast those cards.
That's not to say the game is without flaws, though. It, like Hearthstone, suffers from some poor design choices, like the inclusion of cards with random effects. It's a card game, people! There's enough randomness just based on the fact that you have to draw your cards in a random order! We don't need cards that randomly assign buffs or damage. It just adds needless feel-bad situations where you as the player can't control the outcome of what happens.
The game is also somewhat clunky and buggy. Even with a mouse, it's nearly impossible to avoid misclicks. I can't imagine trying to play on a far less accurate touchscreen device.
The animations, while pretty, get old, and there's no way to speed them up or skip them.
In the end, though, it's the only CCG that has offered enough depth to keep me interested, while being accessible enough financially for me to keep playing it. I'd give it a 7.5/10. With some more polish and a few different design choices (especially regarding random effects), this could easily be a 9.5/10.

I love this game (as you can tell from the sheer amount of hours I have into it). I have played several times through each college, usually with a different goal in mind (i.e. make myself a Gates mage or make my familiar all powerful, things like that), and each time I play I encounter something new. There is a lot of content to this game, and if you don't like text-based games this is not for you. The random events and chooseable adventures are creative and entertaining. I like that we get to decide the curriculum and path for our character as well as the appearance and familiar. Or no familiar, if you simply choose to focus on yourself.
On the negative side,this is a difficult game to grasp at first. Muddling through creating a character was difficult enough, but then I spent ten minutes trying to figure out how to skip to the next day before I found the button (which is so glaringly obvious that maybe I should take the blame for that one!) Then I got so frustrated trying to figure out what was what that I turned it off and played something else. I'm not going to sugarcoat it--you will struggle when learning how to play. The only way I got through it was with help from the guides on here and the Academagia wikia. I personally think it was worth the effort, but I won't lie--it was a lot of effort. Not everyone has that amount of patience.
I doubt at this point whether the sequel will ever be started/finished/released and that is a shame, but this is still great as a stand alone game in its own right. I would definitely recommend it, and I would have no qualms about purchasing Academagia 2 if it ever comes out!

This is an absolute gem of a game. Ever wanted to go to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry?  This is it, or as close as we muggles will ever achieve. After so many hours into the game I can finally say what I like and dislike about the game.
Fisrt and foremost, the gameplay is simply awesome. You are put in a shoes of mercenary company capitan, and you have to manage your company to become the greatest and most formidable force in the world. Simple, isn't it? Well, it isn't. To achieve this dream, you have to kill a lot of things first. And kiling them isn't easy at all. You always need to be careful, because one wrong step can cause you the lives of one of your men.
Death is part of the game. Defeat is part of this game. Starting over is part of this game. Landing on your knees over and over again is part of this game. Those things ARE this game and it's not bad, because the most satisfying part of this game is the feeling of accomplishment, when you finally can stand firmly on your feet. When the brigands start to run away from your company with fear, the noble houses try not to anger you and even orcs and goblins start to retreat in fear from you in battle.
THIS is what this game is about. Loss, defeat, anger and learning. Difficult and challenging but satisfying as hell.
The artstyle is on point. It suits well the dark, medieval, fantastic, brutal tone of the game. Needles to say, I'm a fan of hand-drawn graphics.
Although, like the coin has two sides, so has this game. Not everything is perfect. RNG can sometimes screw you over, you can grind your teeth in anger, when you try for few hours to get a certain item, encounter or character background (freaking occultists man...) and still not get them. The fact, that your bros can start at highly disadvantageous ground, being stuck in a dumb place, being shot right into the face at the first turn before you can act is... Annoying to say the least.
Also, no mod support is really, really, REALLY bad for a game like this. There is oh so much content, that can be put into the game, but there is no mod support to do that. I can even say, that there are more modding possibilities than in Mount and Blade. New races, backgrounds, adding spells into the game, new battlefields, new enemies, sea combat, more weapons, more encounters, more world interactions, story even. There is so much that can be added into the game, that I can't even write it all. Although, no mod support won't allow to add this things into the game. Unfortunately.
So, would I recommend this game? Yes. Wholeheartedly. Can I say that it's worth it's price? I'm not sure. Would I like to add something to it? Hell yeah! Am I sad or angry about the RNG system? Yup, hella angry about the FREAKING CULTISTS NEVER APPEARING FOR ME...
OK, so what about a final, overall grade...?
A+, 10/10, will play again!
