Bastion is a really compelling and very memorable top-down action/RPG with lots of heart. It has a unique tone, great music, and style to spare. It isn’t perfect by any means – the combat is slightly awkward at times and there are a few other mechanics and features that aren’t great - but the pros outweigh the cons, in my opinion. Long story short, I’d say that when it comes to art style, mood, music, and so on, the game is a strong A, while the actual mechanics are a B. Ultimately, I think that the game is stronger than its individual faults, and that the whole project as a sum package is captivating and really worth playing. If you like adventure games and retro stuff, I’d recommend Bastion in a heartbeat.
+ The art style is fantastic. You know when you see great concept art for a game, and then the actual in-game graphics don’t even begin to capture that concept art? Bastion is the rare case where the in-game graphics actually achieve a large part of the wonder, scale, and mood shown in its concept art. The imagery will definitely make people stop and say, "Whoa, what are you playing?" The mission maps are filled with lots of lovingly-rendered clutter and little details, and the character designs run along this really interesting thin line between being cute and charming but also kind of rugged and tough. The visual tone does a great job of setting the mood...a little sad, a little lonely, a little dangerous. It's just an all-around striking and oftentimes stunning visual package.
+ The story is actually quite solid. It seems simple at first, but it's got some unexpected depth to it. I found myself growing unexpectedly invested in the story of the Kid and his comrades. The narrator is awesome, and his voice gives the game such a unique flavor. There’s also quite a surprising amount of lore and little anecdotes that help to create the world and its backstory. By the end of the game, this feels like a truly fleshed-out and real universe with an actual history. I would love to play a full-fledged RPG set in this world, so that I could explore these environments and interact with these characters in a more thorough and in-depth way.
+ As many others here have said, the music really is amazing. It’s got this electronic Western/folk vibe that is extremely evocative and works well with the visuals to produce a very cool effect…a bit lonely, a bit bittersweet, a bit exciting. The music is a huge part of why this game succeeds. The vocal songs are especially great and even beautiful. I definitely think that the original soundtrack is worth buying, some of these tracks will really stick with you for a long time.
+ You've got tons of weapon variety here. I was really surprised by the number of options. You start out with a hammer and shield, but you’ll eventually get a machete, pistols, a flamethrower, a mortar cannon, a spear, trip mines, and several other weapons. You’ve also got a wide number of available super moves, some are which can be unlocked through completing special challenges with each weapon. I really loved having the ability to switch up my weapon loadout to try out different combinations; the weapons are so different that each loadout almost makes you feel like you’re playing a completely new game. If you go through most of the game using the hammer and bow, you’re going to have a very different experience from someone who swears by the calamity cannon and musket.
= The combat is largely satisfying, but the ultimate effect is kind of a mixed bag.  There are some amazing, nail-biting moments of action, and there are some frustrating bits where your attacks clip through enemies or you just slog through a bunch of monsters without anything interesting happening. Some of the enemies are great, some are boring. There are some stunning highs that will make you sit up and play for another hour, and there are some lows that will make you shrug and stop playing. It can be thrilling at times and repetitive at others. The combat and mechanics ultimately average out to being simply good but not spectacular.
I know that this sounds like a pretty big knock against the game - you might be saying to yourself, "Wait, so the combat is just decent and not extraordinary? Why should I bother with this game?" Despite what I'm telling you about the combat, and despite the flaws that I'll talk about in the next few points, I really believe that the overall experience of the game is very worthwhile. If you're willing to accept that this game will give you incredible atmosphere and mood alongside gameplay that is solid but occassionally flawed, I don't think that you'll be disappointed.
- The platformating aspects aren’t very good…the ledges and walkways are extremely narrow and it can be way too easy to fall off the edge of a platform by mistake. This is by design and it's an obstacle that you're expected to overcome, but it’s annoying instead of dynamic or challenging.
- The game is definitely rather short, and levels are all way too linear. You won’t be doing any real exploration or digging for lots of hidden treasures or alternate paths. There are a few collectible items that you can pick up, but they're not even remotely tucked away...they're all just laid out there right in front of you so that you can get them at your ease. I would have liked at least three or four additional missions, some light exploration elements, and a handful of boss battles. Really, why aren’t there any boss battles here? I think that a few bosses would have helped with the pacing and would have just given the missions a bit more focus and pay-off.
- The ranged weapons have an auto-aim function that you can manually adjust, which sounds straight-forward enough, but the whole experience of aiming and adjusting was kind of clunky. Some weapons are better about this than others; the bow is pretty smooth, but others, like the mortar cannon or throwing weapons, are pretty stiff.

Bound to appeal to at least a few Mary Sues and Harry Stus ... especially since those who require (and have the temperament to roll their own) have access to a modding community who can show them how to inject as much Hogwartiana as they care to.
For those of us who get hooked on character creation, that element alone has massive replay (restart?) value:  7 attributes, 7 Colleges, dozens upon dozens of skills, a personal schedule of 6 classes selected from 17 (though a few will be mandated by your choice of college), all tweaked by seven categories of Background options; 10 schools of magic (some informal, some FORBIDDEN) and a bewildering range of on-and-off-campus facilities to train skills for improvement (or cram for exams).
On top of all this, you can use time not spent studying/training/exploring/crafting (and even take the risk of skipping class) to go on Adventures - a variety of missions determined by the calendar, your college, your courseload, and your modified relationships with instructors and fellow students.  There are multiple ways to be competitive - including Rimbal, a not-too-veiled equivalent of Quidditch - or you could spend all of your time alone.
And the basic point of the game is to prepare for your 'sophomore' year ... fresh class options, new missions, hypothetically different instructors, etc. ... not that there's really any way of knowing how long it will take Black Chicken to cook up Year 2, but it is officially on their to-do list.

I'm going to assume you've read the description of this game before you read this review, so I don't have to explain the premise of the game.
Your task is to travel to various levels and collect Cores to restore main hub. (The Bastion) After each time you collectone you can build a shop where you can buy upgrades, passive buffs etc.
To get Cores you need to travel to all kinds of monster-infested areas, kill every thing that moves and make it to the end of the level, where you'll be rewarded with a core and a fast-travel back to the Bastion.
Combat is pretty fun. You have an array of different weapons to choose from. Guns, bows, a hammer, a mortar etc., so there's bound to be something that works for you.
It can get a bit cluster♥♥♥♥y at times, and it's pretty easy to not see where you're walking and fall off the level. Whenever that happens you get smacked back onto the ground and you take some damage. The game is also isometric, which makes it even easier to fall off.
I highly recommend playing this with a controller, since trying to navigate the small levels using the keyboard while 13 different monsters are beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you is like trying to play Expert TTFAF in Guitar Hero after you've had your hands immersed in icewater for 10 minutes.
When you get the hang of it, the gameplay is pretty fun and it's satisfying as hell to turn 12 bloodthristy birds into pâté with a single shot of your shotgun.
The story merges seemlessly with the gameplay, since all of it is narrated while you play by a man with a sexiest voice on earth. Most of what's told is lore about the world got ♥♥♥♥ed. The story focusses more on the Calamity rather than what's going on between you and the other characters. (Which is not necessarily a bad thing.)
This might be because there are barely any other characters. It's you, the narrator and 2 other survivors, and you never really interact with any of them that much. Most of the story events happen while you're off slaughtering the local wildlife and you only hear about them when you get back to the Bastion. Still, the story is good at drawing you in and the characters that are there are likeable. Also the premise is solid and the story nice builds on it. The ending is a bit of an anti-climax though.
The game is over in about 5 hours, and there's not that much to do afterwards except achievement hunting. There's NG+ but it doesn't really add anything new.
In conclusion:  Solid gameplay, solid story. Bit short, but that doesn't make it any less fun.

A well-made source mod that offers a type of gameplay not experienced in other zombie games.
The game is split up into two primary game modes: survival and objective maps. Objective maps give a group of players a linear set of objectives that take players along a map. The objectives in each map aren't all that repetitive and have you completing a variety of tasks that lead you to new parts of the map. This gametype is impossible to solo and some maps demand lots of communication. Survival mode scatters players throughout a map and has them survive either until all the zombies have been killed or the timer runs out. Since there is no map progression, players must hunker down, set up barricades and gather supplies in order to survive.
ZPS was made with teamwork in mind. From my experience, the surivor win-rate in surival mode is about 20-30% and about 5-20% in objective maps. Once a survivor dies they become a zombie, so if you lose too many of your teammates too fast, you will have a harder time as the map progresses. Everything you carry (down to each bullet) has weight that noticably impacts your movement speed and available run energy. People that hoard supplies are not only easy prey for zombies, they are also easily noticable by teammates which will rightfully give you a hard time. Every gun also requires its cooresponding type of ammunition; if your friend runs out of ammo for his AK47, you can toss him a magazine of rifle ammo if you got any.
Being a source engine game, ZPS enjoys new maps and content from the modding community. Although it's not what it was years ago, there's still plenty of maps that were created for you to enjoy now. Just don't expect many more new maps in the future unless you're willing to make them.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone after a more team-based, realistic zombie-survival experience.

Shadow of Mordor is an open world, fantsy RPG which has slight links to the LOTR films. Before playing Shadow of Mordor I was worried that due to me not watching any of the LOTR films (Please don't murder me for not watching them!) I would get really confused when trying to revise the story of the game. It turns out that there are only 2 characters that starred in the film within this game, so if you haven't watched any of the films don't sweat about it as you won't need to, in order to enjoy this game.
The first thing I would like to congratulate this game on is its combat. Shadow of Mordor has the best combat system that I have ever experienced in any game, and i've played a hella load of games! Every kill you get feels badass, whether its an insignificant orc or a warchief, you will leave the battle feeling like your a cold blooded murderer. The executions that you can do after charging your hit streak are gorey, just the way I like it, and a selection of abilities can be equipped onto your bow, sword and dagger to give you that edge in combat. Even after completing the story, I was motivated to go around and just go on a killing spree just to get the satisfaction from the combat system.
The story was fascinating to play through, but was too good to last. I would deliberately stall myself from playing the story missions as I was afraid that I would complete the game too fast, and even when slowly pacing myself through the game it came to an end in the blink of an eye. Even so, the story was addictive and lured you into the game. The story was enjoyable to play through, and i'm not going to give any spoilers, but the game ends with the same feeling that you would get when checking your bank balance after a night out. Disapointment. I get the feeling that the developers were rushing to meet their release date and quickly chucked a few cutscenes in with a crappy end battle and then thought bobs ya uncle. Saying that the intriguing story up until the ending allowed me to forgive the game for cutting it short whilst I was still flacid.
After completing the game I thought to myself, "Oh its okay, the DLC will keep me going for a while." I played through the Lord of the Hunt DLC and it had a similar mission to the main game, being that you had to assassinate all of these warchiefs that were killing little baby Caragors, which I could not stand for. I found this DLC reasonably enjoyable but having the same motif as the original game I kind of shortcutted it, and only assassinated the warchiefs, and didn't bother with all the collectables and slaughtering the other orc captains because it felt like a repeat of the main story.
The other story DLC, The Bright Lord, was again similar to the main game with only slight modifications to the combat and a vaguely different story, leading me to bordom within the first couple of minutes when playing through it. I am interested in the lore of games and like to learn more about the characters, but the DLC was painful to play for me as I knew that the end game factor would be the same as the main game and the Lord of the Hunt DLC, making me give up on it rather quickly.
The graphics have a hyper-realistic sense to them, and from looking at them you could not guess that the game was released in 2014, as they were made to look sexy even in the future. The game is also well optimized as i'm running this game on a Radeon 380 with a 2560x1080 display on high settings with anti-aliasing set to x4, and my game is running at a solid 60fps, so I will give the game props for its optimization. A cool feature that I picked up on was how the grass and foliage would interact with the player, and was a feature that I have rarely seen in games. The orcs within the game are all unique in their own way, and alot of effort has been made to give them their own looks, personality and fighting styles. You will be pushed to find an orc which looks similar to another. (Unless you compare Mogg and his twin brother lmao!).
To conclude, I did love playing through Shadow of Mordor due to its awesome combat and captivating story, implementation of lore from the films, and progression system. I do believe that the story was rather short, and would have loved to have been able to feast on some more content, but it is clear that Warner Brothers games have done a great job in producing an RPG game with a rich story. I'm a big fan of The Legend of Zelda series, so I always keep an eye out for games inspired by it. The first Ittle Dew caught my attention back in 2013, and I had an incredibly fun time with it. On top of being charming, Ittle Dew provided puzzle design that seemed inspired by Zelda but wasn't afraid to do its own thing. I anticipated a sequel for three years, and in 2016 I was finally given one. If you're like me in my love for Zelda and you're seeking out games with similar puzzle foundations, then you should appreciate Ittle Dew 1 and 2. Here is a more detailed breakdown.
Ittle Dew 2 had a really great overworld. It had a good size where it felt large but you were able to find things on almost every screen. There's lots of secrets in the world, from fast travel caves, portals, puzzle caves, and on. These things make the world fun to explore. Furthermore, exploring is made a rewarding experience both through fun gameplay (i.e.the puzzle caves) and good prizes for your efforts.
Ittle Dew has no shortage of clever puzzles, but it accomplishes it in a different way than say a Zelda. With Zelda, you tend to get one item per dungeon, use that item for the rest of the dungeon, and never pull it out again (at least in the 2000s titles). In Ittle Dew, you don't have as many tools at your disposal, but instead are always thinking about different ways to use these tools, and more importantly use them in conjunction with the other tools at your disposal. This philosophy is one of the things that makes Ittle Dew 2 standout from the rest of the pack.
Ittle Dew also isn't scared to provide a challenge where all you need is your sword. It sounds minimalist, but in reality the game designers still did a fantastic job of thinking of clever puzzles that you don't need a lot for. Even some of the puzzles in the dungeons that make use of your items often have multiple ways to go about solving them, and if you're clever enough you can find ways to only use your sword.
If there is one area that Ittle Dew 2 truly stands out, its puzzle and dungeon design. If you're here looking for a puzzle game, then look no farther.
The combat is the most controversial piece of Ittle Dew 2's package. It has both pros and cons to it.
For background, the first game hardly had combat, and if it did it was puzzle combat (where the key to beating an enemy relied less on combat skill and was really just more puzzle work). Fast forward to Ittle Dew 2, and not only did it introduce combat, the combat is hard.
Personally, I enjoyed the combat. It was frustrating at times, especially early on when I wasn't expecting it. It was jarring, and I think it was jarring for a lot of other people as well. However, as I progressed further into the game, I came to really appreciate the combat design. Yes, it's hard, but it's fair. Enemies have patterns and telegraph their next moves, so as much as they deal lots of damage and move quick there is nothing unfair in the game. Beating the boss is a matter of mastering the combat system. So, in terms of that, I feel the combat was well designed and its something I came to really enjoy.
The question I think many people have in regards to Ittle Dew 2's combat system is if the level of difficulty was approrpiate for the game. Remember, Ittle Dew 1 was primarily a puzzle game. Many people returning weren't expecting any combat at all, let alone it being difficult. In other words, when people are buying this game for its puzzles, should they be greeted with difficult combat? Was this the right game to implement it?
People are going to disagree about the answer to the question, because each person is getting a different thing out of the game and has different preferences. The point is its up to you to decide what you want. Are you fan of difficult battles and enjoy mastering combat systems? Or, are you here for the puzzles, and don't care for a more action orientated direction? If you think you would enjoy the combat on top of the puzzles, then this game is for you. If not, then you'd have to evaluate how much it's a deal breaker (or go back and play Ittle Dew 1).
To me, Ittle Dew 2 is a fantastic game and one of the best titles I played in 2016. It has a gratifying overworld, excellent puzzle design, and fun combat. The question is if you want all of these things in one package.
TL;DR Ittle Dew 2 is one of the best titles I played from 2016, and I highly recommend it. The overworld is fun to explore, the dungeons and puzzles are fantastically designed, and the combat is gratifying. However, you need to individually decide if all of these things are what you want out of this game, or if one of them is a deal breaker. While I found each element was fair and extremely well done, do know that there is a tough cross-over in terms of action and puzzles. I loved the entire package and what it provided, but that equation will be different for each person and it doesn't necessarily mean you will. So, I recommend going beyond this TL;DR and understanding each of the games components before making a decision. That said, I think even if you don't like one element of the game, the other should still be more than gratifying enough to make up for it.

Desert Gunner is just a tepid pile of nothing, and that's even if you can run it correctly. It's entirely comprised of awful, repetitive turret sections where you shoot Iraqi soldiers while driving towards Baghdad - at least I assume they're soldiers. The game calls them insurgents, but most insurgents don't have a dozen tanks to throw at you during the average engagement.
Gameplay-wise, aiming your weapons and firing is all you do. This isn't helped at all by the fact that aiming in this game sucks, there's practically no feedback that tells you where you're taking damage from so you can react in time, and the difficulty begins at "brutal" then shortly shoots up to "you're not finishing the first level without cheats." Your small convoy is swarmed with enemy armor, RPGs, and regular rifle-toting soldiers that can still somehow damage your tank's health. Imagine Kaizo Mario with AK47s and you're halfway to Desert Gunner.
Meanwhile, the entire aesthetic is lo-fi and amateur to the point where it honestly looks like one of
. That was probably unintentional, given the player's entire justification for driving through the Arabian Desert is pretty much "they're shootin' at you, kill 'em all!!!" which isn't a good look for a game about one of the least justified wars in modern history.

I wish that the review system for Steam had a "meh" option; because this game is by no means bad, but it isn't really that good either.
Let me explain.  I bought this game 3-odd years ago, and it was a totally different game.  It was buggy and poorly-thought out, but you could see that the core concepts to make an amazing game were really there.
I got bored after a week of playing and didn't play again until a year later.  By then, the game was entirely different.  Each race had cool abilities and unique weapons and armor bonuses; which is still kind of in the game, but not as varying.  The story was subtle, which made it even more fun to be whoever you wanted to be.  You weren't "The Last Protector." You were whoever you wanted to be.
My big problem with the game in its current state is it's unrewarding loot and crafting system, the generic "in your face" story, and the general homogenization of unique features.  Like why did they get rid of the cool, unique S.A.I.L. avatars in favor of the generic humanoid ones?  Why make the loot and weapons so ♥♥♥♥ing hard to find, but not offer a way to create a crafted equivalent?  Why drop the subtle story and replace it with the current boring♥♥♥♥♥version.
Not to mention, the problems and things missing from the game have to be modded in.  There is actually no system in place to accurately tell when your food will rot.  But you'll have so much of it that your food rotting doesn't do anything but make the game that much more annoying to play.
And with all of this, you'd think I'd give this game a negative rating.  But since they included Steam Workshop in the final build, most of this stuff is forgiveable.  Just keep in mind that you'll be installing a fair bit of mods to make the game truly enjoyable.

A deceptively solid strategy game with no frills attached graphics, a satisfying (and anxiety inducing) level of lethality in combat and an excellent level of customisation.
Set in a medieval nation, you control a group of mercenaries as they roam the land taking contracts to fight monsters, bandits and wage the wars of the noble houses. You train, equip and manage your soldiers as you guide them through the hostile and uncaring world of a mercenary in which the classic good vs evil mentality is meaningless - you're there to do a job, get paid and move on and there's often situations where you have to choose between what is "right" and what'll see your men fed and paid for another day.
Combat's deadly and can see your men bloodied, maimed and dead very easily if you get careless, however good use of tactics (and a little luck) means you can often turn unfavorable situations in your favor.
I've been playing the game since it was in Beta and it has a significant amount of content on launch compared to when it first hit Early Access. If you like turn-based strategy combined with an overworld management system similar to XCOM I'd highly recommend you give this title a go.

Have you ever played Terraria and thought "Man, I don't wanna keep on making worlds to find other stuff." or "I like this game, but there's no story." Well, do I know the game for you. The closest thing I can relate Starbound to is Terraria, with it's 2D-survival based gameplay and it's stellar (pun intended) combat. However, I find it to be so much more than space Terraria. You've got quests, and instead of having pickaxes and axes, you have a single tool that you can do just about anything with, and it can be upgraded as you go on. Yeah, you can build a pickaxe, but it breaks over time, and the only benfits it has is that it mines faster and has a larger dig area, which can be fixed with only a few missions in-game. They also have pets that can actually fight, crew members that you can hire, goblin darts, moon ghosts, 8ish playable races, procedurely generated planets, and probably some things that I haven't reached yet, most of my hours are from Pre-release.
tl;dr Fun game, buy it
Also, you can play as Space Cowboys made from Stars, that's pretty cool.

I really enjoyed the original Ittle Dew, so I was excited to get a sequel. You can tell they took a good look at the shortcomings and criticisms of Ittle Dew and tried to improve those areas in the next title, which I really appreciate; that's a hard thing to do and I give them credit for taking a critical look at their product. That said, they went about the "improvements" in entirely the wrong way. The game takes a lot of cheap shots at the player, sending them to opposing corners of the map back-to-back, with all the enemies respawning every time you leave a screen so there's zero reprieve from attack and no reason to bother clearing an area. Baddies are equipped with way too powerful weapons in some areas, and many of those have projectiles that track you. Are tracking projectiles inherently bad? No. When there's 4 enemies on the screen who all fire off 3-8 of these tracking projectiles at the same time so all you can do is try to minimize the damage you take rather that use strategy or skill to avoid it entirely, there's a problem.
The difficulty curve in the dungeons is no joke. The first 6 seem to scale normally, with a natural progression familiar yet new attack types and patterns and puzzles that take on more elements. The 7th dungeon you start to go "huh, this is weird...this is WAY harder than the last one" but you stumble your way through it and head off to the final stage of the game. Which is bat s**t insanity. It's unnecessary backtracking, new enemies that take forever to kill while dealing massive damage, and spikes placed exactly where they make every strategy you've ever come up with for enemies null and void. It also, without any warning, asks you to utilize your tools in ways you have literally never had to in the rest of the game.  Combining functions, applying them at angles, making them loop on themselves, these uses are never used but suddenly they are key to finishing the last stage.
The final boss started out as a cool way to wrap up the game with you having to do puzzles while on the move, which I found to be a nice nod to the story the game has been getting at the whole time. And then, AND THEN, the next part comes. Without getting into spoilers, the same complaints from above come in full force, at the same time, with a time crunch, and sporadic/random health replenishment. I spent 2 hours streaming just the final stage and boss, and we never finished it. I'm morbidly curious what the death counter is for that section alone.
For a game that did so much right in the original, I'm sad to see how much went so wrong in the follow up title, especially seeing that the foundation for a good game is present here beneath all the things that make me want to tear my hair out and lay on my floor in defeat.

The art style, aesthetic, soundtrack and humour in this game are all outstanding and the layers upon layers of secrets are something I haven't seen for years. The dungeon design harkens back to the earlier golden days of Zelda when open plan multiple route dungeons were par for the course. This isn't a retread or cheap knockoff though! Ittle's moveset, the items and the combat are all original. Even the dungeon themes are completely original and delightfully quirky. Smashing your way through an art exhibition whilst fending off disgruntled critics just takes the absurdity of common genre tropes and dials them up to eleven. Furthermore, there's an innovative feature in the game whereby you can play through most dungeons and overworld challenges in any order you please as each puzzle prior to the endgame only asks you to use your starting stick and whatever is found in that particular dungeon.
Sadly though, the difficulty curve suffers terribly as a result of this. Given every item you obtain allows you to simplify or outright bypass puzzles, that they cannot be turned off and that every puzzle in the bulk of the game assumes you have no items from previous dungeons, the difficulty curve for puzzles flatlines for the second through seventh dungeons, before abruptly spiking in the final dungeon and post-game content. The result is a game that is carried by its combat which, whilst better than Ittle Dew 1, is merely fun, not groundbreaking (with optional moves that require three or more keys to be depress simultaneously which is a disaster if your keyboard is ghosted; thankfully they're only mandatory for the super secret third final boss).
There are some challenging puzzles in the game, but to access them you have to begin a new file and attempt the game again beginning with a different initial dungeon. This makes it great for speedrunning, but unlike Ittle Dew 1, I felt little inclination to do so due to the game's length.
What I did feel inclined to do however was complete a second playthrough on the unlockable 1 HP mode. It is here where the game's open design truly shines through! Sequence breaking suddenly becomes significantly harder despite no part of the world being gated off, and the tight balance risk vs reward is incredibly satisfying. There's almost a Dark Souls feel to the way some areas are gated off by combat challenges that can only be overcome by pixel perfect rolls and sequence memorisation, or the slow collection of incremental character boosts and upgrades. If this mode didn't also savage the hilarious dialogue, I'd go so far as to recommend players look up the unlock code and attempt it on their first playthrough.
Overall, its a fun title and I enjoyed it thoroughly and would still recommend it. The developer Ludocity is rapidly becoming one of my favourite indie devs for the love and polish they drench all their titles in; its abundantly clear from everything in game right down to the odd comment on the Steam discussion boards that they adore their work and it shows in the final quality of all their games. My recommendation is to try Ittle Dew 1 first, as it is the more ground breaking of the two titles, and then, if you enjoy that, you'll probably find the sequel's charms hard to resist.

A very simplistic hidden object puzzle game with a good name attached to it, Hound of the Baskervilles offers a quite interesting take on the famous novel.
Let’s get this right out of the way: if you are a Sherlock Holmes purist, stay far away from this. Apart from the presence of Sir Henry Baskerville this game has nothing to do with the novel– not only the titular hellhound is an actual demon, but Holmes even uses magical powers to battle it.
Despite this rather unique use of artistic freedom, the writing is the main strength of this title: both the short plot and the large number of dialogues are great and the actors do an excellent job as well.
The game itself is just a glorified item gathering: you visit rooms to collect things either from the scenery or by playing meticulously crafted hidden object scenes, assemble them into some fairly challenging puzzles, which reward you with even more items. This pattern is repeated from start to finish with not change in the concept.
Don’t be fooled though, the game isn’t easy. It is aimed at the more experienced hidden object players, who will undoubtedly have several hours of great fun with it.

First of all, this game is a 8.5/10 if you like puzzles.

There is a lot more combat than the original, and that helps to rest your brain after solving puzzles.
However, dear devs remember this: the more chaotic the game looks in terms of structure, the more fresh it feels when playing. As a player, I should not know what comes next.
Moving on, sound design was great, music was ok (except the star one, liked that a lot). World themes were pretty original and there was a lot of fun dialogue (found it funnier than the first game, thumbs up to whoever came up with the dialogue lines). Controls were decent, although I found it hard at times to turn and aim properly because aiming was tied to movement controls.
The art was colorful and very nice (I liked that shader that shakes objects' cell shader and makes it look as if sketched) and level design was gorgeous except one case: even though there was a significant amount of cleverly made puzzles, I found the original game to be harder (and better imo) in that aspect. If you get a lot of items in this one you can easily solve 90% of every puzzle there is and I found that to be a let-down as I was not challenged towards the end (compared to the first where the final secret puzzles really melted my mind, maybe I was ready this time as I solved everything pretty fast, dunno).

This is one beautiful and fun game.
The gameplay feels a lot like Assassin Creed with a bit of Batman thrown in. But the combat, which is the most important part of this game is done very well. It feels very satisfying to play and kill Uruks.
Controls are solid, and at least with a keyboard and mouse I didn't have to change anything from the default controls.
The game beginning is very engaging, but it slows down soon afterwards especially once you get stuck in the side quests, which are not very fun. The main story though is certainly fun, and towards the end it gets even better. The voice acting is top notch, especially for the Bright Lord. The cinematic are done very well and fit well with the game.
The game maps are quite small so you will be doing a lot of fighting in the same areas. So it might get a bit repetitive after a few hours into the map. However, the game is paced very well and the frequent unlocks will introduce new concepts and keep things fresh somewhat throughout the game.
I get 144+ FPS on my GTX 1080 and i5 6402P, so the game is very well optimised for PC. I think its important to note that from start to end I did not see a single bug or glitch anywhere. Only in the DLC, I saw a minor sound glitch that fixed itself in about 5 seconds.
It took me about 30 hours to get everything 100% in the DLC and the main game. Considering I got this at a sale, I feel that I definately got my money's worth. I would highly rate this game even at full price. At the discount it goes to, its almost a steal.

Tried this game for about 2 months.  It's a good game.  But why the bad review?  Read on.
1) Pandora game (seal deck format) is too luck based - one of the unique mechanics of this game is, you can save up your mana (faeria) each turn.  So on the first couple turns, unless you are playing vs a rushed yellow deck, you ideally want to cast a big guy on turn 2 to over power your opponent.  But if you opponent has that 1 card to answer your big guy, for example, frogify which turns any creature into a 2/2, the match is pretty much over.  There are also treasure cards which can single handedly turn the game around, assuming you drafted the right treasure for the right situation.
2) constructed - unless you spent money, it will take you a long time to build a collection to make a competitive deck, so I haven't even done enough constructed to comment on this.
3) Timer and griefers - a few days ago I play this one guy who would run out his entire turn timer, every.single.turn.  I don't remember if I won or lost, but I was annoyed enough to stopped playing for couple of days.  So today I played again, guess what?  ran into another guy who does the same!  I actually won that match.  Then queued up again, after about waiting for 3 mins, I ran into that same guy AGAIN!  Played for about 30 mins later, I lost the match.  That really was the last straw for me.  This isn't a complicated game, I don't have the patience to play a 30 mins match.  I want a game that I can just pickup and play.
4) As pointed out in #3, the reason I ran into the same guy is the player pool is really not that large right now.  In pandora, I often run into names I recognize.  Can you imagine that happening in any other mainstream game?   To make matters worse, I constanly run into these clock runners who waste other people's (and their own) time for who knows what reason.
If you have the patience for long matches, and like to play seal deck format (to build up your collection initially), or if you got a lot of money to drop onto this game, it might be for you.
It's a shame because I really do like the game on its own, except for annoyance mentioned.

I may only have 39 hours on Faeria, but I have fully finished all the solo missions and played Pandora mode at least 30 times.
Faeria is a wonderful and completely F2P (Free to Play) Card Game. It offers several solo mission where you defeat AI enemies. There are 2 different types of missions: There is the regular 1v1 battle and then there is the Puzzle battle. In the puzzle battle, you are given a certain situation with lands and creatures already on the board, and you must defeat your foe with the cards you've been given in just 1 turn. This method of training, shows you all types of strategies for when you play the game againt others, may they be AI or People. The RNG (Random Number Generator) in this game is not terribly high, like in other cards games. The cards are quite simple to learn and once learned, there are no surprises you would have to worry about. Altogether I think there's about 300 cards or so. Maybe less actually.
Faeria updates regularly. Solo missions come in packs of 9 missions per pack. The 1st 3 are free, the others need to be bought with ingame currency or RL currency. If the solo pvp battles are too slow for you to earn that currency, just play some Pandora mode. It's the arena mode: You get a selection of 33 cards to choose from, (same for all players) which you make a deck to battle others with. Your chances of winning in this mode rely on your skill to pick and use your deck properly in battle.
I give this game a 10/10   it's honestly the best Card game out there atm.
TL:DR    Faeria is definitely F2P, Play Pandora mode if you need InGame currency fast.

If you have not played the original Ittle Dew first, check out my review, or if you're a puzzle fan, just buy it, you are wasting valuable game time.
Now for the sequel.  In comparing it to the original, there is more.
-More puzzles, BETTER puzzles!  This game maintains its non-linear approach from the original, and ups it to 11.  There are 7 core dungeons, and they can be completed in any order.  Most of the game's dungeons can be completed with just the stick you start with.
-More dungeons, BETTER dungeons!  So many dungeons, and they are all quite non-linear.
-More enemies, HARDER enemies!  More on that later.
-More overworld, larger, more interesting overworld with sights and secrets everywhere.  That is not an exaggeration.  The overworld is filled with so many heartfelt details and just a hilarious amount of secrets.
-More of the same humor.  You found the original hilarious, right?  Well you will not be disappointed!
-More secrets.  If you are familiar with Ludosity's/Daniel Remar's games, you probably already know about secrets in every direction, layered secrets, and even secrets that aren't even secrets!  It's all here.  If you stay focused and take note of everything in sight, it is all very much possible to find.
-Better graphics.  The original looked fine in 2D, but this game uses a 3D approach in the art department.  The core gameplay is the same, it is a sort of top down view, but it's just better.
So about the game's enemies.  In the original, most enemies moved slow and had predictable patterns.  In this game most enemies are fast and will attack you in full 360 degrees, and it is challenging.  Getting knocked out in this game is a slap on the wrist, as it will respawn you at your last checkpoint or at the dungeon entrance with full health.  This is fortunate, because beating the game for the first time without getting KO'd is basically impossible.  Combat is challenging, but a huge portion of the game's optional dungeons and puzzles give you extra life or weapon upgrades.  So if you are good at exploring and puzzling, you can mitigate the challenge.
In closing, if you liked the first Ittle Dew, the only thing that might concern you is the challenging combat; however, losing all of your health is forgiving, and the combat isn't incredibly difficult.  It simply requires a careful, thoughtful approach.  For most puzzling gamers out there, Ittle Dew 2 is a worthy successor to the original, and an excellent purchase.

This game is not just another random, low-quality game on the Steam Store, but one of many of the same type. PLAYERUNKN4WN: Zombie is really an asset flip (a game that reuses the assets of another game), the game it having flipped being UnitZ. UnitZ is a multiplayer FPS sandbox starter kit (or in other words, a template) that can be purchased on the Unity Asset Store. The game has been a popular origin point for a large number of asset flippers, such as the following:
The rest I cannot name, due to a large amount of them out there and tracking them down is actually quite hard.
Even though the game is in Early Access and the developers claim they will update and improve the game, in reality they will likely not do so. You see, they really are just using the Early Access title and promising things as a way of drawing attention to their game. Also, what is there really to improve in such a simplistic and disgustingly designed game that has been reused, that no one would want to actually dedicate time to. This can be proven further by how they market the game. The game has been named similarly to a popular game [PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS], which may lure unsuspecting players to purchasing the game (the chances of that are quite low quite low). The game also promotes how "you will get 5000 achievements" when you purchase it, which is a way of luring achievement collectors to purchase the game and this also makes the game feel more like a complete joke. Going back to my point, all this shows how the developers don't really care much for this game and/or making any original, good quality games, they just want to reuse another game so they have a way of making a quick buck. And this information doesn't just apply to just this game; there are maybe hundreds of asset flippers out there on the Steam Store, some flipping UnitZ, others flipping other games. I advise you to be aware about the existence of asset flippers, refrain from purchasing this game and other similar games, warn your friends about games like these and click that Report this Product button, all of which may help prevent the growth of shady developers like the ones behind this game and prevent them from stealing the hard-earned money of other Steam users.

So to sum up the + and - :

+ TMD is cool device

So all-in-all the game is worth playing if you can get it at < £5 or so on sale but dont expect any depth or challenge to the gameplay - this is a game you play then forget.

Ittle Dew 2 greatly improves on the gameplay of its predecessor, which was essentially a single-player version of the classic co-op game, Goof Troop. The sequel packs a punch at three to four times the original’s length, and mixes the Goof Troop puzzle-solving with far more influence from Nintendo’s classic Zelda titles for the NES and SNES. The self-aware world of Ittle Dew is full of rich humor and clever writing — they’re seriously among the funniest games I’ve ever played.
Ittle Dew 2 is also packed with hundreds of secrets, including not one, but two secret levels, each with their own secret final bosses. One’s a bit more obvious, tied into the characters’ dialogue and the game’s achievement list, but the other is found only by finding all the game’s hidden objects, decoding a number of hidden messages, then standing in a specific place in a specific, obscure room for exactly seven minutes. Doing so transports you to the doubly-secret (and doubly-final) dungeon, housing the game’s most difficult villain: A…farting potato…?

A fine addition to the Ittle Dew series, this game remains similar to a Zelda game in that it's about exploring and finding items for solving puzzles, but has only a few unique tools that are really exercised with some good puzzle variety, rather than simple puzzles that are trivial applications of your tools. Another benefit of the small number of tools is that you never have to go to the menu to select them: they fit right on all your face buttons if using a controller.
The game features more emphasis on combat and avoiding traps than its predecessor, but still brings some great puzzles, largely focused on either putting blocks on switches, hitting switches in sequence, or hitting multiple crystals within a certain amount of time of each other. This time they went with a more non-linear design, which limited the amount of puzzles that could combine tools for most of the game, but I still enjoyed the in-dungeon puzzles a good amount and found the wand they replaced the portal wand with to be interesting to work with. The variation on the ice item compared to the previous game was interesting enough as well.
On the unfortunate side, most of the combat in the game just isn't satisfying. It's often sufficient to just flail your melee weapon at the enemies until they die. It might cost some health, but with frequent shortcuts that can be opened up throughout dungeons, dying isn't much of a problem. The bonus dungeon bosses are somewhat of a challenge, though.
Also, as perhaps a matter of personal preference, I didn't really like the overworld's puzzles, which were largely based on noticing stuff or remembering clues from NPCs. I prefer having all the puzzle elements directly in front of me to work with.

While it's reminiscent of many other games, Singularity is greater than the sum of its oft-borrowed parts. The time & space manipulation in puzzle solving has a Portal-esque feel to it, the gunplay and sci-fi elements are evocative of the Half-Life series, and the alternate reality's sprawling landscapes filled with intricate details and satirical propaganda clearly show that BioShock rubbed off on the developers. In fact, the Time Manipulation Device (TMD) employed by the game is essentially a Plasmid from BioShock – equipped on your hand, you'll use it to do things like reverse or speed up the age of items and enemies to bring variety to combat and navigate the devastated, apocalyptic terrain.
Though Singularity is certainly guilty of taking more than a few elements from other games, it puts its own spin on those elements well and creates enough of an original feel to consider it a legitimately good game in and of itself, making the experience an entertaining entry in the first-person shooter genre. The notes, recordings, and projector footage you find from the past (again, sound familiar?) range from amusing to frightening, and help to further illustrate the game's 1955 & 2010 versions of Russia which you jump to and from in order to rewrite history and correct time travel paradoxes. The consistently thick, tense atmosphere aside, this is the game's strongest asset, I feel, and could've been explored more thoroughly. This and its disappointing length are its greatest flaws, though the fact that the majority of players find the game too short shows just how enjoyable it is. When it was over, I wanted more of it, and I intend on a second playthrough – something the game encourages, as the plot twist at the conclusion recontextualizes the events preceding it.
Singularity isn't the most original or creative game, and it only grazes the surface of deeper themes (the illusion of free will, the responsibility scientists have to mankind, the inherent paradoxes in time travel) in favor of maintaining a breakneck pace, but it does so many things right that its flaws are forgiveable and, in the grand scheme of things, minor. I consider this a good choice for anyone who enjoys action or first-person shooter games, especially the ones I mentioned in this review as well as others in that vein.

Although it's a great game, I can't recommend it to most people unless the devs add a difficulty setting. As it is, I only recommend it if you like to play games on hard whenever given the option. If you usually play on normal, parts of the game will frustrate you (especially if you're a completionist). If you usually play on easy, avoid the game entirely because it will be more frustrating than fun for you.

Shadow of Mordor is an open world, fantsy RPG which has slight links to the LOTR films. Before playing Shadow of Mordor I was worried that due to me not watching any of the LOTR films (Please don't murder me for not watching them!) I would get really confused when trying to revise the story of the game. It turns out that there are only 2 characters that starred in the film within this game, so if you haven't watched any of the films don't sweat about it as you won't need to, in order to enjoy this game.
The first thing I would like to congratulate this game on is its combat. Shadow of Mordor has the best combat system that I have ever experienced in any game, and i've played a hella load of games! Every kill you get feels badass, whether its an insignificant orc or a warchief, you will leave the battle feeling like your a cold blooded murderer. The executions that you can do after charging your hit streak are gorey, just the way I like it, and a selection of abilities can be equipped onto your bow, sword and dagger to give you that edge in combat. Even after completing the story, I was motivated to go around and just go on a killing spree just to get the satisfaction from the combat system.
The story was fascinating to play through, but was too good to last. I would deliberately stall myself from playing the story missions as I was afraid that I would complete the game too fast, and even when slowly pacing myself through the game it came to an end in the blink of an eye. Even so, the story was addictive and lured you into the game. The story was enjoyable to play through, and i'm not going to give any spoilers, but the game ends with the same feeling that you would get when checking your bank balance after a night out. Disapointment. I get the feeling that the developers were rushing to meet their release date and quickly chucked a few cutscenes in with a crappy end battle and then thought bobs ya uncle. Saying that the intriguing story up until the ending allowed me to forgive the game for cutting it short whilst I was still flacid.
After completing the game I thought to myself, "Oh its okay, the DLC will keep me going for a while." I played through the Lord of the Hunt DLC and it had a similar mission to the main game, being that you had to assassinate all of these warchiefs that were killing little baby Caragors, which I could not stand for. I found this DLC reasonably enjoyable but having the same motif as the original game I kind of shortcutted it, and only assassinated the warchiefs, and didn't bother with all the collectables and slaughtering the other orc captains because it felt like a repeat of the main story.
The other story DLC, The Bright Lord, was again similar to the main game with only slight modifications to the combat and a vaguely different story, leading me to bordom within the first couple of minutes when playing through it. I am interested in the lore of games and like to learn more about the characters, but the DLC was painful to play for me as I knew that the end game factor would be the same as the main game and the Lord of the Hunt DLC, making me give up on it rather quickly.
The graphics have a hyper-realistic sense to them, and from looking at them you could not guess that the game was released in 2014, as they were made to look sexy even in the future. The game is also well optimized as i'm running this game on a Radeon 380 with a 2560x1080 display on high settings with anti-aliasing set to x4, and my game is running at a solid 60fps, so I will give the game props for its optimization. A cool feature that I picked up on was how the grass and foliage would interact with the player, and was a feature that I have rarely seen in games. The orcs within the game are all unique in their own way, and alot of effort has been made to give them their own looks, personality and fighting styles. You will be pushed to find an orc which looks similar to another. (Unless you compare Mogg and his twin brother lmao!).
To conclude, I did love playing through Shadow of Mordor due to its awesome combat and captivating story, implementation of lore from the films, and progression system. I do believe that the story was rather short, and would have loved to have been able to feast on some more content, but it is clear that Warner Brothers games have done a great job in producing an RPG game with a rich story. The banter between Talion and Torvin where Talion will mock Torvins high by itself is worth playing the game for. #RoastSimulator.

I was a huge fan of Ittle Dew. It has some brilliant non-linear puzzle design, funny characters, wonderful art style, and tasteful homages to Zelda. So I had high hopes for the sequel, but was let down in many ways. Ittle Dew 2 is much more combat focused, has less charming 3D art, and most of the jokes are references to the first game (many of which are only hazy in my memory). For the first few hours of the game I was really disappointed how different it is, and yet by the end I loved it on its own terms.
Most of the puzzles are simple because they’ve carefully ensure that they can all be completed without the item upgrades. And so, as you progress you gain the ability to ‘cheat’ puzzles with your extra powers. It’s strange for a puzzle game, but it’s an interesting way to show growth. You even find extra keys in secret caves which allow you to skip dungeon puzzle.
Then there’s the combat which feels difficult and tedious at first. But upgrading your weapons to the point where difficult enemies are now trivial feels great. The best tactic early on is to run away when possible. I think the only oversight in the design here is that Ittle should regenerate her health when entering a room, just like monsters do. It doesn’t really make sense having to start a room with low health or search for it when each battle is treated as its own puzzle.
By the end of the game I was satisfied, but didn’t love it yet.
The final boss gives you 1 of 4 keys which begins the question of why to find the other 3. Turns out there’s 4 more advanced dungeons that can only be unlocked by finding most of the secret caves on the island. Tracking down all of those is a joyful treasure hunt on its own. The extra dungeons are also very combat focused, but have a few extra puzzle tricks to teach. Bosses in this game are all a hair too difficult, but they are very fair with specific repeating patterns that can be memorized. The last hour ties up all the dangling story threads and I can’t deny that I really enjoyed my time, even if it wasn’t what I hoped it would be.
No matter what your preferences are, I’d recommend playing Ittle Dew before this game. If this is the ‘Adventure of Link’ of this series, I’m really looking forward to its ‘Link to the Past’.

This is easily one of the best games I've played recently. The puzzles are excellent, and span a good range of difficulties, becoming difficult by the end but not quite "look up the answers" difficult. The art and music are really pleasant and the writing is extremely entertaining; Ludosity has a very specific kind of charm in its characters which shines through well.
The weakest link in the game is probably the combat, which while not bad is unexpectedly difficult and can be unforgiving in many cases, particularly due to its overreliance on the use of the dodge roll mechanic which gives you invincibility frames. The game gives you several other ways to defend yourself, such as deflecting bullets, but on later game enemies everything except the dodge roll becomes impractical or in some cases explicitly useless.
All that said, I absolutely recommend this game, just with the warning that getting 100% completion is an ordeal.

A phenomenal take on the card game formula. While the art style makes it appear like a generic, cartoony turn-based cash trap, the gameplay is surprisingly well designed. The combination of placing, moving and commanding enemy cards along with influencing the game with effect cards is massively complemented by the unique map building system. Players take turns placing land which they need to spawn in and move their cards. Players only able to spawn their own cards on their own land, and certain cards only applicable for certain land types. This adds an entirely new and refreshing strategy element to the gameplay which makes the entire experience feel much less stagnant and more alive then the average card game system.
But while the art style itself is rather typical and the cards are only somewhat creative, they feel much more at home in their world then in most other games. Especially the ever recurrent Yak cards. This also making the world feel more vibrant and alive then the average dry fantasy worlds out there.
The primary drawback is that the game does gate mentionable amounts of content and progress off unless the player pays. Players more likely to get decent currency from daily challenges over actually playing for long periods, currency being borderline mandatory to get new cards. However, this really is a common theme in these types of games is it not. The clever and interesting gameplay well makes up for this, as players are paying to play an actually good game as opposed to a rushed and shotty cash bait.

This game is the best early-access I've ever played, If you're into survival, exploration, and crafting : GET THIS GAME!
It's a very good bargain. The fact that this small Indie a team has a faster, better and friendlier response to its players than other Early-Access games *cough* dayz *cough* should be enough to convince you to buy this, because it means your money did not go to waste, as these devs will fix and solve the bugs you actually post.
But enough about the devs, lets talk about the game!
The intro to the game is pretty generic to survival games (crashing off a plane) but at least you get to make your own martini before descending into your doom. It is also very well made, the intro looks realistic and its not just some stupid black screen at the end of it.
Afterwards you wake up on the raft you climbed on before being blown to ♥♥♥♥ with your trusty paddle and you will find a tiny island : your new home.
There you can gather resources and craft new items and tools necessary for your survival. The crafting in this game is very original, and you will not be disappointed. Instead of depending on a generic crafting screen, this game actually handles that in the physical game world, meaning you have to lay down some sticks, rope and rock before you before you can start crafting your spear.
You have the ability to hunt crabs (easiest) or fish from the ocean, even bigger fish near the reefs and deeper into the water. Hell, if you're brave enough you can actually chase that stupid shark thats been circling your beloved raft for so long, and kill it, and COOK IT! As of now you cant eat shark fin soup, but you can still eat the fin, and other parts.
The cooking is quite realistic, you will have to wait a while before your crabs become crispy and tasty, instead of insta-cooking.
You will have to manage your resources as they are quite finite, which after a while will force you to navigate to other islands in search for more wood and rocks. Especially if you want to build a nice big hut.
This game has a few bugs, but none of them are game-breaking which is something very worth your money these days.
The main reason why I think you should get this game is because it has so damn much potential. And when all the amazing new features start coming in you will start to realize how you should have bought this game early on, you can wait, sure. But you'll miss out on alot of fun. It is always nice to support such a promising game. Even more when you've got community friendly devs, and amazing gameplay.

First let me get this out of the way: I've played this for probably an hour, despite what steam's weird gametime tracking thing says. I've played it on a few different computers which is probably why it says I've played it for such a short time.
Secondly: This is probably the second worst game I've gotten on Steam, the worst obviously being Air Control.
In Desert Gunner, you're a guy manning a turret. In the desert. That's literally it. The "multifacited levels" the game description promises is really just one level where your convoy drives slowly in a straight line and you shoot at things.
Unlike some of the great turret shooters out there (Beachhead 2002, lookin' at you buddy), in this one you'll have NO clue weather or not you're actually hitting anything. You fire and fire and fire and no visible damage or anything happens. Then your'e dead. Start the level over again. But when you start the level over again you won't be able to tell because the whole level is a straight line.
You can switch between guns with the WASD keys, not that the game tells you that. Also, when you start the game up, the three green dots that are offscreen on the main menu are actually "options", "credits", and "exit" respectively. You simply won't be able to read them because the game, on all three computers I've tested it on, the game insists on running on a non-native, non supported resolution.
I've tried it on a 4:3 monitor where it started in 16:9, and a 16:9 where it started in 4:3. No idea why that is, but worth noting: You won't be able to read half the main menu items.
If you're a gun-nut such as myself, you might be interested in reading the technical specs the game has on all the weaponry you'll be using. You'll be significantly less interested when you find out that most of them are downright incorrect, and all of them are wirtten in text with font so small that you can't read them.
All in all, don't waste your dollar. It's not even fun to laugh at like Air Control, it's just a mess. The developer put three seconds of effort into this, so you should treat them similarly.

WAVESHAPER is a game that lots of potential that falls short due to laziness and the devs underestimating their players. Good gameplay, lackluster presentation, scarce content, and an overabundance of hollow, meaningless achievements.
WAVESHAPER's gameplay is simple but appealing: Hit keys to match the oncoming symbols, as they approach ever faster and in more complex matters. Make mistakes, lose health, get streaks going to recover. Get high scores, good flawless streaks, short games that can deal to great bursts of dexterity. I can safely say that the game's basics and core is very good and would lend itself greatly to some truly entertaining short sessions and maybe even some hardcore enthusiasts.
Unfortunately, that's as far as the game's brilliance goes. The gameplay, while good in its core, lacks any depth beyond that. There's simply nothing else to do, and there's only three modes in total and none are really meaningfully different. There's no extra gameplay, and you'll very quickly see everything that there's to offer and accomplish. There's no real long-term replayability beyond just very simplistic leaderboards.
The UI is almost a bit too simplistic. There's only your current score. The game could really benefit from your personal high score, a timer, perhaps something to indicate your current mode. Small details like these can enhance the experience, but they're all lacking. Even some toggleable options would be appreciated. And the leaderboard menus are bland and samey, and hard to navigate. I seriously suggest an overhaul is needed because it's poorly made.
The music is serviceable, but ultimately very forgettable. No catchy tunes, and your presses only give limp bass kicks, or hisses when missed. There's a few tracks but probably none that you'll find yourself thinking about once you put the game down. A game like this could really benefit from a more exhilirating OST to compliment the accelerating gameplay. Even if you insert custom music, the fact that the music the game brings is so boring is definitely not a point in its favor.
The graphics are delightfully simple, but I'm disappointed that it's so monotonous. There's no meaningful variation. No background color change, no background pattern, no customiseable marker (the hit symbols can be custom, that's one good thing), but there's nothing extra, no bonus settings, nothing. It's not just minimalist, it's bare-bones, and there's very little visual candy except some particles. It's just dull to watch with almost no space to express yourself.
But by far the worst aspect of WAVESHAPER is the 120+ achievements. The grand majority of the achievements are hollow, meaningless, and insultingly easy to get. And by that I mean that with minimal effort you can get almost all of them in less than an hour. These range from the absolute brain-dead "Score 5 points in normal" which takes even less time that to complete the tutorial, to completely unrelated ones such as "take a screenshot". This game is bloated with achievements that mean nothing and represent no skill whatsoever, and represent a shallow and clearly lazy selling point. And it a shame because there are actually a few achievements that are not so easy and will take some actual effort to attain, such as "Score 400+ points" or "Go from 1 to 3 health in Hard Mode six times in a run" which actually feel good to satisfy, but the game vomits achievements at you that are empty and just clutter your profile.
Like I said, not everything is bad. There are actually good things to this game. The core gameplay is good, it has tons of stats and leaderboards that while clumsily displayed are actually good info to have, about 5% of the total achievements actually mean something, minor details here and there that indicate that this have been a really fun, exciting, and thrilling game to play. As it is, it's a good concept that barely goes anywhere beyond its simple premise, has no depth, has clearly vacant room for many more features that are nowhere to be seen, and its most offending aspect is that for many, it only serves to allocate asinine awards, attracting avid achievement amassers, against accomplished adepts' ambitions.

Battle Brothers is like a very simplified turn-based verison of Mount and Blade with elements from Darkest Dungeon and Mordheim: City of the Damned sewn in.
You command a warband and each recruit is different due to random backgrounds, traits and appearances given to them. These unique traits interact differently in combat as well as to others in your group and the world around them.
There are ingame events that make the world seem a bit more lively such as random encounters, noble house wars and orc invasions. They add more depth to your story and give you some interesting choices to make.
Quests can get repetitive, but sometime events can occasional change up the contracts.
Combat is straightforward with hits and misses determind by RNGesus. As your warband increases you will need to specialize your men and assemble formations to insure that valued soldiers survive for later game fights. Yes, some of your men are destined to be cannonfodder. Make sure it not your prized Iron Lungs Twohander Hedge Knight.
Finally, the artwork and music for this game went beyond my expections. Images have exquisite attention to detail from character injuries to armor damage depending on if you sustained any in combat. The soundtrack is amazing. There is an appropriate theme for every enemy type you face, ranging from the astounding trumpets of noble houses to the despair inducing choir of the undead legions.
Oh, and free DLC that adds norse serpent-like dragons to hunt. Exactly what this game needed!
I would definitely recommend Battle Brothers.

After beating the game, finding most of the secrets, and getting to the 4th secret boss, I can safely say that despite the many flaws which hurt the experience for some players, I still found it to be enjoyable overall. And to me, that's all that really matters when playing a video game. However, the flaws may be enough to drive the casual player away, and do deserve to be mentioned upfront.
Just as a disclaimer for when I talk about difficulty; I'm a dark souls veteran. The mindset behind the combat is similar, and while I enjoyed the challenge and though it was fair, that might not apply to everyone. You almost have to have a dark souls mindset for the later bosses, so if you can't handle that, this may not be the game for you.
1. Lack of puzzles
The original Ittle Dew was almost entirely puzzles. Combat has gotten an overhaul, and has a lot more emphasis placed on it rather than puzzles. There are some really good ones later in the game, but the problem is that there are basically only two dungeons that will test your knowledge of all of your tools; the final dungeon and the final secret dungeon. Everything else (every single secret area, the first 7 dungeons, and the first 3 secret dungeons) can be done with your original tools and a tool found within the dungeon. They can be challenging, but are still simple and small scale until the end of the game, which is a massive difficulty spike puzzle-wise (not combat, which follows a proper difficulty curve up to that point).
2. Overworld enemies
Not much to say. Fighting them is basically a noob trap; there's no reward for doing so, you run faster than most enemies, so its much safer to just roll past them and run to the next checkpoint or map transition. Then, in metroidvania style, come back when you're overleveled, clear the map, and then start looking for secrets.
3. Player's tools in combat
I will praise the enemies and bosses in this game for having attacks that feel fair, and being easy to overcome once you have the pattern down. That may just be the dark souls fan in me, but I'm used to that, and enjoy it. However, the part of the new combat system I dislike are your tools in combat. Just to note, I'm not talking about the actual items which you can find, but their applications in combat.
Every single tool is one dimentional in its use; for puzzles each item can be used in conjunction, and has unique properties when two techniques are combined. However, in combat, all of these are completely useless. They take too long to set up, and are rarely ever a better option that just using each item normally. I feel this is the largest problem of the combat; your techniques never develop through the game, and each weapon only has face value in usage, so combat gets stale fast.
4. Boss health
To me, I entered each boss room with the mindset of "prepare to die." As Jim Sterling has said, this is not just a catch phase, but a tactic on how to overcome a challenge. Each death gave me more knowledge on the bosses patterns until I knew enough to finally win. A death never frustrated me, because no attack felt unfair, and if I got hit, I knew exactly why. Throughout the entire game, few bosses felt frustrating, and once I was at a boss room, I never left until I beat the boss. Most of them felt pretty easy to me, but I'm more used to the counterintuitive tatics and knowing when some options are inferior, like rolling into projectiles instead of reflecting, since it gets rid of it faster and safer.
With that in mind, I still feel like the bosses health scaling is way off. It feels like items were supposed to upgrade your damage a significant amount more than they currently do. My worst three bosses were cyber jenny 3, slayer jenny (optional miniboss), and the 4th secret boss. On those three, it took much longer than I had the patience for. I knew how to dodge each attack, and the patterns themselves were fairly balanced, but each death meant so much time was added to the boss fight, I was just bored. Not frustrated, or ragequitting, it was just really boring and tedious doing the same button movements to dodge the 3-4 attacks for 10 minutes and having to start all over again if I messed up more than three times.
I'm currently still on phase 1 of that secret boss; when I look at the sliver of damage I deal, it just seems really boring to go back. I know I'm going to have to do it all over again learning the new moves at phase 2; at that point the first phase is just a really long run-up to the actual boss, the part of dark souls I find most boring. It doesn't even have the same feeling as the hardest dark souls bosses, because there they have difficult to avoid attacks but take roughly the same amount of hits as other bosses. Here, the boss is properly balanced, but they just tripled the health to increase the difficulty even more. I can't even take the option of high risk; if the boss took the same amount of health from the new weapon as the first time you hit, then I'd know that I'm supposed to look for chances to use the weapon, which is already challenging with her current pattern (especially since the first shot is given free with the long boss startup). But since it does so little damage, the sword has higher dps while being significantly safer to use.
These flaws will kill the game for some people. If you can look past them and still enjoy the game, then I fully reccomend it at the current price. For others, it may be worth waiting for a 50%-75% sale and trying it then. If nothing else, I reccomend looking out for Ittle Dew 3, which will hopefully fix all these problems. Ittle Dew 2 has kept most of what made the original good, so I have faith that the next one can only be better. I could probably list off everything I feel could make a better game, but that's something for the forums, not here.
