To the folks who are writing reviews about struggling to understand the game, click the big "?" icon on the main menu screen of the game and cycle through all the screens that follow. It serves as a tutorial of sorts and gives you a basis for how the game's 3 character types work differently, as well as a little setting for the story.
Though to be fair even after reading through that tutorial it took me a few rounds to get the hang of the mechanics in action, but it definitely helped.
When you first start a match, you choose among the available yellow flower spaces (the sparkle animations show you where you can move) where you would like to place your 3 characters/pieces. The starting points chosen can help turn the match in your favor once you start to get the hang of the basics of the game, so you'll want to choose carefully, but don't worry too much about it for your first round or two when you're still trying to get the hang of the game.
The gist of a round plays out something like this: you get points for destroying a square, squares with yellow flowers are worth 1 point, magenta flowers are 2, and red flowers are 3, and whatever square your chosen piece is standing on before you move is the one that gets destroyed that turn. Each player in the game gets 3 characters or pieces to move about on the board, and there are a variety of different board layouts chosen seemingly at random each round.
As the game details for you, each character type has a different function. If you are playing as Sylphs, they are able to move through squares that have other characters on them. By contrast, Pixies and Dryads are obstructed by other characters/pieces, even their own teammates. If you are playing as Pixies, they have a chance to randomly change some of the flowers on the squares around them, altering the points values of the squares on the board with each turn (sometimes it fails to alter them). Dryads are perhaps the most complex in that, with Dryads you actually get 4 moves per turn, split between any of your pieces on the board, however only the first move you make destroys a square, and Dryads are limited to moving only a single square at a time, unlike Pixies and Sylphs.
The goal is to be the player with the most points at the end of the round. At the bottom of the main menu of the game you can toggle between Human player and AI Opponent for all 3 of the character types, allowing for up to 3 player local multiplayer by taking turns.
Now I think the part that I can appreciate that most people will not about this game, is that I am intimately familiar with the RPG Maker suite of software, and this game was made using RPG Maker MV engine. I applaud such a creative and unorthodox use of that engine to create an unexpected game type like this.
I only wish the game had more content to explore, more depth to it. More reason to come back to it. There is a great little fun idea here but it feels like it didn't use enough of its potential, and that's a shame since it's such a refreshing idea of a game considering the engine it arose from and the types of games usually seen from RPG Maker.
Even if the game isn't very lengthy, it's still pretty fun while it lasts, and I think the asking price is reasonable as well for what is here. I hope to see more such creative ideas from the developers and I would love to see a sequel to this, or perhaps DLC that perhaps added a few different board types, rules, or modes, or even just other character types would be interesting to explore, having the AI choose randomly from its larger pool of characters.

This is definitely one of the most annoying games I've played in recent years. Shadow of Mordor is derivative trash from head to toe, more so than most non-original IP games in the industry, and almost every aspect of this game feels like it wants to be in or belongs to a different game.
The gameplay is essentially a cross between Arkham series combat and Assassin's Creed movement/stealth ("stealth"), and with a bit of that awful awful MGR auto-platforming drivel, but none of it is executed as well as in the games where those mechanics originate from. Shadow of Mordor essentially takes the worst parts of Arkham and AssCreed and blended them together into a cliche spectacle action game, and threw it onto an open world map for good measure, because lord knows we don't have enough of THOSE in modern video games (I am being completely sarcastic. If a game publisher ever reads this, please stop making open world games. Thanks.)
Like in most modern open world games, the fact that it's open world adds very little to the actual gameplay, and serves little purpose other than to add unnecessary travel time between fights and about a million collectibles strewn all over the place like a pane of glass that fell off a building. The collectibles serve to give you experience points to spend one of the many upgrade trees which unlock mostly core mechanics that should be available from the start, like tapping "Q" to throw batarangs (daggers) like in the Batman games, or (I'm not even joking) causing explosive barrels to explode when you shoot them. The vague RPG mechanics most likely exist so that the game can hop onto the modern gaming RPG mechanic bandwagon and so that players can mindlessly grind collectibles around the map so that they can have a break from the equally mindless two-button combat mechanics that this game has to offer. Look at me mom and dad, I have an experience bar with upgrades too!
The upgrade system likely exists in order for collectibles that give the XP for it can exist, which in turn exist because of the fact that the game is open world instead of level based and linear like most games of this type. This game could have been streamlined by throwing the open world concept into the trash where it belongs, and I guarantee you that the game would have lost nothing of import, and would probably have been better for it.
Combat in this game is simplistic, like how it is in the Arkham games, but more forgiving and with less emphasis on being skillful and having very long combo chains. Instead, a lot of fights boil down into a war of attrition between you and the mass of enemies that will almost surely be outnumbering you and will eventually overwhelm you through sheer numbers. Individual enemies pose pretty much no threat to you, and neither do groups of them unless they have ranged attacks, which can hit you with no warning, their projectiles seemingly passing through their allies as if they were thin air, breaking your combos and hit-stunning you, and also doing a huge amount of damage.
Moving in combat is a nightmare a lot of the time. The animations and geography detection are very janky, and it's very easy to grab onto ledges and climb walls that you had no intention to. Sprinting and climbing on walls are bound to the same key, like in MGR, essentially turning your character into a spastic wall spider. The frequent accidents in movement have the potential to add a lot of frustration to fights, as your character will just as easily interpret an order to jump over an enemy as an order to uselessly cling onto a nearby stone, and vice-versa.
Graphically it looks nice, but what doesn't these days? The soundtrack is alright, but given the source material, they could have done a lot better, just like with almost every other part of this game.
Story doesn't leave much to speak about. Protagonist's family gets killed by the forces of Sauron, now it's his job to brood and enact revenge on the Dark Lord's forces. Whatever.
Overall, I think you'd be a lot better off playing one of the Batman: Arkham games, or even one of the Assassin's Creed titles. This game does not innovate or invent anything new, nor does it improve on anything that existed before it. Also, it takes up 44 gigabytes of hard drive space, but for some reason it requires 90GB to install it. Absolutely inexcusable.
If you love CRPGs and don't mind reading, it is a lot of fun.

I just beat this game in one three-hour playthrough, so, considering that I was compelled to play this game to the end, I thought it would be worth my time to describe the nuances of this hidden EA gem.
====================================================================================
The game is centered around fast-paced, isometric, hack-and-slash combat, and succeeds: It is simply fun and captivating. The UI is friendly, there is replayability, and the tutorial is incredibly helpful to the degree that the long review isn't neccessary. There is a demo so that you can try said tutorial and first few levels. There are alot of similarities in the combat to Dark Souls, so I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys those games for its combat.
====================================================================================
if you are not a fan of the Souls games, but are still interested in this game, or just want to know more in depth before purchase, read on!
First, the
At first glance, the UI in conjuntion with the isometric camera suggests that this game will play mechanically like Diablo, Torchlight, or Path of Exile (all of which I have played, but none of which have greatly captivated me). However, I was plesantly surprised to find that Dragonpath plays more like the From Software's Souls Series, my favorite franchise of all time. The UI is functional and user-friendly, via labeling your custom key/controller bind above each action and explaining each function via mouseover. Speaking of key binds, all actions have costom binds: once upon a time you couldn't unbind the mouse buttons. So, if you, like me, are a fan of Dark Souls, you can be blocking with L1, attacking with R1/R2, interacting with A, dodging with B, using items with X, and healing with Y, and feel right at home with the controller support.
Dragonpath's levels consists of a combat-free starting room, which progresses through combat rooms all the way to the boss room, which upon completion, you can proceed to the next level. The UI features a mini-map, depicting the starting room with a gateway, the boss with a skull, the merchant with a treasure chest, and the room with a secret with a question mark. The mini-map depicts the level as a series of blocks, each representing a room that can be entered or exited in the four cardinal directions if adjacent to another block/room. The levels, and subsequent rooms, with the exception of the secret rooms, are dull and uninspiring by nature of the isometric camera and genre. Furthermore, the level design strongly reminds me of Bloodborne's Chalice Dungeons: the Chalice Dungeons were completely optional, and represented FromSoft's attempt to incorperate rougelite elements into the Souls genre, which failed spectacularly. So despite Dragonpath's repetitive and dull level and room design, I enjoy this game more than Bloodborne's Chalice Dungeons.

200 hours in and I can't say I'd recommend this game to anyone except for the CCG die hards and the money payers.
Faeria has a great concept for a CCG where it is like hearthstone except on a buildable playing field.  There are 4 colors of cards and neutral cards which correspond to the types of land you can build to fufill the requirements to play a given card.  Because you can only play creatures on your own lands whoch also have to be of the corresponding land type, this creates an interesting stategic element where players vie for both land and creature positioning throughout the game.  Creatures have the standard power and life values like Hearthstone and many also have additional effects which can turn the tide of the game.  In addition to creatures, there are also spells and structures which have their own unique effects which vary from the mundane to the ridiculouly powerful.  The combination of the different card types and colors with the additional layer of land building and stragetic positioning really gives a lot to think about in deck building and during gameplay.
So why don't I recommend it?  The problem, like virtually every digital CCG, is the pay-to-win model.  Can you get everything that paying players get without dropping a dime?  Yes, eventually.  But the road required to get there will make you wonder how much someone would have to
to keep going.  Like many other negative reviews will outline in detail, suffice to say that you don't get much gold to buy packs with.  While there's a great single player mode, the majority of it is locked behind steep gold paywalls.  When you do accumulate enough gold to buy packs of cards, they are extremely stingy with what you are likely to get.  In a nutshell, 90% of card packs will give you 4 commons and a rare.  Almost all commons are useless in competitive play and rares form only the foundation of any good deck.  Then to obtain about 15 rares that work cohesively for a given competitive deck is very difficult.  On top of that, to then get the epic and legendary cards that are actually gamechanging in power will require 100s of hours of grinding in order to make just one competitive deck.  To make things worse, ginding will require you to continuously lose against players who have laid down a bunch of cash to get better cards than you.
Some people will make the argument that they were able to reach god-tier (the highest tier of ranked play) without having paid any money.  Unfortunately, this actually means next to nothing because of how the ranking system works, reaching god-teir is a function of the combination of deck strength and number of games played in an inverse relation.  In other words, if you have a competitve deck, it won't take very long to reach god-tier.  However, even if you have a completely garbage deck, you can still reach god-tier if you play enough games.  And, aside from being able to boast about reaching god-tier, the rewards for doing so are stupidly small and you only get it once a month.
Pandora, the other game mode, is a draft mode which also exclusively includes the treasure cards.  These are game breaking cards that, if you are lucky enough to pull 3 good ones, will make the difference between winning 3 games and 9 games.  Pandora games also have a special "opening of pandora" which means that generally speaking, whatever advantage you may have gained in the first 10 turns will likey be completely wiped out due the chaotic and random nature of it.  Unfortunately,
is the mode you need to play consistantly well to make a bunch of gold and earn a lot of packs quickly because the rewards are astronomically higher than ranked mode.  Considering that it is also the mode that will be appealing to most people without all the best cards in the game, it is a shame that success here is based upon luck as much as skill.
Ultimately though, what drove me away after 200 hours is that there isn't enough cards/variety in gameplay.  Basically there are only a handful of top tier decks and then people make their own version of it by changing a few cards.  After playing for so long, I've seen all the different decks and synergies that people come up with and so the game has become stale.  You'll see every deck using the same top tier cards for that particular color/theme.  As expected, many people use the stingy crafting system to just copy one of the top tier decks so that they can avoid wasting what little they've gotten on a deck that isn't good enough/doesn't work.  Will more cards and variety be introduced in the future?  Of course, but as of May 2017, this is still a problem.
So what would I recommend?  If you're not a CCG fan, don't waste your time with this game.  If you still insist on playing it, either be prepared to drop some cash on the game or face the same problems that basically all the free players face.  If you're a CCG fan or die hard, you already know what to expect in a game like this.  Give it a shot, play the inital single player experience the game gives you before the paywalls and play some pandora runs.  It's a game that's fun and stimulating to learn, but doesn't deserve the long term dedication and 100s of hours of play as the game currently stands.

* there is minimal voice acting, but whoever did the grunting sounds for the flexing cactuses needs a pat on the back.
Allow me to reminisce over the first Ittle Dew. I bought it on a whim, due to it looking like a cheap Zelda clone. And to some extent it was. Art style was quirky, dungeons were well thought out, and there were some puzzles that really stretched the old noggin. So when I heard a sequel was coming out, I decided to buy at full price, instead of waiting for a discount, as I and many others usually do. I was hoping for another Zelda clone. And I got one.
As of writing this, I am at the last dungeon, and have gone around doing all the secret stuff. It feels like I'm nearing the end.
The quality improvement over the first is huge. The developers have gone for a cartoony 3D world, which you can see in screenshots. Animation is fluid, controls are good, and the humour is well done. I did chuckle every now and again at all the crazy characters you meet.
The story is very laid back, and knows it. Heroine crashes raft, has to make new one. Go do it. Unfortunately, the raft pieces are in the 8 dungeons scattered around the world. You're free to do them in any order you wish.
This is both a blessing and a curse. On the one hand, the freedom to roam is done very well, and whilst I felt some areas were harder than others, nowhere made me feel like I shouldn't be there at that point. On the other hand, it's clear that puzzle difficulty has taken a hit in order to accommodate this. There's been no puzzles so far that have been real head scratchers. Maybe some super secret final puzzles might be? Maybe I'm just older and wiser?  I don't know. What I do know is, I've breezed through them all. It doesn't help that there's little penalty for dying as well, so racing past enemies, and blindly swinging my stick means the non-puzzle sections are a breeze too. Bosses have been a challenge, but once you spot their patterns, they're easy.
IMPORTANT EDIT: The difficulty level spikes if you're going for the secret dungeons. The last one especially did have me scratching my head for a while, so hard puzzles do exist in the game, they're just right at the end.
Sound design is pretty good (disclaimer: I'm a sound designer/composer), but there were a few hiccups I heard here and there. For example, footstep sounds seem to be timed samples, instead of the traditional triggered ones. This means the speed of the walking sound remains the same, even if you're slowly pushing something. It really put me off initially, but I think that's because I'm more aware of that sort of thing. And those hiccups were overshadowed by some excellent vocal work on enemies. The grunting of the flexing cactuses makes them 10 times better.
Music did its job. Nothing to write home about, but certainly nothing to sneeze at either. Particularly enjoyed the music for stuff that would spoil things if I said them :P.
Finally, the big barrier with this is the price point. Whilst I see the value in this game, indie games like this fall into a slightly cheaper category. Personally, I think the $15 range would have been a much more reasonable price point to entice a larger base of people, and have them feel satisfied they got their money's worth. The $20 price is teetering on the edge of what would be considered good value in this entitled society. And that will be a big deterrent.
Should you buy it? If you enjoy Zelda-esque games, then absolutely! If not at full price, then definitely at a discount. I've certainly enjoyed my time with this!

I assume.  It took me about 16 hours of reading (and fiddling to figure out this and that, but it's all there if you read) to finish one playthrough, which is good and bad.  The game is actually part 1 of a planned 4 part series, each being a year at school.  The game came out in 2010 though, and it's taken them 7 years to be almost ready for part 2.  Now the creators didn't slack off at all during those 7 years, but they did get distracted into making 17 dlc's for the original game.  The dlc's are all included in the steam version so no worries there.  Most of the dlc's though were a bit strange in that they made about a dozen or so new classes, instead of making year 2 and just sticking those new courses as year 2 courses.
So the developers are very involved so that's great, I expect I'll read through this 2 or 3 more times easily getting my money's worth (I figure $1 paid for every hour played is a good investment).  I also expect that year 2 will be out later this year, so like I said, if you like to read, and you like to replay games and have vastly different stories inbetween, then yes this is a very good investment.

Disclosure: I was given a key to review/stream the game and I met and hung out with the developer of the game at PAX.
I think that the price point combined with the art style will lead people to be turned off of the game, and I think the people who decide not to pick it up because they aren't impressed are going to miss out on a wonderful experience.
If you'd rather hear my thoughts over gameplay I have a video here:
Ittle Dew 2 is a top-down action adventure game in the same vein of the open-world 2-D Legend of Zelda games. You are quickly placed into a world with 8 dungeons; 7 of which you can tackle in any order that you see fit.
The gameplay is what you would normally expect from this type of game. You mash the attack button to do damage and you have a dodge roll to help you avoid danger. The idea is that you're to wait for the weak spots in the enemies and although it sounds straight forward, the bullet patterns that you encounter can be tricky enough to catch you off guard. It's cute and childish presentation betray the difficulty in the combat that you encounter in the end-game areas that you can encounter.
When you aren't going to battle with buff cactuses, or pillow fort guards, you're solving puzzles or performing movement challenges. At the beginning of the game these pose no threat, but as you progress the difficulty will increase to the point that you'll find your hands sweating as you go to roll past rotating spike balls, or scratching your head as you try to figure out the push puzzles.
Outside of the gameplay itself, Ittle Dew 2's core strength is the personality residing within its writing and its soundtrack. The game has hilarious quips scattered throughout the dungeons, one moment that specifically comes to mind is in the art-gallery dungeon in which there are a collection of pieces throughout that you can see as you battle enemies. One was an exhibit of trash that was titled, "The Next Dungeon", another was a creepy face which was titled, "You're next, Purely". Although I'm sure it was easy to code, "You're next, {name}" it's the little touches applied throughout that kept me grinning to the point of pain.  Another aspect of the writing that I thought was cute was the 4th wall breaking elements that the writer(s?) weren't afraid to bust out. You have a companion fox with wings that serves as your "Na'vi" that you can refer to at any time and the amount of unique dialogue based on where you are and what you've completed was fairly impressive.
As I mentioned before, the soundtrack is really stellar. A bunch of different styles are employed from your typical starter-area Kevin MacLeod joy tracks, to soothing jazz, to catchy electronica. Writing it out, I could see how that sentence would sound cohesively dissonant, but in practice the tracks help add to the personality of the areas that you're in. It's a total dissapointment that there's no way to buy the soundtrack -- that I'm aware of --  because it's definitely good enough to have playing in the background of activities that I'd find myself doing throughout the day.
My only concern with the game is length. Although there can be some challenging fights that can take you a few tries, or puzzles that can keep you stumped for 5-15 minutes at a time if spacial acuity isn't something you posess (much like myself), the game seems like it could be completed in one or two sittings. My steam time betrays me, because I accidently left the game idling, but I was able to complete 2 out of the 8 dungeons in about 60-90 minutes. If I were to make an estimate based off of that figure, then it would take around 5-6 hours if you were to play the game with the sole purpose of getting to the ending. Length is a contentious issue in games, where some people feel that unnessecary padding hurts games and leads to an overall less interesting experience, whereas other people feel that video games should have a good $/hr ratio. I think that Ittle Dew 2 offers an extremely tight experience in terms of the primary dungeons, and even offers up a secret that you can discover once you find 16 secrets scattered throughout the world. I've yet to see it, but I think 100%ing the game would put you in the 9-10ish hour category if you're going in blind.
Following up on this though, is another aspect of the game that I'm not sure most reviewers will touch upon, which is the speedrun capabilities. Because Ittle Dew 2 is a concise open-world dungeon adventure game, the potential for a speedrun is high, as there are tons of timesaves that can be found in optimized routing, deftly conquering boss fights, and even discovering extra keys in the hub world that can be used in dungeons. These extra keys aren't needed to complete dungeons, but if you were to route out the game carefully, you could potentially use them to save a lot of time. I don't know what a realistic time for an Ittle Dew 2 speedrun looks like yet, but having speedran a bunch of other games, I think this game is very speedrunner friendly without trying to court that demographic.
Ittle Dew 2 plays like a love-letter to the classic zelda games, and at $20 I could understand how someone would look at this and expect something more immediately impressive. I know that personally, even if I had been given a review code, I probably wouldn't have even played it or put a lot of time into it, but fortunately I met someone on the team and that was enough to peak my interest in playing it. After getting my hands on it I feel compelled to discover all of its secrets and get some competitive speedrun times. If you're still skeptical I recommend watching gameplay from someone who isn't as smitten with the game as I am, because I think people would be missing out on a funny, heartwarming experience that stands out admist a sea of Steam games that are all equally begging to be played.

Academagia is a game where you get from it exactly what you put into it. It's less a traditional gamebook and more a sandbox with words. But even armed with a singular goal, you will find yourself greeted with many false starts as you try to discern the rather obtuse mechanics.
The game comes with a manual PDF but it only does a good job at describing the UI elements. The UI itself is "intuitive" in as far as I found out quite quickly which GUMPs locked you out of interacting with other windows. This can be annoying when specifying which skill you want to train/study as you won't be able to easily double check your larger list in the other window. Also, this game exists only in maximized borderless windowed mode as far as I can tell. All these things were sort of jarring at first but now I never notice it as I'm more focused on getting through my week unscathed.
You're not an overpowered god character. You will fail a lot of events no matter what your skills or ability. But you can't afford to be scared of failure as even your feeble attempts to navigate a situation will enlighten your character to new skills that can be trained. Sometimes the best thing to do will be the thing you know you'll have no success doing.
You'll go through a great deal of trial and error trying to connect the pieces of what affects what to glean what you need to accomplish what you set out to do. I think a good example of this is the fact Research (action) is gained from Study Habits (subskill) and not Research (skill.) You might find this happens a lot, where descriptions are less useful and more flavor and it can be overwhelming and a little disheartening in a game where the journey is more important than the destination.
You're very free to do (or not do) all sorts of things in Academagia but it's double-edged in that you've just as much freedom to mess up in ways you may not even comprehend. I'd recommend this game if the idea of learning to fly by repeatedly hurling yourself off a cliff is appealing to you. Things may be rough in a lot of places but when everything aligns finally and you're in the air, it's really rewarding. Just don't be surprised when you go for a second take-off and you plummet again.

SOLVED! Command & Conquer 3 Kane's Wrath not launching/working on Windows 10. after soo long trying to figure out some way to get the game to run on Windows 10, I FINALLY found a solution just when I was messing around in the display driver settings. First of all my laptop is the late 2016 Razer Blade with the GTX 1060 and Core i7 6700HQ. Okay here's how I got it to work on Windows 10, first, make sure the game is not running as an administrator and all the compatibility mode/settings are disabled, I know most people probably enabled these trying to get the game to work (including myself). Okay next, open settings, in the search bar type "device manager" then select it, next select "display adaptors" then "Intel HD Graphics" then go to "driver" and select "Roll Back Driver..." then just give it a minute, the screen may turn blue for a second or whatnot, and that's it! the game should run perfectly! you can adjust it to whatever graphics or resolution you want and you can use a dedicated GPU (if you have one). if this helped you please like this review so others will see! :)
--Edit-- rolling back this driver can cause some other problems like videos on your system and on YouTube playing choppy in fullscreen mode and the only way to fix that is to update the driver back, fortunatly for me, C&C 3 Kane's Wrath still played just fine when I updated back to the latest driver.

Fairyland: Fairy Power is a casual strategy game made with RPG Maker MV. Strange enough that it is a strategy game in that particular engine which is solemnly used for anything other than RPG games.
It features a cute fairy theme and I personally think it would be a very fun game for very young childred too.
That does not mean it's a children's game by any chance.
Gameplay:
The game is set on a board with flowers consisting of 3 different colors. Each color type is worth different "fairy power" points. There are also 3 types of fairies, with their own special mechanic.
The goal of the game is to move your pieces on the board and collect more fairy power than the other fairies which can be human (local multiplayer only) or AI controlled.
As a fan of strategy games, once I grasped the concept of the game, I found it very easy. My first game ended with 52-17-16. This is why I'm categorizing the game under casual.
If you expect a big strategy challenge you will not find it here. The game is good for some casual fun!
Graphics:
Graphics are typical for RPG Maker games. 2D animated sprites on a background board. If you have ever played an RPG Maker game, you know exactly how this game looks.
Music/Sound Design:
The music soundtrack is very relaxing and feels just right on a casual board game. Sounds effects are sparse but that is to be expected as there are few different types of actions that can have sound effects. They all do, by the way.
Pros:
-It is a fun casual strategy game.
-Very light on hardware requirements.
-Cute theme.
-Easy to learn.
Neutral:
-The game is rather easy. If you're looking for a very challenging strategy game, this is not it.
Cons:
-Animations play slow and after a while you will wish there was a way to speed them up.
Conclusion:
A fun game, easy to learn and master. Feels and plays like a board game and it's great for young children too!

While the featured characters are flat, the plot uninteresting, and the pacing awkward, Shadow of Mordor is still an exceptional game. It carries itself on its gameplay, giving you various playstyles that you can easily switch between as they aren't buried in skill trees. A skill tree is present in the game, but it only makes you more powerful, not more specialized. There's no single playstyle that's executed weaker than the others, giving the player a grand deal of agency in how to deal with situations.
Although the protagonist is set and all of the skill tree is acquirable, each weapon of Talion's can be equipped with runes of varying strength that grant certain boons. This is essentially the extent of customization in the game though.
The game is almost entirely composed of repeatable quests with little variety, but it does present a system of randomized named orcs (captains) that the player needs to focus on. The captains are dynamic and will comment on your previous actions (such as if they killed you before or if you tried to kill them with say, fire, but failed). If a random orc kills you, then they become a captain, and if a captain kills you, they get a promotion. Captains differ in strength from a range of about 5-20 (if i remember correctly) and various events will strengthen them (You can influence all events of this sort).
The map is pretty small. It only takes you maybe five minutes to run from one end to the other, and a minute or two if you're on top of a caragor. There are two of them, and the two maps are fairly different, but they're still both tiny. They are fleshed out and each one offers challenges (hunting, gathering, and weapons) unique to them. Although the three types of challenges don't provide much variety in their own respects, I still found them engaging. Hunting challenges require you to kill a certain number of a specific type of animal, gathering challenges require you to find a certain number of a specific plant, and weapon challenges put you in a situation and require you to use one of your three weapons (sword, dagger, bow) to dispatch orcs in a certain way (e.g. shooting fire barrels with a bow).
While the game becomes fairly simple and easy to complete when you become strong enough and all the collectibles are marked on the map and thus easy to locate, its background is rather flushed out, providing the player with a fair amount of access to LotR lore. Artifacts, for example, have a description of what they are and how they were used in the world's history. Each one also provides a unique voiced bit where some (typically) unnamed character speaks either to themselves or talks with someone else about a topic relating to the artifact.
So although the game is straightforward (put in enough time and you'll get 100% completion with no struggle) and simple (the only thing you'll be doing is wandering around and killing orcs, if we're being honest), it's easily worth the twenty dollars if you have the money to spare.

Shadow of Mordor is a great game. Good enough that I bought it twice. Once for the Playstation 4 and again on steam so I could play it in 4k and enjoy the DLC. There are three really good reasons you should get this game. The battle system, the nemesis system, and the story.
Battle System:
The battle system is much like a clone of the Batman Arkham games. It's my favorite battle system that many games have copied since Arkham Asylum but I think this one does a particularly good job. Orcs are vial, irredeemable, scumbags that deserve whatever pain you can dish out to them. It feels great to shank, decapitate, brutalize, poison, feed to Caragores, those nasty Orcs for all they've done.
Nemesis System:
This system was done well in this game and I've seen nothing that comes close to mirroring this system in any other game. This system makes your battles between the orcs feel personal. If an orc manages to "kill" you he will be promoted to a captain and receive additional powers. Because you are a wraith you will come back to life and the Orc will remember your previous encounter. If you had wounded the orc he will spite you for it. If he killed you he'll gloat in your face. This system ties into the story somewhat but I think is good enough to stand on it's own.
The Story:
Even though it's not cannon I think they did a good job incorporating a Tolkien esque story. Lord of the Rings is my favorite book so I am critical of how they make new stories in his world. It's the story of a ranger from Gondor who was stationed at the black gate to keep evil at bay. When the Hand of Sauron comes to kill his family in a blood sacrifice his spirit is bound to that of an ancient elf. I won't say who as discovering his identity is part of the story.
I have yet to play the DLC yet which might make it more challenging but one critique I have for this game is that it gets to easy late game. You become so powerful that you can walk up to the biggest stronghold sound the alarm and completely wreck their base without breaking a sweat. Being able to disable your abilities or making more threatening enemies would be desired late game.
This game is best enjoyed with a controller. I haven't attemted to use a mouse and keyboard.
9/10 this is one of my favorite games and I highly recommend it.

I started this adventure by making myself a martini.  "Where the hell is the stewardess?", I thought to myself as I put a lemon wedge into my glass and promptly set it on fire.  It then occurred to me that I have no earthly idea how to make one.
As I downed my odd concoction, I went back to my seat to enjoy the rest of my flight without any peanuts or crisps.  "Bloody stewardess.", I pondered, "She must be somewhere joining the mile-high club."
Then, kaboom, we crash into the ocean and I find the tiniest little life raft I've ever seen.  I remember thinking, "It's a good thing I was the only survivor...this bloody thing was built for elves!" as I paddled away from the wreckage.
Finally, I came across an island.  This island was not very comfy looking...little more than a clump of rocks and a single tree, but I rowed toward it anyway.  Just as I reached its shore, a larger, more hospitible island appeared on the horizon as if it blinked into being before me.  I continued to row so feverously that I didn't realize I was on land until about halfway across the tiny speck of island I initially found.
Bewildered, but dedicated, I continued to paddle across the sand as the boat moved fluidily over the rocks and grass.  It was almost like water...it even made the same sound that water makes when my oar swept through it.  "What the hell did I put in that martini?  I'm losing my mind..." I pondered quietly to myself as I rowed completely over the tiny island and made my way to the larger.
During my journey, I saw a shipwreck and thought "Ooo, I bet there's fresh food in there for some reason!" so I reached the shore, paddled my boat onto the island safely and exited the mighty elven vessel.  I half-expected the sand to splash and giveway as I jumped out.
I dove to the shipwreck a mere 10 meters from my island and I found something.  It was a shark.  "I wonder if HE knows how to make a decent martini..." I thought, before dying a gruesome death.
11/10 would land-row an elf boat again

Singularity: Good Video Games.
Let's talk about what made me happy:
Pride of place in an FPS: Weapons. They are your primary means of interacting with other entities, and damn are they nice. Many of them are neat spins on regular ol' bread and butter guns, and that's okay, but the look and feel of some guns is just great. The minigun has brake pads around the barrel. The shotgun has this neat locking top pump action. The rifle has a fan that spins as you fire. The Railgun has a timed delay explosive charge. Aside from looking neato frito, they all feel damn great and tear guys up very nicely. The other side of this is the TMD, which has powers and upgrades meted out to it through the course of the game and is great fun to oof at when you hit dudes with it. Seriously I was apologizing to AI for blowing them off their shins and leaving the feet standing. It's pretty grisly.
Speaking of AI, the enemies are neat too. You have monsters and tough monsters and soldiers and tough soldiers, but that's boiling things right down to sump. They all have their neat features,  You can shoot limbs off the creatures and they'll keep coming, sometimes even after they're ostensibly dead. Soldiers will hide behind bigger dudes and try and flank you, though it's standard tactics it's still fun to play with. Between monsters and soldiers, there's a nice gamut of enemies, but though the groups have a nice variety within themselves, it's the way they're placed through the game that's cool. You'll be fighting some monsters and suddenly soldiers will drop in on cleanup, or the guy you're shooting will be clawed from behind, and infighting hell breaks loose either way. It's always fun to be the one in the eye of the storm, and Singularity does it wonderfully.
Let's talk design elements real quick, since Singularity has a bunch I really like. Found Story? Check. Audio logs, notes, interactive items, flashbacks, secrets, all of the good stuff. Oh, what's that, you want wordless little vignettes? You got them too. If you like exploring the world in your FPSs and being rewarded for that with tidbits, you'll feel right at home. Tagging -horror onto your game's genre might have been the "in" thing, but Singularity does the horror elements right. The opening hour or so is filled with jumps and scares, but not jumpscares. You're dropped here and there's noises and movement and OH GOD WHAT IS THAT KILL IT ♥♥♥♥. Give it another couple of hours and you'll be topping those guys left and right, but there's howls in the distance that make you a little uneasy. Most mutant enemies go through this cycle of unknown-scary-identified-understood-kill with impunity. You'll get to know their weaknessess and strategies, but not before feeling a little uneasy that you don't. Another thing I'd like to touch real quick is the set pieces, the kind of ones where you'll be talking about games to a friend and you'll say "Remember that one mission in Singularity, on the bridge, when you-" and they'll go "Yeaahhhh, that was so good!" They're money, all I need to say.
+
Fantastic design all around
Neat writing and backstory
Memorable encounters throughout, including bosses
Heaps of little unf-worthy touches
-
Some genericity in places (playing it safe?)
Gets progressively linear-er
Phase Ticks and Sewers
Expensive as hell for it's age
Singularity is worth playing through if only to get a crash course in what FPS games in the mid-2000s were like, since it cribs stuff from all it's neighbours while managing to remain it's own beast and being very good for it. It also layers some of it's own stuff on top of that, and is, in general, very good. Time well spent (HAH).

Starbound is... an interesting experience.
Contrary to many opinion, this game is closer to being Fallout 4 in 2D rather than Terraria in Space, while I feel Starbound tried to push their idea further than Fallout 4 did, but it ultimately suffers same fate.
It has many, many interesting system and game play, but none of them are exceptioanlly polished and well connected with each other, resulting in double-edged disjointed experience.
As a person who tried translating this game, amount of work Devs put into this game is frustratingly detailed and extreme in size even after all those contents cuts as they progressed. Notice where I said 'Frustrating', this is because Starbound Dev team likely made common development mistake of 'Trying everything that designer throws at the project', which results in immensely bloated project with number of contents that are seemingly impossible to polish.
Main cinematic quests are at best feels disjointed, at worst, it is directly conflicting with interactive building, exploration, collecting, and base management. And that isn't only the cinematic quest's problem.
Still, this also means that you can distract yourselves when you exhausted interest from single content to another. But this advantage is mostly unaccessible if you dislike playing with other people.
As current price tag of 16.99 CAD, this game indeed worth every penny to purchase. So I will recommend it.

Upfront, it needs to be said that this game is not at all new player friendly, with an incredibly steep learning curve and cumbersome mechanics in a very clunky engine.  If you don't enjoy reading, you won't enjoy this game.  You will need to consult the wiki/official forums (fortunately there is a small but extremely dedicated and friendly community) and probably do multiple starts before you get a real sense of what exactly is going on, and failure on events and adventures is to be expected.  That said, if you're patient and enjoy deep, open-ended RPG/simulation experiences, Academagia is really fantastically unique.
The premise can basically be summed up as a Harry Potter simulator.  You create a fresh faced young wizard entering their first of 5 years at Academagia.  From there on, what happens is (mostly) totally up to you.  You choose your background, your curriculum, and what you do with your spare time.  There is no main story per se; your motivations are your own.  You can aim to be the best student, create the largest clique possible, explore all Mineta, master all the varities of magic, complete every adventure possible, whatever suits you.  The one constant is largely fantastic writing, with an incredibly deep lore.  Per all that, this is also about as replayable a game as you can get; you can create numerous completely different characters spending their time on different things, and a staggering number of random events further helps ensure each game feels different from the last.
The engine exists to aggravate and the sheer scope and text reliance may not be for everyone, but if the premise appeals to you and you're the type able to be patient in figuring a game out, there's very little like Academagia out there.  The potential for multiple years is enormous (and the second year at least with an improved engine is a mostly safe bet) , and while the small indie group has clear limitations with their painfully slow development time, the fact they've now put out 17 completely free DLC/updates since first releasing the game shows where their priorities are.

Before reading this review here is some prominent information: The wiki about this game is incomplete and a bit everywhere with its information. If you need help playing, want more information, or just need help playing as a new player please come to the Academagia forums! We're not all bullies that want to Master you into buying this game. Well... At least everyone else isn't >={3 Here is the link to the forums, please come by!
If you like visual novels and dating games with pretty graphics and pretty people, this is not for you. If reading tires you out or you find it boring, then begone! This game is purely text based. This is a virtual "choose your own adventure" about a preteen going to a school of magic. The game is very in depth with it's lore with links that lead you to a "codex" of information about the subject.
When you start a new game you are first sent to a window where you check a box that adds all of the free dlc that has been added to the game so far (seventeen to be exact). When you click to proceed to the next part of character creation you are left with a bit of a lengthy load before entering the next part. As a veteran player this doesn't bother me, but if you're new it can be pretty annoying if you're used to quick loading. The next part of character creation is choosing your name and gender, and after that the hard choices begin. You are given ten points to be used during character creation. Five of those points can be used to raise your attributes frome base one before the game begins, but it's not required. Afterwards you can choose when you were born, where you are from, and an omen of your birth. As you continue on you can choose family history, wealth, and how your parents view you. Do they hate you? Are you the favorite? Or are they just average? There are countless options you can choose from that raise skills, give you spells, or raise attributes. Many of these backgrounds don't actually affect gameplay except in the adventures tied with them and the stats you get from the background. The final part of creation is choosing your college and then classes. Each college has its own values and required classes. Godina for example, has three required classes and three slots for the classes you choose. Each class has its own corresponding adventure that you can pursue during the game, but we'll get to that. After choosing your college and classes, you choose your portrait and off you go to Academagia, adventure awaits!
The beginning of the game sets the tone for your playthrough and makes or breaks it for you. The tutorial is lengthy and done in a series of letters left for you by your rooms previous owner named Gera. You can skip this part and just get into the game and read the letters from your inventory later, but if you're just starting I heavily suggest you buckle down and slave through them to at least get the gist of how things are done. The "game" at its core is relatively easy. You stare at a calender where you choose what you want to do for the day. Go to classes and rest? Sure. Skip classes and study all day? Go ahead. Go to classes and then adventure? WHY NOT. My suggestion? Study and raise your stats. Adventures can be lengthy and are brutal. You will fail, and fail often. Sometimes you can even fail before you begin without even knowing it. If you're starved for content worry not because the game is littered with random events that will hold your attention and even make you laugh once you're done cursing under your breath after failing.
From my biased opinion as a veteran player and long time fan, Academagia is a fun game that has near endless replayability. If you can power through learning how to play and lovw reading, get this game. If you want pretty graphics, semi attractive sprites popping up on your screen, and a linear storyline with a goal, don't get this game.

Academagia is a text adventure that refuses to hold your hand. Don't like reading? Don't get this. Don't like figuring things out on your own? Don't get this. (There is a tutorial in the game. Your mentor that you meet at the beginning is basically your guide to the game. Don't be an idiot and skip this then whine that you have no idea wtf to do.)
The game is absolutely jam-packed with content and lore (it comes with 17 free DLCs.) I've played through the game multiple times and each time I discover something new. New skills to train, new actions to take, new people, new adventures, new places on the campus, and new items.
Once you understand the UI-which is a bit of a learning curve- you can pretty much do anything you want. It will take some thinking and planning. But you can go adventuring with pirates, study gates to other worlds, skip class and build a clique and bully other people. You can shape your character how ever you want. There's no true way to "win" this game.
There is some interesting RNG. You will run into situations (lure an escaped gryphon to its cage, a brawl breaks out in the tavern, you find a mysterious door, etc.) or discover new items, places, tasks randomly. It adds quite a bit of life and excitement to the game.
The game won't go easy on you either, if you fail at an adventure or situation you'll stress out and/or lose vitality. If it gets bad enough, you could have to skip class due to being sick and end up in detention. Don't worry though, because there are tons of different ways to solve problems as they arise (maybe with your Sleuthing skill, your Flattery skill, your Library Knowledge skill, or even your Birds skill. There's a ton of different skills) The game doesn't force you to play any one way.
It's hard not to get lost in the game's world and lore. As someone who loves world-building and lore and freedom to do what ever in a game, Academagia easily ranks as my second favorite game (following closely behind Dwarf Fortress.)
If all that stuff doesn't sound appealing to you, don't get this game.

At first glance, Battle Brothers appears to be a turn-based cousin of the Mount & Blade series of games.  Both games have you play as the leader of a band of mercenaries and have a similar core gameplay loop:
Battle Brothers spices things up in a variety of ways.
The size of your mercenary company is limited to 20 brothers (there is almost no female representation in this game).  They can come from many walks of life.  In the beginning of the game, when you are constrained by low funds, you'll likely find yourself surrounded by farmers, miners, fishermen, and other downsodden physical laborers.  The price of these men is low.  The cost of hiring these sorts is about as much as the cost of 3 weeks of food.  For a decent suit of chainmail, you could hire a group of 5 men.  But then again, life is cheap in the world of Battle Brothers.
Assuming they survive your first few battles, these brothers will level up and you can decide what stats and perks the brother should invest in.  There are 8 stats in this game (HP, Fatigue, Resolve, Initiative, Melee attack/defense, Ranged attack/defense) and you can choose 3 to increase upon each level.  However, the degree of increase is somewhat random (from 1 to 6 points).  Each character usually has some specialties (denoted by 1 to 3 stars next to the stat) that have a higher probability of rolling a higher increase.  The stat rolls also depend to some extent on the character's actions (give a brother a bow, and his ranged attack rolls will be higher).
The game does a good job with making these stats understandable.  For example, Melee attack is the chance to hit with a melee weapon.  Melee defense is the chance
to get hit by a melee weapon.  When calculating a hit, the most simple scenario is:
Most of the content is up to the player to discover.  The game implicitly nudges you to experiment with tactics, weapon types, and unit compositions.  Different enemies generally require different equipment.  An early example is the difference between fighting bandits and wolves.  Against bandits, you'll want some blunt weapons for tearing apart armor.  But against beasts, a thick wall of spears will make short work of them.

Pillars of Eternity is well rounded, solid RPG reminiscent of Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights.  It has a really interesting tabletop RPG feel to it - think Dungeons and Dragons - which compliments game immersion.
I'm only 3 hours into this game but so far it stands out more than any other RPG I've played since KOTOR 2 (another amazing Obsidian game) and I can only see it getting better.  Honestly, if you're a fan of PC RPGs, especially Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights or KOTOR give this game a go.

Bastion is a game where you take the role of "the kid" on his mission to reassemble the mystical Bastion after a catastrophe befalls the world, tearing it to pieces.
The game (even being 4 years old) is gorgeous. Gameplay is diablo-esque, but it takes a good degree of skill; all weapons are varied and viable, each having its pro's and con's, but nothing ever feels "overpowered." The game isn't difficult, but the game designers implement an ingenious "idols" system that unlocks about halfway through the game. Each idol buffs all enemies in a noticable way, with the benefit of garnering you more XP and shards for upgrades. You can remove idols if you feel the games too hard, or add some to make it more difficult. Without idols, the game is incredibly easy, especially when you get some of the better potions.
I really have very few cons with this game. Its rather short if you don't try for everything, especially if you don't use idols, weighing in at most 4 hours. However, I'm going for 100% so I'm on NG+ and buffing things with lots of idols to score more XP/shards for challanges. As well, some of the more fun weapons don't unlock til later, and you cannot replay levels (there are challange areas within the bastion though that can be infinitely replayed, I just wish you weren't forced to fight all 20 waves everytime).
Definitely a worthwhile game if you like hack n' slash RPG's, beautiful artistic games, or quick games. 8/10

I did not enjoy myself while playing this game.  The dark theme was a nice touch compared to the usual bright RPGmaker games but that didn't carry the game enough for me to enjoy this.  You start at level 10? on the bottom of what I can only guess is a 10 floor dungeon.  I got to the 3rd (7th) floor before I stopped playing
The combat is a simple swing harder and faster than the enemy before it kills you, that's kind of the theme with most RPG games but in this game you seem to take damage from out of nowhere, and the enemies have no swing animations.  This makes it really hard to know where it is safe to stand and what is damaging you.  On top of all this, some enemies are massive damage sponges, I was swinging into a 200 health normal enemy doing 7 damage and not every attack was hitting.
EVERYTHING is randomized, aside from Key drops (or at least I got lucky to make it to the 3rd floor with enough Keys to get by).  Drops from chests are random, which means you can save before opening it and you roll the dice on what you get.  Admittadly it appears to keep to a trend of "Chest will give weapon" or "Chest will give stat up".  Learning spells is random too, I got lucky to learn Cure from my first scroll, but I also learned it from my second....  Yay.
With the game being so dark, and so many different tiles I thought I was stuck in the 2nd floor because I was missing an Iron Key.  It was only through sheer frustration that by mashing against the wall that I found a spare Key that allowed me to progress, but the thing is there was another iron door I could of opened (a shortcut-ish door).  Had I used the key on this door I would of ♥♥♥♥ed myself out of a savegame....  Healing could also get you stuck as well, it was only on the 3rd time resting on the first floor that I realised resting cost MP, and with no passive regen and very few healing items that I could find it means you can get stuck with low health and a wall of enemies to get through.
And OMG speaking of the enemies.  I always thought it would be better if a game just filled a room full of enemies to grind EXP and money faster, but this game showed me otherwise.  The first floor has about 6 enemies per room, all locked behind doors (mini-metroidvania-esque).  But the 2nd floor, almost every free tile had an enemy on it.  If there's not an enemy on the tile then there's a stat orb which increases a random stat by 1 depending on the colour of the orb.  Again adding to the randomness of the game.
The first few floors of this game made me feel like this should have a Rogue-Lite tag to it...
There is no options for this game, there's a menu screen for items, magic, status, saving, loading, and two others I can't remember but they didn't do anything important.  There's no remapping for keys, no volume or effects control.  The title screen is literally Start Game, Continue Game, or Quit.
This is by far the worst RPGmaker game I have played, and is the reason I have them turned off in my recommendeds.  It tried a lot of things new and different, but it just didn't hit home for me.  I don't recommend this game, and the only reason I'm not refunding it is because I got it for $1 and it's not worth the time.

Total War Warhammer is an all round great game, but it does have a flaw that prevents it from being a hands down masterpiece. Now even with this flaw I still highly reccomend this game to any fan of dark fantasies and Total War games or RTS's in general.
Reasons why you should get this game Include:
- A vast amount of rich and interesting lore behind the factions, their characters, individual units and locations to delve into. Warhammer has been around for ages and is an established fantasy IP and with good reason. You'll enjoy the game 100 times more if you learn about all the rivalries and history of the world.
- 9 totally unique races/factions to choose from, including ulta violent orcs to manipulative and evil vampire counts. Each faction/race has its individual starting legebdary lords or entirely seperate sub-faction (For example there are the vampire counts and the Von Carsteins who share the same roster but have different starting locations and faction effects)
- Every faction/race has their own unique roster, unlike Total War's historic titles no units are reused like spearmen or armored swordsman were where the only difference was a color change, accent and maybe slightly altered stats. Even when two factions have spearmen like the Empire and Brettonia, the spearmen have different models and stats. This makes every unit unique and not like a copy paste
- Short battles is a common complaint seen in the reviews of this game. I would say this is a good thing. For instance the reason battles were longer in older titles, for example Medieval 2, is that units were very sturdy and could eat arrow volly after volly and not only that but the animations were slower. This often resulted in periods of battles where all you would do is fast forward because you didn't wanna stare at a slow melee grind for 5 minutes. In more recent titles like Shogun 2 and Warhammer the animations are fluid and quick and units take punishment like they should, thus resulting in quicker battles.
Now for the biggest and in my opinion only set back for the game, the price tag.
Unfortunatly you sort of need all the dlc to be able to enjoy this game at its fullest. Unfortunatly again, its 60 bucks standard price and with all its dlc you're looking at about 136 dollars, now i bought everything full price and i don't regret that, I think i got my moneys worth but do yourself and favor and pick it up during one of the major sales like the summer or winter sales.

While the featured characters are flat, the plot uninteresting, and the pacing awkward, Shadow of Mordor is still an exceptional game. It carries itself on its gameplay, giving you various playstyles that you can easily switch between as they aren't buried in skill trees. A skill tree is present in the game, but it only makes you more powerful, not more specialized. There's no single playstyle that's executed weaker than the others, giving the player a grand deal of agency in how to deal with situations.
Although the protagonist is set and all of the skill tree is acquirable, each weapon of Talion's can be equipped with runes of varying strength that grant certain boons. This is essentially the extent of customization in the game though.
The game is almost entirely composed of repeatable quests with little variety, but it does present a system of randomized named orcs (captains) that the player needs to focus on. The captains are dynamic and will comment on your previous actions (such as if they killed you before or if you tried to kill them with say, fire, but failed). If a random orc kills you, then they become a captain, and if a captain kills you, they get a promotion. Captains differ in strength from a range of about 5-20 (if i remember correctly) and various events will strengthen them (You can influence all events of this sort).
The map is pretty small. It only takes you maybe five minutes to run from one end to the other, and a minute or two if you're on top of a caragor. There are two of them, and the two maps are fairly different, but they're still both tiny. They are fleshed out and each one offers challenges (hunting, gathering, and weapons) unique to them. Although the three types of challenges don't provide much variety in their own respects, I still found them engaging. Hunting challenges require you to kill a certain number of a specific type of animal, gathering challenges require you to find a certain number of a specific plant, and weapon challenges put you in a situation and require you to use one of your three weapons (sword, dagger, bow) to dispatch orcs in a certain way (e.g. shooting fire barrels with a bow).
While the game becomes fairly simple and easy to complete when you become strong enough and all the collectibles are marked on the map and thus easy to locate, its background is rather flushed out, providing the player with a fair amount of access to LotR lore. Artifacts, for example, have a description of what they are and how they were used in the world's history. Each one also provides a unique voiced bit where some (typically) unnamed character speaks either to themselves or talks with someone else about a topic relating to the artifact.
So although the game is straightforward (put in enough time and you'll get 100% completion with no struggle) and simple (the only thing you'll be doing is wandering around and killing orcs, if we're being honest), it's easily worth the twenty dollars if you have the money to spare.

Shadow of Mordor is a great game. Good enough that I bought it twice. Once for the Playstation 4 and again on steam so I could play it in 4k and enjoy the DLC. There are three really good reasons you should get this game. The battle system, the nemesis system, and the story.
Battle System:
The battle system is much like a clone of the Batman Arkham games. It's my favorite battle system that many games have copied since Arkham Asylum but I think this one does a particularly good job. Orcs are vial, irredeemable, scumbags that deserve whatever pain you can dish out to them. It feels great to shank, decapitate, brutalize, poison, feed to Caragores, those nasty Orcs for all they've done.
Nemesis System:
This system was done well in this game and I've seen nothing that comes close to mirroring this system in any other game. This system makes your battles between the orcs feel personal. If an orc manages to "kill" you he will be promoted to a captain and receive additional powers. Because you are a wraith you will come back to life and the Orc will remember your previous encounter. If you had wounded the orc he will spite you for it. If he killed you he'll gloat in your face. This system ties into the story somewhat but I think is good enough to stand on it's own.
The Story:
Even though it's not cannon I think they did a good job incorporating a Tolkien esque story. Lord of the Rings is my favorite book so I am critical of how they make new stories in his world. It's the story of a ranger from Gondor who was stationed at the black gate to keep evil at bay. When the Hand of Sauron comes to kill his family in a blood sacrifice his spirit is bound to that of an ancient elf. I won't say who as discovering his identity is part of the story.
I have yet to play the DLC yet which might make it more challenging but one critique I have for this game is that it gets to easy late game. You become so powerful that you can walk up to the biggest stronghold sound the alarm and completely wreck their base without breaking a sweat. Being able to disable your abilities or making more threatening enemies would be desired late game.
This game is best enjoyed with a controller. I haven't attemted to use a mouse and keyboard.
9/10 this is one of my favorite games and I highly recommend it.

Played this game all the way from its inception and I have to say I am dissapointed with the final product in relation to the time they spent on it.
The problems are not with what the game is, it is a good game. It is what it could have been and to me the final execution feels rushed. So many reworks, I think they tried to achieve perfection and got tired with it and in the end released a ill thought out rushed game. Ok here are my main problems.
The questline and story they added is terrible
The main questline features a few basic starter tutorial like missions to get you into the game and then basically has you repeat the exact same quest 6 times before facing a final boss. It is always worrying when the tutorial missions are more interesting and fun to play then any other part of the game. It is also so crazy short. I completed the game in 2 days with little effort which links in to my second issue.
It is very easy
This is basically down to progression not being linked to the questline. Once your out of the starter missions and  you have repaired your ship, you can basically get a a top tier weapon and armor before actually doing any of the main questline. Progression in starbound is not bound to the questline or story. I think this was a design flaw. Sure you can just pace it yourself, but the even bigger issue is this my next point.
You can basically mine everything you need to progress to the next tech tier in one mining run
So for example, when I unlocked tech to let me visit the fiery or frozen stars, basically the stars that had everything but the final ore, I was able to mine enough of every single resource needed to completely max my tech out in one trip. I was able to get enough materials to get all three of the end game armor sets and crafting stations. From one run. Then when you unlock the final planet ore, again one run gives you all the solarium you need to finally max out your armor and anything else you need. Thats it game is pretty much done. You should have a god like weapon by now as they can literally spawn in the most basic of chests anywhere in the game. So if you havent already beaten all the bosses, go and jump about spamming fire and complete them. Thats pretty much it which leads me to my next issue.
I dont see any reason to play on once completed
You may differ with me in opinion here, but I really couldnt see any point in going back to play any more. I mean the fun is in looting and exploring right? So once you have unlocked the hardest difficulty planet there is no point in going to any others as the reward is worthless to you at this point. The side missions and 'town/villages' they implemented with npc missions are utterly pointless. Very low reward for doing repitive tedious missions. So basically 90% of the games worlds are no longer worth visiting at this point. You already have godlike everything which you found in the first chest you encountered on one of these planets. What is the point? I really hope I am missing something here but this was my experience of it. Sure you can max your ship out, sure you can try to build a colony, it all just feels shallow and completely pointless. Like features people wanted which they just added without any thought in relating it to the rest of the gameplay.
I played terraria for weeks and actually found bits of it tough, I dont think I ever saw everything and the final boss was difficult for me and took me quite a few attempts.
I honestly finished starbounds final release in two days and never really had any problems dying.
What could they have done?
Make looting make sense. So rubbish loot on the surface, better loot for quest rewards, more rare items the deeper you go etc.
Make an end game where early game planets are still relevant.
Make other game features like ship and colony building relevant and necessary for the main game questline.
Actually have a decent questline with variation in missions and a lot, lot, lot more of them.
Increase overall difficulty of pretty much everything.
The final 4 tiers of ore are basically split on 2 tiers, 3 of them having equal weighting on a lower tier and then one final ore which lets you upgrade each of these 3 tiers to a final tier (we are talking armor and weaponry here). This was a clear of sign of rushing to me. These should have been four seperate upgrades instead of two.
And so much more I could write all night but I am not going to.

When I first saw
on Steam I immediately had a throwback to the old days when I used to spend hours playing on arcade machines, particularly Metal Slug. At its core the game is a pretty simple 2D beat 'em up sidescroller, however, that doesn’t make it any less fun and engaging than other, more complex, beat ‘em ups.
There isn’t really a story to the game per say, you only have this introductory cutscene with no dialogue that shows your character applying for a
in some sort of special forces. After applying you’re sent to this mansion in order to rescue survivors from monsters, and that is pretty much it. That said, in order to survive longer and to complete objectives, you’ll have to rescue survivors in the mansion by taking them to extraction points. The game manages to gradually get more challenging as time passes, kind of like Risk of Rain. It can get quite hectic after a while, when you’re running from room to room to keep them from collapsing. There are 2 types of survivors, normal survivors that you can find in rooms and some have weapons, and VIP survivors that you can find in certain locations that grant you a power-up upon rescue, such as a revive or cat that instantly kills every monster in your current room.
That said, besides rescuing survivors, you also also have to keep monsters from destroying the rooms of the mansions. You can see the state of each room in the minimap with different colors (green>yellow>red). If you see a room turn red, you should head there as fast as possible and eliminate the monsters before the room collapses. The minimap can be somewhat confusing, especially when certain stairs/elevators don’t take you to the floor directly above/below you but to another floor. Still, each one of the rooms is different from the others and overall the game is very detailed, thus making it easier to navigate through the mansion. Part of this is because of the pixel art, it looks pretty good and has this retro feel to it which reminds me of old games from the arcades.
There is some enemy variety but most of them resort to melee attacks that only differentiate in speed and range, however each one of the enemy types is easily recognizable and distinguishable from the others. As for your own arsenal, there is tons of different weapons to choose from such as, chainsaws, plant vases, shotguns, boxes, books and chandeliers. However, I feel like there is a balance issue with these because melee weapons are split into two different categories, weapons with Area of Effect (AOE) and non-AOE weapons. While non-AOE weapons deal very low amounts of damage they endure a lot more hits, on the other hand, AOE weapons have very low durability but deal high amounts of damage. The way I see it, even though non-AOE weapons endure more hits, AOE weapons are just too good to ignore and I never saw myself using the others unless I had no choice.
One complaint I have about the game is the lack of a tutorial, even though it isn’t that hard to figure out what you have to do. Another thing that is worth mentioning is the fact that in its nature
is very repetitive and that it has only one level, which represents some sort of throwback to the old arcade games. Even though there isn’t much incentive to go back and play it after beating it, you can always compete for the highest score, globally or amongst your friends. There is also some sort of progression, in the sense that after unlocking an achievement you can go to this secret room in the mansion and activate some bonuses.

Imagine if you will..  a job, not just any job but a job that requires you to kill Zombies, monsters, bats, rats, and all sorts of other evil creatures...   I absolutely loved My Night Job from the moment I first installed it and began playing.   Something about running through a mansion slaughtering wave after wave of creatures using every type of weapon imaginable just comes across as fun.  I loved the numerous references to movies, such as the girl from the Ring..  (awesome touch).   Really reminded me of those games I'd play at the China Dragon across from my house.  The Chinese Dragon was Chinese food take out place, with numerous arcade machines, kids from the neighborhood would spend hour in there, trying to beat out high scores..   It was glorious just like this game, kick back and enjoy trying to beat your high score over and over again..
(no real story exist but I made one up in my head) You are Mr. Ponytail McHipster, totally in debt, because what hipster isn't behind in his bills...  Sitting in his recliner, drinking some beer, watching some rock videos, when suddenly a commercial hits, the Army needs YOU, and they are paying loads of cash...  Immediately Ponytail knows what he needs to do, after a quick phone call, and a few handshakes later, McHipster is tossed out of a plane with a walkie talkie and instructions that he needs to kill monsters, save people, and protect the mansion.
Amazing side scroller action, loads of weapons, like film reels, chain saws, shotguns, potted plants and wooden chairs.  The mansion is made up of various rooms, inside the rooms you'll find monsters, various weapons (60 weapons exist, or go all Bruce Lee and fight with your bare hands) Also in the rooms you'll find a hodge podge of various people you have to rescue and take to one of four helicopter ports for rescue.  Saving them give you money, you'll also receive a random gift, whether it's extra money, some healing, or maybe even a nice weapon to help slaughter the hordes of creatures you'll encounter.
The weapons you pick up have a durability bar, which adds some strategy into the game, go into a new room with a nearly broken chair and you run the risk of death or being seriously hurt, pick up a chainsaw and run from room to room like a manic can be fun, but pay attention because once that Chainsaw runs out you'll be left totally exposed..
Occasionally the survivors will give you some extra benefits, like an adrenaline shot that revives you when you die, or a key, others give you attack buffs or a special cat attack that clears out your current room.  Many of the survivors are special references to pop cultural, horror movies, etc etc etc.  This game plays like a hot knife through butter, silky smooth, it gives off a very 80's horror feel.  Fast paced keeping the gamer on the edge of his seat until the very end.
