I already purchased Academagia way back when and have put easily 200 hours into it since then, perhaps even more.
This is a game where you need to know what it wants to be, before going into it. It is whimsical, it is extremely text-intensive and stat-focused, and it really takes some time to get into it. But if you get into Academagia, you definitely don't want to get out anymore.
The character creation is a world on its own. You define the character's attributes, background, inheritance and much more, which in turn defines attributes, skills, money, and a lot of other stuff. Even more, you can also choose one of several school houses and a part of the subjects you want to study, from athletics to zoology and everything in between, like incantation or calligraphy.
After that you arrive at the school and can start to plan your schedule on a calendar, both your social and study life. The more you learn and the more time you spend on the school, the more activities and locations open up, always adding new possibilities to learn stuff, influence people, cast spells, and so on.
Besides skills, getting better in subjects, and making friends, random events and adventures are the heart of the game. The writing is top-notch, though the skill rolls can be pretty unforgiving, especially for newcomers to the game. But failing is learning in this case, and even then the writing is entertaining.
Besides this being a text adventure with RPG elements and the initially steep learning curve, it has to be added that this is only year 1 from several school years that are planned to be released in the future. The end therefore is rather abrupt, but still Academagia Year 1 can hold its own very well.
I've had a lovely time with it and can only recommend it if theme, screenshots and the game mechanics are to your liking.

April seems to have been in many ways a retro month here on Steamified. A number of the games that we’ve featured have been throw backs to gaming and culture’s past. Games such as Holodrive, IS Defense and many more. Today I am pleased to feature My Night Job that has been developed by Webcore Games and published by bitComposer Interactive. Webcore Games is a division of Webcore, interactive solutions agency, that has been operating since 1999. As such they have a large library of games with the overwhelming majority of them being developed for mobile devices. bitComposer Interactive is a growing publisher in the video game industry having published games including The Voice Germany, Galaxy on Fire 2 and Disciples 3: Reincarnation.
My Night Job, as mentioned, is a throwback to the horror movies and the arcade games of the 1980’s. This really is my era so the subject matter and the gameplay is right up my alley. I love that the game is very easy to pick up and play without you really having to think about it. Its great for those short fire sessions of less than an hour when you just want to relax after work or study before you pick yourself back up again to do something else. The game is very easy to learn, very quick to play and an enjoyable arcade smash. Don’t look for enormous depth to the gameplay as the depth isn’t really there and it doesn’t need to be. The depth is arguably in the large number of weapon variety – many of which do very similar things. I believe that Webcore games nailed the match up of survival horror and beat ’em up. As has been mentioned elsewhere the enemies tend to die in one hit so you’re going to want to find weapons that have a large splash/area of effect. These weapons will kill enemies almost as fast as you can see them and in some ways the game becomes an arcade version of wack a mole.
The one major negative that I have with the game is its lack of story which in my opinion gives me a lack of a reason to truly care about the game. Why am I trying to save these people? Why am I killing these monsters? What is really going on? A simplistic story would have been pretty easy to develop and would have added a lot to the game.
Thankfully the game has been Steamified with both achievements – which actually unlock perks within the game which is super cool – and trading cards.
At $7.99 you’re going to be getting your monies worth if you’re looking for a game that you can relax to mindlessly kill a bunch of monsters.

A great game that's NOT for everyone.  First thing to note, I've owned this game for nearly seven years now and rebought on steam to A) support the company and B) make sure I can keep it and it's fully up to date since I originally bought it on a  now defunct player.  So, quel surprise, I'm obviously a fan.  However before you buy it here are some necassary warnings.
WALL OF TEXT INCOMING.  No, that's not  a warning about my review, that's a warning about the game.  To put it mildly this game is full of heavy reading.  Oftentimes it's quite good and fun reading (watch out for the Sad Eyed Hamster of Doom) but if that's not your cup of tea this is not your game.  Second warning, there isn't much of a tutorial.  Now in fairness to the game this is both thematic and a little more fair then you might think since there are actually some pretty useful rewards for failure.  (Seriously, you learn about new skills and after a number of failures you get an improvement to your mental and physical health, along with a few rarer possibilities).  However it is also more then a little fustrating to new players and I don't blame anyone that bows out before the two hour mark based on that.  Third warning, ontop of all that some game mechanics ARE really difficult or obscure, none of the main or necassary ones but if you're wondering about crafting or dueling I don't blame you.  And fourth and final warning, the interface is... a little unintuitive.  It's not too bad, honestly my biggest complaint is I'm using a noticably smaller screen then most people and that makes the font size a little inconvienent for me but I'm not going to compliment it either.
Now, keep in mind this is a game I'm playing seven years after I originally purchased it.  So, yeah, these problems really don't worry me much.  And if they don't worry you then you NEED to get this game.  You play as a new student in a almost steampunk fantasy world not-Hogwarts.  You will have tremendous vareity and reaplayability.  Yes, this is a wizardry school but one playthrough I had an interesting time playing as a scientist, trying to get the non magic disciplines while studying things like math and engineering... yes that was actually INTERESTING trying to make a SCIENCE GEEK.   You can try to be a master mage, the school bully, control your fellow students with forbidden magic... there's a lot of choices here and still things I haven't seen after what's probably closing in on two hundred hours of playtime.
There's way too much for me to go into but here's a few good tips I've found before you start.
Studying (academic side of your classes) isn't a bad idea for a lot of characters.  Your parents will boost your allowance at study level 10 and many classes will give you a boost to one of your fundamental traits at that level.
Train observation (it's under blackmail, not the most intuitive place) it's usually a free action in roughly half the events you'll encounter and succeeding with it will either improve you're chances or give you an alternate course of action.

This review is my personal opinion and as such I'm not going to score things. Subjective terms for my subjective view.
VERDICT: Not Fun
This game has some good points but overall falls flat. If you have enjoyed titles such as Long Live the Queen! , Magical Diary, and other titles similar to the Princess Maker series. I would definitely not reccomend this game.
ART/GRAPHICS: Pretty damn plain and for much of the game not really there.
First off the portraits you have available for the main character are cringe worthy. In addition for my entire playthrough I can't even remember any other character portraits appearing. I'm pretty sure they exist but you have to click on their name link in whatever text you are looking at. If you are trying to play the game versus follow every wiki-ish link in existence (of which there are many and more on that later) then you will likely never see another of the boasted numerous characters portraits or sprites at all...get ready for wall of texts with very little in game art to break it up!
Side note - the user interface is not a pleasure to work with. I guess it has been improved possibly from what I have read but there isn't a whole lot there of substance.
SOUNDS/MUSIC: Inoffensive and oddly enough that's the strong point.
No seriously this one is actually a compliment. Games like this can be huge time sinks and the music in it is extremely repetitive and fairly bland. However after playing hours of hearing the same music, that's kind of a good thing. At the end I even found myself humming to it every now and again!
Sounds are non-existant as far as I could tell or maybe I was lulled into such a coma between the walls of text and the inoffensive music that I didn't even notice them...pretty sure there were none there. I get it text adventure...but some of the better one's have sounds to accentuate what is happening in the text. A minor thing and not necessary, but appreciated when it does exist. The lackluster of this game caused me to notice its absence more.
GAMEPLAY: Seriously dissapointing.
I had some hopes from this game first starting out. The character creation seemed fairly in depth, with lots of unique traits and skills from which you certainly wouldn't be able to be a jack of all trades and would force you to focus. However that is the major downfall of this game, lots of unique appearing options but with no real weight or meaning. There is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of lore, cool spells, lengthy character bios, many different characters! But it all just kind of gets lost, you don't feel attached to any skills as anything other than just another way to progress or make money. People don't feel like they matter (I played the entire game not even socializing much with people and at the epilogue piece everyone was still chummy with me). There is no real attachment to characters and while spells are neat sometimes, they don't really seem useful for anything other than buffing yourself/others and debuffing other characters...and since you can live your life in a bubble without feeling any attachment to the npcs, why bother. If you like spending hours on a wikipedia and following every link you can to get all the detailed information than this is the game for you! It honestly plays like reading a website and following links for source material. I gave it a shot but in the end it's something with a lot of potential that just is not fun to play...and in the end isn't that what games are supposed to be, fun to play?
END RANT - The ending piece! The part where it's supposed to give you your life story and wrap things up...one of the worst I have ever seen. It's the thing that I was hoping would tie together my sea of unique but seemingly pointless endeavors and choices. BUT NO...epilogue thing pulls you through a series of boring♥♥♥♥♥self relfection conversation and conversations with classmates (whose names you never knew or cared about to begin with) in MULTIPLE CHOICE FORMAT!!!What class was your favorite, pick from list of courses you took. What was your best skill, pick from list of skills you leveled up at least semi decently. What do you want to focus on in the future, exactly the same list as the last one...Side note on this, I went with the HIGHLY ILLEGAL MAGIC♥♥♥♥♥♥that is supposed to incur the death penalty. I was like I want to teach this at the school next year. You know what the npcs said about it. NOTHING, just an oh that's an interesting choice. ARE YOU FU***NG KIDDING ME! Out of the sea of blandness this, the epilogue was the most infuriating part of the entire "game".

Bastion is a game where you take the role of "the kid" on his mission to reassemble the mystical Bastion after a catastrophe befalls the world, tearing it to pieces.
The game (even being 4 years old) is gorgeous. Gameplay is diablo-esque, but it takes a good degree of skill; all weapons are varied and viable, each having its pro's and con's, but nothing ever feels "overpowered." The game isn't difficult, but the game designers implement an ingenious "idols" system that unlocks about halfway through the game. Each idol buffs all enemies in a noticable way, with the benefit of garnering you more XP and shards for upgrades. You can remove idols if you feel the games too hard, or add some to make it more difficult. Without idols, the game is incredibly easy, especially when you get some of the better potions.
I really have very few cons with this game. Its rather short if you don't try for everything, especially if you don't use idols, weighing in at most 4 hours. However, I'm going for 100% so I'm on NG+ and buffing things with lots of idols to score more XP/shards for challanges. As well, some of the more fun weapons don't unlock til later, and you cannot replay levels (there are challange areas within the bastion though that can be infinitely replayed, I just wish you weren't forced to fight all 20 waves everytime).
Definitely a worthwhile game if you like hack n' slash RPG's, beautiful artistic games, or quick games. 8/10

Ah, the gladitorial games! The one (blood) sport in which being a skilled athlete meant that you got to keep your head on your shoulders upon winning the match. Well, at least until the next fight. Yeah, I know it was a cruel and undignifying activity which sadly involved slavery as well. You’re not here to see me preaching the merits of modern sports in comparison to our shameful past tournaments. In fact, video games which focus on gladiators and their brutal way of life, seem to have rekindled the interest in both players and developers alike. I still have fond memories of 2003’s Gladiator: Sword of Vengeance but I knew that as I grew up, the management side of the business would also be nicely simulated and of interest to me. The spectacle, the glory and the profits don’t come without sacrifices and careful planning. Creative Storm Entertainment released Age of Gladiators in 2016. Their debut was a complex, albeit text-based simulation while the sequel I’m reviewing today, has promised to improve the existing formula in as many ways as it can.
And let me tell you that the dev team didn’t just aim too high and missed. Age of Gladiators II will first draw your attention with its Sci-Fi setting which is a welcome change of scenery from its predecessor. We have traded the Roman Empire for some new gladitorial contests on a literal, galactic scale. The year is 3000 AD and blood sports are now longer banned by the powers that be. A new Blood League is resurrected and sixty teams are allowed to compete on a professional and highly regulated level. The environment, the rule set and the potential sanctions indicate towards a dystopian scenario. Afterall, even a galactic tyranny can emulate the “panem et circenses” (bread and circuses) edicts of the decadent Romans, right? Gladiators may compete once again but they won’t be using gladius-style short swords that became synonymous with their bloody endeavours.
Players are given the full freedom of choosing everything about their new gladiatorial team. From the owner’s name, gender and previous professional background, to the team composition which can range from selected scouts, trainers, equipment repairmen and doctors. All have their well defined role and are crucial to the firm’s success and legacy. I’d say that half the challenge is not related to the fighting pits at all. Having the best fighters and gear, relies heavily on the skill and motivation of all your employees. As you can imagine, their wages are only a small indicator of their true value. If you’re familiar to any sports management games, you’ll understand the basics of Age of Gladiators II very soon. I really like the open-ended structure and total freedom that doesn’t drag down the narrative thread at all. You’re given the reins and set loose. This will be the story that you’ll be forging in real time. It’s not about luck, it’s about skill and lessons learned over time.
Unlike the first Age of Gladiators, the sequel is fortunately powered by the Unity Engine and it features fights that are fully rendered in 3D. You’ll be reading a lot of stats and messages anyway, between battles. Creative Storm Entertainment made the right choice in expanding the gladiator fights beyond walls of text and dice rolls. One thing that I don’t really understand though, is why blood had to be absent from this whole simulation. By definition a blood sport does involve sanguinary activities. Even the competition itself is named “The Blood League”. So where is the blood or gore? Last time I checked, I wasn't playing a Disney game. You’re actually reading a review from a “nut” that buys blood DLCs in games which their developers took the greedy path and wanted to charge extra for a feature that should have been already implemented. You can’t have warfare without casualties in the same manner in which gladiatorial games were popular because of the gruesome spectacles they promoted. Overall, the game’s performance was smooth and without any unpleasant surprises. Unity doesn’t disappoint me often.
Apart from an underwhelming soundtrack and few sound effects relating to the combat sections, no audio assets are present for any of the characters or the narration itself. Considering the Spartan “tradition” of the first Age of Gladiators, at least the sequel impoved upon that formula. There’s still plenty of room to expand and perhaps feature even memorable voice acting. There’s a lot of text to be read, so a narrator/announcer would fit the story like a glove.
What’s important to understand about Age of Gladiators II is that a hands-on management style is the key to success both early and once you’ve reached the apex of both fame and fortune. Having the most expensive gear, fighters and staff members won’t mean much unless you discover and tap the potential of all those resources. A scout may single out the best marksman from the available roster, but it’s up to the players to guide the gladiator towards the right path which means both survival of the fittest and the smartest fighters in the pit. Automation and auto-resolving (essentially skipping gameplay processes) will yield mixed results. Take your time, learn the basics and you’ll find that this type of strategy isn’t nearly as hard as it may appear at first glance. When you’re not setting your fighters loose in the pits, you can send them off on errands and missions that further solidify the RPG elements of the Age of Gladiators II. A moral compass is well simulated and unlike the ancient gladiatorial games, slavery and the execution of staff/fighters is not only looked down upon, but also penalized by the officials which supervise the Blood League.
I like the fact that as a team manager, the player is encouraged to experiment with various tactics and loadouts. You’ll be able to develop the base of operations in a similar manner to the XCOM series, only that instead of an underground HQ or a space ship, you’re given access to an asteroid which will serve as both corporate headquarters and a training facility. Gaining access to new rooms, requires the mining and clearing of previous debris. Basically, your HQ will grow and become more complex, as you aquire the necessary funds from winning fights and bets (you’re even allowed to bet against your own team). A “loan shark” system has been implemented but I suggest you steer clear from it for as long as you can. Start small, focus on wisely spending the resources you produce by natural game progression and then invest in a few in-game businesses that shall guarantee a steady, albeit small cash flow and income opportunities.
Within its new Sci-Fi environment and auxiliary topics, Age of Gladiators II has managed to distance itself from the previous entry in the series. I wholeheartedly enjoyed the new themes which still improved the established gameplay mechanics of its predecessor. There are few flaws to this title and apart from the nearly non-violent depiction of the fights, no other aspect might require further attention from the developers. An Age of Gladiators III is in the works and it shall hopefully feature the right amount of gore that any gladiator-themed video game deserves.

This is more of a first impressions then a review as i feel that ive barely scratched the surface of this particular game.
Pillars of Eternity or PoE (its unfortunate that it shares the same anagram as path of exile but oh well.), is an Isometric cRPG, which to the uninitiated means Computer Role playing game.  Yes that’s right, there’s a genera called computer role playing games.  Back in the early 80s-late 70s when DnD was a thing, people played these pen and paper style RPGs.  CRPGs are games that are more or less recreations of that pen and paper style with graphics and a computer.  Other similar games would be the original Baldur's Gate games, Fallout 1 &2, Ice Wind Dale, and even Dragon Age: Origins (I don’t consider 2 and 3 Crpgs but thats another conversation for another day).   If you’ve played a game like what I’ve listed above then you will know what to expect from PoE, but it’s most likely that you haven’t played one of the aforementioned titles and that is why you are reading this review.
Just a quick little discussion of CRPGs before I jump into my review, CRPGs tend to be very tactical and story based games.  They tend to use real time combat systems that more or less rely on stat vs stat dice rolls that go on behind the scenes while you are playing the game, to decide many different aspects of the game, anything from whether or not you are successful climbing a wall to how much damage you do when you swing your sword.  These games tend to rely on their world building and stories and require that the person playing them be quite meticulous if they want to be able to play on the normal and higher difficulties.  The combat is real time but allows for the user to pause to issue orders to each of their individual party members before continuing and in this is where most of the strategy comes into play.
With that out of the way, PoE very accurately captures the feel of the old infinity engine games (Baldur’s gate, Ice Wind Dale, etc) while adding new unique features and using its own rule set that is familiar enough for old veterans of the genera but new enough to be interesting.  Things like the addition of a stronghold system, classes that use songs and other mechanics, the endurance/HP system and per encounter spells rather than per rest cycle make the game feel a little more modern while still preserving the feel of nostalgia that comes with those older games.
That being said the game isn’t without its flaws, for example because might is the skill that decides damage, it is actually sometimes better to stack might on your spell caster than to stack int like you would with a traditional wizard.  This feels thematically weird in some cases but honestly it can be overlooked.
I recommend this game for anyone who has played games like Baldur’s gate and really enjoyed those style of games when they played them.  I also recommend this game for people who like story driven experiences (there is a lot of text though most characters are voice acted) and who like a strategic challenge.

===
A very difficult, very niche management game that relatively few players will appreciate and enjoy, but for those that will have the patience to delve into its statistics and management shenanigans, this is certainly a game that can bring great satisfaction.
Age of Gladiators 2 is a team-management game with some turn-based RPG elements. Think of Football Manager right, we all know that one... but with gladiators. In space. A thousand years in the future. And yes there are aliens, and laserbeams, and premature death. And also a ton of numbers, statistics and charts to look at. Mostly that. It is a management game after all, with all the good and bad of it.
===
In Age of Gladiators 2 you will be an enterpreneur running your very own space station inside an asteroid, because asteroids are cool. Ice cold actually. An enterprise that is all about Gladiator fights, to win huge amounts of money, glory, renown and all of that, sounds good right? To do this, Age of Gladiators 2 puts at your disposal a complex set of functions, ranging from hiring your staff such as trainers, medical, engineers, to obviously hiring gladiators, train them to enhanche their statistics, equip them with upgradeable weapons and armor, and even execute them on the spot if they do something wrong, or just make you lose money, that is.
You will have to micromanage all the aspects of your gladiator enterprise: staff, combatants, training, healing, equipment, repairs, finances, debts, loans, morale, third party proprieties to enhanche morale or income, leaderboards, see how your competition is going and act accordingly... there is a whole lot of stuff to do in this title and it can be overwhelming if you are new to this genre or not particularly keen to charts, statistics and lots of numbers. On one side the system is solid and allows a very in depth management, on the other hand, less experienced users will find themselves overburdened and a bit confused with all the stuff going on at once, so keep this in mind before buying.
The gameplay evolves via Turns, each is a day, in a set amount of days a fight draft will initiate and your gladiators will have to fight in either Rookie (non lethal) or Blood (lethal) leagues, obviously the lethal one is the real deal, the other's just for training! At the end of each year, the six best gladiator managers with their teams will dispute a final where in the end will be a only winner. And the next year, all goes on again! Gladiators will get injured, die, be mutilated permanently even. Modern technology and upgrades can aid you but in the end all is about your managing skills and strategy.
Combat can be directly taken control of or just simulated automatically. If you decide to take control, as you should, the game becomes a top-down turn based RPG showing your gladiators against the enemy ones in a hex-cell based arena. Battle system is based on action points, there are 3 attack types, ranging from more accurate to more powerful, consumables, and special moves to get bonuses if you are lucky enough.
Various armor and weapon types, and statistics, play a big role in combat, every move can be the last and attacks that connect well are very lethal, very fast. Combat is rather unforgiving, luck has a big role in it as a critical hit can end a fight in one shot pretty often. Your strategy on whether play it safe or just try hard for that one perfect blow among a lot of missed ones, is up to you, as up to you is equipment and formation.
All considered, combat is pretty solid and is a good reflection of how well you managed your gladiators overall.
The game itself can go on forever, as the fights never really end, it is up to you to decide when to retire and start a new game. Obviously there will be a point where you have it all, your gladiators became demigods and nobody can stand in your way, sure. And that point is at least say, 50-60 hours away, if you are lucky, and good.
No major issues to report.
This is no game for casuals, and not even for hardcore players that have no experience with similar titles. It is a very niche, very difficult management game that few will apreciate to its full extent, and to those players is suggested.

After about 20 hours in game, I thought I'd share some thoughts. This game is brimming with potential. While it is obvious that the game is still in very early alpha, the premise and the promise of new materials that haven't been implimented yet make this game well worth the asking price. There are still numerous glitches such as sharks swimming through the sand on shores and some limited use items never running out of uses, but the glitches that exist aren't game killing. When they do the damage is negligible. They do cause bleeding damage which will continue slowly for up to a week or so of game time but that damage is easily  dealt with as you gain more health from resting than you lose from bleeding. Out of dozens of interactions with sharks, only twice have I been seriously wounded by a shark and never have they managed to kill me. While I like the fact that the sharks aren't overly aggresive, they are simply too abundant (seriously you cant swim more than 30 seconds without seeing one) and not dangerous enough. If nothing else, when they do bite, it should be devestating. Overall this game has a lot of promise. I can't wait for more material to be added.

A surprisingly good game that manages to take the high fantasy setting of LOTR and put a dark spin on it.
Shadow of Mordor can be likened to the Assassin's Creed franchise in how it plays, but also adds in the wraith skills that put a supernatural twist on gameplay, such as teleporting, draining foes, and even mind-control.
The nemesis system, though under-utilized, is also a very interesting feature that shows you the Orc hierarchy of your enemies, and you can either mind-dominate your way up to the Warchiefs, or influence events in Orc society to allow your mind-controlled minions to rise in the ranks. As fun as this system is, the game does make too much use of it outside of a handful of missions.
Story is solid, and plays well into the LOTR setting, but it has a sequel-baiting ending that hints at changing the history of what we know with LOTR. Otherwise, this is a refreshing tale of two souls out for revenge.
I'd recommend it if you're either a 3rd person action/adventure fan, or even a LOTR fan. If you manage to pick up this game on sale, you won't be disappointed.

pay-to-play.  The result of that is that unless you pay the makers of this game real-life money  — on a regular basis — in order play the game, and also in order not to be at an unfair disadvantage in multiplayer, then you probably will have a very unpleasant experience with Faeria.  The rest of this review will expand on these points.
The solo/singleplayer part of Faeria is called “Missions.”  When you start the game, you can play the Missions for free and have fun.  However, after you play two-dozen or so Missions (don’t quote me on that number, because it is merely an estimate off the top of my head) for free, the game suddenly and without warning locks down the rest of the Missions behind paywalls.  To access the rest of the Missions, you first have to pay high amounts of in-game currency, and every time you do pay, it
Missions.  Once you complete those few, then you have to pay yet again before you can access a few more Missions. That process keeps repeating for every few Missions you complete.  In simpler terms:  to keep playing, you must keep paying.
Of course, you are not going to have enough in-game currency to access the Missions you want to play.  That is because the developers want you to buy in-game currency in exchange for real-life currency a.k.a. American dollars.
In my opinion, this tactic is a “bait-and-switch,” because the game never tells you that only the first couple of dozen Missions are free and you will have to pay money, many times, to access the rest of them.
Fans of Faeria might try to rebut the facts I’ve given above, with an argument like: “Your point is invalid because you can earn in-game currency for free, without ever paying real money to the developers.”  But that counter-argument does not negate anything I’ve said, because the process of earning in-game currency is an extremely unpleasant experience.  The tiny amounts of in-game currency you receive for playing the game comes at a very slow snail’s pace. .
I know that sounds complicated, and that is because the game makes it complicated.  But the “solution” to that complication is easy
— and only if  —you pay real-life money for in-game currency every time you instantly want to bypass the paywalls and the aggravation.
I expect that these paywalls were deliberately designed to frustrate players into paying-to-play.
Fans of Faeria might also try to rebut the facts I’ve given above with an argument like: “You can just grind out the in-game currency you need to access singleplayer Missions, by playing multiplayer.”  But that counter-argument fails too, because trying to compete in multiplayer before you have a good deck is
an extremely unpleasant experience.  Even if you choose the form of multiplayer listed as “Casual” (note: it’s
casual), you will be at an inherent disadvantage, because you will be matched against opponents who have much better decks that you. They will have copied their decks from the ones designed by professional eSports players.  Since your multiplayer opponents’ decks are way more powerful than yours, regardless of your skill level, if you play multiplayer, by default, you are going to get owned.
You may be thinking: “Why don’t I just copy a professional player’s deck too, so that I will be on a fair & even playing-field with my opponents in multiplayer.”  That is a great idea, but
do that — yup, you guessed it — unless you first buy good cards with real-life money.  That’s right, the cards you
to play Faeria are also locked behind paywalls within the in-game store.
Yes, again Faeria fans may say: “But you can get all those cards just by playing.”  Except that counter-argument neglects the facts that receiving cards just by playing is an extremely slow grind. And even worse, there are no good places in which you can grind for them, because (as I’ve explained) singleplayer is blocked behind paywalls and multiplayer is horrendous, unless before you enter it, you have first dropped a lot of real-life money to buy good cards, a.k.a. pay-to-win.
You can also “Craft” specific cards you need, but that requires crafting resources, and the game is
with how much crafting resources it gives you.  To craft even one good (i.e. Legendary quality) card takes forever.  And you’d need to craft (or buy with lots of real money) many cards before you’d have a deck that won’t be vastly underpowered in multiplayer.
Faeria also has another mode called “Pandora,” but it too is blocked behind paywalls and mostly inaccessible for free players (they let free players play a little bit of it each day, and then block access to further play).
I understand that the developers need to make some money.  I am not objecting to the principle of making money.  But they can make money in better ways, ways that don’t block any of the game’s content behind paywalls, or gimp free players by leaving them unable to access good cards.
What I am objecting to is promoting the game as free-to-play and implying that paying for content is totally optional, even though in reality that is not exactly true.  The paywalls that block access to game content, and to good cards, will almost guarantee that free players are going to have a bad time with Faeria.

in pretending that it treats free players equally as well as paid players is not ethical.  That is why I spent the time & energy to write this long review.  I hope this review will reveal the bait-and-switch nature of Faeria’s so-called “free-to-play” model before it blindsides & deceives another player like it did to me.

It is in a very early alpha stage, version 0.1 with one hotfix, so there's not much content inside. But what is already in the game works amazingly well. The focus of the game lies more on crafting than on survival, the latter being quite easy with plenty of food and water and weather (seemingly) having no bad consequence. As long as you stay away from white sharks you shouldn't die.
Crafting in this games means first gather different ressources, put them all on the ground and click on it to get a popup menu of stuff you can build with it. You can hunt for sardines, crabs or sharks, I killed a Tigershark quite easily with an axe on my second day. I've build a permanent fire spit, a bed and a hut for myself plus all crude tools like hammer, axe and spear within the first 5 days and that's about all you can build rightnow. There are other islands to explore, each with some shipwrecks that you can dive for loot. There's also the possibility to build an engine so travel with your life raft goes a bit faster, but I don't have all the parts needed yet.
There are also sudden monsuns  where you can't see anything and when you're out on the sea with your raft when a monsun hits, all you can do is let go of mouse and keyboard and wait. Sadly there's no way to let time pass faster in anyway other then sleeping at night, which means long periods of starring at the screen without doing anything.
So, TL;DR: it has content for about two hours realtime after which you've seen all there is but this content is very beautiful and works already well. I'm eager to see what the beta or final version will look like.

My Night Job:
~~~~~~~~~~~

You have been looking for a night job for a while, then you came across the following advertisement in your favourite newspaper . . . “In search of a strong, athletic individual to rescue 100 people in a mansion full of Zombies. The successful applicant needs to be able to use any items as a weapon to succeed!” WOW. . .  that sounds great, here comes my night job!
My night job is a survival side-scroller beat ’em-up game where you have to rescue a certain number of inhabitants and VIP guests from a mansion full of Zombies! At the start of the game, you will be told your objectives, which will include you saving 100 people and making sure that all the rooms (22 in total) are defended and not destroyed. Well, it seems to be a walk in the park when you start your night job, but you will quickly change your mind as the minutes past. Well, I surely did! As the minutes go by, as many zombies seems to find their way into the property and swamp the people as soon as they can.
I forgot to mention a very small but important thing - you start the game without any weapons at all! Fortunately for you, the advertisement above did specify that any items you will find will be useful weapons. It’s true, and you will notice a little blue arrow above different pieces of furniture, crates, tools and more, which means you can find or take a particular object with which to smash the zombies. However, each object takes damage each time you hit a foe. So make sure you find another weapon as fast as possible.
People will be all around the mansion with captions over their heads, “HELP!” Just move towards them and as soon as you past them they will follow you. Some will have weapons and can be very useful to you for a short period of time; after all, you have to lead them to safety before they die. How do you do that? Very simple, guide the survivors towards a helipad to be rescued. Don’t forget to look for the V.I.P’s, they usually hide behind furniture, the little buggers. It is very easy to identify where their might hide; a little coin with a head on one side and one of three power ups on the other side will be display above the furniture. If you manage to escort them safely to one of the five helipads available to you, you will get the power up. One to look for is the lovely nurse,; she has the revive ability at her disposal. You will need it.
The other aspect of the game is to get as many points as you can by hitting as many Zombies as possible without being touched, and to escort people and V.I.P’s to the helipad, surviving as long as you can.
I really enjoyed the progressive difficulty in the game - it is just great!

In My Night Job you find yourself in an old abandoned mansion which is slowly being taken over by hordes of the undead (and other little nasties). Your job is to stop the mansion from becoming overrun by the zombiesque creatures whilst finding and escorting survivors to safety via a helicopter. The gameplay itself is very fun if not a little on the basic side; you'll find various weapons around the map and you must use those to kill as many of the undead as you can whilst evacuating survivors to key locations.
There are multiple rooms in the mansion, all connected to each other in some way and you must navigate through looking for anyone who is still alive. There is a limit on how many survivors you can have with you at once, but worry not, there are evacuation points located around the map where you can drop your survivors off for various rewards (health pack, a loaded gun or cash). When you start you only have your fists as weapons but there are plenty of new things to find that you can kill the zombies with. Most of the weapons in game are melee with the exception of guns (which so far I've only been able to get randomly from the evac point) so be prepared for plenty of close up combat. The weapons seem to come in two varieties, the first being your usual sword-style attack weapons. Things like plates, fish and umbrellas all fall into this category as they do one hit at a time with a small range that only affects those in front of you. The second are AOE weapons and these do damage over an area wiping out many zombies at once. Though MUCH superior in attack damage these weapons have significantly less durability than the other weapons. There is also the very awesome chainsaw which can only be found in one location but can destroy room after room of undead with very little effort; perfect for when you're being stomped in too many rooms.
You'll come across two types of survivors whilst you play: normal and VIP. Normal survivors do nothing special and can be found waiting in rooms in the mansion to be rescued. Some of these survivors will have weapons and others will be completely helpless so you'll have to make sure you have something to defend them because they can and will be attacked whilst waiting for you to rescue them AND while being escorted to safety. The second type are VIPs which can be found by activating certain icons you find in rooms. It seems to be random if you get a VIP or nothing but when you get one you should try and rescue them ASAP. Once you escort a VIP survivor to the evac zone you'll get an added bonus power-up that can be activated one time. For example one of these turns you into a clown that does increased attack damage but can only use fists for a while and another releases a rather angry sounding cat that'll clear the current room for you. These small bonuses can completely turn the tide of the game for you.
There are different types of enemies but most of them are just basic melee attackers with different speeds (besides the odd SuperRobot with guns for hands) and they can be killed pretty easily but make sure to watch your health bar because they can deal lots of damage before you even realise. The undead will attack you and survivors whilst you share a room and slowly fill the rooms you don't occupy. One a room is filled with zombies they will not attack you when you enter and instead start 'stomping', you must stop this happening as quickly as you can. After stomping long enough the room will collapse and once all the rooms collapse you've lost. Survivors cannot spawn in destroyed rooms so the more rooms that are destroyed the less people you can rescue thus making your game a lot harder. Rooms are colour-coded on your map so you can tell the danger levels in each room and quickly work out where you need to go and the best route (I must mention the layout of the mansion is a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥at times).
You can unlock Steam achievements that can then be activated in game for bonuses for that run such as speed boosts, so there is an added incentive to go achievement hunting.
Your achievements are still unlocked though and can still be activated in the special room in the mansion, but other than that there is no progress saved.
There are a few problems with the game thoiugh. Firstly the weapon balance seems a little off in my opinion. Despite AOE weapons having less durability they are still the best option because of the lack of the players health in the game. I think the normal weapons need a bit of a damage boost. Secondly, the lack of tutorial is a real issue. Besides how to move and attack nothing else is explained and you'll have to work things out on your own. VIP survivors need an explanation on how to activate them and what they do when rescued,
, and despite there being a goal of setting explosions I still have no clue how to do this. This may be a later objective but I have no way of knowing if this is the case or not. Lastly I do feel the game could do with another way to regain health than hoping for it randomly as an evac bonus, I'm spending far too much time running 3 or 4 survivors to the helicopter just in the hopes of getting some health. I'll also add that I've noticed that if I rescue 3 or 10 survivors at once the bonus is the same besides cash making it a lot more efficient to do small batches rather than large even though it's more fun to collect as many survivors as you can at once. You should be rewarded on the number you bring (more gun durability, spare health packs).

I didn't expect much, but I was surprised to find a ton of cool game mechanics. The ability to selective age objects, create time warp felds, slow down time when scoping, and use telekinesis opened up a lot of cool gameplay doors. These aren't, perhaps, new features - other games have tried it out before. But this game makes an effort to let you interact with tons of environmental objects, which is nice - it turned an otherwise standard shooter experience into something that felt pretty interactive.
But the game's flaws outrank the fun. In order to get the sound to work, you need to disable any recording devices in Windows. The sensitivity bar won't allow you to go lower than a certain amount (which is still way too high), so instead of trying to find a config file, I just halved the DPI on my mouse. The FOV is artifically low (we're talking probably 65, here) so you get a claustrophobic sense of the world.
I might have been able to forgive these shortcomings (and I did, for a few hours), but the real killer was the unbalanced gameplay. I handled giant mutants, blinking mutants, hordes of russians, and twisted undead with no problem. But at a specific point in the game, you're placed into the position of dealing with enemies who kill you in 2-3 shots, and which you're unable to really fight back against. The swarm of suicide bugs who, with three different hits, will kill you. The blade-armed assassin mutant who could take a literal dozen sniper shots to the head (!!) without being visibly damaged. These encounters took about half an hour to get past (a long time to spend in one encounter), with lots of frustration. And worst, they're surrounded by other no-problem encounters. I had thought to crank down the difficulty and cheese my way through these speedbumps, but you can't even do that.
Add that to the game's general low-res appearance, uninteresting environments (someone said it was all brown - that's true), and unsatisfying sound; and the result was that I simply couldn't find a reason to continue playing.

TLDR: This is a "recommend reluctantly" rating. It's okay at ten bucks. You won't get value received at twenty.
GOOD:
Interesting story, albeit delivered very obliquely so if you like everything spelled out clearly, forget it. Since you're basically working backward in time to the Very Bad Thing That Happened, hearing about it in one-and-two-sentence remarks from various characters, the whole thing won't even begin to make any sense until near the end.
Reasonably good voice acting, although the narrator is much better in his Wry Jeff Goldblum Commentary Mode than in his Heartfelt Big Dramatic Moment mode (those are also the ones which have the worst and most overwrought script).
Interesting locations, good scenery. No load screens while in play. Only one place in the game where you pass a point of no return.
BAD:
Gameplay itself is boring as hell. Use your scanner to find flickering objects. The more important ones will require you to do a quick waveform-matching exercise (which is fortunately easy because it outstays its welcome after the third time you have to do it, and you'll do it a lot more times than that). The others you just click. Some documents don't flicker and you have to find them and click them. When you've unlocked enough of them then Something Happens and you'll need to place an object or some meager interaction. Then you go BACK OVER EVERYWHERE YOU'VE JUST BEEN to find more objects and see what unlocked. Eventually you unsort the story that way. In between, you walk around a lot.
When you finish the game, having explored every act and sometimes checked it multiple times, you'll be told you were still missing half the objects and you won't care enough to go back and find the rest.
Every so often a very simple puzzle will be interspersed to try to break up the grind. It doesn't.
-----
I really wish Steam had a "meh" rating. There's nothing wrong with this game per se. But the story and visuals weren't quite interesting enough to make up for the dullness of the rest of it. At ten bucks, which is what I paid for it, it barely slides into the zone of "I don't regret buying it," and is therefore a recommend. If I had paid twenty for it, it would have tipped the other way and would have been a thumbs-down.

While watching tv late at night our protagonist sees an ad for a night job, the money is good and he signs up right away: said job consists of saving 100 survivors from an house full of monsters before placing explosives to blow everything up.
My Night Job is a very quirky game with perfect art style, frantic beat'em up action and a lot of humour thrown in for good measure: it's very fun to play but sadly doesn't have alot of content going for it.
-the pixelated art is truly great
-catchy soundtrack
-the beat'em up action works well and it's as fun as it is challenging: you also find lots of different weapons to use
-full of humour and references
-mansion design is very good
-unlocking game bonuses through achievements is an interesting concept
-could have used an option to speed up survivor rescue animations and to remove the auto camera change over certain events
-repetitiveness can set in pretty quickly
-once you beat it there's not much to go back to (unless you want to climb the leaderboards or grind for achievements)
-can get slightly glitchy at times
The game has alot going for it: the art style is truly nice and sports a retro vibe while still being very detailed, the catchy retro horror soundtrack is perfect, there's tons of references to horror movies/ games/ comics and the gameplays stays fun despite being challenging.
It'll take several tries before you learn the mansion layout, where every special survivor might be (and what they give once rescued) and how to properly juggle survivor rescuing with room clearing. The game is pretty hard and will require you to be quicky- and a tad lucky- to be able to complete it. Sadly the amount of retries means it can get repetitive pretty quickly as the mansion stays the same and so do your objectives: sure there's a bit of randomization in survivor positions and room attacks but not enough to keep things fresh. And once you beat it, well, you're left with trying to go for an higher score or unlocking achievements (some are pretty grindy).
My Night Job is really fun and should be right down your alley if you like challenging beat'em ups, but the small amount of content and its intrinsic repetitiveness are things you'd consider before you buy.

You can upgrade your person and weapons by exploring and collecting energy cells.
Easy, Normal, and Hard difficulties are available.

A nice (though I wouldn't exactly say "great") story with an intriguing setting. Unfortunately, the game itself has a lot of flaws, and I don't feel like it was worth the time and money.
The story is given entirely via text documents and "mementos". The latter are random objects which you have to find in the world (by using a helpful radar which leads you to everything story-related) and click (and, sometimes, solve a simple boring puzzle) to hear one or two lines of monologue from some story character. There's a lot of these characters, but basically none of them is developed enough to make the player actually care about him/her. Most character stories are also unfinished - I feel like they were just thrown in to make an illusion of a "bigger picture" (and give the player something to collect, of course). Well, it didn't really work for me. The beautiful world was practically the only thing that kept me going. There are a few episodes where you need to find some items and use them on something, but it's very basic (and the game makes sure to highlight the places where you need to put something). The story, as I said, was nice enough, but it didn't have any real surprises - almost everything was clear after the first act, and there were already slight hints about the rest. The endgame simply puts everything you already knew together and briefly fills the gaps. The ending itself is... well, just as bland as the rest.
For an "almost open-world" game, exploration is pretty bad too. Sure, you have enough space to walk around and check around every corner. The problem is - most corners don't have anything around them. And when you do find something, it's just another memento which "rewards" you with a line of boring monologue you couldn't care less about. Think Gone Home on steroids: more space, vast outdoor locations, but nothing conceptually different (except infinitely better story). If you loved Gone Home, this might just be the game for you. Alas, I didn't.
Oh, and there's also the backtracking. Don't get me wrong here - I actually like games which support meaningful backtracking: the kind when the game acknowledges and rewards players which intentionally come back to investigate something they've just learned or realized, or maybe use something they didn't have before. Unfortunately, Empathy's backtracking is the worst kind of meaningless. You can search the whole location, find a lot of inactive (seemingly decorative) objects and decide you are done here - then, once you get back to finishing another story task, your radar suddenly comes alive with a half-dozen markers, leading to these very same items you've already found (but now you can interact with them). So, not only is exploration weak by itself - the game design actively discourages it.
The fact that most of the characters have Russian names and "matching" voices doesn't help either. Yep, we native speakers are long-time used to faux-Russian accents done by amateur Americans who sound like they've never heard an actual Russian speak. But to endure this torture for the whole duration of a game with several dozen invisible characters who can't even pronounce each other's (and occasionally their own) names?! That was the hardest part. Especially when the main developer's name looks like he should at the very least know better than to name a town "Chernosk" without a "v". Sure, that one's at least fixed in the Russian localization, but who cares if there are no Russian voices? Next time, hire a dozen Russian students to voice it if an authentic atmosphere is what you are looking for...
Overall - not a horrible game, it has its charms (mostly visual), but it's definitely not something I would recommend. There are better "walksims" out there.
P.S. On the bright side, the developer is active on the forums and very eager to quickly solve any issue you might have.

Set in a "somewhat postapocalyptic" soviet environment this is a classic First person shooter with some "super-powers" added besides the usual guns. Gameplay is reminiscent of Bioshock, while the setting and atmosphere are close to Metro 2033.
You play as an american soldier sent to investigate closed down and abandoned Soviet facility, where you uncover mistery E99 element and events follow.
What I really liked about the game:
-The gameplay is very solid. You have good amount of different, well-designed weapons (the game keeps giving you new ones right until the end, that way it keeps things interesting). Also you have some superpowers (not from beginning but quite early into the game you get your first one) and the list of the things you can do grows. Timeshift bubble, aging opponents, impulsing all around you, telekinesis. All that good stuff. Overall, the shooting part is fun and makes you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ The 'puzzles' won't take
-The setting. Very gruesome, graphic. Reminiscent of Metro but more "paranormal" stuff.
What is not particularly great but holds up:
-The story. It's pretty linear and straightforward for a game about time-travel and altering history/future, but still it is enjoyable and grips you until the end. The game even has 3 endings, but they are basically the same, just different cut-scenes in the end and you can replay last 1 minute of the game to see them all.
What I disliked:
-For a game that's been out for like 2 years already there's too many bugs. I've had to restart the game around 5 times due to game-breaking bugs (NPCs stuck or disappearing, doors not opening e.t.c) and the thing is - I've wasted good amount of time in each of those instances to figure out that something is wrong. Once there was a sequence where a girl opened some door and I needed to defend her from monsters. Well, the thing got stuck and the monsters spawned endlessly and I couldn't undestand that something is wrong until I wasted all my bullets, medkits, e99 energy and they just killed me (I wasted around 10-15 minutes I think) and after restart the process ended in like 3 monsters and 15 seconds.
All in all, solid title. Recommend to play it if you like shooters, enjoyed Metro 2033 and/or Bioshock.

Cartoon-styled side-scrolling beat'em up game with surprisingly complex and challenging mechanic.
Basically, you're dropped just outside of some big mansion, filled with respawning monsters and "civilians", as well as some items you can use as weapons - from umbrellas and chairs to gas baloons and everyone's favourite - the Chainsaw!
In short, you beat monsters, gather people and led them to rescue (helipads on the edges of the mansion). For each rescue you collect some goodness, like healthkits, guns with ammo etc. After you rescue 100 people, your main goal changing to blow up the mansion, by settling some C4 in the basement. Meanwhile, as you running back and forth through the area, the monsters are growing their numbers, and if they reach some trigger point, they starting to tear the mansion apart - yeah, before you'll be able to save everyone and leave the place.
So, you're not simple bash some monsters - that's the lesser goal, while the three main things are to save people, prevent monsters to crush the house prematurely, and only after you save enough, then blow everything. In The Right Time. Also, you can hunt achievements (such as bash 20 gargoyles with bare hands or save 1000 people), and then Activate those trophies in the Secret Room of the mansion, to get some powerups for that (only 2 at the time, though).
So, yeah, it is quite a challenge. If you're can tolerate a bit of goofy cartoon animation, at its core, the game is quite a solid one. As many people said already, it could only be more fun in some co-op play, which so far is not aviable.
Nonetheless, I recommend "My Night Job" to everyone. It's 8.2/10 mark in my book, for the complexity and overall fun.

Okay, yeah, it's a niche genre. Still, there's a surprising amount of games out there for it. Academagia is, without a doubt, the most in-depth, strategic, number-crunchy one of the bunch. With hundreds of skills spread out across dozens of parent skills, over a thousand Adventures and Random Events, a hundred or more fellow students and professors, and dozens of locations - this is a game that will make you think. Yet layered over all those numbers and depth is a rich literary experience that's both evocative and whimsical.
I bought this game years ago off the developer's website, and I was excited to see the opportunity to support them by buying it again and playing it on Steam.
After working your way through a robus character generator that should give you a hint at the level of depth Academagia offers, you find yourself looking at the screen that controls the majority of the game - your weekly calendar. That's right, if the screenshots didn't clue you in - this is a text and menu-based game.
From this calendar you control your character. Each day has 3 time slots. For weekdays your first two default to attending classes, but you're free to do something else. Skipping class does have its consequences, but will get to that later. What you do with your time is up to you, but it's a big decision. Let's move to the next section and see what you'll be striving for.
Occasional formatting issues can't spoil the incredible writing in Academagia, nor does a lack of modern in-game UI features leave the player helpless (thank you Wikias). Players who accept the text and menu-based nature of Academagia will find a jewel of rich story-telling layered over an incredibly deep, strategic, and crunchy simulation.

Vex is a 3-D puzzle platformer with an arcadey feeling to it. While the game mechanics are kept simple, it is quite challenging and can be hair-pullingly tough at times, yet retains the fun factor that you might expect from a platformer.
(+) Cube Warrior
That title might be a bit misleading, but I couldn’t find a more appropriate title for this section. You are basically a cube that has to go around interweave between other cubes and pass through some timing specific sections to reach the end point of a stage. Some of the power ups available allow you to push cubes aside, so basically you are cube fighting other cubes. The game uses a lot of physics based movement and hence you can even maneuver edges if you get the controls right. The movement can feel a bit clunky in the beginning, but once you get the hang of it, things become easier.
The gameplay is very simplistic and every level has a set amount of enemies and has different power-ups placed in capsule like structures, which give you various abilities. More description will just spoil the game, so trying to be spoiler free, all I would say is that the game has enough variety in elements to keep you going through it’s 2-4 hour long campaign. Note: The last dimension, Quanta, is pretty exciting and adds another tangent to the challenge.
(+) Eyes and Ears:
Visually the game is very simplistic, and isn’t a technical marvel (Well so are many indie titles), but the art direction is good. The different visual settings do impact the look of the game quite significantly. Apart from that, the game looks visually calm during three quarters of it’s run time.
Complimenting the visual calmness are the soothing music tracks which, in similar fashion to the visuals, are only so for three quarters of the game. Yes the Quanta dimension is pretty dark and the music pretty much  reflects it in many ways.
(+) Level Design:
Now, in a platformer, the most important factor for determining a good game is the design of the levels and here Vex does the job brilliantly. The different dimensions allow for various levels that are diverse and feel true to their respective dimensions. The environments are well crafted and as mentioned above the levels can vary from ‘candy eating easy’ to  ‘garment tearingly tough’. So yeah the difficulty slider does swing in various angles. As mentioned above, the movement is physics based, so you can actually use the shape of the cube to your advantage while trying to cross a weirdly angled obstacle. The one thing that developers should have put in was some verticality to the levels which would have made the game more exciting, but well I wouldn’t complain about that, because I enjoyed it irrespective.
(-) The Bummer
Now I can’t pick a very specific flaw from my side, because as I have said in my earlier reviews, I have played relatively less platformers than I have played other genres, and in my recent slew of playing great platformers, Vex continues that trend. One flaw that does come to mind is the lack of a story. The beginning of the game has a short story about the overall plot of the game, but it is never mentioned anywhere in the entire play through, so that’s one. And the other being that it is not something innovative, so these are the only two flaws I can think of. Also, the game does not have any human element added to it- No dialogues, no character etc, which might be a drawback for many modern gamers.
(+) Trivia:
Just to sum up some points that I didn’t elaborate.
There are 45 levels, 40 of which are gained through directly completing the levels, 4 which are found in some secret way and the last one unlocks when you completed the 4 secret levels. For a completionist, this game is perfect since the level of reward for a small replay is getting a whole new level.
The game has three camera modes- First Person (I would rather call it shoulder view), Third person view and Aerial view, so you can play in which ever mode you are comfortable with.

I reviewed the first Age of Gladiators, so I thought I would do the same for the sequel.
First off - it's in space. I big change, definitely, but one that grew on me. The first one was unique for applying a management sim format to the Roman gladiator concept, and this one adds to the unexpected by blasting that combination into a sci-fi space setting. Definitely not a retread.
One of the major benefits of this is the variety of species that you can use as fighters, who have different skill sets related to their biology. I think these differences could maybe be expanded (gladiator officials make it clear that only creatures with a basically human shape can participate in league fights), but there's enough there to keep it interesting. Using cybernetics to repair injured fighters, long range weapons like laser rifles, and cloning dead fighters whose genetics had them winning straight through until they got unexpectedly killed are all components of the gameplay that I certainly haven't seen in a game of this kind.
Bottom line: it's an original take, like the first game in the series, but more so. It's fun to play, not too difficult and not too easy. While some of the sci-fi possibilities could be more fully explored, it's a really strong game and a welcome new spin on the gladiator management sim established by its predecessor.

Despite the negative review, I want to commend the developer for both his commitment to game (like 4/5 patches already) and also for producing a title in a field (strategy/management) that I really, really love.
However, with that said, I'm going to have to (reluctantly) give this game a thumbs down, on one single point alone: the absoloutely atrocious balancing.
In a nutshell the game is either embarrasingly easy (if you directly control all the fights whilst spamming an AP build, even more cheesy with a shield generator in your loadout = win genuinely everything: I was 42-3 when I stopped playing and those 3 were all 'forfeits' because I was bored, endless money from winning ALL bets, and no injuries sustatined from fights so squad always fully powered) or barbarically hard (dont use a 'cheese' build/auto-resolve fights = lose everything, no money because you arent winning anything, all your guys are either critically injured or dead).
In all honesty, I dont think using a 'cheese' build would be all that bad, if the AI did the same - but it doesnt. They usually use pretty suspect tactics, never seem to employ the AP boosting adrenal stims or shields and, on a worryingly regular basis, waste 3AP of their turn using a completely irrelevant stim (ie. a melee character using a stim to buff their ranged aim) instead of attacking you.
Theres a few other minor details, but I feel bad enough with what I've said already, given that i do actually really really *really* want to like this game... if some of the above points are rectified in later patches, I'll happily change my review, but at the minute I can't really recommend the game beyond a couple of hours worth of fun whilst the novelty is still there.

This is more of a first impressions then a review as i feel that ive barely scratched the surface of this particular game.
Pillars of Eternity or PoE (its unfortunate that it shares the same anagram as path of exile but oh well.), is an Isometric cRPG, which to the uninitiated means Computer Role playing game.  Yes that’s right, there’s a genera called computer role playing games.  Back in the early 80s-late 70s when DnD was a thing, people played these pen and paper style RPGs.  CRPGs are games that are more or less recreations of that pen and paper style with graphics and a computer.  Other similar games would be the original Baldur's Gate games, Fallout 1 &2, Ice Wind Dale, and even Dragon Age: Origins (I don’t consider 2 and 3 Crpgs but thats another conversation for another day).   If you’ve played a game like what I’ve listed above then you will know what to expect from PoE, but it’s most likely that you haven’t played one of the aforementioned titles and that is why you are reading this review.
Just a quick little discussion of CRPGs before I jump into my review, CRPGs tend to be very tactical and story based games.  They tend to use real time combat systems that more or less rely on stat vs stat dice rolls that go on behind the scenes while you are playing the game, to decide many different aspects of the game, anything from whether or not you are successful climbing a wall to how much damage you do when you swing your sword.  These games tend to rely on their world building and stories and require that the person playing them be quite meticulous if they want to be able to play on the normal and higher difficulties.  The combat is real time but allows for the user to pause to issue orders to each of their individual party members before continuing and in this is where most of the strategy comes into play.
With that out of the way, PoE very accurately captures the feel of the old infinity engine games (Baldur’s gate, Ice Wind Dale, etc) while adding new unique features and using its own rule set that is familiar enough for old veterans of the genera but new enough to be interesting.  Things like the addition of a stronghold system, classes that use songs and other mechanics, the endurance/HP system and per encounter spells rather than per rest cycle make the game feel a little more modern while still preserving the feel of nostalgia that comes with those older games.
That being said the game isn’t without its flaws, for example because might is the skill that decides damage, it is actually sometimes better to stack might on your spell caster than to stack int like you would with a traditional wizard.  This feels thematically weird in some cases but honestly it can be overlooked.
I recommend this game for anyone who has played games like Baldur’s gate and really enjoyed those style of games when they played them.  I also recommend this game for people who like story driven experiences (there is a lot of text though most characters are voice acted) and who like a strategic challenge.

To be honest I wasn't expecting much.  I've played other gladiator games and so far they've ranged from disappointing to just so-so.  This one, however, turned out to be pretty darn fun.
It's not a complicated game; the most complex parts are the numbers juggling like you'd see in a straight-up regular sports game.  The combat is turn based and very straight forward, with a lot of rock/paper/scissors situations where you find yourself debating between raw damage/protection versus saving room for the game's assortment of power-up gear than can turn the battle when played right or lose it when played wrong.
It has a bit of XCOM style base-building, though nowhere near as complex, and you'll be constantly wishing that next room would
because you will need all of them sooner than you'd like.  This makes strategizing your base development a high priority, as whatever you don't pick today is going be out of reach for an uncomfortably long time.
Yet this all just adds to fun of the challenge: Keeping your team alive and your budget afloat long enough to finally start honing that edge that will make you & your team truly competitive.  A mixture of different races take the place of traditional classes, each with their own fixed special powers that make them all interesting.
Of course it's all not all glitter.  As of this writing the game has barely been out for a week, so there are bugs and a lot of things that can use more polish - in some places, a
more polish.  That being said, however, the developer has shown a shockingly high amount of interest in their product, often leading to multiple patches and updates
Think of that the next time you're looking at those month-long periods of nothing getting fixed that is the halmark of half the crap on Steam.
And in this today's market, finding a complete game (technically a sports game, no less) that isn't destined to become nothing more than a shop-front for DLC and microtransactions is enough to make me give them kudos on general principle.
Again, this isn't a "OMG5Starz" masterpiece, but it
definately far better than I was expecting considering the realitively light $20 price tag.  So it's worth the money, provided that you're into this genre of course.  If it ever goes on sale I'd even reccomend it to people who
into this genre as a good, respectable intro to it.
There could be more bells & whistles, there could be more polish (and from what I've seen that's probably in the works already), but it does what it says on the tin.  The core of this game is pretty solid and does it's job quite admirably.  Anything the developer adds later (from this writing) is all just bonus points that will likely make it worth even more than what they're actually charging.

This game is absolutely phenomenal. It is so deep and well developed. I've spent 4 hours making my first character and working through some of the quests in the first city and I can tell it's going to be a very rewarding and enjoyable game. Now, I'm very early into the game so I'll be sure to update once I develop a better understanding for the game and the mechanics. There is a lot of reading, but there is also a great deal of voice over dialog provided by the more important characters and companions. So far, the voice acting has been on point. The games music is out of this world and the 'Choose Your Own Adventure'-style cut scenes have great sound effects, like the sound of of thunder, heavy breathing or rocks falling. The writing and lore are where the game really hits home. The writers behind this game did an amazing job at creating a world and describing characters actions and emotions with words better than any Triple-A developer has ever done using animation. If you don't mind the reading and you can really get into the lore, this game is going to be one of your favorites. I'm sure it'll be one of mine. I've gone so far as to purchase the Guidebook for even more lore just so I can understand the fantastic world the people at Obsidian Entertainment have put together.
The character development and mechanics are similar to D&D. You have multiple classes ranging from wizards to barbarians and a large array of races, many of which are specific to the world developed in Pillars of Eternity. The attributes are mostly different and the class progression, traits developed and character backgrounds are all their own. In addition, there is a working character biography which develops as you unlock more and more of the story and make it further into the game. I've been holding off to see how mine has developed so far. I'm planning on checking it over once I've completed the game so I can look back and see everything my character has ever done and how he developed as a result of his actions.
The story, lore, mechanics; everything about this game is all its own. It is a gem of a game. It is easy to say that it is not for everyone. It is not exactly 'action-packed' especially compared to modern day games like Dragon Age, Fallout or Skyrim. If you've played Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale you know what it feels like. It's primarily a Roleplaying Game and a Realtime Strategy Game secondarily. Everything about this game has been developed from scratch, and even while it feels like an old-school isometric rpg, it is so much more. The game has done so many things right. It's a game all its own, and it absolutely own's it.
