(Note: Some of this may contain spoilers, and some of the issues listed may have since been remedied. This review was written somewhat shortly after release.)
Like many, I first purchased the game while it was in early access. As it were, I did the usual thing I do in games like this and established a decently-sized farm, and I came to discover two glaring issues: One, the only method of irrigation available beyond watering cans involved dumping water from above using a complex wiring system, and two, it became rather obnoxious to acquire more seeds for certain less-common plants. As such, when I came back to the game in 1.0 I preemptively installed two mods to remedy those issues. One to make watering cans much easier to use, and one to make seeds craftable from produce. However, I was pleasantly surprised when I discovered that you can craft sprinkler systems using the upgraded foraging table. They water a huge area around them with the only cost being the materials required to make them. In addition, once I got into colony building I realized that tenants sometimes pay their rent with seeds from the planet type they inhabit. So, essentially those issues are now null and void.
Now onto my issues with the current game build. While I like the concept of food rotting (thus, giving you a hurdle to get past in the form of acquiring a fridge), I feel the system would benefit by being a tad bit more descriptive than "This should last a good while." In the base game there's no clear indication as to how long something ACTUALLY lasts (which is why I installed a mod that tells you the exact time in hours and minutes before a piece of food rots). Additionally, it's quite cumbersome that perishable foods no longer stack. Design-wise, it makes sense in that two carrots with different levels of decay have different data values, but I think Don't Starve handles that very well. Just average the decay levels of the foods when they get stacked together.
And finally from out of the blue, my third issue with the game as it stands is that there's still hardly anything concerning the Novakids. I think they're mentioned in a codex somewhere and there's one Novakid colonist available, that's about it. I heard somewhere that their lack of prescence is "important to the story," but I played through the story. They ain't mentioned nowhere. Granted, it's stated that they are somewhat nomadic and never write down their history for lack of attention span, but you'd only know that if you read the wiki page. I feel that the prescence of the internet is no excuse to leave out important information from the actual game.
Issues aside, I still love the game, and would highly reccomend it for anyone who likes to explore, build, farm, or any combination of the three. I suppose the purpose behind most of this review is to state that while the game still has flaws (in my opinion), they've fixed my past gripes and are still working on improving the game today. As such, I predict that it'll just get better from here.

To say that Singularity wears its inspiration on its sleeve is to put it very lightly. The game is almost shamelessly derivative, taking the both the style and character building of BioShock, the gravity gun from Half-Life 2, and throwing in a few nods to F.E.A.R. However, this mish-mash of other games' ideas is by no means a bad thing. If anything, Singularity manages to almost play as a "best of" collection of FPS trappings, the ultimate compilation of cool gimmicks and toys seen in the genre over the past five years.

It's taken roughly 3 years, but 1.0's finally here.
Is it the ultimate successor to Terraria? No, absolutely not. That said, this game is still fun in its own right. The various atmospheres make exploration more developed, there are lots of crafting options, lots of decoration options, and randomized loot to find. Mini missions can be given by planet inhabitants to get random rewards, a nice even if little addition. I also liked upgrading the ship and my matter manipulator, and both gave a somewhat fresh feel.
It's nice to have a story and hubworld associated with this game, but it doesn't really leave much of an impact and exists just to give somewhat of a purpose to exploration. I also liked where they were going with the techs early on, but now in 1.0 I feel they're very limited and not as fun to use/unlock.
Equipment progression is a bit linear and you don't really feel that much stronger when you reach the final tier of equipment (which won't take long). Plus towards the endgame, it's practically required. The combat isn't too exciting either, in my opinion.
Overall, while it's certainly not the game imagined when it came out in 2013, it still offers a good amount of fun and is worth at least checking out. I hope future updates expand on the game's potential.

I rate Command and Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath 4/5. Good.
This tactical game (an add-on for Command and Conquer 3) is still extremely difficult but nearly every overly frustrating, unfair or buggy aspect of the original game has been fixed and the new additions of this add-on fit right in. Better than the original in every way, Kane's Wrath is one of the most fun tactical games I have ever played.
The various sides are well-balanced against each other and each side has 3 variants. Each variant which all plays differently while no side has a clear superiority (though the Scrin are still quite a bit over-powerful but their confusing, extremely alien units help make up for their slightly overpowered nature, at least initially). The main campaign is potentially easy (if you play on easy) and has an interesting (though often confusing and disjointed) plot which pretty much requires you to be a fan of the franchise to understand what is going on (but understanding the overall plot is not necessary so far as winning the game is concerned). Skirmish mode really shines with lots of maps and ways to play each battle. The Risk-styled Global Conquest mode is somewhat fun (but is probably the weakest link in this add-on) and feels tacked on to the rest of the game. Global Conquest often involves extremely one-sided tactical battles (one way or another) throughout. Global Conquest mode also does not allow you to use units which you created during one battle in any other battle but the global-domination standpoint of this mode is quite entertaining (but becomes repetitive after 40+ turns).

There is nothing more satisfying than lopping the head off your enemies, or the sound of  a spear taking them them to the grave. This game reminds me of the single player game Final Fantasy Tactics for playstation, which was a lot of fun. This game however is not single player. It's also a collectible card game like Hearthstone. The mechanics of the game however are closer to those of Magic: The Gathering.
Events==Spells
Creatures==Minions
Haste==Charge
Gift==Battlecry
Last Words==Deathrattle
Gods==Heroes
Orb==Face
Faeria==Mana
Lands==Locations for creatures to inhabit.
Wells==Resource nodes for collecting faeria.
The game board is 37 tiles in total, 2 are god orbs, 4 are Faeria Wells. The rest of the 31 tiles start out as sea tiles and are owned by neither player. You get a power wheel as a 'god' and can use it once per turn to generate land over the sea. The 5 types of land are basic(usually called plains or prairies I think), lakes, deserts, forests, and mountains. Plains are not special, meaning you can play 2 of them in a turn instead of just 1. Positioning is important when attempting to play lands, and you cannot convert lands with just the power wheel, except in the case of converting your own basic lands into special lands, but that will use up your only power wheel option that turn. Alternative power wheel options are draw 1 card, and gain 1 faeria.
Every non-neutral card in this game has both a faeria cost and a secondary requirement to play it. I don't know if they made a technical term for it yet, but there's a number below the faeria cost and it indicates the number of lands you need to have to summon it. Fortunately, lands don't deplete for the turn when playing cards, unlike mana crystals, so if you have 2 forests for example, you can play all the cards in your hand that require 2 forests as long as you haven't run out of faeria yet. Your faeria doesn't deplete and restore to maximum from turn to turn like mana crystals do, and you gain 3 faeria passively at the start of your turn, from your god or your orb? Difficult to say.
There are neutral, green, blue, red, and yellow cards. They can all mingle together in a deck if you desire.
Compared to Hearthstone:
Same sized decks, same rarity names and legendary cards may include events in addition to creatures. The other rarity cards you can have up to 3 of in your deck rather than just 2. This definitely makes epic and rare cards feel more valuable, since you can increase their consistency of drawing with more copies, while still making legendary cards feel special.
Creature information:
Haste is a keyword that allows a creature bearing it to nullify 'summoning sickness' and move, attack, and collect faeria on the turn they are played.
Dash is a keyword with a number attached that allows a creature to immediately move that number of spaces in a straight line when being played from hand.
Taunt is a keyword that prevents adjacent enemy creatures from being able to move or attack other creatures or structures that are not in fact bearing the taunt keyword. Certain events can override taunt by moving lands or creatures.
Charge is a keyword with a number attached that allows a creature to move that number of spaces in a straight line before attacking.
Jump is a keyword that allows a creature to move 2 spaces instead of one. It also lets them go over lands already occupied by a creature or structure.
Flying is a keyword that allows a creature to move over any tile not already occupied.
Aquatic is a keyword that allows a creature to move over the sea and lakes, but prohibits them from being on any other sort of tile.
Ranged is a keyword that allows a creature to attack a target in a straight line of sight from a distance, but prohibits them from moving on the same turn.
The single player content is partially free. It seems to be the primary way to earn a colection for new players, aside from playing a lot of games. Doesn't seem to provide very much for free, but it's better than nothing.
The ratio of disenchant to craft for each rarity type except for common is 0.25 to 1, just like in Hearthstone. Common takes a larger penalty, at 0.2 to 1. Still not as bad as Hearthstone's 0.125 to 1.
Mythic cards in this game are the same as golden cards in Hearthstone, except they are flowery-looking rather than class-color purging and animated. And if you like disenchanting the fancy cards, there's good news. The mythic-disenchant-to-craft-regular-version ratios are all(except for common) found to be 1.25 to 1, rather than the 1 to 1 in Hearthstone. And for commons, it's 2 to 1 rather than 1.25 to 1.
At first I thought you needed 3 legendary cards to be competitive in this game, but I realized you can only have 1 of a certain legendary in your deck. I haven't analyzed all the rarity data available yet, there's a lot of data to consume, but at the moment it looks like it isn't quite as difficult as I first thought to make a deck for this game.

While I do feel a couple of the story missions felt lacking overall that complaint makes no sense. The massive varriety of activities, objects, biomes, and materials makes the game well worth playing for any newcomers. To anyone who says the game is abbandoned now that it's launched - new content is still being added. The universe is expanding even if grouches want to pretend its not.
The main story arch is lacking, and I think the balancing they did to the procedural generation to help with story progression negetivly impacted the game, but it's still worth playing through.
A lot of early access games these days don't come through, they get forgotten or fail before they reach their goals. But starbound is a promise that's been fullfilled and is still growing today.

Paranormal sci-fi horror with temporal-weaponry. 2nd playthrough. Definitely worth playing again. Story revolves around a newly discovered (ficticious) element, e99, and the island Katorga-12 where it is exclusively found. E99 holds enormous energetic potential, but is unstable, mutates organic life, and distorts time where it abounds. You are a captain in the u.s. military sent to the island; thought abandoned, to investigate an energy signature which is blinding u.s. spy satelittes. Upon arriving, a temporal wake engulfs you, sending you back in time to 1955. There you find yourself in the same lab facility as it burns. Without hesitation, you rescue a scientist, Demichev. Only before a 2nd temporal wake brings you back to 2010. Demichev was one of two lead scientists heading research into the element and its application. He will continue recklessly pursuing his controversial research without regard for life. His research results in the development and collapse of the singularity, it kills 1000s instantly and mutates any remaning survivors on the island. The result is a paranormal, atemporal mess, torn by violence. Failing to be disuaded, Demichev develops e99 weaponry and quickly rises to power, empowering Russia to conquer the world. The game is primarily about restoring the timeline, but throughout the game you encounter cryptic warnings, written in messages only you can reveal. Perhaps left by a future-you? or by MIR-12? A mysterious organization with knowlecge they couldn't possibly posess, and whose intentions are unclear. As far as enemies, the mutant survivors of the island, warped by the energy of singularity collapse are almost alien. They move incredibly fast, in and out of phase, or can teleport. Others have heightened hearing, but are blind. Still others have become incredibly large. Temporal rifts frequent the game where you can witness events in the past occuring concurrently with the present; revealing the tragic deaths of the inhabitants. Recordings also build this story and reveal what happened in the time since you traveled to 1955. Mostly detailing the exodus of survivors and their horrific deaths attempting to leave. Weapons are also e99 based. Guided rounds, sniper that can slow down time for precise shots, and standard-shooter semi-auto shotgun, assault rifle, and minigun. The most fun is with your TMD, a device you are led to early in the game which embues you with great power. You can create time manipulation fields that age/rejuvenate items or people/mutants, timelocks which freeze time, you can pull things between time-periods, and jump between the years 1955 and 2010. Futher more, you can unleash a blast of energy from your palm that will send enemies flying or will rip them apart. Graphics were out of date even for it's time, but it's just bloody fun to play. And the story line is eery, but enjoyable. Short, but worth your attention, especially if you're into paranormal or sci-fi horror games. Fans of the metro or STALKER series would enjoy, although the feel is much more arcade.

Dev's, you guys are sitting on gold.
I'm a fan of games like Escape Velocity the original, and it's sequal, EV Nova. I also love FTL and other space related games so I might be a tad biased. This game is different than those but somehow retains a similar addiction~  I also like pixel art, customization, and exploration. I just feel like this game has a really great feel.
I did not expect there to be much to do in it's early access state. But seeing where the Dev's are in the development process and seeing how much crafting and customizing there is/will be has got me excited to say the least!
You start in a little tiny pixelated spacecraft in a star system next to a space station. You can zoom in and out and open up a menu for your ship and stations. You mine asteroids and pick up ore's and craft new items/kit's ect. Your ship can take damage and be repaired. You can warp to other star systems and mine more exotic planets and asteroids as well as explore other wrecked ships and destroyed space stations to collect their goodies!
There is already tons of crafting objects in the menu but no fear you can check a box to show only the itmes you are able to craft. You can add remove/upgrade parts from your ships and stations. Your starting ship called the "Venture" does not have much cargo space, so you may find yourself storing things on your home station which you can frequent anytime to drop off or pick up items. Once you have collected/explored enough content you will start to upgrade lasers to mine faster or possibly purchase/build a new and better ship.
It is possible to generate systems for new games using seeds similar to the way it worked in minecraft. Some have called this terraria in space and I can see the relation but this game feels very unique in it's own right.
The game is composed of tiles so customization and modding should be avaiable and simple for most everyone making future options and new content limitless~
Core mechanics seem solid and as I am writing this I am looking forward to diving back in.

Singularity. Singularity. You know, this is what some people described this game: 'Half-Life combined with Bioshock'. Is that right, or wrong? Well, half right, half wrong. While you do feel like you are playing that kind of game, it's not that kind of game at all. And I will explain every one bit why this game does not deserve a 7/10, an 8/10, or a unbelievable 9/10.
First off, the game does not have a memorable story. You play as this army guy- yeah, how original. Anyway, you are at this weird Russian island where this new powerful and rare element called the 'E-99' was found, and the Soviet Union was planning to use this against the USA, when something went horribly wrong.
In the first hour, you actually feel like you are in this dangerous place where something really went wrong, and you need to find out why. But the game quickly tells you everything about the plot in the first 4 hours, and the only momorable thing is the characters, and a good plot twist at the end.
Speaking of characters, this game's 'characters' are not great at all. At least Half-Life didn't have a lot of major characters, it was all just Gordon, and Bioshock had a lot of great characters, while this game doesn't have any of those. There's this heroine character which is so blend I wanted to smack her in the face because she did not have any point to the plot except for her first appearance.
There's also this scientist guy who looked to be kind at first, but he goes beyond and becomes kind of crazy at the end. And there's the antagonist, which is... well, he's bad and he has a scar. That's about it. He also tries to take over the world but- (OF COURSE!) Okay, I'll stop with the characters now.
The story itself? It's not too bad. It makes sense at best, but it takes away immersion once the Russian soldiers start attacking you, and the monsters become so easy, drawing you away from this atmosphere of 'a island where something went horribly wrong'.
The gameplay is great. It's the only thing worth anything in this game. This device- the TMD, short for Time Manipulation Device, can do so much fun stuff like making people older, making objects newer, a energy blast, or telekinesis powers. It was so fun trying out this powers, and since the gun play is very average, you start wanting to use more of this powers, rather then the guns, which is not a good gameplay design.
You can never beat Bioshock using the plasmids majority of the time, you use them so you can kill people more easily, not to kill people. Well, some of them can, but you still use the guns or the wrench majority of the time.
Still though, you can have fun with it, so it is kinda good in my book. But still, it does not makes this game a great game.
This game deserves a maximum of 6/10. It's above average, I still have to say that it's better then most of the modern CoD games, but it's not a great game in the slightest. I can't decide if it's a 'good' game or not, but even if it was obvious that the game was good, I would still have given the game 6/10 because the price tag is too high- 30$ for this game? Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath is actually an expansion pack for Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars, which I haven’t covered yet, and played these in the wrong order; that being said, I can still give a review on this game as an individual release.
Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath was released in early 2008 before actually being released on the 360 console if you can believe it. This is the first C&C game I have played since Generals in 2003. This game takes place between the time of Tiberian Sun and the start of Tiberium Wars plot wise, so if you want to play the games chronologically, start with this one before Wars.
The single player campaign has 13 levels which are divided up into three different sub-stories which follow Kane’s plot.  In all good C&C fashion, there are two types of missions, base building missions and more stealth operation missions. The base building missions can normally be completed by overrunning your enemy with your army of tanks an d troops, and just play the numbers game. There is a good amount of buildings to use, but there are only handfuls which actually have some real use in terms of game play. If  you want to be playing this game optimally, there are really only 4 or 5 buildings you’ll be using.  The second type of mission which gives you control of a smaller force of units, meaning you have to use an element of either stealth or well planned attacks in order to complete objectives. These missions are the hardest, but they present the greatest amount of fun in this title.  They really do give you a serious element of strategy and planning which is what you would expect to see from a C&C game.
This game is eight years old now, and whilst none of the C&C games ever had super amazing graphics, some may be put off by the graphically old style to this game. There are some low texture qualities to be seen in abundance,  but you really only see these if you are zoomed as far in as you can go, and you will hardly ever want to do this as you are overseeing the whole battlefield anyway.  The game is fully voice acted and has very well made cut scenes in between levels which have live action taking place, with some celebrity cast members such as Joseph Kucan returning as Kane, Carl Lumbly, and Canadian actress and fashion model, Natasha Henstridge
The base building missions are really quite ease – like I said you can just use the numbers game against the opponents and overrun them with a huge army. Where the game challenges is the other missions. The game can be played on varying levels of difficulty so you can tailor it to how much of a threat you want your adversaries to cause you.
All of the thirteen missions come with their main objective, along with optional objectives for you to complete. Completing these bear no real game play bonus’ apart from a higher rank at the end of the mission, what they do offer you is a greater knowledge of the lore and plot going on behind the scenes, so fans of the series should definitely be taking the time to read through the extra bits of story you get.
The game took me just about fifteen hours to finish; I am very happy with that length of time for a RTS game like this, and it matches the full price tag quite fairly too. The multiplayer scene is fairly dead on this game as the official servers were taken offline, so it’s only a single player experience from now on. The game has a few other game modes which include a Risk style game, and of course, just general skirmishes against the AI, all of which add to the replay ability of this game.
The only major technical issue I had whilst playing, was that I could not get the game to run in 4k resolutions. Whilst it is an option in the menu, the game will crash when trying to select it. 1080p works fine and runs at over 60 FPS all of the time when maxed out.  Keyboard and mouse is an absolute must whilst playing too; even though the game was released on xbox360, the controller doesn’t work on the PC title for some reason?
In conclusion, Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath is a quality C&C release, whilst it may not be as fully polished as the previous games in the series, it still has some really stellar gameplay and an interesting plot. The price tag of £9,99 is right on point as well. You cannot go wrong with picking this game up now.

So I'm about three hours in now, and actually having a lot of fun. Its not as deep as I hoped, but still a really solid squad manager for a detail orient statistic loving player.
As for gameplay, it took me a few tries to get a decent start going, but on the fifth try I got it right. I am now "Rotwound," a rather arachnoid ex-fighter. Gonna say, not too fond of the gladiator stylization, but whatever, pushing on. Rotwound opened the game by hiring a vorcinne (the hairless spider dude, 'cause there's also a spider yeti, yeeeah) scout who can hire other spider dudes at the beginning. The scout found a couple ok fighters, but most importantly Slowsin (the spiderdudes have rather menacing portmanteaus as names) who is an excellent melee fighter with loads of damage and accuracy, but not much hp. Slowsin is given an axe and medium armor and an adrenal booster, and sent out to fight. This he does with great joy and abandon. Fairly quickly "Slowsin" racks up ten kills, and is renamed "Executioner," for reasons "Rules and Guidelines" does not let me make a joke about. Executioner has now led Rotwound's gladiator asteroid team of spider dudes to 14-0 victories and speicializations in axes, medium armor, and adrenal boosters. The old spiderdude scout found another few badass spiderdudes, and then went to recruit what are apparently constipated trolls. He found a very scary constipated troll, who is now training to be more scary. This brings the story of Rotwound and Executioner to day 90, at which point they have not lost a gladiator, fight, or limb, because apparently Rotwound can live up to his name 'casue amputations are a thing. I think. There's something about cybernetics later on. Gonna keep updating this as I play for while.

And it looks like it could be, there are numerous base upgrades that sound a bit crazy, and I haven't even gotten into research. Gonna recommend it right now because I've had a fun night (yes, rules and guidelines). Also gonna update my review as I continue to play, so I apologize if I recommend something terrible because of my unnatural enjoyment of spreadsheets right now.

Not typically too much of a politically correct person, I mean I'm thrilled when a game gives me the option to sacrifice virgins to demons, but the whole "gladiator" thing feels unnecessary. Few days later-
Still enjoying it. Started a second game with a ant dude called Oda. He started with a team of expert ant dude swordsmen using forcefields. Tanky units. Oda ended up with two real master swordsmen, Miyamoto and Kenzai, who were eventually backed by a troll sniper called Frank. While Evil Maze isn't really a bad game, it isn't that great either. It's a generic grid-based action RPG with a sketchy English translation.
The gameplay is basic RPGMaker action RPG, with pretty weak feedback in terms of receiving damage from enemies, making it seem like just their bad mojo is enough to make you hurt. At the start you are very liable to die, but this quickly reverses once you start finding equipment, at which point there's rarely a threat big enough to make you care. Just make sure you don't softlock yourself in the second level by unlocking the wrong doors.
As far as the graphics, sound and music are concerned, I'm pretty sure everything in the game uses stock RPGMaker assets, excluding probably the main character (and the "CGs"), but I wouldn't know. Oh, and the "lewd factor" of the game is absolutely not worth the money, if that's what you're looking for. You could literally just download the official patches to get the images without bothering to play.
The game is very RNG-heavy, including things like damage dealt/received and spells learned from scrolls, et cetera, which might make some people want to savescum (especially learning spells, as useless as they are).
The DLC is worth even less than the base game, yet paired together they cost triple the base cost of the game.
Unless you're a crazy game collector, there's no reason to get this game, even as a joke of some kind.

Excellent turn-based tactical game.
-The AI is great and feels like it's living and thinking.
-The writing is enjoyable and invests you even more in your grunts and makes it more agonizing when they inevitably die.
-Difficulty balance is fantastic; expect lots of challenge and game overs, and for campaigns to go very well only for sudden misteps to have disasterous consequences.
-Balance and mechanics make having to decide when to retreat from battles another interesting (and even fun) tactical decision to agonize over.
-Hit chance percentages appear accurate (which I would have expected would be a given until 2K's XCOM), tactics prevail over RNG and good play will mitigate the impact of random chance messing over the player but bad play is punished immediately and severely.
-DIfferent enemies require not just different tactics, but also different optimal weapons loadouts (often you can anticipate this and switch things up ahead of time), adding more depth and variety to combat.
-It feels both more difficult and yet much more fair than most turn-based tactics games.

After nearly 90 hours of playing, I've got to update/upgrade my review.
This game has some serious potencial if the creators wish to do something with it, e.g. adding a real story, adding more late game content (Elves anyone?), making Magic somewhat more diverse than just "Mind control! Fear! Entangle!"
But that is just nitpicking, really. It's a great game. You start out with your Farmers, Rat Catchers, Fishermen, Cultists and Ne'er-do-wells and level them to the most Badass Warriors Ever, who take on hordes of undead, giant orks, the big Lindwurm, terrifying Geists and really ugly Nachzehrers.
Gameplay's a bit repetitive, go there, kill things, get reward, but the spirit really reminds one of those nice skirmish-based tabletops or X-COM and Mordheim and the likes: Build up your team, customize them, train them, equip them, get attached to them and their little flaws and merits- and then cry havoc, as they die from one random crossbow-bolt in the big battle of a noble house or get a one-hit-crit from some big green monster.
16/10, blood for the blood god.

Let me start off by saying I would definitely recommend this game and that you should definitely try it because it is a really good game. You don't even have to read the rest of this review, just go back up and buy it. But continuing on with the actual review, like I said, it is a really good game.
The combat initially starts off quite slow but as you progress and earn new weapons and fight harder enemies, the combat becomes a lot faster and more intense. It is a normal top-down hack and slash but with less hacking and slashing and more dodge-rolling and poking when you have a gap. For the length of the game, there are a decent amount of weapons and all of them have a decent amount of upgrades.
The main drawing point of the game, I would say, is the story. The game plays out with the narrator describing your every move and slowly the story unfolds. The story itself, is really interesting and enjoyable and the ending is both heartwarming and heartbreaking, depending on how you view life. But all in all, the story is really good and definitely worth paying attention to.
Finally, the actual design of the game is fantastic. The soundtrack is fitting and the art style is unique and beautiful.
So like I said at the beginning of this review, go and buy this game. It is definitely a game that is worth your time.

This game is very immersive and uses intuitive mechanics. Forming words to deal with your situation is very fun and the amount of thought behind how and what you use the words for keeps me very much intertained. The adventure is fun and pulls you in with great aestetics, but be warned it is not very long (for me it took 4 hours to beat it). They do have some minigames on the side that are entertaining at first but quickly lose their luster. This game is a good example of doing one thing amazing and stopping the game, albeit a little early, for the sack of avoiding the feeling of being repetitive. If the length doesn't turn you away from this game then it is definitley for you.

The Good:
The setting (abandoned Soviet Military research base, what's not to like?)
The Plot (although it's a bit patchy in places there are some genuine scares to be had but they may be underwhelming for some people)
The atmosphere (you do genuinely feel creeped out reading through the diary entries and audio logs of what happened before you arrived and seeing 'flashbacks')
Some of the more sophisticated weapons (like the rifle which allows you to steer your explosive bullets straight into enemies)
The powers and time travel work really well and are easy to use without feeling like a gimicky add on
The Bad:
The puzzles (there's about 3 basic types which just get repeated over and over and which mostly rely on you spotting the EXACT piece of rusty metal you need in a room full of bits of random rusty metal)
The enemies (the AI is really dumb and the difficulty just gets ramped up through the game by increasing their health and making some enemies immune to some of your abilities)
The difficulty (it's a really easy game to finish and the higher difficulty ratings don't change things much since I've already completed 2 separate playthroughs taking my time to explore everywhere)
The Meh:
Other than the 'exotic' weapons you've got the bog standard FPS arsenal (i.e. pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, rocket launcher and grenade launcher)
The Boss battles (by and large the bosses are just bullet sponge versions of the normal enemies with some form of highlighted weakspot that may as well just be a sign saying 'shoot here')
The Graphics are pretty good for a game this old (I suppose they would have been better when it was first released, but they're starting to show their age)
Overall verdict:
A solid and pretty good but (understandably) underrated FPS, but not quite worth paying full price for. My advice is (unless you REALLY REALLY want it) wait for it come on sale and grab it.

It's a decent game, but it has a lot of technical problems and is missing some key features. If you liked Half Life 2, Bioshock and Timeshift, but for some reason don't want to play them again, you could buy Singularity. I would say it's not a good game, but a fun game. 4/10.
Let's start with the bad. There are no subtitles. Just none, at all. Considering there are usually a lot of sounds and music in the background, and all characters speak with a Russian accent, this is a gigantic problem. Also, it's just rediculous for a game from 2010 to not have subtitles.
The second problem are the options. There barely are any graphical options, and even less for audio options. The lack of the latter makes the subtitle problem even worse; you can't just lower the SFX or Music so you would hear the voices better.
The graphical options might be a result from a (bad) port. Another minor result of this might be a problem with the controls. In the beginning of the game, you can use a melee attack. However, at some point you get a new power, which is binded to the melee key, and from this moment you can no longer use your melee attack. My guess would be that it's because it was the same button on console, they made it the same button on PC as well. This sucks, since the new power you get on that button is vastly inferior to your regular melee attack.
Another control-related problem is the Use/Reload key. For some reason, they put both on the same key, and you can't change that. That means that you either don't have E as Use key, or the R as Reload. You get used to this quickly, but there is still no reason for this to be inconvienent.
The graphical options are bad, and possibly as a result, so are the actual graphics. The style is OK, but the texture quality is decent for the best objects, and it's terrible for some. There are some other problems that bothered me in the beginning, but I got used to fairly quick One of them was animations that would get interrupted by other animations, making it look rediculous. For instance, the recoil animation on your pistol is actually longer than the minimum time between shots, resulting the in recoiling animation ending halfway to display the shooting animation. They either should have made the animations as long as the action that they belong to, or they should have made them go over in eachother better.
Another graphical problem is a minor problem with a specific weapon: You are sort of invisible. There is a special weapon that lets you guide a bullet, and it uses a bulled-mounted camera to do so. If you turn the bullet 180 degrees, and look at the position that your character is standing, there is nothing there. Nothing at all. In the meantime, your enemies do see you and keep firing at you. This looks rather rediculous; the enemies fire at thin air...
That were most of the big complaints. It's quite a list, and it's the reason I would never call this a good game. I did however finish the game, and most of the time spent I enjoyed myself. That means there must some redeeming qualies.
Actually, there is one. The gunplay. It's a shooter, and in the end the most important part is the combat. Which is very enjoyable. There are quite some weapons and they vary greatly. That is, however the only good part, and it's still not perfect. There are many weapons, but I used most of them only for a little while, before realizing it's vastly inferior to my main weapon: the Shotgun. It's so strong that it kills almost all enemies in one shot. With your sprint you are fast enough to avoid most damage, get up close, and one-hit them. This is fun, but it also means that it's not possible without thinking "This is so much weaker than the Shotgun" on most other weapons. The only other 2 weapons that I used sometimes were the Sniper and the Minigun, both to deal with enemies from afar.
Apart from the gunplay, there's not much to the gameplay. You can use Time-powers in combat, but it's pointless. Depending on the enemy, it's either a useless slow, or an instant kill, and even if it's an instant kill it costs a ton of energy (you can only do this twice in a row, three with upgrades I guess), while you could also just use your shotgun for the same effect. I never had any ammo problems while I did have energy problems, and this is while I always used guns and very rarely the energy powers.
The story is enjoyable, but predictable and full of plotholes and half-explained events. For instance, there are some occasions that you change things in the past that change the future (in big and small ways). The problem is that all characters seem to know this while there is no way they could know. The explanation they give has to do with leaving notes, but it makes no sense, and it would imply that everyone believes something because it's written on a wall somewhere. Another big problem with the story is a spoiler for the ending, so skip it if you want to.
That were just some examples of mistakes in the story, and overall I would say this makes the story very forgettable.
There are some more problems related to both story and gameplay. The first is the Time-Slow thing you can do while zoomed in with the Sniper. It's quite fun, but for some reason you can use this before you character ever comes in contact with Time-altering powers. It is a real Time power, and not just holding your breath or something, since it's called something like Time Dialation. There is no explanation given for this, whatsoever.
The last thing I want to point out is the pointless use of the time altering power on objects. You can make objects yourger and older, which is used for puzzles and hidden areas. It's quite fun, but you can also use it on ammo chests, audio logs and stairs, in which case it's often just pointless waiting. If you find an audio log, instead of just listening to it, you have to repair it by making it new again (i.e. press the Q button) and wait for the animation. The same with ammo chests, and stairs; you just have to wait a second before you can use the object. The idea is fun, but if you have to wait a second before using any object it's just tedious and annoying.
So overall, there's not much to this game. Nothing is exceptional, and the fun part (the shooting) get's harder to enjoy because of missing features and technical problems. In general, I think a 2010 game by Raven, published by Activision should have been much better, and it's just unacceptable to not have subtitles in this day and age. The concept was OK, and if they put a bit more time and effort in, I think it could be a very good shooter. Alas, now it's just a below-mediocore shooter. The only reason to buy this would be if all the things below are true:
1. It's on sale for $5 or less.
2. You really liked Half Life 2, but have no desire to play it again.
3. You really liked Bioshock, but have no desire to play it again.
4. You really liked Timeshift, but have no desire to play it again.
5. You don't like to listen to music while playing games (since if you do you won't hear a word from the story)
6. You know you can get over major and minor problems in graphics, contols, and desing for the sake of enjoyable shooting.

Singularity is one of those hidden gems that seem to only attract its real fans long after its demise and relegation to the scrap heap. Don't misunderstand that as the game being bad, because it most certainly is not. Singularity is everything that used to be fun in the FPS genre, before mainstreaming took it over. Essentially, Singularity is a popcorn shooter with fluid non-stop combat, lots of enemies, a great story, a lengthy singleplayer campaign and a neat RPG-lite character building system that borrows from System Shock/Bioshock without completely ripping them off.
Your average shooter fan won't like Singularity since it speaks more to the 90s gamers out there, so be warned if you're expecting something modern. That being said, If you want a solid FPS with a clever gimmick, an entertaining story and some great level design....here you go. Thank me later.

I really don't play much in the "brawler" category, but from the little I've seen, Monolith really did their homework. "Shadow Of Mordor" only has one gameplay loop, when it really comes down to it. Sure, there's a stealth "subloop" that you can get into, but in the end, the game always comes down to how you enter and exit a chain of dispatching orcs in up-close combat.
Monolith got that experience extremely "right," mostly by way of their skill progression system. There's an almost magical balance between the combat remaining an interesting challenge while Talion grows more and more powerful. In my playthrough, things got noticeably easier as time went on, but it never got too easy or too rote. There are a lot of skills that you can weave together for maximum benefit, and "Shadow" is pretty decent at rewarding mastery, at least in the immediate sense.
The downside of all that Talion can do is that the game sometimes struggles to figure out what you want. It never became a scourge, but there were still plenty of instances where Talion wouldn't, say, climb up a wall, because the combat system was telling him that "spacebar" meant "dodge" when I wanted "climb." In that same vein, I was sometimes a little perplexed about what Talion would and would not tackle vertically - some walls that clearly looked like giant collections of handholds actually weren't, apparently. (This is a bit jarring when your super-rad wraith-ranger can climb almost anything, but then arbitrarily says, "Nope, can't climb that thing which looks like it would incredibly easy. Sorry.")
The "Nemesis" System is an interesting idea that does play well, but it has a couple of problems.
First, as it turns out, there's only so much actual meat on that bone. At first, the constantly self-replacing cast of procedurally-generated baddies is pretty nifty. Later on, though, you start to shrug your shoulders as you realize that what you're doing isn't having any real, permanent effect on what's going on. At some point, when you're highly (or totally) upgraded and have all the runes you want, hammering away at one more Uruk Captain doesn't mean anything.
Second, the Nemesis System has a noticeable penchant for cooking up opponents who are actually tougher than high-level story encounters. There were some regular captains that emerged that caused me far more trouble than Sauron's Black Captains, the supposed terrors of Mordor. (They're actually rather a gang of pushovers, if you ask me.) Once you've faced a high-damage, quick-firing, ranged-attack orc who's immune to all regular damage, a big bad who hits hard (but slowly) and is taken down by moves that are easy to pull off is a bit of a let-down.
...and the ending isn't much of a payoff. I don't want to spoil it, but I will say it's abrupt and offers almost nothing in the way of closure. It's sort of reminiscent of "Mass Effect 3," where you get this nagging feeling that the developer ran out of money, time, and ideas when it was time to actually plonk a climactic capstone on their experience. Story-wise, Monolith does a nice job with giving you collectibles that trickle juicy bits of lore down to you, but I found myself wishing that the various characters would have gotten more "airtime" instead.

Cyto is a well thought-off Indie puzzle game in an attractive and colourful setting. It was developed by the Ukrainian studio Room 8 and succeeds admirably in what it sets out to do: to provide no-nonsense, casual gameplay. The core gameplay is built around a more than decent physics engine that allows for puzzles of gradually increasing difficulty. By carefully adding new gameplay elements, the developers kept my interest for quite some time, and the above average, colourful graphics help a lot to provide quite some hours of carefree entertainment.
There is even a story behind it all: you play as Cyto, who has lost his/her memory and needs to collect snippets of memory during a voyage through space and several worlds/universes. By collecting these snippets, more and more levels and worlds are unlocked, as are parts of the - basic - storyline. In some ways, Cyto reminded me of World of Goo: there too, one basic but flexible physics-element provided some quite interesting challanges. Cyto is generally less hardcore and more forgiving: the puzzles get seldomly really difficult, and there is always the option to skip a certain level. This grants the game a more casual character, as does the relaxing and very appropriate music.
Mission accomplished - Cyto comes with Steam trading cards, but misses achievements which could have been easily implemented into this kind of game.
Overall score: 8/10

Battle Brothers is definitely one of my favorite games in my library.  Highly recommended!  If I could give more than just a thumbs up, I would.  I think it's fair to say, however, that it's not for everyone, for a few reasons.  But I'll start with the positive first and why I think you should definitely purchase Battle Brothers (especially while it's on sale!).  My reviews tend to be lengthy so....TL;DR, buy it if you're into turn based strategy.  But expect a hard journey.
For starters, the atmosphere of the game is really cool.  It does a really nice job of plopping you down into the gameworld, and from the very beginning, literally everything you do is up to you.  The music certainly adds to the atmosphere and is exceptionally well tailored to the game.  While I think all of the music is really good, I think some of the combat music really shines.  Some of the ambient presence in the game, like when you're in town, is a nice touch, although a bit repetitive at times.
The gameplay is awesome.  I've read some reviews that describe it as being repetitive after a while.  While this is true to a degree, I also feel that you kind of get out of it what you put into it.  In my current playthrough, I've almost completed a full year in-game.  It truly feels like my company is a crew of hardened, grizzled veterans.  One of my best members is missing his nose, has permanent brain damage and is almost always last to act in battle, but he hits like a truck and seems to survive the worst anyone can throw at him at this point.  A few others have been with the company since the beginning or very early on, and then there are some less seasoned fighters to fill the gaps that were left in losing some of my best members.  What I'm getting at is that you've got to have some interest in your crew, be invested in their personal story.  If you can't immerse your own imagination into the world of Battle Brothers, you will likely be one of those people who just sees it as being repetitive after a while.
Combat mechanics are really well executed.  I've seen numerous complaints whining about RNG and how it's "too hard".  It's supposed to be hard.  If you're just playing to always win and never lose anyone, you're playing the wrong game.  It doesn't hold your hand.  If you send a level 5 member with medium armor and a spear against an orc warrior, don't be surprised if you lose him.  That's not a fault of RNG as much as it is a lack of judgement.  The game is well balanced but hinges greatly on your ability to make good decisions.  Once you understand how to leverage things like morale, different weapon types/combinations, perks, etc. in your favor, the playing field starts to change.  Also it helps to realize that you have to approach a battle against orcs differently than a battle with the undead.  You could sum all this up in a single word:
.  The more negative reviews I see that complain about RNG, the more I start to feel that a number of those negative reviews were by people who don't want to put much thought into the things I just mentioned.
I feel that the late game crises deserve a mention too.  For those of you who just have to have an ending in a sandbox game, the late game crises are your ticket.  There are three of them, and they can change the map permanently (i.e. losing a settlement), and add some interesting events to the game.  At this point, I've completed all three, and I still continue to play, but after each one, you are given the option of retiring.  You can make a lot of gold doing quests during the different events, especially during the Noble Wars, and even more so if you've done a nice job getting your reknown up.  Also, the different random events that can happen at any time add a lot of flavor to the game.  The devs clearly put a lot of thought and imagination into these, and with over 100 hours of game time, I still have been running into events that are new to me.
Okay, call me a fanboy...but I honestly don't have much to put here.  I suppose there are a few small annoyances for me.  I'll admit that the combat, as much as I praise it, can be frustrating.  But the outcomes are always more interesting when you just play them through to the end.
While I enjoy that the game really doesn't hold your hand at all, I do think there are times it could do a better job of at least pointing you in the right direction.  I can't think of any specific examples here though.  I did notice though that occasionally you'll get a quest where you're supposed to track someone down, and it says to follow such and such tracks west or wherever, but there won't actually be any tracks.
Also, I've seen a few people mention that it'd be nice if there was a more detailed breakdown of budget for your party expenses.  That's a neat idea but honestly, the tool tip when you hover over your gold or supplies is 100% clear about how long they each will last you.
It's disappointing that there will be no more development for the game, beyond bug fixes and such, and that there is no modding.  For some, this is a deal breaker.  I'll still continue to enjoy it, but agree that mods would at least extend the life of the game beyond it's final development.  There's SO much that modding could bring to Battle Brothers.  But don't let that deter you from giving it a try, it really is an awesome game.  You just have to put a little bit of time and thought process into it, and I think that's fair considering that it's a strategy game.  Immerse yourself as the commander of your company, explore, and don't be afraid to lose a strong party member.  At the end of the day, the stories that arise out of your specific journey will make it very memorable.
If you read this far without falling asleep, you should go ahead and just buy the game already.  ;)

Get this if you like turn-based tactics, medieval settings, and difficult games. Don't expect a strong roleplaying experience.

The game is essentially a loop of take on a mission, defeat some enemies, get rewards, gear up and supply your mercenaries, then repeat. It's ok if you like the combat. If you don't like the combat, you probably won't like this game and could safely refund it in 2 hours.
To the developers credit the writing is strong and decision to choose different end-game situations is cool.  But the game can become repetitive.
Do not listen to people who say this is like Mount and Blade without giving any explanation.
Unlike Mount and Blade, Battle Brothers does not have:
- a player character who battles and who you can upgrade
- the possibility to become a lord then a king
- the possibility to have your own castle and fiefs
- no raiding towns or cities
- horses
- a strong economic game. You can trade in Battle Brothers, but you cannot do it solely without forsaking essential experience for your mercenaries.
- tournaments
- a marriage system
- mostly importantly, mod support
I think the above really needs to be addressed because the comparison to Mount and Blade is so common yet so often misleading. There are similarities but in my opinion they are few.
Overall this is a great game. If the developers add more content it could be amazing.

Short Version : Its good, reasonably stable, atmospheric but empty at the moment. Easy to survive with not many dangers or things to actually do. Buy if have an active imagination and can keep yourself amused, or wait until more content is added as this game has tonnes of potential... if completed.
My experience of the game has been mostly positive, it was stable and ran at a decent frame rate on my PC (Intel i7 4ghz nVidia GTX 780 16 gigs rame SSD) and gltitches were minimal really solid opening for a early access alpha.
Visually the game is atmospheric with some especially noteworthy lighting, take particular note of the moonlight and sunset though sunrise did have some shadow flickering issues.
The islands are generic tropical but pleasing to the eye with some nice water effects, diving below the waterline was well implemented.
Controls and physics are reasonable, the movement can be clumsy at times especially near objects or climbing trees and moving about wrecks.
Object physics are well implemented with some neat additions to manipulating in game objects in a reasonable fashion, it works much like how you would expect it in many cases.
Content is currently rather limited, with very few craftable items and structures available and there really isnt a whole lot to do in the game currently, its up to you the player to amuse yourself in the game.
Challenge is currently limited as well, as surviving is easy if somewhat tedious as crossing islands is long and dull but a reasonable expectation given the set piece of the game, and more content is forthcoming and should provide for more challenges to survivial.
In its current state this game is a well crafted and stable alpha that is fun to play initially and can amuse for a while, but will sooner rather than later show itself to be shallow and lacking.
I would reccommend the game if you have an active imagination, would be happy to enjoy the visuals and pretend to be a castaway and set own goals to amuse yourself... I would not buy this title at the moment if you want action or a harsh survivial trial with goals and achievements to strive for.
For an Alpha its a very good start, has tonnes of potential but its early days and the developers will need to keep up the good work.

This is definitely a step in the right direction from the original. Revised certainly has its own uniqueness and doesn’t feel as clunky as its predecessor.
I used a wired XBox 360 controller for this review. The left thumbstick moves Typo, A is to jump, RT is to push and pull letters, and B is to carry letters. Levels are cleverly designed with words in mind. Keep your eyes peeled for letters hidden or discarded as you may miss a letter. Letters and words can be pushed, picked up, thrown, and dropped to fit, create, and activate sequences throughout the levels.
There are also collectibles to find in the form of little quotes. They aren’t too tough to find if you pay close attention to how the level is set up. Sometimes going off the beaten path will reward you with an achievement and a couple quotes. Pay attention to these quotes because the word that is in all caps is often times the word related to what you need to do in the next part of the level. The majority of the story is told through the quotes as well.
You’ll come across enemies that you can’t fight yourself, so you’ll have to use your wits and take note of your surroundings if there is a word to be unscrambled or a word that tells you what to do. There will be instances where these red lasers are above certain areas. These lasers mean that you can’t go beyond them holding a letter. Pay close attention to these areas as there might be other ways to solve the puzzles.
Puzzles aren’t too troublesome and require players to unscramble or come up with words that pertain to the situation. Words such as run, turn, and open are just a few of the words that you will be unscrambling in order to get out of tight situations or activate objects. They do, however, get more complex as the levels go on. There is a system where there will be hints in case a puzzle proves too difficult. There are moments where it’s difficult to figure out what to spell or how to progress
Controls are smooth and responsive. The XBox controller worked well and felt very natural to use. Keyboard and mouse was a little difficult for me as I’m better at playing these games with a controller, but to each their own.
Controls this time around feel leagues better than they did the first time around.
The game looks like it feels, dark and foreboding. It reminds me of Limbo with it’s almost all monochromatic scale. Music was gloomy and dreary, directly relating to the bleak situation at hand. It fit the scenes in each level and didn’t take away from the overall feel.
Typoeman: Revised is a great word game and an atmospheric puzzle platformer. It’s clever enough to keep you guessing, challenging enough to keep you entertained, and fun enough to keep you engaged. The only downfall I can see is that the game has moments where it’s hard to figure out how to proceed and it’s really short. It can be completed in roughly 2 hours. Although obtaining all the collectibles could prolong that if that’s what you’re into.

A charming innovation on the CCG genre; part puzzle and part deckbuilding. Plentiful (172!) and enjoyable single player mission content ('Puzzle' levels are fantastic at teaching more complex mechanics) with active updates to complement the interesting card mechanics. Single player bosses all have their own distinct playstyle and type of colour deck they prefer, keeping the encounters fresh and immersive - speaking of which, the game has a gorgeous aesthetic. Multiplayer is active and functions much like Hearthstone, with ranked and casual modes. I wish I could leave it there...
F2P players beware however - after a few introductory missions the single player content is locked behind insurmountable paywalls. You might receive 100 gold for a level up, but will have to pay 4000 gold for one of these single player 8-mission campaigns, and 2000 gold for an 'Arena' (Pandora) ticket!! It is worth mentioning that crafting costs, especially for powerful legendaries, are steep. This might not be a problem for those willing to shell out, but for all the fun I've had this is the end of the road for me and I anticipate many other F2Players as well.
Premium currency is available, and mainly useful for buying cosmetic upgrades (which can cost up to 10000 gold from what I saw). Pre-ordering the upcoming expansion (€9) grants players those cards immediately, while the rest must wait (CHECK COMMENTS).... suffice to say I am not impressed with the business model, and would hope the devs reconsider. I would love to return to Faeria someday.

As far as game play goes this is a series that has not aged too well. Pathfinding is awful unit, controls are no always intuitive, telling the difference between passable and impassable terrain is sometimes near-impossible and some units feel useless while others will end up being the only units you ever build. Unlike its successor in Red Alert 3 this game doesn't really beg comparison to more modern RTS games such as Starcraft 2 however I will say that in pure gameplay terms this is no longer a groundbreaking RTS.
That said though the campaign is fun and fits in with the story of the universe quite nicely. It doesn't do too much to advance the greater plot and at times the cutscenes can feel a bit limited to simply Kane monologues. All in all the campaign is nice if a bit sparse compared to C&C3.
Missions can be quite unique and fun and fit in well with the story. If you are more a fan of straight up kill the enemy missions unlike SC2s method of always having a gimick that changes gameplay this may be more of the RTS for you.
The Risk-like Global conquest mode is dull and uninteresting after one playthrough it doesn't add anything to the game and battles are rushed and uninteresting. Skirmish is better if you are looking for fun vs AI battles.
Overall I feel this is a game that hasn't aged too well in comparison to those that followed however the core game and capaign is still good and fun if you are a fan of the series or genre.

You've read through Umineko and met all these characters... now fight with em!
Golden Fantasia (GF) is a 2D fighting game where you pair two characters from Umineko together to fight. I'm going to be upfront here and say my experience with fighting games is pretty minimal, so I am not the person to ask when it comes to how this fares in relation to other fighting games. But what I do know is that the "pairing" this game has is a core part of the game, and you will need to use both characters in your matches. Thankfully all of the characters seem balanced with their individual strengths and weaknesses, so you won't feel like half of your team is dead weight. Also when you are not using a character in your team, they give you a bonus like taking less damage or gaining points you need for special moves quicker. It all seems like a well-crafted game, but you are better off asking someone who actually knows fighting games than me.
As for the part that was the whole reason I bought this game... namely to play with Umineko characters in short but entertaining story modes and use the attacks they had in the main series, then I was very satisfied with what GF had. The character pairings you choose determine the stories you get, which range from comedic bits to "what if" scenarios to stuff found in the original game. It is all good fun for me. :D
I need to say right now that if you have an interest in the story of Umineko, you should finish that BEFORE you check this game out. While you obviously don't get full explanations, there are some pretty hefty spoilers that can be found in some of the game's stories as well as the "unmasked" personalities of some characters. There is also the fact that the game has playable characters from the whole series including Willard H. Wright who isn't introduced until Chapter 7, but I find that to be a bit less important than one story mode (kinda) telling you who the "culprit" really is. I will grant that some of these plot points might fly over people's heads and that I am hyper-sensitive to them because I already knew the full story of Umineko and was actively looking for spoilers in this game. Still, my recommendation is that you should finish all of Umineko before you play this game unless you don't care about some spoilers.
There are some issues with this game. There was a translation issue when the game first came out (which is the cause for many bad reviews), but this was quickly patched. Multiplayer likely has a tiny player base as well, which is liable to decrease over time. Controls for now need a third party program to change them (see a pinned thread in this game's discussions) or add new ones for people like me who have a keyboard.
But... none of that detracted from the fact that I got to impale people as Lucifer (the Stake of Purgatory), throw popcorn at people as Lambdadelta, fire off "Blue Truths" as Battler, shoot people as Rosa, swarm people with Bernkastel's cats and other magics, and many many more. I find all of this pretty neat. It is one thing to see Dlanor use engrish and a crazy face to sentence someone to death in the Umineko VN. It is quite another to use Dlanor to do that yourself in this fighting game. ^_^

First of all keep on mind this is a game made with fans of Umineko on mind. A lot of the dialogue, movesets, endings and fanart, and the Meta system are all refences to the original work. So if you're planning to get into this When They Cry story, I recommend you to read either the Visual Novel or the Manga first (Avoid the anime like the plague).
However, as a game on its own Golden Fantasia is a very solid fighting game and quite stands out with very unique mechanics never seen in any other game of this genre. A tag battle system with each character having unique passive abilities makes very interesting combinations with their gimmicks working together (And individual HP to fuse together, making tanky teams or glass cannons). Each character has simple command lists with many of them sharing the same inputs, so casual players can quickly learn their favorites and master basic combos. And the super bar takes a very different route with the active character building bar for their partner.
But if you're fan of Umineko you'll know what really stands out of this game is the Meta system. This is where many of the big showdowns will come with each player countering each other's Meta by spending super bar, or failing to do so as the winning side will have not only their two abilities active but also infinite supers for a brief seconds. Depending of your team the Meta activation can have more importance than others (Characters like Bernkastel abuses the Meta with a powerful super and longer Meta duration. While some others will just use it to cancel moves in the middle of a combo or to nullify the opponent's Meta).
The flaws of Golden Fantasia might show when compared to the competition. The rounds of this game can be very long depending of the teams, so you might want to lower the HP if battles are feeling tedious. The combos you can pull out are very straightforward and there might not be much to experiment with, and if so most likely requires a lot of super bar which makes them situational (Maybe the exception is teams with Virgilia due her ability). Lastly is the fact that is a PC fighting game, and even though got a highly improved netplay compared to the original release there won't be many players from a franchise mostly known for its Visual Novel.
I am gonna heavily recommend this game for Umineko fans no matter if you read the Mangagamer version, the fan translation by Witch Hunt many years ago, or the Manga (The Anime as I said, just no). For those who just saw this game in the store I'll say to give it a try as well, but since is a spoilerfest right from the first minutes into the game you must really not care about the original source and wanna try something very different from other fighting games.

Kingdom: Classic is a game about building your castle and men up from a simple campfire to a full blown keep with heavy stone walls and catapults. Please...give me...more thumbs up buttons to click, for Bastion!!!
This little game swept me off my feet and reeled me in at the first few seconds of starting it...
First of all - Logan Cunningham is probably the best choice -ever- to be a narrator! His calm, deep and yet somehow so soft and pleasant voice follows the player throughout the whole game, and it could not have been a better 'companion'. The little parts of story that he tells you (well, or is telling Zia, in game, whilst The Kid goes and does the hard work) are a great little adition to your adventures. A more serious look at the past of that world, a bit of a comical insert (especially if you roll off an edge. *cough* Totally not me. *cough*), a touching, warmhearting little story...all of it is like a puzzle of vocal little pieces, that you have to put together to understand what has happened in the world of Bastion. And quite honestly - it's a brilliant way of making the player 'dive into the Bastion's Universe' and enjoy the game, his own actions during the game, whilst getting told facts or stories about the world (or the particular creatures that he's fighting currently.
Second - the gameplay and looks. Amazing! As in...I could not have wished for better, from a little indie (and at the current moment - already OLD indie) game! It's rather beautiful and eerie, fluently swapping between various enviroments even on the same level. Yes, of course, the actions, combat itself will be simple and noone should expect some ultra-super-duper-gazillion-slashes-in-air-in-a-wave-like-motion-before-smacking-a-mob. But I still found it extremely enjoyable. Mostly due to the fact that you actually get such a weapon and playstyle variety, that even some of the new games pale in comparison! The mix and match of the combat possibilities is amazing.
Third - the soundtrack! It's brilliant! Going from a heart-pumping rythm that makes you want to score the best...to an almost tear-jerker, as you listen to some more emotional parts of the story, told by the excellent narrator....
If I knew it was so amazing, I would have bought it for the full price as well! An excellent little game that kept me entertained with every second I spent on it. And oh you bet - I will be going back into it, to get those achievements and explore the rest of the weapon combinations... :D

I was chosen to be a Linux beta tester of Typoman Revised and I must say I was quite impressed how well the game was ported over to Linux and how well it performs despite being in a beta. I didn’t run into any game-breaking bugs or issues. Although it's still in ongoing Linux/SteamOS beta testing, if all goes well the developer will release the Linux edition on Feb 10th!
Charming, yet dark, German developer Brainseed Factor behind Typoman Revised blends puzzle and platforming elements into a polished pulp of passion and forges a noteworthy game that now works on all three Operating systems (Windows, Mac & Linux). Easy to describe, Typoman uses letters to forge its “Hero”. Literally, the character’s design is an H, E, R and O. Even the enemies and obstacles are made up on consonants and vowels. In order to advance through each level, gamers have to create words to activate and traverse the terrain, creating words like “on” and “off” in easy situations and much complex verbiage in later levels. The end result is a platformer that works, it’s got a bit of “Mario” and “Pitfall” in it, but thanks to the puzzle elements has that something “extra” to make it stand out of the crowd.
Much of the speciality has to do with the games look. Right from the start, Typoman creates a sense of wonder and fun that you’ll enjoy. Dark and gritty with an endearing air, Typoman will instantly draw connections to another fantastic platformer, “Braid.” It’s here where much of the intrigue is created, jumping around, climbing and swinging. But at the same time, the dangers that wait may be too much for the average gamer. Simply put, you will die quite a bit in Typoman. At times, you’ll have no idea how to remedy your situation.  Then, just wait until the boss battles, where you’re platforming skills won’t be enough, you’ll have to spell the proper words at a pace that may take your brain some time to get used to.
Typoman Revised as a platformer alone is fun, everything works the way it should and is fun in spite of its later difficulty. The puzzle elements too are a hit, but create another layer to the action. The end result is a unique blend of puzzle and platforming that I really enjoyed and wouldn’t mind a sequel down the line (maybe a bit longer this time). I can full heartedly recommend Typoman to all of you who are interested in a uniqe puzzle platformer!
PS:"I like the game so much that I will buy it as soon as it officially comes out for Linux".

EvilMaze is a hack and slash RPG Maker game with a heroine with big boobs. The only character potrait that this game has is the heroine and both of her potrait and sprite will change based on her equipments. Most of the equipments will have a lack of clothes. On the other side, there are a lot of hidden "secrets" in this game.
Most (if not all) graphics in this game are using standard RTP assets. The mapping looks messy with all of the items placed in the map and some areas are annoying enough which make you have to traverse through several floors in order to go to the place that you want (i'm talking about layer 8).
The heroine will change her appearance whenever you change her equipment, both in sprite and potrait. In the potrait, some equipments will have less clothing, which somehow made her looks like in a beach instead of prison.
There are different musics in the area and most (if not all) is also using RTP. The music selection fits with the background though.
There isn't much story in the game except of a woman which wakes up in a "prison" full of monsters and trying to get out of it. However, most of the in game text looks messy. There isn't even a generalization for capital letters. There is a "Copper key", "silver Key", "Iron key", and "Golden key" in the game (notice the capital letter). "g" letter is also cut midway.
This game has a small amount of floors for a hack and slash game; It only has 10 non randomized floors which is shown as layers. Each floor has its own theme and some floors are uniquely designed. There are a lot of items and enemies scattered in each floor. The maps in each floor is also not very big and can be traversed quickly.
The game also has a lack of tutorial which make it hard to understand. After you start a new game, you'll be brought to a prison with no dialogues at all. People with no exploring habit will stuck at this point for a long time while people with exploring habit will find a weapon in the area after inspecting almost every possible places in the map. After that, the game will abruptly giving you instructions in a wall of text which i intepret as "press F to attack". The thing is, it actually also gives an instruction for assigning a quick slot which is important after you obtain a spell later on.
After you get out of the prison, the game will provide you with the last tutorial about attacking and enemy attack range. However, it is missing an important thing: MP. It doesn't provide a tutorial that you can rest on the bed and resting in the bed will use 1 MP. I don't know about it until i am retrying the game several times in order to figure out what to do.
This game has several secret spots in each floors. Most of the useful items will be placed in these very spot which makes you have to inspect every wall in every direction to make sure you don't miss any.
You need keys to unlock some doors in order to access some area. However, there is no enough set of keys available if you choose to use them all. You need to use the keys efficiently or you have to spend money to buy them.
The game randomly crashes when i played it and it ruins my save file once. Luckily i have a backup save for it so i don't have to redo the game.
In some floors, there will be some bosses. These bosses is just a normal enemies with better stats, except the final boss. The final boss can move and has its own aoe attack. However, they are not that difficult to beat as long as you have all secret equipments in the area.
Your character can learn spells through a scroll which is obtainable from inspecting the area or buying the scroll from a merchant. Using spells cost MP and the only way to recover MP is by using items or picking up glowing light in some of the floors.
There is a merchant in some of the floors which will sell some items including permanently enhancing stat items. However, they are quite expensive so you have to save some money to buy it. There is also a money trick which involves a skill although it will take a long time to generate the money.
Pros:
- 10 floors
- Lots of secrets
Cons:
- Unclear tutorial
- Random crash
- Easy boss
