Should you buy it - $30 is a little bit much for a four year old game but it is a good game and if you really like FPS's, Yes
Should you buy it on sale - Absolutely
Singularity is a standard FPS with just a little bit more that sets it above the norm.
Visuals : The visuals in the game wont destroy your graphics card or anything but it does tax it a little bit. The scenery and set pieces look very nice, sometimes really pretty. There is no reuse of areas that I can tell ( aka same corridor syndrome ) and you will get a good feeling of progression ( you can visually see getting closer to your goal). The enemies look nice but dont change much in the looks area but at least you dont get the same guy but his time hes red! Overall - Good looking game that helps to visually immerse you into the world.
Story and Setting : (Spoiler Free) The setting is an Island off the coast of Russia that has some dirty little secrets and as a US special forces soldier you have to infiltrate the island and find out what is going on. As a base story it is just like most of the other FPS games out there but Singularity adds a nice twist on the basic formula that makes it feel new and refreshing. Overall - The story wont break the bank on amazing plots but it will engage you very well and help to keep you playing to find out what happens next.
Gameplay : This is were the game really sets itself above a normal FPS. It has a slight rpg feel with upgradeable weapons and skill selecting although neither is a game changer or breaker. It has good gun play and the powers that you use are fun and work well but what this game does really well is that it lets you play the way you want to. No, there is no stealth or anything like that, it is all action and if something is in your way it has to die but the game gives you incredible freedom on how it dies.   You can play and complete this entire game with nothing but guns or once you get your powers you can complete the entire game with those. It never limits you and it gives you plenty of ammo or easily throwable items no matter which way you want to play. Overall - The gameplay is great and gives you a great feel of freedom that never tells you how you should play it
Replayability : While the story does give this game a little bit of replay ( you might want to play again just to see all the clues you didnt understand in the first playthrough ) and the gameplay lets you play it again in differnet ways, there is really no reason to play it more than a few times.
Personal overall enjoyment - This game was a good change of pace to me for normal FPS's. I enjoyed playing the game and was glad of the purchase I made. I will probably play it again sometime down the line and have no problem recommending it as a good game.

When I first saw the trailer for Typoman: Revised, the thing that stood out to me was the idea of blending a word game with a puzzle platformer. Using words to change the environment is a clever idea and showed a lot of potential for a puzzle platformer. For the most part the game lives up to this potential since the word mechanic works well. While the puzzles are a little on the easy side, the game does a really good job using the mechanic to create a unique experience.
I really enjoyed my time with Typoman: Revised but I did have two issues with the game. First the game is pretty short at only 2.5-4 hours long. Also while I didn't really have many issues with it, the game does have a problem where it only accepts certain words in some situations where other words should also work. This can be frustrating when you create words that should work but weren't the word the designers were thinking of so they don't work.
If Typoman: Revised's concept sounds interesting to you, you will probably really enjoy the game as long as the game's length doesn't bother you. If the idea of a word based puzzle platformer doesn't really interest you though, it probably won't be for you.

'Singularity' is an action FPS which delivers not only a satisfying experience in terms of atmosphere and visceral combat but also tries to spice things up with a few gimmicks. These gimmicks mostly revolve around time and gravity manipulation mixed in with an above standard FPS-shooting experience.
Most of what 'Singularity' has to offers has been seen in different games: the package here is just a variation based on known ingredients. I might be reading too much into this, but I believe one could make a drinking game out of all the reference/homages/rip-offs presented. FEAR, Dead Space, Bioshock 1 and Clive Barker's Jericho all seem to get, at the very least, a tip of the hat. I also saw some of Half-Life 2, Resident Evil and even a little bit of Silent Hill (with walls ageing as you pass by) and Portal (in the form of the blue and orange slider to age or revert objects). Even the spectral plants reminded me of Final Fantasy – Spirits within, but that might be pushing it a bit.
Anyway, in my book, these references do not diminish the game. Just don't expect anything ground-breaking here. The most original aspect of 'Singularity', to me, came in the form of the grenade-launcher, which uses a rolling and jumping remote controlled brightly orange ordnance. Not very effective, but quite entertaining.
What really worked for me was the atmosphere of the game. I enjoyed the slower parts, but I was also in the mood for it: I didn't expect balls to the walls action all the time. I let the game set its hooks into me and do its schtick. The environments really helped in that regard, with pleasing aesthetics and exploration worthy level-design.
Still, I'm not too sure about the overall tone of the game. Granted, with that many references, it must be hard to keep a semblance of coherence. What I mean by disturbing changes in tonality is going from tense and oppressing almost survival-horror experiences to flat-out drawn-out stand-off fire-fights against dozens of enemies. Or jumping the shark with an giant boss battle, for little to no reason. Sure, it was very impressive and entertaining but it also seemed completely out of place. I guess 'Singularity' is like a blended mix: a smooth experience overall but with some chunks here and there.
Since the story revolves around time travel and time manipulation you should expect a convoluted mess plot-wise. If you thought Bioshock Infinite's was headache inducing and lacking in basic sense, then be ready for the plot of 'Singularity'! I'm just gonna say it but, by the end, the story doesn't really make sense. It tries, and it helps to think about it in terms of “constants and variables” but that still leaves a whole bunch of plot holes to fill. Regardless, it didn't really bother me since I did enjoy trying to wrap my head around the story and tried to figure it out. And while the endings did not offering the best of explanations, they still managed to reach a satisfying conclusion, and even offer some options for the player.
But the strongest part of the game is the combat. With a decent arsenal and a bunch of gimmicks, not to mention the environmental kills, the player is really spoiled for choice. Ageing an enemy ; turning him into a zombie so he will attack his former friends ; creating a time bubble as a shield for the player, or a trap for the enemies ; using melee energy waves ; sniping in slow-motion ; using guided missiles or bullets ; rolling grenades around corners ; burning, freezing or exploding enemies with different barrels ; or just shooting them with rifles, shotguns, railguns, gatling-guns ; etc. are some (most?) of the options at your disposal. It helps that there is a decent variation of enemies, -ready victims for your tools-, and that the impacts of bullets is quite satisfying. That their limbs don't seem to attached to their bodies also helps, as do their death animations. The game has a little bit of gore going for it. And on top of that, you have character perks and upgrades as well as limited weapons upgrades to round things up and tune the action to your affinities.
Still, this doesn't mean that the game is without flaws. With such destructive power literally at the fingertips of the player, the game could stand to be a little bit more challenging. By being careful, you will avoid most deaths, and apart from the suicide-spiders (are those floods? Did I miss a Halo reference?), the enemies are manageable.
The run time of the game is decent, but I would have liked a bit more. To give you an idea, it took me less then 10 hours for my first playthrough on hard, and less then 5 for the second one, also on hard.
Also, the video game logic present here can be quite silly: going back in time to change the present is fine, doing so to get a box in the past to use as a stepladder in the present is lazy. Still, when one wields a hammer, everything looks like a nail, so if you have a device that can bend time and space on your hand... Yeah...
Finally, on both playthroughs, one of the NPC glitched as he was in the middle of some explanation and, while it didn't break the game or anything, the exposition would have been nice to hear. Still, as it was rather obvious, so I just looked up the completed scene on the internetz.
In conclusion, when all is said and done, I'm really glad to have bought and played 'Singularity'. It's a safe yet entertaining experience. It is worth your time, if there is a steam-sale for it, grab it if you like those kind of games. While perhaps lacking in intuitive controls at the begin, with all the different abilities you can use, it is still a game that I will launch from time to time, like the first FEAR actually.

Total War: Warhammer is a dream come true for me, and no doubt it will be for all Warhammer Fantasy fans. Just when I thought Games Workshop was abandoning the franchise in favor of 40k after the End Times and Age of Sigmar erased the Old World, they give us this with Creative Assembly's help, and the blend of Total War gameplay and Warhammer lore is one of the greatest things I've played.
Most of the negative reviews come from the presence of DLC, some of it being from day one. While this is frowned upon by most, it has been common practice by Creative Assembly since Shogun 2 and, while costly, the DLC is mostly worth it. There have also been a pretty good amount of free DLC, including the massive Bretonnian pack that came with three new factions.
With that said, it's classic Total War gameplay with things never seen before, such as magic and flying units, gigantic monsters and unbelievable siege weapons. It works wonderfully. The animations are gorgeous. I'm sixty hours into the game and I still don't get tired of zooming into the battle to watch my units fighting for their lives in real time, the blood of their enemies covering their exhausted bodies. The variety in races and factions is incredible, as none of them plays the same, unlike in Shogun 2 where every faction had more or less the same units with a few differences. Playing as Greenskins feels like playing as Greenskins and nothing like the Empire.
Total War: Warhammer is possibly the greatest love letter to the Warhammer Fantasy universe in the history of gaming, and it's a damn good Total War game on its own merit. What else is there to say? Be sure to buy the Blood for the Blood God DLC to include that gore and blood in your massive cinematic battles, enter the Old World and pray Sigmar and Ulric in the hope that they'll grant you victory. You'll need it.

Shadow of Mordor has been the game that I have been waiting for for years.  In my old game collection I had Lord of the Rings: War in the North, Battle for Middle Earth II and Conquest. I am a Lord of the Rings fan for almost a decade and after War in the North I was excitedly waiting for a new game.
In general it is very well portrayed with a good intro and with good features such as showing battery level. The game plot is very linear but it keeps interesting with the 'history lessons'. Due to the linear story replaying the story is not really worth to do, unless you are a big fan like me. The other gamemodes, 2 of which require you to buy DLC, are probably worth digging into (I don't have those DLC). The free ones are objective where you have to kill a certain amount of warchiefs and captians. Certain goals give you bonus score and the amount of score is posted on an online leaderboard. Gives a little competitive feeling but it wasn't a necessity. The stealth in this game is almost the same from assassins creed, which makes sense because it is published by Ubisoft.
The story starts off very sad and dark to somewhat heroic. I find the main character to be both an hero and an anti-hero. Once you play enough story you'll discover why I make this statement. The story gives an intresting approach on how they made the one ring. If it is the true version I don't know, I need to read the books, but I doubt it is the real version.
EDIT: 9gag to save the day!

Also notice that golum is in the story. He's more of a side character here and it's not really clear how he got into mordor. (I'll be connecting a bit with the LOTR story here). I think that he got here because he got captured by the orcs for torture, in the beginning of the first movie they tortured him to know the whereabouts of the ring, after the torture they released him and that's maybe the reason that we encounter him. It also gives an idea when the story is in the Middle-Earth history.
The killing captians and warchiefs is different due to a new system, they call it the nemesis system, it is pretty fun and keeps the game exciting. The captians  themselfs are trying to climb up the ladders by trying to gain power by recruiting, feasting, trials in combat or beast hunts. Or they can try to kill each other for a position. Every captain or warchief has it own strengts and weaknesses so they are not as killed easily as general orcs. There is also a chance that random captians return once you killed them, this is based on how you kill them if you chop off their head they are really dead but they can survive a kill by arrows or a stealth takedown of some sort. Talking about arrows I'll give an example of a captain that I was fighting. There was this captain that could be killed by a charged headshot. I killed him like that from afar. He then returned to the spot I was at and almost one shot me but one of his abilities is that they ignore you when you are in last chance struggle, means they won't kill you, he then returned to the same guarding spot I killed him from earlier and I did the same thing because his weakness was the same. After that he did the same thing but he now literally was unkillable. He became a Defender which you can't jump on, can't be damaged by stealth, can't be damaged by arrows, and the ignoring while he almost killed you.
Overall a good 3th person fighting game with a decent story, it is a bonus when you are a Lord of the Rings fan to pick this up otherwise I wouldn't recommend this if it isn't your kind of game.

Having got this on sale, I would recommend this game. There are a lot of things that I hate/love about this game but the amount of time I have played this gives an indication of how long it would take to complete the game (including side missions and what not). Here are pros and cons:
Pros:
- You definitely get the Lord of the Rings feel, scenery, Orc encampments, human prisoners, even combat.
- The Nemesis system is very well executed. It keeps the game going more and it's very interesting to see that the Orc that killed you got 'promoted' and is now a captain.
- The executions are the best that I have seen in any game, they are very well designed and feel very impactful.
- The Orcs are amazing too. From their voice acting to their behaviour it really does feel like you are killing Orcs from Lord of the Rings and not some generic Orc.
- There are differnt ways to complete some missions however most of them require you to kill a target in steathily.
Cons:
- The story is rather lackluster. I won't spoil it but I found it rather uninteresting and didn't really care about the story much.
- Once you have finished the game (and DLC if you choose), there isn't any real reason to play the game again. Nothing really to do once you have completed the game.
- Side mission gave almost nothing. I did them to get 100% but they don't reward you with much, if anything at all.
- DLC was a disappointment, there were no new areas to explore, it was just added features on top of what was already there.
- 57 GB?????
Combat could go either way as you are just right clicking to attack but I found executions so cool that I could live through it.
Overall it isn't a bad game but it isn't AMAZING either. I'd recommend this game for when it is on sale. You most certainly get your money's worth then, however I wouldn't really bother with DLC.

I really enjoy this game, it's one of those "Easy to Play, Hard to Master" types, which I really adore.
It's VERY similar to Clash Royale (mobile game), the graphic style is worse than in Clash (In my opinion), but the game itself is made with grater care.
It's not as Pay2Win as Clash Royale - No "Player Levels", no waiting 4h-24h for chests to open, no card levels (You have to collect "card pieces", but once You collect them all, You permanently unlock a card and it can't be upgraded), You get 1 free tournament entry everyday, Paid Currency(Gems) is used to purchase additional tournament tickets, premium emotes and skins for cards (Pink Rats FTW!)
There are currently 88+ cards in game with different rarity levels (The rarer the card, the harder it is to get it, and it cost more in shop), Your deck must contain of 10 unique cards (no duplicates), and must be balanced (both offensively and defensively), the games are really intense and great to watch!
I still think it lacks some content, there is no possible option to cooperate with friends, no 2v2 matches (yet!)
But it has potential, since there are a lot of possibilities (I would LOVE to play "Boss challanges", where Your enemy is Computer, but with additional perks, like he is generating x2 elixir from the start of the game, or has unlimited deck, or drops bomb at Your Main Tower every 10s).
I really hope it gets bigger, better, prettier and more competetive in the future!
My final rating would be 8.5/10.

A caveat: I played the game an hour after release, this review is the day after. Supposedly bug fixes are being done on the game, my opinions may change if the game is fixed.
An excellent game in many regards, but the version has new netplay that replaced the old. For many, playing online is unplayable - even when the previous version (non steam ver which I've played hundreds of hours of) worked fine with these players. For some, the new netplay works but there are some egregious problems.
1: someone joining a full lobby can disconnect currently playing people.
2: if you direct IP connect, the game crashes afterwards - forcing you to reboot & reconnect after each match.
3: desyncing is a huge problem, a streamer demonstrated this - he was unable to play vs his friend reliably.
4: i personally (and i'm sure others) often have disconnects near the end of matches. this might be due to desync as well.
5: no spectator mode, making me wonder what the point of having a lobby system is - I am hugely disappointed by this lack of feature... though it was technically not promised, I just assumed it would be in the game.
6: no way to set delay, the game forces you to play with roll back and 0 delay. Other modern fighting games have options for the players to choose if they want choppy "teleporting" netplay at times, or a bit of delay + less choppy ness; the steam version does not. This lack of settings might be the reason people are having problems, though I cannot say for sure.
7: there are people who play the game with a keyboard, some of them are very unhappy with the lack of control options as well as the changes to keyboard controls from the non-steam ver.
I cannot speak to the translations in story mode because I don't speak/read Japanese, but it's nice to have some kind of translation.
A real let down that the netplay, in it's current form on release, is so utter garbage for so many people. I will change my opinion accordingly if it is fixed.

The game is simple, yet very well polished. You wake up devoid of any memory of what has happened or why you're in the ruins of a ruined civilization. All you can do is follow the glowing alchemical technology of this world, and let the gameplay itself guide and give hints about the story.
I really dig the show don't tell approach to storytelling here. They use animations rather than cheap journals or hidden logs to tell you whats happening. Breach away from all those generic walking simulator tropes.
That said there is a fair bit of walking around, derping about with broken things, hunting for glowing bottles of liquid. Its relaxing but might not be for everyone. Having played through a fair chunk Im not really even sure if anything can kill you aside from falling to your death.
Overall I liked it and would recommend it as a simplistic puzzler that is fairly relaxing. its also got that lost altantis feel to it.

Let me address some of the negative reviews quick;
If you don't like this game because of mechanics or feel, then respect.  If you are out here giving this game a bad review because of the command list, then you shouldn't even be playing fighting games.  It's very obvious that the lay out is; A, B, C, Tag, Taunt.  The command list couldn't be easier to understand.  If it truly elludes you, google is your friend.  I found a translated move list and break down of all mechanics in a matter of seconds.
Now for the game;
I havent played online yet but I hear there aren't any lobbies.  That sucks.  Hopefully that gets addressed but it probably won't.  The number one thing for any online fighting game is lobbies in my opinion.  We grow as a community by sharing tech and watthcing others and how they react to various situations in comparison to ourselves.  The game itself however, is really good.  LIKE REALLY GOOD.  This isn't your traditional anime fighter.  If you are looking for endless strings of combos and touch of death, go DL BlazBlue or MaHvel.  This has more of a King of FIghters vibe with tons of spacing fundementals and short punish, street fighter esque, combos.  The tag system and ability mechanics allow for pretty intense extenders to give a true anime feel.  The sprites can sometimes look a little stiff and awkward but doesn't really effect the gameplay and honestly only adds to the charm.
TL;DR
7/10 - It's pretty solid.  I don't really know anything about the story or lore.  Never heard of this.  I'm a fighting game fan and I like this.  Feels........right?!  I would have scored higher had I known anything about this but there was no build up hype.  Mix up situations and defensive options create that hype in game.  Worth.

If you like wander-around-solve-puzzles games, the puzzles in this are too few and too easy--a few old standards you've seen a thousand times (a mirror/beam puzzle, a "turn on all the lights" puzzle, etc).
If you like a good story, you'll find this one is cryptic and unsatisfying, assuming you can even figure out what the heck is going on. (I like it when a game doesn't spell everything out, but I have my limits, and I suspect here the story is deliberately opaque to conceal how little of it there is.)
If you like walking simulators, though, boy howdy is this the game for you. Apart from a few areas where you have to run like hell so the game's one nemesis doesn't get you, and the occasional puzzle or climb/jump exploration area, you walk. A LOT. Especially in the game's enormous chapter 3 (which is most of the game). When you look at a save file and you find out what chapter 3 is actually CALLED, you'll think a cruel joke has been played on you.
It's a pretty game, with good visuals and sounds, and it plays fair; pretty much everything important is very clearly lit or marked so you don't have to do an endless scavenger hunt in acres of scenery.
Recommended, barely, but not at full price.

Played 200 hours of this before it was on Steam, just on and off over the years after finishing the visual novel, and it got me into fighting games. It's one of my most cherished games of all time and possibly the reason a number of fighting games felt disappointing to me afterwards. I don't have much negative to say about it.
There's no fancy game modes, just the most basic stuff. Arcade, Versus, Training. You might expect more nowadays but in the end it is all you need.
The mechanics are incredibly solid. Game is a lot less air time-y than most anime fighters, with air-dashing and double jumping being a privlege only certain characters enjoy, making them more distinct and keeping things from getting too crazy. The block bar and how you refill or attack it matters. Projectiles have their place, but never feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Tag and SP system mean the fight is constantly changing, and you are encouraged to play other characters to find new ways to play. The tag system also makes bad match ups far less of something to worry about. Metaworld feels fun as hell to refute back and forth to force through for a critical special.
There's a decent chunk of strategy in who you pick to play, and lots of ways to play whatever duo you choose. Every character has an ability they grant to their partner when they are called in in some situations, and the two are combined when a metaworld declaration is made, which can be fun in an obvious way (combine healing with damage reduction or no tag out debuff with increased block bar damage) or take skill and knowledge to use (granting a cancel to a special of a character of your choosing or increasing stun damage dealt). Characters lending different amounts of health to their team add a bit there as well, playing with Black Battler and enjoying his improved moveset without compensating for his much lower health will turn you into a glass cannon.
The art is gorgeous. Every stage is two combined due to the metaworld mechanic, and there are nice small details like background characters being either replaced or not being there at all if they were chosen for the match, and the painting in the entrance hall suitably changes when certain characters make a meta-world declaration in that stage. The shadow of the clock ticking down to midnight as the timer nears zero is just perfect. The (too brief) loading screens are chosen randomly from hundreds of pieces of fan art varying in quality from professional to talented fan to beginners with a bit of passion, and it can be a joy to look through the new pieces you "unlock" as you play the game.
The music is mostly hand picked from the many tracks from the visual novel. If you have read Umineko then you know what that means; 10/10 tracks everywhere. Many of them fit incredibly well in a fighting game, giving a blood pumping "11th hour" feeling while some are just really fun, like the character select music's insane babble and Tsurupettan playing on the Touhou concert stage. The official voice actors from certain versions of the novel and the anime are here too, and do an excellent job.
The characters, of course also being from the visual novel, all have the 60-70+ hour beast backing up their characterization and motivation despite being fighting game characters, and they didn't slack on including it in the smaller details either. For certain matchups there are unique introduction/victory animations, special move voice bits, or meta declaration lines. Every match up also has multiple lines for both pre- and post-match banter in arcade. Every new little detail feels great when you discover it, like Jessica's stunned animation being an asthma attack or Rosa's defiance in her lines against Beatrice.
The arcade mode's stories are not based on single characters due to the tag system, and so there are about 40 pairings who have a story for it. Each one ends with a CG or two (which is then added to your collection) and vary quite a bit in tone. Some have your pairing cause the murders, while one is simply them demanding better food from their masters and rebelling, and many will be siblings or lovers bonding despite the bloodshed. There's also a rather difficult optional boss at the end of arcade and it's always fun to see how far you can get this time with your team.
If you dig Umineko or just 2d fighters in general and don't mind the few rough edges from it being a doujin fighting game then give it a shot.

The bad:
-the graphics put me off buying the game for a long time. After playing the first hour I grew to like them, but the characters are only rendered as a torso with head and equipment. This feels a bit ugly at times.
The good:
- best turned-based strategy game I've played, including xcom 1+2. You get to choose character equipment, formations and character build through a solid leveling system and see what happens in combat. Every choice matters and you get plenty of moments where you feel like a hero slaying the last monster with the last arrow from your last uninjured dude.
- Great immersion. The game makes you feel like a badass mercenary by a combination of high risk/high reward decisions, text-based interactions with the various factions and settlements and global events that put you to the ultimate test.
- Replayability. I've played a bunch of hours and can already tell this will be a game I'll play regularly. I wouldn't be surprised if I got a couple of hundred hours of fun out of it.
Conclusion: One of the best games for strategy gamers with a nice RPG-flavour as a bonus. I say this as someone who play mostly strategy games like xcom, total war (rome 1, medieval 1+2 and shogun 1+2) etc.

This game's got a few things going for it, and those things are very well done. But what it's lacking takes too much from the game that it doesn't feel like a whole game at all. At least, it doesn't provide enough depth to be worth the asking price.
As the other review states, it's like a flash game, one you'd find for free online. That's an accurate description; it plays like a flash game: fast paced and very simple. Unfortunately the price tag doesn't match the simplicity it offers. You could describe it as mindless fun, but to me this phrase conveys the notion of a game that isn't too deep/complicated/sophisticated in it's gameplay
but yet requires quick, successive tactical decisions based on the immediate situation (as opposed to a thought out strategic approach before facing each conflict/battle in game (do I need to buy more ammo, is my $ better spent on upgrades, is there an alternate approach to the mission). Unfortunately this game doesn't touch on any of that sort of tactical depth that even a simple top down shooter should have.
The store page mentions "If you like stealth gameplay, you can avoid direct enemy contact and try to outsmart them..." But for the most part, gameplay consists of holding down the fire button of the automatic rifle or shotgun and spamming bullets in front of you as you walk through the level, and only mixing things up when you encounter multiple enemies: now you backpedal as you spam bullets at the enemies (or strafe if you're fighting guards). on every level and with
and
there's no meaningful decision to make about which weapon to use: just use best one for the situation, or whichever is most fun for you. The only thing close to stealth in this game is the ability to bounce grenades off walls to hit enemies around a corner or to just not shoot the enemies that are facing away from you (but if you have to pass them, you have
but to shoot them (unless you can dodge every bullet and enemy until you reach the end of the level.))
The video with the cool graphics and bumpin' music are what sold me on this game (and the sale). The video looks like a collection of the most tense moments of the game, showing some neat popping out from the corner and shooting and frantic running in circles while shooting at the bugs swarming the player. But the latter is the majority of the gameplay. There's no reason to pop out and take shots when you can accomplish the same thing (dodging bullets) by strafing and spamming your own bullets (because there's no reload or ammo to worry about). In the latter case, if you're not backpedalling then you're forced to run in circles or get mauled by the bugs (though backpedalling is ALWAYS the winning strategy- again, leaving you without a meaningful choice to make about how to approach the situation).
Then there's level design. Every level but 3 are linear. There is a labyrinth level which is hardley a maze, but again, still only one direction to go. One is completely open with no hallways, just single obstacles you walk around. And the other level (that actually contains a loop in it!) is the bonus level. It's the best level in the game, lots of enemies and they come at you from different directions at one point.
There's no story. No text to explain anything, why you're doing what you doing. But hey, the guards are shooting at you so you have to kill them, and the bugs are ugly (and they're bugs), so you have to kill them, too.
So we're lacking meaningful choices of:
- What path to take to the end of the level
- Where/how to move your character in relation to the enemies
- When to shoot (or conserve ammo)
- When to kill enemies or slip past them
- What weapon to use
(- No choices to affect story)
The last one I don't count against the game, because not every game needs, or even
have a story that the player can alter. (Interactivity is, for the most part, in the gameplay which is the player's way of being involved in the story the developer is telling through the game.) But I mention it because having it could've added a lot seeing as how the game is lacking so many choices elsewhere.
Other few negatives include no rebindable controls and one set resolution (though you have the option to go fullscreen).
I'm not trying to dissuade anyone from buying this game, I just want to let people know what they're in for. I'd say this game is worth a dollar for some mindless fun. I did find it mildly enjoyable spraying lead into those bugs and seeing the bloody mechanical mess they leave. So let me now mention the positives for this game.
But also a negative too. They don't look right. Blood is too bright/pale, and then doesn't match the blood color of the bugs.
(gave me a laugh!)
Yeah, you're going to get chomped on a few times, so it's good to be able to make like Jesus and be bread for the world and still live. (And also just like Jesus, when you do die, you can always resurrect (and retry the level ;)) Those damn bugs still eatin' you? Try it on an easier difficulty setting.
Here you go, make something interesting and invite a friend over to play your level. There's no scripting though.
Nice
2D lighting effects. Makes this look more professional.
Player walking sounds are decent and weapon sounds are nice and consistent with the different weapon types. I wish the bugs would make a pinching or chomping noise or something when they attack you (or maybe I just can't hear it?).
Buy this just for some good music to listen to while you blow the brains out of some bugs.
Character looks great holding each of the weapons and I love the look of the bugs (and their corpses.) The guards are "bleh", though.
So if you don't mind the negatives I've mentioned (including the price), then I'd say buy this game. It's really just the price that's keeping me from recommending this, as one can still have some fun with it despite all the negatives.

This is one of the worst puzzle games I’ve ever played. I don’t even know where to start.
So the object of the game is to wait for some colored dots to spawn, then click on a variety of stationary tools to get them to fly into receptor objects. Sometimes the dots will fly wildly all over the screen until you activate magnets to suck them up. Other times they will break or decay and need to re-spawn. Yet other times they don’t respawn, so if you mess up the puzzle you need to start all over. There are a few good ideas, but what game doesn’t have a few good ideas? Here, it’s completely destroyed by a large number of issues:
* Non-deterministic physics. When I first played the game, the introductory level told me to “just watch.” Then physics glitched out and two particles collided when they should not have, breaking the level and leaving me staring at the screen until I realized I had to restart. Things didn’t get much better from there.
* Most of the puzzles don’t involve planning, but having highly precise aim and timing. This is “I know what I need to do, but it’s taking me two hundred tries to do it: the game”
* Solved the puzzle? – Great, now you have to do it again. Four times. For some reason, clearing most stages requires you to repeat the exact same actions several times in a row, usually four times, sometimes more. All the while, the physics could glitch out at any time and require a restart.
* The only texture in the game is the space background. White textureless models are hard on the eyes and make it difficult to distinguish between different objects.
* Twitch-reaction solutions are very frustrating when they require quickly clicking on multiple tiny objects.
* Camera controls are a joke; the camera and the game can’t be controlled at the same time, and it resets at the beginning of every level.
* The only music is a few 12-second ambient loops. Sounds are unremarkable. (The voice-overs for the tutorials were decent, though)
* It is impossible to play this game in full-screen if you have multiple monitors, it will crash instantly. You need to edit a config file just to let it run.
In short, this game is irritating, obtuse, unrewarding, glitchy, and visually awful.
On the bright side, I got all of the achievements in under 5 hours… so if you’re an achievement hunter, go for it, just don’t expect to have much fun.

I've played only the bare minimum of the game. My expectations have been more or less met so far. I can't say conclusively that the game is a winner until I've played it a lot more. But I figure I should add my voice to the chorus.
In short, yes, you should probably buy the game.
, apparently the game requires quite hefty amounts of memory, but seeing as I have 32GB of ram, I ... well, I didn't even notice.
, if you dislike games with
and prefer ARPGs, then stop reading right now and go look at some other game. If you don't mind a slower paced game with a lot of reading, keep on going.
I can't really comment too much about the story with only few hours under my belt. But it seems quite interesting, and rather sombre. There is a touch of Arcanum here in how everything feels so melancholic. But that could just be the initial areas. I haven't really met too many characters, and only one companion.
I am not spoiling things too much to say that due to circumstances you can somehow touch people's souls and perceive their past lives. There's been some pretty excellent writing on that front, and it definitely makes you wonder exactly what is up with yourself?
As an interesting detail you can in the Inns hire adventurers for money, and you can spec these adventurers up yourself however you wish. So I guess it looks like you could create a typical 4 adventurers group by yourself. Well, assuming you have the money...
The game looks quite beautiful, as long as you are fine with the faux-isometric view and prerendered (mostly, there's some animation and it has fairly dynamic light) backgrounds with 3D models walking around. The screenshots give you a fair idea of what the game actually looks like, and if the so far fairly muted and violet/purple/blue color palette is fine with you, go ahead. The game in general seems pretty dark as far color palette goes, and definitely leans towards cool color choices. It's not monochromatic or anything, but it there is a clear preference towards purple or blue where possible.
On the technical side of graphics, you can zoom in and out of the screen. Which is quite nice if you want ot see an overview of the area. I can't really do full zoom because my screen resolution is so high (2560x1440) and the background gets a bit blurry in full zoom at that resolution. You can also adjust the font size dynamically, which helps as there is a lot of text to be read in this game.
As  a side note there is an option to have every character in the game have big heads (think of bobbleheads) when they move around in the map. Hilarious but kind of ruins the somber mood.
There are also parts what I'd call "text adventure" scenes. In fact, they have nothing to do with that. It's more like dialogue cutscenes. What happens is that in the game you sometimes are prompted with a screen where there's an illustration and (usually) several choices. For example, you find a rock cliff. You can examine the cliff, or try to climb it or leave it.
If you succeed, you end up to the top of the wall and can get the "hidden" treasure. These sections are well illustrated and written, and I feel like they add to the game more than detract. My first thought was they saved a lot of money that would have spent on stupid one-off animations when they did this. There's been several instances of this technique already, and I think they worked quite well.
However, if you think the main storytelling element of the game is the graphics, combat and so forth, this won't work for you. It works only if you realize that the game is mostly conveyed through text, and thus these "text adventure" sections are a natural continuation of this medium.
In conclusion, I recommend the game.

A very novel idea that offers a wealth of possibilities and concepts to play with, Typoman taps into a world whose premise is simply too big to adequately explore even with a AAA level budget - words crafted into tools to progress through puzzle environments, wordscramblers allowing multiple solutions (sometimes as simple as the difference between RAISE, RISE, and UP, but a difference all the same) to problems and some genuinely satisfying moments when something clicks and you finally crack that puzzle you've been staring at a while.
I won't lie, there came points where I was about ready to give up - some of the puzzles you either get them immediately or you sit there staring at them forever, and personally the soundtrack didn't gel with me - often the level tones and sound effects were screechy or stressed a note too long and too hard, but on the whole the level design was great, and especially the look of the antagonist words were top notch.
A flawed but nonetheless intriguing and enjoyable venture - I think it's worth your time.

You play as Talion, a captain serving at the Black Gate of Mordor. Sauron's forces siege the garrison, kill your wife and son and finally end your life as well. Your body merges with a soul of an ancient elf and together you seek revenge. Yes. Yes, it is a revenge story and to be honest the story is pretty much none existant.
You are introduced to different characters as you progress in the story. You're introduced to exactly 3 characters. Yup. That's it. You'll meet a dwarf, a woman and an older woman. None of them get enough screen time and as a result you don't really care about any of them.
However that's not why the game is loved...
Gameplay, while quite simple, is just so amazing.
You can parkour Assassin's Creed style through an open world map while brutaly killing thousands and thousands of orcs. There are fast travel points (towers) to unlock just like in Far Cry 3&4, monsters to tame and ride, slaves to free, challenges to do, collectibles to..collect and did I mention you can also murder hundreds upon hundreds of orcs?
You have the freedom of choosing how you want to uproach each situation. You can be a stealthy sniper and shoot 'em all down from distance with your bow. You can just jump right in and go berserk or you can use stealth and take them down one by one or take control of the orcs and make 'em kill each other.
It feels more like a stealth game at first since you get overrun by orcs easily but as you progress in the game and unlock new skills and weapon runes you become a bonafide buttocks.
Not only are there survival and hunting challenges in the game (picking flowers and killing innocent animals) but there are also 3 different weapon challenges scattered across the world: Dagger, sword and bow.
Each of these challenges make you use different skills from your skilltree and try out different approaches making the gameplay a bit less redundant because let's be honest, the game can get a bit repetitive. Especially those slave freeing missions.

Its like terraria, except better in almost every aspect.
Ignore the haters, this is legitimately a good game.

To anyone who says the game is abbandoned now that it's launched - new content is still being added. The universe is expanding even if grouches want to pretend its not.
The main story arch is lacking, and I think the balancing they did to the procedural generation to help with story progression negetivly impacted the game, but it's still worth playing through.
A lot of early access games these days don't come through, they get forgotten or fail before they reach their goals. But starbound is a promise that's been fullfilled and is still growing today.

Fantastic. Exceptional. Tremendous. Choose your flattering adjective, because it'll perfectly describe Shadow of Mordor.
If you have played with the recent Batman games (Rocksteady), you'll feel very familiar with this game's mechanics; and if not, you'll find SoM to be quite easy to pick up, learn, and play. The approachability to its combat mechanics is perhaps this game's greatest strength, with so many routes for tackling the game's challenges - do you choose to go brute force, stealth, ranged, or a combination of all three? All flavors are satisfying, but, perhaps most satisfying, is the visceral combat that's perfectly complimented by bone crunching force and gore galore that'll satisfy the orc slaughtering desires of your teenage-angst-power-fantasy-trip you latentely have in the back of your brain.
With combat being so fun to play, the story acts as a secondary - almost a backdrop to the mayham that ensues. Thankfully, the game is wise to this and never presses exposition heavy scenes that remove you from more orc slaughtering. What is there does compliment the Lord of the Rings canon appropriately and finely sets up the vengeance (and justification for the ridiculous orc slaughtering that ensues) for the main character. Additionally, the voice acting is really quite top-notch, expertly done to compliment the emotions the game's characters suffer through.
Visually this game looks nice, with the free-form combat a definite highlight. Animations of orc slaughtering are always entertaining and there's so much variety here that it really can't get old. The only nitpick is the fairly mundane environs with only average levels of detail and variety, but this can be so easily dismissed based on the absolutely excellent enemy animations and combat mechanics.
In addition to the game's mechanics, it introduces a clever enemy leveling system, whereby the game's enemies "level up" with your successes and failures, further highlighting the stupendous combat mechanics - both on scene and off scene.
For anyone even remotely interested in action video games, this is a MUST buy.

When I initially heard about Starbound, I had been told it was "Terraria in Space" but after playing it for quite a while, it's definitely managed to do something very special compared to its predecessor. Starting with an apocalyptic event causing your character to be stranded on a striken ship in space, you mine resources, build things on planets and in your starship to set about exploring the universe. This proves to be an incredibly simple and very efficient set up for an excellent twist on Terraria's forumla.
Starbound was actually quite hard for me to get into initially, because it overwhelms you quite quickly with information and the sheer amount you can do. There are multiple crafting stations on hand to start with, there are a lot more options for how you explore and what to do - like do you build on your starship or on the planet? Mining is also faster, with most resources being close to the surface and easily accessible (compared to say, mining gold in Terraria). Once you have the ship and can explore freely, this leads to a compelling gameplay loop of just cruising to new planets, exploring them for alien settlements, hidden ruins or secret bases, then jetting off elsewhere.
Even after many hours of play so far, this hasn't got old because there is a huge variety to these places you can visit. From abomination filled labs, to prisons that have been taken over to the inmates to perfectly peaceful villages full of NPCs to interact with. There is a huge variety to see and do in Starbound, with the various biomes on its multitude of planets offering interesting things to see constantly. It's also frequently worth raiding these places, as they often have minerals, items and equipment required to advance the game. Oddly enough, I actually haven't done a lot of mining in Starbound - a lot of the needed resources can be got just by visiting multiple planets and raiding their various facilities/dungeons if you would rather not mine.
One thing I really like about Starbound, compared to Terraria, is the way it handles boss encounters. In Terraria you had to build boss arenas and then summon your boss in it - so that you could actually fight it. In Starbound, you're usually taken to a specific boss arena and that's where you fight the enemy. This turns out to work well, with bosses fought in areas that feel fair and that give you enough room to employ reasonable strategies to defeat them. Without you needing to spend 30+ minutes trying to set up a suitable arena to give you the best chance possible first. Many of these bosses (without spoiling anything) also have suitable checkpoints, so if you die it's not terribly difficult to get back.
Overall even at around 30 hours in, I've not seen anywhere near everything that Starbound has to offer. It's especially good, because you can build and found your own colonies - convincing various aliens to move in. This aspect of the game has me especially excited, being able to build my own colony somewhere and then populate it with NPCs - who generate items, rent and even quests. This is a really great game, with a more forgiving difficulty curve than Terraria and a fantastic twist on space exploration/minecraft style buiding. Definite recommendation.

Warden, as you explore the valley, flee the darkness and seek eternal light, you will find the keys to our past and future.
A great exploration and puzzle game. The details and the soundtrack also add to the atmosphere and the story, as you learn about the valley's rise and fall.
The game can be quite beautiful if not for Cry Engine's heavy requirements. Some artifacts can appear even on low settings.
One really weird thing is the locked "Qwerty pattern": the game will use input based on where keys are on a Qwerty keyboard, instead of using the actual keys. This means the usual movement keys work on all keyboards, but you will need to find where the Qwerty M key is in order to open the map.

-EDIT: Most of the Japanese text issues are already fixed, and the remaining ones (credits, system voice unlock message, replay save prompt) are being worked. Now all those people who couldn't play the game because the move list didn't say "Sommelier Finger" instead of "ソムリエフィンガ" next to the clear picture of a quarter circle backwards + A/B/C can train in peace.
On to the actual review:
PROS:
-ROLLBACK NETCODE. It still has its share of minor issues to iron out as it gets wider usage, but what has been implemented here is vastly superior to the original Japanese PC version, and more than most poverty games get. (Did the *original* releases of Chaos Code and Blade Arcus even have netplay at all?)
-Set in the universe of an absolutely fantastic Visual Novel, which I strongly recommend to any mystery fan. There are enjoyable references to the source material scattered throughout everything, including the fantastic music and art.
-A very unique tag-team system. Characters share health, but not meter. Characters build meter for their partner, not themselves, to encourage tagging and emphasize resource management. Each character has a unique buff applied upon tagging out, and whether you use your tag in neutral, as an attack, or as a means of escape determines the length of time before you can tag again.
-With only 3 attack buttons, a tag button, and a taunt, learning to play is relatively easy compared to most "anime" fighters, and yet strategy and combos can still become quite complex.
--If doing combos or classic quarter circle/shoryuken motion fighting game inputs is too hard, the game has the condescendingly named, but quite helpful, "Princess Mode," which vastly simplifies everything.
-Even the "worst" characters can usually function rather well as partners for others, by covering their weaknesses or providing scary damage/mixup scenarios. I don't think anyone is unviable.
-Rapturous Sommelier Finger
-The Devs are Poverty FGC and Umineko fans themselves, and are currently interacting with the community via an official Discord server to resolve issues, mentor new players, and improve the overall experience.
-Some of the Arcade endings are hilarious, some are rather touching.
CONS:
-There doesn't seem to be a spectate feature...? The original release didn't have one, but I don't think it had lobbies, either. This makes it hard to do any sort of well-publicized netplay tournament.
-The AI on Hard has a tendency to repeatedly wait for you to attack and use an invincible reversal of some sort. Like running into a wakeup Shoryuken masher who never guesses wrong. It also kinda input reads in general, but what fighting game AI doesn't?
-There's not much narrative relevant dialogue in the Arcade mode aside from the intros and endings, which is a bit disappointing for a game based on one of the longest written works of all time.
-Obviously making a ton of casually interested players extremely salty by releasing with some texture errors in the movelist/unlock notifications was a bad move.
Overall, 8/10 would fight against the unforgivingly difficult living embodiment of cynical fan-theories again.

It does mean each game will probably be slower than you've experienced in other games, but it is way worth it. The board isn't just a fancy path between you and the enemy, but also includes, at each four remaining corner, a well you can gather additional mana from. This mechanic gives you one more level of control and variety in the way you play, and ensures strong combinations have to fulfill one more condition (favorable board position) than just holding the cards and the mana.
Moreover, Faeria seems to be designed so that it doesn't get in your way. First, by default, the game will add a description of special abilities every time it appears on a card (you can turn it off in the options). Second, rather than locking cards to certain classes like Hearthstone does, you can put any combination of cards in your 30-card deck. Finally, rather than letting your hand decides what you can do (if anything), your are given one free action per turn (amongst placing land, drawing one more card, or gaining one more mana) on top of playing any number of cards from your hand.
As long as you are willing to play multiplayer PvP, the progression (gold income) is fast (by completing the daily quest, often done in two or three games, you can buy a pack of 5 cards every two day or so). The singleplayer side is also rather rich, with simple AI games and challenges, as well as puzzles taking advantage of the board mechanic of the game. The special reward for singleplayer is merely cosmetic, as you can get everything else (just card packs) without ever touching it.
A word on the "Arena" mode of Faeria, called Pandora, as explanations are generally missing from the game itself: it adds a twist on the regular draft format by adding special cards ("treasures") that activate in the middle of the game. The game doesn't feature a vanilla draft to this day. Each time you get in a Pandora run, the cards presented to you in the draft belong to only three (plus colourless) of the four colours of the game, meaning that one colour will randomly be absent. A Pandora coin (a single run) costs two thousand gold *but* you are given a Training Coin daily to play either singleplayer (warning: doesn't count towards your daily quest, but still rewards you basic gold and xp), or multiplayer (which counts). Winning three multiplayer training runs awards you a free pandora coin, which you can accumulate.
Downsides include an oddly placed tutorial (the game considers you have to know how to play even before you set a password), at least *some* lack of ingame documentation on how some effects interact (some of which are explained in loading screens, but some things you'll have to read up elsewhere or learn empirically), and a lack of singleplayer content once you are done with the (fairly numerous) solo packs.
In all, I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for an original, fair cards game even for casual multiplayer, as it is easy to pick up and offers you plenty of opportunities to play every mode and be rewarded with progression no matter the outcome.

Umineko: Golden Fantasia or previously known as Ougon Musou Kyoku Cross is a traditional 2d Fighting game with heavy focus on tag-team mechanics.

Refer to the forums to find other issues and see if they might apply to your setup.
Otherwise a great game with a rough start on launch, but I believe in the Developers to sort out any major issues within the next few days.

Bastion is a game that is almost flawless. However, its singular flaw is easy to overlook as it’s something that Bastion lacks; one small but important element that would have transformed Bastion from an amazing game into a masterpiece.
Positives:
- Simple Story with Complex Themes
- Naturally Evolving Gameplay
- Beautiful World
- Solid Music
Negatives:
- Characters are distanced by Narration
The story is presented and unfolds in a simple yet elegant manner. As such, it would be all too easy to say the story itself is simple. It is anything but. The story gives focus to four characters, but only one of them ever talks (with one exception at the very end). He is the narrator. He is telling the protagonist’s story as it unfolds, as the player makes it unfold. He is the creator of the Bastion, a haven for if and when disaster strikes. The disaster that plagues this world, the calamity, has literally torn the world apart. Because it is presented so simply, much of what the story is about also comes across just as easily. It is not till the very end, when you learn what the Bastion is, that the complexity of the story falls into place. There are two choices to make at the end of the game, but both choices are very powerful in a very fundamental way. And both will leave the player with plenty to reflect on.
The gameplay is excellent, and evolves as the game progresses. The controls are extremely intuitive, with clear descriptions displayed as each new feature becomes available. Anything more non-intuitive about the gameplay is explained through the descriptions as well as special challenge levels designed to teach the player about the new weapons they discover. Bastion is a game where you use WASD to move, and aim using the mouse. It works phenomenally well. These aren’t the only controls, but nothing about the control-scheme is complicated or bloated. I’d be lying if I said that the gameplay was simple; there’s a surprising level of depth and complexity to it. But it’s presented to the player in such a simple way that anyone could easily pick it up without difficulty.
Thinking about it now, the gameplay in Bastion is also fundamentally influenced by choice. There are various weapons to choose as the primary and secondary weapon, different tonics that can give the protagonist different abilities, the power of the gods which provide great rewards but at greater risk. Even the three level tiers of each weapon have two options per tier to choose from. And nothing is restricted; you can change tonics and weapons later in the game, you can turn on or off the power of the gods, you can switch between the two options of each level tier of a weapon. Bastion has a significant focus on choice and consequences, something that is expressed through both its story and its gameplay.
There is one element of gameplay that has the protagonist jumping from platform to platform. This is actually a bit frustrating. However, it only appears for the final level of the game, and it lasts just long enough to be enjoyably challenging.
The world of Bastion is beautiful. It’s not the most beautiful 2D game I’ve played, but Bastion’s style in conjunction with its puzzle-like nature makes for a unique visual experience. The world forms from beneath the protagonist. I never really understood this, but at the same time it never broke my suspension of disbelief. Humorously, even the narrator passes this off as unimportant right at the beginning of the game! And it works. The beautiful world that forms beneath the protagonist’s feat is cemented as reality by using such simple, yet clever writing.
The music of Bastion does an excellent job of setting and expressing the atmosphere of each moment. It also stands on its own as a solid soundtrack. While there are soundtracks that I overall like better than Bastion’s, there are specific tracks in Bastion that I just love. My favourite is the track ‘Mine, Windbag, Mine’, which for me personally is perfection.
I had a very difficult time figuring out why Bastion is not one of my favourite games. The execution of everything seemed, as far as I could tell, perfect. But Bastion does have a fundamental flaw. The issue goes back to the decision to have the story expressed through only the narrator and the progression of the game. The player gets nearly everything from the narrator, but that also distances the player from the characters. As a consequence, there is no opportunity to build a personal connection to the characters and their individual situations. The filter of the narrator severely dilutes their personalities. Moreover, the backstories of the characters are never shown; they are described by the narrator during several challenge levels.
Truthfully, I do feel for these characters, especially when their backstories, as explained by the narrator, are quite heartbreaking. But it’s the same sort of feeling you get when you hear about a tragedy. It’s saddening, but in a very disconnected and impersonal way. Being told about a tragedy just can’t compete with watching it, watching the characters experience it, and then watching the characters grow because of it. That I felt as much as I did is truly a testament to Bastion’s strengths; the writing, the delivery by the narrator, and the timing of the delivery are all consistently strong.
Bastion, though its technical execution is perfect, lacks one element that keeps it from being a masterpiece. Despite this, Bastion is still a very good game with some clever and thought-provoking ideas. It is definitely worth a playthrough.

Battle Brothers is a fun game. The turn-based combat is well-balanced and difficult. Even on easy, I play to try and not lose any of my men (at least the good ones), and it's a challenge. You can only take one quest at a time, and journeying to that location rarely involves surprises or interruptions -- if so, just one. It's kind of refreshing, because you don't have to pay attention during the journey. But could use a lot more variety. You don't care what quests are at all, just walk somewhere and fight a battle. The one variation is that on a certain type of quest, you get offered more money to betray your employer. But that variety only underlines how little of that there is in the game.
The turn-based battles almost all involve the same line of enemies running at you at the beginning. There are a few types of monsters and a few types of humans. 10 hours in, I'm still happy to fight them, but it needs some different setups.
For $20 or less is a good bargain. I think $30 is too much unless they plan on expanding it or adding modding. Expeditions: Vikings has a similar combat and character leveling, but an actual story with real choices and a ton of variety. The simpler game mechanics of Battle Brothers could have a longer shelf-life, if they add more variety or let the community do it.

Remember the feeling of entering Morrowing and encountering an enemy for the first time? How, no matter how you spec your character or position yourself it seems like every attack you make fails or misses? When even the simplest of enemies can easily overwealm you, all because you can't actually hit the bloody thing? If you enjoyed that, Battle Brothers is the game for you. It has taken that feeling and packaged it up as a tactical, turn-based combat game.
You run a control a squad of up to 12 men. You need to feed them, equip them, and keep them happy. The last part is easy, since they won't be alive long enough to be sad. This is because all of their attacks will miss, and the enemy will kill them in one or two hits.
You have a choice between ranged and melee equipment. Different classes of melee equipment do different kinds of damage. For example, hammers are good against armour, and axes are good against shields. Or so I'm told. None of them will actually hit the enemy so it doesn't really matter which of the numerous health bars they don't affect.
Ranged weapons come in the form of bows and crossbows. You can fire a bow a couple of times each turn, and a crossbow uses all of your action points to reload and fire. It doesn't matter which you choose since neither will hit the enemy, although sometimes they will hit your own soldiers.
There's also a few thrown weapons, like nets and axes. No idea if they're any good, I figured they'd probably miss.
It may seem like I'm just saying that you spend each turn missing attacks on the enemy. That's not true for EVERY turn, though. Sometimes you won't be able to make an attack. As well as the enemies, you also have to battle fatigue. In addition to 'Action Points' each action you take (like moving or attacking) also builds up fatigue. If your fatigue is too high you just can't attack. To reduce it, you skip your turn.
Money is earned by completing contracts. There's a bit of variety to these. Some of them are "go over there and kill things". Others are "Stay here and kill things". Sometimes you'll find a "go over there, and you might not have to kill things". Money earned for completing the contracts is really low. Early, 'easy' contracts will pay 100-200 gold. A crap new recuit will cost more than this, and a GOOD recruit will cost you about 2000-4000 gold. Same with weapons and armour.
This is a beautiful game with some good ideas, but is let down by the uninteresting and frustrating combat. The balance is almost entirely non-existent. If this gets patched in the future I'd be happy to give it another go, but for now I'm done with it.

This is what the transition from Baldur`s Gate to the new generation of rpgs should`ve looked like!
Obsidian Entertainment delivers one of the best (hot candidate for spot 1) rpgs i`ve ever played.
Stunning visuals, great artstyle mixed with bright, yet still sometimes very eerie colour-schemes create a scenario between distant lands (similiar to the style Guild Wars 2 evoked) and some dark age-witch-hunting-tale (or Lords of Salem). The soundtrack is phenomenal, beeing it pubs with their uplifting instrumentals or dark dungeons and caves filled with strange sounds, magic and weapons flying through the air.

All this is carried by fantastic voice-works (actors and writing) which is witty at times, funny and always engaging.
The story and scenario OE created are simply put brilliant, they basicaly created their own, new little universe which offers typical fantasy cliches ala dwarf and elv, but goes way beyond that. The story leaves enough suspense to keep you wondering about the grand scheme of things and reminds me often enough of the good ol Baldur`s Gate 1 times (minor spoiler: your will soon start talking to dead people).
The writing in general is perhaps the best currently available concerning rpgs since the infinity engine products. Every small text (and there`s a lot) is delivered with so much depth and passion.
But the best thing above all: we finaly get to see complex rpg again. Deep stat- and talent-systems, great pausable realmtime combat, which blows any sort of tactics other games since ICWD or BG1/2 have shown out of the water. Tons of passive and active abilities, classes and subraces and whatnot. There`s currently no better crpg system available for pc gamers, heck i`ve even stopped my IWD-addiction ;)
Skill/statchecks for conversations and "events"..it`s all here.
All this glory is presented with so much love for detail you wouldn`t believe it. The UI offeres functions en mass, heck you protagonist can even aquire cosmetic pets (like a poor little doggy in your first major town), you get your own little homebase, can send npcs on mission, get side-lore all couple of steps ...heck you can even choose your prefered language setting in the options menu...just reminds you of what rpgs-players had to deal with the last couple of (many) years. I sincerly don`t know how OE plans to top Pillars of Eternity 1 cause it`s downright filled with greatness and goodies everywhere.
If you got the slightest inch of love for rpgs you will need to play this...only downside beeing you will probably never be able to play one of those "shallow as hell tripple A publisher rpgs"(lookin at you Bioware) again.
GOTY definitly and perhaps even far more than that.
Thanks Obsidian for serving us something amazing again.

Wanna find out what happens when Half Life 2 meets Call of Duty? Raven Soft did.
Pros
- Legitimate Time Travel Plot
- Secrets throughout the game
- Dead Space style upgrade terminals for weapons and character
- Optimized very well
- Immersive
- TMD is useful
- Good characters that are for the most part fleshed out
- Puzzle Gimmicks
- Fun Boss fights
- Multiple Endings
- Time Stop/Slow-Mo Gimmick
Cons
- Generic Russian Enemies
- Hardest Difficulties make the enemies feel like sponges
- Felt very short
- Press F and the puzzles are gone
- Lack of control and ingame video options
Not going to lie to you guys. This is a gem, a true gem. One of the best shooters from "Last Gen" and I am glad it was Raven Soft that  brought it to us, too bad the game is so short. The game itself revolves around the main character polluting the past and corrupting the future, obviously for spoiler reasons I won't say anymore about the story other than that. One of the biggest draws for me was the secrets. The secrets in this game feel very much like Bioshock. The customization reminds me so much of Dead Space, both of these, the secrets and customization, are NOT complaints. This game also has puzzles much like in Half Life 2 and the games special tool, the TMD (Time Manipulation Device) is used to solve many of them, this does lead into one of my biggest complaints about the game, when you press F the TMD displays foot prints on where to go next if you are lost, while nice, this ability has no drawbacks to prevent you from constantly using it, basically trivilizing one of the gimmicks this game has to offer just by pressing F. Pressing F also leads into my next point, control options and video options. This game has basically none of either, you can change a few basic controls but things like reloading are tied into the USE button as well, so things get very confusing, very quickly. Lastly, I would like to talk about general game design. In terms of actual character design and appearence everyone felt very generic, this is actually a bit ok though as the story itself is a big enough draw to keep you going, rather than the characters, who themselves have great personalities, just terrible designs. In terms of boss design, the few bosses this game has are ♥♥♥♥ing sweet, they all are very different and they are really fun, one of the ones in mid game felt very unique, I won't spoil it, but it involves a train.
10/10 - Despite the flaws, most specifically its length, the unique story, gameplay, and the time travel gimmicks help keep this game at the top of my list, I highly recommend this to lots of people, not very often a give a game a 10!

This game is to the Heroes Rise trilogy what Andromeda is to the Mass Effect trilogy: not offensively bad, but not nearly as good as what came before. Instead of a gripping superhero story, it's an unabashedly obvious bout of virtue signalling under the paper-thin veneer of a superhero story. Even as someone who generally agrees with the message of understanding and tolerance, it's hard to understand and tolerate the hamfisted presentation and drastically reduced player agency.
There were some parts that made me laugh, though. Like the part where the game invents new social issues for superheroes that weren't present in previous games, then has the characters complain about how said social issues were completely ignored in those games. Or the part when a bunch of reality TV producers declare that they need to protect and look out for the player character, then in the same breath say that he needs to be a symbol of pride and independence.

You play as Talion, a captain serving at the Black Gate of Mordor. Sauron's forces siege the garrison, kill your wife and son and finally end your life as well. Your body merges with a soul of an ancient elf and together you seek revenge. Yes. Yes, it is a revenge story and to be honest the story is pretty much none existant.
You are introduced to different characters as you progress in the story. You're introduced to exactly 3 characters. Yup. That's it. You'll meet a dwarf, a woman and an older woman. None of them get enough screen time and as a result you don't really care about any of them.
However that's not why the game is loved...
Gameplay, while quite simple, is just so amazing.
You can parkour Assassin's Creed style through an open world map while brutaly killing thousands and thousands of orcs. There are fast travel points (towers) to unlock just like in Far Cry 3&4, monsters to tame and ride, slaves to free, challenges to do, collectibles to..collect and did I mention you can also murder hundreds upon hundreds of orcs?
You have the freedom of choosing how you want to uproach each situation. You can be a stealthy sniper and shoot 'em all down from distance with your bow. You can just jump right in and go berserk or you can use stealth and take them down one by one or take control of the orcs and make 'em kill each other.
It feels more like a stealth game at first since you get overrun by orcs easily but as you progress in the game and unlock new skills and weapon runes you become a bonafide buttocks.
Not only are there survival and hunting challenges in the game (picking flowers and killing innocent animals) but there are also 3 different weapon challenges scattered across the world: Dagger, sword and bow.
Each of these challenges make you use different skills from your skilltree and try out different approaches making the gameplay a bit less redundant because let's be honest, the game can get a bit repetitive. Especially those slave freeing missions.

This is my first review and I have to do it because I love this game.
It's a perfect video game reimagining of the Warhammer universe, creating the epicness and brutality of the world.
Campaign: My first time playing this is with the Empire, wherein I experienced so much retries and setbacks, being attacked on all fronts. Just when I was trying to eradicate of the world of Vampires, beastmen raid my towns and a giant WAAAGH that broke through the dwarves dove deep into my territory. Barely having the time to replenish my army, Chaos came knocking at the North. As much as it is stressful, it is very enjoyable, that I feel I really am the Emperor in this war-ridden universe. After finishing it, I now played the dwarves and while it is a lot easier, the same feeling of having such responsibility given to, now High King, is just as fun.
Battle: While I have to admit I miss the formations from Rome and Shogun II, the availability of various races, monsters and creatures made the warfare just as fun. I remembered using the LotR mod for Medieval II before, but now I'm playing it as it is, where most battles are really fun to watch, and a joy to win. It is so satisfying to defend civilization from the dreaded Warriors of Chaos with battle weary veteran dwarves of multiple wars, holding till the last breath. I never played competitive in my life so I have no comments on that.
I played TW games before like Rome, Medieval II and Shogun II (even bought Atilla but haven't touched yet) but never have I actually enjoyed something like this, moreso because I'm more of a fan of fantasy than history. I highly recommend this to anyone who's a fan of the Warhammer universe, grand scale RTS and fantasy.

EDIT:
Since the original posting of this review, the game has been patched a number of times to reach proper localization standards. None of the issues listed in the original review remain, except for a few awkward sounding lines, but nothing too unforgivable.
However, I still personally am not that happy that it was this bad at launch, so I do intend to leave my rating and the original content of this review as it was first presented below.
-------------
ORIGINAL:
The long and short of it is: For 25USD, you'd think they'd actually translate the Command Lists.
The Long of it is:
I'm glad this game has a western release, as a fan of Umineko, alongside the real game proper, but this release is so LAZY. I haven't had the chance to check the improved netplay, but I'm gonna run on some decent faith that it's actually better here, but.
My biggest gripe is how absolutely garbage the localization is. The text in the arcade mode ranges from acceptable to "Did literally anyone look at this? Once?". Stuff like the UI and the Credits, okay, you can kinda get away with not translating those, especially the former, since they're part of that Engrishy charm, sure.
But the Command List is not touched at all from the Japanese version. I cannot read Japanese. I bought the English release of this game. I cannot read how to use most of the character's moves. Plenty I can just gleam or guess with trial and error, but basically any move that has a pre-requisite other than "is a super" is completely lost on me.
I paid 25 dollars for a fighting game, and I cannot figure out how to play most of the characters. That is just completely unnacceptable. I'll likely refund this because I cannot play it. All the resources for this game are also in Japanese, so its not like I can go elsewhere to look at a moveset.
If they fix this, that'd be great! But if they don't really soon, or at least acknoledge they left a lot of the game untranslated, I'm just getting a refund. I'd rather not! But I likely will. Completely, utterly unacceptable for a 'localization'.
