I bought Aporia: Beyond the Valley on Humble Bundle with  zero knowledge of what I was purchasing other than the genre of the game and I am so happy I did. Aporia: Beyond the Valley is visually stunning, the puzzles are not all that difficult, but still rewarding and the music is lovely. It's a perfect mix of relaxing and eerie, which may sound obscure, but it works. There is a nice element of uncertainty and mystery in the picture told, puzzle driven story that kept me curious and wanting to play straight through to the end. I will admit, I did wish the game had a little bit of a narrative at times as I found pieces of the plot a bit difficult to follow, but was still easily able to put it all together in the end and admittedly even through wanting a tinge of narrative, the somewhat open player interpretation was also a breath of fresh air.
The only issue I have with the game is the map. I can't stress it more how much I would have liked the map to have an icon showing where the player is. Of course one can look around the environment and figure it out, but when you're running around in tunnels, through hidden passageways and looking for tiny shards in random locations it's helpful to be able to press the map button and recap. I also wish the achievements were open, because hot damn, I would have killed 'em. Who doesn't love those sweet, sweet achievements amirite?! (Aw well, will just have to speed through it a second time).
If you like single player, explortion and adventure driven, visually stunning puzzlers you'll love Aporia.

Kanes Wrath further spices up the C&C3 universe in terms of gameplay by adding a handful of new units as well as multiple sub-factions. These sub-factions also have their own exclusive units and overall play styles; in addition there's a new game mode known as global conquest to which the player tries to achieve global domination. STORY:
What really sells this game as a MUST PLAY is the story, assuming you're a Tiberium Universe fanatic.
Overall, Kanes Wrath is an expansion pack soley intended to tell the story of Nod and Kanes actions that consist of 13 missions seperated into three acts. These acts cover just about two decades from 2034 to 2052.
To avoid spoiling the campaign, I'll keep this brief.
As the player, your perspective is LEGION -an A.I. created by Kane intended to be CABALS successor- and throughout the duration of this campaign, Kane instructs LEGION to do his bidding until the A.I's true purpose can be done (hint CABAL's purpose).
As the player, you'll experience what Kane was up to post-Tiberian Sun (post-Second Tiberium War) as well as pre-C&C3 (pre-Third Tiberium War); in addition to actually experiencing battles of C&C3 from a different perspective. After that, you'll experience post-C&C3 events.

Don't get me wrong, I love the concept of composing characters and actions by nothing but words, but this game doesn't really gel with me. Personally, I'm more right-brained, which means that subjects like word problems, mathematics, and coding do not bode well with me. This makes me more of an artist at heart, so it's no surprise that I'd be totally stumped at EVERY single word scramble puzzle.
I swear, if I actually wanted to finish this game, there's a good chance that I'd just refer to a walkthrough of a gameplay video from the Wii U version over a dozen times! That's not very fun if you'd have to resort to doing that.
The fact that this game takes place in a bleak environment doesn't really help me get through it either. The environment is very well done, but it sort of ruined my sense of motivation.
When I was younger, I never liked word finders. I always felt like I had to find these concise words in a sea of scrambled letters, which was incredibly nerve wracking. Advanced Crosswords were intimidating to me for different reasons, mostly because I had to stuff together words in boxes based on convoluted hints that I wouldn't get.
Point is, if you hated word scrambles, or crosswords to an extent, then you're not gonna have a good time with this game's puzzles. Again, this is an amazing game in it's own right. But I feel it alienates the right-brained thinkers, and favors the left-brained thinkers based on the composition of the puzzles that this game has.

Although Reality 2.0 is a decent enough episode on its own, its miniature playing field, repetitive puzzle design, and some of the high-contrast visuals feel like a gigantic step back from the previous chapter.
How do you follow up an episode where Max, the psychotic rabbit became the President of the United States? If we look at Reality 2.0, then the answer seems to be with filler.
For example, the largest contribution to playtime is the amount of complexity of the trial-and-error puzzles tied to the episode’s gimmick, cyberspace (plus a text adventure segment at the end, where the bright neon letters on the dark background were not a good idea).
This space is also a cop-out, because Reality 2.0 is the only part in the entire season where we never physically leave the starting neighbourhood, we just get a Tron-like neon copy of it as a “new” playing area.
Still, even fillers can be entertaining, and luckily the franchise-defining funny quips and the occasional absurd humour still manages to hold together Reality 2.0 long enough to get us through the episode.
(By the way, most mentioned websites still work, after all these years.)

The game is unforgiving and I get that, I mean, that's part of the advertising. You play as Talion, a captain serving at the Black Gate of Mordor. Sauron's forces siege the garrison, kill your wife and son and finally end your life as well. Your body merges with a soul of an ancient elf and together you seek revenge. Yes. Yes, it is a revenge story and to be honest the story is pretty much none existant.
You are introduced to different characters as you progress in the story. You're introduced to exactly 3 characters. Yup. That's it. You'll meet a dwarf, a woman and an older woman. None of them get enough screen time and as a result you don't really care about any of them.
However that's not why the game is loved...
Gameplay, while quite simple, is just so amazing.
You can parkour Assassin's Creed style through an open world map while brutaly killing thousands and thousands of orcs. There are fast travel points (towers) to unlock just like in Far Cry 3&4, monsters to tame and ride, slaves to free, challenges to do, collectibles to..collect and did I mention you can also murder hundreds upon hundreds of orcs?
You have the freedom of choosing how you want to uproach each situation. You can be a stealthy sniper and shoot 'em all down from distance with your bow. You can just jump right in and go berserk or you can use stealth and take them down one by one or take control of the orcs and make 'em kill each other.
It feels more like a stealth game at first since you get overrun by orcs easily but as you progress in the game and unlock new skills and weapon runes you become a bonafide buttocks.
Not only are there survival and hunting challenges in the game (picking flowers and killing innocent animals) but there are also 3 different weapon challenges scattered across the world: Dagger, sword and bow.
Each of these challenges make you use different skills from your skilltree and try out different approaches making the gameplay a bit less redundant because let's be honest, the game can get a bit repetitive. Especially those slave freeing missions.

Fantastic. Exceptional. Tremendous. Choose your flattering adjective, because it'll perfectly describe Shadow of Mordor.
If you have played with the recent Batman games (Rocksteady), you'll feel very familiar with this game's mechanics; and if not, you'll find SoM to be quite easy to pick up, learn, and play. The approachability to its combat mechanics is perhaps this game's greatest strength, with so many routes for tackling the game's challenges - do you choose to go brute force, stealth, ranged, or a combination of all three? All flavors are satisfying, but, perhaps most satisfying, is the visceral combat that's perfectly complimented by bone crunching force and gore galore that'll satisfy the orc slaughtering desires of your teenage-angst-power-fantasy-trip you latentely have in the back of your brain.
With combat being so fun to play, the story acts as a secondary - almost a backdrop to the mayham that ensues. Thankfully, the game is wise to this and never presses exposition heavy scenes that remove you from more orc slaughtering. What is there does compliment the Lord of the Rings canon appropriately and finely sets up the vengeance (and justification for the ridiculous orc slaughtering that ensues) for the main character. Additionally, the voice acting is really quite top-notch, expertly done to compliment the emotions the game's characters suffer through.
Visually this game looks nice, with the free-form combat a definite highlight. Animations of orc slaughtering are always entertaining and there's so much variety here that it really can't get old. The only nitpick is the fairly mundane environs with only average levels of detail and variety, but this can be so easily dismissed based on the absolutely excellent enemy animations and combat mechanics.
In addition to the game's mechanics, it introduces a clever enemy leveling system, whereby the game's enemies "level up" with your successes and failures, further highlighting the stupendous combat mechanics - both on scene and off scene.
For anyone even remotely interested in action video games, this is a MUST buy.
To the orc slaughtering!

Enter the world of Typoman: Revised! Typoman is a ‘cute thing in big scary world’ game where you are assembled as a series of letters that may or may not be foreshadowing what the main character will become. Despite being a cute thing in a big scary world that totally isn’t based in WW2,  you have one special, unique gift: You can assemble a series of hodgepodge letters in order to create words that alter your environment. Will this odd, typographic world hold ink? Let’s find out.
The game starts off as you, the player being nothing more than a letter ‘O’. You quickly assemble the shackles of a body out of other letters and parts, and you’ll travel across the 2D lands solving puzzles, assembling words, and slamming your head on the nearest wall out of frustration for what should be the easiest version of word scramble you’ve ever seen. Mind you, not necessarily in that order.
“But what does one do in the game?” I hear the reader cry.
Whelp, that’s it. You will platform your way with your character while you solve what are almost intentionally the equivalent of word scrambles. Mind you, it’s already about two steps higher than the average indie job, and this ‘revised’ version (something we’ll talk about later) does deserve the title of being revised to at least some degree. The platforming itself is well enough, and the platforming puzzles (which are different than the other puzzles in the game) are decent enough if a bit basic. The game presents itself well and we were surprised by the diversity of puzzles in the game when it came to mixing up the word portions and the platforming portions. The problem isn’t the platforming, but the word scrambles.
To diverse, there are two types of word scramble puzzles in the game. One is where the letters are already in front of the player and the player then just has to make the correct word, and then there are the word puzzles through the press machines. These differ from the normal puzzles in which you have near infinite letters at your disposal, and you have zero clue what word you’re supposed to use. Sometimes it’s the same word you’ve used previously, other times it’s words you’ve never used. The difference is while there’s a ramp in word scrambled difficulty, the puzzles themselves only share common traits at random. In short, while there’s a difficulty curve in the game, the puzzle elements that ramp up in difficulty aren’t the types of puzzle elements you truly master, rather succeed at through trial and error. And when the game ‘does’ introduce puzzle elements that could ramp up in difficulty, they almost never bring them back later making them one-off elements of the game. There’s also the problem of certain puzzles being overly specific with word choices. For example, rather than using the word ‘raise’ to open a door that opened a previous door, this time the word was ‘split’, and ‘raise’ or ‘open’ weren’t even options. Figure that one out.
As for the ‘revised’ part of the title, this is the PC port of Typoman, which was originally released on the Wii U in 2015. Most of the revisions seem to come in the form of bug fixing, graphical improvements, and puzzle elements being switched up while (sometimes) making the puzzle more or less difficult.
This makes it out like I hate the game, and I don’t. Truthfully, I find the concept of assembling words to help you solve puzzles intriguing. Similar to ‘Scribblenauts’ on the DS except targeted at people who really like word scrambles. The problem is that while certain elements of the game’s puzzles (arguably the game’s bread and butter) have some cohesion, that cohesion all falls flat towards the third chapter of the game. It’s not bad if you’re really into that concept, but if you’re hoping that this game will bring you into the game idea with open arms and welcome you with a fresh bag of crisps, prepare to be met with open arms to only later be slapped in the face several hundred times. The puzzle elements work, but because what gameplay elements do and what do not carry forward are borderline random, which makes getting ‘better’ at the game to be nearly impossible.
Oh, and the game also has a story or something. The game doesn’t care enough to have it be in anything more than floating quotes, so why should we? It’s not explained, and you miss out on story elements if you miss jumps at certain points in the game. Don’t get me wrong, a story doesn’t have to be crystal clear. However, I draw the line at ‘so murky aliens probably live at the bottom of this puddle’ levels of vagueness. With that being said, the first 30 minutes of the 2-3 hour experience will probably cue you in as to what the whole world is one big analogy for. Specifically, a quote about burning books.
Visually, the game looks quite nice if the ‘small cute thing in big scary world’ is your type of visual style. Even then, some of the words entwined with the scenery looked nice and the lighting effects looked quite nice. Particularly, the early stages have some nice detail.
Audio wise, it’s not ‘horrible’ but it’s certainly not incredible by any means. The first few chapters and their music work well enough, but the third chapter falls short. The big problem is the fact that there’s no way to adjust sound at all, and even with the computer at 50% volume, I had to physically take my Sennheiser 598s off because the volume was physically hurting my ears and I shouldn’t have to do that. That being said, the audio isn’t terrible, but one particular music track at the last 20 minutes or so was borderline screeching, and I have a good feeling that such an audio effect was almost entirely due to the audio volume of the game.
Control wise, it plays fine with a controller. The keyboard and mouse controls are rather ‘iffy’ but, the controls were fine with a controller. As for the settings, you have one extremely generic ‘graphics’ slider and that’s it. Nothing else. The game looks fine as-is and ran incredibly well on my system, but that’s not a surprise.
So, despite my gripes with the game, was it fun? Yes. Well, yes in parts I should say. It’s fun in short, chapter-based bursts and if you’re really amazing at word scrambles and you just can’t get enough word searches and word scramble, this game should keep you interested. However, if you thought like myself that this game would be ‘Scribblenauts but with words’, you’re mistaken. Worse yet, with no tutorial and the gripes mentioned previously, this game left me lukewarm at best. Unless you’re really into word scrambles, our conclusion is to wait until this concept is at a deep discount or to try the demo first. In the end, Typoman: Revised is a neat ‘Scribblenauts meets words’ concept, but doesn’t truly deliver on its execution in the way most players would expect.

A very, very very tentative recommendation on my part.
The author always had a tendency to stray heavy into politics with his books, and this time I believe he finally hit the extreme. There is very little hero’ing in this game, but a lot of talk about discrimination of the physically disabled. None of it is particularly subtle, and while it wasn’t all that bad, I don’t feel like ever reading through all of it ever again.
Which is a bit of a shame, because everything else is pretty damn neat. Your character is forced to make some pretty hard decisions, and I found myself quite attached to the persona I have crafted for the game. The story is engaging, and I certainly enjoyed it, even if it wasn’t what I was expecting. I certainly don’t regret buying and reading it, and seeing how Zachary (the author) managed to cut down on the obvious preaching in Versus book that followed this one, I’m looking forwards to the continuation of the series.
That being said, the author seriously needs to stop with the cliffhangers. The main plotline is nowhere near resolved by the end of the book, and we’re already teased with the next main plotline. I guess it fits the theme (constant crises that plague every comic book series in existence), but it’s getting a bit old by now.  I’ll revisit this review later if the series jumps the shark, but for now, as stated earlier – a very careful recommendation. 6,5/10

I think this is nonetheless a great story, despite many of the critics are pointing out that this story is more like a preaching phamphlet. In fact, if you have read the hero rise triology, you would find out that this particular author has always been incorporating ideas of social equality into his works. Only in the orginal triology, is about the powered and the non-powered, and in this story is about the ani-powered, and the other more acceptable powered. The former issue is easier to accepet, in fact a lot of superhero comics have been talking about it for quite a long time. The latter, however, is more like the homosexual marriage issue, to most people is not that big deal, and if you spend nearly all the time talking about it, people will be angry, like what we can see in the comment section.
But is this story worth recommending? I guess it is. Though the author always tries to preach his ideas about social justice, you can somehow still focused on saving your sister's life without giving your efforts away for some petty injustices. Although eventually you will be forced back to caring more for the ani-powered because your sister always has been an equality advocater, it wasn't awkward. In fact, it actually gives me more thoughts about how I should love and protect my family. The last time I had such experiences was when I finished TWD S2.
Therefore, if you actually enjoyed good stories, and can put up with the propaganda like preachment, this story might worth purchasing.

Zombie Panic! Source is a co-op oriented Survivor vs Zombie multi-player survival horror mod.
In the mod, players can generally participate in timed matches against the opposite team, or the humans try to solve objective-based missions.
One thing that really separates Zombie Panic! from Left 4 Dead is that if you die, you will become a zombie. To prevent yourself from going the way of the undead, you will have to arm yourself with shotguns, rifles, explosives and more.
In addition to a lot of last man (or zombie) type matches, as previously mentioned, there are also objective-based scenarios. In these modes, humans will often have to find resources like wood boards or gas canisters, turn cranks and knobs, or do a combination of both.
Zombie Panic! Source is an overall good-looking mod with some minor clipping issues.
So if you are looking for another interesting take on the oncoming zombie apocalypse, Zombie Panic! Source is not a bad choice.

-The art style was interesting.
-It was pretty straightforward.
-Easy game.
-Music is decent.
-Can beat it and get a refund within the two-hour limit.
Cons:
-Way too short. I know it's an episodic game but one and a half hours? Really?
-The puzzles are incredibly easy. They require absolutely no thought.
-The jokes are either terrible memes, Internet references, dated jokes, or bad puns. Sometimes it's all of those wrapped in one.
-The voice acting isn't good. The accents are poor and the quality drop in some of the voice clips are obvious that most lines are phoned in.
-The characters aren't memorable. I only really liked Sherlock. They are so incredibly bland that I had that big cyclops guy with me the whole time (who you probably only use like four times) and I don't even remember his name. When explaining it to a friend I could only describe them as "Main guy", "cyclops servant", "Sherlock", "creepy bug guy", "old beard guy", etc. You only meet every character once (excluding Sherlock) so there's no point in remembering their name.
-"Geoff the Murderer", really? That was the reason I had to take a break from playing because that was so cringe.
In the end it's not worth the price for less than two hours of gameplay. I mean, unless you wanna play it and then refund it because you'll definitely beat it under the two hour limit. It's good if you want an easy point and click game but for the price you can get better point and click games that are the same price or cheaper. People who are a fan of the genre probably won't get much enjoyment out of the gameplay because of how straightforward it was. Because of the price I probably won't buy the next episode unless it's like a dollar or something.

I would recommend this on sale, for sure. Full price is out of the question, however, given the plethora of DLCs for the game and CA moving on the part 2.
Pros:
- Great art, beautiful landscapes, good animations.
- Terrain plays a solid role in the tactical combat. There are times I have won, and lost, simply because they/I had to fight up a hill to the artillery.
- The core races are varied tactically, albeit subtly. Empire is balanced across the board, the orcs have crappy units with phenomenal leaders, the dwarves have solid infantry with great ranged and artillery units, and the vampires rely on squishy mobs to flood the field while elite units and spellcasters finish the fight.
- Tactical combat itself is very solid and enjoyable (except you, seiges!).
- Leveling up heroes is tons of fun. The most fun I had with the game was during my empire campaign, where each Lord took an office, earned himself a hold, and defended from there. Great times!
- Tons, and tons, and tons, of mods.
Cons:
- All the races fall into a strategic grind of "build big economy to field big army, gar."
- The quest structure is flawed, imho. As far as I can tell, all the hero quests require walking places, as in "get a character to The Silver Road." That is a gross misuse of an army or a hero for 5+ turns, and one I never felt was cost effective.
- Chaos sucks. Hard. You build an army balanced toward a foe. Then you have 4+ doomstacks of a different foe sweep down, all while you are rapidly rebalancing your army. That said, you will feel great if you manage to kick them back north!
- Auto-resolve needs some work, as expected.
- For as much as I love the tactical combat, it relys a bit too much on hammer and anvil military theory. Lock 'em up, smash them down.

These desperate cries for attention affected the boys relationship with his parents, and they drifted further and further apart. On day, the boy was at school, and it was a normal day until the school received a call from his parents work. Both of his parents were killed by a fire at their work building. Their death made the boy realise how much he really cared for them, and he fell into a deep depression. The boy grew up greiving for his parents, and regretting his actions. RNG: The Game.
The game is unforgiving and I get that, I mean, that's part of the advertising. But I didn't realize that meant that in battles you'll have turns where you miss, miss, miss, and the enemies get a lucky crit, and all of a sudden your favorite guy is instantly dead. Of course there's no substitute for good strategy and if you're placing your soldiers tactically and wisely you'll lessen this, but there are still going to be battles where an enemy archer gets lucky and you're going to lose men. I like difficulty but this feels unfair and arbitrary, especially when you've perfectly placed a shieldwall and lol who cares your frontline is now butchered because the other guy succeeded on a swing that had a 1% chance to hit and now you're dead or crippled.
Feel free to tell me to git gud but with RNG being such an integral part of the combat you can't even reliably do that. It all comes down to dice rolls and as much as I love the art style, the depth to the weaponry and the writing that ends up screwing you sooner or later.

Imagine a less politically involved version of Mount and Blade with tactical turn based combat instead of real-time third/first person and that is pretty much what you have.
Ignore the cries of too much RNG. It's tactical and if you use focussed tactics both in building and using your units then the RNG is not obtrusive at all. This said, it's a difficult game with a fairly steep learning curve which makes it understandable that many would put their feeble tactics being crushed down to bad rolls. This is a game you will want to keep on beginner level for quite some time before moving on. In fact I myself hated Battle Brothers for a fair while before it captured me.
The only criticism I have is that by late game everything can become a bit samey especially after several playthroughs.
It remains an eminently worthy buy on the rare occasions it is on sale. Is it worth its full price? Well that depends more on you than the game itself.

My first time playing Battle Brothers I went through 20 hours almost entirely non-stop. I normally don't like procedurally generated single player games, they tend to have a "wide as an ocean but deep as a puddle" feel to it. But this game feels like The Black Company novel by Glen Cook in video game format. It's such a blast running around the countryside leading a band of mercenaries, making decisions that dramatically effect your group and the world. The combat is almost as tactical as chess, and the AI is good at always exploiting the tiniest weakness you present it. You tend to get attached to your unique fighters with their storylines and quest decisions. The turn-based combat is brutally unforgiving and the sound effects are entertaining.  Getting good at the game requires some experimentation to understand it all but it's surprisingly intuitive.

Typoman: Revised is a 2D puzzle platformer that requires you to use letters to make words in order to solve the puzzles.
You play as the hero and your body is made up of the letters spelling 'HERO'.  It’s a game about good versus evil, and there isn’t much depth to the story. You will need to find and gather all the collectible quotes as you play though, in order to read it.
As you progress through the chapters, you encounter various words and letters, and you need to build specific words to complete the puzzles. It would have been nice to be able to type out words instead of moving letters individually, but it wasn't a big deal. There isn’t any direct combat in the game, but you use words as weapons in some levels, as well as on the final boss fight, and it was enjoyable.
There are a wide variety of words that you can make, but not all of them have a function. The part of the game that was the most challenging for me was figuring out which function I needed to perform. Once you know what you need to do, it’s then a matter of finding the right synonym using the letters you have available at the time.
The game took me just over 4 hours to complete, and there were just a few collectibles that I missed. I don’t feel the need to replay it, but there are several achievements that are still available. I enjoyed the word puzzles, and the game overall. I feel that the price is just a little too high for the game’s duration. I’d recommend checking it out if you’re someone who enjoys word puzzles, and puzzle platformers.

I have been a fan of Obsidian for as long as I can remember.  Growing up during the birth of gaming, and testing my limits during the golden age of RPG's has made me salty. The tepid products gracing the shelves, physical and digital, in the last decade have just made it more righteous a feat for what this group has accomplished with crowdfunding.  The genre "feels" like DnD.  It ''feels'' equally Baldurs Gate (I and II).  It "feels"... pretty damn good.  I can't remember the last time I have been so absorbed in a story.  Cliche is not always a bad thing, especially when most of the attempts to stray have been fickle, no, fecal, at best.  If it ain't broke don't fix it yada yada.  Well guess what.  It wasn't fixed.  It was polished.  The feel of the new universe is comforting like a bed you can climb in, but the sheets are new.  And wow is the thread count high.  I cannot think of a single reason you should not try this game... I take that back.  If you have given in to the new era of having yoru hand held and never experiencing challenge through puzzle, adventure, and best of all High Fantasy story telling at its apex, then please avoid.  For the rest of you who are reading this, and watching the videos, and scanning screenshots, I promise.  I expected good.  I was delivered great.  Obsidian, you have won my trust back.  And the next back i will do, is back your kickstarters should you go that way again.  For a crowd sourced game to feel so... dare I say triple A...  I just hope that this proves you aren't going the way of Square-Enix, and forgetting why your fans play what you make.  We love RPG's, and I love this game.  My favorite in longer than I can remember. 10/10
Some small bugs exist.  Negligible.  They are so minor in comparison to the Leviathan you have wrought. Now if you'll excuse me, I have a world to save and you have a game to buy.

Total War: Warhammer is not a perfect game, but it is an improvement over past titles in the series without a doubt, and has already sucked up hours of my life, and will continue to suck up hours more.  There are some things that get my goat, but what game ever developed was perfect in the eyes of everyone that played it?  And I'm more of a critic than most.
I just don't like seeing an Orc Warboss kill 136 Longbeards in a battle.  I think that's cheesy, as I know, no matter how big or awesome at combat a man or creature is, being surrounded by two hundred peasants is going to result in a solitary 'hero' being poked full of holes sooner rather than later (to say nothing of the battle hardened veterans heroes routinely make mince meat out of), but people love this kind of mind numbing ubermensch crap, so it's in the game, and I have to deal with it.  Every faction has heroes, and while some are better than others, they can at least be countered and dealt with on the battlefield, even if legendary.  So, it's not a big, unbalanced deal.  It's just dumb.
I also don't like the way that half the units in this game are useless.  Why even put Empire Spearmen or Ungor Herds into the game if they exist solely to be replaced by better units later on?  The game tries telling me that they're worth something, that they are there to counter large creatures, but a full card will disintegrate in seconds when charged by Minotaurs or a Terrorgeist, and I've seen AI opponents field as many as four cards of each in a single stack.  So why put a chew toy in the center of your Empire army when your economy can sustain Hippogryph Knights with halberds instead?  The answer of course is the ability to field 9 stacks instead of 4, but why burden yourself with 9 fluffy stacks when you can win the game with 4 hard ones?  So much unnecessary clicking!
Likewise, I haven't found much use for spells and abilities.  I once tried fighting a battle with Balthaser Gelt against a vastly superior Vampire Count army.  His Final Transmutation spell and Fireball Ring proved too much for Von Carstein to handle, but his other spells had little impact on the battle, and all my anti-large and armor piercing damage did little against the 8 cards of Blood Knights and 4 Terrorgests that descended on my halberdiers and zweihanders.  Nor have I seen much magical impact in other battles.  The big flashy spells of doom might do wonders against hordes of low-tier infantry, but you rarely see such armies, particularly in the late game, so the spells are more flash than bang compared to a charge from Knights Errant or a Giant, not to mention unwieldy (try picking out a hero in a mass of zombies without pausing).  As I play more, I'll experiement with spells and abilities, particularly buffs and debuffs, but my gut tells me they're all but useless outside of a multiplayer battle.  I just don't see the point of reducing a melee attack of 450 to 375, or 45 to 37, or whatever.  It can be a big difference, but a wrecking ball is a wrecking ball and I doubt the difference between a Feral Mammoth and a card of Empire Spearmen can be mitigated in any meaningful way.
The campaign map is better than ever at least.  Diplomacy almost makes sense.  You still get the occasional neutral faction that doesn't want a trade agreement boost to their economy, because, reasons, but at least the whole world doesn't go hostile the second your borders touch.  Being able to coordinate war targets with military allies is OMFG awesome though.  I didn't give it much thought at first, but in a moment of desperation, as Franz was beset by large stacks of Vampire Counts, Chaos Warriors and Norsca, I reached out to three Kharaks, Tilea, Middenheim, Hochland and Bretonnia for assistance.  I was soon bombarded with messages of agreement from my allies, and watched stack after stack of erstwhile idle Dwarfs and men on the march.  My heart leapt with unadulterated joy to see that, undiminished by the loss of Nordland and the Dwarfs' flat refusal to go to war with the Vampire Counts.
Battlefield maps are also better, if not a little stale.  Some additional terrain features would be nice to help make a position defensible (like buildings in a city-defense map) but at least I'm not marching to the highest, furthest corner of a cliff to crush the remnants of the army I had just defeated earlier in my turn.  Previewing the battlefield is nice, and knowing where reinforcements are going to come from BEFORE the battle starts is a wondrous, logical, beautiful thing.
My biggest complaint is that the challenges this game poses are less like challenges and more like endurance trials.  Beating the 'grand campaign' is a question of patience and endurance.  How much wack-a-mole can you play with Beastmen Herds, Orc incursions and waves of Chaos invasion?  You have options as to how you do it, the factions each have their own little nuances to master, but at it's core, that's all it is: mole whacking, again and again.  Likewise, battles tend to devolve into the same experience.  Cards break and route, coming back, again and again until they're shattered, or else the battlefield devolves into a remarkable chaos as fleeing units reform and fight one-on-one battles with the cards you sent to pursue, believing erroneously that they would ensure that fleeing card stays fleeing.  It's because of this that I auto-calculate 99% of my battles.  Fighting most battles feels too much like work, and less like playing a game, and besides, the cold-hard math does a far better job of preserving my squishy units than I do.
I almost took back my recommendation after writing the above.  Almost.  Instead, I'm going to boot Warhammer back up, and see if I'm not wrong.  I'm going to try fielding an army of useless units and buff them to bejeezus and see what I can do commanding a battle personally.  I'm going to go and wack some more moles.

Overall: a jarring but interesting departure from the first three Hero Rises books that some may find and intriguing if overally preachy. Takes a while to find its footing.
Details: as a huge fan of the original trilogy, I immediately bought Redemption Seaon. Although it drops you into the action, a large amount of text slows you down considerably at the start. As you slog through some exciting sequences, the action then stops to a crawl and continues so for a while as the author not only introduces you to the new characters but bashes over the head ad naseum with the book's take on prejudice against certain aspects of the  superhuman community (Ani's, Disembodied, Morphs, and in general those who don't look like your standard Greek god/goddess).
What should be an interesting new viewpoint from the more standard (if fun and glamorous) superhero fare of the first trilogy and build a strong foundation instead blankets the story in a heavy weight. I kept waiting for the lecturing to stop and the plot /action to begin. That, along with a long wait before you can start individlualizing your character and a constantly changing power set/appearance, led to a disconnect between myself and viewpoint character that led me to put the book down for over a month.
The action is much lighter with far fewer battles than the earlier books but what is there works well enough. The exception is a well-written final battle that raises the stakes, introduces unique villains, and instills a sense of dread. It's over too quickly and easier than anticipated but these are minor quibbles give its otherwise slick execution. Hopefully we will see more action in the sequel.
The book is best when it focuses away from its heavy reliance on the heavy-handed prejudice storyline to focus on the characters who well drawn and layered. Even the final badguys have a shocking backstory twists that paints them and the theme of prejudice in a new light.
I would also criticize the early attempt to force your character to take a strong stance one way or another. By not doing so, I was eliminated early despite doing reasonably well in the competition. It discourages readers from exploring who their character might be and might become as they learn about their new storyline. In trying to stand out early, you may (as I did) define your character in a way that you will later regret.
Final Summary: the book is a frankenstein of sorts: half Prodigy and half Hero Project. It suffers from a very slow setup in the beginning and only partial progression through the title's "Redemption Season." Although it has a strong climax, that the new season of the Hero Projection has far to go may be unsatisfying for some. The GOOD news is that it sets up for a better second book, just as the fine Hero Rises Prodigy set the stage for the even better Hero Project. Also, while the plot is slow with a heavy-handed theme, the characters are as interesting and enthralling as ever.
A 6.5/10 with an anticipated higher score for the next book in the series.

First of all, I'm a huge fan of Choice of games. I've only played a few, but these are among the best storytelling I've ever seen, no matter the media.
Second, I played the Heroes Rise trilogy, and I loved every moment of it. So I had rather high expectations about Redemption Season, as the sequel to one of my new favorite licence.
And I was kind of scared, seeing this only rated as "Variable" (in French), compared to the other games, which all have received really good reviews.
I just completed my first run, achieving almost the best score of Legend possible, and I'll most certainly replay it.
I get why so many peoples seems disappointed in this episode. ** minor spoiler here ** As some said, the game revolve heavily around the segregation among the Powered, and mostly toward Ani Powered, Morpho Powered and Disembodied. And some find you actually barely see it in game. I completely agree. Though, it's a logical and good narrative choice. Inside of the Hero Project, heroes are secluded and receive as less as possible informations from the "outer world" (like in most reality show). It's actually only logical, that you can't go on the streets and see this by yourself. ** end of spoiler **
As usal, the narrative is extremely good, the story really got me to actually care deeply for characters, a thing that happens more than often with Choices of Game, and particularly Heroes Rise. So far, in my opinion, it's the storyline that offer exchanges with the most characters (and they're all unique and deep). I'm kind of discouraged by some aspects of the story, for personnal reasons. Plus side: if you've played the first trilogy, many informations about what has been going on behind the scene can be foud here and there. To me, it explained a lot of situations I found rather dubious, and seems a bit more logical now. If you have one, I highly recommand to load one of your previous game, seeing the consequences of your choices and getting news from your previous self (and his/her group) is really a plus.

I've played the first 3 Heroes Rise games and am I very big fan, however I almost didn't by this one because of the number of very persuasive negative reviews. However in the end I found the prospect of a cameo from my hero, Specs, in a new series too hard to resist so I took the plunge and gave the redemption series a try. I am very glad I did.
strangely, depending on your perspective, this could be both the strongest and most flawed entry in the heroes rise series. After playing it I can certainly see why there is a split between positive and negative reactions. While the negative reviews are not without merit, I can safely say that the flaws they highlight are not as severe as they make it seem.
Let's get right into it: There are definitely author tracs in this game. Heroes Rise has always been a particularly progressive series and issues of discrimination and underrepresented persons are obviously very important to the author. While these themes have always been present in ther series,  In The Redemption Project, they are now a dominant element of the story. Fans who just want a superhero/scifi adventure might find themselves disappointed with these political issues being so prominent this time. There's still plenty of superheroic action sequences and reality show drama to be enjoyed, but they now share equal stagetime with your character grappling these issues.
While these issues don't feel out of place, since the game has given you a main character who is practically guaranteed to have a reason to care about them at least a little, there are points where I couldn't help but feel the game was lecturing me a bit. These segments aren't nearly as jarring as when it happened in Heroes Rise: The Hero Project, but this is still a game that needs you to meet it halfway more then any of the others did since while in the previous series you had a rather typical comicbook superhero with a familiar backstory, this time you have a superhero with an unusual powerset that is also heavily disenfranchised. So even though your hero is still quite customizable, unless you are an underrepresented person yourself, you might find it'll take more effort on your end to care about your character and put yourself in their shoes than in the previous series. At least I found it took a little while for me, but once I did I became utterly hooked.
This game is bigger and longer then any of the previous in the series. The interesting, well developed characters that have a way of forcing you to care about them and hard decisions that I've come to expect from this series are all still here. (in fact I get the sense that the writer has actually improved quite a bit!) There were several times when I was faced with a decision that was so tough that I had to stop playing and leave my chair to really think about what I wanted my character to do, which has always been my favorite part of this series. The writing, characters, and the game's ability to present you with tough choices that make you second guess yourself after making them are the biggest strengths here and I found myself even more engaged by them then I was even in the previous series.
The biggest weakness has been touched on in other reviews, at a few points I had the game wagging its finger at me a bt regarding some of the choices I have made. One was when another character was explaining how they are forced to sacrifice their ideals to survive in the competition and I was presented with 2 previous "bad" choices my character could use to realize how him and this other character are alike, and 1 previous "good" choice that he could use to reflect on how he acted differently. The other instance was near the end where a character with similar ideals as my main character railed into me for falling short by voting the way I did in an elimination. For a game about choice it feels weird to be judged in this way, and I don't know if it was due to the choices I made early on but I definitely felt nudged in a certain direction, particularly when my character had an epiphany and became highly motivated to start breaking down barriers near the end of the game. Personally though I thought it was alot of fun for the game to confront me about my earlier decision like that. It was an opprotunity for my character to realize that while he is still confident that he made the right call, it was still very much not a perfect decision, and he is not perfect either. There are no easy answers here.
The bottom line is that I came into the Redemption Season expecting myself to not like it and I was very surprised to find that it is actually now my favorite of the entire series. If you are a fan of heroes rise I definitely recommend giving this one a shot, if only just to see if you end up liking it as much as I did. It's definitely a bold and different direction from the previous games but alot of what made them great is still here and I found myself warming up to the new elements as i got more invested in the story and the new main character. However, If you are new to the series, I recommend trying the previous trilogy first.
If this game is the first in the series, (I always feel the necessary introductory nature of first installments makes them particularly weak) then needless to say I am very excited.

This game is very good.
Obviously, if the Warhammer setting doesn't appeal, it's not a plus (or may even be a minus, depending on your preferences).
With regards to the game itself, it has advantages and disadvantages over previous games in the series.
On the strategic level, it's greatly simplified over many of the more recent games in the series.  A few of the most obvious changes are:
There are no faction politics.
Province management is minimal.
There are no province governors.
There are pretty much no choices regarding how to develop a province beyond whether you want it to be generating cash or generating armies.
Many factions cannot be negotiated with, only fought.
Which all seems pretty poor, but the battles are, quite simply the best Total War has ever managed (except Warhammer 2, which I'll mention below).  The principle two reasons why boil down to:
Variety -
There are genuinely different faction rosters; Vampire Count armies are different from Wood Elf armies, are different from Troll armies, are different from Dwarf armies, are different from Chaos armies, are different from Empire armies, are different from Brettonian armies (and so on) in ways that the historical titles simply cannot be.
Specifically, all the "regular" kinds of Total War units (shock/melee/light/missile cavalry, sword/armour-piercing/spear/polearm/direct-firing-ranged/indirect-firing-ranged foot soldiers, varied artillery) are present, but there are also monstrous units, flying units, chariots, war engines, spellcasters, ethereal troops, fearsome and terrifying units and so on.
There are nine playable races, each with numerous legendary lords to use.  These races play in significantly different ways, again, in ways that historical titles simply cannot do.  This is also true on the campaign map.
The inclusion of so many factors in the battles leads to an excellent variety of options being available to the player both in preparation (building armies and choosing skills for lords and heroes on the campaign map) and in the execution on the battle maps.
and Action -
There is a sweet spot for exciting action here; cavalry, monsters, pikes, artillery, and even sometimes the "regular" infantry all seem to be interesting and powerful in different ways.
The inclusion of terrifying units, magic and hero units make for a more interesting and exciting battlefield, again, in ways that a historical title probably couldn't.
Personally, having been playing these games since the original Shogun: Total War (pre-Mongol Invasion), I've always been of the opinion that the game truly shines on the battle map; the strategic map exists principally to make decisions that determine the circumstances of what battles you will fight.  Although the simplification on the strategic level are a shame in some ways, the vastly increased options and excitement on the battle map more than make up for it.
The final plus point is that whatever you buy here in terms of the base game and DLC is not simply lost by being made obsolete by Total War: Warhammer 2 (and #3 when it gets released).  Everything you buy here is available as content to play in the Mortal Empires campaign of TW:W2, which thus offers even more options for variety on and off the battlefield and probably manages to create even better action than this title.
tldr: Best Total War title up to its release because the battles are so awesome.  Warhammer 2 is better, but everything you buy for Warhammer 1 is playable in #2 as well, so nothing is lost.

First of all let me say, that in general I really like the Choice of Game games. I really love interactive novels where the reader forwards the plot by conscious decisions. Also I really like the superhero genre. The preceding trilogy, Hero's Rise, was great.
However THP:RS falls flat. Somehow heroic deeds of superheroes are only second to the social commentary. Social commentary per se are nothing bad. But here it feels artificial and academic. You are being told that people are oppressed several times, but this oppression rarely is ever shown. A dystopian scenario with real oppression like slavery, forced labor, ghettos would have been a wonderful basis for a "rise to greatness" superhero story, where the hero manages to actually change something.
Instead the "oppression" is constantly talked about in sermon-like expositions and seems oddly out-of-character and out-of-place.
Ironically for a game that for a good part deals with identification, it is rather hard to identify with the main character. The hero powers are a great idea per se, but the daily changes are so radical, it's as if the MC constantly changes with them. Also, in a game where you want to drive the plot with your decisions how the MC should act, it is very obvious that the MC is often "nudged" into the "right way". If you don't walk that path, it could lead to punishment and a dissatisfying resolution.
All in all, I'm missing the superhero story here, with all the cheese and stereotypes from the superhero genre. Conluding: I really can't recommend this game, as my high hopes after the really good first trilogy were not met.
A similar interactive novel from Choice of Games from the superhero genre which I do recommend is: Community College Hero: Trial by Fire. Check that out instead!

I saw this one pop up elsewhere and I'd never heard of it - randomly fancying a new game I gambled on it, and while it has faults, and a lot of them, it really is a very, very original game and in places a quite stunning one.
Aporia sees you wake up as an unnamed protagonist in some kind of tomb. Through the medium of a vial and a mount you find yourself watching an in-game animation, itself telling a story. Once the story is done, out into the wilderness you go to discover 'what happened here'. You are surrounded by crumbling buildings, skeletons, and evidence of some widespread disaster from ancient times.
The way the story is told is unique - there's not a word of text or spoken dialogue - it's all through pictures and animation films in game - it's refreshing, and makes the narrative very different to anything you'll see elsewhere.
Aesthetically the game is quite beautiful - stunning sunsets, horizons, grand valleys and huge expanses make it visually very impressive, but not so much technically (more on that later).
The audio experience too is deep and rich, with ambient music which fits the environment perfectly and plenty of spooky sound effects to make you feel you're not alone.
And on this narrative and visual experience, it's a great game and worth your time - but my God it is flawed.
Never has a game been so Jekyll and Hyde as Aporia is.
See, the problem with this game is it's just too ambitious. It looks like an indie game gagging to be a triple AAA game but fails miserably and ends up technically resembling a Crysis mod. My God it's rough round the edges - the amount of graphic glitches in here is just embarrassing for this level of production. Shadows which move with mouselook, textures which flicker like mad, non-colission detected surfaces in places and far too many areas in which there is no sound at all - quite simply the devs didn't think we'd go there, so there's no production in them at all.
The third chapter is just littered with these technical issues and it makes it feel cheap and like a mod - yes, it's on Cryengine, and yes, the ideas and aesthetics are lovely, but the technical implementation of the visuals is diabolical at times - textures which barely even quality as 720P, framerate which is hopeless in places, and environments which at times seem big for the sake of being big.
To call the technical quality of Aporia rough round the edges is extremely generous.
BUT
BUT
It IS quite an experience, and these multitude of technical issues do not ruin that - sometimes you think they might, but they never quite do.
Had this been produced by an AAA dev on a high budget the polish would have been impeccable - you get the feeling it was just too ambitous a project for these guys.
But they did a good job within limitations, and did produce a very original game indeed.
It's just a pity it's one whos flaws are so glaringly obvious they often overshadow the good stuff.
But yes, I'd still recommend. And I'd recommend the devs spend a couple of months ironing the issues out.

I have been a fan of Obsidian for as long as I can remember.  Growing up during the birth of gaming, and testing my limits during the golden age of RPG's has made me salty. The tepid products gracing the shelves, physical and digital, in the last decade have just made it more righteous a feat for what this group has accomplished with crowdfunding.  The genre "feels" like DnD.  It ''feels'' equally Baldurs Gate (I and II).  It "feels"... pretty damn good.  I can't remember the last time I have been so absorbed in a story.  Cliche is not always a bad thing, especially when most of the attempts to stray have been fickle, no, fecal, at best.  If it ain't broke don't fix it yada yada.  Well guess what.  It wasn't fixed.  It was polished.  The feel of the new universe is comforting like a bed you can climb in, but the sheets are new.  And wow is the thread count high.  I cannot think of a single reason you should not try this game... I take that back.  If you have given in to the new era of having yoru hand held and never experiencing challenge through puzzle, adventure, and best of all High Fantasy story telling at its apex, then please avoid.  For the rest of you who are reading this, and watching the videos, and scanning screenshots, I promise.  I expected good.  I was delivered great.  Obsidian, you have won my trust back.  And the next back i will do, is back your kickstarters should you go that way again.  For a crowd sourced game to feel so... dare I say triple A...  I just hope that this proves you aren't going the way of Square-Enix, and forgetting why your fans play what you make.  We love RPG's, and I love this game.  My favorite in longer than I can remember. 10/10
Some small bugs exist.  Negligible.  They are so minor in comparison to the Leviathan you have wrought. Now if you'll excuse me, I have a world to save and you have a game to buy.

I've read a number of reviews here, and having just finished playing through for a second time I figured I should chime in with my own perspective. So, here goes:
THP: Redemption Season is one of those games where I feel like it was expressly built to be part of a series. I see it as an introductory game in many ways - it introduces a huge number of characters and concepts, not the least of which being your own character. However, this often means there's a bit of information overload. Since it is, technically, a new series that builds off the old one, this is something veterans of the world will have to endure. Perhaps most prominently is the tone that is set by the author - your character is just scraping by financially and has experienced discrimination rather heavily. Whether that leads you to becoming an activist or a recluse (or neither, but you are rewarded for sticking to one path) is something you decide in game. Many of the people you interact with have been discriminated against in some way or another, and there's a lot of clashing subcultures and personalities. It makes for an interesting dynamic, though there are times in which, as other reviewers noted, this comes across as over the top (or in their words, preachy). Personally, it wasn't much of a big deal to me - I saw it more as representation and the author writing from the perspective of a disenfranchised main character. However, it is worth noting for other people who may be made uncomfortable with those sorts of things.
Overall, I enjoyed the game, the characters, and the writing, but like all things there are flaws that take away from the experience. I would certainly recommend THP: Redemption Season, but only with the warning that it is most definitely an introduction to this new series and can, at times, feel more like an introduction than a full game. Still, I am very excited for the next part, which should be coming out sometime early 2017.

When I read through all the negative reviews I felt that I had to write one that isnt two years old so here we go (conclusion at the bottom):
You may see that I am not really good on writing reviews so I just try to tell you how I feel with the game atm.
First I have to say that I enjoyed the game in Early Access and Recommended it in my previous review. I backed Starbound 2 1/2 years ago and followed its development throughout this time. Many things have changed since e.g. enraged Koala but unfortunately not to the best for the game.
I have played it around forty hours after the 1.0.5 patch but now I have no reason to play any further as I finished the story and have achieved everything that doesn't requires grinding (e.g. the armor aficiando achievement) and seen everything that made me feel "Wow, ... That is nice!" To me it seems like this is because the game isn't challenging me anymore after I am done with the (a little bit obvious) story, the only "challenge" is to grind for materials on a poisonous planet where I just have to "eat" bandage after bandage to survive the poisonous rain (though I have a poison Resist EPP Module???!1!!). When you have a short look at my playtime you will see, that I have played Starbound 100 hours before the 1.0 Update.
I feel like I enjoyed the pre-1.0 time more than after the 1.0 Update.  Before the "Great Combat Update" every weapon was different to each other, but with the Update they introduced Weapon groups in which the Weapons only distinguish in Damage and Ability. Each Axe feels as odd as all the other Axes, Melee Swords have had the "Block" Ability removed as it was ported to the shields. The Block Ability was the one I most enjoyed as you can stand where you are and wait for the moment to take your turn against all the random monsters out there. Random monsters were removed too, they are now generated by an engine that has rules so after you have visited every Biome just once you are done with finding new monsters that look like "I gonna slaughter you if you aren't careful". There once were Big monsters like the ones you can only find in quests now. In that stage of the game I always was like "**** let me get outta here!!1!!!" or "I have to bunker down and sneak kill this mob" because I was caugt by surprise and these monsters were a particularily good challenge. The point is, that the game at its current stage misses this randomness I really enjoyed when I played the pre-1.0-Builds. I can foresee what could be on a planet easily so I dont bother to search on it if it hasnt the ressource I need.
That takes me to the next point of the randomness that I regret the absence of:
Planet generation. You can see, which Ore is on a planet so you can weigh if visiting this planet is worth. This is primarily a good feature and I enjoyed to see it ingame but now I decide if I visit the planet only by the Ores generated down there. When you haven't had this feature you had to beam down and look what the planet has to give and maybe you were surprised by a strong monster that dropped a cool weapon or by an avian city you didn't expect. So I feel like the new Randomness Engine makes it job so good that I can expect what it will "randomly" generate. So I am not surprised by a Floran village on a Magma Planet anymore or can't find Glitch on an Ocean planet.
A feature I liked very much were the Asteroid Fields in Koala, Giraffe and so on:
They were very dangerous as you died when you fell in the wrong spot. The early availability of the 3 techs takes this danger away easily.
In Asteroid Fields there were all kind or ressources in small amounts but it was fun to seek if you could find the one ressource you need while you were jumping around with 0.2 G and had to be extremely cautious. Now you can find Gold, Silver and Copper there, Ressources you don't need for anything beside crafting Wires and some furniture.
I just want to say that I don't like the Inventory Interface at all, it is kinda weird and not very clear.
The last thing I would like to mention is the difference of Mob generation in Multiplayer:
I had a session (around 1 year ago) with a friend and saw a Mob that looked really nice and wanted to show it to my friend (we sat next to each other) but when I pointed at it and looked at my friends monitor I saw an entirely different kind of Mob. It was fun to see what the engine generated there. Of course it is nice to see the same Mob as a friend standing next to you (ingame) but it's again predictable as the generation rules are set.
When I have more to write about I will edit this review but I think I won't edit it to "Recommended". Farewell Starbound :*
(Beside, the Soundtrack should be really good but the Preorder Soundtrack wasn't updated for 3 years now :C )
Conclusion:
I can't recommend this game anymore as I miss the depth of the older versions inter alia visible in the predictable randomness. If you are fine with 40 hours of gameplay (40 hours cause that was my maximum time I wanted to play it) for 15 or 20 € (not sure, so long ago I backed it) then I say "GO FOR IT!!!!". The Soundtrack should be good as well.
But when you like randomness that is not bound to generation rules (Monsters that look the same all the time) and love it when a game is unpredictable, I can't recommend it to you. The Randomness is to predictable to be fun.
If you have a question on my opinion, leave a comment.

Aporia: Beyond the Valley starts off not unlike LoZ: BotW, but nearly immediately distinguishes itself as a standout Walking Simulator of the highest order. There are threats aplenty, albeit not from anything that moves around (although there is a creepy thing after the first chapter that made my skin crawl)...
It's a lonely thing about a woman awakened after a long time, and her adventures through the remains of the civilization she left behind. It's at once beautiful, lonely, joyous, puzzling, and heartbreaking as you wander around. The story is told with the environment and the occasional rotoscope-style cutscene that requires you to maintain focus in order to see what it is you need to know. Tooltips are pictoral rather than textual, and none of it is particularly intrusive. You have it when you need it, and not before. Controls are simple with keyboard and mouse, which is a massive bonus, and most of the truly active things you're going to do are bound to the mouse.
Could one have done this on a mobile device?
It's possible, but it would lose a lot in the transition. I have very little to fault here, if we're  being honest. Maybe... Being able to hold my breath a bit longer? Not that it matters, because you'll rarely need to even gwet to the point where you're taking significant damage. Even if you do, chances are that there are healing items enough growing nearby.
All in all a simple game that provides loads of mystery, exploration and fun for kids and adults alike.

You wake up in this gorgeous world without any clear objectives. As you explore, and progress through the world, you learn about the story along the way. The story is told visually with animated projections. I love the way the story is told. With the game having absolutely no dialog or text, I admit that did feel a little uncertain about some of the details along the way, but overall I liked the story.
The gameplay is largely that of a walking simulator with a focus on exploring the world and solving various puzzles to progress. The world can be explored freely, and to get the most out of Aporia, I definitely suggest exploring thoroughly. If you don’t, you might miss out on some of the story elements. I liked the exploration, but I regret not saving the game prior to hitting the point of no return because now I can’t go back to explore the island further.
You have a tube of glowing liquid that’s required for unlocking doors, and growing vines to climb. This fluid is consumed when you use it, so you’ll need to keep refilling by finding more supply around the world.
As far as the puzzles go, some of the puzzles might make you stop and think for a bit, but overall they aren’t very difficult. There really aren’t that many puzzles either, so I was hoping for there to be more, but Aporia seems to focus more on creating an immersive world to enjoy rather than throwing an abundance of puzzles at you.
The game took me about 4 hours, and as long as you explore thoroughly, there isn’t much in the way of replay value unless you want to just bask in the game’s beauty.
Aporia: Beyond the Valley is a good game, and I expect those enjoy walking around, exploring, and soaking in a beautiful immersive world would like Aporia. With that being said, I personally would have liked a lot more puzzles, so I’m glad I got Aporia at a sale price.

"Aporia: Beyond The Valley" is a first-person adventure game with a decent amount of puzzles (some small, some more complex), a story that is told without words, and a few areas that encourage exploration.
The story, which chronicles the rise and fall of a foreign civilization, is told on murals that you find in the world, as well as short animated sequences (where you can see, but not hear, key people interact with each other). The story isn't very complex, but I appreciated that there was more depth to it than a simple "good vs evil" structure, I found it interesting and (at times) touching. The presentation through very basic animations of figures that look like colored cardboard cut-outs is probably not for everyone's taste - I did not like it at first, though it did grow on me while I was playing. Nevertheless, while I appreciate that the devs tried to do something unusual here, I have to say that well-written texts would have worked better for me than those crude and sometimes unclear animations.
The game's puzzles are varied, engaging, and fairly easy, most of them have appropriate cues that a player with open eyes will notice. They usually require the player to manipulate the environment in the correct way, for some you also need o collect a few items first. Some puzzles are very small (like a standard water barrel puzzle, where you swap water between barrels until the water level in the largest barrel meets the target height), others take longer (like redirecting a ray of light through several areas via mirrors), and sometimes the small puzzles combine to a bigger meta-puzzle. While many of the puzzles don't make much sense in the game's world, the solutions are always logical. In general, I found Aporia's puzzle design very good.
Unfortunately most of the game is very linear, you just follow a pre-defined path and remove obstacles as you go. There are a few semi-hidden corners that you can explore, but you quickly learn that that's a waste of time: the only thing that you can find, is more fuel for your light source, or plants that give you health, but you'll find more than enough of either on the main path already. This made the first two chapters of the game fairly boring, I was just walking across a lifeless and not particularly exciting map. However, this changed in the third chapter, which consists of a large explorable area with lots of puzzles that you can engage at your choosing, and which includes 18 optional collectibles that reward exploration. Unfortunately the game's remaining chapters regressed back to a more linear design (just with larger areas than the first two), but by that time the story had become more interesting, so the linearity did not bother me as much as in the beginning. In any case, players can easily spend the majority of their playing time in the more enjoyable third chapter, especially if they are tackling the optional puzzles as well.
Graphically I found Aporia surprisingly unimpressive for a CryEngine game. Some of the screenshots looked pretty good, but in the game, even at Ultra settings, it was almost impossible to get a crisp image. There was always some fog or blur in the way, and since the game does not offer any detailed graphics settings, there was no way to fix that. Areas that could have looked very good, like the dark cathedral with its many glowing energy lines, were ruined by massive aliasiang. The lighting was especially bad - instead of highlighting the features of the map, it is often so terribly overdone that it just
them by blinding the player. By contrast, interiors are often so dark that it's impossible to appreciate anything. There also isn't much variation to the graphics, and not much detail to the textures. All the wood in the game has exactly the same color. All the stone walls have aged in exactly the same way. Almost the entire game is held in tones of brown and grey, the only elements of color are the murals, which are too abstract to be considered beautiful. The water shader is extremely primitive. There aren't many interesting structures either - apart from an altar and the cathedral, the game's architecture looks bland and repetitive. While all that doesn't make the game look
- these are still decent graphics in a powerful engine -, I feel that the artists and the art direction have just not put this engine to its best use. I would have appreciated a bit more imagination and variety in that area.
Sounds are mostly functional, though it always feels out of place for me when I hear the sounds of rich animal wildlife in a completely dead looking world that shows no signs of any fauna whatsoever. Music is very sparse in the game, but when it's being used, then it's usually very good. The music and sound for the ending sequences was particularly well done, with just the right balance of emotions.
The game's controls are, unfortunately, one of its weakest points. It insists on WASD movement (not even arrow keys work), and the keys cannot be rebound, so people with French or Dvorak keyboards, or left-handed mice, or certain disabilities, or simply different preferences than the devs, are simply out of luck. On top of that, the key layout is bad even for WASD users, since the "View Map" function has been assigned to the "M" key - which is impossible to blind-type when you have one hand on your mouse and the other on WASD, as the game forces you to do. So whenever you want to look at your map, you have to break your immersion and look at your keyboard first. A developer has mentioned in the forum that they will try to patch a key rebind feature in, but it is inconceivable to me why such a basic feature that is so important for a smooth interaction with the game, is treated as an afterthought.
There's also a second problem with the input: Many interactions, such as turning a wheel or opening a lid, require you to "grab" the item by holding the left mouse button, and then move your mouse to perform the action. This can be a very immersive means of interaction, as games like Amnesia have shown, but in Aporia, I often had to literally fight these controls in order to get things done. From lids falling back onto chests because I just couldn't raise them high enough, to wheels for which I had to run my mouse across the entire length of my desk for a single revolution, to endless frustration with positioning mirrors because my "hand" would suddenly lose its grip - Aporia's implementation of this input method just didn't work for me.
On a more positive note, the game - despite being new - ran very stable for me. I encountered only one crash, and no game-breaking bugs (though others have reported an issue that made one puzzle unsolvable; the devs are looking into this).
Taking everything into consideration, I recommend this game to fans of adventure puzzle games, who can appreciate a decent story even if it isn't very accessible and requires "work" to understand it, and who can appreciate exploration even if it's limited to only one area. It's a decent game, perhaps even a good one, it just doesn't really offer all the freedom and beauty that's being advertised. Don't be deterred if you find the first two chapters boring, it gets much better afterwards.

This game is the bastion of a well-designed RPG, and game (heh). Now that we've got that one pun out of the way, I truly do think that Bastion is one of the best RPG games out there, especially because it focuses on untraditional aspects of a game, and focuses on making a game a piece of art.
Obviously, Bastion does the RPG-part of an RPG well. The plot is pretty well-crafted (no big holes), and I truly do buy into the story of the game. The characters are well-made, and while they lack a bit of depth (the game is a bit short compared to, let's say, Skyrim), they're still pretty cool. The in-game mechanics also are pretty good, and fit into the RPG-ish genre: you run around on an isometric platform, using your weapons to defeat the many nefarious enemies you'll encounter. You upgrade (and sidegrade) your character, weapon choice, and even game difficulty as the game goes on. All things normal for an RPG, and all things done well.
I think where the game excels is the concept of art, and art in the game. First of all, the game is very visually appealing. According to the creators, Supergiant Games, the entire game is hand-painted; I've got to give kudos to their painting. The landscape is breathtaking, enemies really do look and feel like enemies, and each part of the map has its own special graphical feel (e.g. forests, swamps, cities). From an audio standpoint, there's also this narrator that accompanies you around the game, and he's one of the best serious narrators I've encountered. In addition, the soundtrack is absoutely amazing. Whoever they hired to do their sound really puts you into the game: common RPG tropes like "boss-fight music" are done very well, and the atmosphere is set during troughs of playtime. I've even added some of the songs on Spotify, and that's something I rarely see from video games.
The game is also replayable (there's a new game + mode), and has a mechanism called "shrines" that can make the game harder, for better rewards. Plus, as you level up and gain access to more weapons, different playstyles are available.
Overall, Bastion is one of the best RPGs I've played in a long time, and I definitely think it's worth its selling price. It functions well as an RPG game, but also has the added bonus of being a well-developed piece of art. If you're someone who likes games that are both fun to play and fun to just watch and listen, Bastion's definitely the game for you.
